## Workload, burnout, and well-being

- “AI to the rescue: Exploring the potential of ChatGPT as a teacher ally for workload relief and burnout prevention” states that teachers’ average time on non-teaching tasks is substantial. Prior teacher workload studies revealed that teachers spend significant time on two non-teaching activities: lesson planning and preparation of teaching and learning materials. Findings from a study conducted in England showed that primary teachers self-reported more than 60 working hours per week, a total number of hours that was found to be significantly higher than time spent by secondary teachers. Secondary school teachers have described increased workload concerning the amount of time spent on class preparation due to the difficulty of a subject they teach. Teachers from Poland confirmed that extensive non-teaching workload is associated with higher levels of teacher burnout. Almost half of the interviewed teachers reported that increased administrative tasks contributed to their already heavy workload. The increase in workload was not due to teaching responsibilities but rather the addition of new demands without removing previous tasks. [4]

- “Early Childhood Teachers of Color in New York City: heightened stress, lower quality of life, declining health, and compromised sleep amidst COVID-19” reported that 6 early educators were asked to respond to text messages every half an hour over a 4-day workweek to report what they were doing; the researchers then constructed a time-use diary for each participant. Texts were sent in 30-minute intervals (6:30am-11pm, unless participants indicated they had gone to sleep earlier). The study collected 816 entries (34/day, 4 days, 6 participants). [4]

- “Teacher Procrastination, Emotions, and Stress: A Qualitative Study” summarized professional tasks on which 16 teachers reported procrastinating into four main categories: correcting students’ work, administration and organization, preparing lessons, and evaluating students on their general work and performance. Delaying work on administrative and organizational tasks was mentioned most frequently (11 teachers), including organizing field trips, structuring one’s paperwork and lessons, and organizing parent-teacher conferences. Correcting and evaluating students’ work was mentioned by 10 teachers, including evaluating and correcting students’ written exams and homework. A further task mentioned by seven participants was evaluating students on their general work and test performance, including procrastinating on grading tests and writing report cards at mid-term and at the end of the year. Six teachers also reported procrastinating on preparing and structuring their lessons. [20]

## Administrative workload and digital tools

- “Electronic school diary for statistical analysis of student progress” investigated the effects of using a digital diary to facilitate the calculation of administrative statistics of teachers and classroom caregivers. The purpose was to explore the use of an electronic diary (e-diary) in supporting teachers and classroom caregivers to successfully complete administrative work related to completing the school diary. A quantitative design was used to obtain data from teachers and classroom caregivers through questionnaires. The sample included 12 elementary school teachers 0-5 and 8 lower secondary teachers 6-9. A closed-ended questionnaire according to the Likert scale was used for data collection. The study showed many potential advantages in using a digital diary at school to facilitate administrative tasks. Teachers and classroom caregivers were very satisfied with the integration of the e-diary to successfully complete the statistical tasks calculated automatically from the electronic diary. [22]

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

The gathered findings are dominated by review, survey, qualitative, and comparative papers about AI in education, with a smaller number of studies that directly compare AI-generated output with human output in K-12 or school-teacher contexts. The most directly relevant evidence to the research thread is the comparative K-12 lesson-plan study and the evidence around specific teacher tasks such as lesson planning, grading, feedback, and administrative work.

### Directly relevant K-12 comparative evidence and task-level evidence

**Connecting Feedback to Choice: Understanding Educator Preferences in GenAI vs. Human-Created Lesson Plans in K-12 Education - A Comparative Analysis**  
This paper is the clearest direct comparator in the raw results for K-12 lesson planning. The snippet says:

- “Developing rigorous, engaging, and personalized lesson plans is a cornerstone of effective K-12 education, yet it remains a timeconsuming and cognitively demanding task for educators.”
- “According to the TALIS 2018 Survey [30], U.S. educators spend an average of seven hours per week on lesson planning, with an additional three hours required for students with diverse needs, such as disabilities or language barriers.”
- “This workload detracts from direct student interaction-arguably the most rewarding aspect of teaching.”
- “Recent advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI (GenAI) powered by large language models (LLMs), offer promising solutions to streamline lesson planning.”
- “A May 2024 Impact Research survey [12] found that 79% of teachers reported using GenAI tools like ChatGPT [31] for lesson planning.”
- “Despite this growing adoption, GenAI tools still exhibit critical limitations: their lack of domain-specific knowledge often results in lesson plans that are contextually inappropriate, pedagogically unsound, or factually inaccurate [6,36].”
- “Our study addresses this by systematically comparing GenAI-generated lesson plans with those crafted by experienced curriculum designers in a K-12 setting.”
- “To evaluate the viability of LLM-generated lesson plans, we conducted a comparative study using pairwise evaluation methods.”
- “We assessed lesson plans generated by models such as customized prompt-based GPT-4 and fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b against humancreated plans.”
- “Educators rated these plans across four key dimensions: relevance, quality, and usefulness of the warm-up, main task (explain and reinforce), and cool-down sections, along with overall quality.” [source text from snippet_search result; study design not explicitly labeled in the raw snippet, so design not reported] [1]

**Augmented teachers: K–12 teachers’ needs for artificial intelligence’s complementary role in personalized learning**  
This paper is a K-12 teacher study focused on what teachers need from AI. The abstract says:

- “Empowering K-12 teachers for personalized learning using artificial intelligence (AI) is an open challenge.”
- “AI systems often fall short of meeting the needs of teachers, hindering the educational process or even causing conflicts.”
- “In Study 1, we conducted a focus group interview (n = 15) to identify the roles that teachers envision AI augmenting for personalized learning.”
- “We identified eight key roles: personalized curriculum design, development of instructional materials, foundational learning support, self-reflection support, student evaluation, career guidance, student management, and administrative task support.”
- “In Study 2, we examined the preferences of 128 teachers from various school levels (elementary, middle, and high school) with regard to how they envision the use of AI in their classrooms.”
- “Our analysis revealed that teachers have differing preferences for AI roles based on the school level.”
- “Elementary school teachers placed emphasis on student assessment and management, while middle and high school teachers prioritized self-reflection support and career guidance.”
- “Teachers underscored the significance of maintaining a complementary relationship with AI, pursuing shared objectives, and fostering sustained interaction, with the aim of evolving into ‘augmented teachers.’” [study design not explicitly labeled in the abstract; design not reported] [2]

The body snippets add task-specific detail:

- “The questionnaire asked 11 questions, which focused on teachers’ needs regarding roles for personalized education.”
- “Participants were presented with two questions (Cronbach’s α = 0.845), employing a 5-point Likert scale to assess their perception of the necessity and effectiveness of ai performs an analysis of academic schedule data and administrative tasks organized by time periods.”
- “an ai chatbot designed to assist with academic scheduling provides teachers with guidance on their activities for each time slot.”
- “The teacher efficiently manages administrative tasks with the support and guidance offered by the ai chatbot.”
- “To investigate teachers’ preferences for the eight augmented teacher roles identified in Study 1, scenarios were created as examples for each role (see Figure 1).”
- “Storyboards are well-suited for collecting opinions from participants who may lack knowledge or experience with AI (Zimmerman & Forlizzi, 2017).”
- “To design and create eight scenarios for augmented teachers’ roles (See Table 4), we conducted three rounds of brainstorming sessions.”
- “Three subject experts were recruited. Two of the experts are from the field of educational technology, and the other is from artificial intelligence.”
- “On average, the experts have 12 years of research experience in AI for education.”
- “In addition to these experts, we further tested the feasibility and usability of the storyboards with two teachers with experiences in K-12 settings.”
- “Each storyboard consisted of four cut scenes: (1) depicting the challenges faced by a traditional teacher in their role, (2) illustrating AI’s engagement as a complement to address these challenges, (3) showcasing the collaborative synergy between a human teacher and AI as they jointly fulfill a role, and (4) presenting the performance of an AI-augmented teacher.”
- “As illustrated in Figure 1, each scene was presented using images and keywords, accompanied by a descriptive sentence to enhance participants’ comprehension of the storyboard.”
- “Based on the experts’ feedback, we modified the expressions and explanations in the storyboards (See Appendix A, Supplementary material).” [2]

A second snippet from the same paper provides direct administrative-task evidence:

- “About half of the teachers (8 out of 15) expressed their expectations for AI to assist with administrative tasks.”
- “They referred to a messenger group chat utilized by lead teachers to collectively address administrative issues and share information (P02).”
- “This collaborative platform inspired the notion of implementing a chatbot or similar tool to assist in tackling complex patterns within their administrative responsibilities.”
- “Furthermore, due to the yearly repetitive nature of school tasks, teachers expressed their desire for AI to take on the role of providing guidance for administrative tasks.”
- “Several teachers (P03, P06 and P10) expressed a desire to receive support from AI in performing administrative tasks according to the academic schedule.”
- “If AI can assist in administrative tasks by analyzing the tasks performed annually and providing guidance, such as which tasks should be completed in the current month and which tasks should be addressed in the following month, it would enable teachers to anticipate and prepare in advance.”
- “This would alleviate the ambiguity and concerns of human teachers and prove to be highly beneficial (P10).”
- “Teachers expected that with the help of AI, they would be able to perform administrative tasks more efficiently and without mistakes.” [2]

**The AI Revolution in Education: Will AI Replace or Assist Teachers in Higher Education?**  
Although this is higher education, it includes very relevant task-level teacher productivity statements. The snippet says:

- “Teachers need to allocate a certain amount of time in handling administrative tasks such as attendance checking, assignment and classroom monitoring, and paperwork.”
- “With the introduction of AI, not only can these tasks be relieved from teachers, but also be accomplished in a much more efficient way.”
- “Multiple studies and reports have provided evidence to support the notion that the time-consuming administrative tasks involved in the teaching and learning process can be done through AI technologies while not compromising the tasks quality (Chen, Chen & Lin, 2020; Felix, 2020; UNESCO, 2021).”
- “A survey revealed that teachers spend as much as 15% of their time on such tasks (McKinsey & Company, 2020).”
- “Utilizing AI technologies for these tasks can save time, allowing teachers to focus on addressing students’ learning needs.”
- “AI has the capability to assist teachers in student assessment, as developments in natural language processing facilitate applications such as plagiarism detection, assessment scoring, and automated feedback provision (Chen, Chen & Lin, 2020; Goksel and Bozkurt, 2019).”
- “Owing to their dependence on algorithms and data, AI technologies can provide more objective and efficient feedback compared to human teachers (Celik, Dindar, Muukkonen & Järvelä, 2022; Terzopoulos & Satratzemi, 2019).” [review/report-like discussion; design not reported] [3]

A later snippet from the same paper says:

- “Teachers agree that generative AI technologies improve their time efficiency and reduce costs, the technologies ‘speed up routine tasks’, ‘fasten the pace of lesson preparation’, and design assessments.”
- One teacher said it can “help me finish some administration work, especially regarding course logistics and tutorial registration, as these are very timeconsuming and labour-intensive” and “generate some email templates”.
- “Students also perceive similar benefits.”
- A student noted, “For future teaching, I believe that the use of ChatGPT will reduce teachers’ workload for answering students’ questions. I may also use it to generate some lesson plans.”
- “AI technologies are as virtual tutors, providing personalized learning experiences and immediate feedback on student responses.”
- “One teacher commented, ‘I think AI like ChatGPT could be used as a personal tutor. But instead of showing the answers directly, providing advice or directions might be better.’”
- “In addition, some teachers also perceive using these technologies to provide students with immediate feedback.”
- “For instance, a teacher suggested, ‘Perhaps it’s possible to have ChatGPT review student writing and give them feedback on how and where to improve their writing’.”
- “A student also agree that teachers can use generative AI technologies such as ChatGPT to ‘provide immediate feedback on student responses.’” [3]

**AI to the rescue: Exploring the potential of ChatGPT as a teacher ally for workload relief and burnout prevention**  
This is one of the strongest teacher-workload sources and is directly about teacher workload relief. The snippet says:

- “The primary objective of this study was to investigate how incorporating AI-generative ChatGPT as a teacher assistant can alleviate teacher workload.”
- “A literature review on teacher burnout and ChatGPT explicitly focused on teacher workload and teaching responsibilities.”

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

No direct study was retrieved that explicitly and simultaneously quantified both:
- gross time savings from AI use by K-12 teachers, and
- net time savings after verification, editing, revision, or quality-control costs.

However, several sources in the retrieval set speak directly to components of the research thread: teacher time savings, workload relief, lesson planning efficiency, quality control / critical review / revision requirements, and the need for human oversight. All relevant statements gathered from the searches are preserved below.

1. **Perils and Opportunities of ChatGPT: A High School Perspective** [1]  
   The snippet states that this was “not meant to be formal research, but rather a collection of our opinions and ideas.” It reports that “Three teachers-an English teacher, a computer science teacher, and a media arts teacher-provided their responses. Seven students, all 11th graders (16 or 17 years old) at State College Area High School at the initial stage of recruitment in Spring 2023 also participated.”  
   Relevance to the research thread: teacher opinions / high school perspective only; no time savings, verification, editing, or productivity effect sizes reported. [1]

2. **Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Technologies in Education According to Primary School Teachers: Opportunities and Challenges** [2]  
   The abstract says: “This research aims to determine primary school teachers' opinions about using AI tools in education. The research was conducted using a case study. The participants are 16 primary school teachers determined by the criterion sampling method. Data were collected through a semi-structured interview form and analyzed with content analysis. According to the findings, teachers stated that AI tools may have advantages and disadvantages in educational environments. While teachers are concerned about the adverse effects of artificial intelligence tools on students, they also recognize their cognitive and socio-emotional contributions. Teachers also stated that artificial intelligence can make teachers' jobs easier but can only partially replace them. The results help understand primary school teachers' opinions regarding using artificial intelligence tools in the learning process.”  
   Study design label: case study.  
   Relevance: directly about primary school teachers and AI making teachers’ jobs easier, but no explicit time savings or editing/verification costs. [2]

3. **Mapping the landscape: A bibliometric analysis of AI and teacher collaboration in educational research** [3]  
   The introduction snippet states: “AI offers numerous benefits in education, including personalized learning, administrative efficiency, and enhanced instructional methods, [but] it also raises important concerns about the evolving role of educators. Teachers must adapt to technological advancements while preserving the fundamental principles of effective teaching, ethical considerations, and personal connections with students.”  
   It also states: “By facilitating seamless communication, data sharing, and co-creation of research materials, AI can potentially revolutionize how teachers collaborate on research projects.”  
   Relevance: discusses AI, teacher collaboration, and administrative efficiency. No teacher time-savings effect sizes or verification/editing costs reported. [3]

4. **Can AI grade your essays? A comparative analysis of large language models and teacher ratings in multidimensional essay scoring** [4]

   It further says: “supporting time-consuming tasks like essay scoring is crucial, and technical solutions can offer valuable assistance to alleviate the workload on teachers.”

For instance, LLMs can support lesson preparation through automated question generation, facilitate teacher collaboration via conversational AI, and support the evaluation and feedback generation for student errors.”

The raw snippet and database outputs indicate that the evidence base on K-12 teacher AI productivity is concentrated in studies of lesson planning, formative feedback, grading, assessment support, personalized learning, and teacher perceptions or adoption, with results varying by grade band, subject area, and school context.

A review-style source, **Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence in K-12 education (2017-2022)**, states that the review searched Web of Science and six databases indexed in EBSCO host, used a PRISMA flow chart, and reviewed **66 AI studies**. It reports that themes in the studies include AI as a predictor and indicator of academic behavior or performance, AI curriculum design, integrating AI in various subjects, evaluation of AI in education, AI to enhance learning environments and school operations, AI ethics, and the equity and safety of AI. It also reports that AI methods were grouped into Supervised Learning, Unsupervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning, and that AI technology applications were Machine Learning (ML) model building tools, intelligent tutors, chat bot, educational games, AI robots and virtual reality devices. It says AI applications were mostly used by teachers for ML model demonstration, academic performance prediction and behavior prediction, while AI was used by students for scientific discovery learning, improving learning experience and data driven decisions. It concludes that practitioners can use the findings to implement AI in K-12 education, and researchers can build on the gap in research on AI K-12 education. [1]

A recent arXiv paper, **Thematic and Task-Based Categorization of K-12 GenAI Usages with Hierarchical Topic Modeling**, includes the section “GenAI in K-12 Education: Promise and Early Trials.” It states that advocates have touted GenAI’s potential to personalize learning and reduce teacher workload, and that early responses in schools ranged from outright bans to cautious, exploratory integration. It reports empirical examples including:
- **Jauhiainen and Guerra**: a classroom study with **110 pupils (ages 8-14)** in Uruguay, where ChatGPT & Midjourney were used to dynamically personalize science lessons (texts, illustrations, exercises) in real time, leading to improved engagement and learning outcomes.
- **Almohesh**: a **quasi-experimental study** involving **250 Saudi primary students**, showing that ChatGPT-based assistant use significantly enhanced learner autonomy in live online classes.
- **Ng et al.**: an SRL-bot powered by ChatGPT during a secondary science course, reporting gains in subject knowledge, motivation, and self-regulation among **74 tenth-graders**.
- **Fokides and Peristeraki**: ChatGPT feedback on primary-aged students’ English and Greek essays against teacher comments; ChatGPT produced more accurate and detailed feedback in English but was less reliable in Greek.
- **Levine et al.**: high school students using ChatGPT for brainstorming, drafting, and revision; AI suggestions helped students clarify their own voice and engage in deeper reflection.
- **Zheldibayeva et al.**: 11th graders using the CGScholar AI Helper, finding that AI feedback supported writing development and elicited improvement suggestions from students and their teacher. [2]

The same paper also says that teachers and educators most frequently use AI to support upstream planning and content development tasks, particularly lesson generation, assessment, and administrative work, and that many existing studies rely on self-reported data or small samples limited by subject area or geographic scope. [2]

A related arXiv paper, **How K-12 Educators Use AI: LLM-Assisted Qualitative Analysis at Scale**, reports that in a national survey of **979 K-12 math and science educators**, **50%** reported having used generative AI. Of those users, **57%** indicated infrequent use (monthly or rarely), while **42%** reported more regular use (weekly or daily). A majority also reported using AI for lesson planning (**76%**), assessment development (**61%**), instructional support (**50%**), and differentiated academic support (**32%**). It says a study with **11 mathematics teachers** found educators used generative AI to accelerate workflows in lesson planning, generate engaging and differentiated activities, and design learning tasks aligned with higher-order thinking skills. It also reports that K-12 educators in Idaho rural areas expressed curiosity and optimism about generative AI, particularly for out-of-classroom tasks such as lesson planning, assessment, and administrative work. The paper concludes that educators most frequently use AI for upstream planning and content development tasks, but that many existing studies are self-reported or small and geographically limited. [3]

The same paper also reports that teachers viewed AI as a powerful tool for reducing workload and enabling more personalized instruction, while concerns remained around accuracy, usability, and the need for ethical guidelines. [3]

A specific field or pilot study, **Generative AI in K-12 Education: The CyberScholar Initiative**, reports that CyberScholar is a Generative AI assistant tool that aims to provide formative feedback on writing in K-12 contexts. It says the study explored how students worked with CyberScholar in diverse subject areas, including English Language Arts, Social Studies, and Modern World History classes in **Grades 7, 8, 10, and 11** in **three schools in the Midwest and one in the Northwest of the United States**. Data were collected through implementation observations, surveys, and interviews by **121 students and 4 teachers**. The thematic qualitative analysis revealed that the feedback tool was perceived as a valuable tool for supporting student writing through detailed feedback, enhanced interactivity, and alignment with rubric criteria. Students appreciated the tool’s guidance in refining their writing. The study says that, for the teaching side, the findings indicate a shift in teachers’ roles, from serving primarily as evaluators to guiding AI feedback processes that foster better student writing and critical thinking. [4]

A different paper, **Generative AI and ChatGPT in School Children’s Education: Evidence from a School Lesson**, is a case study focused on a Social Sciences (History) curriculum lesson designed for **4th-6th-grade pupils**. It reports that in **July 2023**, a total of **110 pupils** of **8-14 years of age** in **four different classes** participated in and completed the lesson, and their learning experiences were assessed both quantitatively and qualitatively. The study was conducted in **two schools in Montevideo, Uruguay**. ChatGPT-3.5 was the main application utilized for the generation of the test and related material. The abstract states that it was possible to use ChatGPT-3.5 to personify learning material so that it would meet the knowledge and learning skills of pupils with different levels of knowledge, and that a clear majority of pupils enjoyed learning the generative AI-modified material. It concludes that there is promising potential of generative AI use in school education, supporting pupils’ motivated learning and skills development, but that these tools need to be developed, refined and optimized to create impactful, inclusive, and sustainable learning in schools to benefit pupils, teachers and education managers alike. [5]

The paper **Opportunities and risks involved in using ChatGPT to create first grade science lesson plans** states that lesson planning is an essential and time-consuming part of teaching. It says teachers reportedly spend an average of **seven hours per week on lesson planning**, making it even more time-intensive than grading, and that teachers in the United States reported working **53 hours per week**, including planning, teaching and grading. The paper says the study used an exploratory case study design to facilitate researcher testing of generative AI, that ChatGPT responded to prompts and the researchers performed document analysis on the outputs, and that the desired science lesson on heredity was aimed at first grade students. It states that within **30 minutes** the researchers could generate and substantially refine a lesson plan that accurately aligned with the desired curriculum framework and the **5E model of instruction**. However, the iterations included questionable components, missing details, and a fake resource. The conclusion says ChatGPT efficiently produced a lesson plan that accurately used the 5E model, but that using generative AI should not replace the teacher’s expertise related to effective pedagogical practices and contextual factors, and that teachers would need to strengthen the AI-generated lesson plan to replace problematic components, fix inaccuracies, and fill in missing details. It also says educators should avoid solely relying on AI to generate lesson plans in light of potential limitations. [6]

The same paper says that generative AI can potentially support teachers in lesson planning by making the process of generating an outline more efficient, and that recent research on using generative AI for lesson planning has used a similar approach and achieved comparable findings that ChatGPT can produce a good first draft of a lesson plan, but a critical revision process is also necessary. It also says future research could continue to probe generative AI tools to take stock of their capabilities and accuracy for use in designing instruction, including each tool’s capacity to reflect contextual elements, such as grade level and school culture. [6]

The paper compares lesson plans generated by a customized GPT-4 model and a fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model against human-created plans, with educators rating them across warm-up activities, main task, cool-down activities, and overall quality. The abstract reports that human-authored lesson plans were generally favored, particularly for elementary education, where educators emphasize student engagement, scaffolding, and collaborative learning.   - **AI and Chat GPT in Language Teaching** discusses EFL assessment and evaluation, real-time feedback, and the evolving role of teachers. [45]
- School context:
  - **Designing Technology to Support the Hospital Classroom: Preliminary Findings** reports that hospital teachers often rely on older curricula, learning is often assessed through in-classroom observations of mastery, and technology and internet use by students is often restricted, which may inhibit opportunities to use AI and other technical resources in the classroom. [46]
  - **The Impact of Large Language Models on K-12 Education in Rural India** says rural K-12 schools in India face significant limitations in technology adoption, with digital access disparities, lack of teacher training, and skepticism toward AI’s role in education. [47]
  - **Identifying Rural Elementary Teachers’ Perception Challenges and Opportunities in Integrating Artificial Intelligence in Teaching Practices** reports that teachers view AI tools as pedagogical instruments that can help them build transdisciplinary connections and reduce the rural-urban gap; the quantitative survey item on reducing the rural-urban gap received a high agreement rating of **4.6**, and **22.4%** of qualitative codes were assigned to this category. [48]
  - **AI in Pakistani Schools** emphasizes the need for training and infrastructure to ensure inclusive and effective implementation in Pakistani K-12 schools. [14]
  - **The factors affecting teachers’ adoption of AI technologies** includes elementary and secondary schools and reports broad familiarity and active use of generative AI tools across disciplines. [13]

Some sources emphasized that AI can reduce workload but should not replace teacher expertise:
- **Opportunities and risks involved in using ChatGPT to create first grade science lesson plans** says using generative AI should not replace the teacher’s expertise and that teachers must critically analyze outputs, ask follow-up questions, and adapt lessons. [6]
- **AI to the rescue** says ChatGPT can help teachers allocate more time to other responsibilities. [9]
- **Augmented teachers** says teachers want AI as a complementary role, not a replacement, and want sustained interaction that preserves teacher authority. [16][19]
- **Implementation Considerations for Automated AI Grading of Student Work** says teachers valued rapid narrative feedback but distrusted automated scoring and emphasized the need for human oversight; teachers edited feedback, clarified grades, and recontextualized comments to maintain pedagogical coherence. [44]
- **We Should Not Be Like a Dinosaur—Using AI Technologies to Provide Formative Feedback to Students** says AI-generated feedback is appreciated by both students and teachers, but the teacher needs to have the last word when AI takes over formative feedback procedures. [49]
- **Teachers’ use of generative AI: a ‘dirty little secret’?** says teachers use generative AI for creating resources such as lesson plans, assessment tasks and learning activities, saving teachers’ time and effort, and for marking and feedback on students’ work. [50]

The evidence also repeatedly notes that higher-quality AI use depends on scaffolds, human review, and context-specific adaptation:
- **Opportunities and risks involved in using ChatGPT to create first grade science lesson plans** states that a critical revision process is necessary. [6]
- **Connecting Feedback to Choice** says human-AI collaborative lesson planning is needed and that GenAI should be an assistive tool rather than a replacement. [7]
- **How K-12 Educators Use AI** notes that many existing studies are self-reported or limited by subject area or geographic scope. [3]
- **Implementation Considerations for Automated AI Grading of Student Work** says AI should augment rather than replace educator judgment. [44]
- **Teachers’ AI-TPACK** says real-world applications require attention to instructional settings, subject domains, and student demographics. [11]
- **Artificial Intelligence Integration in Teacher Education** says preservice programs, especially in elementary teacher education, have not adequately kept up with integrating AI concepts into their curricula. [51]
- **Teacher training in the age of AI: Impact on AI Literacy and Teachers’ Attitudes** says teachers primarily employ AI applications for lesson planning, creating exercises, and adapting content for diverse student groups, followed by grading and assessment, and that implementation remains limited. [52]
- **How to Assess AI Literacy: Misalignment Between Self-Reported and Objective-Based Measures** says many existing items are overly technical for K-12 educators, and that future work should design subject-specific and grade-divided (primary and secondary) scenario-based items. [53]

Across the outputs, the main pattern is that K-12 teacher AI productivity evidence is strongest for:
- lesson planning and instructional design,
- grading and feedback,
- assessment scoring,
- differentiated support,
- teacher workload relief,
- and school-context-specific constraints and opportunities.

However, the raw outputs also repeatedly state that evidence is limited, often observational, qualitative, survey-based, exploratory, or early-stage, with few rigorous causal studies directly focused on K-12 teacher productivity. [2][3][36][37]

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

The gathered material repeatedly indicates that AI-enabled grading and feedback tools in education are positioned as time-saving, workload-reducing, and feedback-turnaround-improving systems, but most authentic K-12 evidence stresses teacher oversight, teacher adaptation, and human validation rather than fully automated final grading. In the K-12-specific classroom implementation literature, teachers used AI-generated rubrics, grading feedback, and formative feedback, but did not treat AI output as final; instead, they edited feedback, clarified grades, recontextualized comments, and retained interpretive control [1]. The same study reports that teachers valued the AI’s rapid narrative feedback for formative purposes, distrusted automated scoring, and emphasized the need for human oversight [1]. Students welcomed fast, revision-oriented feedback but remained skeptical of AI-only grading [1]. A second snippet from the same paper states that teachers valued the AI’s rapid narrative feedback for formative purposes, but distrusted automated scoring and emphasized the need for human oversight, while students were skeptical of AI-only grading [1]. A further snippet from the same paper says the platform’s AI-powered grading features were used in a co-design pilot with 19 teachers, where the goal was “to speed and scale formative feedback, elevate depth of student thinking, while preserving teacher authority over final grading judgments,” and 13 of the 19 teachers submitted feedback survey forms [1]. Another snippet from the same paper says “students loved the prospect of getting a grade and feedback with such a quick turnaround, rather than waiting the 2-3 weeks that it usually takes me to grade their writing,” and that teachers preferred narrative feedback over numerical grades [1]. The study also states that student responses varied, with some benefiting from lowstakes feedback with a quick turnaround while others experienced cognitive overload or usability challenges [1].

The same K-12 implementation paper includes a direct statement that, even among teachers critical of AI limitations, the system’s utility was its ability to streamline initial feedback, reduce turnaround time, and make space for higher-order instructional moves [1]. One teacher quote states, “I see AI grading tools as a kind of new TA: it gives fast, helpful first-pass feedback that enables students to make improvements right away, but I still review and make final grading decisions” [1]. Another quote states, “I took the feedback and put it in the AI Chat. . . told it, ‘give me one paragraph in teacher voice,’” showing adaptation and teacher mediation of AI output [1]. Another teacher quote says, “I asked if [students] would be ok if the AI graded all their work and they all said no! They want to know I’m reading their work. They want me to see their jokes and emotions. They feared that AI would just be like a checklist. I thought her [the AI assistants] feedback was better than mine though. (But they thought it’d be great as a presubmission self check grade)” [1]. Another quoted statement says AI grading tools are “a kind of new TA” giving “fast, helpful first-pass feedback” while the teacher still reviews and makes final grading decisions [1]. The study explicitly notes that automation accelerates routine processes but teachers retain interpretive control, and that teacher mediation was essential to address discrepancies between comments and grades [1].

Related K-12 evidence from a secondary-school formative feedback study reports that AI-generated feedback is appreciated by both students and teachers and provides immediate subject-specific, concrete, and relevant feedback [2]. In that study, the sample consisted of 26 students and 13 teachers at five secondary schools in Norway, using five different AI plug-ins and four different knowledge bases for feedback optimization [2]. Interviews and unstructured observations were used to collect data [2]. The findings indicate that AI-generated feedback is appreciated by both students and teachers, provides immediate subject-specific, concrete, and relevant feedback, and that high-performing students were motivated to further improve their writing [2]. However, some students found the feedback too general or complicated, and teachers who had not conducted whole-term periodic planning struggled with using AI for formative assessment purposes [2]. The paper also states that the teacher needs to have the last word when AI takes over formative feedback procedures [2].

A high-school lesson-planning study using MagicSchool AI reports that AI accelerates lesson planning, supports differentiated instruction, and fosters creativity, but also requires critical teacher oversight, effective prompt-engineering skills, and significant adaptation to align with classroom dynamics [3]. It states that AI’s outputs often lack readiness for immediate use and require refinement to ensure pedagogical soundness [3]. The study used data from 38 teachers, collected through post-workshops open-ended questionnaires and focus group interviews [3]. It emphasizes the importance of targeted training and professional development [3].

A broader K-12 teachers’ needs study reports a focus group interview with n = 15 and a second study of 128 teachers from elementary, middle, and high school levels [4]. It identified eight key AI roles: personalized curriculum design, development of instructional materials, foundational learning support, self-reflection support, student evaluation, career guidance, student management, and administrative task support [4]. Elementary school teachers emphasized student assessment and management, while middle and high school teachers prioritized self-reflection support and career guidance [4]. Teachers underscored the significance of maintaining a complementary relationship with AI, pursuing shared objectives, and fostering sustained interaction, with the aim of evolving into “augmented teachers” [4]. A follow-up discussion section states that teachers expect AI to augment their roles in those eight key roles and that human-AI complementarity needs to adapt to school level [4].

A related conceptual and review literature stream repeatedly states that AI in education can automate routine tasks, including grading and feedback, and free teachers to focus on higher-order tasks. One review states that AI-based educational platforms “purport to streamline workflows and provide rapid, individualized feedback” but concerns remain about pedagogical alignment, teacher agency, and learner impacts [5]. Another review states that AI is used to automate grading, create instructional materials, and provide real-time feedback to students, allowing teachers to focus on facilitating learning and developing critical thinking skills [6]. One paper states that “Essay, test, and assignment grading is a time-consuming activity that may be made much more efficient for teachers with the use of AI-powered automated grading and feedback systems,” and that instructors can spend more time with their pupils by using these systems’ sophisticated algorithms, which evaluate replies quickly and accurately [7]. Another paper states that AI-driven automation manages duties like scheduling, grading, and report preparation efficiently, streamlines processes, and frees up time for teachers to focus on engaging pupils in meaningful ways [8]. One conceptual review states that AI can automate grading homework and tests, that “This time could be used to work on professional development, interact with students, and prepare for class,” and that “Since grading consumes up to half of educators’ time, the potential time savings are enormous” [9]. It also states that “AI can be trained to grade a range of subjects and assessments including essays, problem-solving questions, and even graphing assessments” [9]. Another review says AI-based feedback tools use advanced algorithms and natural language processing to provide personalized and timely feedback, and that traditional feedback methods, such as manual grading and assessments, are often timeconsuming and resource-intensive for educators [10].

Several studies and reviews specifically mention feedback turnaround. One paper states that “Current automated essay scoring systems can not only give an overall holistic writing quality score for student writing, but they can also give feedback, guidance, and even model writing samples to assist students with improving their writing” [11]. Another paper states that automated scoring can reproduce advantages of multiple-choice scoring, including “speed, consistency, transparent scoring logic, constant avail-ability, and lower per-unit costs,” and because it is based on productive samples of student writing, it provides detailed performance-specific feedback [12]. The same paper says Criterion’s design is intended to help writers achieve competency and fluency by “providing real-time evaluation of their work” in terms of grammar, usage and mechanics, style, and essay structure [12]. Another paper says AI-powered tools “can grade essays, multiple-choice exams, and other forms of testing, and they can also give students immediate feedback” [13]. Another paper states that integrated AI in Microsoft Teams automatically grades assignments based on customizable rubrics, generates a detailed report for each evaluated task, and provides “automatic, immediate feedback” based on clear criteria [14]. Another paper says that AI-powered assessment tools offer real-time feedback on student performance, enabling teachers to adjust their strategies accordingly [15]. Another paper states that AI can provide real-time assistance to students through chatbots and virtual assistants, offering immediate help with assignments, answering queries, and providing feedback [16]. Another paper says AI can be used to provide useful feedback to students and teachers and to assist students in improving their academic writing skills [17].

The evidence also repeatedly emphasizes that human review and adaptation remain necessary. In one K-12 co-design pilot, teachers did not treat AI output as final; they exercised discretion, editing feedback, clarifying grades, and recontextualizing comments to maintain pedagogical coherence [1]. That paper explicitly says the model where automation accelerates routine processes but teachers retain interpretive control emerged as a key condition for productive use [1]. It also says teacher mediation was essential to address discrepancies between comments and grades, underscoring that AI should augment rather than replace educator judgment [1]. Another paper says AI systems “often fall short of meeting the needs of teachers, hindering the educational process or even causing conflicts” and that teachers underscored the significance of maintaining a complementary relationship with AI [4]. Another paper states that AI-generated rubrics served as strong starting drafts, improving structure and clarity, but teachers emphasized the necessity for oversight due to occasional misalignment with instructional priorities and the need for substantial editing [18]. A separate paper on AI-supported rubric generation says teachers expressed conditional willingness to adopt AI rubric tools when workflows support easy customization and preserve teacher control [18]. Another paper says “When numerical scores lack clarity or consistency, but written comments hold pedagogical value, the role of the AI should be reimagined: not to replace teacher judgment, but to scaffold learning through accessible, timely, and editable feedback” [1].

In the literature on non-AI digital or semi-automated alternatives, there are several examples of rubric-based grading, LMS-supported feedback, and computer-managed workflows. One paper on Gradescope, Canvas, and open-ended assignments says these tools provide valuable options for grading open-ended assignments and that Gradescope has made grading “easier and faster,” with features such as rubric-based grading for transparency and consistency, dynamic rubric creation, and group assignments [19]. Another paper says linking each rubric item with corresponding feedback allows gradetools to scale the provision of detailed individualized feedback, and that prompt codes can expedite the provision of repeatable feedback across different questions and students [20]. The same paper says gradetools supports the provision of unique feedback on the fly and dynamic update of the rubric [20]. Another paper says previous annotations can be reused to speed up the code review process because remarks or suggestions tend to recur frequently when reviewing submissions for the same assignment [21]. It also says manual assessment feedback is delivered asynchronously and that students can only see manual source code annotations and grades after a teacher has explicitly published the feedback [21]. Another paper says the workshop comment setting in a peer-feedback system was changed from optional to forced, and that training with screencasts supported peer feedback practices [22].

The search results also surfaced older and non-K-12 or broader-education studies that still speak to grading and feedback turnaround. A study on content-specific computer-generated feedback with EssayCritic in Norwegian upper secondary school states that the target class and comparison class both significantly improved grades, and that the feedback from EssayCritic gave content-specific cues and students included more ideas in their essays than the comparison class, which struggled when giving feedback to each other [23]. A paper on teacher’s feedback on students’ writing ability states that project 1 was the essay grade before feedback and project 7 was the essay grade after feedback, using a rubric that included organizational skills, idea development, language use, and creativity and originality; it says there was an increase in students’ essay scores before and after teacher feedback, and that the significance would be tested using paired t-tests [24]. Another paper on teacher feedback reports that teachers provide homework feedback via oral or written praise, criticism, written comments, rewards, general review of homework in class, and grading, and that these practices are important instructional tools [25].

There are multiple review and bibliometric papers indicating the broader state of AI in K-12 education. A systematic literature review of AI applications in K-12 education reports that the review covered articles and conference papers published between 2011 and 2021 in Web of Science and Scopus, with 2075 documents initially extracted and 210 identified for further investigation [26]. It categorized AI applications into Student performance, Teaching, Selection, and Behavior tasks, and Other [26]. It says Machine Learning and Intelligent Tutoring System were the most common approaches [26]. Another K-12 review reports that among the studies, most were in high school (n = 45), followed by middle school (n = 32), and elementary school (n = 13), and that most of the studies included K-12 students (n = 53) as participants [27]. It also notes that one study was conducted in a preschool setting (n = 1) and predicted student performance at age 8 [27]. Another systematic review says AI in K-12 education includes 169 extant studies from 2011 to 2021 [28]. Another bibliometric review states that AI-based feedback tools in education are strongly associated with keywords like feedback, students, education, teaching, assessment, ChatGPT, learning analytics, automated writing evaluation, and personalized feedback [29].

The search results also surfaced several non-K-12 or higher-education studies that still provide directly relevant mechanisms about grading speed, feedback generation, and human oversight. One arXiv paper says an LLM-powered feedback engine generated feedback on students’ essays based on rubrics used by teaching assistants, and that TAs considered using AI feedback as suggestions during their grading could expedite grading, enhance consistency, and improve overall feedback quality [30]. The same paper says they performed think-aloud studies with 5 TAs over 20 1-hour sessions [30]. Another arXiv paper says AI-powered assessment and grading features in a classroom pilot allow teachers to generate or refine standards-aligned rubrics and automatically create feedback and grades for student work, with the goal “to speed and scale formative feedback, elevate depth of student thinking, while preserving teacher authority over final grading judgments” [31]. That paper says of the 19 teachers, 13 submitted feedback survey forms, and that over half (56%) used the platform for in-class formative assessments [31]. It also says “Students loved the prospect of getting a grade and feedback with such a quick turnaround, rather than waiting the 2-3 weeks that it usually takes me to grade their writing” [31]. Another arXiv paper says it estimates per-essay grading time from timestamps between the first and last action on each essay, but the snippet does not report a quantitative time-saved result in the raw excerpt [32]. The same paper says AI-derived scores were used instead of TA grades because TA first-draft grades were provisional, there was high rater variance, a single uniform human rating was infeasible, and AI rubric-level scores were more internally consistent than TA scores [32]. It also states that 88.7% of rubric-level AI judgments matched TAs’ final judgments [32].

The search results included a number of papers and reports that reiterate the theme that AI can reduce grading burden but does not replace teachers. One review says AI can “streamline various educational processes such as generating questions using prompts, grading, and content creation, reducing the workload on educators and enabling them to focus on higher-order tasks including thinking and problem solving” [9]. Another review says AI can be used by tutors to personalize assessment and provide timely feedback addressing individual learning needs, and that the benefit of AI in assessment is that it can reduce human subjectivity and time taken for assessment [17]. Another paper says AI can automate grading and feedback, enable teachers to spend more time with students, and that “Teachers can save time and concentrate on other crucial facets of education by adopting AI technology to automate feedback and grading” [33]. Another paper says “Automated scoring of answers is not meant to serve as a replacement to a human evaluator, but, merely as an aid to the evaluator” [34]. Another paper says AI grading tools already exist and that humans are more prone to mistakes than automated essay scoring systems, but current systems are not efficient enough to replace good writing teachers [35]. Another paper says AI can help reduce the burden on teachers by improving the accuracy and timeliness of feedback [36]. Another paper says AI-generated rubrics, feedback, and grades can optimize educators’ time, allowing them to focus more on interactive teaching and less on manual grading, and that students receive consistent and valuable feedback in a very short time [14]. Another paper says “ChatGPT holds great potential to considerably decrease teachers’ workload,” can be used as a feedback tool, can create tests and rubrics, and can be used for automatic grading of assignments, especially for text-based courses [37].

The tool output also included multiple studies on automated essay scoring, AI-assisted scoring, and human–AI scoring comparisons. One ERIC abstract states that a total of 923 essays from 23 classes of 12 senior high schools in Taiwan were manually and electronically scored, and the study investigated consistency between human raters and an automated essay scoring system [38]. Another ERIC abstract says a quasi-experimental study compared point-based, rubric-based, and rubric-plus-written-feedback-based grading methods in middle school science classrooms with 136 7th and 8th grade students from Midwest USA [39]. Another ERIC abstract says the current educational system relies heavily on manual grading, posing challenges such as delayed feedback and grading inaccuracies, and introduces “GRAD-AI” as an advanced AGT that combines automation with teacher involvement for precise grading, timely feedback, and personalized support [40]. Another ERIC abstract says AI-assisted automated scoring of picture-cued writing tasks can greatly reduce teacher workload and shorten the time needed for providing feedback to learners [41]. Another ERIC abstract states that “The purpose of this paper is to propose a novel method for automatically scoring student responses to picture-cued writing tasks” and that grading assignments is inherently subjective and time-consuming [41]. Another paper says the West Virginia Department of Education’s auto grading initiative dates back to 2004 and was looking to expand statewide writing assessment “without having to pay more teachers to hand-score the tests” [42]. Another paper says “There is currently no adequate evaluation mechanism for grading essays and short responses; the computer-based evaluation system only works for multiple-choice questions” and that the project studied different uses of ML and how to improve efficiency of essay scoring using AI and other algorithms [43].

A large set of review papers and bibliometric analyses in the gathered material describe the broader ecosystem in which K-12 grading and feedback automation sits. One review says AI applications in K-12 education are categorized into Student performance, Teaching, Selection, and Behavior tasks, and Other [26]. Another says AI in education is being implemented in tutoring and assessment [44]. Another says AI-based feedback tools focus on personalized and timely feedback to learners and are motivated by the time-consuming and resource-intensive nature of manual grading and assessments [10]. Another systematic scoping review says LLM-based educational tools can automate question generation, feedback provision, and essay grading but raises practical and ethical concerns [45]. Another paper says AI in educational assessment increases consistency, personalization, and scalability and can analyze large data with multiple sources [9]. Another paper states that AI can provide “feedback that meets” the criteria of timely, relevant, and objective feedback [9]. Another paper says “Artificial intelligence powered digital writing assistant in higher education” is a randomized controlled trial, but the raw snippet in the available output did not include details about time savings or K-12 settings [46].

The search results also included a wide range of contextual and theoretical papers on AI in education, teacher roles, digital competencies, and ethical issues. One paper says the use of AI in education can transform educational practices and that teachers are required to undergo in-service training [47]. Another paper says AI in education should not compromise instructional integrity [3]. Another paper says AI-driven automation could make it possible to save money on hiring many teachers and other staff while still providing high-quality education, but quality control and fine-tuning the AI become key teacher responsibilities [8]. Another paper says the role of the educator will be to oversee the work of AI [8]. Another paper says AI supports teachers by automating routine tasks, providing actionable insights, and enhancing instructional planning [48]. Another paper says “AIEd plays many roles and has many advantages, such as improving teacher productivity, offering support, and resolving issues” [48]. Another paper says AI can reduce administrative burdens by managing student records, tracking attendance, and handling other logistical tasks, freeing teachers to focus on their core responsibilities [48]. Another paper says “Teachers who are familiar with these technologies can incorporate them into their lesson plans to provide continuous support, even after school hours” [16]. Another paper says “Understanding AI also encourages educators to explore and implement cutting-edge pedagogies, such as flipped classrooms and gamified learning environments” [16].

The gathered material also includes one paper on automated feedback and assessment in a hybrid educational environment using Microsoft Teams, which states that integrated AI generates detailed reports for each evaluated task, including the grade obtained and specific feedback for each rubric criterion [14]. It says the system addresses delayed or absent teacher feedback by providing automatic, immediate feedback based on clear criteria, optimizing educators’ time and allowing them to focus more on interactive teaching and less on manual grading [14]. Another paper states that automated grading systems can help reduce the burden on teachers by improving the accuracy and timeliness of feedback [49]. Another paper states that AI can automate grading, provide immediate feedback, reduce bias or grading errors, and enable teachers to save time [50].

No direct K-12 field study in the gathered material reported a clean, directly comparable “net time saved after review and adaptation versus non-AI digital and human-only alternatives” in a way that was numerically explicit in the raw excerpts. The closest explicit time-related statements in the gathered raw outputs are qualitative or partial: “reduce turnaround time,” “fast, helpful first-pass feedback,” “quick turnaround,” “waiting the 2-3 weeks that it usually takes me to grade their writing,” “grading consumes up to half of educators’ time,” “grading by artificial intelligence may actually be more reliable in some cases,” and “speed and scale formative feedback” [1, 9, 31]. The raw output also includes a non-K-12 web result claiming “AI-assisted grading significantly reduced grading time by 88%, from 50 to 6 minutes per report” in a paper titled “Hybrid Instructor AI Assessment in Academic Projects: Efficiency, Equity, and Methodological Lessons,” but that paper was only mentioned in open web search text and not fully represented in the other database outputs [51]. The raw search outputs also mention a Commercial or tool-specific claim that grading 100 multiple-choice or short-answer math quizzes manually takes 4–6 hours while using an AI tool reduces this to 20–40 minutes, and that reviewing 35 essays manually takes 7–10 hours but with AI-assisted scoring and feedback generation it takes 1–2 hours of review; however, these claims came from an openAI web-search result pointing to a commercial blog post and were not backed by a directly retrieved academic study in the tool outputs [52]. Another open web search result says a Gallup-Walton survey found teachers using AI grading tools reclaim an average of 5.9 hours per week, equating to six full work weeks annually, but that was also not represented as a directly retrieved academic paper in the academic database outputs [52].

The search outputs repeatedly emphasize a stable pattern across sources: AI grading and feedback systems are promising for reducing workload, accelerating turnaround, and supporting formative assessment, but the authentic K-12 evidence in the raw outputs consistently treats them as teacher-centered, human-in-the-loop tools rather than full replacements for manual grading. The strongest directly K-12-specific implementation evidence in the raw output is the co-design pilot with 19 or 20 teachers, where teachers used the system for rubrics, assessments, narrative feedback, and revision cycles, while editing and validating the AI output themselves [1]. The strongest directly K-12-specific non-K-12-but-school-relevant evidence includes the Norwegian secondary school feedback study with 26 students and 13 teachers [2], the high-school MagicSchool AI lesson-planning study with 38 teachers [3], and the K-12 teacher-role study with n = 15 and n = 128 [4].

## Executive Summary

The evidence base indicates that AI-enabled tools can plausibly improve K-12 teacher productivity, but the strongest conclusion is narrow: the benefits are most credible for draft generation and first-pass support in lesson planning, feedback, communication, and some administrative text work, while the evidence for reliable net time savings in authentic K-12 practice remains limited. Across the retrieved studies, the dominant pattern is human-in-the-loop use: teachers use AI to produce a draft, then verify, edit, contextualize, and finalize it. That makes AI best understood as an augmentation tool rather than a substitute for teacher labor [20][23][29][39][140][208].

The strongest causal evidence in the retrieved set is indirect but informative. A randomized controlled trial in K-12 human–AI complementarity, “Designing for human–AI complementarity in K-12 education,” tested Lumilo smart glasses that provided teachers with real-time analytics and metacognitive support during middle-school mathematics instruction; in the randomized field study, students in the Glasses + Analytics condition showed greater learning gains on linear equation solving than students in both comparison conditions, and the intervention also shifted teacher attention toward lower-pretest students, with n=286 analyzed students and n=8 teachers/18 classrooms [232]. A second randomized study, “Physics task development of prospective physics teachers using ChatGPT,” found that prospective physics teachers using ChatGPT 3.5 produced high-school physics assessment tasks with correctness comparable to textbook-generated tasks, but tasks were less clear and less often contextually embedded; the study reports n=26 participants and 103 tasks total (n=51 ChatGPT, n=52 textbook), with effect sizes d=0.38 for clarity and d=1.04 for context [61]. These trials do not directly measure teacher time saved in K-12 classrooms, but they do show that AI can improve or at least support workflow performance in task generation and classroom orchestration when carefully designed [61][232].

The strongest quasi-experimental and observational evidence aligns with that story but also exposes the limits. A quasi-experimental study in underserved middle-school settings reported a 40% reduction in lesson preparation time and a 30% reduction in administrative tasks when AI-powered education tools were deployed, alongside student achievement gains; however, the study is broader than teacher productivity alone and is not the same as a K-12 teacher-specific time-use trial [250]. An observational study of generative AI grading for high-school mathematics found that AI-powered grading platforms were useful for rubric generation, grading, and feedback in real classroom settings, but the finding is still implementation-oriented rather than a clean estimate of net productivity [208]. A mixed-methods comparative study of K-12 mathematics educators found AI-generated lesson plans were preferred in some structured components, while human-created plans were preferred overall, especially in elementary contexts; this suggests AI may reduce drafting burden without displacing teacher judgment [67]. In a second observational study, K-12 educators in Pakistan reported adoption and perceived impact of AI tools, but the evidence remains self-report and descriptive rather than causal [146]. Together, these findings support the idea that AI can improve task efficiency in some workflows, but they do not yet establish large, durable, generalizable productivity gains across K-12 teaching [67][146][208][250].

Tier 1 is answered only partially: the literature is consistent about what counts as productivity—time saved, faster completion, workload reduction, feedback turnaround, and administrative burden—but it is much less consistent in how these outcomes are measured, and many studies remain focused on perceived usefulness, adoption, or feasibility rather than direct productivity metrics [20][23][140][142][226]. Tier 2 is partially answered: teachers already rely on LMS tools, reusable comments, rubrics, translation supports, and clerical help, but direct head-to-head comparisons between AI and those existing supports are rare [235][208][268]. Tier 3 is also partially answered: the literature identifies mechanisms such as draft generation, personalization support, automated grading suggestions, translation, and communication drafting, with implementation conditions including training, prompting skill, human review, privacy and policy constraints, and integration into existing workflows [29][39][142][235][270]. Tier 4 remains unresolved in its most decision-relevant form: there is promising but still thin evidence that AI reduces workload or speeds turnaround, and the evidence is weakest on net time saved after verification, on comparisons to non-AI digital tools, and on whether productivity gains persist across elementary, middle, and high school contexts [61][67][208][250]. Overall confidence is moderate for the claim that AI can help with specific K-12 teacher tasks and low for the claim that it reliably produces large net productivity gains across schools. The single most important caveat is that verification, editing, compliance, and contextual adaptation can erase a substantial portion of gross drafting speed, so “faster output” should not be equated with “net productivity gain” [20][23][208][235].
