It describes successful establishment of cross-institutional structures, including a common learning evaluation group and revised benchmarking statements, but does not report a single pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Implementation of IPE policy, curriculum restructuring, and institutional partnerships

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that implementing practice-based IPE required substantial coordination of placements, facilitators, and practice educators, and that resource constraints limited scale and consistency. At the same time, the programmes created workable models for delivering interprofessional placements and, in some sites, allowed large numbers of students to participate (e.g. about 7,000 in South East London targeted, 96 in the North East pilot sample), but no standardized workload metric or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Placement logistics, facilitation burden, recruitment of practice educators, and delivery feasibility

finding.finding_summary: Students and facilitators reported gains in teamwork, understanding of professional roles, confidence, reflection, and collaborative problem-solving through participation in practice-based IPE. These are qualitative findings from reflection sheets, interviews, and focus groups; no quantitative effect size or sample-level summary statistic is reported.
finding.measure: Student/facilitator reflections, interviews, and focus groups on teamwork, role understanding, and collaboration
finding.study_size: 96 student participants in the North East case study; qualitative accounts from facilitators and students

paper_profiles.title: The Promises and Challenges of Artificial Intelligence for Teachers: a Systematic Review of Research
paper_profiles.population: K-12 teachers (in-service and some pre-service teacher studies included in the review)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a systematic review of empirical research on how teachers use artificial intelligence (AI) applications and machine learning methods in education. The authors were motivated by a gap in the literature: AI in education had been studied extensively from the learner or system perspective, but much less from the perspective of teachers as end users and as contributors to AI development.

The review covered 44 journal articles published in Web of Science-indexed journals over roughly the prior 20 years, with studies spanning K-12 contexts and a small number of pre-service teacher studies. The authors coded each study for the kinds of teacher data collected, the roles teachers played in AI research, the advantages AI offered teachers, the challenges teachers faced, and the AI methods used. Teacher data sources were most often self-reports, grading, and observation data, while teachers frequently served as models to train AI algorithms or as sources of data for prediction and automated assessment.

Overall, the review concludes that AI can support teachers’ planning, implementation, and assessment work, especially by helping them identify student needs, monitor learning in real time, provide immediate feedback, reduce workload, and automate scoring. At the same time, the authors highlight important limitations, including AI’s limited reliability, technical capacity, context dependence, and the lack of multimodal data and teacher involvement in system design. The paper argues for more research on pre-service teachers, richer data modalities, and stronger collaboration among teachers, researchers, and AI developers.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, AI was consistently reported to improve teacher productivity by supporting planning, real-time monitoring, immediate feedback, intervention, and automated assessment. The review does not report a single pooled effect size; instead, it synthesizes 44 studies and notes recurring benefits such as reduced teaching workload and time savings (e.g., AI-based peer tutor recommender systems and automated essay scoring).
finding.measure: Teacher workload, time savings, monitoring/feedback efficiency, and automation of scoring/assessment tasks
finding.study_size: 44 studies reviewed; individual study sample sizes varied

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that AI adoption in teaching practice is shaped by institutional and implementation factors such as technical infrastructure, teachers’ technological knowledge, AI reliability, and context dependence across settings. It also highlights systemic gaps, including limited teacher involvement in AI development and limited use of multimodal data, while arguing these issues constrain broader educational adoption.
finding.measure: Implementation challenges, infrastructure constraints, teacher involvement in AI development, and applicability across settings
finding.study_size: 44 studies reviewed; individual study sample sizes varied

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing education with AI: Exploring the transformative potential of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review article examines the emerging role of artificial intelligence in education, with particular attention to chatbots and ChatGPT. The paper asks how AI tools may transform teaching and learning, what benefits they may provide for students and teachers, and what ethical and practical concerns accompany their use.

The article is not an empirical intervention study; instead, it synthesizes existing literature on AI technologies in education, including intelligent tutoring systems, automated grading, learning analytics, adaptive systems, and chatbots. It discusses how these tools may support individualized instruction, instant feedback, student engagement, language learning, assessment, and teacher workload reduction, while also raising concerns about bias, privacy, academic integrity, transparency, and over-reliance on technology.

The paper’s context is broad K-12 and higher education rather than a single grade band or program. Its main conclusion is that AI has meaningful potential to improve productivity, personalization, and educational support, but successful implementation requires teacher training, responsible use, and attention to ethical safeguards. The authors call for further research on how ChatGPT and related tools can be effectively integrated into educational practice.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI tools, especially chatbots and automated grading systems, can reduce teacher workload by handling repetitive tasks such as assignment evaluation, scoring, and providing feedback. It cites examples like Gradescope, Autolab, AutoGradr, and Repl.it as tools that can save teachers many hours and redirect time toward lesson planning, student support, and professional development; however, no original effect size or study sample is reported because this is a review article.
finding.measure: teacher workload, grading/scoring time, administrative task efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The review emphasizes that successful AI adoption in education depends on institutional factors such as teacher training, support, policy, privacy, ethics, and responsible implementation. It does not report original institutional outcome data, but it repeatedly frames AI integration as requiring organizational preparation to avoid bias, inequity, and academic integrity problems.
finding.measure: teacher preparation/support, ethics/privacy considerations, institutional implementation conditions

finding.finding_summary: The article identifies literacy-related uses of AI, including personalized writing feedback, summarization, and language-learning support through chatbots and tools such as Grammarly, InstaText, and QuillBot. It cites prior studies suggesting these tools can improve writing performance and reading comprehension, but the paper itself reports no new literacy outcome data or effect sizes.
finding.measure: writing assistance, reading comprehension, text feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses AI chatbots as useful for language acquisition and speaking-related practice, including providing conversational interaction, pronunciation correction, and feedback in foreign-language contexts. It references prior work on AI chatbots improving speaking performance, but provides no primary empirical estimates in this review.
finding.measure: language learning, conversational practice, pronunciation correction

finding.finding_summary: The review states that AI-enabled personalized learning can increase student motivation, engagement, confidence, and reduce anxiety. These claims are supported by cited literature, including AI interventions that reduced anxiety, but the article itself does not present original data or effect sizes.
finding.measure: motivation, engagement, confidence, learning anxiety

finding.finding_summary: The authors note that AI tools can support self-reflection, self-directed learning, self-regulation, critical thinking, creativity, and collaboration through individualized feedback and interactive learning environments. These are synthesized claims from prior studies rather than findings from a new empirical evaluation.
finding.measure: self-regulation, critical thinking, creativity, collaboration

paper_profiles.title: Basic psychological need theory: Advancements, critical themes, and future directions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This editorial reviews two decades of research on Basic Psychological Need Theory (BPNT), a mini-theory within Self-Determination Theory. The paper’s central purpose is to synthesize conceptual and empirical advances, clarify what counts as a basic psychological need, and organize the literature around five themes: whether the shortlist of needs should be expanded, the consequences of need frustration, the relation between psychological and physical needs, the role of need-supportive and need-thwarting contexts, and the universality of need effects across people and settings.

The article does not test a new educational intervention or AI tool; instead, it surveys prior studies and special-issue contributions, many of which are correlational, longitudinal, or experimental across domains such as education, work, sport, relationships, and health. The review emphasizes that autonomy, competence, and relatedness satisfaction reliably support well-being and adjustment, while need frustration predicts ill-being, disengagement, and compensatory behaviors. It also highlights emerging candidate needs such as novelty, morality, and beneficence, but argues that further evidence is needed before expanding the core need set.

For K-12 relevance, the paper discusses school-based work showing that need frustration predicts lower autonomous motivation and disengagement among students, and it references educational contexts when describing how need satisfaction and frustration operate. However, the paper is primarily a theoretical and narrative review of motivation research rather than a study of classroom practice or AI use. Its main conclusion is that BPNT provides a powerful framework for understanding how supportive or thwarting environments shape motivation, adjustment, and well-being, and that future work should more rigorously test universality, measurement, and contextual mechanisms.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed literature, satisfaction of autonomy, competence, and relatedness is repeatedly linked to better well-being, adjustment, and autonomous motivation, while need frustration predicts ill-being, stress, anxiety, depressive symptoms, and disengagement. The paper summarizes findings from many studies rather than reporting one new estimate; for example, it notes that semester-to-semester increases in need frustration predicted parallel increases in disengagement among Korean high school students (3-wave longitudinal study).
finding.measure: Need satisfaction/frustration, autonomous motivation, disengagement, ill-being indicators (stress, anxiety, depressive symptoms)

finding.finding_summary: The review discusses need-related processes that support self-regulation, proactive coping, and motivational persistence, but these are secondary to the paper’s main focus on basic psychological needs and well-being. It cites evidence that need frustration is associated with compensatory and reactive behaviors, including disengagement and oppositional defiance, which are relevant to self-regulation and persistence.
finding.measure: Disengagement, oppositional defiance, compensatory behaviors

paper_profiles.title: A critical review of flipped classroom challenges in K-12 education: possible solutions and recommendations for future research
paper_profiles.venue: Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper systematically reviews empirical research on flipped classrooms in K-12 education to identify how the approach is implemented, what outcomes it affects, and what challenges arise in practice. The authors searched eight databases, applied PRISMA-style selection criteria, and included 15 peer-reviewed empirical studies published through September 2016.

The review focuses on the structure of flipped learning activities, student achievement, student attitudes, and implementation barriers. Across the reviewed studies, K-12 flipped classrooms typically used video-based pre-class instruction and in-class group work, brief review, and individual practice. The authors found that flipped classrooms generally produced neutral to positive achievement outcomes compared with traditional instruction, while student attitudes were mixed but often positive.

The paper also synthesizes common challenges into student-related, faculty-related, and operational categories, including disengagement with videos, heavy teacher preparation time, and unequal access to technology. Based on these findings, the authors propose a rudimentary flipped classroom model and 10 implementation guidelines intended to improve adoption in K-12 settings. The paper is primarily a review and recommendation piece rather than a single primary effectiveness study.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed K-12 flipped classroom studies, student achievement was generally neutral to positive relative to traditional classrooms. Of the nine direct comparison studies discussed in detail, five reported significantly better performance in flipped classrooms (e.g., Bhagat et al. 2016; Chao et al. 2015; Schultz et al. 2014; Tsai et al. 2015; Huang and Hong 2016 on some aspects), while four found no significant difference; no study reported a detrimental achievement effect.
finding.measure: Student achievement outcomes from comparison studies (quasi-experimental or historical control comparisons)
finding.study_size: 15 studies reviewed; 9 direct comparison studies for achievement synthesis

finding.finding_summary: Students were generally satisfied with flipped classrooms, but attitudes were not uniformly positive. Several studies reported higher engagement and course satisfaction, while others found resistance to the new format, lower satisfaction than traditional instruction, and complaints about pre-class workload and video-based learning.
finding.measure: Student attitude, satisfaction, and engagement data from surveys, interviews, instructor reflections, and observations

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that flipped classrooms increased opportunities for peer interaction, group discussion, collaboration, and problem solving during class. Students also reported benefits for note-taking, self-directed preparation, and working through problems in class, suggesting gains in collaboration and metacognitive learning behaviors.
finding.measure: Reported collaboration, problem-solving, note-taking, and self-directed learning behaviors in reviewed studies

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies substantial operational tradeoffs in K-12 flipped classroom implementation. While the approach can reallocate class time toward interactive activities, it also imposes high upfront teacher workload for video and material creation, requires monitoring of out-of-class preparation, and depends on student access to technology and school infrastructure.
finding.measure: Reported implementation challenges, teacher preparation effort, and technology/infrastructure requirements

finding.finding_summary: The review shows that successful flipped classroom implementation depends on institutional support, including IT infrastructure, staff assistance, and teacher professional development. The authors argue that schools need to provide computer resources, technical support, and training to sustain implementation, but the paper does not measure institutional outcomes directly.
finding.measure: Institutional support needs and implementation conditions identified across reviewed studies

paper_profiles.title: A comparative analysis of international frameworks for 21st century competences: Implications for national curriculum policies
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how eight influential international frameworks define 21st century competences and how they address curriculum implementation and assessment. The authors ask which competences are emphasized across the frameworks, whether the frameworks provide guidance for implementing these competences in educational practice, and whether they propose ways to assess them. The analysis is grounded in a curriculum-representations lens that distinguishes intended, implemented, and attained curriculum, allowing the authors to compare policy intentions with evidence from educational practice.

The study is based on document analysis of 32 documents drawn from the official websites of the selected frameworks and related international initiatives. The frameworks include P21, EnGauge, ATCS, NETS/ISTE, NAEP technological literacy, OECD-DeSeCo/New Millennium Learners, the EU key competences framework, and UNESCO’s ICT competency framework for teachers. The paper also reviews three international studies on implementation in practice (EU member states, OECD countries, and SITES) to understand how national systems and schools take up these competences.

The main conclusion is that there is strong horizontal consistency across frameworks about the importance of collaboration, communication, ICT literacy, creativity, critical thinking, and problem-solving, but vertical consistency is weak: policy intentions are far ahead of classroom implementation and assessment practice. The authors argue that ICT is central both as an argument for new competences and as a tool for supporting learning and assessment, yet in practice most systems still assess traditional knowledge more than complex competences. They conclude with recommendations for clearer operational definitions, stronger links between core subjects and 21st century competences, better integration of ICT literacies, and more explicit national frameworks to support implementation and assessment.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds strong alignment among international policy frameworks about what 21st century competences are, but much weaker alignment between policy intentions and classroom implementation. Across the reviewed international studies, many countries had adopted these competences in curriculum policy, yet school-level practice lagged behind and assessment remained a major weakness.
finding.measure: Document analysis of 8 frameworks and 3 international implementation studies (EU, OECD, SITES)

finding.finding_summary: Across the frameworks, the most consistently emphasized competences were collaboration, communication, creativity, critical thinking, problem-solving, and the ability to produce quality products. The paper does not estimate effects of an intervention; rather, it synthesizes policy guidance and notes that these skills are widely endorsed but not yet consistently enacted in practice.
finding.measure: Comparative analysis of competence frameworks and implementation documents

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that several frameworks view ICT as a means to make assessment more efficient, including faster result availability and reduced scoring and feedback time. This is framed as a policy/design claim rather than an outcome test, and no quantitative effects are reported.
finding.measure: Framework recommendations on ICT-supported assessment processes

paper_profiles.title: AI to the rescue: Exploring the potential of ChatGPT as a teacher ally for workload relief and burnout prevention
paper_profiles.venue: Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can function as a teacher assistant to reduce workload and help prevent burnout, especially by supporting lesson planning and content development, which the authors identify as major time-consuming contributors to teacher stress. The study is motivated by the growing interest in generative AI in education and the UAE’s push to integrate AI tools into schooling.

Using an explanatory research approach, the authors tested ChatGPT with task-specific prompts for lesson planning and material generation in English, science, and math for students ages 12-15 and 16-18. Generated lesson plans were evaluated against the 5Es instructional model, and the authors iteratively refined prompts when outputs were weak. The paper is based on analysis of ChatGPT-produced lesson plans and materials rather than classroom implementation with students or teachers.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT can generate usable lesson-planning drafts and supplementary materials, but quality depends heavily on prompt specificity, iterative feedback, and human review. The tool showed the ability to adapt to prior context and, in some cases, autonomously use the 5Es framework after earlier prompting. The authors argue that ChatGPT may reduce teacher workload and free time for other responsibilities, but it should be used cautiously as a support tool rather than a replacement for teacher expertise. They also emphasize training teachers to craft effective prompts and balancing AI output with professional judgment.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT can reduce teacher workload by speeding up lesson planning and content development, especially when teachers provide detailed, task-specific prompts and iterate based on the model’s outputs. In the authors’ testing across Grade 7 English, Grade 8 math, and Grade 10 science, ChatGPT produced lesson-plan drafts and supplementary materials that the authors judged could free teachers’ time for other responsibilities, although first attempts were often incomplete and needed revision.
finding.measure: Quality of ChatGPT-generated lesson plans and content materials evaluated against the 5Es instructional model; qualitative assessment of workload-relief potential
finding.study_size: n=3 prompt-tested lesson-plan cases (math, science, English)

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and higher education (teachers and learners across primary, secondary, tertiary, and professional development contexts)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities, challenges, and responsible use of large language models (LLMs), especially ChatGPT, in education. Rather than reporting a single empirical study, it synthesizes early research and proposes a conceptual framework for how LLMs may support learning and teaching while also introducing risks related to bias, copyright, privacy, overreliance, cost, and fairness.

The paper discusses use cases across student and teacher contexts, including content generation, personalized practice, feedback, assessment support, lesson planning, and professional development. It argues that LLMs can improve engagement, reduce some instructional and grading burden, and enable new forms of educational interaction, but only if implemented with strong human oversight, pedagogical guidance, fact-checking, and institutional policies.

The focus is broad rather than experimental: the authors review emerging applications and research examples from language learning, writing support, assessment, and conversational tutoring, then derive mitigation strategies for responsible adoption. Their main conclusion is that LLMs are promising educational tools, but current deployment should be cautious, ethical, and complemented by teacher expertise and curricular safeguards.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce teacher workload by supporting lesson planning, generating quizzes and practice materials, automating feedback, and semi-automating grading. However, this is presented as a conceptual claim and review of early examples rather than a direct empirical estimate of time savings for K-12 teachers.
finding.measure: Teacher workload / time savings from lesson planning, feedback generation, and grading support

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes that successful LLM adoption depends on institutional strategy, governance, privacy and security policies, copyright compliance, fairness measures, and teacher training. It also warns that inadequate implementation can worsen inequity, bias, and misuse, so the institutional impact is framed as conditional rather than uniformly positive.
finding.measure: Institutional governance, policy, privacy/security, fairness, and implementation readiness

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly argues that LLMs can both support and potentially undermine durable skills such as critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, and fact-checking. It notes that LLMs may help prompt deeper questioning and exploration, but overreliance may reduce learners’ independent reasoning unless teachers deliberately embed critical-thinking activities.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, fact-checking, collaboration, and related 21st-century skills

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT as an AI L2 Teaching Support: A Case Study of an EFL Teacher
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how an EFL teacher used ChatGPT in actual teaching practice over seven months and what kinds of prompt-writing and verification strategies shaped the usefulness of the tool. The study is framed around practical teacher support: lesson planning, in-class implementation, and assessment, with special attention to how the teacher refined prompts over time and checked the reliability of outputs.

The authors conducted an exploratory single instrumental case study of one private language-school teacher in Spain who used the free version of ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) from January to June 2023. Data came from the teacher’s ChatGPT history, lesson plans, and a semi-structured post-interview, then were analyzed thematically. The teacher used ChatGPT for curriculum suggestions, activity generation, vocabulary lists, real-time Q&A, text editing, automated grading, language tests, and creative/self-assessment tasks for learners of varying ages and proficiency levels.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT can meaningfully support language teachers, especially for lesson preparation and resource generation, and can also aid classroom interaction and assessment when used with strong prompt-crafting skills and critical evaluation. The paper emphasizes that the teacher’s effectiveness improved as she developed a five-step prompting strategy and cross-checked outputs with credible sources, colleagues, and students. However, the authors also note limitations for more advanced-level materials and stress that teacher expertise remains essential for spotting inaccuracies and biases.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT supported reading and writing instruction in this case study by generating reading-comprehension tasks, writing prompts, sentence/text edits, and composition feedback. The teacher reported that these outputs improved comprehension, retention, and the personalization of writing support, though some assessment outputs differed from official Cambridge scoring by up to 3 points in the example shown (n=1 essay).
finding.measure: Reading comprehension tasks, writing prompts, sentence/text editing, composition feedback, and Cambridge FCE writing-scales scoring
finding.study_size: n=1 teacher; student work examples reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that ChatGPT was used to support speaking practice and real-time language interaction through role-play, simulated conversations, and prompt-driven classroom Q&A. The teacher observed increased participation and enthusiasm when ChatGPT-mediated activities were used, but the evidence is qualitative and based on classroom examples rather than quantified fluency gains.
finding.measure: Speaking practice, simulated conversations, role-play, real-time Q&A, and teacher-reported participation/enthusiasm
finding.study_size: n=1 teacher; classroom examples with her students

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT appeared to increase student engagement, enthusiasm, and participation, especially in activities designed for children and adolescents. The teacher reported that the tool made lessons more enjoyable and productive and helped tailor materials to students’ interests and needs, but these findings are observational and not experimentally measured.
finding.measure: Teacher interview and observation of student participation/engagement during ChatGPT-supported lessons
finding.study_size: n=1 teacher; multiple class groups across seven months

finding.finding_summary: A central finding is that the teacher and students needed prompt crafting and critical thinking to use ChatGPT effectively. The paper describes a five-step prompt strategy that improved output quality over time and a set of verification practices (cross-checking sources, fact-checking, peer review, and bias checking), indicating strong emphasis on metacognition and critical evaluation rather than direct measured gains.
finding.measure: Prompt crafting practices, reliability-check strategies, and critical evaluation of AI outputs
finding.study_size: n=1 teacher; instructional cases with students

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT substantially reduced teacher workload by helping with lesson planning, activity generation, vocabulary lists, assessment rubrics, automated grading, and feedback drafting. The teacher explicitly stated that the tool saved time and allowed more personalized feedback, and the paper concludes that ChatGPT can alleviate workload and streamline planning and assessment processes.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported workload reduction, lesson-planning support, assessment support, and time saved

paper_profiles.title: What if the devil is my guardian angel: ChatGPT as a case study of using chatbots in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines early adopters’ concerns about using ChatGPT in education. Rather than testing a classroom intervention, it uses ChatGPT as a case study to explore how an advanced conversational AI is being discussed, perceived, and experienced in educational contexts.

The study uses a three-stage qualitative design: (1) social network and sentiment analysis of 2,330 tweets about ChatGPT in education, (2) content analysis of 19 publicly recruited interviewees who had experience using ChatGPT in education, and (3) hands-on user experiences from three educators who tested ChatGPT across ten educational scenarios. The authors focus on issues such as educational transformation, response quality, usefulness, personality/emotion, and ethics.

Across all three stages, the paper concludes that ChatGPT is seen as potentially transformative and useful for education, especially for generating content, aiding instructional design, and reducing teacher workload, but that its use raises substantial concerns about accuracy, fairness, cheating, privacy, manipulation, and lack of human-like emotional responsiveness. The authors argue against outright bans and instead call for new teaching philosophies, responsible-use guidelines, upskilling in prompt/questioning skills, and more research on human–machine collaboration in education.

finding.finding_summary: Participants widely perceived ChatGPT as useful for reducing instructional workload and helping teachers prepare teaching materials, outlines, and quizzes. In the interviews and user scenarios, educators reported that ChatGPT could generate content quickly and support instructional design, although output quality varied and sometimes required substantial checking and revision.
finding.measure: Interview perceptions; hands-on educator scenario testing of content generation and assessment creation

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT was viewed as helpful for writing-related tasks such as thesis support, essay generation, and providing model answers, suggesting potential support for literacy production. At the same time, the paper reports concerns that it can facilitate cheating and produce inaccurate or misleading text, so its literacy-related utility is offset by reliability and integrity problems.
finding.measure: Interview reports and user scenarios involving essay writing, short-answer generation, and written content quality

finding.finding_summary: The study repeatedly identifies implications for critical thinking, prompt/question-asking skill, and judgment about AI output. ChatGPT was seen as potentially useful for stimulating learning, but also as risking laziness, reduced critical thinking, and overreliance on generated answers; the authors explicitly argue that users need stronger critical-thinking and prompt skills to use it effectively.
finding.measure: Interview themes and qualitative scenario analysis of prompt sensitivity, answer quality, and ethical concerns

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on institutional concerns including cheating, privacy, fairness of access to content, data security, manipulation, and policy responses such as school bans. The authors conclude that simply banning ChatGPT is insufficient and recommend guidelines, policies, and responsible-AI approaches for educational use.
finding.measure: Tweet discourse, interview responses, and educator scenario testing of cheating, privacy, and manipulation concerns
finding.study_size: n=2330 tweets; n=19 interviewees; n=3 educators

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported that interacting with ChatGPT felt exciting, fun, and sometimes emotionally engaging, but also disappointing because it lacks genuine empathy or emotional value. The user scenarios showed that ChatGPT does not meaningfully express emotions or support reflective engagement in the way a human might, limiting its social-emotional realism.
finding.measure: Interview themes and educator scenario testing of emotional responses and reflection prompts

paper_profiles.title: Exploring High School EFL Teachers' Experiences with Magic School AI in Lesson Planning: Benefits and Insights
paper_profiles.venue: Voices of English Language Education Society
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This qualitative exploratory case study examines how Indonesian high school EFL teachers used MagicSchool AI for lesson planning after a workshop, with a focus on the benefits, limitations, and implementation features that shape its usefulness in practice. The authors are interested in whether generative AI can reduce lesson-planning burden while still supporting pedagogically sound, contextually relevant materials.

The study involved 38 high school English teachers in Central Java, Indonesia, who completed open-ended questionnaires and participated in focus group and stimulated recall interviews. Teachers reported that MagicSchool AI can speed up material and assessment preparation, help differentiate instruction, and provide new ideas that expand their teaching repertoire. However, they also stressed that the tool's outputs often require substantial refinement, that effective use depends on prompt-engineering skill, and that weak internet access can undermine productivity gains.

Overall, the paper concludes that AI is best understood as a collaborative support tool rather than a replacement for teacher expertise. The main practical takeaway is that productivity benefits are contingent on strong human oversight, adequate teacher training, and supportive infrastructure, especially when AI-generated materials must be adapted for diverse classroom needs.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that MagicSchool AI reduced time spent on lesson-planning tasks, especially material preparation and assessment generation. For example, respondents said the tool was faster than ChatGPT because of structured prompts and pre-designed fields, but they also noted that follow-up prompting and editing sometimes reduced the overall time savings (n=38).
finding.measure: Teacher-reported time efficiency in material preparation and assessment design; open-ended questionnaire, focus group, and stimulated recall interview data

finding.finding_summary: Teachers said MagicSchool AI helped generate lesson materials, differentiated texts, and varied classroom activities aligned with EFL teaching needs. The study did not measure student academic achievement directly; instead, it documented teacher-perceived usefulness for lesson planning and content generation in high school English classes (n=38).
finding.measure: Teacher-perceived usefulness for EFL lesson material creation and differentiation

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that AI use encouraged teachers to practice prompt engineering, critical evaluation, and adaptation of AI outputs, which the authors frame as important durable skills. At the same time, teachers emphasized that these skills were necessary because AI outputs were often not classroom-ready and required human judgment, so the net effect was mixed rather than purely beneficial (n=38).
finding.measure: Teacher reflections on prompt-engineering skill, critical thinking, and adaptive judgment

paper_profiles.title: Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education – where are the educators?
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.population: Undergraduate; Postgraduate; Higher education students and institutions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper systematically reviews research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education from 2007 to 2018. The authors ask how the field has developed over time, how AI in education is conceptualized, what ethical challenges and risks are discussed, and what kinds of AI applications are being used across the student life cycle. Their search across EBSCO Education Source, Web of Science, and Scopus yielded 146 peer-reviewed articles from an initial pool of 2,656 records.

The review organizes AI applications into four main areas: profiling and prediction, intelligent tutoring systems, assessment and evaluation, and adaptive systems and personalization. Most studies were quantitative, came primarily from computer science/STEM authors, and focused on undergraduate contexts. Across the literature, the authors found a strong emphasis on technical performance and prediction accuracy, but very little critical discussion of ethics, privacy, bias, or costs. They conclude that AI research in higher education is growing, but that educators are underrepresented and the field needs stronger pedagogical grounding and more attention to ethical and institutional implications.

Because this is a broad systematic review rather than an intervention study, the paper synthesizes findings qualitatively and descriptively across many technologies and outcomes. It suggests that AI can improve prediction, automate some assessment tasks, and support tutoring or personalization, but also notes limits such as calibration needs, short evaluation windows, and the absence of longitudinal evidence in most studies. The review is useful for mapping the field, but it does not itself estimate a single pooled effect on learning or productivity.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed higher-education studies, AI applications frequently improved operational efficiency by automating prediction, assessment, feedback, and some tutoring tasks. The review notes that machine learning approaches outperformed logistic regression in classification accuracy in all profiling/prediction studies, and that automated grading systems could reduce the cost and time of employing multiple human assessors; however, the paper does not report a single pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Prediction/classification accuracy, agreement with human raters, and reported reductions in cost/time or workload

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies multiple institutional uses of AI, including admission decisions, course scheduling, dropout prediction, student retention, course planning, and alignment of students with professional competencies. These applications were described as supporting timely intervention and institutional decision-making, but the evidence base was mostly technical and short-term, with no pooled estimate of institutional impact.
finding.measure: Institutional decision support, admission/course scheduling accuracy, dropout/retention prediction, and administrative utility

finding.finding_summary: Several included studies used AI to predict or support student engagement, motivation, and self-regulation. Examples in the review include machine-learning models for student engagement at the Open University UK and a model predicting academic motivation from online behavior; these studies generally reported useful predictive performance, but the review does not provide a single combined effect size.
finding.measure: Student engagement, academic motivation, and related behavioral indicators in learning environments

finding.finding_summary: The review includes AI-supported collaborative learning and automated feedback for collaborative writing, which touch on durable skills such as collaboration and metacognition. However, evidence is limited: most studies are small, short-term, and focused on system functionality rather than durable skill outcomes, and the review does not report a pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Collaborative learning interactions, collaborative writing processes, and related process indicators

paper_profiles.title: Adoption of Artificial Intelligence in Schools: Unveiling Factors Influencing Teachers’ Engagement
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference of Artificial Intelligence in Education 2023
paper_profiles.population: K-12 public school teachers (Grade 5 to Grade 12)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses why AI-based adaptive learning platforms, despite evidence of student learning benefits, are adopted slowly in real-world K-12 schools. The authors argue that prior work has focused too narrowly on technology features and individual teacher attitudes, while underexamining broader school-level factors such as workload, trust, support, governance, and ethics.

To study this, the authors developed and validated a survey instrument for measuring holistic factors influencing adoption of adaptive learning platforms in schools. They implemented the survey with 792 public school teachers from Grade 5 to Grade 12 in a country-level K-12 context, then linked survey responses to platform log data on teachers’ active days during the first half of the 2022-2023 academic year.

The results show seven factors associated with adoption: workload, ownership/trust, perceived support, knowledge/confidence, classroom orchestration, product quality, and ethics. Correlations with real-world engagement were positive and statistically significant for many items, especially helpful professional development, belief in platform success, satisfaction, helpful feedback, trust, content quality, and perceived efficiency. A predictive model using the survey data explained 24.4% of the variance in teachers’ engagement (R2 = 0.244), suggesting that school-level and teacher-level factors jointly help explain adoption behavior. The paper concludes that reducing workload, strengthening ownership and support, and addressing ethical concerns may improve teacher engagement with AI tools in schools.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined whether the adaptive learning platform affected teacher workload and other efficiency-related aspects of use. Teachers’ mean response on the workload factor was 3.09, suggesting the platform was seen as neither clearly adding to nor reducing workload overall; however, items such as helpful professional development (r=0.246), platform efficiency (r=0.181), and no extra lesson planning (r=0.113) were positively associated with teachers’ active days on the platform.
finding.measure: Teacher survey factors on workload/efficiency, plus real-world engagement measured by active days on the platform
finding.study_size: n=792 survey respondents; engagement correlations based on platform log data
finding.effect_size: r=0.246 (largest reported correlation for a workload-adjacent item); R2=0.244 for predictive model

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally studies school-level conditions for AI adoption, including governance, support structures, leadership belief, teacher ownership, and privacy/ethics. The survey and predictive model show that institutional and organizational factors are strongly tied to engagement, with items like helpful professional development, community support, leadership’s belief, and trust significantly correlating with active use, and the model explaining 24.4% of variance in engagement.
finding.measure: School-level adoption factors, leadership/support items, and teachers’ real-world engagement with the platform

finding.finding_summary: Although the paper is not primarily about student social-emotional outcomes, it substantively measures teacher engagement-related attitudes and beliefs such as trust, ownership, satisfaction, self-efficacy, and perceived support. These constructs were positively associated with engagement, including trust in the platform (r=0.179), self-efficacy (r=0.109), and belief in success (r=0.226).
finding.measure: Teacher trust, ownership, self-efficacy, satisfaction, and support-related survey items

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively touches collaborative and metacognitive dimensions of teacher use, especially through the teacher empowerment and interaction factor and classroom orchestration. Items such as part of community (r=0.154), opportunity to share (r=0.106), and can find balance (r=0.132) were positively associated with engagement, indicating that collaborative and self-management-related conditions matter for adoption.
finding.measure: Teacher survey items on community, sharing, orchestration, and balance in classroom use

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conceptual article examines how artificial intelligence is reshaping educational practice, with a focus on three competencies the author argues are essential for the AI era: AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. The paper is framed around concerns that students and teachers may use generative AI uncritically, misunderstand its limitations, or rely on it in ways that undermine learning, academic integrity, and fair assessment.

The paper draws on informal discussions and teaching experience at a Swiss University of Applied Sciences (Kalaidos University of Applied Sciences in Zurich) and supplements this case-based discussion with a narrative literature review. It describes the institution’s response to ChatGPT through internal AI guidelines that permit AI use with transparency and critical reflection requirements, and it proposes workshops, formal AI literacy courses, updated guidance, and dedicated staffing to support responsible adoption.

A second major contribution is a pedagogical discussion of how prompt engineering can be used to improve learning, including examples of zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought, self-consistency, automatic prompt engineering, generated knowledge prompting, and tree-of-thought prompting. The article concludes that AI can be beneficial in classrooms and academic work if students and staff are trained to use it as a sparring partner rather than a substitute for human thinking, but it does not present direct empirical outcome data on productivity or learning gains.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI literacy and prompt engineering can strengthen students’ critical thinking and metacognitive skills by requiring them to evaluate AI outputs, detect hallucinations, and refine prompts. No quantitative effect sizes are reported; the claim is supported by conceptual discussion and cited prior literature rather than direct measurement in this study.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, metacognitive reflection, and prompt-engineering proficiency (conceptual/pedagogical outcomes)

finding.finding_summary: The article repeatedly claims that AI tools can help teachers and students work more efficiently, for example by supporting curriculum creation, case-study generation, brainstorming, and other academic tasks. However, the paper provides no empirical productivity metrics, sample sizes, or effect sizes; the evidence is anecdotal and illustrative rather than experimental.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, curriculum preparation, and academic task efficiency (described via use cases)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that institutions benefit from adopting AI guidelines, workshops, formal documentation rules, and dedicated AI support positions to manage generative AI use. The central finding is institutional and normative rather than empirical: a 'culture of AI' is presented as a way to improve governance, transparency, and responsible adoption, but no outcome data are reported.
finding.measure: Institutional policy, governance, and implementation practices

paper_profiles.title: Learn to Machine Learn via Games in the Classroom
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates ArtBot, a serious game designed to teach children and adolescents basic concepts in artificial intelligence and machine learning, especially supervised learning and reinforcement learning. The authors are interested in whether a game-based approach can increase AI literacy, engagement, and reflection among K-12 learners, while also revealing design tradeoffs that affect usability and sustained participation.

ArtBot was developed as part of the EU LearnML project and deployed across web browser, Windows, and Android platforms. The paper analyzes anonymous gameplay telemetry from more than 2,000 users over roughly one year, plus survey responses from 130 students and 35 educators collected during workshops, teacher-training events, and school demonstrations in Greece, Malta, and Norway. The study examines how players used the game, what settings they changed, where they dropped off, and how they evaluated the experience.

The main findings are that ArtBot was generally well received and appeared to support understanding of AI/ML concepts: students and teachers reported that the game was easy to use, fun, and helpful for learning how AI works. At the same time, the telemetry shows important tradeoffs: the browser version was the most accessible, but it also complicated analysis; manual labeling in the supervised-learning mini-game was often skipped or auto-sorted; later reinforcement-learning levels suffered from retention drop-off; and some level designs and parameter choices did not provide enough novelty or agency. Overall, the paper concludes that game-based AI instruction is promising for classroom use, but the learning content and interaction design need refinement to better sustain engagement and make the instructional mechanisms more explicit.

finding.finding_summary: The game was designed to teach core AI/ML concepts, and both students and teachers reported that it helped them understand how artificial intelligence and machine learning work. In the student survey (n=130), the item "The ArtBot game helped me understand how Artificial Intelligence works" had a mean of 4.0/5 (SD=1.0), and teachers (n=35) gave a mean of 4.2/5 (SD=1.0) for the same idea; teachers also rated understanding machine learning through the game at 4.2/5 (SD=0.9).
finding.measure: Survey ratings of understanding how AI works and what machine learning is

finding.finding_summary: The authors report that players explored algorithm parameters, varied settings, and reflected on how changes affected outcomes, indicating some gains in critical thinking and problem solving around ML systems. In the SL mini-game, 32% of players changed algorithm settings and 25% repeated labeling, while in the RL mini-game players experimented with rewards, penalties, learning rate, and exploration settings across levels, suggesting engagement with underlying causal relationships rather than passive play.
finding.measure: Gameplay telemetry on parameter changes, retries, and exploratory behavior; survey feedback about thinking and problem solving

finding.finding_summary: Players and educators reported high enjoyment, ease of use, and willingness to use the game again, indicating positive engagement and motivation. Among students (n=130), mean ratings were high for ease of play (4.2/5, SD=0.9), fun (4.0/5, SD=1.1), and willingness to play again (3.9/5, SD=1.1), while only 11% endorsed the game as boring; teachers (n=35) similarly rated fun at 3.8/5 (SD=0.8) and willingness to play again at 4.0/5 (SD=1.0).
finding.measure: Likert-scale survey ratings of enjoyment, boredom, and willingness to replay; gameplay retention/engagement indicators
finding.study_size: n=130 students; n=35 teachers; n=2,222 unique users

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not measure teacher productivity directly, but it does present evidence relevant to implementation workload and usability tradeoffs. The browser-based version was the most convenient for classroom use because it required no installation, yet the authors note that browser analytics were harder to interpret; teachers also requested more guidance and tutorials, suggesting that the tool may reduce some access barriers while increasing the need for instructional support.
finding.measure: Survey feedback on ease of use and implementation; qualitative feedback on need for guidance and tutorials; platform adoption patterns
finding.study_size: n=35 teachers; telemetry from n=2,222 users

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported strong willingness to use ArtBot in classrooms and believed it would help children understand AI, suggesting promise for institutional adoption of AI literacy resources. In the teacher survey (n=35), 4.1/5 (SD=1.0) agreed they would like to use the game in the classroom, 4.2/5 (SD=0.8) in future teaching, and 4.3/5 (SD=0.7) believed it would help children understand AI.
finding.measure: Teacher survey responses about classroom adoption and perceived educational value

paper_profiles.title: Reflection on whether Chat GPT should be banned by academia from the perspective of education and teaching
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and higher education (discussion spans school and university contexts)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an opinion essay that asks whether ChatGPT should be banned in academia, with a focus on education and teaching. Rather than presenting new empirical data, it synthesizes arguments for and against ChatGPT use, emphasizing both academic-integrity risks and potential educational benefits.

The article argues that ChatGPT and similar AI tools can support learning, content generation, personalized tutoring, and teacher/research productivity, but that they also raise concerns about cheating, over-reliance, privacy, bias, and weakened critical thinking. The author discusses how schools, especially K-12 systems, have responded with bans or restrictions, while also highlighting voices that advocate integrating AI into instruction with appropriate regulation.

The paper’s core conclusion is that outright bans are not the best approach. Instead, it recommends regulated integration of AI tools into education, combined with updated curricula, assessment reform, and stronger governance to protect academic integrity and student development. The piece frames ChatGPT as part of a broader digital transformation in education that should be managed rather than prohibited.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT can reduce workload and improve efficiency for educators and researchers by automatically generating text, helping with literature reviews, answering questions, and supporting academic writing. However, this is a conceptual claim in an opinion essay rather than a directly measured empirical result, so no effect size or sample size is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher/researcher workload and task efficiency (conceptual discussion)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT creates institutional tradeoffs: it may support digital transformation and more effective educational systems, but it also creates academic-integrity risks that have led schools and universities to ban or restrict use. The paper cites policy responses in multiple jurisdictions, but it does not present original empirical evaluation of those policies.
finding.measure: Institutional policy responses, academic integrity concerns, and educational governance (conceptual discussion)

finding.finding_summary: The article argues that ChatGPT may help students with knowledge access and learning efficiency, but over-reliance could weaken independent thinking, critical thinking, exploration, verification, and summarization abilities. These claims are presented as expert/author interpretation rather than measured outcomes, so no quantitative effect estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, independent thinking, exploration, verification, and summarization (conceptual discussion)

paper_profiles.title: The Promises and Challenges of Artificial Intelligence for Teachers: a Systematic Review of Research
paper_profiles.population: K-12 teachers (in-service and limited pre-service teacher studies)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper systematically reviews empirical research on how teachers use artificial intelligence (AI) applications and machine learning methods in education. The authors ask what kinds of data have been collected from teachers, what roles teachers play in AI-based research, what advantages AI offers teachers, what challenges arise in classroom use, and which AI methods are most common.

The review covers 44 journal articles from the Web of Science database published between 2004 and 2020, focusing on in-service K-12 teachers and a small number of pre-service teacher studies. The paper does not evaluate a single intervention; instead, it synthesizes patterns across studies involving AI tools such as automated scoring, predictive models, tutoring/feedback systems, and classroom sensing/monitoring applications. Teachers were most often used as data sources for training AI or validating automated assessment systems, with much less evidence of teachers actively co-designing systems.

The review concludes that AI can support teachers in planning, implementation, and assessment, especially by identifying student needs, providing timely feedback, reducing workload, and automating parts of scoring and monitoring. However, the authors also identify important tradeoffs and limitations, including limited reliability, limited technical capacity, slow or insufficiently adaptive feedback, context dependence, and weak school infrastructure. Overall, the paper argues that the field is promising but still underdeveloped, particularly in multimodal data use and in meaningful teacher participation in AI development.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, AI was repeatedly reported to reduce teacher workload, support timely monitoring, speed up feedback, and automate parts of assessment. The review synthesized evidence from 44 studies and found that teachers benefited from AI in planning, implementation, and especially assessment, with workload reduction and task automation being central themes rather than a single pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, monitoring efficiency, immediacy of feedback, automation of scoring/assessment
finding.study_size: n=44 studies (systematic review); individual study sizes varied

finding.finding_summary: The reviewed literature suggested AI can improve teacher engagement and enjoyment by making teaching more interesting and by enabling more responsive classroom interaction, but it can also produce boredom when feedback is slow or systems are hard to use. These findings were qualitative and descriptive across the included studies rather than based on a pooled quantitative estimate.
finding.measure: Teacher enjoyment, engagement, perceived interest/boredom, interaction quality
finding.study_size: n=44 studies (systematic review); individual study sizes varied

finding.finding_summary: The review found that AI adoption in schools is constrained by broader institutional factors, including limited technical infrastructure, lack of teacher technological knowledge, and context-dependent systems that do not transfer well across settings. At the same time, the paper argues that more teacher involvement in AI development could improve institutional uptake and implementation quality.
finding.measure: School infrastructure readiness, teacher AI knowledge, transferability across settings, teacher participation in AI development
finding.study_size: n=44 studies (systematic review); individual study sizes varied

finding.finding_summary: Several AI applications were used to support teacher decision-making, including identifying student needs, selecting activities, and informing interventions, which the review framed as improving pedagogically meaningful judgment. The evidence base was descriptive and drawn from multiple studies rather than from a single comparative effect estimate.
finding.measure: Teacher decision-making, instructional judgment, selection of learning activities, intervention timing
finding.study_size: n=44 studies (systematic review); individual study sizes varied

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing education with AI: Exploring the transformative potential of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and broader education stakeholders (not empirically sampled; literature overview)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how artificial intelligence—especially chatbots and ChatGPT—may transform teaching and learning, while also highlighting ethical and practical risks. Rather than testing a specific intervention, the authors synthesize existing literature on AI in education to describe likely applications such as personalized learning, automated feedback, assessment support, and administrative assistance.

The article is a narrative review focused on the educational context broadly, with particular attention to how AI tools could benefit teachers and students. It emphasizes that AI can support individualized instruction, reduce repetitive grading and other routine tasks, and improve productivity, but it also raises concerns about privacy, bias, academic integrity, lack of human interaction, and the need for teacher training and institutional support.

Because the paper is a conceptual review rather than an empirical study, it does not present original participant data or quantitative results. Its main conclusion is that AI tools like ChatGPT have substantial promise for education, but responsible implementation requires careful attention to ethics, governance, and pedagogical alignment.

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that AI tools can reduce teacher workload by automating repetitive tasks such as grading, scoring, and feedback generation. It specifically states that chatbots and systems like AutoGradr and Repl.it can save teachers many hours that can be redirected toward lesson planning, student support, and professional development, but it provides no original empirical estimate.
finding.measure: teacher workload / time saved through automated grading, scoring, and feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes that successful AI adoption depends on teacher training, institutional support, and ethical governance, while warning that AI can worsen inequality, create bias, and raise privacy and academic integrity concerns. These are presented as institutional tradeoffs of implementation rather than measured effects, so the conclusion is mixed.
finding.measure: institutional readiness, ethical risks, and implementation considerations

finding.finding_summary: The review claims AI can increase student motivation, engagement, confidence, and reduce anxiety through personalized learning and interactive support. However, this is a synthesis of prior literature rather than a new empirical test, so no effect size or sample size is reported here.
finding.measure: motivation, engagement, confidence, and anxiety

paper_profiles.title: War of the chatbots: Bard, Bing Chat, ChatGPT, Ernie and beyond. The new AI gold rush and its impact on higher education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the rapid emergence of generative AI chatbots, especially ChatGPT, Bing Chat, Bard, and Baidu’s Ernie, and argues that they are already reshaping higher education. The authors frame the paper as a response to the post-ChatGPT “gold rush,” focusing on how these tools affect assessment, teaching, learning, academic integrity, and institutional responses.

Rather than evaluating a classroom intervention, the paper combines a narrative review of English- and Chinese-language literature with a comparative, author-conducted test of selected chatbots on tasks relevant to higher education. The paper situates the bots in their corporate and geopolitical context, discusses limitations such as hallucination, bias, outdated knowledge, and jailbreakability, and contrasts those weaknesses with some strengths, especially GPT-4 and Bing Chat’s internet access and sourcing.

The main conclusion is cautious and skeptical: current bots are powerful but unreliable, so they should not be treated as authoritative substitutes for human judgment or assessment. The authors argue that higher education institutions should adapt assessment and teaching practices, explicitly address academic integrity, and develop informed policies for responsible use rather than relying on bans alone.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI is forcing higher education institutions to rethink assessment policy, academic integrity rules, and teaching practice. It concludes that outright bans are impractical and that institutions should respond with updated assessment designs, clearer policies, and more thoughtful integration of chatbots.
finding.measure: Narrative review and comparative analysis of policy-relevant implications for higher education institutions

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses how chatbots may support or undermine critical thinking, writing, and evaluation skills in higher education. It highlights opportunities for students to use chatbots for brainstorming and drafting, but stresses that hallucinations, errors, and overconfidence make critical evaluation essential.
finding.measure: Comparative performance on higher-education tasks and literature-based discussion of critical evaluation demands

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses heavily on writing-related uses of chatbots, including essay generation, drafting, summarization, and writing support. It reports that GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 performed better than Bing Chat and Bard on the authors’ higher-education test set, but also emphasizes persistent weaknesses in accuracy, sourcing, and hallucination.
finding.measure: Higher-education text-generation and writing-related comparative tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper compares chatbot performance on a multidisciplinary set of academic tasks relevant to university assignments and examinations. It concludes that GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 outperformed Bing Chat and Bard, but none of the bots reached an ‘A’ or ‘B’ level overall, indicating substantial limitations across academic domains.
finding.measure: Multi-disciplinary higher-education test of chatbot responses

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that chatbots can save time by generating drafts, summarizing documents, and helping with writing and sourcing tasks, with examples such as Microsoft Copilot and Mollick’s classroom workflow. At the same time, it warns that these productivity gains are offset by the need for careful checking because outputs may be inaccurate or hallucinated.
finding.measure: Narrative discussion of time-saving and workload-reduction uses of chatbots in teaching, writing, and institutional work

paper_profiles.title: Adoption of Artificial Intelligence in Schools: Unveiling Factors Influencing Teachers’ Engagement
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference of Artificial Intelligence in Education 2023
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses why AI-based adaptive learning platforms, despite evidence of positive student-learning effects in controlled and real-world studies, are adopted slowly in schools. The authors argue that adoption depends on more than platform features or individual teacher attitudes, and they seek to identify a broader set of school-level and human factors that influence teachers’ real-world engagement with adaptive learning platforms.

The study develops and validates a survey instrument for measuring holistic adoption factors in K-12 schools. Drawing on literature review, expert discussion, and pilot feedback, the authors created a 30-item survey and administered it bilingually to 792 public-school teachers in a country-wide K-12 context. Exploratory factor analysis yielded seven factors: workload, teacher ownership, perceived support, knowledge/confidence, classroom orchestration, product quality, and ethics. The paper then correlates these factors with teachers’ active days on the platform and fits a predictive model using survey responses and platform log data.

Results show that teachers’ engagement is most strongly associated with professional development/support, belief in the platform’s success, satisfaction with the platform, trust/ownership, content quality, and ease of use. Workload matters in the sense that teachers want the platform to avoid adding work, while classroom orchestration and privacy concerns also matter. The prediction model explains about 24% of variance in engagement (R2 = 0.244), suggesting that school-level and human factors meaningfully predict uptake, though much variance remains unexplained. The paper concludes that scaling AI in schools requires minimizing workload, building trust and ownership, strengthening support, and addressing ethical concerns, not just improving technical features.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers’ engagement with the adaptive learning platform was strongly related to whether it was perceived as reducing or at least not increasing workload, and to whether it supported efficient use in practice. The workload factor itself had a mean of 3.09 (roughly neutral), while 'Platform is Efficient' correlated significantly with active platform days (r=0.180516, p<.001); the predictive model explained 24.4% of variance in engagement (R2=0.244, n=792 teachers, with platform-log engagement data).
finding.measure: Teacher-reported workload/efficiency perceptions and real-world engagement with the adaptive learning platform (active days from log data)

finding.finding_summary: Teachers’ real-world engagement was associated with supportive, motivational, and self-regulatory beliefs such as professional development usefulness, belief in the platform’s success, trust, and self-efficacy. Significant correlations with active days included 'Helpful CPD' (r=0.246061, p<.001), 'Believe in Success' (r=0.225836, p<.001), and 'Self-Efficacy' (r=0.108566, p<.05), indicating that engagement rose when teachers felt confident and motivated to use the platform.
finding.measure: Teacher self-efficacy, trust/ownership, professional development support, and active days on the platform

finding.finding_summary: The study substantively examines teacher collaboration, classroom orchestration, and control/coordination skills needed to integrate the AI platform into practice. 'Part of Community' and 'Opportunity to Share' were both significantly associated with engagement (r=0.154447, p<.01; r=0.106320, p<.05), and the orchestration factor reflected teachers’ ability to balance platform use with other classroom activities, which also correlated with engagement (e.g., 'Can Find Balance' r=0.131564, p<.01).
finding.measure: Teacher community participation, sharing opportunities, classroom orchestration/balancing, and active days on the platform

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally studies school-level conditions for AI adoption, including governance, leadership, support structures, and ethical/privacy expectations. Items such as 'Leadership’s Believe' (r=0.139671, p<.01), 'Access to Help' (r=0.134303, p<.01), and privacy concerns (ethical factor) were linked to engagement, and the authors conclude that scaled adoption depends on whole-school infrastructure and governance rather than only teacher-level attitudes.
finding.measure: School-level governance/support perceptions, privacy/ethics concerns, and active days on the platform

paper_profiles.title: Generating and Evaluating Tests for K-12 Students with Language Model Simulations: A Case Study on Sentence Reading Efficiency
paper_profiles.population: K-12 (grades 1-8+; with some adult participants in training/evaluation)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the high cost and time burden of developing and calibrating educational assessment items, especially when schools need multiple parallel test forms over the school year. The authors focus on silent Sentence Reading Efficiency (SRE), a K-12 reading fluency measure that depends on both answer accuracy and response time, and ask whether large language models can help generate, calibrate, and assemble high-quality test items that behave like human-authored items.

The approach combines GPT-4 item generation with a fine-tuned LLaMA-based item-response simulator trained on prior student response data. The simulator predicts how past students would answer unseen items and how long they would take, allowing the authors to estimate item difficulty and ambiguity without collecting responses for every candidate item. They also propose an optimal-transport-inspired method for matching generated items to a human-developed reference test form to create parallel versions with similar psychometric properties.

The study uses several evaluation settings: computational validation on held-out item-response data, a crowdworker experiment (n=50, with 44 analyzed) comparing human-generated, parallel AI-generated, and ambiguous AI-generated forms, and a school deployment with 234 California students in grades 2-8 (231 analyzed after exclusions). Across these evaluations, the filtered AI test form closely matched the human test form in total scores and difficulty, with correlations of r=0.92 in crowdworkers and r=0.93 in the school study. The item-response simulator also predicted item accuracy and response time better than a readability baseline, suggesting that LLMs can meaningfully reduce assessment-development workload while still requiring human review for safety and appropriateness.

finding.finding_summary: The AI-generated, filtered parallel test form closely matched the human-authored reading efficiency test. In the school study with n=234 students in grades 2-8 (231 analyzed after exclusions), total scores on the AI form were highly correlated with the Lab form (r=0.93), and the forms showed similar difficulty and item-level behavior.
finding.measure: Silent Sentence Reading Efficiency (SRE) total scores; item difficulty and median response time

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can substantially reduce the cost and time required to generate and calibrate K-12 assessment items by automating item generation, item-response simulation, ambiguity screening, and parallel-form construction. While no direct teacher workload metric is measured, the central contribution is a workflow intended to replace or reduce labor-intensive expert item writing and large-scale calibration.
finding.measure: Assessment item generation/calibration workflow efficiency; parallel test construction process

finding.finding_summary: The paper demonstrates a deployable assessment pipeline for K-12 classrooms and schools, with a real-world school evaluation showing that AI-generated items can produce comparable test forms when experts remain in the loop. The work suggests institutional usefulness for creating multiple parallel forms for ongoing school monitoring, though it also emphasizes human review, safety, and deployment caution.
finding.measure: Real-world K-12 deployment feasibility; parallel test form comparability
finding.study_size: n=234 school participants; >30 school partners in data collection

paper_profiles.title: New Curriculum, New Chance – Retrieval Augmented Generation for Lesson Planning in Ugandan Secondary Schools. Prototype Quality Evaluation.
paper_profiles.venue: Ndejje University Second Annual Research Dissemination Symposium 2024
paper_profiles.population: Secondary school teachers in Uganda (Ugandan secondary schools)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This working paper addresses the challenge of poor and obsolete lesson planning in Ugandan secondary schools, especially under the country’s shift to a new competency-based curriculum. The authors argue that teachers need support producing lesson plans that are both technically sound and aligned with government-approved curricular materials.

To address this problem, the study develops and evaluates a prototype lesson-plan generator using Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG). The system retrieves information from government-accredited textbooks and uses a Cohere LLM via LangChain to generate lesson plans in the official Ugandan format. The prototype was trained on three Secondary 1 textbooks (ICT, Mathematics, and History) and generated 24 lesson plans, which were then rated by three independent experienced raters using an adapted Lesson Plan Analysis Protocol (LPAP).

The main finding is that the generated lesson plans achieved average LPAP scores of about 75–80%, which the authors interpret as “very good” technical quality. The paper compares these scores favorably to a prior Rwandan study of human-written lesson plans that did not exceed 50%, suggesting the RAG system can support higher-quality lesson planning than manual approaches reported in similar regional studies.

At the same time, the paper emphasizes important tradeoffs and limitations.
