The system can hallucinate when the underlying textbook lacks sufficient content, as illustrated by one lesson plan that addressed the wrong topic. The study evaluates technical quality rather than classroom outcomes or teacher productivity directly, and it relies on a small prototype sample and university raters rather than everyday classroom users. Overall, the paper concludes that RAG has promise for improving lesson-planning quality and potentially reducing teacher workload, while cautioning that human oversight remains necessary.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that a RAG-based lesson-plan generator can produce technically strong lesson plans from government-approved textbooks, implying improved teacher productivity in lesson planning. Across 24 generated lesson plans (n=24), the average LPAP score was about 75–80%, and none scored below 65%, which the authors interpret as efficient support for creating usable plans more quickly. However, the study does not directly measure time saved, workload reduction, or comparative productivity versus teachers.
finding.measure: Lesson plan technical quality using the Lesson Plan Analysis Protocol (LPAP) as a proxy for support to lesson-planning productivity

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests the prototype could help implement Uganda’s new competency-based curriculum more efficiently by generating lesson plans aligned with government-approved textbooks and official format requirements. The authors conclude that the tool can support curriculum implementation and may be useful to government and publishers, but these claims are inferential rather than directly measured in the study.
finding.measure: Alignment of generated lesson plans with the Ugandan curriculum and official lesson-plan format

paper_profiles.title: Automatic Short Answer Grading via Multiway Attention Networks
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of automatic short answer grading (ASAG), which aims to score student free-text responses against reference answers. The authors argue that ASAG can reduce the cost and monotony of manual grading for teaching professionals while providing consistent scoring across many open-ended K-12 questions and domains.

The proposed approach is a deep learning framework built around transformer encoders and a multiway attention mechanism. The model separately encodes student and reference answers, uses self-attention and several cross-attention variants to capture semantic overlap and differences, and then aggregates these representations to predict whether an answer is correct. The paper evaluates the model on a large real-world K-12 dataset of 120,000 student-answer pairs labeled as correct/incorrect, with a 30,000-sample test set.

Results show the proposed model outperforms several baselines, including logistic regression, gradient boosted decision trees, CNNs, Bi-Transformer, MaLSTM, and a prior multiway attention model. The best reported performance is accuracy = 0.8899 and AUC = 0.9444, compared with the strongest baseline accuracy = 0.8825 and AUC = 0.9375. The paper concludes that multiway attention improves automatic scoring performance and could support scalable short-answer grading in K-12 contexts, but it does not directly measure teacher productivity, time saved, or grading quality tradeoffs in practice.

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents automatic short answer grading as a cost-effective approach that can reduce monotonous and tedious grading workloads for teaching professionals. Empirically, the proposed model improves classification performance on a K-12 short-answer grading task, reaching accuracy = 0.8899 and AUC = 0.9444 on a dataset of 120,000 answer pairs, which suggests potential efficiency gains for grading workflows. However, the study does not directly measure teacher time saved or actual workload reduction.
finding.measure: Binary correct/incorrect short answer grading performance; accuracy and AUC

paper_profiles.title: MAGIC: Multi-Agent Argumentation and Grammar Integrated Critiquer
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of automated essay scoring (AES) and automated essay feedback (AEF), especially the tradeoff between scoring accuracy and useful feedback. The authors argue that existing systems are mostly optimized for numerical score prediction and are often evaluated on pre-secondary or lower-grade writing, leaving a gap for college-level argumentative writing with detailed trait-level feedback.

To address this, the paper introduces MAGIC, a zero-shot multi-agent framework in which separate small LLM agents evaluate prompt adherence, persuasiveness, organization, vocabulary, and grammar. An orchestrator agent then combines the trait-level judgments into a holistic score and integrated feedback. The authors create a GRE essay dataset with holistic scores and additional trait-level annotations, and evaluate MAGIC against single-prompt baselines using open-weight LLMs (Llama 3.1 8B, Gemma 3 12B, Gemma 3 27B).

The main findings are that MAGIC improves score agreement with human raters and also produces feedback judged to be strong in quality, naturalness, specificity, and relevance. On the GRE dataset, MAGIC increased QWK for all tested models (e.g., Gemma 3 12B from 0.607 to 0.762; Gemma 3 27B from 0.613 to 0.766) and reduced RMSE. Feedback evaluations showed MAGIC was preferred over human-written feedback more often than the baseline, though the authors note possible judge bias and modest human–judge agreement. Overall, the paper suggests multi-agent LLM systems may improve the productivity and scalability of essay scoring and feedback generation, with the main tradeoff being that automated feedback can be somewhat less lexically rich than human feedback.

finding.finding_summary: MAGIC is presented as a zero-shot framework intended to reduce the workload of human raters by automating holistic scoring and detailed essay feedback. On the GRE dataset (n=48 essays), MAGIC improved agreement with human scores across all tested models and produced feedback judged competitive with human-written feedback, suggesting a productivity benefit for essay assessment workflows.
finding.measure: Automated essay scoring agreement with humans (QWK, RMSE) and feedback quality comparisons versus human feedback
finding.effect_size: QWK improved by 0.126-0.155 depending on model; RMSE reduced by 0.144-0.269

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies college-level argumentative writing performance in automated essay scoring and feedback generation. Across the 48 GRE essays, MAGIC improved holistic scoring agreement with human raters and yielded strong per-trait agreement on writing dimensions such as prompt adherence, organization, vocabulary, and grammar, indicating better automated support for writing assessment.
finding.measure: Holistic essay scores, per-trait writing scores, and generated writing feedback quality
finding.effect_size: Holistic QWK improved from 0.605-0.613 to 0.731-0.766 across models; per-trait agreement was moderate to substantial

paper_profiles.title: Human or AI? Comparing Design Thinking Assessments by Teaching Assistants and Bots
paper_profiles.population: Secondary school teachers and pre-university teachers (MOE, Singapore); study task involved secondary-school design thinking poster samples
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This exploratory study examines whether an AI grading system can support assessment of design thinking artifacts more efficiently than teaching assistants (TAs) and how teachers perceive those scores. The paper is motivated by a common problem in large design-thinking classes: rubric-based grading of multimodal student posters is labor-intensive, time-consuming, and inconsistent across assessors.

The authors built a custom GPT-4o-based journey map grader using a validated rubric with three dimensions: empathy and user understanding, identification of pain points and opportunities, and visual communication. The study was conducted during a June 2025 teacher workshop in Singapore with 33 in-service teachers from secondary schools and pre-university institutions. Teachers first scored ten anonymized student samples manually, then reviewed a separate set of ten samples with unlabeled AI, TA, and hybrid scores and indicated which they agreed with most; open-ended responses and a focus-group discussion provided qualitative data.

Quantitatively, AI and TA scores showed low agreement with instructor benchmark scores on empathy and pain points, with slightly better agreement on visual communication. Teachers preferred TA-assigned scores in six of ten comparison samples, while hybrid averages were never the top choice. Qualitatively, teachers valued AI’s speed, consistency, and potential for formative feedback and student self-reflection, but worried that it missed contextual nuance, creativity, and the subjective aspects of visual reasoning. The paper concludes that AI graders may be promising as supportive formative tools, but they are not yet ready to replace human judgment in summative assessment of creative, multimodal work; hybrid models with human oversight are recommended.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers and the authors report that the AI grader could make assessment faster and more consistent than manual scoring, which was described as slow, tedious, labor-intensive, and time-consuming. The study did not measure time savings experimentally, but qualitative feedback emphasized AI’s potential to reduce grading burden and provide immediate formative feedback for large cohorts.
finding.measure: Perceived grading speed, consistency, and workload burden from teacher survey responses and focus-group discussion
finding.study_size: n=33 teachers; 10 student samples per task

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests AI feedback may support self-reflection and self-directed learning, but also highlights limitations in capturing the nuanced reasoning required for creative and contextual judgment. Teachers saw value in AI for iterative formative feedback, yet the low agreement with human scores on empathy and pain points indicates that AI did not reliably assess deeper interpretive aspects of the task.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of AI-supported formative feedback and alignment on rubric dimensions requiring interpretation
finding.study_size: n=33 teachers; 10 sample comparisons per scoring condition

finding.finding_summary: On design-thinking journey map assessment, AI scores aligned poorly with instructor benchmark scores for empathy and pain points, but somewhat better for visual communication. Instructor vs AI agreement was 20% for empathy (kappa = -0.026), 20% for pain points (kappa = -0.039), and 50% for visual communication (kappa = 0.242), indicating that AI performance varied by rubric dimension.
finding.measure: Agreement between AI-assigned, TA-assigned, and instructor-assigned scores on design-thinking journey map rubrics

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI-based grading could help scale assessment in large, multi-section educational settings and reduce reliance on teaching assistants, but only if used within hybrid models with human oversight. Teachers were cautiously optimistic about adoption, yet concerns about trust, nuance, and high-stakes use led the authors to recommend institutional safeguards and professional development.
finding.measure: Teacher acceptance and perceived readiness for AI-assisted assessment in a workshop setting

paper_profiles.title: Co-Designing Interdisciplinary Design Projects with AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a GPT-based planning assistant, IDPplanner, can help teachers design higher-quality interdisciplinary project plans under time constraints. The authors motivate the study by noting that interdisciplinary, design-based planning is cognitively demanding and time-consuming, especially when teachers must align activities to curriculum standards, design-thinking processes, and 21st-century competencies.

The intervention is a custom GPT chatbot that scaffolds a ten-step planning workflow and is grounded in Design Innovation, Singapore MOE syllabuses, and 21st-century competencies. In a within-subject, counterbalanced workshop, 33 in-service Singapore teachers created two versions of the same interdisciplinary project plan: one manually and one with AI assistance. Plans were evaluated with a six-dimension rubric and complemented by open-ended teacher reflections.

The main findings are that AI-assisted plans scored significantly higher for Curriculum Alignment, Design Thinking Application, and Coherence & Flow, with a marginal advantage for Assessment Strategies. Qualitative feedback suggests the tool improved structure, sequencing, and idea generation, but teachers still needed to adapt outputs to local syllabus, class profile, and student needs. Overall, the paper argues that AI can serve as a pedagogical planning partner that reduces planning complexity and supports curriculum alignment, while human teacher judgment remains essential for contextualization and deeper interdisciplinary integration.

finding.finding_summary: In a within-subject workshop with 33 in-service teachers, the AI-assisted planning condition improved the efficiency and structure of interdisciplinary project planning. Teachers reported that IDPplanner helped generate ideas, organize sequencing, and reduce planning complexity, and the authors conclude that it can reduce workload during the planning phase. Quantitatively, AI-assisted plans outperformed manual plans on several rubric dimensions relevant to planning productivity, including Curriculum Alignment (M=4.08 vs. 3.67, d=0.54), Design Thinking Application (M=3.85 vs. 3.00, d=0.81), and Coherence & Flow (M=4.00 vs. 3.42, d=0.64).
finding.measure: Teacher-rated project plan rubric scores and qualitative reflections on planning process/workload
finding.study_size: n=33 teachers; 19 project plans formally scored (13 AI-assisted, 6 manual); 38 evaluations
finding.effect_size: d=0.54 to d=0.81 on key planning-quality dimensions
finding.std_deviation: Manual vs AI SDs reported as 0.65 vs 0.48 (Curriculum Alignment), 1.04 vs 1.07 (Design Thinking Application), 0.79 vs 0.57 (Coherence & Flow)

finding.finding_summary: The study directly assessed planning-related durable skills embedded in interdisciplinary design work, especially design thinking and structured collaboration around project design. AI-assisted plans scored significantly higher on Design Thinking Application (M=3.85 vs. 3.00, p=.005, d=0.81), and teachers noted that the chatbot scaffolded the Discover–Define–Develop–Deliver process with guiding questions and logical sequencing. The paper also suggests the tool supported teachers’ collaborative planning and problem-structuring capabilities, although deeper conceptual integration still depended on human expertise.
finding.measure: Rubric score for Design Thinking Application; qualitative reflections on planning structure, sequencing, and collaboration
finding.study_size: n=33 teachers; 19 project plans formally scored

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that IDPplanner may help bridge institutional capacity gaps in schools by supporting teachers who lack deep interdisciplinary planning expertise and by aligning plans to national syllabuses and school frameworks. Teachers indicated that AI-generated plans could still require school-level adjustment, but the tool was viewed as a useful planning partner for institutional curriculum design and teacher development. Evidence is primarily indirect, drawn from teacher ratings and reflections rather than school-level outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher reflections on curriculum alignment, contextual fit, and institutional adaptation needs

paper_profiles.title: A GPT-based Code Review System for Programming Language Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of providing immediate, personalized programming feedback in growing K-12 classes while avoiding the cheating risks associated with direct AI assistance. The author argues that traditional online judge feedback, peer review, and instructor review are too slow, too generic, or too labor-intensive for introductory programming education, especially for younger learners.

To address this, the paper proposes and evaluates a GPT-4-based code review system for Python programming that integrates code correctness checking and learner-friendly code review comments. The system was designed to give feedback only on learner-submitted code, annotate specific lines needing fixes, avoid directly revealing solutions, and present comments in a supportive tone and markdown format. The system was built and iteratively improved using logs from an existing online judge system, prompt engineering, and UI refinements.

The evaluation involved software education experts rather than students: three experts participated in a usability test of the initial system, and six experts/developers participated in a later survey of the improved system. The improved version was tested on 108 code samples for correctness-check behavior and 92 error-code cases for response-time analysis, and API token costs were estimated using OpenAI pricing. The paper concludes that the improved system became stricter at identifying several error types, reduced response time and API costs, and preserved generally positive perceived quality of code review feedback, suggesting usefulness as a programming learning support tool for primary and secondary school students.

finding.finding_summary: The improved GPT-4-based code review system reduced response time for code review comments by at least 12% and up to 58% compared with the initial system. The paper also reports up to an 8.53% reduction in estimated OpenAI API call cost per request, and expert feedback indicated the system shortened grading/review time while maintaining useful feedback.
finding.measure: Response time for code review comment requests; estimated API call cost per call
finding.study_size: n=92 error codes for response time; 27 questions for token/cost estimates
finding.effect_size: Response time improvement: 12%-58%; cost reduction: up to 8.53%

finding.finding_summary: The paper positions the GPT-based tool as suitable for teaching programming to primary and secondary school students and argues it can support instructional workflows by providing immediate feedback at scale. However, the institutional evidence is limited to expert usability judgments and system-performance tests rather than implementation at the school or policy level.
finding.measure: Expert usability feedback and perceived suitability for K-12 programming instruction
finding.study_size: n=3 usability experts; n=6 survey participants

paper_profiles.title: Automatic code generation from sketches of mobile applications in end-user development using Deep Learning
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and broader end-user development context
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem that turning hand-drawn user-interface sketches into App Inventor wireframe code is time-consuming and error-prone, especially for end-user developers and for computing education contexts. The authors propose Sketch2aia, a web-based tool that uses deep learning to detect common UI components and their positions in sketches and then automatically generate App Inventor .aia code for the corresponding wireframes.

The technical approach is built around a custom dataset of 279 sketches derived from 165 App Inventor app screenshots, manually labeled and used to train a YOLOv3 object-detection model with transfer learning. The system detects nine common UI components plus the screen itself, groups them into App Inventor-compatible layouts, and outputs importable code. The paper reports an F1 score of 0.88 and mean Average Precision of 87.72% on the test set, with lower performance for rare classes such as ListPicker.

The authors also conducted a preliminary user study with 29 participants, including 6 young people and 1 teacher from a K-12 educational context, alongside students, researchers, and professors. Participants generally judged the generated wireframes to correspond well with sketches, and they rated the tool as highly usable and useful (average SUS 92.16; 100% reported it useful). The main limitation noted was imperfect layout reconstruction, while the main benefit was reduced time and effort in moving from sketch to App Inventor wireframes.

finding.finding_summary: Sketch2aia reduced the effort and time needed to turn sketches into App Inventor wireframe code. The paper reports that generating wireframes for a three-screen application took about 58 seconds, and participants rated the tool as useful for saving time in the app development process; the study also found an average SUS score of 92.16, indicating excellent usability.
finding.measure: Time to generate wireframe code; perceived usefulness; System Usability Scale (SUS)

paper_profiles.title: Tareas matemáticas abiertas como respuesta didáctica a la inteligencia artificial generativa en contextos post-IA
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how mathematics teaching can preserve meaningful student mathematical activity in so-called post-AI contexts, where generative AI tools can solve many conventional school tasks automatically. The central concern is not whether AI can produce answers, but how task design and classroom regulation can prevent students from bypassing interpretation, decision-making, and validation.

The author analyzes a secondary-school classroom experience in which open mathematical tasks were implemented as a didactic response to generative AI. The study uses a qualitative, descriptive–interpretive approach and examines student work, classroom interactions, and teacher observations through four lenses: open-task design, student mathematical agency, human–AI complementarity, and modeling/validation practices. A didactic regulation device called COMPAS structures the activity through phases such as understanding the situation, organizing assumptions and data, modeling, exploring results, validating, and socializing conclusions.

The main conclusion is that, when tasks are intentionally open and the use of AI is explicitly regulated, students retain epistemic control over mathematical activity even in the presence of generative AI. AI functions as a partial support for exploration or checking, while students remain responsible for interpreting the situation, choosing assumptions, and validating solutions. The paper argues that preserving the formative value of mathematics in post-AI settings depends more on task design and pedagogical regulation than on simply restricting or allowing AI use.

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that open mathematical tasks, supported by explicit didactic regulation, sustain students’ mathematical activity in secondary school. Students remain engaged in interpretation, modeling, and validation rather than delegating the work to generative AI, and the paper concludes that they retain epistemic control over the mathematical process. No quantitative effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Student mathematical work on open tasks; modeling and validation practices; epistemic control over mathematical activity

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that the task design fosters students’ agency, decision-making, argumentation, and critical validation of results. In classroom discussion, students compare models, question assumptions, and evaluate the plausibility of AI-generated and student-generated solutions, indicating strengthened metacognitive and critical thinking practices. No quantitative effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Student agency, argumentation, critical evaluation of assumptions, and validation practices during task resolution

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses AI primarily as a tool that can support exploration or checking, but it does not evaluate teacher productivity, workload, or time savings. Because the study is qualitative and centered on student mathematical activity rather than teacher efficiency, there is no empirical evidence that AI tools improved operational efficiency in this classroom context.
finding.measure: Teacher productivity / workload / task efficiency

paper_profiles.title: AI Conversational Tutors in Foreign Language Learning: A Mixed-Methods Evaluation Study
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings 14th Panhellenic Conference iCT in Education
paper_profiles.population: Undergraduate/Adult foreign language learners (Spanish B1/B2 profile used in simulated interactions); not K-12
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the design, user experience, and transcript-based quality of AI conversational tutors for foreign language learning. The author asks what design patterns are common in current AI language tutors, how specialized language-tutor apps compare with general-purpose voice AI models, and how tutor quality can be evaluated systematically and possibly automated.

The study uses a mixed-methods approach centered on simulated learner interactions with four specialized language-learning apps (Talkio, TalkPal, Univerbal, Langua) and two general-purpose voice AI systems (ChatGPT and Gemini). The author created a Spanish learner profile (B1/B2), conducted short conversational practice sessions, collected chat transcripts, and then applied a ten-dimensional evaluation framework. The framework was scored by five LLM-based “artificial experts,” with inter-rater reliability assessed via Cronbach’s alpha.

The paper concludes that AI language tutors share useful features such as free chat, contextual hints, corrections, and feedback reports, but differ substantially in responsiveness, handling of breakdowns, feedback quality, and privacy handling. Specialized tutors often provide richer pedagogical scaffolding than general-purpose models, while ChatGPT can nevertheless produce high-quality conversational exchanges. The author argues that key design priorities for future tutors include clear representation of dialogue, contextual correction without interrupting flow, and better privacy safeguards for voice data.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies speaking/conversation practice in AI language tutors and finds that these systems can support natural, supportive language interaction with contextual correction. Specialized tools and general-purpose voice models both enabled Spanish conversational practice (B1/B2 profile), with ChatGPT and the best specialized tools producing fluid exchanges; however, some systems had issues with interruptions, missing corrections, or limited handling of unfinished utterances.
finding.measure: User experience of conversational speaking practice; transcript-based dialogue quality; voice interaction fluency
finding.study_size: n=6 tutors/tools (4 specialized language apps + ChatGPT + Gemini); one simulated learner profile per tool

finding.finding_summary: The study’s evaluation framework includes conversational features linked to critical thinking and reasoning, and the discussion notes that some tutors guided learners into further reasoning rather than only correcting errors. T4 especially emphasized critical thinking over the learner’s argument, and the paper identifies this as a desirable design pattern, but no learner outcome was experimentally measured.
finding.measure: Transcript-based evaluation of tutor initiative and reasoning-oriented prompts

finding.finding_summary: Although the paper is not about teacher productivity, it does argue that AI tutors provide scalable, cost-effective alternatives for language practice and describes automated transcript-based quality evaluation as a way to streamline tutor assessment. The main evidence is comparative system analysis and the use of LLMs as evaluators, rather than a direct measurement of teacher workload or time savings.
finding.measure: Scalability/cost-effectiveness claims; automated transcript-based evaluation workflow

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks Middle School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether teachers should remain “in the loop” when using generative AI to personalize middle school mathematics tasks, and what the productivity and student-experience tradeoffs are when teachers use ChatGPT to modify curriculum problems. The authors focus on the practical question of whether AI can save teachers time while also producing personalized tasks that students find interesting and relevant.

Seven 7th-grade mathematics teachers in six U.S. schools participated in training on personalization and then used GPT-4o / ChatGPT to adapt 143 Illustrative Mathematics problems across two units. The researchers logged teacher prompts and time spent, recorded sessions, and collected student ratings and open-ended feedback from 521 students (with subsets responding to different items). The paper analyzes teacher prompting practices, student reactions, and changes over time from Unit 4 to Unit 6.

The main finding is that teacher-in-the-loop personalization did not become especially time efficient: teachers spent about 4 minutes per personalized problem on average, and time actually increased from Unit 4 to Unit 6. Teachers used prompts to control grain size, realism, and ownership, often revising LLM outputs to improve contextual realism and age appropriateness. Students tended to prefer finer-grained, specific popular-culture references rather than broad generic categories, but they were also sensitive to whether the reference matched their own interests. A moderate amount of prompting (about 3-5 prompts per problem) was associated with better student ratings, suggesting that some iteration helps, but too much or too little prompting is less effective. Overall, the study concludes that teacher-in-the-loop GenAI personalization offers professional learning benefits but does not yet appear to be a clear time-saving solution.

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively studies personalized middle school mathematics task creation, but it does not measure student math achievement or learning gains. Instead, it reports that teacher-generated personalized math problems were rated higher when teachers used 3-5 prompts (B=0.240, SE=0.085, p=0.0073), suggesting better task quality in that prompting range, while other analyses show no direct performance outcome.
finding.measure: Mathematics personalized problem ratings; teacher prompt patterns during math task generation

finding.finding_summary: Students’ reactions indicate that personalization influenced interest and perceived relevance. Average student ratings were modest overall, and ratings were significantly higher in Unit 6 than Unit 4 (interestingness: 2.27 to 2.56; closeness: 2.28 to 2.66; B=0.33, SE=0.095, p=0.0012), showing improved engagement-related perceptions over time.
finding.measure: Student ratings of problem interestingness and closeness to interests; open-ended feedback about interest
finding.study_size: n=521 students; ratings collected for 52-53 problems

finding.finding_summary: The study examines teacher prompting, iteration, and revision practices with ChatGPT, which reflect problem-solving and metacognitive task refinement. Teachers improved in crafting more personalized problems over time, but this came with more prompts and more time rather than greater efficiency, indicating growth in iterative prompting skill but not in streamlined execution.
finding.measure: Teacher prompting practices; number of prompts per problem; time to create personalized problems

finding.finding_summary: The central finding for efficiency is that teacher-in-the-loop GenAI personalization was time-consuming and did not become clearly more efficient with experience. Teachers averaged 3.2 prompts and 246 seconds per problem overall, and Unit 6 took longer than Unit 4 (4.6 vs. 3.2 prompts/problem; 286 vs. 204 seconds/problem), indicating increased workload rather than time savings.
finding.measure: Time spent creating personalized problems; number of prompts per problem

paper_profiles.title: Need of AI in Modern Education: in the Eyes of Explainable AI (xAI)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book chapter argues that AI is increasingly important in modern education, but its complexity and opacity create problems for trust, transparency, and fairness. Rather than studying a classroom intervention or a teacher-facing tool directly, the chapter focuses on explainable AI (xAI) methods as a way to inspect model behavior, understand feature importance, and diagnose bias in educationally relevant decisions.

The empirical case study uses the UCI Adult Census Income dataset and trains an XGBoost classifier to predict whether an individual earns more than $50K, using that income as a proxy for parental economic advantage in education. The authors compare multiple explanation methods, including permutation importance, SHAP, LIME, decision-tree surrogates, submodular picking, and FairML, to see whether different xAI tools reveal similar feature attributions and whether they expose bias. They find that several methods emphasize features such as marital status, education level, capital gain, age, sex, race, and nationality, but FairML specifically surfaces dependence on sensitive attributes and suggests strong bias in the model.

The chapter concludes that feature-importance methods alone may miss unfairness, that LIME can be unstable, and that fairness audits are necessary alongside explainability. Its broader educational implication is that AI systems used in educational decision-making should be transparent, accountable, and carefully checked for bias, especially when socio-economic status is involved. However, it does not evaluate teacher productivity or K-12 instructional outcomes directly; its contribution is primarily conceptual and methodological, with a small observational model-analysis example.

paper_profiles.title: Towards The Ultimate Brain: Exploring Scientific Discovery with ChatGPT AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can be used as a co-author and creative assistant in scientific discovery, specifically by generating the text, tables, figures, and even argumentative structure of a paper in theoretical physics. The author frames the work as a meta-experiment: an AI-generated paper about using AI to create and benchmark hypothetical physical theories.

The approach is a gamified, prompt-driven interaction in which the human author instructs ChatGPT to define a fictional generalized probabilistic theory, score it against criteria such as generating a limerick, evaluating determinants, and verifying nonlocal correlations, and then refine the theory into a hypothetical "GPT4" that satisfies all criteria. The paper further asks ChatGPT to produce a black-hole text adventure game, a probability formula for AI surpassing humanity, and proof-like reasoning about predictive power. No human subjects or K-12 learners are studied; the context is an adult academic/self-experiment in AI-assisted writing and concept generation.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT can generate coherent, flexible, and surprisingly sustained output across scientific, mathematical, and creative prompts, but that these outputs are not reliable scientific evidence. The author explicitly notes that the model is not capable of conducting experiments or producing original scientific contributions on its own, and that the paper should be interpreted as a demonstration of generative capability rather than a rigorous scientific result. For K-12 education purposes, the paper is only indirectly relevant because it concerns human-AI collaboration and productivity, not classroom instruction or teacher performance.

finding.finding_summary: The paper demonstrates that ChatGPT can generate plausible scientific-sounding explanations, mathematical expressions, and proof-like arguments in response to prompts about generalized probabilistic theories, black-hole physics, and uncertainty quantification. However, these outputs are explicitly framed by the author as speculative and not scientifically rigorous, so the work shows generative scientific-style reasoning rather than validated scientific reasoning performance.
finding.measure: Quality/coherence of AI-generated scientific and mathematical text; prompt-based demonstrations of theoretical physics reasoning

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that ChatGPT can generate a full scholarly manuscript structure, including narrative sections, tables, figure captions, limericks, and references, on a highly abstract topic. The author claims the model produced much of the paper text and ancillary components, demonstrating breadth in academic content generation rather than learning outcomes in a specific school subject.
finding.measure: Generation of academic paper components and formatted scholarly prose

finding.finding_summary: The central claim is that ChatGPT can assist with drafting, revising, and structuring a paper, thereby supporting human productivity in scientific writing. The author repeatedly describes the model as useful for content generation, literature-style prose, and iterative refinement, but also notes that substantial hand-holding and correction were required and that the outputs were not independently reliable.
finding.measure: Human-AI co-writing/productivity in generating and revising a scientific manuscript

paper_profiles.title: Shiksha Copilot: Teacher-AI Collaboration for Curating and Customizing Lesson Plans in Low-Resource Schools
paper_profiles.population: Middle School and High School teachers (Grades 5–10) in low-resource public schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether and how an AI-assisted lesson planning system can support teachers working in low-resource, multilingual public schools in Karnataka, India. The central problem is that teachers in these settings face heavy administrative burdens, limited instructional materials, multilingual teaching demands, and little time for lesson planning. The authors investigate Shiksha Copilot, a human-in-the-loop system that uses LLMs plus human curators to generate curriculum-aligned lesson plans in English and Kannada.

The system was deployed in government schools and used by 1,043 teachers and 23 curators. In the curation phase, curators reviewed and edited LLM-generated learning objectives and lesson plans, and in the distribution phase teachers customized the curated plans for classroom use. The study combines system logs, surveys, and interviews with teachers, curators, and mentors, making it a large-scale mixed-methods evaluation of teacher-AI collaboration in a Global South context.

The findings show that Shiksha Copilot was most successful as a workload-reduction and workflow-support tool. Teachers used it for both bureaucratic documentation and instructional planning, and the system reduced lesson-planning time, record-keeping effort, and teaching-related stress. English-language lesson plans were generally high quality and required little editing, while Kannada translations needed substantial linguistic revision. Teachers often adapted plans offline and relied on their own professional knowledge, suggesting that the tool augmented rather than replaced teacher expertise. The paper concludes that AI can meaningfully support teacher productivity in low-resource settings, but only when paired with human oversight, local linguistic adaptation, and integration into existing school practices.

finding.finding_summary: The system reduced lesson-planning workload and bureaucratic effort for teachers. Across surveys, interviews, and logs, teachers reported lower stress and less time spent on record-keeping and planning after using Shiksha Copilot; the paper specifically states that the tool “significantly reduced” time and effort, though it does not report a causal effect size.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported lesson planning time, administrative/record-keeping effort, and teaching-related stress (Teacher Stress Scale); platform usage logs
finding.study_size: n=406 matched survey respondents; n=1,043 teachers deployed; interview sample n=22 teachers

finding.finding_summary: Shiksha Copilot influenced teacher workflows beyond individual lesson preparation by supporting administrative documentation and shaping how teachers interacted with school-level expectations. The paper reports that the tool eased bureaucratic workload and helped teachers meet record-keeping requirements, but also notes that staffing shortages and administrative demands constrained broader pedagogical change.
finding.measure: Teacher interviews, system logs, and survey responses about work practices and administrative use

paper_profiles.title: DeBiasMe: De-biasing Human-AI Interactions with Metacognitive AIED (AI in Education) Interventions
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of Workshop: AI Augmented Reasoning (CHI ’25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper argues that current AI literacy approaches overemphasize technical proficiency and underemphasize human cognitive biases that shape how learners interact with generative AI. The paper focuses on anchoring bias, confirmation bias, automation bias, and related human-AI feedback loops, proposing that AI literacy should include metacognitive support so students can monitor, evaluate, and regulate their own prompting and interpretation of AI outputs.

The paper presents DeBiasMe, an in-development metacognitive AI literacy intervention for university students. DeBiasMe is framed around deliberate friction, bi-directional human-AI interaction, and adaptive scaffolding. The prototype includes two main components: a prompt refinement tool that flags potential bias before a prompt is submitted, and a bias visualization map that highlights possible biases in AI-generated responses after output is received.

The evidence base described in the paper is limited and largely conceptual, but it does reference initial mixed-methods user research with university students using surveys and interviews to identify support needs around bias awareness, AI understanding, and critical thinking. The author also reports that an earlier prototype version was reviewed through usability heuristics, think-aloud studies, and expert reviews, suggesting promise for making implicit biases explicit and actionable. Overall, the paper concludes that AI literacy tools should move beyond automation and prompt engineering toward learner-centered, bias-aware, metacognitive support, though it does not report rigorous outcome data for educational effectiveness.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that a metacognitive AI literacy intervention can support critical thinking and self-regulation in AI use by making human and AI biases visible at both the prompt and response stages. This conclusion is based on conceptual design work plus initial mixed-methods user research with university students, but no quantitative outcome effect sizes are reported.
finding.measure: Bias awareness, AI understanding, and critical thinking needs identified through surveys and interviews; usability/think-aloud/expert review of prototype

paper_profiles.title: Meaningful human control: actionable properties for AI system development
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how human control and moral responsibility can be preserved as AI systems become more autonomous and operate in complex socio-technical environments. The authors argue that the philosophical idea of meaningful human control has been influential but remains too abstract for practical engineering use, especially when designers need concrete requirements for AI systems that act in the real world.

Using an iterative abductive reasoning process across engineering, computer science, philosophy of technology, ethnography, and design, the paper proposes four actionable properties for AI systems: an explicit moral operational design domain (moral ODD), mutually compatible human and AI representations, alignment between control authority and ability, and explicit links between AI actions and responsible human decisions. The paper illustrates these ideas using two application scenarios: automated vehicles and AI-based hiring. It is not an empirical evaluation of a deployed educational technology; instead, it is a conceptual design paper aimed at helping researchers and practitioners translate meaningful human control into system requirements, governance, and oversight practices.

The main conclusion is that meaningful human control can be made more actionable through system-level design properties, but these properties are necessary rather than sufficient for ethical AI. The paper emphasizes that effective implementation requires transdisciplinary work, contextual analysis, and socio-technical design beyond the AI model itself. It also notes that moral responsibility can be supported by transparency, explainability, logging, shared representations, and organizational procedures, but that no purely technical solution can guarantee ethical outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: NormCode: A Semi-Formal Language for Auditable AI Planning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a core problem in modern AI workflows: multi-step LLM systems are difficult to audit because data flow is implicit, intermediate states are opaque, and context pollution can cause reasoning errors. The authors argue that in high-stakes domains such as legal, medical, and financial decision-making, systems need step-level traceability so auditors and developers can see exactly what each step received and produced.

To solve this, the paper introduces NormCode, a semi-formal language and execution framework for AI planning. NormCode enforces explicit data isolation between steps, separates semantic operations that invoke LLM calls from deterministic syntactic data-plumbing operations, and provides multiple human- and machine-readable formats (.ncds, .ncd, .ncn, .ncdn) plus a compiler and runtime orchestrator. The paper also describes a visual Canvas App, checkpointing, and debugger support to make workflows inspectable and resumable.

The paper is primarily a systems/design paper rather than a K-12 education study. Its validation consists of two demonstrations: a self-hosted compiler pipeline showing expressive completeness and a base-X addition benchmark showing correct execution (100% accuracy up to 150-digit numbers). The authors conclude that NormCode can improve auditability, debuggability, and transparency in complex AI workflows, but they do not evaluate teacher productivity, student outcomes, or K-12 classroom use.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that NormCode improves workflow debuggability, checkpointing, and traceability, which can reduce time spent diagnosing failures in multi-step AI systems. However, the evidence is qualitative and systems-oriented; no controlled measurement of productivity, task time, or workload reduction is reported.
finding.measure: debuggability, checkpointing, auditability, and workflow inspection in a compiler/planning system

paper_profiles.title: Privacy and Copyright Protection in Generative AI: A Lifecycle Perspective
paper_profiles.venue: 2024 IEEE/ACM 3rd International Conference on AI Engineering - Software Engineering for AI (CAIN)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the legal, technical, and governance challenges that arise when generative AI systems are trained on large-scale datasets containing personal and copyrighted material. The authors frame the problem as one of privacy and copyright protection across the full data lifecycle, arguing that isolated techniques such as differential privacy, machine unlearning, or data poisoning are insufficient when considered separately.

Rather than evaluating a single intervention empirically, the paper proposes a lifecycle perspective that maps key risks to stages such as problem formulation, data collection, model training, deployment, and downstream distribution. It discusses challenges including consent acquisition, transparency and access, consent modification and withdrawal, provenance and attribution, side effects of protection mechanisms, continuous monitoring, and downstream reuse of outputs. The paper is oriented toward AI engineering and policy design, with the goal of motivating integrated guardrails and an AI bill of materials for compliance.

The context is generative AI systems such as large language models and text-to-image models, with examples drawn from current legal disputes and privacy/copyright regulations in the EU and US. The paper does not study K-12 learners or teachers, nor does it report direct experimental evidence on educational outcomes or productivity. Its main conclusion is that privacy and copyright protection for GenAI should be treated as lifecycle-wide, socio-technical governance problems requiring coordinated technical and organizational solutions.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI creates significant system-level privacy and copyright governance challenges across the data lifecycle, and that existing isolated techniques only partially address them. It does not report a study with effect sizes; instead it provides a conceptual mapping of risks and a call for integrated compliance mechanisms such as consent tagging and an AI Bill of Materials.
finding.measure: Lifecycle governance challenges, legal/compliance considerations, and proposed protection mechanisms

paper_profiles.title: Designing AI Systems that Augment Human Performed vs. Demonstrated Critical Thinking
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2025 ACM Workshop on Human-AI Interaction for Augmented Reasoning (AIREASONING-2025-01)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper asks how generative AI should be evaluated and designed when the goal is to augment human critical thinking. The authors argue that much current research conflates two distinct constructs: performed critical thinking, meaning independent reasoning done without AI assistance, and demonstrated critical thinking, meaning reasoning or outputs produced with AI assistance.

The paper is not an intervention study; instead, it synthesizes prior literature from psychology, education, and HCI to propose a conceptual distinction and to explain why it matters for evaluating AI tools. The authors note that many existing studies measure only final AI-assisted outputs, which may overstate gains in human capability because they capture demonstrated rather than performed thinking.

The paper's main contribution is a design and research framework. It argues that AI systems can improve demonstrated critical thinking by helping users produce better outputs faster, but that this does not necessarily improve independent critical thinking skills and may even encourage overreliance. The authors recommend future research designs that separately measure performed and demonstrated critical thinking, including pre/post interventions and longitudinal studies, and they suggest AI interfaces should scaffold reasoning processes rather than simply provide answers.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI may improve demonstrated critical thinking in final outputs, but this does not necessarily translate into improved performed critical thinking done independently by users. The authors synthesize prior studies and examples (e.g., ChatGPT-assisted writing and coding) to conclude that AI can boost efficiency and output quality while potentially reducing practice of independent reasoning, but no new empirical effect size is reported in this paper.
finding.measure: Critical thinking conceptual distinction and prior-study synthesis; no direct empirical measure in this paper

finding.finding_summary: The paper states that LLM-based systems can increase productivity and efficiency in tasks such as writing, coding, information analysis, and decision-making. However, this is presented as background synthesis rather than a direct empirical test in this paper, and the authors emphasize that efficiency gains do not guarantee improved human capability.
finding.measure: Productivity/efficiency in AI-assisted tasks discussed in prior literature

paper_profiles.title: Breaking Bad Behaviors: A New Tool for Learning Classroom Management Using Virtual Reality
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a low-cost immersive virtual reality system, “Breaking Bad Behaviors” (3B), designed to train classroom management skills for teacher education. The main problem addressed is that classroom management is difficult to practice systematically in real classrooms because disruptive student behavior is unpredictable, while conventional approaches such as theory, video analysis, and role-play do not provide the same realism, control, and immediate feedback.

The system simulates a classroom of up to 24 semi-autonomous virtual students and lets an instructor control disruption levels, individual student behaviors, dialogue, and feedback using a desktop interface. The trainee teacher wears a head-mounted display and interacts verbally and nonverbally with the virtual class, while the instructor can provide synchronous audio cues and asynchronous post-session evaluation. The paper focuses on technical design and a first usability/acceptability evaluation rather than learning outcomes.

The evaluation includes latency measurements and a user study with teacher/instructor pairs using a seven-minute classroom management task. Results suggest the system meets key requirements for affordability, mobility, believability, safety, and comfort, with average end-to-end latency around 73 ms (SD 45) and frame rate around 75 fps. The authors conclude that the initial results are promising and that the platform is a feasible foundation for future research on the effectiveness of immersive VR for classroom management training.

finding.finding_summary: The system is designed to reduce teacher-training setup burdens by using low-cost consumer hardware and free software, with no special infrastructure, calibration, or extensive rigging required. The authors report that the platform is easy to install and use in a classroom, supports rapid creation of new scenarios and behaviors, and allows instructors to control sessions and provide feedback through a single interface.
finding.measure: System usability, affordability, mobility, and ease of control for training sessions

paper_profiles.title: Developing Critical Thinking Skills through School Teacher Training 'Training and Development Personnel' Model and Their Determinants of Success
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Information and Education Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem that primary school teachers may not be developing critical thinking skills effectively, and argues that teacher training needs to be better aligned with teachers’ actual needs and training design principles. The author examines a “Training and Development Personnel” model intended to improve teachers’ critical thinking through more relevant, participatory, and better-structured professional development.

The study was conducted with 37 elementary teachers in Wonosobo Regency, Indonesia; 17 were alumni of Satya Wacana Christian University’s blended learning program. The training model was implemented in stages and then validated through participants’ self-assessments of training efficiency and perceived gains in critical thinking. The paper also used stepwise regression to identify which training features were most associated with improvement.

Results suggest the model was perceived as efficient and effective, with several training features improving after implementation. The strongest determinants of critical thinking improvement were knowledge elaboration, teacher participation, and good image result; together these three variables explained 70.8% of the variance in the regression model. The author concludes that the training model can be replicated to support teacher professionalism and critical thinking, though the evidence is based on self-report and correlational analysis rather than a controlled experiment.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the training model was associated with improved critical thinking skills among primary school teachers. In the final regression model, knowledge elaboration, teacher participation, and good image result together explained 70.8% of the variance in teachers’ critical thinking self-assessments (F=11.493, p=.001), suggesting a substantial positive association.
finding.measure: Self-assessed critical thinking skills after training

finding.finding_summary: Participants rated the training model as efficient, with a mean efficiency score of 3.33 on a 4-point scale (median=3, SD=0.63). The paper interprets the training as more efficient and effective after implementation than before, but the evidence is based on participants’ self-assessments rather than objective productivity measures.
finding.measure: Self-assessed training efficiency

paper_profiles.title: Teacher Quality and Student Achievement: A Review of State Policy Evidence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how teacher qualifications and state policies are related to student achievement across U.S. states. Using a 50-state policy survey, state case studies, the 1993-94 Schools and Staffing Surveys, and NAEP data, the author asks whether states that invest more in teacher preparation, licensing, recruitment, mentoring, and professional development tend to have stronger teacher workforces and higher student achievement.

The analysis synthesizes prior research and then compares state policy environments and achievement trends. It argues that teacher qualifications—especially preparation, certification, and subject-specific knowledge—are strongly associated with reading and mathematics achievement, even after controlling for student poverty and language status. The paper highlights states such as North Carolina and Connecticut as examples of comprehensive reforms that coincided with sizable achievement gains, while states with weaker standards and less investment in teacher learning tended to have poorer outcomes.

The paper is not an experiment; it is a cross-state policy and achievement analysis combined with a narrative review of prior studies. Its main conclusion is that teacher quality policies matter at the state level, and that investments in teacher education, mentoring, and professional development are plausibly linked to improved student performance and more equitable outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: Across states and in the cited NAEP analyses, stronger teacher qualifications and more professional training were associated with higher reading performance. The paper reports that 4th-grade students of teachers who were fully certified, had master's degrees, and had professional coursework in literature-based instruction did better on reading assessments, though the relationships were described as modest.
finding.measure: Reading achievement / NAEP reading assessments

finding.finding_summary: Teacher qualifications were strongly associated with mathematics achievement across states. The paper cites Texas district analyses where combined teacher expertise measures explained more of the variation in reading and mathematics achievement gains than student socioeconomic status, and North Carolina/Connecticut reforms coincided with large gains in mathematics. Ferguson's Texas study is described as showing strong links between licensing exam scores, master's degrees, and experience and student math outcomes.
finding.measure: Mathematics achievement / NAEP mathematics / state test scores

finding.finding_summary: The paper briefly notes that students of fully certified teachers with literature-based instruction coursework performed better on reading assessments, and it also cites evidence that strong teacher preparation can matter for language arts outcomes. However, language fluency is not a central focus and is addressed only indirectly through reading-related findings.
finding.measure: Reading/language arts assessments

finding.finding_summary: The paper's central focus is state policy and institutional change: states with stronger licensing standards, better enforcement, mentoring programs, and professional development investments had better-qualified teachers and, in many cases, higher achievement trends. It highlights North Carolina and Connecticut as examples where comprehensive teacher-policy reforms were followed by substantial system-wide gains and reductions in emergency hiring and shortages.
finding.measure: State policy conditions, teacher qualification distributions, hiring practices, state achievement trends

paper_profiles.title: Leadership empowering behaviour as a predictor of employees’ psychological well-being: Evidence from a cross-sectional study among secondary school teachers in Kohat Division, Pakistan
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether school leaders’ empowering behavior is associated with teachers’ psychological well-being in secondary schools in Kohat Division, Pakistan. The authors frame empowering leadership as a potentially beneficial management approach that may improve organizational productivity by giving employees more authority, information, and autonomy.

The study used a cross-sectional, non-experimental correlational design with a stratified random sample of 564 secondary school teachers (520 respondents; 92.2% response rate). Teachers completed the Leader Empowering Behavior Questionnaire and Ryff’s Psychological Well-being Scale. The analysis included descriptive statistics, Pearson correlations, and multiple linear regression.

Results showed a strong positive association between overall leadership empowering behavior and teachers’ psychological well-being (r = 0.780, p < 0.01). Regression results indicated that the overall model explained 65.6% of the variance in psychological well-being (R2 = 0.656), and all six empowering leadership subdimensions were significant positive predictors, with accountability for outcomes the strongest predictor. The authors conclude that empowering school leadership is linked to better teacher well-being and recommend adopting empowering behaviors to support healthier and more productive school workplaces.

finding.finding_summary: Overall leadership empowering behavior was strongly and positively associated with teachers’ psychological well-being (r = 0.780, p < 0.01) in a sample of n=520 secondary school teachers. In regression, the model was significant (F = 162.840) and explained 65.6% of the variance in psychological well-being (R2 = 0.656), suggesting that empowering leadership practices were linked to better teacher functioning and productivity-related well-being.
finding.measure: Teachers’ psychological well-being (Ryff’s Psychological Well-being Scale) as predicted by principals’ leadership empowering behavior (LEBQ)

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported relatively high psychological well-being on Ryff’s scale (M=4.78, SD=0.122), and higher leader empowering behavior was associated with higher well-being. The relationship was statistically significant and positive (r = 0.780, p < 0.01), indicating that more empowering leadership coincided with better teacher well-being, autonomy, and positive relations.
finding.measure: Psychological well-being (autonomy, environmental mastery, personal growth, positive relations, purpose in life, self-acceptance)

finding.finding_summary: The study found that empowering leadership behaviors at the school level were significant positive predictors of teachers’ psychological well-being, with the regression model explaining 65.6% of variance (R2 = 0.656). All six dimensions of empowering leadership were significant predictors, especially accountability for outcomes (β = 0.312) and coaching for innovative performance (β = 0.280), implying potential institutional benefits for school leadership and productivity.
finding.measure: Association between principals’ leadership empowering behavior and teachers’ psychological well-being in secondary schools
finding.confidence_interval: 0.070–0.103 for accountability for outcomes B; other CIs reported in paper

finding.finding_summary: Several leadership subdimensions closely tied to durable workplace skills were positively related to teachers’ psychological well-being, including self-directed decision making (r = 0.369) and self-development (r = 0.377), with both also remaining significant predictors in regression (β = 0.137 and β = 0.095, respectively). The findings suggest that autonomy, self-management, and skill development in leadership practices are associated with better teacher functioning.
finding.measure: Self-directed decision making and self-development subscales of leadership empowering behavior; psychological well-being outcome

paper_profiles.title: Implementation strategies to promote measurement-based care in schools: evidence from mental health experts across the USA
paper_profiles.population: School mental health providers and researchers serving K-12 students in the USA
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a practical implementation question in school mental health: which non-AI implementation strategies are most feasible and important for increasing school mental health providers’ use of measurement-based care (MBC). MBC involves routine collection and use of student progress data to guide treatment decisions, but the paper notes that it is underused in schools despite its promise to improve care quality.

The authors used a modified Delphi approach with 52 U.S.-based stakeholders (31 school mental health providers and 21 researchers) to rate 33 implementation strategies across two survey rounds, then refined the list based on quantitative ratings and qualitative feedback. The study also compared provider and researcher perspectives and identified several strategies that stakeholders viewed as especially promising, including assessing readiness and barriers, identifying champions, developing a usable implementation plan, offering a provider-informed menu of free brief measures, providing training materials, and reducing burdensome documentation.

The final output was an empirically derived list of 21 strategies tailored to MBC in schools, with six top-rated strategies in the high-feasibility/high-importance zone. The paper concludes that implementation support in schools should focus on training, workflow support, and reducing paperwork burden, and that stakeholder-engaged strategy selection can improve the fit of implementation efforts to school contexts.

finding.finding_summary: Stakeholders rated workflow- and documentation-related strategies as highly important and feasible for improving MBC implementation in schools. The top-rated strategy in Survey 1 was "make implementation easier by removing burdensome documentation tasks" (importance M=4.61, feasibility M=3.89; n=46), and in Survey 2 this remained one of six top-rated strategies (importance M=4.28, feasibility M=3.37; n=46), indicating that reducing paperwork burden was seen as a key productivity support for school mental health providers.
finding.measure: Stakeholder ratings of implementation strategies related to documentation burden, workflow adjustment, and implementation feasibility/importance
finding.study_size: n=52 overall; key strategy ratings n=46
finding.std_deviation: Survey 1 SD=0.68 (importance) and 1.18 (feasibility) for the documentation strategy; Survey 2 SD=0.94 (importance) and 1.18 (feasibility)

finding.finding_summary: The study found strong support for system-level implementation supports, including readiness assessment, champions, implementation planning, local policy, consultation/coaching, fidelity monitoring, and facilitation. These results suggest that institutional structures and governance-related supports are viewed as necessary for scaling MBC in schools, although the paper reports stakeholder perceptions rather than downstream institutional outcome effects.
finding.measure: Delphi survey ratings of system-level implementation strategies (e.g., champions, local policy, facilitation, fidelity monitoring)
finding.std_deviation: Survey 2 SDs ranged from 0.69 to 1.13 for top system-level strategies; exact SD per strategy reported in Table 3

finding.finding_summary: Although the paper does not test student outcomes directly, its central focus is improving the implementation of measurement-based care intended to monitor and adjust mental health treatment for children and adolescents. The authors argue that effective implementation of MBC in schools has the potential to improve the quality of care and support better progress monitoring for student mental health treatment, but no direct student social-emotional outcome effect was measured.
finding.measure: Not directly measured; implementation strategy ratings for supporting MBC in school mental health services

paper_profiles.title: A narrative review of the physiology and health effects of burnout associated with veterinarian-pertinent occupational stressors
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This narrative review examines burnout in veterinary medicine, focusing on the physiological, cognitive, mental health, and workplace effects of chronic occupational stress. The paper argues that burnout is not best understood as an individual failing, but as a work-related syndrome arising from chronic mismatch between job demands and available resources, insufficient recovery time, and organizational factors such as workload, culture, and practice management.

The review synthesizes literature from veterinary medicine and adjacent healthcare fields to explain how burnout affects sleep, autonomic and inflammatory function, cognition, mental health, and professional functioning. It emphasizes that while individual wellness strategies and resilience-building may offer short-term relief, sustainable prevention and recovery require systemic changes to workplace structure, workload, and organizational support. The paper is explicitly framed around veterinarians, trainees, and clinical staff, but its conceptual conclusions are meant to generalize to healthcare professions more broadly.

Because this is a narrative review rather than an empirical intervention study, it does not test a specific program or produce original outcome estimates. Its main contribution is to summarize existing evidence that burnout is multifactorial and that interventions aimed only at individuals are less likely to have lasting effects than organizational and system-level solutions.

finding.finding_summary: The review concludes that chronic occupational stress and burnout reduce workplace functioning, including performance, efficiency, and the ability to sustain high-quality work. It cites evidence that burnout is associated with impaired attention, executive function, and task performance, and argues that individual-only wellness strategies do not produce durable improvements when underlying workplace conditions remain unchanged.
finding.measure: work performance, cognitive task performance, burnout-related occupational functioning

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues strongly that organizational and systemic interventions are necessary to address burnout, because interventions focused only on individuals are usually temporary and insufficient. It emphasizes that workload, workplace culture, practice management, and system design are central drivers of burnout and that changing these conditions is required for sustainable improvement.
finding.measure: organizational/workplace factors influencing burnout; effectiveness of systemic vs individual-focused interventions

paper_profiles.title: The Longest Way Round Is The Shortest Way Home: An Overhaul of Surgical Ward Rounds
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative review of surgical ward rounds and the factors that shape their quality, efficiency, and safety. The authors argue that ward rounds are central to patient care but are often underprioritized, poorly standardized, and constrained by staffing, communication, documentation, and time pressures.

The review synthesizes literature on ward round structure, team composition, communication, leadership, education, simulation, checklists, record keeping, and technology. It discusses proposed solutions such as standardized ward round protocols, dedicated multidisciplinary rounds, checklists, simulation-based training, structured documentation, electronic patient records, and improved mobile communication tools. The context is hospital surgical practice in the UK and similar healthcare systems, not K-12 education.

The main conclusion is that ward rounds should be standardized and prioritized to improve patient care, reduce communication failures, and support education and teamwork. The paper does not present original experimental data; rather, it reviews prior studies and guidelines to recommend organizational and workflow reforms.

finding.finding_summary: The review concludes that standardizing ward rounds, using checklists, structured documentation, and better communication tools can improve workflow, reduce disruptions, and save clinician time. It cites prior studies showing consultant-led ward rounds twice daily reduced inpatient stay from 10.4 to 5.3 days (p < 0.01) with no increase in readmissions, and that mobile communication tools improved response time and information transfer.
finding.measure: Ward round duration, inpatient length of stay, documentation quality, communication efficiency, response time

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that institutional reforms are needed to prioritize ward rounds through staffing, consultant presence, multidisciplinary participation, and governance changes. It highlights that structured ward round practices, daily consultant-led reviews, and ward safety checklists can improve care consistency and reduce preventable complications, indicating an organizational-level impact rather than an individual-only effect.
finding.measure: Adoption of ward round standards, multidisciplinary participation, institutional care processes

paper_profiles.title: Preparing for Accelerated Third Order Impacts of Digital Technology in Post Pandemic Service Industry: Steep Transformation and Metamorphosis
paper_profiles.venue: The Future of Service Post-COVID-19 Pandemic, Volume 1
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter develops a conceptual theory of how digital technology adoption changes service organizations across three orders of effects: first-order convergence, second-order re-engineering, and third-order dynamic metamorphosis. The author argues that COVID-19 accelerated technology adoption under severe time pressure, but that rapid digitization can produce unintended long-term consequences if organizations do not anticipate deeper changes in workflows, structures, and business models.

The paper is not an empirical study of K-12 schooling or teacher workflow. Instead, it synthesizes literature and uses six service-sector cases from the same edited volume to illustrate the theory, including one chapter on education services. The education example describes distance learning, learning management systems, and AI-enabled EdTech as first- and second-order changes, with broader institutional redesign as a possible third-order effect. The overall conclusion is that organizations should look beyond simple digitization of routines and prepare for more fundamental transformation of service operations.

finding.finding_summary: The chapter argues that digital technology adoption can produce first-, second-, and third-order organizational change in service systems, culminating in structural metamorphosis and new business models. This is a conceptual/theoretical claim rather than a measured intervention effect, so no effect size, confidence interval, or sample size is reported.
finding.measure: Conceptual analysis of service-sector digital transformation and illustrative cases from the volume

paper_profiles.title: Implementation of an Electronic Mental Health Platform for Youth and Young Adults in a School Context Across Alberta, Canada: Thematic Analysis of the Perspectives of Stakeholders
paper_profiles.population: Secondary school stakeholders in K-12 settings (primarily high school; educators and school mental health staff)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the anticipated barriers and facilitators to implementing the Innowell electronic mental health (eMH) platform in secondary schools across Alberta, Canada. The study was motivated by the growing need for youth mental health supports, the expansion of digital mental health tools, and the limited evidence on how such tools function in school settings.

Using a qualitative descriptive approach, the authors conducted 8 focus groups with 52 school stakeholders from 11 school divisions, including teachers, administrators, psychologists, counselors, social workers, and community connectors. Participants discussed implementation challenges related to youth access, consent and confidentiality, device/internet availability, school staff workload, liability, and the risk of identifying more mental health needs than schools can currently support. They also identified facilitators such as youth empowerment, stronger therapeutic relationships, easier access to resources, system flexibility, collaboration across services, and continuity of care.

The paper concludes that implementing eMH in schools is promising but requires careful pre-implementation planning. The authors recommend clear consent and confidentiality policies, training and supervision for school staff, attention to socioeconomic and access barriers, and crisis-response protocols so that digital screening and monitoring do not overwhelm existing school and community mental health services.

finding.finding_summary: School stakeholders identified both barriers and facilitators at the organizational and system level for implementing the Innowell eMH platform. Key issues included consent policies, confidentiality, liability, workflow fit, interoperability, training needs, and the risk of identifying more youth needing care than available services can support; facilitators included cross-system collaboration, continuity of services, and the possibility of system transformation.
finding.measure: Qualitative focus group themes on implementation barriers and facilitators

finding.finding_summary: Participants repeatedly described concerns that the platform would add to already high caseloads, increase time burden, create work duplication, and be difficult to integrate into existing school workflows. At the same time, they noted that the platform could improve prioritization, monitoring, and coordination if it fit existing processes and reduced silos.
finding.measure: Qualitative focus group themes on staff workload, workflow integration, and care coordination

paper_profiles.title: GPT (Generative Pre-trained Transformer) – A Comprehensive Review on Enabling Technologies, Potential Applications, Emerging Challenges, and Future Directions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
