finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that V-MATH could support scalable, curriculum-aligned mathematics preparation at the institutional level by creating a structured dataset (about 500 exam sets from 220 official PDFs) and aligning outputs with the Vietnamese Ministry of Education and Training specification matrix. It presents the system as a plug-and-play tool for standardized exam preparation and teacher support, but does not evaluate policy adoption, governance, or school-level implementation outcomes directly.
finding.measure: Dataset construction, specification-matrix compliance, alignment with national exam format

paper_profiles.title: Connecting Feedback to Choice: Understanding Educator Preferences in GenAI vs. Human-Created Lesson Plans in K-12 Education – A Comparative Analysis
paper_profiles.population: K-12 mathematics educators (elementary, middle, and high school contexts)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether K-12 educators prefer lesson plans created by human curriculum designers or by generative AI systems, and which parts of the lesson plan are stronger or weaker across author types. The study is motivated by the growing use of GenAI tools for lesson planning and the need for evidence on whether they can meaningfully assist teachers without sacrificing pedagogical quality.

The authors compare lesson plans produced by a customized prompt-based GPT-4 model, a fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model, and human-created lesson plans sourced from open repositories. Twenty experienced K-12 mathematics educators evaluated 529 lesson plan pairs across warm-up, main task, cool-down, and overall quality, using blinded pairwise comparisons and optional written comments. The paper combines quantitative preference analysis with qualitative thematic coding and topic modeling to understand both what educators prefer and why.

Overall, educators still preferred human-created lesson plans for warm-ups, main instructional tasks, and overall quality, especially in elementary grades. However, AI-generated plans—particularly GPT-4 and the fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model—were more competitive for cool-down activities, and fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b sometimes outperformed human plans in high school comparisons. The qualitative findings suggest that educators value human plans for differentiation, student discourse, scaffolding, and contextualization, while AI plans are often praised for structure and coherent wrap-ups. The authors conclude that GenAI is best viewed as a collaborative planning aid rather than a replacement for teacher expertise.

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests GenAI can reduce educator workload by assisting with lesson planning, but it does not directly measure time savings or productivity gains. Across 529 evaluated lesson plan pairs from 16 educators, the authors conclude that AI-generated plans can serve as an assistive tool, especially for structured components like cool-downs, potentially lowering the cognitive burden of drafting plans.
finding.measure: Educator preferences for AI-generated vs. human-created lesson plans; qualitative comments about planning usefulness and workload
finding.study_size: n=16 educators; 529 lesson plan pairs; 2116 binary evaluations

paper_profiles.title: EZYer: A simulacrum of high school with generative agent
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents EZYer, a generative educational agent system designed to support high school mathematics teaching and learning. The authors argue that existing AI education tools often have incomplete service, weak interactivity, limited performance, and insufficient quality assurance, especially for generating structured courseware and notes. EZYer combines a Teacher Module for generating teaching materials and LaTeX Beamer courseware, a Student Module that simulates classroom dialogue through five roles (Teacher, Assistant, Top Student, Struggling Student, and Note Taker), and a Controller that filters, scores, and corrects content.

The system is evaluated using 100 generated Beamer files and 100 Notes files, which are scored by five large language models across five dimensions: content accuracy, knowledge coverage, usability, formatting correctness, and visual design and appeal. The evaluation is not a human-subject study or classroom experiment; rather, it is a system-quality assessment of generated outputs. Results reported in the paper are uniformly positive, with especially strong scores for content accuracy and knowledge coverage, and somewhat weaker scores for usability and visual design. The paper concludes that EZYer has promising application prospects for high school mathematics instruction and may help reduce teacher workload by automating lesson-material preparation and note generation, while noting limitations in speed, scope, and lack of manual evaluation.

finding.finding_summary: EZYer-generated Beamer courseware and notes were rated highly for mathematics content quality in a system-level evaluation. Across 100 generated Beamer and 100 Notes documents, the average content accuracy scores were 4.74 for Beamer and 4.70 for Notes on a 0-5 scale, indicating that the generated materials were considered mathematically rigorous and suitable for high school mathematics instruction.
finding.measure: LLM-rated content accuracy of generated math Beamer courseware and notes
finding.study_size: n=100 Beamer documents; n=100 Notes documents

finding.finding_summary: The paper positions EZYer as a tool that can raise teachers' lesson-preparation efficiency by automatically generating structured teaching materials, exercises, LaTeX Beamer presentations, and notes. However, this claim is primarily conceptual and system-oriented; the paper does not report direct measures of teacher time saved or workload reduction in a user study.
finding.measure: System functionality for automatic generation of teaching materials, Beamer slides, exercises, and notes

finding.finding_summary: The Student Module is designed to simulate classroom interaction and deepen understanding through multi-role dialogue, including prompting, extension, challenge questions, and note synthesis. The evaluation does not directly measure learner outcomes such as critical thinking or metacognition, but the paper claims the interaction structure is intended to support deeper conceptual understanding and more comprehensive review.
finding.measure: Design of multi-role instructional dialogue and note synthesis

paper_profiles.title: Evaluation Report on Large Language Models Solving High School Mathematics Questions
paper_profiles.extended_summary: This report evaluates the performance of eight large language models (LLMs) on high school mathematics exam questions from Chinese college entrance examinations spanning 2019–2023. The authors focus on whether LLMs can solve exam-style math problems accurately and efficiently, and whether prompting strategies can improve performance. The study is framed as an educational application assessment rather than a classroom intervention.

finding.finding_summary: The models showed uneven performance on high school mathematics questions, with notable strengths in some item types and weaknesses in others. For single-solution accuracy, the best models reached 0.95 on comprehensive questions (ERNIE-Speed-128K) and 0.50-0.57 on easier item types, while multi-solution accuracy peaked at 0.64 for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and 0.63 for ERNIE-Speed-128K. Results indicate LLMs can solve some math tasks well, but logical reasoning and harder problem types remain inconsistent.
finding.measure: Accuracy on multiple-choice, fill-in-the-blank, comprehensive, and difficulty-level mathematics exam questions; multi-solution correctness

finding.finding_summary: The report explicitly evaluates logical reasoning and creativity as problem-solving competencies. Logical reasoning scores ranged from 0.28 (Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) to 0.42 (Hunyuan-lite), and creativity-related measures such as richness and complexity varied substantially across models, with GLM-4-Flash showing the highest complexity (68) and the largest average number of solutions (4.5 per question). This suggests LLMs differ considerably in higher-order reasoning and multi-solution generation rather than just answer accuracy.
finding.measure: Logic score, number of guidance attempts, success rate of chain-of-thought guidance, richness (number of solutions), complexity score, weighted creativity score

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally measures response time as a proxy for efficiency and compares models across question types and prompting conditions. Efficiency differed widely: gemma-2-9b-it and Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct were fastest on some single-solution tasks (e.g., 0.32 s and 0.39 s on fill-in-the-blank/multiple-choice tasks), while GLM-4-Flash was much slower on question-and-answer tasks (16.01 s) and multi-solution tasks (7400 s total). Prompting sometimes improved both speed and accuracy, but not consistently across models.
finding.measure: Response time in seconds for single-solution and multi-solution math problems; speed change under different prompts

finding.finding_summary: The paper also evaluates prompt responsiveness and guidance effects, which are not a separate academic subject outcome but are tied to task performance in exam-style problem solving. Under different guiding prompts, several models improved accuracy by 5%-22%, with Spark-lite showing the largest improvement under prompts A/C (+13%) and GLM-4-Flash improving most under prompt B (+22%). This indicates prompting can materially change model performance on structured academic tasks.
finding.measure: Accuracy and speed improvement under prompt-based guidance conditions

paper_profiles.title: Connecting Three Pivotal Concepts in K-12 Science State Standards and Maps of Conceptual Growth to Research in Physics Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines which physics concepts are both foundational in K-12 science and especially difficult for students to learn. The authors analyze concept maps from Project 2061, review K-12 state science standards from four U.S. states, and synthesize prior physics education research on student misconceptions and effective instructional approaches. They aim to identify a small set of "pivotal" concepts that deserve emphasis in teacher preparation, curriculum design, and instruction.

The paper finds that Newton’s laws, conservation of energy, and geometrical optics are the concepts that best satisfy all three criteria: they are central in the conceptual landscape, appear across state standards, and are persistently challenging for students. The article gives a detailed account of common misconceptions in force and motion and conservation of energy, such as motion implying force, confusion between velocity and acceleration, and difficulty recognizing conservation of energy in novel problem structures. It also describes research-based instructional strategies that have shown success, including prediction-before-demonstration activities, guided inquiry, and conceptual explorations using experiments and graphs.

Overall, the paper argues that K-12 science instruction would benefit from focusing more deeply on a smaller number of coherent concepts rather than broad superficial coverage. It is primarily a synthesis and conceptual analysis rather than an original intervention study, but it provides practical guidance for educators and professional development providers on how to structure instruction around the most challenging foundational ideas in physics.

finding.finding_summary: The paper synthesizes extensive evidence that students have persistent conceptual difficulties with foundational physics reasoning, especially Newton’s laws and conservation of energy. It reports that many students retain non-Newtonian beliefs after traditional instruction, while research-based activities such as prediction-before-demonstration and guided explorations can improve understanding; however, the paper does not report a single new effect size from an original study.
finding.measure: Conceptual understanding of force and motion; conservation of energy reasoning; conceptual diagnostic responses (e.g. Force Concept Inventory, conceptual multiple-choice items)

paper_profiles.title: AI-Fuzzy Markup Language with Computational Intelligence for High-School Student Learning
paper_profiles.venue: 2021 IEEE CIS Summer School on Computational Intelligence for High-School Student Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reports on the 2021 IEEE CIS Summer School on Computational Intelligence for High-School Student Learning, an outreach and instructional event organized for students and teachers from Taiwan, Japan, Indonesia, and other countries. The paper’s central question is not an intervention efficacy trial, but rather whether a summer-school format using lectures and hands-on AIoT / AI-Fuzzy Markup Language (AI-FML) activities can help younger learners understand core computational intelligence concepts.

The program included introductory lectures on fuzzy logic, neural networks, and evolutionary computation, plus AIoT workshops using tools such as the AI-FML learning platform, AI-FML Lab, NUWA Lab, and the Kebbi Air robot. Participants worked in small groups, explored parameter effects in fuzzy systems and PSO training, designed robot expressions, and produced short reports and feedback surveys. The authors describe the event as engaging and educational, emphasizing that students quickly understood basic CI principles and that the workshop provided useful co-learning experience with real-world AIoT applications.

The sample included 214 registered attendees, with about 22% high-school students and additional elementary students, university students, teachers, and other participants. Based on reports and feedback from 78 attendees who completed at least two-thirds of the program, and 80 short reports / 77 surveys, the authors conclude the school was well organized and effective as an outreach model for introducing CI at an early age. However, the paper provides no controlled comparison, so its claims are descriptive and based on participant feedback rather than causal evidence.

finding.finding_summary: Participants in the summer school engaged with introductory content on fuzzy logic, neural networks, evolutionary computation, and AIoT applications, and the authors report that feedback showed students understood the principles of computational intelligence to a higher degree than in previously organized schools. This conclusion is based on participant reports and surveys rather than a controlled test; no standardized outcome scores or effect sizes are reported.
finding.measure: Short reports and feedback surveys about understanding of computational intelligence concepts
finding.study_size: n=80 reports; n=77 surveys; 214 registered attendees total

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the summer school and AIoT workshop stimulated student interest, motivation, and participation in future research adventures, based on qualitative feedback from attendees and a teacher comment. These are descriptive impressions from the event, not measured with a formal engagement or motivation instrument.
finding.measure: Participant feedback comments on interest, motivation, and engagement

finding.finding_summary: Students worked in teams during breakout-room AIoT workshops, interacted with robots, and completed tasks such as examining fuzzy-system parameters, designing robot expressions, and presenting short reports. The paper suggests these activities supported collaboration and practical problem solving, but provides no direct measurement of durable skills or comparative effect estimates.
finding.measure: Group workshop participation, task completion, and short reports
finding.study_size: n=10 teams reported (8 high school, 2 elementary)

paper_profiles.title: Identification of Books That are Suitable for Middle School Students Using Artificial Neural Networks
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of efficiently identifying books that are appropriate for middle school students. The authors argue that book selection for school curricula is time-consuming and potentially subjective, and they propose an automated screening approach to help institutions, educators, and families quickly judge suitability.

The study builds a custom dataset of 416 books labeled as suitable or unsuitable for middle school children, using sources such as Turkish Ministry of National Education-approved books, Oxford/Cambridge library sources, Gutenberg texts, and books with R ratings or age ratings indicating inappropriate content. After preprocessing the text, the authors extract 14 features from each book using sentence- and word-level sentiment analysis with VADER plus a manually created bad-words list, then train an artificial neural network (ANN) to classify books. The ANN is reported to achieve 90.06% consistency overall, with 91.2% accuracy for appropriate books and 80.7% for inappropriate books on a sample test set of 83 books.

The paper concludes that the approach can serve as a screening tool for ministries, schools, teachers, parents, and students to support book selection for middle school curricula. However, the authors note important limitations: the model struggles with academically complex texts and would likely improve with a larger training set and a domain-specific academic jargon list. The work is primarily a technical classification study rather than an intervention study in classrooms, and its main contribution is an automated text-suitability screening method for educational materials.

finding.finding_summary: The proposed ANN-based screening tool is presented as a way to expedite the book selection process for middle school curricula and reduce the need for manual reading-based review. On a dataset of 416 books, the model achieved 90.06% consistency overall and 91.2% accuracy for appropriate books and 80.7% for inappropriate books on a sample test set of 83 books.
finding.measure: Book-suitability classification accuracy / consistency for automated screening

finding.finding_summary: The paper explicitly frames the model as a tool for institutional decision-making, including use by the Ministry of National Education, schools, teachers, parents, and students. The authors argue it could function as a preliminary reference source and a screening tool for curriculum book selection, potentially standardizing and accelerating institutional review processes.
finding.measure: Proposed institutional usability of the book-screening system

paper_profiles.title: Beyond Answers: Large Language Model-Powered Tutoring System in Physics Education for Deep Learning and Precise Understanding
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of providing personalized, effective physics tutoring with large language models (LLMs), especially for tasks requiring deep conceptual understanding rather than simple answer retrieval. The authors argue that generic LLM tutoring can produce plausible but incorrect guidance in physics and may not support students’ error analysis or reflective learning.

To address this, they propose Physics-STAR, a prompt-engineering framework that structures LLM tutoring into three stages: knowledge explanation, error analysis, and review suggestion. The approach is tested in a small controlled pretest-posttest experiment with 12 high school sophomores, divided into three groups: traditional teacher-led review, unguided GPT-4o tutoring, and GPT-4o guided by Physics-STAR. Students completed conceptual, computational, and information-based multiple-choice questions on gravity and spaceflight.

Results show that all three methods produced similar gains on conceptual and computational questions, but Physics-STAR performed better on information-based questions, improving average post-test scores to M=5 versus M=2.5 in the other two groups, and reducing completion time slightly. The paper concludes that LLM tutors can support physics learning when carefully scaffolded toward student-centered explanation and error analysis, and that prompt design matters for improving deeper understanding and efficiency on complex tasks.

finding.finding_summary: Physics-STAR improved students' performance on information-based physics questions, which required interpreting diagrams and applying the law of gravity, compared with both teacher lecture and generic GPT-4o tutoring. In the post-test, the Physics-STAR group scored M=5 on information-based questions versus M=2.5 in the other two groups, with a modest reduction in completion time (M=257s vs. M=262s and M=271.5s).
finding.measure: Pretest-posttest multiple-choice physics questions on conceptual, computational, and information-based understanding of gravity and spaceflight

finding.finding_summary: The authors report that Physics-STAR fostered deeper learning behaviors such as reflective learning, error analysis, and critical thinking during problem solving. This is supported mainly by the higher performance on information-based items and the discussion's interpretation that interactive Q&A helped students understand and correct misconceptions.
finding.measure: Performance on information-based physics items and observed interaction patterns during tutoring

finding.finding_summary: Physics-STAR improved efficiency on the most complex question type by reducing completion time relative to the other two conditions. For information-based questions, the Physics-STAR group averaged 257s compared with 262s for generic GPT-4o tutoring and 271.5s for teacher lecture, while also showing higher scores.
finding.measure: Completion time on physics test questions

paper_profiles.title: Perspectives on astronomy: probing Norwegian pre-service teachers and middle school students
paper_profiles.venue: Physical Review Special Topics - Physics Education Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates Norwegian pre-service science teachers and middle school students' understandings, beliefs, and ways of responding to astronomy questions before and after astronomy instruction. The authors adapt and translate the Introductory Astronomy Questionnaire (IAQ) into Norwegian, creating the NIAQ, and use it to probe views on astronomy content, the nature of scientific theories, the size and scale of the universe, and how astronomers learn about the universe.

The study is set in Norway and includes 41 pre-service teachers in a university college course and 535 year 8 and 387 year 10 middle school students from eight schools around Oslo. The pre-service teachers completed pre/post questionnaires around their astronomy instruction; the middle school comparison used year 8 as a pre-test group and year 10 as a post-test group because the latter had already completed the standardized astronomy module. Data included free-response and multiple-choice items, analyzed with grounded-theory-style coding and descriptive comparisons.

Main findings were that pre-service teachers improved in their ability to explain astronomical concepts and showed some gains in content knowledge, but they also exhibited a concerning drop in pedagogical responses and a shift toward more authoritative, less student-centered explanations after instruction. Middle school students showed little or no improvement on several astronomy knowledge measures, and substantial misconceptions persisted about distance and size scales in the universe; these misconceptions were also gender-stratified, with female students scoring lower on the ranking tasks. The paper concludes that the adapted instrument reveals meaningful misconceptions and that further work is needed to understand both instruction and teacher preparation in astronomy education.

finding.finding_summary: The study found some pre/post improvement in pre-service teachers' astronomy understanding and explanatory ability, including better brief explanations of stars, planets, and more complex ideas such as why Earth remains in stable orbit. However, middle school students showed little to no improvement on knowledge of sizes and distances in the universe, and substantial misconceptions remained after instruction.
finding.measure: NIAQ free-response explanations and multiple-choice/ranking tasks about astronomical objects, theory, and distance/size relationships
finding.study_size: n=41 pre-service teachers; n=535 year 8 students; n=387 year 10 students

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that pre-service teachers' scores improved on the explaining task for astronomical objects, and that question 5b was a statistically significant predictor of later course success on the NIAQ and Force Concept Inventory. This is an academic content outcome specific to astronomy rather than a general literacy, numeracy, or scientific reasoning measure.
finding.measure: NIAQ explaining task scores and later course performance / Force Concept Inventory scores

finding.finding_summary: Pre-service teachers' opinions about how interesting, important, and open-ended astronomy and physics are started high and increased slightly after instruction, but these changes were not statistically significant. The paper also reports that more than 80% believed life likely exists elsewhere in the universe, with exoplanet coverage appearing to strengthen that belief, but this is more a belief/perception finding than an affective intervention effect.
finding.measure: Likert-type opinions on interest, societal importance, and how much remains to be discovered in physics/astronomy; beliefs about extraterrestrial life
finding.study_size: n=41 pre-service teachers; middle school sample also assessed on similar opinion items

finding.finding_summary: A notable result was that pre-service teachers gave fewer pedagogical responses after instruction when asked how they would respond to hypothetical students, shifting from student-centered to more authoritative explanations. Pre-instruction, more than one-third responded pedagogically, whereas post-instruction fewer than 10% did so.
finding.measure: Coding of free-response explanations as pedagogical versus authoritative

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not directly measure teacher workload or productivity, but it does show that the adapted questionnaire could generate rich information through free-response analysis, and that a multiple-choice format alone would have missed much of this detail. This is more about assessment utility than a demonstrated productivity gain, so the evidence is indirect and limited.
finding.measure: Use and analysis of the NIAQ free-response versus multiple-choice format

paper_profiles.title: Evaluation of ChatGPT and Microsoft Bing AI Chat Performances on Physics Exams of Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates the performance of two large language models, ChatGPT and Microsoft BingChat, on Vietnamese high school physics exam questions drawn from the National High School Graduation Examination (2019–2023). The authors use a curated VNHSGE physics subset of 200 multiple-choice questions to compare model accuracy across difficulty levels (knowledge, comprehension, application, and high application) and against the performance distribution of Vietnamese students on the same exams.

The central finding is that both models can answer many lower- and mid-level physics questions, but they struggle substantially with high-application items that require multi-step reasoning. BingChat is generally more accurate, while ChatGPT is described as more stable/consistent. When compared with Vietnamese student score distributions, both models underperform students overall, though the authors note that the models may still be useful as supportive tools for immediate feedback, individualized practice, and assisting teachers and students during learning activities.

The paper is not an intervention study; it is a benchmark-style evaluation of LLM performance on educational physics questions in a Vietnamese secondary-school context. It highlights both the promise of LLMs for education and the limitations of current models for complex subject-specific reasoning, especially in a non-English setting.

finding.finding_summary: On Vietnamese high school physics exam questions (n=200), ChatGPT and BingChat performed adequately on knowledge/comprehension items and some application items, but both struggled on high-application questions requiring multi-step reasoning. Average accuracy was 61% for ChatGPT and 66% for BingChat, compared with Vietnamese student averages of 6.39/10 in the referenced score comparisons; the paper concludes the models are not yet capable of replacing human reasoning in this physics context.
finding.measure: Accuracy on multiple-choice high school physics exam questions; converted exam scores compared with Vietnamese student score distributions
finding.study_size: n=200 questions; student comparison data from Vietnamese national exam cohorts (exact comparison n not reported in-text)

finding.finding_summary: The study directly evaluates LLM performance on a subject-specific high school physics exam dataset from Vietnam and finds that both ChatGPT and BingChat underperform Vietnamese students overall on physics content. BingChat was more accurate than ChatGPT on average (66% vs. 61%), but neither model handled high-application physics problems well.
finding.measure: Exam-question accuracy on Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination physics items

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs could support students and teachers by providing immediate feedback, individualized learning experiences, and help with generating practice/test materials and reducing teacher workload. This is presented as a potential benefit rather than a measured productivity outcome; no direct workload effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Potential teacher/student support functions discussed in relation to model use

paper_profiles.title: Development of a test in German language to assess middle school students’ physics proficiency
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a measurement gap in German-language physics education research: the lack of a freely accessible, psychometrically evaluated achievement test for middle school students’ physics proficiency. The authors argue that researchers in Germany often rely on ad hoc tests built from released TIMSS items, but the available German-language pool is too limited to support a strong instrument, and open-ended TIMSS items are inefficient and difficult to score objectively.

To address this, the authors developed a 20-item multiple-choice, single-select test in German by translating and adapting released TIMSS science items for primary and middle school. They first assembled a 40-item pool, administered it to 177 eighth-grade students in Hamburg, and then used Rasch modeling, item-wise Wald tests for differential item functioning, Andersen’s likelihood ratio test, and correlations with external variables to evaluate item quality and construct validity.

The final test retained 20 items spanning physics content areas such as mechanics, optics, thermodynamics, electrics, magnetism, and acoustics. Psychometric results suggested adequate model fit, acceptable person-separation reliability (0.78), excellent item-separation reliability (0.97), and generally satisfactory coverage of student proficiency, though the authors note gaps at the very low and high ends of the proficiency range and underrepresentation of electrics. Correlations with science interest and self-concept were positive and moderate, supporting validity evidence, while the paper concludes that the instrument is promising for research use but should be expanded and validated further in other grade levels and contexts.

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that the finalized 20-item German TIMSS-based test provides a valid and sufficiently reliable measure of middle school students’ physics proficiency. After removing 20 items with differential item functioning from the original 40-item pool, the remaining test showed acceptable Rasch model fit (Andersen’s LR test: LR=11.82, df=19, p=0.89) and strong psychometric properties for assessing physics knowledge and proficiency.
finding.measure: Physics proficiency test performance / Rasch-estimated person parameters

finding.finding_summary: The paper found moderate positive correlations between estimated physics proficiency and students’ science interest and science self-concept, suggesting the test behaves as expected with respect to motivational and self-belief variables. Correlations were r=0.45 with science interest and r=0.34 with science self-concept (both p<0.01) among n=177 eighth-grade students.
finding.measure: Correlations between physics proficiency and science interest / science self-concept

paper_profiles.title: Abstract book of Supporting Health By Technology XIV
paper_profiles.venue: Supporting Health By Technology XIV 2025 (conference abstract book)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This document is a conference abstract book for the 14th edition of the Supporting Health by Technology conference, not a single paper. It contains keynote descriptions, program listings, and multiple abstracts spanning digital health, AI, wearables, remote monitoring, co-design, and implementation research, primarily in adult healthcare contexts.

Because the provided text is an abstract collection rather than one discrete study, the relevant material for this retrieval question comes mainly from an oral presentation on students’ mental well-being. That abstract reports a qualitative study of student counsellors’ views on chatbot features for supporting higher-education students’ mental well-being, alongside broader conference content on AI-enabled health tools and implementation challenges. The student-focused abstract is exploratory and formative: it identifies themes about students’ needs, the importance of a non-judgmental and community-oriented design, and desired chatbot features, but does not yet report outcome effects on users.

Overall, the document offers adjacent evidence on AI tool development, acceptability, and implementation tradeoffs, but very limited direct K-12 evidence. The most relevant finding for the user’s question is that AI tools are often valued for support and personalization, yet implementation depends on explainability, usability, workflow fit, and stakeholder trust. No K-12 teacher productivity outcomes are reported in the provided text.

finding.finding_summary: In the student-wellbeing RCT of ROOM (n=208; 104 intervention, 104 waitlist control), the intervention did not produce significant improvements on primary or secondary mental health outcomes. These outcomes included emotion regulation skills, stress symptoms, anxiety, depression, and resilience, although exploratory analyses suggested benefits only among highly engaged subgroups.
finding.measure: Emotion regulation skills, stress symptoms, anxiety, depression, resilience, and app uptake/engagement

finding.finding_summary: Several abstracts focus on implementation, governance, and fit of AI/digital tools in care settings rather than outcome effects. For example, the palliative-care recognition tool was viewed by home care professionals as potentially improving care and communication, but its adoption was limited by insufficient explainability, browser/device issues, and workflow integration problems.
finding.measure: Professional perceptions of implementation, usability, explainability, and workflow fit
finding.study_size: n=6 home care teams; 6 focus groups

paper_profiles.title: Abstract book of Supporting Health By Technology XIV (June 10th & 11th 2025, Enschede, The Netherlands)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This abstract book compiles the conference program and abstracts for Supporting Health By Technology XIV, a digital health conference focused on the design, evaluation, and implementation of technology-enabled care. The included abstracts span many topics, especially AI, digital mental health, remote monitoring, personalization, and implementation science. As a collection, the volume is not a single study but a conference proceedings-style source containing multiple independent studies with varying methods and populations.

Because the user-provided text includes multiple abstracts, the most directly relevant items for the retrieval question concern AI-enabled tools, implementation considerations, and productivity/workflow effects. Several abstracts describe qualitative or mixed-methods studies of AI tools in care settings, including concerns about explainability, data quality, usability, and clinician trust. Other abstracts report pilot or feasibility findings for predictive modeling and remote monitoring systems, typically in adult healthcare contexts, with themes centered on whether these tools improve identification, support decision-making, or reduce workload. Overall, the proceedings suggest that AI tools may offer operational benefits, but successful use depends heavily on workflow fit, transparency, and implementation support.

finding.finding_summary: Across several abstracts, AI tools were described as potentially improving care efficiency through earlier identification of risk, better triage, and support for decision-making, but also creating usability and implementation burdens. For example, the palliative care recognition tool was seen as helpful for timely flagging, yet professionals reported insufficient explanations, unreliable re-flagging behavior, and weak EHR integration; no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Professional perceptions of AI tool usefulness, workflow fit, and implementation usability; qualitative focus groups and pilot use in EHR/workflow settings
finding.study_size: n=6 home care teams; 6 focus groups for the palliative care tool; additional qualitative studies included n=34 interviews for COPD RPM

finding.finding_summary: The papers repeatedly emphasized that AI adoption depends on governance, implementation readiness, and institutional fit rather than technical performance alone. Multiple abstracts highlighted the need for clear guidelines, data governance, explainability, and better integration into electronic systems; the COPD RPM and palliative care studies both found that organizational processes and stakeholder alignment were central barriers and facilitators, but no quantitative institutional outcome was reported.
finding.measure: Implementation readiness, stakeholder alignment, data governance, and integration into care pathways/EHRs

paper_profiles.title: Abstract book of Supporting Health By Technology XIV
paper_profiles.venue: Supporting Health By Technology XIV (conference abstract book)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This document is a conference abstract book for the 14th Supporting Health by Technology conference held in June 2025. It compiles keynote descriptions, oral presentations, posters, and demonstrations focused on digital health, artificial intelligence, implementation, co-design, and evaluation of health technologies across a range of adult and student populations.

Several abstracts are relevant to AI and technology adoption, including work on AI-based suicide risk prediction, AI-assisted detection of palliative care needs, and machine learning for postoperative monitoring and ECG interpretation. Other contributions examine user needs, co-design, and implementation barriers for mobile interventions, chatbots, smartwatches, and remote monitoring tools, often using qualitative or mixed-method approaches. The included studies generally emphasize sociotechnical fit, explainability, user engagement, and implementation challenges rather than large-scale efficacy effects.

Because this is an abstract book rather than a single empirical paper, the document does not report one unified study or a common intervention effect. The abstracts collectively suggest that AI and digital tools may support clinical decision-making, monitoring, and personalization, but successful use depends on data quality, usability, clinician trust, and workflow integration.

finding.finding_summary: Across the abstracts, AI and digital health tools were reported to have potential to improve clinical workflows, monitoring, and decision support, but implementation was constrained by data quality, explainability, integration problems, and stakeholder alignment. Multiple studies emphasized that adoption depends on sociotechnical fit, clinician trust, and workflow integration rather than model performance alone.
finding.measure: Qualitative implementation experiences, feasibility findings, and design/acceptability evidence across multiple conference abstracts

finding.finding_summary: Several abstracts described AI and digital tools as potentially improving efficiency by supporting earlier detection, prioritization, or decision-making, such as flagging palliative care needs, detecting postoperative deterioration, and reducing diagnostic delays. However, these benefits were offset by usability issues, false alarms, limited explainability, and incomplete integration into existing systems, which reduced practical uptake.
finding.measure: Feasibility, workflow, and user-experience findings from AI tool implementation and evaluation abstracts

finding.finding_summary: The only clearly outcome-oriented student wellbeing RCT reported no significant impact of the ROOM intervention on primary or secondary mental health parameters, including stress, emotion regulation skills, anxiety, depression, and resilience. Exploratory analyses suggested benefits only among highly engaged users, indicating that engagement quality may matter more than simple exposure.
finding.measure: Stress symptoms, emotion regulation skills, anxiety, depression, resilience, and app usage in a student wellbeing RCT

paper_profiles.title: Abstract book of Supporting Health By Technology XIV 2025
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This document is a conference abstract book for the 14th Supporting Health by Technology conference (2025) rather than a single paper. It includes keynote descriptions, oral presentations, posters, and workshop abstracts spanning digital health, AI in healthcare, implementation science, and co-design methods. The relevant content for this retrieval focuses on an oral presentation about a chatbot for student mental well-being, but the provided text is only a partial abstract book and does not contain a fully developed empirical paper.

Across the included abstracts, the recurring problem is how to design, implement, and evaluate digital health tools so they are usable, acceptable, and fit real-world care workflows. The student-well-being chatbot abstract specifically uses semi-structured interviews with 14 student counsellors in the Netherlands to identify needs and requirements for a mental health chatbot for higher education students, with the aim of informing later prototype development. Because the data shown are preliminary and qualitative, the main conclusion is that chatbot design should be guided by user needs, stakeholder perspectives, and implementation considerations such as trust, avatar design, and support for counsellors, but no outcome effect is reported in the excerpt.

finding.finding_summary: The student-counsellor study is formative rather than evaluative: it identifies needs and requirements for a chatbot to support student mental well-being, but it does not test whether the chatbot improves stress, anxiety, or well-being. The abstract reports that data analysis was not finished at the time of writing, so no outcome effect size or direction on student well-being is reported.
finding.measure: Needs and requirements for a chatbot supporting student mental well-being; qualitative themes from semi-structured interviews

finding.finding_summary: The abstract notes that some student counsellors expressed a personal interest in using the chatbot to support them during sessions with students, suggesting a potential workflow-support role. However, the study does not evaluate workload reduction, time savings, or productivity outcomes, so no empirical efficiency effect is reported.
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness of chatbot for supporting counsellors in student sessions

paper_profiles.title: Abstract book of Supporting Health By Technology XIV (conference abstracts)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This document is a conference abstract book for the 14th Supporting Health by Technology conference held in June 2025. It contains multiple short abstracts spanning digital health, AI in healthcare, implementation science, and co-design of eHealth tools, rather than a single study focused on one intervention or population.

Because the supplied text is an abstract book, the relevant evidence comes from a collection of individual presentations. The excerpts include qualitative co-design work, feasibility and evaluation studies, and several AI/ML methods papers in healthcare settings. Many of the studies focus on implementation, usability, personalization, and clinician or patient acceptance of digital tools, with some RCT evidence among university students and several early-stage feasibility or prototype studies.

For the specific sub-question on AI tools and productivity in K-12 schools, the provided text does not contain direct K-12 evidence. The closest adjacent evidence in the text concerns university-student mental health tools and clinician workflow/decision-support in healthcare, but these are not directly transferable to K-12 teacher productivity. Overall, the excerpt is best treated as a mixed conference proceedings source with heterogeneous study types and mostly early-stage, implementation-oriented evidence.

finding.finding_summary: The abstract on AI in automatic recognition of palliative care demand reports that home care professionals believed the AI model could improve care by helping them identify the palliative phase earlier and support communication with general practitioners. However, they also reported substantial usability and reliability limitations, including insufficient explanations for flags, browser/device compatibility issues, and extra steps to locate flagged clients, which reduced actual use during the test period.
finding.measure: Home care professionals’ perceived usefulness, explainability, usability, and implementation experience of an AI model embedded in the EHR
finding.study_size: n=6 home care teams from 2 home care organizations; 6 focus groups

finding.finding_summary: The same palliative-care AI feasibility study found that professionals saw institutional value in the tool for improving timely recognition of the palliative phase and for prompting better documentation practices. At the same time, the study identified implementation barriers at the organizational and system level, including weak integration into the EHR, insufficient transparency, and low uptake during the short test period, indicating that impact depended heavily on better implementation support.
finding.measure: Implementation feasibility and institutional fit of an AI tool in home care EHR workflows
finding.study_size: n=6 home care teams from 2 organizations; 6 focus groups

paper_profiles.title: Modern Trends in the Development of Science and Society: Proceedings of the International Scientific Conference
paper_profiles.venue: Modern Trends in the Development of Science and Society: Proceedings of the International Scientific Conference
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conference proceedings volume collects multiple short papers spanning education, economics, technology, psychology, law, and other fields. For the purposes of this extraction, the relevant paper is a pedagogical discussion of survival-skill education in wartime Ukraine and a companion paper arguing for the effectiveness of survival training courses during emergencies. Both pieces focus on the broader question of how education can strengthen preparedness, resilience, and national security under conditions of war.

The first paper argues that survival skills should be integrated into school, college, university, and professional development curricula, including modules in existing safety and civil defense courses. It emphasizes self-protection, first aid, orientation, communication, psychological resilience, and decision-making under stress, but does not report original empirical testing. The second paper reviews criteria for effective survival courses—practical training, accessibility, relevance, psychological preparation, and modern technologies—and concludes that such courses improve preparedness and trust in institutions, again without presenting primary quantitative results.

Overall, the relevant papers are conceptual and practice-oriented rather than experimental. Their main conclusion is that survival education is strategically important in wartime Ukraine and should be standardized, expanded, and supported with practical exercises, simulations, and digital tools to build a more resilient society.

finding.finding_summary: The papers argue that integrating survival-skill instruction into the educational system would strengthen national security, civic preparedness, and institutional resilience in wartime Ukraine. They recommend adding modules to existing curricula (e.g., 'Defense of Ukraine,' safety, and civil defense) and developing standardized training and certification, but they do not report empirical effect sizes.
finding.measure: Conceptual analysis of curriculum integration, preparedness, and national-security relevance

finding.finding_summary: The papers emphasize improved psychological resilience, stress resistance, self-control, and adaptability as central outcomes of survival training. The discussion is theoretical and cites prior work on practical training and simulation, but it does not provide original measured effects.
finding.measure: Psychological preparedness, stress resistance, self-control, resilience

finding.finding_summary: The papers highlight decision-making under stress, critical thinking, teamwork, and practical problem solving as competencies developed through survival education. No direct evaluation data are reported; the claims are normative and based on educational rationale rather than measured outcomes.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, decision-making, teamwork, adaptation to risk situations

paper_profiles.title: Engaging Teachers to Co-Design Integrated AI Curriculum for K-12 Classrooms
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how K-12 AI education can be made more accessible by integrating AI concepts into teachers’ existing core curricula rather than treating AI as a standalone computer science topic. The authors argue that many teachers want to teach AI but need more scaffolding, clearer tools, and curricular supports to do so, especially in non-CS subjects.

To explore this, the researchers ran a two-day remote co-design workshop with 15 K-12 educators from diverse subject areas and grade bands. Teachers received introductory presentations on AI, explored AI learning tools, and then worked in small groups with researchers to design integrated lesson plans that embedded AI into social studies, ESL, literacy for students with learning disabilities, and an exemplar physics curriculum. The study used workshop audio, participant questionnaires, and artifact analysis with thematic coding.

The main findings are that teachers value AI curriculum that supports evaluation, engagement, logistics, and collaboration, and that integrated AI lessons can be built around three points of connection: data, reflection, and ethics. The paper concludes that co-design with teachers can generate implementable AI curriculum ideas and that embedding AI into core subjects may expand access to AI learning for students outside computing classrooms. The authors also note tradeoffs of remote co-design, including the need for more time, clearer scaffolding, and better grouping by subject expertise.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the workshop increased engagement and confidence related to teaching AI: participants’ self-rated familiarity with AI increased from an average of 4.8/7 to 5.8/7, and their confidence about integrating AI into their curriculum averaged 5.6/7 by the end of the workshop. The workshop also increased enthusiasm for teaching AI in ways that connect to students’ interests and real-world contexts.
finding.measure: Self-reported familiarity with AI; self-reported confidence integrating AI into curriculum; workshop feedback

finding.finding_summary: The co-design process explicitly targeted and supported collaboration, reflection, and discussion of AI ethics and design choices. Across the workshop, teachers identified collaboration as a key curriculum value and designed activities that required students to work in groups, reflect on data and model behavior, and reason about ethical implications, indicating strong emphasis on durable skills such as collaboration, critical thinking, and metacognition.
finding.measure: Workshop discourse, curriculum drafts, thematic coding of co-design discussions

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not measure teacher workload directly, but it does identify concrete supports teachers said they needed to make AI curriculum feasible: scaffolding, clear tool guidance, evaluation ideas, and logistical support for classroom implementation. Teachers also reported that some AI tools were hard to choose between and wanted more explicit information about when and how to use them, suggesting that better-designed curriculum/tooling could improve classroom implementation efficiency.
finding.measure: Teacher reflections on curriculum design feasibility and logistics; workshop discussions

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests that integrated AI curriculum could broaden institutional access to AI education by embedding AI into core K-12 subjects such as social studies, ESL, and literacy, including for students with learning disabilities and non-CS classrooms. Teachers and researchers co-created draft curricula and identified design considerations that could support wider adoption, but the paper does not evaluate school-level implementation or policy change.
finding.measure: Curriculum drafts, workshop outcomes, teacher perceptions of adoption potential

paper_profiles.title: Shiksha Copilot: Teacher-AI Collaboration for Curating and Customizing Lesson Plans in Low-Resource Schools
paper_profiles.population: Middle School and High School teachers (Grades 5–10) in low-resource public schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies whether and how an LLM-based, human-in-the-loop lesson planning system can support teachers in low-resource K-12 settings. The central problem is that teachers in government schools in Karnataka, India face heavy administrative burdens, limited instructional materials, multilingual classrooms, and severe time scarcity, making lesson planning both difficult and bureaucratically important. The authors ask how teachers collaborate with AI, what challenges arise when using LLM-generated lesson plans in non-English-medium classrooms, and how such a tool reshapes teacher work practices.

The intervention is Shiksha Copilot, a teacher-facing system that combines retrieval-augmented generation, human curator review, bilingual English-Kannada translation, and optional chat and question-generation features. The study deployed the system across 757 schools in Karnataka and involved 1,043 teachers and 23 curators; the analysis draws on logs, 43 interviews, and pre/post surveys from 406 matched respondents. Curators first reviewed and refined AI-generated learning objectives and lesson plans, and teachers then customized the curated plans for classroom use.

The findings suggest that the system was useful mainly as a productivity and workflow support tool. Teachers used it to reduce lesson planning time, ease record-keeping, and lower stress, while also shifting some practice toward more activity-based pedagogy. English lesson plans were generally high quality and required few edits, but Kannada translations often needed substantial linguistic revision. Teachers rarely recorded their own customizations in the platform, but interviews showed they frequently adapted plans mentally and with outside resources. Overall, the paper concludes that teacher-AI collaboration can be effective when AI is embedded in a human-reviewed, curriculum-aligned workflow, but that language quality, contextual fit, and systemic constraints limit broader pedagogical change.

finding.finding_summary: Shiksha Copilot reduced teacher workload by easing bureaucratic documentation, lowering lesson planning time, and reducing teaching-related stress. The paper reports measurable reductions in lesson planning time and stress from pre/post survey and usage evidence, though no single overall effect size for the productivity outcomes is provided in the text excerpt.
finding.measure: Teacher stress scale; weekly time spent on lesson planning and administrative tasks; platform usage/logs; interview reports
finding.study_size: n=406 matched survey respondents; 1,043 teachers total; 5,542 teacher-created lesson plans in logs

finding.finding_summary: The tool helped teachers satisfy administrative documentation requirements and fit into existing school workflows, but broader institutional constraints limited deeper change. The paper finds that staffing shortages, bureaucratic demands, and low-resource conditions constrained wider pedagogical transformation even when the tool improved day-to-day workflow fit.
finding.measure: Interviews with teachers, curators, and mentors; survey items on support/resources; workflow and usage analysis

paper_profiles.title: Using ChatGPT for Science Learning: A Study on Pre-service Teachers' Lesson Planning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This preprint examines how pre-service elementary science teachers think about using ChatGPT in science lesson planning, and what they believe its benefits and risks are. The study addresses a gap in the early ChatGPT-in-education literature by moving beyond general speculation and analyzing concrete lesson plans and survey responses from teachers-in-training.

The authors worked with 29 pre-service elementary teachers at a Korean teachers' university during a short professional-learning sequence in 2023. Participants were introduced to ChatGPT, discussed possible science-education uses, and then created lesson plans for a 45-minute elementary science class that had to integrate ChatGPT and one or more instructional methods (e.g., cooperative learning, POE, learning cycle, analogy generation, concept mapping). The researchers evaluated the plans with a modified TPACK-based rubric and also analyzed open-ended survey responses and simulated chat logs.

Overall, the pre-service teachers envisioned wide-ranging uses for ChatGPT across science topics and instructional approaches, and their lesson plans scored relatively high on the modified rubric (M=3.29/4, SD=.91). They were stronger at aligning ChatGPT with curriculum goals and instructional strategies than at selecting the best ChatGPT functions for a given lesson, suggesting a need for more professional development on practical AI use. Qualitatively, participants saw ChatGPT as useful for questioning, individualized support, and formative feedback, but they also worried about inaccurate information and student over-reliance. Many proposed safeguards such as using multiple information sources, teacher feedback, and structured peer interaction.

finding.finding_summary: Pre-service teachers generally believed ChatGPT could support science learning through questioning, prediction, explanation, exploration, and formative feedback. In their lesson plans, ChatGPT was integrated across science domains and instructional methods, and the modified TPACK-based lesson-plan rubric averaged M=3.29/4 (SD=.91), suggesting reasonably strong planning quality for science instruction. The paper does not measure student science achievement directly; instead, it shows teacher candidates' perceived instructional fit and planned use of ChatGPT for science inquiry-related activities.
finding.measure: Modified TPACK-based Technology Integration Assessment Rubric (TIAR) applied to science lesson plans; qualitative analysis of lesson-plan design for science instruction

finding.finding_summary: Participants expected ChatGPT to increase students' motivation, interest, active participation, and self-directed learning. The survey responses indicate that 9/29 pre-service teachers saw ChatGPT as supporting individualized and self-directed learning, and others linked it to motivation and interest, though these were anticipated rather than measured outcomes. The study also notes that over-dependence on ChatGPT was a concern, so any positive social-emotional effects were seen as contingent on careful classroom structuring.
finding.measure: Pre-service teachers' open-ended survey responses and lesson-plan rationales about anticipated student motivation, interest, and self-directed learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly discusses critical thinking, digital literacy, and collaboration as key student skills associated with ChatGPT use. Pre-service teachers believed ChatGPT could stimulate consecutive questioning and critical thinking, while also requiring students to compare outputs against other sources and work within structured group interactions to avoid over-reliance. These findings are based on lesson plans and open-ended survey responses from 29 participants, not on measured student skill gains.
finding.measure: Qualitative coding of lesson plans and survey responses about critical thinking, digital literacy, and collaboration strategies

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests ChatGPT could improve instructional efficiency by helping with lesson planning, role-play scripting, summarizing student-generated scenarios, and providing quick feedback. In the rubric, pre-service teachers scored highest on 'instructional strategies & ChatGPT' (M=3.48/4, SD=.99), and they frequently described ChatGPT as a tool that could support the teacher's work and help manage large classes through individualized support. These are perceived productivity gains from teacher candidates' plans, not observed classroom efficiency outcomes.
finding.measure: Lesson-plan rubric scores plus qualitative descriptions of teacher support, feedback, and planning efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT could help teachers and schools broaden access to personalized learning and AI literacy, but it also raises institutional concerns about reliability, access costs, and the need for professional development. The discussion explicitly notes subscription cost as a barrier for underresourced teachers and students, and calls for future support around prompt engineering, teacher preparation, and equitable use of open-source LLMs.
finding.measure: Qualitative analysis of participant concerns and discussion of implementation barriers (cost, training, equity, reliability)

paper_profiles.title: Towards Evaluation Guidelines for Empirical Studies involving LLMs
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a methodological problem: how to conduct and report empirical studies that involve large language models (LLMs) in software engineering research in ways that are valid and reproducible. The authors argue that the rapid adoption of LLMs has created new reproducibility and validity challenges because model outputs can vary by version, configuration, prompts, backend infrastructure, and non-determinism.

The paper is a position paper and taxonomy of study types rather than an intervention study. It classifies empirical LLM studies into four broad categories: LLMs as tools for researchers, LLMs as new tools for software engineers, studies of how people use LLMs, and benchmarking LLMs on software engineering tasks. For each category, it proposes preliminary reporting guidelines such as declaring LLM use, reporting model version and date, documenting configuration, publishing prompts, using open models as baselines, and applying human validation.

The population/context is software engineering researchers and, more broadly, empirical researchers working with LLM-based systems. The paper concludes that current reporting practices are insufficient for reliable replication and that the community needs more tailored guidelines for different study types, along with further work on ethical issues and threats to validity. It does not present new empirical results about an educational intervention or tool; instead, it offers a framework intended to improve the quality of future research.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce the time and effort required for empirical researchers by automating tasks such as data collection, preprocessing, analysis, annotating artifacts, and generating summaries or literature reviews. However, this is presented as a conceptual claim supported by examples from prior work, not as a new empirical effect estimate from this paper.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The main contribution is a set of preliminary evaluation and reporting guidelines for empirical studies involving LLMs, aimed at improving validity, reproducibility, and community standards in software engineering research. The paper does not quantify institutional impact, but it clearly focuses on research practices, governance of methods, and standards for future studies.
finding.measure: existence and content of proposed evaluation/reporting guidelines; methodological classification of study types

paper_profiles.title: AI Conversational Tutors in Foreign Language Learning: A Mixed-Methods Evaluation Study
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings 14th Panhellenic Conference iCT in Education, Rhodes, October 2025
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines AI conversational tutors for foreign language learning, with a focus on how state-of-the-art tools support speaking practice, contextual feedback, and conversation quality. The author asks three questions: what design patterns are common in these tutors, how their user experience compares with general-purpose AI models, and how tutor quality can be measured systematically using transcript-based evaluation.

The study uses a mixed-methods approach. First, the author manually interacted with four specialized language-learning apps (Talkio, Talkpal, Univerbal, and Langua) using a Spanish learner profile and free-chat scenarios, documenting user experience, breakdown handling, feedback style, and privacy/disclosure issues. Second, the author compared voice-mode interactions with ChatGPT and Gemini as general-purpose AI tutors. Third, transcript-based quality scoring was conducted on six tutors using a 10-dimensional rubric, with five LLMs serving as artificial expert raters. The study found that the specialized tools shared useful features such as conversational practice, contextual hints, and feedback, but differed substantially in fluidity, correction quality, and handling of unfinished utterances; privacy consent for voice data was absent across the apps. In the comparison with general-purpose models, ChatGPT produced a richer and more instructional interaction than Gemini, but both lacked some of the specialized feedback and complete transcript annotation of dedicated language tutors.

Overall, the paper concludes that effective AI language tutors need robust conversation representation, contextual repair of communication breakdowns, and feedback that supports learning without disrupting conversational flow. The quality-evaluation phase suggested that strong tutors combine systematic corrective scaffolding, coherent dialogue, supportive style, and rich vocabulary, and that even general-purpose tools can deliver high-quality conversational experiences in this domain. The paper also emphasizes the need for privacy safeguards around voice data and proposes an automated evaluation framework for future research.

finding.finding_summary: The paper found that the specialized AI tutors and general-purpose voice models all supported foreign-language conversation practice, but they differed in fluency, feedback quality, and handling of breakdowns. Specialized tools such as T1 and T4 were judged to provide stronger learning support, while T3 was less fluid and T6 (Gemini) lacked clarity and timely feedback; ChatGPT (T5) scored highly on transcript-based quality despite some missing transcript segments in voice mode.
finding.measure: User experience with voice-based conversational practice; transcript-based rubric scores for dialogue quality and feedback
finding.study_size: n=6 tutors (4 specialized apps + ChatGPT + Gemini); one expert interaction per tutor for UX phase

finding.finding_summary: The evaluation framework explicitly assessed and compared conversational tutors on qualities related to critical thinking and guided reasoning, such as tutor initiative, coherence, and value of learning. T4 in particular was described as encouraging further reasoning and critical thinking, while T3’s role-play approach raised questions about effectiveness and value.
finding.measure: 10-dimensional transcript rubric including tutor initiative, coherence, and value of learning; qualitative judgment of reasoning support

finding.finding_summary: Across the specialized tools and ChatGPT, the study reported generally supportive, encouraging, and empathetic interaction styles that likely support learner engagement and persistence. T2 and T4 were described as friendly and constructive, while T1’s messages were supportive but sometimes hindered by latency and T3 was less responsive to breakdowns.
finding.measure: Qualitative user experience assessment of tutor tone, encouragement, empathy, and interaction flow

finding.finding_summary: The paper notes that AI conversational tutors offer scalable, cost-effective alternatives to human tutoring for speaking and conversation practice, implying productivity benefits relative to traditional instruction. However, this is framed as a general design rationale rather than a direct measurement of teacher workload or time savings, and the study itself did not quantify operational efficiency outcomes.
finding.measure: Qualitative discussion of scalability, availability, and cost-effectiveness of AI tutors; no direct workload metric

paper_profiles.title: Connecting Feedback to Choice: Understanding Educator Preferences in GenAI vs. Human-Created Lesson Plans in K-12 Education – A Comparative Analysis
paper_profiles.population: K-12 mathematics educators (elementary, middle, and high school contexts)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether K-12 educators prefer lesson plans created by generative AI systems or by human curriculum designers, and what features drive those preferences. The authors focus on a practical problem in education: lesson planning is time-consuming, and AI tools are increasingly marketed as ways to reduce teacher workload, yet there is limited direct evidence comparing AI-generated lesson plans with human-authored ones in real K-12 settings.

The study compares lesson plans from three sources: a customized prompt-based GPT-4, a fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model, and human curriculum designers. Twenty experienced K-12 mathematics educators evaluated 529 lesson-plan pairs across warm-up, main task, cool-down, and overall quality dimensions, with 2,979 optional comments analyzed using thematic analysis and topic modeling. Educators were blinded to author source. The authors report that human-created lesson plans were generally preferred overall, especially for elementary settings and for components requiring student discourse, scaffolding, differentiation, and engagement. GenAI plans were seen as increasingly competitive for cool-down/closing sections and, in some high-school comparisons, a fine-tuned model outperformed human plans. The paper concludes that GenAI is best positioned as an assistive planning tool rather than a replacement for educator expertise, with stronger performance when tuned for specific instructional contexts.

finding.finding_summary: Educators and the authors frame GenAI as a tool that can reduce lesson-planning workload and cognitive load, with the study concluding that AI can serve as an assistive planning tool rather than a replacement for teacher expertise. However, this paper does not directly measure time saved or productivity gains; the evidence is based on educator preference for AI-generated lesson plans over human ones in some components, especially cool-down sections.
finding.measure: Educator preferences for AI-generated vs. human-created lesson plans; qualitative comments on workload/cognitive load
finding.study_size: n=20 educators; 529 lesson-plan pairs; 2,116 measure-level evaluations

paper_profiles.title: Designing for human–AI complementarity in K-12 education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how AI tutors and teachers can be designed to work together more effectively in K-12 classrooms. The authors argue that many human-AI partnerships fail because they are not designed around the complementary strengths of each party, and they present Lumilo, mixed-reality smart glasses that give teachers real-time analytics about students’ learning, metacognition, and behavior during AI-supported class sessions.

The paper combines participatory design, iterative prototyping, and field testing in middle school math classrooms. Teachers with prior experience using AI tutors helped shape the design through classroom observations, storytelling, card sorts, speed dating, and replay-enactment prototypes. The final field experiment involved 343 middle school students across 18 classrooms, 8 teachers, and 4 schools/districts, comparing business-as-usual AI-supported instruction, a minimal glasses condition, and a glasses-plus-analytics condition.

The main conclusion is that Lumilo improved student learning relative to both control conditions, with the analytics-enabled version outperforming the minimal monitoring version. The tool changed teacher behavior by directing attention toward students with lower prior knowledge, and this redistribution of teacher attention reduced the usual “rich get richer” pattern seen in AI-supported learning. The paper frames these results as evidence that carefully designed human–AI complementarity can improve both instruction and student outcomes in real classrooms.

finding.finding_summary: In the in-the-wild experiment, students in the Glasses + Analytics condition showed greater learning gains on a linear equation solving pre/post test than students in both the No Glasses and Glasses-only conditions. The study included 286 analyzed students (from 343 enrolled) across 18 classrooms, and the authors report that the full Lumilo condition improved post-test performance and attenuated the usual advantage for higher-pretest students.
finding.measure: Linear equation solving pre-test and post-test scores

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that teachers using Lumilo spent more time helping lower-knowledge students and provided encouragement and motivational prompts, suggesting improved student engagement and persistence in AI-supported math sessions. Evidence is indirect and comes from classroom observation and process data rather than a standalone social-emotional outcome measure.
finding.measure: Classroom observations of teacher-student interactions; student engagement-related behaviors in AI tutor sessions

finding.finding_summary: Teachers using Lumilo appeared to better support students’ metacognition by prompting them to reflect on their work and by using the tool’s alerts plus raw error examples to infer underlying causes of student difficulty. The paper describes this as a form of human-AI complementarity, but it does not report a separate standardized metacognition test; evidence comes from field observation and behavior tracking during the classroom pilots and experiment.
finding.measure: Observed teacher prompting and student reflection during AI-tutored math work; teacher attention allocation
finding.study_size: n=286 analyzed (and 14 teachers, 15 classrooms in pilots)

finding.finding_summary: Lumilo improved teacher decision-making and classroom orchestration by helping teachers identify which students most needed help and by reducing the time needed to detect student difficulties. During the pilot work, teachers using the tool spent about 24 seconds per visit per student on average, and the system’s alerts and remote screen monitoring enabled more targeted, efficient attention allocation in the classroom.
finding.measure: Teacher attention allocation, classroom orchestration behavior, and time spent per student visit
finding.study_size: 14 teachers, 15 classrooms, 304 students in pilots; 8 teachers, 18 classrooms, 286 students in experiment

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that participatory design and real-world field evaluation are necessary for effective AI deployment in schools, and it presents a replicable design approach for teacher-AI partnerships. This is primarily a conceptual and design implication rather than a policy or governance outcome measured directly in the study.
finding.measure: Participatory design process and field deployment of Lumilo in K-12 classrooms

paper_profiles.title: LLMs to Support K–12 Teachers in Culturally Relevant Pedagogy: An AI Literacy Example
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a practical implementation gap in K–12 education: teachers often want to use culturally relevant pedagogy (CRP), but they lack time, training, and ready-to-use resources. The authors ask whether large language models (LLMs) can help teachers adapt AI literacy lessons so they better reflect students’ cultural and demographic contexts.

To explore this, the paper introduces CulturAIEd, an LLM-powered tool that combines student demographic information, a culturally responsive teaching checklist, rubric-based feedback, and just-in-time coaching. The study used a small exploratory pilot with four secondary teachers from the U.S. and East Asia, who completed lesson-adaptation tasks and interviews while working on AI literacy activities aligned with AI4K12 guidelines. Participants first adapted activities without support, then with a CRT checklist, and finally with CulturAIEd.

The main conclusion is that teachers viewed the tool as helpful for making culturally responsive modifications more efficiently. Post-survey responses and interview data suggest increased confidence in identifying opportunities for cultural responsiveness and in making CRP-informed lesson changes. The authors emphasize that these results are preliminary and based on a very small sample, but they argue that LLMs may reduce planning burden and support CRP integration in emerging areas like AI literacy, while also warning about risks such as bias, overreliance, and superficial “routinized” use of CRP.
