finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that CulturAIEd streamlined CRP-related lesson adaptation by integrating student demographics, providing rubric-based feedback, and reducing the time and research needed to customize activities. In the pilot with n=4 secondary teachers, 3/4 strongly agreed that the tool saved time, and participants described the workflow as highly efficient, though no objective time-on-task measure was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived time savings, workflow efficiency, and teacher-reported ease of lesson adaptation

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests CulturAIEd could help schools and teachers integrate culturally relevant pedagogy into AI literacy instruction despite common institutional barriers such as limited time, limited training, and inconsistent support. However, this is based on a small exploratory pilot (n=4) and qualitative feedback rather than school-level outcome data, policy change, or implementation at scale.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of institutional barriers and tool support for CRP implementation

paper_profiles.title: Automating RT Planning at Scale: High Quality Data For AI Training
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a core bottleneck in AI-enabled radiotherapy planning: the scarcity of large, standardized, high-quality training data. The authors argue that clinical treatment planning is time-intensive, subjective, and difficult to curate at scale because of heterogeneous contours, planning preferences, and missing optimization objectives across institutions.

To address this, they introduce AIRTP (Automated Iterative Radiotherapy Planning), a pipeline that uses AI-based auto-contouring, scripted planning in Varian Eclipse via ESAPI, RapidPlan/scorecard objectives, and iterative optimization to automatically generate deliverable RT plans. The system is deployed on cloud GPU nodes and is used to release the HMM-RT dataset, a multi-cohort, multi-site dataset covering head-and-neck and lung cancer, with 3,730 plans from 1,622 patients.

The study evaluates plan quality using dose-volume histograms and plan scorecards, and reports that AIRTP-generated plans are comparable in quality to manually produced clinical plans while reducing planning time from roughly 3–6 hours to 0.1–1 hour per plan. The paper also demonstrates plan reproducibility from 3D dose distributions and presents the dataset as a benchmark and training resource for dose prediction and other downstream RT AI tasks. Overall, the work is mainly a systems/data paper focused on automation and dataset scaling rather than clinical outcome evaluation.

finding.finding_summary: The AIRTP pipeline substantially reduced RT planning time relative to manual planning. The authors state that manual planning typically requires 3–6 hours per plan, whereas their automated pipeline produces plans in about 0.1–1 hour, while maintaining comparable plan quality based on DVH/scorecard comparisons.
finding.measure: Radiotherapy planning time per plan; plan quality via DVHs and scorecards

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s main institutional contribution is the release of a large public dataset and challenge infrastructure for RT AI research. The authors report 3,730 plans from 1,622 patients across head-and-neck and lung cohorts, claiming the released dataset contains more than 10 times as many plans as the largest existing well-curated public dataset.
finding.measure: Dataset scale and public release; number of plans and patients released

paper_profiles.title: Fast evaluation of far-field signals for time-domain wave propagation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a numerical-analysis problem in time-domain wave propagation: how to recover or “teleport” far-field signals from data recorded on a finite spherical boundary without having to extend the computational domain. The authors focus on exact and approximate frequency-domain kernels that map solution data from one radius to another, including the asymptotic case of evaluating the waveform at infinity.

The approach is mathematical and computational rather than educational. The paper derives exact teleportation kernels for spherical-harmonic multipoles of the 3D wave equation, analyzes the instability of exact sum-of-poles representations at large spherical-harmonic index due to catastrophic cancellation, and then proposes kernel compression via rational approximation using well-conditioned evaluation along the imaginary axis. The authors test the method numerically for high-ℓ kernels, study empirical scaling laws for the number of poles and residue magnitudes, and demonstrate accurate pulse teleportation and asymptotic-waveform evaluation in wave-equation simulations.

The context is numerical solution of PDEs in physics, not K-12 schooling. The paper’s main conclusion is that compressed kernels can substantially improve numerical stability and accuracy relative to exact pole sums, while still enabling efficient post-processing to recover far-field signals. It also argues that the method may extend to other hyperbolic equations on non-flat geometries, including gravitational-wave applications.

paper_profiles.title: Foundations of GenIR
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter surveys foundational ideas in generative AI for information access (IA), focusing on how modern large language models (LLMs) change retrieval, synthesis, and generation paradigms. The core question is not whether a specific intervention improves learning outcomes, but how generative models can be used to produce tailored information, synthesize grounded answers from external sources, and support more capable information access systems.

The paper organizes the field into two broad directions. First, it describes information generation, where models directly create answers, content, or multimodal outputs from prompts, covering topics such as Transformer architecture, scaling laws, training stages, prompt optimization, and multimodal generation. Second, it describes information synthesis, especially retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), modular retrieval, generative retrieval, and domain-specific modeling. The chapter argues that synthesis is often more reliable than pure generation because it can reduce hallucination and incorporate external knowledge, but it also highlights unresolved tradeoffs around efficiency, controllability, inference cost, and the practical limits of scaling.

The chapter is best understood as a conceptual and technical overview for researchers and practitioners in information retrieval and generative AI rather than an empirical education study. It does not evaluate K-12 learners, teachers, or schools directly, but it is relevant to adjacent discussions of AI tools that might support educator productivity through retrieval and synthesis workflows. Its main conclusion is that generative AI substantially expands the design space of information access systems, yet many foundational research questions remain open, especially around reliability, optimization, and system-level integration.

finding.finding_summary: The chapter discusses generative AI and RAG as technologies that could improve information access efficiency by generating tailored responses, synthesizing evidence, and reducing manual retrieval burden, but it does not empirically test any productivity or workload outcomes. No effect sizes, sample sizes, or measured efficiency gains are reported because this is a conceptual survey rather than an intervention study.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Auto-Evaluation: A Critical Measure in Driving Improvements in Quality and Safety of AI-Generated Lesson Resources
paper_profiles.venue: AI + Open Education Initiative / AI and Open Learning Submissions
paper_profiles.population: Elementary (PreK-5th) through High School (K-12) teachers and lessons across ages 5-16
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a practical problem in AI-assisted lesson generation: how to evaluate and improve the quality and safety of AI-produced educational resources at scale. The authors argue that because lesson content must be accurate, pedagogically sound, and safe, AI tools for teachers need systematic evaluation, not just generation. They present Oak National Academy’s AI lesson assistant, Aila, and an accompanying auto-evaluation agent designed to score lesson outputs against 24 quality and safety benchmarks.

The core empirical case study focuses on multiple-choice quiz distractor quality, especially whether answer options are minimally different and appropriately challenging. The authors compared an LLM-based auto-evaluator with 20 qualified teachers (19 usable after one participant was excluded), who rated 311 multiple-choice questions drawn from 4,985 lessons spanning primary and secondary subjects. The team used thematic analysis of teacher justifications to refine the evaluation prompt and add few-shot examples, then re-tested alignment.

Results showed that the original auto-evaluator was overly strict and often scored quizzes lower than teachers did. After prompt refinement, agreement improved: mean squared error decreased from 3.83 to 2.95 (p=0.00640) and quadratic weighted kappa increased from 0.17 to 0.32. The paper concludes that auto-evaluation can help rapidly improve AI-generated lesson materials and that integrating expert teacher feedback into evaluation prompts improves alignment, with potential application to broader quality and safety evaluation workflows.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that an LLM-based auto-evaluation agent can help evaluate AI-generated lesson resources quickly and efficiently, reducing the need for purely manual review. After prompt refinement using teacher feedback, agreement with expert human evaluators improved, with mean squared error dropping from 3.83 to 2.95 (p=0.00640) and quadratic weighted kappa rising from 0.17 to 0.32 on 311 quiz questions.
finding.measure: Auto-evaluation agreement with human teacher ratings; mean squared error (MSE); quadratic weighted kappa (QWK)
finding.study_size: n=311 quiz questions rated by 19 qualified teachers
finding.effect_size: QWK increased from 0.17 to 0.32; MSE decreased from 3.83 to 2.95

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents a scalable evaluation workflow for institutional use in AI lesson-production systems, showing that iterative human-in-the-loop auto-evaluation can improve quality assurance procedures. It argues that the approach can serve as a framework for other organizations building similar AI educational tools, with stronger alignment between automated and expert judgments after refinement.
finding.measure: Alignment between automated and expert evaluation process; thematic analysis-informed prompt revision
finding.study_size: n=4985 lessons in the dataset; n=311 quiz questions in the case study

paper_profiles.title: Why do Experts Disagree on Existential Risk and P(doom)? A Survey of AI Experts
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates why AI experts disagree about existential risk from advanced AI and the likelihood of catastrophic outcomes (“P(doom)”). The study asks whether disagreement is driven by different worldviews about AI systems (as controllable tools versus uncontrollable agents), by differing familiarity with AI safety concepts, or by reactions to different AI safety arguments.

The author surveyed 111 AI professionals, including academics, industry researchers, and AI safety researchers, all of whom had graduate-level ML coursework or at least one year of professional ML experience. The survey measured familiarity with both empirical ML concepts and theoretical AI safety concepts, agreement with nine AI-safety belief statements, desired AGI timelines, and responses to short reading interventions drawn from AI safety and mainstream AI coverage.

The main findings are that experts cluster into two correlated belief profiles: an “AI as a controllable tool” view and an “AI as an uncontrollable agent” view. Most respondents agreed that technical AI researchers should worry about catastrophic risk (77%), but many were unfamiliar with core AI safety concepts such as instrumental convergence (only 21% had heard of it) and scalable oversight (23% fairly well/know it well). Lower familiarity with AI safety terminology was associated with greater skepticism about catastrophic risk, while the short reading interventions produced only modest, non-definitive shifts in beliefs. The paper concludes that a substantial expertise gap in AI safety literacy may underlie some expert disagreement, and that clearer conceptual grounding may improve communication about AI risk.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examines expert beliefs relevant to AI governance, AI safety prioritization, and risk communication rather than educational outcomes. Among 111 AI professionals, 77% agreed that technical AI researchers should be concerned about catastrophic risks, but the author also found strong disagreement on AGI timelines and only modest, non-definitive opinion shifts after exposure to different AI-safety readings. These findings suggest broad concern about safety alongside persistent disagreement that has implications for research agendas and policy discourse.
finding.measure: Survey agreement with AI safety and AGI risk statements; reactions to short reading interventions

paper_profiles.title: Digital Audio Processing Tools for Music Corpus Studies
paper_profiles.venue: Oxford Handbook of Music and Corpus Studies
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter reviews digital audio processing tools used in music corpus studies, with an emphasis on how researchers can extract musically relevant information from recordings rather than only from scores or other symbolic representations. It explains the underlying signal-processing concepts needed to understand audio analysis, including time-frequency representations, filters, and feature extraction at low and high levels.

The chapter then surveys a range of widely used tools for manual, semi-automatic, and automatic analysis, including GUI-based tools such as Audacity, Sonic Visualiser, and Tony, as well as code-based toolkits such as MARSYAS, Aubio, Essentia, jAudio, MIR Toolbox, LibROSA, MSAF, and Madmom. The focus is on what each tool can do, what kinds of features it extracts, and the tradeoffs between manual annotation, semi-automatic workflows, and fully automatic methods.

The chapter’s broader argument is that audio corpus research has expanded the kinds of musical questions that can be studied, especially for non-notated and performance-based music, but current automatic methods are still not accurate enough to replace human annotation in many settings. As a result, the most productive near-term approach is often a hybrid one: use software to scale analysis while accepting some error, and rely on manual intervention where higher accuracy is required. The chapter is not an empirical study of K-12 education; it is a methodological review aimed at researchers and advanced practitioners in musicology and music information retrieval.

paper_profiles.title: Leveraging contact network structure in the design of cluster randomized trials
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a design problem in cluster randomized trials for infectious disease interventions: how to balance statistical power with public health benefit when clusters are connected through contact networks. The authors argue that in outbreak settings, standard parallel or stepped-wedge CRTs may not use available network information well enough to reduce transmission during the trial itself.

They propose a family of "connectivity-informed" trial designs that rank clusters by their between-cluster connectivity and then vaccinate more-connected clusters earlier, either with static rankings or adaptive re-ranking as the trial progresses. The paper evaluates these designs with simulation of Ebola-like epidemics on a network-structured agent-based model, comparing epidemic control outcomes and power to detect vaccine effects across 1,000 simulated trials.

The simulations suggest that connectivity-informed designs can reduce peak infectiousness and cumulative incidence, with up to about a 20% reduction in cumulative incidence relative to traditional staggered CRTs, but this comes at a cost in statistical power. Adding a short holdback period to the randomized designs recovers much of the lost power while preserving most of the public health benefit. The main conclusion is that network-aware CRT design can improve outbreak control, especially when rapid epidemic suppression is more important than precise estimation of vaccine efficacy.

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that connectivity-informed cluster trial designs can improve public health impact during outbreaks by reducing cumulative incidence and peak infectiousness while preserving some ability to estimate treatment effects. In simulation of 1,000 Ebola-like epidemic trials, these designs lowered cumulative incidence by about 20% relative to standard staggered CRTs, but they reduced power unless a brief holdback period was added.
finding.measure: Epidemic control metrics in simulated cluster randomized trials: peak infectiousness, cumulative incidence, time to epidemic end, time to Re<1, and statistical power

paper_profiles.title: Guidelines for Empirical Studies in Software Engineering involving Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a methodological problem rather than an educational intervention: how empirical software engineering studies should report and design research involving large language models (LLMs) to improve reproducibility and replicability. The authors argue that LLM-based studies are especially vulnerable to non-determinism, model drift, opaque training data, prompt sensitivity, and weak reporting, all of which can undermine validity and make findings difficult to reproduce.

To tackle this, a 22-researcher collaboration developed a taxonomy of seven study types for LLM involvement in software engineering and eight reporting/design guidelines. The guidelines cover declaring LLM usage, reporting model versions and configurations, documenting tool architecture, disclosing prompts and logs, validating outputs with humans, using open LLM baselines, choosing appropriate benchmarks and metrics, and reporting limitations and mitigations.

The paper is explicitly about software engineering research methods and LLM use in SE tasks, not K-12 education. Its context is empirical research and software engineering practice, with examples drawn from annotation, judging, synthesis, simulation, tool building, usage studies, and benchmarking. The main conclusion is that careful, specific disclosure and validation practices are necessary for trustworthy LLM-based empirical studies, and that “reasonable efforts” toward reproducibility should be expected despite the inherent instability of LLM systems.

paper_profiles.title: The AI generation gap: Are Gen Z students more interested in adopting generative AI such as ChatGPT in teaching and learning than their Gen X and millennial generation teachers?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how Generation Z undergraduate students and Generation X/Generation Y teachers in higher education perceive, understand, and intend to use generative AI tools such as ChatGPT. The authors were motivated by the rapid rise of GenAI in education and the need to understand whether younger students are more receptive than their teachers, especially given concerns about academic integrity, accuracy, bias, and overreliance.

The study used an online mixed-methods survey with 583 participants (399 students and 184 teachers), combining closed-ended Likert-scale items with open-ended questions. Quantitative analyses compared students and teachers on frequency of GenAI use, perceived benefits, knowledge of limitations, and concerns; qualitative thematic coding identified intended uses and worries about adoption. The context was higher education, primarily in Hong Kong with some participants from mainland China and other regions.

Findings suggest that Gen Z students were somewhat more enthusiastic and more frequent users than teachers, and were more likely to believe GenAI could save time, improve writing, and positively affect teaching and learning. Teachers were more cautious, especially about factual inaccuracies, bias, manipulation, and students becoming over-reliant or using GenAI to get ahead. Both groups nevertheless saw value in GenAI for productivity, information synthesis, writing support, and administrative tasks, while also emphasizing the need for guidelines, policy, critical thinking, and responsible use. The study concludes that GenAI should be integrated thoughtfully rather than banned, with institutions supporting AI literacy and clearer assessment and governance practices.

finding.finding_summary: Both students and teachers reported intending to use GenAI for productivity-related tasks such as summarizing information, drafting emails, writing literature reviews, and assisting with data analysis. In the quantitative survey, students were more likely than teachers to agree that GenAI could help them save time (students M=4.16, teachers M=3.90; t=3.38, p<.001), indicating perceived productivity gains rather than measured performance gains.
finding.measure: Self-reported perceived time saving / productivity and intended use for administrative and writing tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally examines perceived effects on writing and broader transferable skills. Students were more likely than teachers to believe GenAI could help them become better writers (students M=3.29, teachers M=3.06; t=2.07, p=.039), but both groups also worried that reliance on GenAI could undermine originality, creativity, critical thinking, and evaluative skill development. No direct performance test was reported; the evidence is based on self-reported perceptions and intentions.
finding.measure: Self-reported beliefs about writing improvement, originality/creativity, and critical thinking / evaluative skill implications

finding.finding_summary: Writing support was one of the most common intended uses of GenAI for both groups, including improving grammar, proofreading, essay structure, and generating or refining text. Quantitatively, students were more likely than teachers to agree that GenAI could help them become better writers (students M=3.29, teachers M=3.06; t=2.07, p=.039), but participants also raised concerns that using GenAI for essays could reduce originality and creativity.
finding.measure: Self-reported perceived writing support and writing quality implications

finding.finding_summary: The study highlights a strong institutional need for policy, guidelines, and assessment redesign around GenAI use in higher education. Both students and teachers agreed that institutions should have a plan for managing GenAI risks, and qualitative responses repeatedly called for clear strategies, responsible-use protocols, and updated assessment practices; however, this is a perceived governance need rather than a measured institutional outcome.
finding.measure: Self-reported agreement with need for institutional policy, governance, and assessment change

finding.finding_summary: The paper touches on comfort, anxiety, and engagement with learning, but does so indirectly through attitudes toward GenAI rather than direct measurement of social-emotional outcomes. Students were more likely to see GenAI as a useful student support tool because of anonymity (students M=3.73, teachers M=3.53; t=2.07, p=.039), while teachers were more concerned that GenAI could reduce opportunities to interact and socialize during coursework (teachers M=3.43 vs students M=3.09; t=-3.16, p=.002).
finding.measure: Self-reported perceptions of comfort, anonymity, and social interaction during coursework

paper_profiles.title: Opportunities, challenges, and benefits of AI innovation in government services: a review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review examines the opportunities, challenges, and benefits of artificial intelligence (AI) adoption in government services. The paper is motivated by the growing interest in AI for public-sector innovation, while noting that governments face practical barriers such as limited technical expertise, procurement complexity, privacy and bias concerns, and uncertainty about how to evaluate AI impacts in real-world settings.

The article synthesizes existing literature rather than reporting a new empirical study. Its conceptual lens is organizational theory, which the authors use to frame how internal capabilities, regulatory conditions, stakeholder expectations, and resource constraints shape AI adoption in public administration. The review highlights common application areas such as predictive decision-making, document review, sentiment analysis, virtual agents, and service automation, and it uses examples from agencies in New South Wales, the UK NHS, France, and Belgium to illustrate potential uses and benefits.

The main conclusion is that AI can improve administrative efficiency, productivity, and public service delivery, but those gains depend on supportive organizational conditions and responsible governance. The paper emphasizes that successful adoption requires capacity-building, workforce training, trustworthy data practices, procurement reform, and attention to ethics, accountability, fairness, privacy, and legitimacy. Because the paper is a narrative review with no original outcome data, its value is chiefly as adjacent evidence about public-sector AI productivity and institutional change rather than direct causal evidence.

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that AI can improve administrative efficiency, streamline procedures, reduce workloads, and increase productivity in government service delivery. However, it does not report a new empirical estimate; instead, it synthesizes prior literature and examples such as Revenue NSW and NHS workflows that suggest faster processing and automation benefits.
finding.measure: Administrative efficiency, workload reduction, and productivity in government operations

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that AI adoption in the public sector can transform governance, improve public service delivery, and support smarter policy-making, but it also raises significant institutional challenges related to accountability, bias, privacy, procurement, and legitimacy. The review is not a quantitative evaluation; it synthesizes case examples and prior studies to argue that outcomes depend heavily on organizational and regulatory conditions.
finding.measure: Governance, policy-making, institutional readiness, and public service delivery outcomes

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence in local governments: perceptions of city managers on prospects, constraints and choices
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how city managers perceive artificial intelligence (AI) in local government services and operations, addressing a gap in empirical research on public-sector AI adoption. The authors focus on the question of how city managers view AI’s prospects, constraints, and deployment choices, especially in cities with active smart-city and AI agendas.

The study uses semi-structured interviews with 14 city managers from eight local governments in Australia and the United States. Interview data were analyzed using summative content analysis with NVivo and Leximancer, producing themes around AI adoption areas, cautionary areas, challenges, effects, impacts, knowledge base, plans, preparedness, roadblocks, technologies, deployment timeframes, and usefulness.

Findings suggest that managers are broadly optimistic about AI’s ability to create efficiencies, improve productivity, automate routine decisions, and manage repetitive tasks, with applications in asset management, service delivery, data analytics, maintenance, and public services. At the same time, they express substantial caution about bias, black-box systems, privacy, cybersecurity, transparency, legal uncertainty, funding constraints, staff readiness, and public trust. Overall, the paper concludes that local governments are experimenting with AI incrementally rather than comprehensively, and that wider adoption depends on better regulation, governance, capacity building, and stakeholder engagement.

finding.finding_summary: City managers consistently reported that AI is useful for creating efficiencies, improving productivity, automating routine decisions, and managing repetitive tasks and processes in local government. This was based on interviews with 14 city managers; the paper does not report quantitative effect sizes, but the theme was present across all interviews and was linked to service delivery, customer service, and performance review.
finding.measure: Interview-derived perceptions of AI usefulness for efficiencies, productivity, routine decision automation, and error reduction

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that AI is expected to reshape local government institutions by changing adoption practices, increasing experimentation, and widening capability differences across councils. Interviewees also anticipated institutional risks such as budget pressure, legal uncertainty, staff resistance, trust issues, and a widening knowledge gap between councils that can and cannot afford AI.
finding.measure: Interview-derived perceptions of institutional impacts of AI adoption on local government governance, capacity, preparedness, and planning

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI is already widespread in the Public Sector
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how widely generative AI is already being used across UK public-sector work, and whether workers think it can improve productivity and reduce bureaucratic burden. The authors frame generative AI as a bottom-up technology that can be adopted directly by individual workers, unlike traditional centralized public-sector IT systems.

The study uses an online survey administered in November 2023 to 938 UK public service professionals across the NHS, schools, universities, social care, and emergency services. Respondents reported awareness and use of generative AI, trust in outputs, understanding of risks and accountability, and perceptions of productivity, bureaucracy, and public-service improvement. The paper is descriptive and correlational: it does not test an intervention, but instead characterizes adoption patterns and self-reported perceived effects.

The main findings are that generative AI use was already common in this sample: 22% reported using it, with especially high uptake in universities and schools. Users were generally optimistic and believed the tools enhanced productivity and could substantially reduce administrative burden; NHS respondents, for example, estimated bureaucracy could fall from about 50% of work time to under 30% if AI were deployed effectively. At the same time, respondents reported unclear guidance and unclear accountability, suggesting that uptake is growing faster than governance and organizational support.

finding.finding_summary: Public service professionals reported that generative AI improved their productivity and could reduce administrative burden. Among 938 respondents, 22.28% said they used generative AI, and users were 15% more likely to agree that GenAI could reduce time spent on bureaucracy; those users also expected over 5% more time savings on administrative tasks on average (about two additional hours per week). NHS respondents estimated bureaucracy could fall from about 50% of work time to under 30% if AI were effectively deployed.
finding.measure: Self-reported productivity enhancement; self-reported percentage of work time spent on bureaucracy/administration and expected reduction if AI were deployed effectively

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds high uptake and optimism about GenAI in public services, but also substantial governance gaps. Only 32% of respondents felt there was clear workplace guidance on GenAI, and 53% said they understood who is accountable for AI outputs, indicating institutional readiness is lagging behind adoption.
finding.measure: Survey responses on workplace guidance, accountability, optimism about public service improvement, and missing out on AI opportunities

paper_profiles.title: Assessing Generative AI Value in a Public Sector Context: Evidence from a Field Experiment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI can improve productivity on complex knowledge-work tasks in a public-sector setting, where direct evidence from K-12 is limited and task demands differ from commercial workplaces. The authors focus on whether AI changes task quality and completion time for work that involves document comprehension and data analysis.

The study was run at the Central Bank of Ireland with 143 staff members (about 7% of the workforce) in a preregistered randomized experiment. Participants completed baseline assessments and were then randomized to either a control condition or a treatment condition that provided access to GPT-4o-based web applications tailored to the task. Two representative tasks were studied: extracting and synthesizing information from Solvency and Financial Condition Report documents, and answering questions from quantitative reporting templates using insurance data.

Results were mixed and strongly task-dependent. For the document task, Gen AI improved answer quality by 17% and reduced completion time by 34%, with larger gains for lower-performing participants and for questions whose answers were concentrated in one part of the document. For the data task, Gen AI reduced quality by 12% and did not significantly change completion time. The authors conclude that generative AI can boost productivity in public-sector knowledge work, but the benefits depend on task structure, user skill, prompting behavior, and the need for human oversight.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that generative AI improved productivity on one task but not another. In the document-comprehension task (n=143 staff overall), access to GPT-4o-based tools increased answer quality by 17% (mean score 2.21 vs 1.89; mean difference 0.32) and reduced self-reported completion time by 34% (33 vs 50 minutes; 17-minute difference). In the data-analysis task, quality fell by 12% (36.5/40 control vs 32.3/40 treatment) and completion time did not differ significantly (33.5 vs 32.5 minutes).
finding.measure: Task answer quality scores and task completion time
finding.effect_size: Documents: +0.32 quality points and -17 minutes; Data: -4.241 quality points, no significant time effect

finding.finding_summary: The study directly evaluates AI adoption in a public-sector institution, showing that generative AI could improve some forms of knowledge work but may harm others depending on task structure. The evidence is based on a preregistered field experiment at the Central Bank of Ireland and is used by the authors to discuss implications for public-sector workflow design, training, and human oversight.
finding.measure: Public-sector task performance in a central bank / financial regulation context

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence, rationalization, and the limits of control in the public sector: the case of tax policy optimization
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the social, ethical, and political implications of using AI in the public sector, framed through Max Weber’s theory of rationalization and bureaucratization. The authors argue that AI is best understood not as a radical break from existing bureaucratic systems, but as a continuation and intensification of long-running processes that impose calculability, efficiency, and instrumental rationality on social life.

To make the argument concrete, the paper uses a thought experiment about AI-driven tax policy optimization in a nation-state aiming to reduce economic inequality. The proposed system would use continuous experimentation and reinforcement learning to optimize tax policy based on data about incomes, wealth, and taxpayer behavior, potentially automating taxation and policy adjustment. The paper does not present a human-subjects empirical evaluation; instead, it analyzes a hypothetical AI governance scenario alongside related work such as Kasy (2018) and Zheng et al. (2022).

The main conclusion is that AI-driven policy optimization could improve efficiency and make normative goals more explicit, but it also creates important tensions: it can exclude competing values, instrumentalize citizens, and undermine self-determination. The authors argue that these risks are not primarily failures of AI systems, but consequences of their success as tools of rationalization. They conclude that transparency and safety measures are useful but insufficient to resolve the deeper normative issues raised by AI in public administration.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI systems can improve the efficiency, consistency, and calculability of public-sector decision-making, including tax administration and policy optimization. However, this is presented as a conceptual claim and thought experiment rather than an empirical test, so no effect size, sample size, or statistical estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of policy efficiency, consistency, and calculability in tax administration

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central contribution is a normative analysis of how AI-driven tax policy optimization could reshape public institutions and democratic governance. It argues that AI may help make normative goals explicit and subject to scrutiny, but also risks concentrating decision power, overriding competing values, and changing the relationship between citizens and the state; no empirical effect size is reported because the paper is argumentative rather than empirical.
finding.measure: Normative and conceptual analysis of public-sector governance, bureaucracy, and democratic deliberation

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing Communication Quality between Government and Citizens: The Role of AI Modification
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether AI language modification improves the quality of written communication between government agencies and citizens. The authors focus on a central public-administration question: whether AI can improve not only informational clarity, but also relational and trust-related dimensions of communication, such as politeness, feeling heard, empathy, and trust.

The intervention studied is AI-assisted rewriting of real government-citizen messages using GPT-4o. The researchers selected 20 real message-response pairs from a Chinese public message board and modified them to produce clearer, more polite, and more empathetic versions. They then used a vignette-based survey with 220 citizens and 214 civil servants in Mainland China, asking participants to rate original versus AI-modified messages across five interaction contexts: service requests, policy inquiries, complaints, suggestions, and emergencies.

Results from paired t-tests and mixed-effects regression analyses show that AI-modified messages were consistently rated more favorably on all measured dimensions for both audiences. Citizens perceived AI-modified government responses as clearer, more satisfying, more polite, more empathic, and more trustworthy. Civil servants also perceived AI-modified citizen messages as clearer, easier to reply to, more polite, and more respectful, with the authors arguing that AI can reduce administrative burden and improve communication efficiency.

The paper concludes that AI modification can enhance both the informational and relational quality of government-citizen communication, although the authors also note that some effects are context-sensitive and that concerns about emotional flattening may be less severe than critics suggest. Because the study is vignette-based and perceptual rather than behavioral, it provides adjacent evidence for productivity and efficiency gains in public-sector communication rather than direct evidence of operational performance in K-12 settings.

finding.finding_summary: AI-modified citizen messages were rated as easier for civil servants to respond to, indicating lower communication burden and higher processing efficiency. In the mixed-effects models, AI modification had a positive coefficient for easiness of reply (not shown in the excerpted table for the civil-servant outcomes, but described in the results) and in the citizen-side models AI modification also improved response clarity and satisfaction, suggesting smoother two-way communication overall. The study is vignette-based with 214 civil servants and 220 citizens (N=1,320 evaluations from citizens; N=1,284 from civil servants).
finding.measure: Civil servants' ratings of information clarity and easiness of reply for citizen messages; citizens' ratings of clarity and response satisfaction for government replies
finding.study_size: n=214 civil servants; n=220 citizens; 1,284 civil-servant evaluations and 1,320 citizen evaluations

finding.finding_summary: AI-modified communication improved perceived trust, politeness, empathy, and responsiveness in government-citizen exchanges, suggesting institutional benefits for public administration. In the citizen-side mixed-effects regressions, AI modification increased trust toward government by 0.268 (95% CI: 0.152–0.379), expressed politeness by 0.339 (95% CI: 0.251–0.429), and feeling of being heard by 0.244 (95% CI: 0.130–0.355), all p < 0.001 or p < 0.05. The study directly frames these effects as improvements in digital governance and administrative communication quality.
finding.measure: Citizen perceptions of trust toward government, feeling heard, politeness, empathy, satisfaction, and clarity in written government responses
finding.effect_size: 0.268 for trust; 0.339 for politeness; 0.244 for feeling heard; 0.271 for empathy; 0.280 for satisfaction; 0.105 for clarity
finding.confidence_interval: trust: 0.152–0.379; politeness: 0.251–0.429; feeling heard: 0.130–0.355; satisfaction: 0.246–0.428; clarity: 0.000–0.201; empathy: 0.161–0.388

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI as a lab partner: a case study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This case study examines how high school students use ChatGPT during a physics laboratory session on acoustic levitation and measuring the speed of sound in air. The paper addresses a practical question in AI-in-education research: when students have limited prior knowledge and only vague lab instructions, what kinds of help do they seek from generative AI, and how does that interaction affect their learning and problem solving? The authors frame the work with variation theory to interpret how students’ awareness shifts during the lab.

Seven student groups (n=19) in Swedish high school physics courses participated in a lab where they collected data with an acoustic levitation setup and then used the free version of ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) as needed. The study collected video recordings, chat logs, written notes, and pre/post group interviews. The lab design intentionally left the analysis somewhat underspecified so that students would need to ask ChatGPT for formulas, conceptual explanations, or help interpreting the task.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT functioned more like a quick-reference lab partner than a reliable autonomous helper: it was useful for simple explanations, formula retrieval, and basic checks, but students often struggled to judge correctness unless they already had relevant background knowledge. Groups with stronger physics knowledge could more effectively probe and verify ChatGPT’s answers, while weaker groups tended to accept vague or misleading responses and sometimes drifted away from the intended learning goals. The paper concludes that generative AI may support laboratory learning, but only when students have sufficient prior knowledge and guidance to evaluate outputs critically; teachers remain essential for directing attention to the relevant scientific ideas.

finding.finding_summary: Students used ChatGPT to identify relevant formulas, interpret acoustic levitation, and support analysis of the speed of sound, but the tool’s usefulness depended strongly on students’ prior physics knowledge. Groups with more background knowledge could better detect incorrect or misleading answers, while less prepared groups often accepted vague responses and sometimes formed incorrect explanations (e.g., about how levitation works).
finding.measure: Qualitative analysis of lab interactions, chat logs, and pre/post interviews during a physics laboratory on acoustic levitation and speed of sound

finding.finding_summary: The study found that ChatGPT sometimes supported students’ problem-solving and metacognitive checking, especially for groups that actively cross-checked answers and asked follow-up questions. However, overreliance and weak question formulation limited these benefits for many groups, and the paper emphasizes that students need training in how to ask good questions and evaluate AI output critically.
finding.measure: Qualitative observation of problem-solving behavior, follow-up prompting, and group discussion during the lab

finding.finding_summary: Students generally viewed ChatGPT as helpful for quick explanations and simple support, but most remained skeptical about using it for calculations or analysis. Some groups expressed trust in its ability to provide reasonable estimates, while others were cautious and felt the need to double-check facts, indicating mixed effects on confidence, trust, and reliance during the lab.
finding.measure: Pre- and post-lab group interviews about perceived usefulness and trustworthiness of ChatGPT

paper_profiles.title: Responsible AI Adoption in the Public Sector: A Data-Centric Taxonomy of AI Adoption Challenges
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 59th Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences (HICSS 2026)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines why responsible AI adoption in the public sector remains difficult, focusing specifically on data-related and governance-related barriers rather than on AI model performance itself. The authors argue that responsible AI frameworks are often aspirational because they overlook foundational conditions such as data quality, interoperability, governance, and institutional pressures that determine whether AI can actually be adopted in lawful, fair, transparent, and sustainable ways.

To address this gap, the study conducts a systematic literature review of 43 papers on AI and public sector data ecosystems, then refines the findings through validation with 21 experts from public administration, information systems, and related fields. Using the TOE framework and Institutional Theory, the authors develop a taxonomy of 13 challenges spanning technological, organizational, environmental, and cross-cutting dimensions. These include limited access to suitable data sources, poor AI-ready data, weak governance, human-AI misalignment, low literacy among stakeholders, privacy/security risks, and economic and environmental sustainability concerns.

The paper is not an intervention or outcome study; instead, it provides a diagnostic conceptual framework for researchers and practitioners. Its main conclusion is that public sector AI adoption problems are socio-technical and institutionally embedded, and that progress in responsible AI depends on improving data ecosystems, governance arrangements, and institutional readiness—not only on better algorithms or tools.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that responsible AI adoption in the public sector is constrained by a mix of technological, organizational, and environmental barriers that are reinforced by coercive, normative, and mimetic institutional pressures. Based on a systematic review of 43 studies and validation by 21 experts, the authors identify 13 recurring challenges, including weak governance, legal ambiguity, accountability gaps, privacy and transparency concerns, and coordination failures across agencies.
finding.measure: Systematic review synthesis and expert validation of AI adoption challenges in public-sector data ecosystems

paper_profiles.title: Artificial Intelligence in Government: Why People Feel They Lose Control
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This working paper asks how citizens perceive the use of artificial intelligence in public administration, with a particular focus on whether AI-driven efficiency gains come at the cost of perceived control and trust. The authors frame AI adoption as a principal-agent problem, arguing that delegating administrative tasks to AI creates structural tensions around assessability, dependency, and contestability.

To test these ideas, the authors field a preregistered factorial survey experiment with a stratified UK adult sample recruited through Prolific (main study n=1,198; pretest n=301). Participants evaluated vignettes about AI use in three government domains: tax administration, welfare benefits, and bail risk assessment. The vignettes varied whether AI was described as beneficial only or as also creating assessability, dependency, or contestability risks.

The main finding is that AI framed as improving efficiency modestly increased trust in government, but it also reduced perceived control. When AI delegation risks were made salient, trust and perceived control both fell substantially, and support for expanding AI use declined. The paper concludes that even when AI delivers short-term efficiency gains, public reactions may become negative once people recognize the governance and accountability costs of delegation.

finding.finding_summary: When AI was described as handling routine government tasks and producing tangible efficiency benefits, trust in government increased by an average of 0.5 points on a 1-7 scale (from 3.21 to 3.71; β=0.36, 95% CI [0.28, 0.43], p<0.001). This result comes from a factorial survey experiment with n=1,198 UK adults; the paper does not report an effect size in standardized mean-difference terms, but characterizes the gain as moderate.
finding.measure: Perceived trust in government after vignette exposure to AI-enabled routine government service delivery

finding.finding_summary: The study shows a dual institutional effect of AI in government: efficiency-focused AI vignettes increased trust, but all AI risk conditions (dependency, contestability, assessability) significantly eroded institutional trust and increased perceived loss of control. In the main experiment (n=1,198), perceived loss of control rose from 4.14 in the human condition to 5.43 in the dependency and assessability conditions and 5.36 in the contestability condition; the authors also report large, statistically significant treatment effects on AI delegation preferences, with 65.6% to 70.5% of respondents preferring less AI under risk-framed conditions.
finding.measure: Trust in government, perceived loss of control, and AI delegation preference in response to government AI vignettes
finding.confidence_interval: Dependency 95% CI [0.80, 0.97]; Contestability 95% CI [0.76, 0.92]; Assessability 95% CI [0.80, 0.97]

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks Middle School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether teachers should remain “in the loop” when using generative AI to personalize mathematics tasks for students. The authors focus on a practical question with growing relevance in AI-enabled instruction: whether teacher-mediated use of ChatGPT can produce meaningful personalization while also being time efficient enough to justify the workflow.

Seven seventh-grade math teachers from six U.S. schools used GPT-4o/ChatGPT to adapt existing Illustrative Mathematics problems for their students’ interests across two curriculum units. The study analyzed 143 personalized problems, 558 total prompts, ChatGPT interaction logs, teacher audio/video, and student survey responses from 521 students (with 446–454 open-ended responses across items and 52–53 problems receiving closed-ended ratings). The paper codes teacher prompting behavior, student reactions, and measures of teacher efficiency, then compares teacher performance and student ratings across Unit 4 and Unit 6.

The main conclusion is that teacher-in-the-loop personalization is feasible but not especially time efficient. Teachers spent about 4 minutes per problem on average and often needed multiple prompts to refine realism, cultural fit, readability, and mathematical clarity. Student feedback suggested they preferred smaller-grain, more specific popular-culture references, while teachers often used broader categories and spent substantial effort making contexts realistic. Teachers appeared to improve in sophistication over time, but not in speed; in fact, they used more prompts and more time in the second unit, though student ratings of interestingness and closeness also improved. The authors argue that this approach can support teacher learning and better monitoring of depth and appropriateness, but that it may not scale well for fine-grained personalization.

finding.finding_summary: Teacher-in-the-loop personalization was time-consuming. Across 143 problems, teachers used 558 prompts (3.2 prompts/problem, SD=2.6) and spent an average of 246 seconds per problem (about 4 minutes, SD=165.7). The authors conclude that this process did not become particularly time efficient as teachers gained experience; in Unit 6 teachers actually used more prompts and more time than in Unit 4.
finding.measure: Teacher time spent creating personalized problems; number of prompts per problem

finding.finding_summary: Student interest and perceived closeness to their interests were modestly positive overall, but limited. For the 53 problems with closed-ended ratings, the mean interestingness rating was 2.46/5 and mean closeness rating was 2.53/5, suggesting only moderate engagement. Student open-ended responses often indicated preference for specific popular-culture references, but many also said the problems were uninteresting or not aligned with their preferences.
finding.measure: Student ratings of interestingness and closeness to interests; open-ended feedback on interest
finding.study_size: n=521 students; closed-ended ratings for 53 problems; open-ended responses from 446-454 responses per item
finding.effect_size: B=0.240 (3-5 prompts vs other prompt counts)

finding.finding_summary: The study primarily centers on mathematics problem personalization rather than achievement outcomes, and it does not measure learning or test performance. Still, the paper reports that teachers frequently had to correct mathematical realism, quantities, and context fit (e.g., 76 prompts about numbers/quantities and 64 about realism of the context), while relatively few prompts addressed mathematical clarity (16 instances). The authors note that students’ ratings were higher when teachers used 3-5 prompts, but no direct learning gains were measured.
finding.measure: Quality/realism of personalized mathematics problems; student interest/closeness ratings, not achievement
finding.effect_size: B=0.240 for student ratings when using 3-5 prompts; no achievement effect reported

finding.finding_summary: Teachers appeared to improve their ability to craft interesting problems with GPT-4o over time, but this improvement came with greater effort rather than efficiency. The authors describe growth in prompting sophistication and in the ability to monitor realism, age-appropriateness, and ownership, though they do not report a direct durable-skills metric or standardized assessment.
finding.measure: Teacher prompting practices and qualitative evidence of growth across Unit 4 vs Unit 6

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI for FFRDCs
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper discusses how generative AI and large language models can support the work of federally funded research and development centers (FFRDCs), which routinely handle large volumes of policy documents, scientific papers, and other text-heavy materials. The central problem is that these workflows are slow to execute manually and often involve sensitive data that cannot easily be sent to external cloud services.

The paper presents OnPrem.LLM, an open-source, privacy-conscious toolkit for document intelligence that supports local or hybrid deployment. It includes modules for ingestion, retrieval, summarization, classification, extraction, agents, and a Streamlit-based web UI, with emphasis on auditability, structured outputs, and on-premises use in sensitive government contexts.

Rather than reporting a controlled evaluation, the paper provides illustrative case studies using publicly available examples such as the National Defense Authorization Act, Request for Information responses, Federal Acquisition Regulation text, and NSF awards data. The main conclusion is that LLMs can accelerate summarization, classification, extraction, and question answering for oversight and strategic analysis, while still requiring human oversight and safeguards against hallucination, over-reliance, and data exposure.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can substantially reduce time spent on text-heavy workflows in FFRDC settings, such as summarization, coding open-ended survey responses, extraction, and document question answering. It gives a qualitative example that coding RFI responses can be reduced from weeks to minutes, but does not provide a controlled experiment or quantitative effect size.
finding.measure: Time needed for summarization, classification, extraction, and question answering in document-analysis workflows

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents generative AI as a tool for improving oversight, strategic analysis, and horizon scanning in government research institutions. It emphasizes on-premises deployment, auditability, and data sovereignty as institutional benefits for sensitive public-sector contexts, but provides no formal outcome evaluation.
finding.measure: Oversight quality, strategic analysis capability, and institutional data-governance practices

paper_profiles.title: Artificial Intelligence Driven Course Generation: A Case Study Using ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can be used to efficiently generate full educational course materials, addressing the practical problem of time-consuming and resource-intensive course development. The author argues that while AI is already used for tutoring, grading, and administrative tasks, there is limited empirical evidence on its use for producing complete, high-quality course content.

Using a qualitative case study design, the paper documents the generation of an 87-page Multimedia Databases course for a first-year master's program in Systems and Multimedia at Chahid Cheikh Laarbi Tebessi University in Algeria. The workflow included translating the official outline from French to English, expanding it into sections and subsections, generating theoretical explanations, practical examples, assignments, supplementary materials, and formatting everything in LaTeX. The resulting content was immediately reviewed by the author, checked with Detectia and Turnitin for originality, reviewed by two English teachers and two field experts, and then approved by a university scientific committee.

The paper concludes that ChatGPT can produce comprehensive course materials in less than one day with high originality and acceptable academic and linguistic quality. The author emphasizes substantial time savings, scalability, customization, and potential cost reductions, while also noting limitations related to prompt quality, the need for human oversight, and ethical concerns such as accuracy and bias. The study positions AI as a tool that can free educators to spend more time on interactive and personalized teaching.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT substantially reduced the time required to create a complete course package. The paper reports that an 87-page, 10-chapter Multimedia Databases course with practical assignments was generated in less than one day / within a few hours, suggesting major productivity gains for educators in course preparation.
finding.measure: Time to generate complete course content; originality checks; expert review of generated materials

finding.finding_summary: The generated course was reviewed and approved by university teachers, field experts, and the faculty scientific committee, indicating that AI-assisted content creation can be institutionally acceptable within higher education governance processes. The paper argues this may support scalable curriculum development and reduce institutional resource burdens.
finding.measure: Expert review, committee approval, institutional acceptance of course materials
finding.study_size: n=1 course case study; 2 English teachers; 2 field experts; informal feedback from 15 students

paper_profiles.title: Artificial Intelligence in Deliberation: The AI Penalty and the Emergence of a New Deliberative Divide
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether informing people that artificial intelligence, rather than humans, performs key tasks in deliberative democratic processes changes their willingness to participate and their perceptions of deliberative quality. The authors focus on a central tension in AI-enabled civic participation: although AI may improve information processing, moderation, fact-checking, and summarization, it may also affect public trust, voice, and recognition.

To test this, the authors ran a preregistered survey experiment with a representative sample of adults in Germany (n=1,850). Respondents were shown descriptions of deliberative tasks such as balanced participation, topic selection, content summarization, argument structuring, fact-checking, disruption detection, translation support, and role-play empathy, with each task randomly attributed to either AI or human facilitators. The outcomes were willingness to participate in such deliberative formats and an index of perceived deliberative quality.

The study finds a clear "AI-penalty": participants were less willing to engage in AI-facilitated deliberation and rated AI-facilitated deliberation as lower quality than human-led formats. The penalty was moderated by attitudes toward AI: higher perceived AI benefits, lower AI risk perceptions, greater AI anthropomorphism, and in one case more AI experience, reduced or eliminated the penalty. The authors conclude that AI in deliberation may create a new participation divide based on AI attitudes, not traditional demographic or educational inequalities.

finding.finding_summary: Information that deliberative tasks were facilitated by AI rather than humans reduced perceived deliberative quality and willingness to participate, indicating a clear AI-penalty for AI-enabled deliberative institutions. In the pooled experiment (total observations=11,000 from n=1,850 participants), AI-enabled formats were rated lower in quality (b = -0.29, 95% CI [-0.32, -0.26]) and drew lower participation interest (b = -0.30, 95% CI [-0.34, -0.26]).
finding.measure: Willingness to participate in deliberative formats and index of deliberative quality

finding.finding_summary: Although the paper is not a direct skills intervention study, it centrally examines whether AI-facilitated deliberation affects participants' willingness to engage in activities requiring deliberation, judgment, and collaborative discussion. The treatment reduced interest in participating in such formats overall (b = -0.30, 95% CI [-0.34, -0.26]), suggesting a negative effect on engagement with deliberative processes that depend on durable skills.
finding.measure: Willingness to participate in deliberative formats

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI in Knowledge Work: Perception, Usefulness, and Acceptance of Microsoft 365 Copilot
paper_profiles.population: Adult employees in a non-university research organization
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This preprint examines how employees in a large non-university research organization perceive and use Microsoft 365 Copilot during its early rollout. The paper asks whether scientific and administrative staff differ in their assessments of usefulness, ease of use, output quality, and reliability, and whether these perceptions change over time across two repeated cross-sectional survey waves.

The study was conducted during a technical pilot in a German research organization. In May 2024, 550 employees received Copilot licenses and were invited to participate in surveys; the analysis focuses on two measurement points: T01 (November–December 2024; n=106) and T02 (March–April 2025; n=90), split between administrative and scientific staff. The survey used established technology-acceptance constructs and also asked about task-specific usefulness for typical knowledge-work activities such as information gathering, analysis, text creation, learning, feedback, and networking.

Results show generally positive perceptions of Copilot, especially for structured, text-based tasks. Administrative staff rated usefulness and output quality higher at T01, but scientific staff showed significant gains over time in perceived usefulness and ease of use, suggesting learning and routinization effects. Perceived reliability stayed positive and relatively stable, while harm from incorrect output remained low. The paper concludes that generative AI appears most useful for formalized language- and information-based work, and that successful implementation depends on context-sensitive training, governance, and alignment with task profiles rather than technical capability alone.

finding.finding_summary: The study found generally positive and improving perceptions of Copilot’s usefulness for productivity-related work. Scientific employees showed a significant increase in perceived usefulness from T01 to T02 (d=0.42, p=.022; n=106 at T01 and n=90 at T02 overall), and the usefulness scale explicitly captured performance improvement, effectiveness, workload reduction, increased productivity, and faster task completion.
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness scale (5 items) covering performance improvement, increased effectiveness, workload reduction, increased productivity, and faster task completion

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes organizational implementation effects, showing that Copilot adoption changed acceptance perceptions over time and that success depended on context-sensitive implementation, role-specific training, and governance. Although the findings are based on subjective survey data rather than objective organizational metrics, the authors argue that generative AI can create organizational value when embedded appropriately in work processes.
finding.measure: Survey-based acceptance, implementation, and task-usefulness perceptions in a non-university research organization

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI and LLMs in Industry: A text-mining Analysis and Critical Evaluation of Guidelines and Policy Statements Across Fourteen Industrial Sectors
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how companies and organizations across 14 industrial sectors are writing and implementing guidelines and policy statements for generative AI and large language models (LLMs). The central question is not whether AI works in a controlled experiment, but how industry is governing its use amid concerns about efficiency, safety, privacy, bias, intellectual property, and regulatory compliance.

The authors collected 160 policy documents and related statements from companies spanning sectors such as healthcare, finance, publishing, translation, construction, consulting, fashion, entertainment, journalism, pharmaceuticals, and legal services. They then used text-mining methods, including tokenization, TF-IDF, and KMeans clustering, to identify recurring themes and sector-specific patterns in AI governance.

Across sectors, the paper finds strong interest in using generative AI to improve productivity, automate repetitive work, and enhance decision-making, but with heavy emphasis on human oversight, transparency, and security. The conclusions are largely descriptive: organizations are adopting AI cautiously and unevenly, and most documents frame AI as a tool to augment human work rather than replace it. Because the study analyzes policies and public statements rather than measuring outcomes directly, it provides adjacent evidence about expected productivity gains and operational efficiency, but not causal evidence of those gains.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that across many industries, organizations describe generative AI and LLMs as tools to improve productivity, streamline workflows, automate repetitive tasks, and enhance operational efficiency. This is a document-based synthesis of 160 company guidelines and policy statements, not an outcome evaluation, so no effect size or sample-level productivity estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Company guidelines and policy statements describing productivity, workflow automation, and operational efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that organizations across 14 sectors are developing AI governance structures, policies, and principles to manage risks such as privacy, bias, safety, and intellectual property concerns. The main institutional impact is the emergence of sector-specific and cross-sector AI governance frameworks, but the paper does not measure downstream institutional performance effects.
finding.measure: Presence and content of AI governance guidelines, policy statements, and organizational principles

paper_profiles.title: Cyber Humanism in Education: Reclaiming Agency through AI and Learning Sciences
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues that generative AI in education should be understood not as an external tool to be adopted or resisted, but as part of the cognitive and institutional infrastructures of learning. The central problem is how to preserve and expand human agency, epistemic judgment, and democratic participation when large language models increasingly mediate reading, writing, coding, feedback, and decision-making.

To address this, the paper develops a framework called Cyber Humanism in Education, built around three pillars: reflexive competence, algorithmic citizenship, and dialogic design. It then connects this framework to existing AI/digital competence frameworks and illustrates it through higher-education case studies, including prompt-based learning activities and a Conversational AI Educator certification in the EPICT ecosystem. These cases are presented as design examples rather than controlled evaluations.

The paper’s context is higher education and educator professional development, with examples drawn from social sciences, digital humanities, and engineering. Its main conclusion is that prompt-based learning and structured educator certification can support more reflective, governed, and human-centered AI use, while also surfacing tensions around workload, equity, bias, and the risk of cognitive outsourcing. The paper is conceptual and practice-oriented; it does not report experimental impact estimates, but argues for new professional roles and institutional governance mechanisms to support AI-rich learning environments.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that conversational AI tools and prompt-based learning can support productivity in educator work and student tasks by helping generate, explain, and refine outputs more quickly, but it does not provide quantitative evidence of gains. It also emphasizes that these same practices may increase workload for educators because designing reflective, governed AI activities requires time, iteration, and institutional support.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of educator workload, task completion, and AI-assisted productivity in certification and classroom design

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents the Conversational AI Educator certification and related cyber-humanist practices as mechanisms for reshaping institutional AI governance, professional roles, and policy alignment. It argues that these structures can formalize educator agency, support institutional AI strategy, and create communities of practice around responsible AI use, but again does not test these effects empirically.
finding.measure: Institutional design, professional certification model, and governance implications for AI use in education

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly emphasizes reflexive competence, metacognition, critical evaluation, and dialogic engagement as intended outcomes of prompt-based learning. It argues that students comparing prompts, analyzing hallucinations and bias, and justifying AI-assisted decisions can strengthen critical thinking and epistemic agency, but the evidence remains illustrative rather than measured.
finding.measure: Reflexive competence, metacognition, critical evaluation of AI outputs, and dialogic engagement in prompt-based learning activities

paper_profiles.title: Improving municipal responsiveness through AI-powered image analysis in E-Government
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether machine learning can improve responsiveness and efficiency in municipal e-government workflows, specifically for citizen-submitted image-based petitions. The author argues that existing e-government systems have focused heavily on text, while image submissions are increasingly common for reporting urban issues such as potholes, waste disposal, illegal parking, and infrastructure damage.

Using anonymized data from a Romanian municipality for the year 2022, the study builds an image-analysis pipeline combining preprocessing, Faster R-CNN for object detection, and a fine-tuned ResNet-50 for classification. The system was trained on 5,712 citizen-submitted images and evaluated on a train-validation split, with manual annotation by municipal public services analysts. The paper reports a validation classification accuracy of 92.8% and average processing time of 3.1 seconds per image, compared with an estimated 8 minutes per case in the traditional manual workflow.

The main conclusion is that AI-based image analysis can substantially reduce administrative workload, accelerate issue triage and response, and improve consistency and responsiveness in municipal service delivery. The author presents the work as a proof-of-concept for e-government 3.0, emphasizing scalability, cost-effectiveness on relatively modest hardware, and the potential to support more transparent and citizen-centric governance. However, the paper also notes important limitations, including a lack of an independent test set, potential generalization issues, and the need for further validation in other municipal contexts.

finding.finding_summary: The proposed AI workflow substantially improved municipal processing speed and labor efficiency for citizen-submitted image cases. On a Dell XPS 9510 laptop, average processing time fell from about 8 minutes per case in the manual workflow to under 7 seconds per case in the ML workflow, a reported time savings of approximately 98.5%; the system also processed up to 500 cases per hour.
finding.measure: Case processing time; throughput; workload/time savings in municipal petition handling

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that ML-based image analysis improved the accuracy and responsiveness of public institutions in handling e-petitions. The model achieved 92.8% validation accuracy on 5,712 citizen-submitted images and was used to automate report generation and citizen communication, suggesting improved service delivery and institutional responsiveness.
finding.measure: Classification accuracy; responsiveness of municipal service delivery; automated report generation and citizen communication

paper_profiles.title: Harnessing the Potential of Gen-AI Coding Assistants in Public Sector Software Development
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI coding assistants, especially GitHub Copilot, can improve software developer productivity in the Singapore public sector, where secure and compliant development is a major constraint. The authors frame the work as an engineering productivity pilot under GovTech Singapore’s Engineering Productivity Programme and focus on the development phase of the software lifecycle, where AI assistants might reduce repetitive coding work, accelerate learning, and improve output quality.

The study deployed GitHub Copilot for Business over four months (Oct 2023–Jan 2024) with 70 volunteer developers working on public-sector applications via SHIP-HATS/GitLab. The evaluation combined telemetry (prompt acceptance and accepted lines of code) with a SPACE-based survey completed by 40 respondents, mostly from GovTech. Reported findings include a 22% reduction in coding time, a 28% increase in coding speed, a 24% average productivity increase, and strong satisfaction gains (95% reported being able to focus on more satisfying work). Junior developers appeared to benefit more than senior staff, while security benefits were limited and not clearly improved. The paper concludes that coding assistants can yield meaningful productivity gains in public-sector software development, but these gains are moderated by context, expertise level, and security/compliance constraints.

finding.finding_summary: The pilot found meaningful productivity gains from GitHub Copilot in public-sector software development. Across 70 participants, respondents reported a 22% reduction in coding time, a 28% increase in coding speed, and a 24% average productivity increase; the authors further estimate this translates to roughly a 12% overall developer productivity gain because about half of developers’ time was spent in the IDE.
finding.measure: Coding time reduction, task completion speed, productivity increase from telemetry and SPACE survey responses
finding.study_size: n=70 pilot participants; n=40 survey respondents
finding.effect_size: Reported 22% coding time reduction; 28% coding speed increase; 24% productivity increase; estimated 12% overall productivity gain

finding.finding_summary: The survey showed strong gains in developer satisfaction and perceived fulfillment. A large majority of respondents (95%) agreed that coding assistants let them focus on more satisfying work and feel more fulfilled at their jobs, suggesting positive effects on motivation and work experience.
finding.measure: Developer satisfaction, job fulfillment, perceived ability to focus on satisfying work
finding.effect_size: 95% agreement on improved satisfaction/fulfillment; 90% said the department should provide coding assistants

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports learning acceleration, especially for less experienced developers. Around three-quarters of respondents agreed that GitHub Copilot helped them learn new languages faster, indicating improved skill development and onboarding support; interviews also noted that learning gains may be weaker or risky for developers without strong fundamentals.
