finding.measure: Self-reported learning acceleration / learning new languages faster

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI coding assistants can improve public-sector software delivery and should inform institutional policy and tooling decisions. It recommends governance actions such as AI usage playbooks, security/compliance policies, and consideration of cloud vs self-hosted deployment to enable broader adoption across an estimated 8,000 public-sector developers.
finding.measure: Institutional recommendations, adoption implications, and public-sector deployment considerations

paper_profiles.title: Assessing the Quality of AI-Generated Exams: A Large-Scale Field Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models can generate high-quality, course-specific exam questions for college classes. The authors focus on a practical educational problem: instructors spend substantial time creating assessments, and there is limited evidence about whether AI-generated items can match human-created questions in real classroom settings.

The study introduces an iterative refinement pipeline that repeatedly generates, critiques, and revises multiple-choice questions using instructor-provided materials such as syllabi, course descriptions, and prior homework or exams. The resulting questions were deployed in a large field study across 182 college classes in the United States, with a final analyzed sample of 91 classes and 1,686 students; 71 classes received AI-generated exams and 20 statistics classes received benchmark questions drawn from a public AP Statistics exam.

Student responses were analyzed using item response theory to compare difficulty, discrimination, and test information. The AI-generated items were, on average, somewhat easier than the standardized-test benchmark questions but slightly more discriminating, and the AI-generated 10-question exams showed higher maximum test information and reliability in this sample. The authors conclude that generative AI can produce customized assessments with psychometric properties comparable to expert-written items, potentially reducing instructor workload and expanding access to high-quality assessments.

finding.finding_summary: The study argues that AI-assisted exam generation can reduce instructor time spent creating assessments by automatically producing and refining course-specific multiple-choice questions. Although the paper does not directly measure time savings, it positions the approach as a way to make high-quality assessments more readily available and to offload question creation from instructors.
finding.measure: AI-generated exam question production and refinement workflow; qualitative claim about instructor workload reduction

finding.finding_summary: Across 91 college classes and 1,686 students, the AI-generated questions performed comparably to expert-created standardized-test questions in psychometric quality. The paper reports that the AI items were somewhat easier on average (mean difficulty βAI = -0.45 vs βSTD = 0.35; difference E[δβ] = -0.79, 95% credible interval [-0.94, -0.65]) and slightly more discriminating (mean αAI = 1.3 vs αSTD = 1.2; difference E[δα] = 0.09, 95% credible interval [-0.0918, 0.253]).
finding.measure: Item difficulty, item discrimination, and test information from item response theory on multiple-choice exams
finding.confidence_interval: difficulty difference 95% CrI [-0.94, -0.65]; discrimination difference 95% CrI [-0.0918, 0.253]

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing healthcare: the role of artificial intelligence in clinical practice
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review surveys the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in clinical practice, with emphasis on how AI may improve diagnosis, treatment selection, patient engagement, population health management, and healthcare workflow. The paper is framed around the broader question of how AI can be responsibly integrated into healthcare systems and what benefits and risks accompany that integration.

The article synthesizes indexed literature from PubMed/Medline, Scopus, and EMBASE with no time constraints and English-language limits. It discusses AI applications including machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, large language models, virtual health assistants, predictive analytics, and clinical decision support across settings such as diagnostics, laboratory medicine, emergency care, genomics, treatment optimization, mental health, and patient education.

Overall, the review concludes that AI shows strong promise for improving accuracy, reducing costs, saving time, and reducing human error in healthcare, while also supporting clinicians with decision-making and automating some routine tasks. At the same time, it emphasizes major implementation barriers such as data quality, privacy, bias, cybersecurity, lack of transparency, and the need for human oversight. The paper is largely descriptive and synthesizes prior findings rather than reporting a single original empirical study.

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that AI tools can improve workflow efficiency, reduce costs, and save time in healthcare settings, particularly by automating routine tasks, supporting decision-making, and streamlining laboratory and emergency department processes. It cites prior studies showing improvements such as faster laboratory turnaround and better triage/resource allocation, but the paper itself does not report a new pooled effect estimate.
finding.measure: workflow efficiency, time savings, cost reduction, task automation

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses AI’s influence on guideline development, regulatory frameworks, implementation standards, and healthcare governance. It argues that AI can accelerate evidence synthesis and guideline updating, while also noting the need for transparency, ethical oversight, privacy protections, and coordinated institutional regulation.
finding.measure: guideline development, regulatory frameworks, healthcare governance

paper_profiles.title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI): Concepts, Taxonomies, Opportunities and Challenges toward Responsible AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a broad survey of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) rather than an empirical study of a specific intervention. It asks what explainability means in machine learning, why it matters, what goals it serves, and how existing methods can be organized into a coherent taxonomy. The authors argue that explanation must be defined relative to the audience, because the details that make a model understandable depend on who is receiving the explanation and for what purpose.

The paper reviews roughly 400 prior contributions and organizes them into two main families: transparent models and post-hoc explainability techniques. Transparent models are discussed through the lenses of simulatability, decomposability, and algorithmic transparency; post-hoc methods include text explanations, visualizations, local explanations, explanations by example, simplification, and feature relevance methods. The paper also distinguishes a set of goals for XAI, including trustworthiness, causality, transferability, informativeness, confidence, fairness, accessibility, interactivity, and privacy awareness.

Its main conclusion is that XAI is a foundational requirement for the practical deployment of AI in high-stakes settings, but the field still lacks agreed-upon definitions and robust metrics for evaluating explanation quality. The authors ultimately connect XAI to a broader notion of Responsible AI, arguing that explainability must be considered alongside fairness, accountability, privacy, and security when deploying AI in real organizations. Although the paper is highly relevant to responsible AI and institutional deployment, it does not present original educational or productivity outcome data.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that explainable AI is crucial for the practical deployment of AI in real organizations and should be part of a broader Responsible AI framework alongside fairness, accountability, privacy, and security. This is a conceptual claim supported by a review of approximately 400 XAI contributions, not by a new empirical evaluation.
finding.measure: Conceptual review of XAI literature and taxonomy development

paper_profiles.title: Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE): Explanation and Elaboration
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an explanatory companion to the STROBE Statement, which was developed to improve how observational studies are reported. It does not test an AI intervention or an educational program; instead, it explains the rationale behind each of the 22 checklist items used to report cohort, case-control, and cross-sectional studies clearly and transparently.

The article is aimed at researchers, journal editors, and reviewers working with observational health research. It draws on empirical reporting literature and methodological examples to show why details such as study design, participant selection, variable definitions, measurement, bias, study size, and statistical methods should be reported. The main conclusion is that better reporting improves critical appraisal, interpretation, and reuse of observational evidence, but the paper itself provides no original empirical results and no intervention effect estimates.

Because this is a reporting guideline/explanatory document, the paper’s relevance to the retrieval question is indirect: it is methodological evidence about research transparency rather than evidence of productivity gains from AI tools for educators or public-sector workers. It may be useful only as adjacent background on observational study quality and reporting standards.

paper_profiles.title: Exploring utilization of generative AI for research and education in data-driven materials science
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative AI can be used to support research and education workflows in data-driven materials science. The authors organized a hackathon (AIMHack2024) involving about 30 participants from academia and industry, with the goal of exploring practical uses of AI for software trials, AI-assisted tutorials, and GUI development.

The paper presents three case studies. First, participants used ChatGPT to learn and trial ImageJ for object counting, including handling overlapping circles with watershed segmentation. Second, the authors tested MyGPT as an AI tutor for PHYSBO, finding that response accuracy improved substantially only after supplying full documentation PDFs rather than URLs alone. Third, they used ChatGPT to convert a PHYSBO Python workflow into a Windows executable and then into a GUI with file selection, input dialogs, and output options, demonstrating that generative AI could accelerate routine development and documentation tasks.

Overall, the paper argues that generative AI can reduce effort in learning unfamiliar software, generating tutorials, and building simple end-user tools, but that human verification remains necessary because AI can produce plausible but incorrect outputs. The context is a materials-science research environment rather than K-12 education, but the paper is relevant as adjacent evidence on productivity gains from AI tools for educators and other knowledge workers.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that generative AI reduced the effort required to learn unfamiliar software, generate tutorials, and convert Python scripts into executable GUI tools. In qualitative demonstrations with about n=30 hackathon participants, ChatGPT-enabled instructions allowed successful use of ImageJ, and MyGPT plus structured documentation produced executable PHYSBO tutorials that converged to an accuracy of 0.9742 in a validation run.
finding.measure: Task completion and workflow efficiency in software learning, tutorial generation, and GUI/executable creation; validation accuracy for generated hyperparameter-optimization tutorial
finding.study_size: n=30 participants in the hackathon; additional single-case demonstrations not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The hackathon emphasized critically evaluating AI-generated content by cross-checking outputs against manuals, literature, and actual software behavior. Participants learned to verify whether AI-generated instructions were functionally correct, indicating gains in critical thinking and metacognitive checking rather than a directly measured test score.
finding.measure: Observed ability to verify AI-generated responses and judge correctness during software trials

paper_profiles.title: BoilerTAI: A Platform for Enhancing Instruction Using Generative AI in Educational Forums
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents BoilerTAI, a human-in-the-loop platform that integrates generative AI into online educational discussion forums to help instructional staff draft responses to student questions. The research question is whether GenAI can reduce instructional workload when used to pre-answer forum posts, while still preserving response quality and student experience.

The system was piloted in four first- and second-year computer science courses at Purdue University, each with enrollments of about 200 students. One teaching assistant per course used BoilerTAI to generate first-draft responses, which were then reviewed, edited, reprompted, or approved before posting. The study used a mixed-methods design combining Likert-scale surveys of four teaching assistants with qualitative feedback and usage metrics collected over a 3.5-month trial.

The results suggest that BoilerTAI improved instructional efficiency and response quality from the TAs’ perspective. Three of four participants reported improved efficiency, all four reported improved quality, and open-ended comments indicated reduced cognitive load and time savings. Teachers also perceived student reception as positive and the responses as relevant and personalized, but oversight remained necessary: half of the TAs reported needing to significantly correct or alter AI suggestions about half the time. The paper concludes that GenAI can augment instructional workflows in large undergraduate courses, but human review remains essential for accuracy and contextual fit.

finding.finding_summary: BoilerTAI improved instructional workflow efficiency for teaching assistants in four undergraduate computer science courses (n=4 TAs). On a post-trial survey, 75% (3/4) of participants somewhat agreed that their efficiency improved, and open-ended responses described reduced cognitive load and time savings when drafting forum replies.
finding.measure: TA self-reported efficiency, cognitive load, and time-saving perceptions on Likert-scale survey plus open-ended feedback

finding.finding_summary: The platform appears to support a narrower durable-skill outcome related to reducing cognitive effort in response formulation, allowing TAs to focus more on correctness rather than drafting from scratch. This was based on qualitative feedback from 4 TAs, who reported that the scaffolded AI responses made the task less mentally taxing.
finding.measure: Perceived cognitive load during response drafting

finding.finding_summary: Teaching assistants reported that BoilerTAI made responding to student inquiries easier and less burdensome, which may support persistence and reduced frustration in routine instructional tasks. The paper’s evidence is limited to TA perceptions from n=4 and does not report direct student motivation or engagement outcomes.
finding.measure: TA-reported perceived burden and ease of use

paper_profiles.title: Integrating Generative AI into Cybersecurity Education: A Study of OCR and Multimodal LLM-assisted Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how generative AI can be integrated into a legacy cybersecurity lab platform to provide real-time instructional support during experiential learning. The authors argue that students in technical STEM settings often need simplified explanations of dense instructional slides, and that AI assistants could reduce comprehension barriers while being easier to deploy than resource-intensive multimodal systems.

The study extends the Cybersecurity Labs-as-a-Service (CLaaS) platform with a zero-shot OCR-to-LLM instructional assistant. When students click an in-platform button, slide images are converted to text with Tesseract OCR and passed to an LLM to generate a simplified explanation. The paper also benchmarks this text-only pipeline against a multimodal LLM that interprets slide images directly, comparing instructional quality, computational overhead, and token/cost usage across different slide types.

The implementation was evaluated in a live university cybersecurity course with undergraduate and graduate students. Students provided 42 usefulness ratings on a 1–10 scale, with an average score of 7.83, suggesting positive perceived value. The comparative analysis found that OCR-to-LLM performed comparably to the multimodal model on text-dominant slides at much lower overhead and cost, while multimodal models were better on visually dense or screenshot-heavy slides. Overall, the paper concludes that a lightweight OCR-based generative AI pipeline is a practical and scalable way to support learner comprehension in technical education contexts.

finding.finding_summary: In a live university cybersecurity course, students rated the usefulness of the OCR-to-LLM instructional assistant an average of 7.83 out of 10 across 42 responses. The paper reports that the simplified AI-generated instructions were generally perceived as helpful for understanding lab slides, especially for text-centric content.
finding.measure: Student usefulness ratings of AI-assisted instructional slide explanations on a 1–10 scale

finding.finding_summary: The OCR-to-LLM pipeline delivered comparable pedagogical value to a multimodal LLM on text-dominant slides while requiring significantly lower computational overhead and operational cost. The paper also notes a token-based comparison for one example: 392 tokens for OCR text input versus 1105 tokens for image-based multimodal input, indicating a substantial efficiency advantage for the lighter-weight approach.
finding.measure: Computational overhead and operational cost comparison between OCR-to-LLM and multimodal LLM pipelines; token usage for example slide processing

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT outperforms crowd-workers for text-annotation tasks
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can perform manual text-annotation tasks as well as or better than human annotators, especially crowd-workers on Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk). The motivation is methodological and practical: many research, policy, and NLP workflows require labeled text, and human annotation is costly and time-consuming. The authors compare zero-shot ChatGPT classifications against both trained annotators and MTurk workers using the same annotation instructions and codebooks.

The study uses four datasets of tweets and news articles (n=6,183 total) drawn from prior content-moderation research and a new 2023 tweet sample to reduce concerns about memorization. Tasks include relevance detection, stance detection, topic identification, and frame detection. ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo) is evaluated at two temperatures and compared on accuracy and intercoder agreement. Across datasets, ChatGPT outperforms MTurk on most tasks by about 25 percentage points in accuracy on average, and its intercoder agreement is higher than both MTurk and trained annotators across all tasks.

The paper also reports a major cost advantage: ChatGPT annotations cost less than $0.003 per annotation, about thirty times cheaper than MTurk. The authors conclude that large language models could substantially increase the efficiency of text classification and may already be preferable to crowd-annotation for many tasks, though they note the importance of prompt quality and further testing across languages, task types, and models.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT substantially improved annotation productivity relative to MTurk and trained human annotation. Across four datasets (n=6,183), zero-shot ChatGPT accuracy exceeded MTurk by about 25 percentage points on average, and per-annotation cost was under $0.003, roughly 30 times cheaper than MTurk. Intercoder agreement was also higher for ChatGPT (about 91% at temperature=1 and 97% at temperature=0.2) than for MTurk (about 56%) or trained annotators (about 79%).
finding.measure: Annotation accuracy, intercoder agreement, and per-annotation cost for text classification tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that large language models could transform institutional text-annotation workflows and disrupt the business model of crowd-work platforms such as MTurk. This is an institutional-level implication drawn from comparative performance and cost evidence rather than from a direct policy intervention. No causal effect size for institutional change is reported.
finding.measure: Comparative feasibility and cost of AI-based versus crowd-based text annotation

paper_profiles.title: Towards Anatomy Education with Generative AI-based Virtual Assistants in Immersive Virtual Reality Environments
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether a generative AI-based virtual assistant can support anatomy learning in an immersive VR environment. The authors motivate the work by arguing that conventional anatomy instruction and many existing VR anatomy systems are limited by low interactivity and rigid, pre-scripted interactions, and that conversational AI may provide more adaptive, personalized support.

The study introduces a VR anatomy environment built in Unity that integrates ChatGPT-3.5, speech-to-text/text-to-speech services, and two assistant configurations: an embodied avatar and a screen-based text assistant. Sixteen adult participants from the University of Delaware completed a within-subject pilot study with a 2×2 design crossing assistant configuration with cognitive complexity of questions (knowledge-based vs. analysis-based). The evaluation measured task completion time, number of interactions, quiz score, usability (SUS), task load (NASA-TLX), presence (IPQ), and qualitative feedback.

Quantitatively, the study found no significant differences in task completion time, usability, task load, or presence between avatar and screen configurations. However, participants scored significantly better on knowledge-based than analysis-based questions within the avatar condition, and they generally needed more interactions with the avatar than the screen. The authors conclude that both configurations appear usable and that generative AI may be more helpful for lower-complexity questions, while more complex analytical questions remain challenging. They suggest future work on accuracy, larger samples, multimodal input/output, and combining avatar and screen modalities for improved learning support.

finding.finding_summary: In a within-subject pilot study with 16 participants, performance depended on question complexity in the avatar condition: participants scored significantly higher on knowledge-based than analysis-based anatomy questions (t = -1.78, df = 15, p = 0.04). The paper reports average scores of 0.75 for knowledge-based versus 0.43 for analysis-based questions in the avatar condition, suggesting the system supported simpler recall more effectively than higher-complexity analysis.
finding.measure: Multiple-choice anatomy quiz scores by Bloom-style cognitive complexity (knowledge-based vs. analysis-based)

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined cognitive complexity demands and the interaction of the AI assistant with users’ problem solving, including how many interactions were needed and whether users could reason through anatomy questions. Participants required more interactions in the avatar condition, especially for analysis-based questions, indicating that the assistant supported some higher-order reasoning but did not eliminate the need for active user reasoning and clarification. The authors interpret this as evidence that generative AI is more effective for direct answers than for complex analysis.
finding.measure: Number of interactions with the virtual assistant; performance on analysis-based vs. knowledge-based questions
finding.std_deviation: Avatar number of interactions: SD=11.87 overall; analysis-based SD=12.83

finding.finding_summary: The paper examined whether the AI virtual assistant configuration improved task efficiency, using task completion time as a key outcome. There were no significant differences in task completion time between avatar and screen configurations, and average completion times were nearly identical overall (avatar M=159.23 s, screen M=159.06 s), suggesting no measurable productivity gain from one configuration over the other in this pilot.
finding.measure: Task completion time for answering anatomy questions in VR
finding.std_deviation: Avatar SD=149.25 s; Screen SD=152.94 s

paper_profiles.title: Transforming Software Development with Generative AI: Empirical Insights on Collaboration and Workflow
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative AI tools such as ChatGPT and GitHub Copilot are changing the work practices of software development teams. The central question is not whether GenAI improves code in a narrow benchmark sense, but how it affects everyday workflow, productivity, learning, and collaboration among knowledge workers. The authors frame GenAI as a tool that can automate repetitive tasks, speed up learning, and alter team communication patterns.

The study is based on 13 semi-structured interviews with software professionals in Norway, including developers, data scientists, managers, designers, and technical leaders. Participants described using GenAI for assistance when stuck, interactive learning, boilerplate code generation, copywriting, and working with existing code such as refactoring, debugging, translating, and writing tests. The paper argues that GenAI often increases individual efficiency, motivation, and perceived productivity by reducing tedious work and providing immediate feedback.

At the same time, the paper finds potential tradeoffs at the team level. Because people increasingly turn to GenAI instead of human colleagues for quick support, the usual learning loop in agile teamwork may weaken, reducing knowledge sharing and possibly affecting team performance. The authors conclude that GenAI is useful for speeding routine work and enabling more creative tasks, but it may also shift collaboration patterns and require new team practices such as prompt engineering and pair prompt engineering.

finding.finding_summary: Interviewees consistently reported that GenAI made them more efficient by reducing time spent on repetitive or manual work. One manager said a bid that would normally have taken a lot of time was completed in 20 minutes, and multiple participants described faster code generation, refactoring, test writing, and boilerplate creation; the study reports that most informants felt AI reduced the amount of time developers spent on projects.
finding.measure: Perceived time savings / productivity in software development tasks

finding.finding_summary: GenAI was reported to support learning, metacognition, and problem-solving by helping participants get unstuck, think through problems, and learn new technologies faster. However, the authors also note a tradeoff: relying on GenAI instead of colleagues may reduce pair programming and human knowledge sharing, which can weaken collaboration in agile teams.
finding.measure: Interview-reported collaboration, learning, and problem-solving practices

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported higher enjoyment, motivation, and work satisfaction when GenAI reduced tedious tasks and gave immediate feedback. The paper states that freeing time from repetitive work increased motivation to experiment with the technology and made work feel more fun and rewarding.
finding.measure: Interview-reported motivation, enjoyment, and work satisfaction

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that widespread GenAI use may alter team-level coordination and the learning loop in agile organizations. While individuals become more efficient, reduced reliance on coworkers for help could decrease knowledge sharing and shift collaboration patterns, potentially affecting overall team performance and work structures.
finding.measure: Observed/elicited changes in team collaboration and knowledge-sharing dynamics

paper_profiles.title: Understanding the Practices, Perceptions, and (Dis)Trust of Generative AI among Instructors: A Mixed-methods Study in the U.S. Higher Education
paper_profiles.population: Undergraduate and graduate instructors in higher education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how U.S. higher-education instructors use generative AI (GenAI), how familiar they are with it, and how they conceptualize trust and distrust in GenAI for teaching and learning. The authors motivate the study by noting that most prior work in education has focused on students or on general perceptions of AI, while the instructor perspective—especially the distinction between trust and distrust—has been less studied.

The study surveyed 178 instructors from a single research-focused university in the mid-Atlantic United States in March 2024 and also analyzed 294 open-ended responses using an inductive qualitative approach. The quantitative survey measured GenAI familiarity, current use in instructional tasks, intentions for future use, and trust/distrust dimensions such as efficiency, personalization, misinformation, creativity, and student skill development. The qualitative component explored instructors’ examples and concerns, including blind distrust, social justice concerns, academic integrity, pedagogical risks, and additional faculty burdens.

Overall, the paper finds that instructors were moderately to highly familiar with GenAI concepts but used GenAI only sparingly for direct instructional tasks. Many instructors wanted more training and clearer institutional guidance. The authors conclude that trust and distrust are related but distinct constructs that can coexist, and that familiarity with GenAI and teaching level are associated with different trust/distrust patterns. The paper argues for calibrated (dis)trust and more systematic support for instructors as GenAI becomes more embedded in higher education.

finding.finding_summary: The paper found that instructors perceived GenAI as potentially making college instructors more efficient, but actual direct instructional use remained limited. In the survey, 75.8% to 64.0% of respondents reported never using GenAI for many instructional tasks, while only up to 2.8% used it routinely for text/code generation; 61.6% also said they personally needed more training to use GenAI effectively. The study is descriptive rather than causal, so it does not estimate productivity gains, but it documents perceived efficiency benefits alongside low adoption (n=178).
finding.measure: Survey items on perceived efficiency and self-reported use of GenAI for instructional tasks

finding.finding_summary: The study found substantial demand for institutional support, with 75.7% of instructors saying the university needed more training channels or support around GenAI and 55.1% reporting their own training and experience were insufficient. Qualitative responses also raised concerns about policy, academic integrity, disability accommodation, and possible administrative misuse of AI-related efficiencies, indicating that GenAI adoption has institutional governance implications beyond individual classroom use (n=178; 294 open-ended responses).
finding.measure: Survey items on training needs and open-ended responses about institutional policy, governance, and implementation

finding.finding_summary: Instructors generally believed GenAI could enhance student problem-solving skills, but many also worried it would undermine critical thinking, analytical skills, and independent problem-solving. The paper reports both positive trust items (e.g., enrichment/problem-solving) and distrust items (e.g., demotivation and skill degradation), but the evidence is attitudinal rather than performance-based, with no direct student outcome measures or effect sizes reported.
finding.measure: Survey items on perceived effects of GenAI on student problem-solving, critical thinking, and skill degradation; qualitative open-ended responses

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses writing-related concerns and uses writing tasks as an example of GenAI-mediated instructional work. Instructors worried that GenAI could restrict student creativity, homogenize writing, and weaken students’ ability to write clearly; several also noted plagiarism and overreliance in writing assignments. However, these are perceptions and anecdotes rather than measured changes in writing performance, and no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Survey items and open-ended responses about writing assignments, creativity, and language use

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes instructor concerns about GenAI in coursework broadly, including assignment design, exam policies, and course-specific integration across disciplines. One reported use case was using GenAI to develop assignments, but the study does not evaluate student learning in a specific academic content domain. Because the outcomes are framed at the level of instructional practice rather than a subject-area achievement measure, this is a secondary rather than central outcome.
finding.measure: Survey items on instructional uses and future intentions for GenAI in course design and assessment

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks Middle School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether teachers should remain “in-the-loop” when using generative AI to personalize mathematics tasks for students. The authors ask how teachers prompt ChatGPT to modify existing middle-school math problems, what students think of the resulting personalized problems, and whether the process is time-efficient for teachers.

Seven 7th-grade mathematics teachers from six U.S. schools worked with GPT-4o/ChatGPT to personalize 143 Illustrative Mathematics problems for 512-521 students (the paper reports both counts in different places; the analytic sample for student data is 521). Teachers participated in training, then used ChatGPT during recorded Zoom sessions to revise problems toward broad class interest areas such as sports, food, or specific popular-culture references. The study analyzed teacher prompts, chatbot interactions, time spent per problem, and student survey feedback on interestingness and closeness to their interests.

The findings suggest that teachers actively managed the depth, grain size, and ownership of personalization, but the process was not especially efficient: personalizing a problem took about 4 minutes on average and did not become clearly faster with experience. Student feedback favored finer-grained, specific references, but students’ preferences were heterogeneous, making teacher-mediated personalization difficult to satisfy at scale. The authors conclude that teacher-in-the-loop personalization can support professional learning and content quality control, but it is time-intensive and may not achieve the small-grain personalization many students prefer.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers and students worked on personalized middle-school mathematics problems, and students’ ratings of the problems improved from Unit 4 to Unit 6. The paper reports that average interestingness rose from 2.27 to 2.56 and average closeness rose from 2.28 to 2.66 on 5-point scales, with the unit effect statistically significant (B=0.33, SE=0.095, t=3.49, p=0.0012).
finding.measure: Student ratings of problem interestingness and closeness to interests for personalized mathematics word problems

finding.finding_summary: The study found that personalized problems were sometimes rated as more interesting by students, and teachers believed the process could support engagement with mathematics. Student ratings averaged 2.46 for interestingness and 2.53 for closeness overall, indicating only modest engagement, but there were meaningful gains in Unit 6 compared with Unit 4.
finding.measure: Student self-reported interestingness of problems and closeness to personal interests

finding.finding_summary: Personalizing a single problem with ChatGPT was time-consuming for teachers and did not clearly become more efficient over time. Teachers used an average of 3.2 prompts per problem and spent about 246 seconds per problem; Unit 4 averaged 204 seconds per problem versus 286 seconds in Unit 6, and Unit 4 versus Unit 6 differences actually increased for both prompts (B=1.26) and time (B=70.4 seconds).
finding.measure: Teacher prompts per problem and time spent creating each personalized problem

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not directly measure teacher or student durable skills, but it does show iterative prompting, problem revision, and reflection that the authors interpret as professional learning and improved prompting practice. Teachers increased their ability to craft interesting problems, but this did not translate into better efficiency, so the durable-skill implication is mixed and indirect.
finding.measure: Teacher prompting behavior and iterative refinement of personalized tasks

paper_profiles.title: A Review of Generative AI in Computer Science Education: Challenges and Opportunities in Accuracy, Authenticity, and Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews recent literature on the use of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude in computer science education, with a particular focus on three recurring issues: accuracy, authenticity, and assessment. The authors synthesize 52 papers published between 2019 and 2024 from major academic databases and organize the evidence into these thematic areas.

The review finds that generative AI can improve efficiency, provide real-time feedback, and support creative coding work, but it also introduces substantial risks, including hallucinations, error propagation, bias, and ambiguity about authorship. The paper argues that human oversight remains essential and that hybrid AI-human assessment models, bias-detection frameworks, and AI literacy are needed to use these tools responsibly.

Although the paper is framed around computer science education, its main contribution is conceptual and synthetic rather than primary empirical testing. It concludes that AI can be valuable for teaching and learning, but successful adoption depends on balancing productivity gains with safeguards for academic integrity, fairness, and accurate assessment. The review also identifies gaps in long-term evidence and calls for more empirical work on adaptive, context-aware AI systems.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed literature, generative AI was consistently described as improving efficiency by providing real-time assistance, instant feedback, and automated support for routine tasks such as coding help and grading. The review does not report a single pooled effect size, but it synthesizes multiple studies indicating reduced educator workload and faster student task completion, especially in large classes and formative assessment contexts.
finding.measure: Efficiency, real-time feedback, grading workload, and task support in educational workflows

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that GenAI can support problem-solving, creativity, and critical thinking by giving students immediate feedback and alternative solution paths, but it can also weaken these skills when students over-rely on AI-generated outputs. The paper synthesizes concerns that hallucinations, blurred authorship, and AI-assisted shortcuts may reduce independent reasoning and deep learning, while guided use may strengthen experimentation and reflection.
finding.measure: Problem-solving, critical thinking, creativity, and learning quality in coding tasks

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that generative AI is pushing institutions to revise assessment policies, academic integrity rules, and AI literacy practices. It recommends hybrid assessment models, clearer policies distinguishing AI-assisted from student-authored work, and investment in bias detection and AI-detection tools, but it does not quantify institutional effects.
finding.measure: Assessment policy, academic integrity practices, and AI literacy / governance recommendations

paper_profiles.title: The future of generative AI chatbots in higher education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the future role of generative AI chatbots in higher education institutions, focusing on both opportunities and challenges associated with tools such as ChatGPT. The central problem is how HEIs can harness AI to improve teaching, learning, research, and administration while managing risks such as academic integrity violations, privacy concerns, bias, and difficulty detecting AI-generated content.

The study uses a narrative literature review (NLR) of recent academic publications, drawing on sources from databases such as Google Scholar and Scopus and limiting inclusion to English-language articles published between 2021 and February 2024. Rather than testing a specific intervention, the paper synthesizes prior literature to describe likely future applications of generative AI chatbots in higher education, including student support, research writing assistance, and administrative task automation.

The paper concludes that generative AI chatbots have substantial potential to streamline routine administrative work, enhance student learning experiences, and support research activities, but that successful adoption depends on ethical guidelines, stakeholder training, human oversight, collaboration across disciplines, and ongoing evaluation. Because the paper is a narrative review, its findings are conceptual and synthesis-based rather than experimental, and it recommends more empirical studies in real educational settings.

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that generative AI chatbots can streamline routine administrative tasks in higher education, such as admissions inquiries, course registration, fee payments, and appointment scheduling. It also suggests that chatbot support can free staff time for more strategic work and improve academic productivity, but it does not report original effect sizes or quantitative estimates.
finding.measure: Administrative task streamlining / staff time saved / academic productivity

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on institution-level implications of adopting generative AI chatbots, including changes to teaching, learning, research processes, policy development, ethical governance, and institutional efficiency. It concludes that HEIs need clear guidelines, training, human oversight, and interdisciplinary collaboration to implement these tools responsibly; however, the study provides no direct institutional outcome data.
finding.measure: Institutional policy, governance, and implementation considerations

paper_profiles.title: The Potential and Implications of Generative AI on HCI Education
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 5th Annual Symposium on HCI Education (EduCHI '24)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative AI (GAI) can be incorporated into an undergraduate Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) and Interaction Design module, with the goal of understanding both the pedagogical opportunities and the limitations of these tools in design education. The authors argue that, while generative AI is increasingly discussed in computer science education, there has been less attention to its role in HCI education specifically. They therefore designed a 10-week module activity in which students used tools such as ChatGPT, Bard, and Claude to generate personas, scenarios, and functional requirements.

The study took place in a third-year optional undergraduate computing module delivered in English over 10 weeks in 2023. Students completed coursework centered on designing a GAI-powered web tool for generating HCI design resources, and they also participated in a dedicated practical session where they experimented with AI tools in groups. After the module, all 86 enrolled students were invited to complete a survey; 12 responded. The authors used grounded-theory-style qualitative analysis of the survey responses to identify themes around AI as a mirror for learning, AI as a persona, overreliance on AI for evaluation, and contradictory student attitudes toward creativity, bias, and cheating.

The main conclusion is that GAI can support deeper understanding of HCI concepts, especially personas, scenarios, context, and design evaluation, by making students reflect on the quality of their inputs and the outputs produced by the system. Students reported that the module was engaging and relevant, and the authors interpret this as evidence that GAI can function as both a pedagogical tool and a design material. At the same time, they caution that students may attribute too much evaluative and analytical capacity to GAI, so educators need to teach its limitations more explicitly and create structured opportunities for critical discussion. The paper ultimately frames GAI integration as a worthwhile but carefully scaffolded educational practice, especially when aligned with the TPACK framework.

finding.finding_summary: Students generally reported higher engagement and interest when generative AI was incorporated into the module. On a 1-5 engagement rating, 10/12 students selected 4 or 5, 2 selected neutral, and none selected a negative impact; the mean rating was 3.92. Qualitative comments described the module as more relevant, interesting, fun, and engaging.
finding.measure: Student self-reported engagement with the module (1-5 rating) and qualitative survey comments

finding.finding_summary: The study found that working with GAI supported students' understanding of personas, scenarios, context, and design evaluation, and encouraged reflection on prompts and outputs. Qualitative responses suggested improved critical thinking and metacognitive reflection, for example by revising prompts incrementally, recognizing shallow outputs when context was missing, and using AI to test their understanding of design concepts.
finding.measure: Qualitative survey responses about understanding of personas, scenarios, requirements, context, and evaluation

finding.finding_summary: The module's direct instructional focus was on HCI/interaction design concepts rather than a conventional academic subject area. Students reported that GAI helped them better understand and apply key course concepts such as personas, scenarios, requirements, and the design process, with positive impact reported across all topics on the post-module ranking figure. No numerical item-level values were reported beyond the qualitative summary that the impact was positive across topics and strongest for personas and scenarios.
finding.measure: Student rankings of GAI's impact on understanding course topics; qualitative survey responses

finding.finding_summary: Students described GAI as making parts of the design process faster or easier, especially idea generation, brainstorming, and evaluating design drafts. Several comments indicated that AI helped them generate multiple resources in less time and supported mundane tasks, though the paper does not report formal time-on-task or productivity measures.
finding.measure: Qualitative survey responses about use of GAI for brainstorming, generation, and evaluation during coursework

paper_profiles.title: Privacy Preserved AI School for Personal Assistant (GOD model)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper proposes the Guardian of Data (GOD) model, a privacy-preserving framework for evaluating and improving personal AI assistants on-device. The central problem is how to measure and train proactive, personalized AI behavior without exposing sensitive user data or undermining user trust. The authors argue that conventional personalization benchmarks are insufficient because they focus on reactive tasks, centralized data, and limited privacy protections.

The proposed system runs inside a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) and generates curriculum-based exam-style tasks of increasing difficulty, from simple factual recall to cross-domain reasoning and proactive recommendation. It also includes secure data connectors, anti-gaming safeguards, and a token-based incentive mechanism intended to reward useful personal data contributions while preserving privacy. The paper further sketches how the framework could support imitation learning and reinforcement learning from human feedback to improve on-device personal assistants over time.

The paper is primarily a conceptual system paper and does not report a human-subject evaluation or empirical K-12 study. Its examples and motivation are drawn from personal-assistant use cases such as scheduling, travel, shopping, and proactive reminders, rather than classroom or school contexts. The main conclusion is that privacy-preserving evaluation and training could enable more trustworthy personalized assistants, but the paper presents this as a proposed architecture and future direction rather than a validated intervention.

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes that on-device personal AI assistants could improve productivity by proactively handling tasks such as scheduling, trip planning, email summarization, and reminders. However, no empirical study is reported; the claimed productivity gains are conceptual and illustrated through example workflows rather than measured outcomes.
finding.measure: Conceptual productivity/task efficiency in personal-assistant workflows

finding.finding_summary: The framework is designed to support proactive assistance and context-aware planning, which could relate to time management and multi-step reasoning. These are proposed capabilities of the system, but the paper does not empirically measure improvements in these durable skills.
finding.measure: Conceptual multi-step reasoning, planning, and time management support

paper_profiles.title: Rethinking AI Evaluation through TEACH-AI: A Human-Centered Benchmark and Toolkit for Evaluating AI Assistants in Education
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable / framework paper spanning K-12 and higher education contexts
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a gap in how generative AI systems for education are evaluated. The authors argue that current evaluations overemphasize technical measures such as accuracy and task efficiency while underweighting human-centered concerns such as learner agency, ethical alignment, accessibility, and classroom workflow. To respond, they propose TEACH-AI (Trustworthy and Effective AI Classroom Heuristics), a domain-independent benchmark framework and toolkit intended to guide the design and evaluation of educational AI assistants.

The paper is based on a scoping review and synthesis of 126 sources spanning early intelligent tutoring systems, the transformer era, and recent generative AI work. From this literature, the authors derive ten evaluation components: explainability, helpfulness, adaptivity, consistency, learning exploration, usability, ethics/responsibility, accessibility, workflow coordination, and refinement. These components are translated into a checklist and example indicators/metrics such as trust ratings, usability scales, fairness audits, and workflow coherence measures.

The paper is conceptual rather than empirical: it does not test TEACH-AI on a deployed system or report participant outcomes. Its main conclusion is that education AI evaluation should move beyond correctness and efficiency toward a stakeholder-aligned, human-centered, and context-sensitive framework. The toolkit is positioned as a practical starting point for researchers, designers, educators, and policymakers to assess AI assistants in education, with future work planned for co-design, iterative validation, and scalable implementation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively focuses on educator workload reduction and task efficiency as one motivation for educational GenAI, especially in administrative tasks such as auto-grading and instructional content generation. However, it does not empirically test productivity gains; instead, it proposes workload-related indicators within the TEACH-AI framework and cites prior work to justify the need for better evaluation of these efficiencies.
finding.measure: Task efficiency, teacher workload, auto-grading and instructional content generation as evaluation constructs

finding.finding_summary: This paper centrally targets evaluation standards, governance, and institutional decision-making around AI in education. It proposes TEACH-AI as a stakeholder-aligned benchmark intended to support policymakers, designers, researchers, and educators in establishing value-aligned evaluation practices, but it does not report empirical institutional outcomes.
finding.measure: Benchmark framework adoption potential, stakeholder-aligned evaluation criteria, policy-relevant assessment checklist

paper_profiles.title: Beyond Replacement or Augmentation: How Creative Workers Reconfigure Division of Labor with Generative AI
paper_profiles.venue: CSCW / conference paper (venue not explicitly reported in provided text)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how creative professionals actually use generative AI in workplace settings, moving beyond the familiar “replacement vs. augmentation” framing. Rather than treating AI as simply automating or assisting human labor, the authors examine how workers actively reconfigure division of labor, role boundaries, and accountability when working with tools like ChatGPT, Midjourney, and Adobe/Firefly-integrated systems.

The study is based on 17 remotely conducted, ethnomethodologically informed interviews with workers in 12 creative agencies in the United States and Canada. Participants included creative directors, art directors, copywriters, strategists, producers, and related roles. Across examples, the paper shows that workers use prompting as reflexive delegation: they assign AI a persona or role, iteratively repair outputs, and adjust tone, style, and responsibility boundaries so the output becomes intelligible and acceptable to clients and internal stakeholders.

The main conclusion is that generative AI does not simply replace or augment labor in a stable way; instead, it creates ongoing workplace work to make AI contributions usable, trustworthy, and accountable. The paper highlights three recurring practices: configuring AI roles through prompts, repairing AI boundaries when outputs are off-target, and “templatizing trust” so outputs can be scaled and reused while still satisfying client, brand, legal, and ethical constraints. It also reports practical productivity gains in parts of creative production, such as substantially reduced turnaround times for reusable voice assets, but these gains are inseparable from additional interpretive and managerial work by humans.

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that creative workers use generative AI to save time on tedious production tasks and to scale reusable outputs. One participant described a voice-production workflow that fell from a 14–21 day turnaround to about 2–3 days, and another said AI allowed more retouching work to be completed without extra weeks or extra people. However, these gains depend on substantial human prompting, editing, and boundary-repair work.
finding.measure: Turnaround time, workflow efficiency, and perceived time saved in creative production tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that generative AI changes organizational practice by reshaping division of labor, accountability, disclosure norms, and client-facing workflows in creative agencies. Participants described new policies, disclosure expectations, and internal procedures for when AI can be used, how outputs are framed for clients, and how brand/legal concerns are managed.
finding.measure: Reported organizational practices, disclosure rules, use policies, and stakeholder/accountability management

paper_profiles.title: Large Language Model-Powered Chatbots for Internationalizing Student Support in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether an LLM-powered chatbot can improve student support and internationalization services in a higher-education setting. The authors focus on a chatbot built with GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4-Turbo, LangChain, Chroma vector storage, and OpenAI embeddings, designed to answer questions for international and Moroccan students at Al Akhawayn University (AUI) using only university-provided information.

The study is primarily an implementation and evaluation report rather than a causal experiment. The chatbot was tested on four internal test sets covering general capability, provocation/sensitivity, information retrieval, and multilingual support, and then evaluated by AUI students on a subset of general-capability responses using Likert-scale ratings for quality, relevance, correctness, formality, and human-likeness. The final survey set included 11 evaluators (10 Moroccan, 1 international) and 79 ratings per metric. Bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals were reported, with mean scores around 4/5 across the five metrics, suggesting strong perceived performance.

The main conclusion is that a relatively simple retrieval-augmented chatbot pipeline can provide accurate, engaging, and professional student support while being cost-effective and scalable for higher education internationalization. The authors argue that such systems may improve information access and student support, though they also note limitations such as small sample size, limited data coverage, and some hallucination in edge cases. Future work is proposed on larger-scale evaluation, broader datasets, and stronger assessment of translation and response-time performance.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the LLM chatbot improved the efficiency and accessibility of student support by providing timely, relevant, and comprehensive answers to international and Moroccan student queries. In the survey evaluation, the chatbot received high mean ratings across quality-related measures (e.g., correctness CI [4.18–4.47], relevance CI [4.02–4.41]), suggesting it can handle information retrieval and support tasks effectively, though no direct time-savings measure was reported.
finding.measure: Student survey ratings of chatbot response quality, relevance, correctness, formality, and human-likeness; internal testing of information retrieval and multilingual response handling
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CIs: Quality [4.06–4.43], Relevance [4.02–4.41], Formality [4.24–4.47], Correctness [4.18–4.47], Human-Like [3.87–4.32]

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLM chatbots can support higher-education internationalization by improving student support, information access, and institutional responsiveness. The chatbot was designed around official university information and multilingual support, and the authors conclude it could be adopted by other institutions as a scalable, low-cost digital service.
finding.measure: Survey-based evaluation of the chatbot in an institutional support context; qualitative assessment of chatbot deployment for international student services

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating Multimodal Generative AI with Korean Educational Standards
paper_profiles.population: Elementary (PreK-5th), Middle School, High School, Undergraduate
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces KoNET, a new benchmark for evaluating multimodal generative AI systems using Korean national educational tests. The authors argue that existing AI benchmarks are heavily English-centric and often do not compare model performance against human performance, making it difficult to assess real educational utility in non-English contexts.

KoNET converts four Korean exams into a multimodal multiple-choice QA format: elementary, middle school, high school, and college scholastic ability tests. The benchmark includes question difficulty annotations and, for a subset of college exam items, human error-rate data from approximately 505K students, enabling comparison between AI error patterns and human error patterns. The paper evaluates 18 open-source LLMs, 20 open-source MLLMs, 4 closed-source LLMs, and 4 closed-source MLLMs using OCR and chain-of-thought prompting.

The main finding is that performance improves with larger models, but closed-source systems substantially outperform open-source systems on Korean educational content, especially for multimodal tasks. The authors also find that CoT prompting generally helps, OCR can materially affect results, and model error patterns only weakly correlate with human error rates. Because the paper is primarily a benchmark study rather than an intervention study, it provides adjacent evidence on model capability and evaluation quality rather than direct evidence of educator productivity gains.

finding.finding_summary: Models show improving performance on mathematics-heavy items as scale increases, with closed-source multimodal systems achieving the strongest results on the Korean exam benchmark. For example, gpt-4o-2024-05-13 scored 83.4 on KoNET overall, and closed-source MLLMs reached 73.3-83.4 overall, while open-source systems were generally much lower on the Korean subsets.
finding.measure: Accuracy on math and broader multiple-choice questions in KoNET, including mathematics-related items from Korean educational exams

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark includes substantial Korean reading and text-comprehension content, and models performed variably depending on language and comprehension complexity. The paper reports that AI models do better on comprehension tasks but weaker on memorization-heavy questions, and that performance declines on more advanced Korean curricula and culturally specific text. KoCSAT human error data were used to compare model and student performance on reading/comprehension-type items.
finding.measure: Accuracy on Korean language, reading comprehension, and text-based multiple-choice questions; comparison of model error rates with human error rates on comprehension items

finding.finding_summary: KoNET spans elementary through college-level Korean educational content across many non-language subjects, and model performance generally rises with model size but drops as curriculum level and subject complexity increase. The paper reports strong closed-source performance on the benchmark overall (e.g., gpt-4o 83.4 for closed-source MLLM, claude-3-5-sonnet 80.6), while open-source models lag substantially on Korean-specific educational content.
finding.measure: Accuracy on Korean educational benchmark questions across subjects such as social studies, science, history, arts, and vocational topics

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s human-vs-model error analysis suggests models and students differ in problem-solving patterns, with AI excelling more on comprehension-oriented items and humans doing better on memorization-oriented items. This is relevant to higher-order reasoning and metacognitive challenge, but the paper does not directly measure durable skills as an educational outcome.
finding.measure: Error-rate comparison between AI models and human examinees on KoCSAT items, including comprehension and memorization-heavy questions
finding.study_size: approximately 505K students for human error-rate data; 327 questions with human error rates

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents KoNET as a benchmark intended to support realistic evaluation workflows, and it shows that LLM-as-a-Judge can closely match manual grading, with agreement accuracy between 96.9% and 98.3% across five tests. This suggests a potentially efficient automated evaluation method, though the study does not measure educator workload directly.
finding.measure: Agreement rate between LLM-as-a-Judge grading and manual grading; benchmark evaluation workflow efficiency

finding.finding_summary: KoNET is framed as infrastructure for more valid, multilingual, and human-referenced evaluation of AI systems in education, with potential relevance for the AI tutoring market and broader benchmarking practices. The study argues that incorporating Korean national tests and human error rates can improve institutional assessment of model capability in non-English educational settings.
finding.measure: Benchmark design and comparative evaluation framework for AI systems in Korean educational standards

paper_profiles.title: Mathify: Evaluating Large Language Models on Mathematical Problem Solving Tasks
paper_profiles.venue: NeurIPS'23 Workshop on Generative AI for Education (GAIED) / arXiv
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models can be adapted to solve high-school mathematics problems, with a focus on problems drawn from NCERT 11th and 12th standard textbooks. The authors introduce a new curated dataset, MathQuest, containing 223 word problems across 14 mathematics domains, and also augment a smaller arithmetic dataset (Math-401) to create a larger training set for model fine-tuning.

The study fine-tunes three open-source LLM families—LLaMA-2, WizardMath, and MAmmoTH—using QLoRA and evaluates them with exact-match accuracy on MathQuest and several external math reasoning benchmarks (GSM-8K, DeepMind, NumGLUE, SimulEq, and Math-401). Results show that fine-tuning improves performance across models, and that MAmmoTH-13B performs best on MathQuest after fine-tuning, reaching 24.0% exact-match accuracy. The paper concludes that these models can serve as baselines for high-school math question answering, but the work also notes that the models still struggle with more complex expressions and nested brackets.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports improved mathematical problem-solving performance after fine-tuning open-source LLMs on augmented arithmetic data. On MathQuest, the best model (MAmmoTH-13B) achieved 24.0% exact-match accuracy after fine-tuning, compared with 12.2% before fine-tuning; across the model family, performance improved on the evaluated math benchmarks, though accuracy remained limited on harder sets.
finding.measure: Exact-match accuracy on MathQuest and related math reasoning datasets
finding.study_size: n=223 for MathQuest; benchmark evaluations reported on 100-sample test sets for several datasets; training data n=241,600, validation n=30,200, test n=30,200 for augmented Math-401

paper_profiles.title: Could ChatGPT get an Engineering Degree? Evaluating Higher Education Vulnerability to AI Assistants
paper_profiles.population: Undergraduate and graduate higher education students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether modern AI assistants, especially GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, can successfully answer assessment questions from university STEM courses well enough to threaten the integrity of higher-education evaluation. The authors frame this as a problem of “assessment vulnerability,” meaning that if AI tools can solve enough exam and assignment questions, students may be able to obtain passing grades without demonstrating the intended learning outcomes.

To study this, the authors built a dataset of 5,579 textual questions drawn from real exams, assignments, and practical exercises across 50 courses at EPFL in Switzerland. The dataset spans 9 degree programs and includes both multiple-choice and open-answer questions in English and French. They evaluated GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 using eight prompting strategies, then graded responses automatically for MCQs and with a GPT-4-based grading pipeline for open answers, supplemented by human grading on a subset of responses.

The main finding is that GPT-4 can answer a large share of university assessment questions correctly: 65.8% on average under majority voting across prompts, and at least one prompting strategy produces a correct answer for 85.1% of questions. At the program level, GPT-4 could pass non-project components of many courses across all examined programs at common passing thresholds, with especially strong performance in code- and text-heavy subjects and weaker performance on mathematically derivational tasks. The paper concludes that higher-education assessments, especially unsupervised ones, are already vulnerable to AI assistance and should be redesigned with generative AI in mind.

finding.finding_summary: The study finds substantial vulnerability of higher-education assessment systems to AI assistants. Using a dataset of 5,579 questions from 50 EPFL courses, GPT-4 answered 65.8% of questions correctly on average under majority vote, and at least one prompt yielded a correct answer for 85.1% of questions, implying that many course assessments and degree programs could be passed with AI support.
finding.measure: Course assessment vulnerability; percentage of questions answered correctly; percentage of courses passed at various thresholds

finding.finding_summary: As an academic task-performance measure, the models show high success on university-level STEM assessment questions. GPT-4 achieved 65.8% average accuracy across the question bank and could reach a passing threshold on 83% to 100% of courses depending on the degree program and threshold, with strongest results on code/text-based questions and weaker results on derivation-heavy problems.
finding.measure: Accuracy on university assessment questions; course pass rates

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI assistants can support some learning tasks but may also let students circumvent the acquisition of foundational knowledge and problem-solving skills. Performance drops on more complex questions and higher Bloom’s taxonomy levels, suggesting weaker support for deeper reasoning even though many lower-level tasks are answered correctly.
finding.measure: Performance by question difficulty and Bloom’s taxonomy complexity
finding.study_size: n=376 Bachelor questions with instructor difficulty labels; n=693 Master questions with instructor difficulty labels; n=207 Bloom-coded questions

finding.finding_summary: The models struggle more on mathematically demanding questions, especially those requiring derivations and extensive computations. The paper reports that performance is lower on harder and more mathematical assessments, although exact effect sizes are not given; this relative weakness contrasts with better results on code- and text-based items.
finding.measure: Accuracy on derivation-heavy and computation-heavy assessment questions
finding.study_size: subset of the 5,579-question bank; exact mathematical subset not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Across STEM courses, GPT-4 performs well on many assessment questions but its accuracy declines as cognitive complexity increases. On Bloom’s taxonomy annotations, performance is higher for remembering and understanding than for analyzing and applying, indicating weaker scientific reasoning on more complex tasks.
finding.measure: Accuracy by question complexity and Bloom’s taxonomy level

paper_profiles.title: Computer Science Education in the Age of Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual review and position piece about how generative AI is reshaping computer science education. It asks what benefits and risks LLMs such as ChatGPT and Copilot create for programming instruction, debugging, feedback, assessment, and curriculum design, and argues that traditional assessments centered on producing code from scratch are becoming less valid as a measure of understanding.

Rather than reporting a single empirical intervention, the paper synthesizes emerging studies and examples from the literature to propose pedagogical and policy responses. These include AI-augmented pair programming, flipped classroom models, process-based assignments, oral examinations, reflective writing, and explicit AI literacy instruction. The discussion spans introductory programming, broader CS curricula, and HCI-oriented computing education contexts, mostly in higher education.

The paper’s main conclusion is that generative AI should be treated as a tool for exploration, refinement, and productivity, but only within instructional designs that preserve deep learning, critical evaluation, and academic integrity. It argues for redesigned assessments focused on process and explanation, clearer institutional policies on acceptable AI use, and faculty/student training to ensure responsible and equitable adoption.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI can substantially improve educator and learner productivity by reducing time spent on routine coding, debugging, prototyping, and assessment-related tasks. A notable anecdotal example states that an MSc-level cloud-based secure document-sharing system was produced in under 8 minutes with generative AI support, illustrating very large task-speed gains, but this is not presented as a controlled empirical estimate.
finding.measure: Task completion speed / productivity in coding, debugging, prototyping, and assessment preparation

finding.finding_summary: Across the cited studies and the paper’s synthesis, AI tools are portrayed as supporting debugging, critical evaluation, reflection, and collaborative problem solving, but also as risking over-reliance and superficial learning if students simply accept AI output. The paper does not report a single pooled effect, but it emphasizes that learning gains depend heavily on whether students review, refine, and explain AI-generated code rather than use it as a shortcut.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, debugging, reflection, collaboration, and problem-solving in programming coursework

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses substantively on computer science learning, especially programming and HCI-related design work, and argues that AI assistance can improve coding support, personalized feedback, and student performance when embedded in well-structured pedagogy. It cites studies reporting improved student scores and better-quality submissions, but the paper itself is a narrative synthesis rather than a direct evaluation.
finding.measure: Programming performance, code quality, and learning outcomes in CS coursework

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper is institutional policy and assessment redesign: it recommends vivas, process documentation, disclosure rules, faculty development, and explicit AI-use guidelines. The claimed impact is institutional rather than measured experimentally, aiming to improve integrity, assessment validity, and responsible adoption of AI across CS departments.
finding.measure: Institutional policy, assessment design, and governance practices

paper_profiles.title: Teachers’ AI digital competencies and twenty-first century skills in the post-pandemic world
paper_profiles.population: Educators (primarily teachers; no specific K-12 sample studied)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conceptual paper addresses the question of what digital competencies teachers need to teach effectively in AI-enhanced, post-pandemic learning environments. The authors argue that the rapid expansion of AI tools in education has created both opportunities and challenges for teaching, learning, assessment, and teacher workload, but that teachers often lack the technical, pedagogical, and ethical preparation to use these tools well.

Rather than testing an intervention, the paper synthesizes prior research and uses examples from the literature to propose an expanded framework for teachers’ AI digital competency. It aligns AI-related skills with the DigCompEdu framework and revises P21’s twenty-first century learning framework, emphasizing professional engagement, digital resources, teaching/learning, assessment, learner empowerment, information/media literacy, communication/collaboration, content creation, responsible AI use, problem solving, creativity, and life/career skills.

The paper’s context is broad and post-pandemic, spanning online and blended learning settings and drawing on examples from K-12 and higher education research, but it does not report original empirical data. Its main conclusion is that teacher AI competency should be understood as more than technical know-how: educators also need ethical awareness, pedagogical adaptability, and broader twenty-first century skills to support AI-enabled teaching and student learning.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues, based on prior studies, that AI tools can reduce teacher workload and improve efficiency by automating repetitive tasks such as grading, feedback, paperwork, and some administrative functions. However, this is a conceptual synthesis rather than a direct empirical test, so no original effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, efficiency of grading/feedback/administrative tasks

finding.finding_summary: The article centrally discusses AI-related durable skills including critical thinking, collaboration, communication, creativity, metacognition/self-regulation, and life/career skills. It synthesizes literature suggesting that AI-supported environments can foster these skills, but the paper itself provides no primary empirical measurement or effect estimate.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, collaboration, communication, creativity, self-regulation, and related twenty-first century skills

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes framework-level and institutional recommendations for teacher education, curriculum design, and policy around AI competency, arguing that schools, universities, and professional organizations should adopt standards and professional development supports. This is a conceptual policy contribution rather than a measured institutional outcome.
finding.measure: Framework and policy recommendations for digital competency standards and professional development

paper_profiles.title: The AI Revolution in Education: Will AI Replace or Assist Teachers in Higher Education?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI, especially ChatGPT, will replace teachers or instead function as a complementary tool in higher education. The authors frame the issue around broad concerns in AI in education: AI’s capacity to automate routine and administrative work, versus its inability to replicate human qualities such as empathy, creativity, cultural sensitivity, moral guidance, and social-emotional support.

The study uses a survey of 384 undergraduate/postgraduate students and 144 teachers from Hong Kong universities, combining closed-ended items with open-ended responses.
