Quantitatively, both groups showed openness to AI-assisted teaching and learning, but neither strongly believed AI would replace teachers; students were somewhat more optimistic about AI’s academic benefits and 24/7 availability, while teachers were more concerned about threats to transferable skills and less confident about detecting AI use in assignments. Qualitatively, respondents described AI as useful for course design, brainstorming, writing support, research assistance, personalized feedback, and reducing workload, but not capable of replacing the social-emotional, pedagogical, and mentoring roles of human teachers. Overall, the paper concludes that AI is best viewed as an augmenting partner rather than a replacement for teachers, though it also warns that poor AI literacy, academic misconduct, and weak governance could make AI work against educators.

finding.finding_summary: Respondents reported that generative AI can speed up routine tasks, reduce workload, and improve time efficiency for teachers. Qualitative responses described uses such as fast lesson preparation, administration work, email templates, assessment design, and course logistics, while survey items indicated moderate agreement that AI is useful because it is available 24/7 and can support coursework guidance.
finding.measure: Survey perceptions of AI usefulness for teaching/learning efficiency; open-ended teacher and student responses about workload, lesson preparation, administration, and feedback

finding.finding_summary: Participants viewed generative AI as helpful for writing development. Students rated the statement that AI can help them become better writers higher than teachers did (students M=3.32, SD=1.162; teachers M=3.01, SD=1.273; t=2.577, p=.010), and qualitative comments noted support for sentence structure, grammar, vocabulary, and essay critique/correction.
finding.measure: Survey item on improving writing; open-ended responses on writing assistance and essay critique
finding.study_size: n=527 for the writing item (384 students, 143 teachers)

finding.finding_summary: The paper found that AI is perceived as supporting some durable skills but threatening others. Survey results showed teachers were more concerned than students that AI would hinder generic/transferable skills such as teamwork, problem-solving, and leadership (teachers M=3.48, SD=1.238; students M=3.10, SD=1.227; t=-3.087, p=.002), and qualitative responses echoed fears about reduced critical thinking and originality. At the same time, respondents also saw AI as useful for brainstorming, idea generation, and supporting research and decision-making, which can aid critical thinking when used well.
finding.measure: Survey item on generic/transferable skills; qualitative perceptions of critical thinking, creativity, collaboration, and idea generation
finding.study_size: n=525 for transferable-skills item (385 students, 140 teachers)

finding.finding_summary: A central conclusion is that generative AI cannot replace the social-emotional competencies provided by human teachers. The paper argues, based on qualitative responses and literature review, that AI lacks emotions, empathy, trust-building, cultural sensitivity, and the ability to provide human connection, role modeling, and motivational support that students value.
finding.measure: Qualitative perceptions about teacher irreplaceability, human connection, empathy, emotions, and social-emotional development
finding.study_size: n=528 total survey participants, with qualitative responses from both students and teachers

finding.finding_summary: The paper identifies institutional risks and governance needs around generative AI, including academic integrity, privacy, ethics, equity, and regulation. Teachers were more concerned than students about AI’s negative impact on transferable skills, and qualitative findings stressed the need for AI literacy, guidance, and regularity mechanisms to manage misuse, plagiarism, over-reliance, and loss of trust in assessment.
finding.measure: Survey perceptions of AI’s impact on skills and AI detection; qualitative comments on governance, ethics, privacy, equity, and academic misconduct

paper_profiles.title: New Era of Artificial Intelligence in Education: Towards a Sustainable Multifaceted Revolution
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how artificial intelligence may affect education, with a particular emphasis on higher education. Rather than conducting a primary empirical study, the authors perform a scoping review of recent literature (2019–June 2023) drawn from Scopus and Google Scholar to map the main applications, benefits, and challenges of AI in education.

The review organizes the literature into four major application areas: personalized learning, intelligent tutoring systems, assessment automation, and teacher–student collaboration. Across these areas, the paper argues that AI can improve learning experiences, automate time-consuming instructional tasks, and expand access to quality education, while also raising concerns about privacy, bias, reliability, and the erosion of human interaction.

The paper’s context is broad but centered on higher education and education systems more generally, with examples ranging from chatbots and automated grading to adaptive tutoring and generative AI tools such as ChatGPT. Its main conclusion is strongly pro-adoption: AI should be integrated into education, but only with guardrails to limit misuse and ethical harm.

finding.finding_summary: The review concludes that AI can reduce teacher workload and improve productivity, especially through grading automation, question generation, lesson-plan creation, and scheduling support. The paper states that around 40% of teachers’ time is spent on grading and related activities, implying that automation could free substantial time for direct student support, but it reports no original effect size or controlled comparison.
finding.measure: Teacher time/workload; grading and related instructional tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI can improve institutional efficiency, broaden access to quality education, and support more scalable delivery models, especially through AI-driven platforms, MOOCs, and low-cost digital resources. These claims are synthesized from the reviewed literature rather than tested in a single empirical study, and no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Institutional access, scalability, and cost efficiency of educational provision

paper_profiles.title: Pre-service teachers' attitudes towards artificial intelligence and its integration into EFL teaching and learning
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Language and Cultural Education
paper_profiles.population: Undergraduate and postgraduate pre-service EFL teachers in Slovakia
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how pre-service EFL teachers in Slovakia perceive artificial intelligence (AI), how much they know about it, and how they view its integration into English language teaching and teacher education. The study was motivated by a lack of evidence from Central Europe and by the need to understand whether future teachers are prepared to adopt AI tools in education.

The author used a cross-sectional knowledge-attitude-practice (KAP) survey administered online to 137 pre-service English language teachers at a Slovak university. The questionnaire included Likert-scale items on AI knowledge, positive and negative attitudes, and reported practices, plus one open-ended question about AI tools used for EFL learning/teaching. The sample consisted mostly of female undergraduate students, with a small share reporting prior AI training.

Findings show low self-reported understanding of AI's computational principles and limitations, but substantially more positive views of AI in EFL than negative ones. Most respondents wanted AI education included in their curriculum, believed AI would improve education and EFL teaching/learning, and expected AI to reduce workload and improve assessment objectivity. At the same time, many thought teachers might lose some skills and that AI could make teaching less personal. The paper concludes that EFL teacher education should update curricula to include AI-related training and ethical reflection.

finding.finding_summary: Respondents expected AI to improve teacher productivity and reduce workload. In the KAP survey (n=137), 67 students (48.90%) agreed that AI implementation would reduce teachers' workload, 72 (52.55%) agreed it would make assessment procedures more objective, and 64 (46.71%) expected AI to help with repetitive tasks such as pronunciation drills.
finding.measure: Self-reported expectations about workload, assessment objectivity, and repetitive-task support

finding.finding_summary: The study directly assessed attitudes toward including AI in the teacher-training curriculum. A total of 88 respondents (64.24%) agreed that AI education should be included in their university curriculum, with 37 (27.01%) strongly agreeing. The paper concludes that EFL teacher education programs should update curricula and provide seminars/workshops on AI.
finding.measure: Agreement that AI education should be included in the university curriculum

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests both support for and concern about AI's effects on teacher skills and judgment. While respondents generally supported AI use, 73 students (53.28%) agreed that EFL teachers might lose some skills when using AI, and 67 (48.90%) agreed teachers should be careful using AI tools in class. This is an attitude measure rather than a direct test of skill change.
finding.measure: Self-reported concern about skill loss and cautious AI use

paper_profiles.title: Assessing teachers’ readiness and perceived usefulness of AI in education: an Estonian perspective
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines Estonian teachers’ readiness to use AI in education, their perceived usefulness of AI tools, and which factors predict actual AI use in teaching. The paper is motivated by the rapid growth of AI in education and the need to understand whether teachers are prepared to adopt tools that can automate administrative work, support individualized learning, and improve lesson efficiency.

The authors surveyed 3,848 teachers from 133 Estonian general education schools in autumn 2024. The instrument measured readiness (knowledge, access to software, school management support, access to relevant content) and perceived usefulness (efficiency in conducting lessons, individualized instruction), then compared teachers who had used AI tools with those who had not. Analyses included factor analysis, group comparisons, and logistic regression predicting AI use.

Results showed that 53.2% of teachers reported using AI tools, with higher reported use in basic schools than in upper secondary settings. Teachers who used AI rated both readiness and perceived usefulness significantly higher than non-users, with large group differences on the item-level comparisons (e.g., Cohen’s d ranging from 0.501 to 1.022). Logistic regression indicated that readiness, perceived usefulness, and age were significant predictors of AI use, while teaching experience was not. Overall, the paper concludes that teacher confidence, access, and perceived value of AI are central to adoption, and that professional development and school leadership support are important enablers of integration.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers who had used AI tools rated AI as improving lesson efficiency significantly higher than non-users. On the item “Using artificial intelligence enhances my efficiency in conducting lessons,” AI users reported M=3.69 (SD=0.99) versus M=2.41 (SD=1.17) among non-users; Welch’s t=27.845, p<0.001, Cohen’s d=0.923.
finding.measure: Perceived efficiency in conducting lessons; self-report questionnaire item AI_2

finding.finding_summary: Institutional readiness factors were associated with AI use, including school management support and access to software/content. In logistic regression, readiness and perceived usefulness were strong predictors of AI adoption, and readiness items explicitly included school management support and access to resources.
finding.measure: School-level and institutional readiness items; logistic regression predicting reported AI use

finding.finding_summary: Teachers who had used AI tools rated the relevance of AI for individualized instruction higher than non-users, but the endorsement was more cautious than for efficiency. On “Using artificial intelligence allows me to better implement an individualized approach to students,” users reported M=3.25 (SD=1.14) versus M=2.43 (SD=1.07) for non-users; Welch’s t=22.537, p<0.001, Cohen’s d=0.743. This reflects perceived support for pedagogical decision-making and individualized teaching, a durable-skills-related instructional capability.
finding.measure: Perceived ability to implement individualized instruction; self-report questionnaire item AI_6

paper_profiles.title: Attitudes of Czech Teachers Towards the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines Czech teachers’ subjective feelings about the introduction of artificial intelligence into schools. The study asks whether teachers are worried about AI, whether they see it as helpful, and whether they have experience using it in their work.

Using in-depth interviews, the author interviewed five primary and secondary school teachers aged 35 to 48. The analysis, based on open coding, identified three themes: fear of AI introduction, acceptance of AI as inevitable, and AI as help for teachers. Teachers were especially concerned that students would misuse AI to cheat or plagiarize, and they felt that teaching and assessment practices would need to change as AI becomes more common.

At the same time, some teachers already used chatbots and other AI tools for lesson planning, differentiation, and simplifying preparation. These teachers described AI as a tool that can reduce workload, save time, and improve efficiency. The paper concludes that Czech teachers largely expect AI to become a normal part of schooling, while emphasizing the need for ethical guidance, critical use, and changes in pedagogical practice.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers described AI as a tool that helps with lesson planning, creating teaching materials, differentiation, and reducing preparation time. In the interviews (n=5), respondents said AI can make their work more efficient, reduce workload, and save time, though no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported workload, preparation time, and perceived efficiency from in-depth interviews

finding.finding_summary: The study found that teachers believe AI will require changes to teaching, testing, and assignment design, and that schools must adapt to AI's presence. At the same time, some teachers were concerned about cheating and plagiarism, indicating both perceived institutional benefits and risks; no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of school-level changes, assessment practices, and AI-related risks

finding.finding_summary: Teachers worried that students might rely on AI too much, weakening independent thinking, writing, and the ability to formulate meaningful thoughts. The same interviews also suggested AI could support students in learning to use technology critically and effectively, but the paper does not provide direct outcome data or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of students' independent thinking, writing, and critical use of AI

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the future of learning and the relationship between human intelligence and AI. An interview with Professor Rose Luckin
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an interview article with Professor Rose Luckin about artificial intelligence in education, with a strong emphasis on the ethical, practical, and conceptual implications of generative AI for teaching, learning, assessment, and institutional change. Rather than testing a specific intervention, it synthesizes Luckin’s views on AI in education, her learner-centred design framework, the Golden Triangle Framework, and the need for educator-developer-researcher collaboration.

The discussion is situated primarily in higher education and broader education systems, though it repeatedly references K-12 schooling, school leadership, and classroom practice. The interview highlights concerns that current AI deployments are outpacing regulation and educator understanding, and argues that teachers must remain in the loop rather than using AI as an autopilot. It also stresses that AI should be introduced through careful, staged, ethically governed collaboration and that assessment systems must be redesigned to measure more meaningful forms of learning than memorization.

Because this is an expert interview and not an empirical study, the paper does not present original participant data, comparisons, or measured effects of AI tools on teacher productivity or student outcomes. Its main contribution is conceptual and practical guidance: AI can support education when grounded in human-centred design, ethical governance, and robust partnership across educators, researchers, and developers.

finding.finding_summary: The article argues that AI in education requires coordinated governance, ethics, and collaboration across educators, researchers, developers, regulators, and community groups. No empirical effect sizes are reported; the paper instead offers a conceptual case that AI adoption can be beneficial if institutions build the right partnerships, infrastructure, and safeguards, but risky if deployed without them.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of governance, ethics, institutional collaboration, and AI readiness in education

finding.finding_summary: The interview suggests AI may improve teacher-facing and institutional workflows through automated feedback, automated grading, data analysis, and better product evaluation processes, but it does not measure productivity gains directly. Luckin emphasizes that effective use depends on staged rollout, staff capability, and avoiding semi-functional tools in high-stakes classrooms; no quantitative evidence is reported.
finding.measure: Discussion of automated feedback, grading, progress analysis, and developer/educator workflow support

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses AI’s role in assessment and broader learning design, arguing that AI should help redesign assessment toward more authentic measures of learning rather than memorization. It claims AI can support personalized feedback and analysis of student progress, but provides no direct outcome data, sample sizes, or effect estimates.
finding.measure: Assessment redesign, formative feedback, and student progress analysis

finding.finding_summary: Luckin argues that AI should support higher-order learning such as critical thinking, creativity, and metacognition by shifting assessment away from rote recall and by enabling learners to reflect on and challenge their understanding. This is a conceptual claim rather than a measured finding; no empirical evidence is provided in the interview.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, creativity, metacognition, and higher-order assessment design

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly emphasizes learner engagement, trust, and agency as important conditions for successful AI use in education. However, these are discussed as design goals and ethical considerations rather than as measured outcomes, and no data are provided on engagement or motivation effects.
finding.measure: Learner engagement, trust, and agency in AI-supported learning

paper_profiles.title: Editorial 6(2): Personal digital assistant or job killer? Generative AI and the teaching profession in higher education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This editorial examines the rise of generative AI in higher education and asks whether it will function as a teacher’s assistant or a job killer. The piece situates ChatGPT and related large language models within broader historical and labor-market debates about automation, academic work, and the changing role of university teachers. It argues that the current AI moment should be understood against a backdrop of pre-existing pressures on higher education, including casualisation, intensification of work, and the devaluation of learning under neoliberal accountability regimes.

The article’s main purpose is not to report a new empirical study, but to synthesize emerging examples and commentary on how teachers might use generative AI productively. It describes potential uses such as brainstorming, summarising readings and student feedback, drafting texts and emails, creating lesson plans and curricula, generating data visualisations, and supporting presentations and workflow automation. It also highlights concerns about hallucinations, ethical risks, and the danger of outsourcing critical thinking, arguing that AI may yield productivity gains only when used critically and with appropriate human oversight.

The editorial’s overall conclusion is that generative AI is unlikely to replace teachers wholesale, but it may significantly reshape teaching and knowledge work by augmenting some tasks and leaving others stubbornly human. The authors stress that access to hardware, software, training, and institutional support will shape who benefits from AI, and they call for critical AI literacy rather than uncritical adoption. Because the piece is an editorial and does not present original empirical data, its evidence base is primarily illustrative and argumentative rather than experimental.

finding.finding_summary: The editorial argues that generative AI can substantially improve teacher productivity on administrative and teaching-related tasks such as summarising student feedback, drafting text, creating lesson plans, and generating visualisations. One concrete illustration notes that GPT-4 can organise and summarise 100 student responses in less than a minute, compared with about an hour for a human teacher, though no original study data are reported.
finding.measure: Illustrative productivity examples and task-completion time comparisons described in the editorial

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI and Firm Productivity: Field Experiments in Online Retail
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether generative AI improves firm productivity in real-world settings, and whether the gains come from supply-side efficiency or demand-side value creation. The authors study a large cross-border e-commerce platform and use a series of randomized field experiments to evaluate seven GenAI deployments across consumer-facing workflows, including pre-sale customer service, search query refinement, product description generation, push-message creation, ad-title optimization, chargeback defense, and live-chat translation.

The interventions were implemented over roughly six months in 2023–2024, with random assignment at the consumer or product level and fixed prices and inputs across treatment and control conditions. The paper uses transaction-level outcomes such as sales, conversion rates, cart value, clicks, and product-level performance to estimate GenAI's causal effects on revenue-based productivity. The main finding is that most GenAI workflows increase sales and conversion rates, with effects ranging from no detectable impact to 16.3% sales growth; the largest gains occur in customer service and search-related applications.

The authors conclude that GenAI raises productivity primarily by reducing market frictions and improving consumer experience, rather than by changing spending intensity or post-purchase outcomes. They also find no deterioration in returns or ratings, and evidence that less experienced consumers benefit more. Overall, the study provides large-scale causal evidence that GenAI can improve productivity in online retail through demand-side channels while holding labor and capital inputs constant.

finding.finding_summary: Across seven randomized field experiments in a large online retail platform, GenAI adoption improved workflow performance and raised sales, with treatment effects ranging from 0% to 16.3% depending on the workflow. The paper interprets these gains as productivity improvements because prices and inputs were held constant, and it reports especially strong effects in the pre-sale chatbot and search-related workflows.
finding.measure: Sales (total consumer expenditure), conversion rates, clicks, and workflow-specific performance metrics
finding.study_size: n=44,614 to n=13,715,528 depending on experiment; five experiments with granular data
finding.effect_size: 0% to 16.3% sales lift; conversion rates +1% to +22% across workflows

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not directly measure student social-emotional skills, but it does examine consumer experience proxies that reflect reduced friction and easier decision-making, especially conversion rates and satisfaction-related outcomes. The main reported evidence is that GenAI increases conversion rates and, in one workflow, consumer satisfaction, without worsening returns or ratings.
finding.measure: Conversion rates, consumer satisfaction, return rates, customer ratings
finding.effect_size: Conversion rates +1% to +22%; satisfaction +5.2% in Live Chat Translation

paper_profiles.title: Augmented Computational Design
paper_profiles.venue: Artificial Intelligence in Performance-Driven Design: Theories, Methods, and Tools Towards Sustainability (book chapter)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter argues for a formalized approach to augmented computational design (ACD), in which design problems are reframed as discrete decision-making problems that can be addressed through AI. The authors distinguish two dual tasks in generative design: mapping, which learns the relationship between many design decisions and a few outcomes of interest, and navigation, which attempts to infer design decisions from desired outcomes.

The paper develops a mathematical framework using vectorized decision and performance spaces, Jacobian approximations, singular value decomposition, and pseudo-inverses to explain how AI can support both evaluation and derivation in generative design. The discussion emphasizes that AI is most appropriate when design spaces are high-dimensional, nonlinear, and difficult to model with first-principles methods, and it highlights the importance of interpretability and explainability.

The illustrative case study applies the framework to Dutch building energy modelling. Using 269 input parameters from the NTA 8800 model, the authors run 20,000 Sobol-sampled simulations, perform global sensitivity analysis to reduce the inputs to 15 influential parameters, and train a shallow Bayesian Belief Network to approximate three energy performance outputs (BENG 1, BENG 2, BENG 3). The chapter concludes that this surrogate model can support faster policy and design exploration, though the paper is methodological and theoretical rather than an evaluation of classroom or K-12 educational outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The chapter presents a data-driven surrogate modeling workflow intended to improve the efficiency of design and policy analysis by approximating a complex energy model with a smaller Bayesian Belief Network. In the case study, 20,000 simulated samples were reduced from 269 inputs to 15 influential parameters, which the authors report explained about 90.45% to 92.30% of the final energy performance score. No formal effect size, confidence interval, or standard deviation is reported because this is a methodological chapter rather than an empirical comparison study.
finding.measure: Model approximation and computational tractability for building energy performance analysis
finding.study_size: n=20000 simulation samples; 269 original inputs reduced to 15 inputs

finding.finding_summary: The chapter argues that the surrogate model can support Dutch government energy policy analysis, including subsidy planning and building-code-related decision making, by providing a more tractable approximation of the NTA 8800 model. The reported workflow is positioned as useful for institutional-scale analysis because the original model is described as too slow, opaque, and difficult to use for early-stage policy and design decisions. No inferential effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Usefulness of a meta-model for building energy policy analysis and regulatory decision support

paper_profiles.title: Modular Belief Updates and Confusion about Measures of Certainty in Artificial Intelligence Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines a conceptual problem in artificial intelligence research: the confusion between absolute measures of belief and measures of change in belief (belief updates) when reasoning under uncertainty. The authors define a property they call modularity for belief updates, show how modular updates can be derived from probability theory (using the likelihood ratio / weight of evidence), and argue that this distinction has been poorly understood in the AI literature.

The paper focuses on two influential expert systems, MYCIN and INTERNIST-I, and argues that both systems implicitly treated elicited certainty-like quantities as modular belief updates when they were in fact closer to absolute probabilities or other non-modular quantities. Through theoretical analysis and examples, the authors show that assuming modularity inappropriately can imply problematic independence assumptions and can distort reasoning. The work is primarily a conceptual/review paper aimed at the AI expert-systems community, with implications for how uncertainty should be represented and elicited from experts.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that modular belief updates can make knowledge acquisition, explanation, maintenance, and computation easier because they reduce the need to model complex interactions among evidence. However, it concludes that the apparent efficiency gains can be misleading when modularity is assumed inappropriately, because the resulting representations may be conceptually flawed and can impair correct reasoning. No empirical effect sizes or sample sizes are reported because the paper is theoretical rather than experimental.
finding.measure: Conceptual analysis of knowledge acquisition, explanation, and maintenance burden in expert systems

paper_profiles.title: Bias Amplification in Artificial Intelligence Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues that a major present-day risk of artificial intelligence is not only future automation or job loss, but the amplification of bias already present in training data. It explains how different forms of bias in machine learning datasets and model design can lead to representative harm and allocative harm, particularly for marginalized groups, and uses examples from hiring, advertising, facial recognition, chatbots, and criminal justice to illustrate these risks.

The paper is not an empirical study of a specific AI intervention or educational setting; it is a policy and conceptual discussion focused on governance, standards, and public-sector oversight. The author contends that governments should establish data standards, transparency requirements, and accountability mechanisms to reduce bias amplification, and that diversity in development teams and datasets is necessary to support fairer AI systems.

Because the paper is primarily argumentative and synthesizes examples from prior reports rather than presenting original data collection or a controlled evaluation, it does not provide direct evidence about educational outcomes or teacher productivity. Its relevance to K-12 AI research is indirect, centered on policy implications for responsible AI deployment rather than measured effects in schools.

paper_profiles.title: Certifiable Artificial Intelligence Through Data Fusion
paper_profiles.venue: AAAI Fall Symposium Series (AAAI FSS-21): Artificial Intelligence in Government and Public Sector
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual review and position paper about how to certify artificial intelligence and machine learning systems, especially in safety-critical and human-machine teaming contexts. Rather than testing an educational intervention, it surveys existing standards and proposes the Multisource AI Scorecard Table (MAST) as a framework for evaluating AI systems across sourcing, uncertainty, interpretability, transparency, consistency, accuracy, and visualization.

The paper’s main argument is that AI certification should be tied to intended use, performance bounds, and operational conditions, with verification and validation used to manage expectations about what an AI system can and cannot do. It discusses examples from aviation, security, and image fusion, including a notional image-fusion case where performance varies by distance and method (e.g., anisotropic diffusion versus CNN), but these examples are illustrative rather than a controlled study. The paper does not study K-12 learners, teachers, or classrooms directly; it is about general AI governance and certification methods.

For the image-fusion example, the authors compare two methods using metrics such as mutual information, PSNR, SSIM, standard deviation, and spatial frequency, and conclude that there are tradeoffs between speed and accuracy and that certifiable performance bounds may depend on conditions such as distance. However, the paper does not report a teacher productivity task, an education-specific comparator, or any direct K-12 evidence.

paper_profiles.title: Human-in-the-loop Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues that modern AI systems are built on knowledge extracted from the interactions and everyday work of people, and that this creates an unfair situation in which the original knowledge producers are not compensated. The author frames this as a “knowledge theft” problem and proposes Human-in-the-loop Artificial Intelligence (HIT-AI) as a normative paradigm for making AI more responsible and equitable.

The paper does not report an empirical study, intervention, or evaluation in schools. Instead, it sketches conceptual requirements for HIT-AI, emphasizing explainable AI, symbolic and distributed representations, trusted technologies, virtual identity protocols, privacy-preserving mechanisms, and possible copyright extensions. The discussion is broad and includes examples from many domains, including a brief mention that chatbots and MOOCs may replace teachers and professors, but no K-12-specific data, participants, or outcomes are presented.

Overall, the paper’s main conclusion is that AI systems should trace knowledge provenance and repay the people whose data and activity made those systems possible. Because it is a conceptual position paper without direct evidence, it provides no measured findings about teacher productivity, student learning, or school outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Enterprise AI Canvas: Integrating Artificial Intelligence into Business
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper proposes the “Enterprise AI Canvas,” a structured framework for planning how artificial intelligence can be integrated into business operations. The paper argues that existing canvases either focus too much on business strategy or too much on technical machine-learning details, and that successful AI adoption requires both perspectives to be discussed together.

The framework is organized into two parts: a business view (value, success metrics, decisions and optimization, organization, sponsor, and domains) and a model/data view (prediction and action, features, data sources and processing, domains and data quality, constraints, and evaluation/monitoring). The paper is conceptual and illustrative rather than empirical, and it uses a supermarket replenishment example to show how the canvas might be filled out in practice.

The intended audience is business and technical teams in organizations considering AI deployment, especially managers, domain experts, and data scientists. The main conclusion is that jointly specifying business goals, operational decisions, organizational change, and data/model requirements early can improve the feasibility and alignment of AI projects, but the paper does not test the framework experimentally or report quantitative outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: This is a conceptual framework paper, not an empirical study of teacher or school productivity. It proposes that AI systems may improve operational decisions and reduce manual work in business settings, but it provides no measured evidence of workload reduction, time savings, or task efficiency. The supermarket example is illustrative only and does not report experimental results.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses organizational change, sponsorship, and integration of AI into workflows, emphasizing that AI adoption can alter roles, decision rights, and management structures. However, these claims are conceptual and not evaluated with data, so there is no empirical estimate of institutional impact.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: OAK4XAI: Model towards Out-Of-Box eXplainable Artificial Intelligence for Digital Agriculture
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem that machine-learning results in digital agriculture are often accurate but difficult to interpret and reuse because they are stored as black-box models or in disconnected reports. The authors argue that farmers, agronomists, managers, and data scientists need a way to understand what a model means, what its inputs and outputs are, and how its concepts and transformations relate to domain knowledge.

To address this, the paper proposes OAK4XAI, an ontology-based knowledge map framework for explainable AI. The framework separates knowledge items from their explanations: mined results are stored as linked-data knowledge maps, while concept definitions, transformations, and relationships are stored in a domain ontology called AgriComO. The paper describes the architecture, ontology design, and a web-based knowledge browser that retrieves and explains agricultural knowledge items, with examples focused on soil pH prediction and transformation definitions.

The context is digital agriculture rather than K-12 education, and the paper is primarily a systems/framework contribution rather than an empirical evaluation of learner or teacher outcomes. The main conclusion is that an ontology-backed knowledge map can improve transparency, usability, and interpretability of mined agricultural knowledge, and the authors suggest it may help different stakeholder groups better understand and compare machine-learning models.

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims the OAK4XAI framework improves the efficiency of locating, interpreting, and reusing mined knowledge items by organizing them into a searchable knowledge repository with ontology-backed explanations. No controlled user study or quantified time-savings results are reported; the evidence is limited to system description and illustrative examples (e.g., searching "predict SoilPH").
finding.measure: Knowledge retrieval/explanation capability in the Knowledge Browser; qualitative system functionality

finding.finding_summary: The framework is presented as a reusable knowledge-management and explainability infrastructure that could support decision-making, model comparison, and standardization across agriculture knowledge repositories. The paper does not report institutional outcome data, but it argues that the ontology and linked-data architecture can improve transparency and governance of AI knowledge assets.
finding.measure: Framework/architecture for knowledge management and explanation

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (education stakeholders broadly; no specific empirical sample)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the potential opportunities and risks of large language models (LLMs), especially ChatGPT/GPT-3, for education. The paper asks how LLMs may be used to support learning and teaching, and what challenges arise around bias, privacy, plagiarism, verification, and overreliance. Rather than presenting a single empirical study, it synthesizes early research, examples, and conceptual arguments about educational applications of LLMs.

The paper discusses use cases for both learners and teachers. For teachers, it highlights possible support for lesson planning, personalized feedback, assessment, content generation, and professional development; for learners, it highlights tutoring, writing support, quiz generation, explanations, and dialogue-based practice. The authors also discuss broader concerns such as data privacy, copyright, fairness, environmental sustainability, and the difficulty of distinguishing human- from model-generated work.

Overall, the paper concludes that LLMs are promising but require careful, responsible integration into education with human oversight, critical thinking, fact-checking, and institutional safeguards. Because it is a position paper, its contributions are primarily conceptual and forward-looking rather than direct measured evidence of effects.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can save teachers time on tasks such as lesson planning, personalized material creation, feedback, and semi-automated grading. However, this is presented as a conceptual opportunity rather than direct empirical evidence; no study-level effect size or sample is reported.
finding.measure: teacher workload / time saved on planning, feedback, assessment, and content generation

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes institutional implications of LLM adoption, including copyright compliance, privacy and security, bias mitigation, governance, sustainability, and policies for fair access. These are discussed as risks and implementation requirements rather than measured outcomes, so no effect size or sample is reported.
finding.measure: policy, governance, privacy/security, copyright, sustainability, and access considerations

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly suggests that well-designed LLM use could support critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, and fact-checking by prompting reflection and inquiry. It also warns that overreliance may undermine these skills, making the overall argument mixed and conceptual rather than empirically measured.
finding.measure: critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, and fact-checking

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes LLMs as useful for reading and writing support, including summaries, outlines, grammar correction, style improvement, and writing feedback. These claims are illustrative and based on examples and cited prior work, not on direct original measurement in this paper.
finding.measure: reading comprehension and writing support tasks

paper_profiles.title: A systematic literature review of empirical research on ChatGPT in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses an early-stage evidence gap: how ChatGPT has been used in education and what empirical studies have found about its effects on learning and teaching. The authors systematically reviewed 14 empirical studies published through April 10, 2023, following PRISMA 2020 and Okoli’s review procedures, and extracted study characteristics, uses of ChatGPT, and main findings.

The reviewed studies spanned mostly higher education, with one elementary-school study and several studies that did not specify level. Across qualitative, quantitative, and mixed-methods studies, ChatGPT was used by students as a virtual assistant for on-demand answers, feedback, writing support, language support, self-directed learning, and personalized learning; teachers used it to create lesson plans, quizzes, activities, and resources. The review concludes that ChatGPT can improve productivity, writing/language support, and some learning processes, but it also raises concerns about inaccuracies, overreliance, reduced creativity/collaboration, and academic integrity. The paper emphasizes the need for training, clear guidelines, and further research on safe and effective educational use.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, ChatGPT was used to support writing, summarizing, paraphrasing, idea generation, and essay composition, with reported improvements in students’ writing performance and language-related writing tasks. However, the review also notes concerns that overuse may reduce deeper engagement and collaborative learning, and no pooled effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Writing tasks, essay composition, summarizing, paraphrasing, grammar checking, and self-reported writing/language proficiency

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that ChatGPT helped participants translate content, change linguistic tone, and check grammar, supporting language accessibility and proficiency development. These findings were based on included studies in English education and language-related tasks, but the review did not report quantitative effect sizes.
finding.measure: Translation, tone adjustment, grammar checking, dictionary-like use, and language proficiency tasks

finding.finding_summary: Several included studies found ChatGPT supported students in mathematics by helping them understand mathematical concepts, assisting with geometry operations, and improving problem-solving performance. The review describes these as positive effects on mathematical learning, but it does not provide pooled statistics or standardized effects.
finding.measure: Mathematics problem-solving, geometry operations, and understanding mathematical concepts

finding.finding_summary: The review includes multiple non-language, non-math subject areas where ChatGPT was used to support learning, including computer engineering, construction education, journalism, early education, and social science education. Reported benefits included improved hazard recognition, deeper subject understanding, and better academic task completion, but the synthesis is descriptive rather than effect-estimating.
finding.measure: Hazard recognition, subject comprehension, journalism writing, and task completion across varied disciplines

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that ChatGPT could enhance motivation, engagement, and the learning experience, but it also notes concerns that frequent use may reduce students’ motivation to attend class and may weaken collaborative competencies. The evidence is drawn from several included studies and is not summarized with quantitative effects.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, learning experience, and collaborative learning competencies

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT was reported to improve critical thinking, reasoning, problem-solving, and hazard recognition in some studies, but the review also states that overuse may negatively affect innovative capacities and collaborative learning competencies. No meta-analytic effect size was reported; the synthesis is based on the included primary studies.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, reasoning, problem-solving, innovation/creativity, and collaboration

finding.finding_summary: Teachers and students used ChatGPT to reduce time spent on tasks, generate lesson plans and quizzes, and increase productivity and efficiency. The review specifically states that educators’ productivity and efficiency improved when ChatGPT was used for content generation, resource creation, preplanning activities, and answering questions, but no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher productivity, efficiency, workload, time savings, and task completion efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that effective integration of ChatGPT requires structured training, support, and clear rules or regulations, and it calls for ongoing work with policymakers and stakeholders. This is an institutional-level recommendation emerging from the reviewed studies rather than a measured outcome, and no quantitative effect was reported.
finding.measure: Training needs, guidelines, policy/regulation needs, and stakeholder collaboration

paper_profiles.title: The application of artificial intelligence assistant to deep learning in teachers’ teaching and students’ learning processes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This brief research report examines whether an AI-assisted, intelligent in-class teaching model can improve deep learning in a university course compared with traditional instruction. The paper is motivated by the claim that AI can support teachers with intelligent lesson preparation, real-time classroom monitoring, personalized instruction, and after-class tutoring, thereby improving both teaching efficiency and student learning outcomes.

The intervention was implemented in a public foundational course on career development and employment guidance, using three rounds of action research. The experimental class (n=40) received an intelligent in-class teaching model supported by AI-related tools/platforms, while the control class (n=40) used a traditional in-class teaching model. Students were evaluated through pre-test/post-test knowledge tests, SOLO-taxonomy coding of personal resume work, questionnaires on deep learning state and ability, and interviews about emotional experience.

Findings suggest the AI-assisted model outperformed the traditional model on several measures. The experimental class showed more students reaching deeper SOLO levels across rounds, significantly higher post-test scores (experimental mean 73.75 vs control 59.58; p=0.000), and better post-test ratings on deep learning state and ability dimensions. Interview data also indicated students preferred the intelligent classroom and reported improved motivation, practical skills, and collaborative inquiry. The paper concludes that AI-based instructional design can support more effective, personalized, and efficient teaching and learning in higher education, though it also notes the need for broader and more objective future studies.

finding.finding_summary: The AI-assisted intelligent in-class teaching model improved academic performance on a personal resume design and production task in a career development course. In the post-test, the experimental class (n=40) scored higher than the control class (n=40), with means of 73.75 vs 59.58 and a statistically significant difference (p=0.000).
finding.measure: Personal resume design and production test scores

finding.finding_summary: Students in the experimental class reported improved deep learning motivation and more positive learning experience after three rounds of action research. Post-test questionnaire results showed significant differences between groups on the state of learning/deep learning motivation dimension (p=0.013), and interviews indicated students preferred the intelligent classroom and felt it helped them learn faster and stay more motivated.
finding.measure: Deep learning state, motivation, and emotional experience questionnaires; follow-up interviews
finding.study_size: questionnaire n=78 valid responses; experimental/control n=40 each; interviews n=15
finding.std_deviation: reported dimension SDs varied; see Table 3

finding.finding_summary: The intelligent in-class teaching model improved students’ deep learning ability, including problem solving, teamwork, innovation, and related learning strategies. Post-test differences favored the experimental class on deep learning ability overall (p=0.004) and on subdimensions such as problem solving (p=0.035), teamwork (p=0.001), and innovation (p=0.013).
finding.measure: Deep learning ability questionnaire subscales and SOLO-based work classification
finding.study_size: questionnaire n=78 valid responses; experimental/control n=40 each
finding.std_deviation: reported dimension SDs varied; see Table 3

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI-assisted teaching improves teaching efficiency by supporting intelligent lesson preparation, real-time monitoring, personalized courseware, and after-class Q&A tutoring. Although no direct teacher workload metric or effect size was reported, the study consistently frames the intervention as improving efficiency in teaching and learning and helping teachers grasp students’ learning conditions more effectively.
finding.measure: Teacher teaching efficiency / intelligent lesson preparation / real-time classroom monitoring (conceptual and self-reported in discussion and questionnaire items)

paper_profiles.title: Students’ voices on generative AI: perceptions, benefits, and challenges in higher education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.population: Undergraduate and postgraduate students in higher education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how university students in Hong Kong perceive generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, with attention to their familiarity, willingness to use these tools, perceived benefits, and perceived risks. The authors situate the study in the rapid rise of GenAI in higher education and ask how student perceptions may shape effective integration of these technologies into teaching and learning.

The study used an online survey with 399 undergraduate and postgraduate students from six Hong Kong universities, combining closed-ended Likert items with open-ended questions. The quantitative data were analyzed descriptively and with correlation tests, while the qualitative responses were thematically analyzed. Students generally reported a good understanding of GenAI limitations and a positive attitude toward using GenAI for learning, future careers, writing support, research support, multimedia creation, and routine administrative tasks.

At the same time, students expressed concerns about accuracy, transparency, privacy, plagiarism, over-reliance, reduced critical thinking and creativity, job displacement, weakened human values, and the lack of clear institutional policies. Knowledge of GenAI and frequency of use were positively associated with willingness to use GenAI, but concerns were not significantly correlated with knowledge. The authors conclude that GenAI could support teaching and learning, but effective integration requires AI literacy development, ethical guidance, and institutional policy frameworks.

finding.finding_summary: Students saw GenAI as potentially helpful for brainstorming, idea generation, and feedback on writing, but they also worried it could reduce critical thinking and creativity through over-reliance. The paper does not measure a causal effect on these skills; it reports perceived benefits and risks from 399 surveyed students and qualitative responses.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of GenAI’s effects on critical thinking, creativity, and idea generation

finding.finding_summary: Students frequently identified GenAI as useful for writing support, grammar improvement, paraphrasing, feedback on written work, and brainstorming. This was based on survey responses and open-ended comments from 399 university students; no direct performance outcome or effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of writing assistance, grammar support, paraphrasing, and feedback

finding.finding_summary: A major perceived benefit was time saving and workload reduction, including immediate answers, 24/7 availability, faster feedback, easier literature searching, summarizing, data analysis, and handling repetitive administrative work. The study is perception-based rather than experimental, so it does not estimate actual productivity gains.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of time saving, workload reduction, and task efficiency

finding.finding_summary: Students linked GenAI to broader institutional concerns, especially policy uncertainty, academic integrity, transparency, privacy, and potential effects on the value of university education and student-teacher relationships. The study suggests a need for institutional guidance and governance, but it does not evaluate a policy intervention or institutional outcome.
finding.measure: Student concerns about policy, governance, academic integrity, privacy, and educational value

finding.finding_summary: Students generally reported willingness to use GenAI and saw it as supportive, available, and helpful for personalized learning, but they also expressed concerns about dependence on the technology and its possible effects on motivation and personal development. The paper measures perceptions only, not changes in engagement or self-regulation.
finding.measure: Student willingness to use GenAI, perceived support, and concerns about over-reliance/motivation

paper_profiles.title: Using ChatGPT as a Lesson Planning Assistant with Preservice Secondary Mathematics Teachers
paper_profiles.population: Undergraduate; Graduate preservice secondary mathematics teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This qualitative study examines how preservice secondary mathematics teachers (PSTs) used ChatGPT as a lesson-planning assistant while preparing microteaching lessons in a secondary mathematics methods course. The authors were interested in two questions: how PSTs reacted to ChatGPT’s mathematical output and what they found useful or not useful when using it to plan a mini-lesson.

Twenty-two PSTs at a public urban university first solved a selected mathematics task on their own, then prompted ChatGPT to solve the same task and to help draft aims and objectives for a lesson. They continued using ChatGPT informally during lesson preparation and later reflected on its usefulness after teaching. The data consisted of the PSTs’ written reflections, ChatGPT outputs, and lesson-planning artifacts, analyzed through deductive qualitative coding grounded in a reflective framework.

The main conclusion is that PSTs were generally able to use ChatGPT as a starting point for planning, especially for pedagogical elements such as objectives, misconceptions, assessment ideas, and rough lesson outlines, but they did not use its output unchanged. However, PSTs often failed to recognize mathematical errors in ChatGPT’s responses, even when they solved the problems correctly themselves. The authors conclude that teacher education should emphasize critical reflection and AI literacy, particularly for evaluating mathematical correctness and pedagogical quality.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT’s mathematical accuracy was limited: among 19 comparable PST-ChatGPT problem-solving instances, PSTs were correct in 15 cases while ChatGPT was correct in only 6. There were 5 cases where both were correct, 10 where the PST was correct but ChatGPT was incorrect, 3 where both were incorrect, and 1 where the PST was incorrect but ChatGPT was correct. PSTs often failed to identify ChatGPT’s errors, suggesting limited reliability for mathematics problem solving.
finding.measure: Correctness of solutions to secondary mathematics tasks (algebra, geometry, data analysis, percent) and PST evaluations of ChatGPT’s solutions
finding.study_size: n=19 comparable problem-solving instances (n=22 PSTs total; 3 not coded for this analysis)

finding.finding_summary: PSTs found ChatGPT useful for generating and revising lesson-planning components such as aims, objectives, prior knowledge, misconceptions, homework ideas, and lesson outlines. Of 22 responses, 20 indicated changes to aims/objectives after using ChatGPT, and several PSTs reported incorporating ChatGPT-generated suggestions into their lesson plans. The evidence is qualitative rather than experimental, but it indicates clear perceived usefulness for planning support.
finding.measure: PST reflections on usefulness for lesson planning; reported changes to aims, objectives, assessments, misconceptions, and lesson structure

finding.finding_summary: The study found that ChatGPT prompted metacognitive and critical reflection, with PSTs evaluating whether the output was useful, accurate, and aligned with lesson goals. The authors argue that reflective analysis was central to how PSTs used the tool, and many PST comments explicitly described using ChatGPT as a starting point for comparison, revision, and critique rather than as a final authority.
finding.measure: PST reflective statements about ChatGPT’s output, accuracy, and usefulness

finding.finding_summary: PSTs reported that ChatGPT helped them plan more quickly and provided ready-made ideas, outlines, objectives, and assessment prompts, which reduced effort during lesson development. Although the paper does not measure time savings directly, multiple reflections describe ChatGPT as a helpful planning tool or starting point that improved efficiency in drafting lesson components.
finding.measure: PST reflections on lesson-planning usefulness, including planning support, idea generation, and drafting assistance

paper_profiles.title: The Effects of an Artificial Intelligence Voice Chatbot on Improving Vietnamese Undergraduate Students’ English Speaking Skills
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Learning, Teaching and Educational Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether practicing English speaking with an AI voice chatbot improves Vietnamese undergraduate students’ speaking performance, and how students perceive the tool. The paper was motivated by persistent speaking difficulties among Vietnamese EFL learners, including limited opportunities to practice, low confidence, and insufficient exposure to spoken English.

The intervention used Andy English Bot, an AI voice chatbot, over an 8-week quasi-experimental mixed-methods study with 30 non-English-major undergraduates at Can Tho University, Vietnam. Students completed pre- and post-speaking tests, a questionnaire, and semi-structured interviews after practicing with the chatbot during class sessions and self-study time. The speaking tests targeted fluency and accuracy, and the qualitative data explored students’ experiences with pronunciation, grammar, vocabulary, confidence, and ease of practice.

Results showed statistically significant gains in overall speaking performance as well as in both fluency and accuracy after the intervention (paired t-tests, p < 0.05 for all comparisons). Students reported that the chatbot helped them improve grammar, pronunciation, vocabulary, and confidence by providing repeated practice, native-like input, visible text feedback, and unlimited speaking time. The study concludes that AI voice chatbots can be a useful tool for English speaking instruction, while noting limitations related to small sample size, limited topics, and some speech-recognition issues.

finding.finding_summary: After the 8-week intervention with Andy English Bot, students’ English speaking performance improved significantly on the speaking tests, with gains specifically reported for fluency. The paired t-test for fluency was significant (Pair 1: pre-test vs post-test, p = .000, n = 30), and the mean paired difference was -0.4333 with a 95% CI of [-0.5528, -0.3139].
finding.measure: Pre-speaking and post-speaking speaking test fluency scores

finding.finding_summary: Students reported greater confidence, comfort, and motivation to speak English after using the AI voice chatbot, and questionnaire responses indicated overall agreement that the chatbot improved their speaking. Interview data suggested the unlimited time and nonjudgmental practice environment reduced pressure and encouraged more frequent speaking.
finding.measure: Questionnaire ratings and semi-structured interview themes on feelings, confidence, and motivation

finding.finding_summary: The intervention also produced significant gains in speaking accuracy, which the paper attributes to improved grammar, vocabulary, and pronunciation. The accuracy paired t-test was significant (Pair 2: pre-test vs post-test, p = .000, n = 30), with a mean paired difference of -0.2833 and a 95% CI of [-0.3872, -0.1795].
finding.measure: Pre-speaking and post-speaking speaking test accuracy scores

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT: Bullshit spewer or the end of traditional assessments in higher education?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the emergence of ChatGPT and asks what it means for learning, teaching, and assessment in higher education. The authors combine a desktop literature review with hands-on experimentation using ChatGPT to explore its capabilities, limitations, and likely implications for education.

The paper situates ChatGPT within the broader history of AI in education, especially student-facing, teacher-facing, and system-facing applications. The authors argue that ChatGPT is powerful enough to challenge conventional written assessments, but also unreliable enough that it should not be treated as a substitute for human judgment. They emphasize opportunities for more innovative assessment design, flipped learning, and feedback support, while cautioning that the model can generate inaccurate, generic, or fabricated content.

The article is not an empirical study of learners or teachers in schools; it is primarily a conceptual and exploratory higher-education piece. Its main conclusion is that educators and institutions should adapt assessment and teaching practices rather than simply banning ChatGPT, since AI-generated text tools are likely to become part of everyday academic work.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that ChatGPT can produce conceptual explanations, draft essays, and generate responses within roughly 60-120 seconds, suggesting potential time savings for writing and explanation tasks. However, the authors also found substantial limitations: the tool produced generic and shallow content for a 2000-word essay prompt, failed to provide reliable citations, and struggled with some language tasks, so its productivity benefits are context-dependent rather than consistently positive.
finding.measure: Informal task completion speed and output quality during author experiments with ChatGPT

paper_profiles.title: Using ChatGPT for Science Learning: A Study on Pre-service Teachers' Lesson Planning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how pre-service elementary science teachers in Korea envisioned using ChatGPT in science lesson planning, and how they perceived its usefulness and risks. The authors address a gap in empirical research on generative AI in education by moving beyond speculation and analyzing actual lesson plans and survey responses rather than only opinions about ChatGPT.

Twenty-nine pre-service teachers in a university science education course received short instructional sessions on ChatGPT and science-teaching methods, then created lesson plans for a typical 45-minute elementary science class. Their plans were evaluated with a modified TPACK-based rubric, and open-ended survey responses plus attached simulated chat transcripts were qualitatively analyzed. The study found that participants imagined ChatGPT across many science topics and instructional methods, scored relatively high overall on the rubric (M=3.29/4, SD=.91), and were especially strong at aligning ChatGPT with instructional strategies. However, they were less effective at choosing appropriate ChatGPT functions, and they identified both suitable and unsuitable uses.

The paper also reports that pre-service teachers viewed ChatGPT as useful for question generation, self-directed learning, individualized support, and formative feedback, while worrying about inaccurate information and student over-dependence. Participants suggested mitigation strategies such as using multiple information sources, teacher guidance, peer discussion, and structured classroom interaction. Overall, the authors conclude that ChatGPT has broad perceived potential for science instruction, but that future teacher professional development should focus on more careful functional selection, critical evaluation of AI outputs, and classroom structures that prevent over-reliance on the tool.

finding.finding_summary: Pre-service teachers expected ChatGPT to improve planning and instructional efficiency in science lessons by helping organize role-play activities, generate and refine prompts/questions, summarize lengthy student-generated scenarios, and provide rapid feedback. In the analyzed lesson plans, ChatGPT was also used as a supplementary information source and to support individualized or adaptive instruction, suggesting perceived productivity gains for teachers and students; however, the paper does not report a task-time comparison or direct workload reduction measure.
finding.measure: Lesson-plan analysis of ChatGPT uses; TPACK-based rubric (instructional integration and function selection) and qualitative survey responses about usefulness

finding.finding_summary: Participants believed ChatGPT could support scientific inquiry processes such as prediction, explanation, exploration, and concept understanding in elementary science. The lesson plans emphasized using ChatGPT for learning content like ecological balance, solar system and stars, and acids and bases, and the discussion noted that ChatGPT could bolster scientific inquiry and cognitive gains when used with teacher guidance; nevertheless, no direct student learning outcomes were measured.
finding.measure: Lesson plans and survey responses about science-content integration and inquiry-oriented instructional use

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that participants believed ChatGPT could foster critical thinking through continuous questioning and comparison with other sources, and could support collaborative learning structures such as jigsaw, role play, and group discussion. The study also found that teachers intentionally proposed classroom structures to prevent over-dependence and encourage reflection, indicating a perceived benefit for critical thinking, collaboration, and self-regulation rather than a measured effect on these skills.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses and coded lesson-plan strategies; references to critical thinking, collaboration, and reflection

finding.finding_summary: Pre-service teachers repeatedly anticipated that ChatGPT could increase students' motivation, interest, active participation, and self-directed learning. These claims were based on perceptions in survey responses and lesson-plan rationale, not on observed student engagement data, so the finding reflects expected rather than directly measured gains.
finding.measure: Survey responses on perceived usefulness; lesson-plan rationales referencing motivation, interest, participation, and self-directed learning

paper_profiles.title: Connecting Feedback to Choice: Understanding Educator Preferences in GenAI vs. Human-Created Lesson Plans in K-12 Education – A Comparative Analysis
paper_profiles.population: K-12 mathematics educators (elementary, middle, and high school contexts)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether K-12 educators prefer lesson plans created by humans or by generative AI, and which parts of lesson plans differ most in quality and usefulness. The authors frame lesson planning as a time-consuming, cognitively demanding task and investigate whether GenAI can serve as a practical assistive tool for curriculum development.

The study compares three sources of mathematics lesson plans: human curriculum designers, a fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model, and a prompt-engineered GPT-4 model. Twenty experienced K-12 math educators evaluated pairwise comparisons of lesson plans across four dimensions: warm-up, main tasks, cool-down, and overall quality. The dataset included 529 complete lesson-plan pairs and 2,116 binary evaluations, plus 2,979 written comments analyzed using topic modeling and manual thematic coding.

Results show that human-authored lesson plans were generally preferred overall, especially for elementary grades and for instructional components requiring pedagogy-sensitive design such as warm-ups, main tasks, group work, student discourse, and support for multilingual learners or students with disabilities. However, AI-generated plans, especially GPT-4, were comparatively strong in cool-down activities and structured wrap-up tasks, and the fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model became more competitive at higher grade levels, especially high school. The authors conclude that GenAI is best positioned as a collaborative planning aid rather than a replacement for educator expertise, with the strongest use cases in structured lesson components and lesson summarization.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies whether GenAI can reduce lesson-planning burden by producing lesson plans that educators judge as usable alternatives to human-created plans. In pairwise preference tests, educators preferred GPT-4 over LLaMA-2-13b fine-tuned 57.7% to 42.3%, and human-created plans over GPT-4 58.7% to 41.3%; the authors interpret this as evidence that GenAI can serve as an assistive planning tool, especially for structured components like cool-downs, though human plans remain preferred overall.
finding.measure: Educator pairwise preference judgments of lesson plan quality/usability across warm-up, main task, cool-down, and overall lesson plan
finding.study_size: n=16 educators; 529 complete lesson plan pairs; 2,116 total evaluations

finding.finding_summary: The study is entirely focused on K-12 mathematics lesson plans aligned to CCSSM, so it substantively concerns mathematics instruction. Educators preferred human-created lesson plans overall, especially in elementary grades, but the fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model became more competitive in middle and high school, including a 59.2% preference over human-created plans in high school.
finding.measure: Pairwise educator preferences for mathematics lesson plans aligned to Common Core State Standards for Mathematics
finding.study_size: n=16 educators; 529 complete lesson plan pairs

finding.finding_summary: The paper examines instructional features closely related to durable skills such as collaboration, discourse, and structured reasoning within lesson plans. Human-created lesson plans were preferred for fostering meaningful student discourse and structured group work, while AI-generated plans were sometimes seen as more structured for some high-school-level content and wrap-up activities.
finding.measure: Educator comments and pairwise preferences regarding lesson-plan features such as group work, student discourse, and cognitive demand
finding.study_size: n=16 educators; 2,979 comments plus 2,116 binary evaluations

finding.finding_summary: Although the paper does not measure student motivation directly, it evaluates educator preferences for lesson-plan elements tied to engagement and supportive instruction. Human-authored plans were favored for warm-ups, developmental appropriateness, and supports for multilingual learners and students with disabilities, while GenAI plans were often described as more structured but less engaging or less supportive.
finding.measure: Educator preferences and qualitative comments about engagement, warm-up relevance, and scaffolded supports

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses implications for curriculum development and responsible AI integration in K-12 schooling, concluding that GenAI can function as a collaborative planning aid within institutional lesson-planning workflows. The evidence is indirect and based on educator preference rather than policy or organizational outcomes, but the authors explicitly frame the findings as guidance for AI adoption in educational content creation.
finding.measure: Educator judgments about the suitability of human vs. GenAI lesson plans for classroom use

paper_profiles.title: LessonPlanner: Assisting Novice Teachers to Prepare Pedagogy-Driven Lesson Plans with Large Language Models
paper_profiles.venue: UIST '24 (ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge novice teachers face when preparing lesson plans: choosing effective instructional strategies, finding appropriate teaching materials, and organizing content into a coherent lesson structure. The authors argue that large language models (LLMs) could reduce this burden, but that existing chat-based interfaces do not sufficiently support lesson-planning workflows or pedagogical structure.

To investigate this, the authors first ran a formative study with six novice teachers and teaching assistants to identify needs and design requirements. Based on those findings, they built LessonPlanner, a web-based LLM-assisted lesson-planning system grounded in Bloom’s Taxonomy and Gagne’s Nine Events of Instruction. The system supports metadata-driven prompt templates, outline generation, block-based editing, preset pedagogical actions, and flexible regeneration/copy/edit interactions.

They then evaluated LessonPlanner in a within-subjects study with 12 university students with little or no teaching experience, who planned lesson materials for familiar Data Structures topics using either LessonPlanner or a baseline ChatGPT web interface. They also conducted expert interviews with six teachers across educational levels. The study found that LessonPlanner improved the quality of outcome lesson plans and reduced workload during planning compared with the baseline, while expert interviews suggested the tool was especially helpful for structuring lessons and generating inspiring content. The paper concludes that LLMs can support lesson-planning productivity when embedded in pedagogy-aware interfaces rather than used as generic chat tools.

finding.finding_summary: In a within-subjects study with n=12 university students acting as teachers, LessonPlanner significantly reduced perceived workload in lesson-plan preparation compared with the baseline ChatGPT web interface. Participants reported lower NASA-TLX-style workload across the planning process, and the paper concludes that the system eased users’ workload while preparing lesson plans.
finding.measure: Lesson-planning workload (NASA-TLX-derived questionnaire) comparing LessonPlanner vs. baseline ChatGPT web app

finding.finding_summary: The system significantly improved the quality of outcome lesson plans in the within-subjects study with n=12 participants. Quality was rated by an experienced Data Structures teacher using CIPP-inspired criteria, including alignment with objectives, teaching materials, balance of theory/practice, teaching strategies, and detail; LessonPlanner outperformed the baseline ChatGPT interface.
finding.measure: Lesson plan quality ratings using CIPP-adapted rubric

paper_profiles.title: Linking Artificial Intelligence Principles
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Workshop on Artificial Intelligence Safety (AAAI-Safe AI 2019)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to compare, connect, and analyze the large and growing set of published Artificial Intelligence (AI) principles. The authors argue that existing AI principles differ in emphasis, vocabulary, and scope, and that no single proposal is complete.
