To address this, they introduce the Linking Artificial Intelligence Principles (LAIP) platform for semantically linking principles across organizations.

Methodologically, the paper compiles 27 AI principle documents from academia, non-profits, governments, and industry. The authors manually define 10 high-level topics (e.g., humanity, fairness, privacy, safety, accountability) and expand keyword sets using word2vec similarity to measure topic coverage and keyword coverage across proposals. They also compare topic frequencies by type of publisher and represent the resulting linkages using Semantic Web standards (RDF/OWL).

The paper is not an intervention study and does not evaluate educational outcomes. Its main conclusion is that AI principles share overlapping themes but also reflect distinct priorities by organization type: corporations emphasize collaboration more, governments emphasize security more, and academia emphasizes accountability more. The authors recommend combining multiple AI principles into a comprehensive framework rather than adopting any single one in isolation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds substantial variation in which ethical topics are emphasized across AI principle documents, suggesting that organizational and governance perspectives shape institutional AI policy framing. Based on 27 AI principle proposals, the authors report that corporations mention collaboration more, governments mention security more, and academia mentions accountability more, indicating complementary but uneven policy priorities rather than a single consensus framework.
finding.measure: Topic coverage and keyword frequency across 27 AI principle documents; comparative topic frequencies by publisher type

paper_profiles.title: Unmasking the giant: A comprehensive evaluation of ChatGPT’s proficiency in coding algorithms and data structures
paper_profiles.venue: ACM conference paper (venue not specified in provided text)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates ChatGPT’s ability to solve Python programming problems focused on algorithms, data structures, and strings. The authors ask whether ChatGPT can generate correct code, how its code quality compares with human solutions, whether it may have memorized training data, and how wrong its incorrect solutions tend to be. They compare GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 across 2,792 LeetCode coding prompts, using both complete prompts (problem text plus examples and constraints) and incomplete prompts (problem text only).

The study uses LeetCode as the primary benchmark and PyLint to assess code quality. It also compares model performance against human submission statistics on LeetCode, and separates results into train-set and test-set problems based on whether the problems/solutions were plausibly present on the internet before or after the September 2021 cutoff used by ChatGPT training. The context is coding assessment rather than education intervention, and the relevant population is programming tasks akin to undergraduate computer science work, not K-12 learners.

Main findings are that GPT-4 generally outperforms GPT-3.5, especially on the training-set problems, but humans outperform both models on the test set. Performance drops substantially on harder problems, and most wrong answers are not close to correct: when ChatGPT fails, its code usually still executes but often passes only a small fraction of test cases. PyLint analysis shows many warnings and convention issues, with undefined-variable errors dominating runtime failures. The incomplete-prompt experiment suggests a mix of memorization and generalization, since the models sometimes solve partially redacted test-set problems but do much better on training-set-like items.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies ChatGPT as a coding productivity aid by measuring whether it can generate correct Python solutions, how often its code runs without runtime errors, and how code quality varies across 2,792 LeetCode prompts. GPT-4 substantially outperforms GPT-3.5 overall, but on unseen test problems humans still outperform both models; for incomplete prompts, the models still solved 10-19% of test items correctly, suggesting some utility for filling in missing code-task details.
finding.measure: Correctness of coding solutions on LeetCode; runtime errors; PyLint code-quality issues; fraction of test cases passed by wrong solutions
finding.study_size: n=2792 coding prompts (723 complete train-like + 673 incomplete train-like; corresponding test-set prompts as reported)

paper_profiles.title: Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup as an Evaluation Domain for Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.venue: AAAI-2019 Workshop on Games and Simulations for Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues that Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup (DCSS), a complex single-player roguelike game, is a strong evaluation domain for AI and cognitive systems. The authors focus on why DCSS is attractive as a benchmark: it is partially observable, dynamic, stochastic, open-ended, and requires long-horizon strategic planning, rich knowledge use, and explanation capabilities.

The paper describes an ongoing effort to build an API that would let AI agents interact with DCSS through structured state objects and action commands. The API is intended to support research on planning, reinforcement learning, knowledge extraction, explainable AI, tutoring, and human-agent interaction, including spectators and chat-based interaction. The paper also summarizes human tournament performance data from prior DCSS competitions and uses those results to motivate DCSS as a benchmark for comparing AI systems against human play.

The paper does not present an experimental intervention or evaluate an educational technology in K-12 settings. Instead, it provides a domain analysis, a lower-bound complexity argument for DCSS state/action space, and a discussion of future research directions. Its main conclusion is that DCSS fills a useful gap among simulated environments because it combines high complexity with turn-based decision-making that does not penalize slow deliberation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses an AI API and benchmark domain, but it does not evaluate any productivity, workload, or efficiency intervention. No empirical results are reported on task completion time, teacher workload, or other operational outcomes; the only quantitative information concerns human game-play statistics used as motivation for benchmarking.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: To what extent is ChatGPT useful for language teacher lesson plan creation?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether ChatGPT can help language teachers create lesson plans, and whether making prompts more specific improves the quality and consistency of the generated plans. The authors focus on zero-shot prompting with ChatGPT-4.0 and evaluate outputs against a lesson-plan rubric aligned to ACTFL world-readiness standards and an edTPA-based template used in a university foreign language teacher preparation program.

The researchers generated 50 lesson plans by entering five prompts, each repeated 10 times in new chats. The prompts increased in specificity from a general lesson request to one that also included a lesson-plan format, standards guidance, and a detailed checklist of required elements. Outputs were scored on the presence or absence of 25 rubric criteria, then analyzed with descriptive statistics, ANOVA, Jaccard distance, NMDS, PERMANOVA, ANOSIM, and hierarchical clustering to examine prompt effects and variability.

The main finding is that ChatGPT can generate generally high-quality lesson plans for foreign language teaching, but more specific prompts do not reliably produce better output. The most useful addition was an explicit checklist of required criteria, while adding a template or standards language sometimes lowered scores or narrowed the plan in unhelpful ways. The authors also found substantial non-determinism: identical prompts often produced meaningfully different lesson plans, sometimes differing by at least five rubric elements. They conclude that teachers can use ChatGPT to streamline lesson planning, but they should critically evaluate and revise outputs because generated plans may include outdated pedagogical practices, weak cultural integration, or other anachronistic features.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT was generally useful for generating foreign language lesson plans, suggesting a productivity benefit for teachers. Across 50 generated plans (5 prompts × 10 iterations), outputs were often high quality, and the best prompt condition (P.5, with a checklist of required criteria) produced the highest mean rubric score at 21.6/25. The authors conclude that the tool can streamline lesson planning, although the improvement was not linear with prompt specificity.
finding.measure: Lesson-plan rubric score / presence of 25 required lesson-plan criteria; word count

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates ChatGPT’s ability to generate foreign language teaching materials, specifically high school Spanish lesson plans. Output quality was generally strong, but alignment with pedagogical goals varied by prompt, and the inclusion of a checklist improved completeness more than a template or standards prompt alone. The study also identified recurring weaknesses in culture integration and some instructional components.
finding.measure: Lesson-plan rubric criteria for foreign language pedagogy / edTPA-aligned lesson plan components

paper_profiles.title: Learning to Plan by Updating Natural Language
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how large language models can be made better at complex reasoning tasks by learning a reusable natural-language task plan rather than relying only on one-shot or few-shot prompting. The authors argue that LLMs often produce incomplete or factually incorrect plans when asked to solve complex tasks, so they introduce a "learning to plan" method that iteratively updates a natural-language plan using error feedback from training examples.

The method works in two phases. In training, the model identifies wrong samples, prompts the LLM to generate candidate plan updates, verifies them on a validation set, compresses overly long updates, and appends the best update to the plan. In testing, the learned plan is inserted into the prompt to guide inference. The experiments are run on 8 reasoning datasets spanning mathematical, causal, logical, symbolic, and combinatorial reasoning, using ChatGPT and also some open-source models such as Vicuna. Results show that the learned plan improves zero-shot and few-shot performance over direct CoT prompting, self-plan baselines, and Automatic Prompt Engineer, and that a learned plan can even transfer from one LLM to another (e.g., from ChatGPT to GPT-4).

finding.finding_summary: On the AMPS math dataset (10 tasks), ChatGPT + Learning-to-Plan improved average zero-shot CoT accuracy from 48.3% to 66.6% (+18.3 points) and few-shot CoT accuracy from 64.0% to 73.9% (+9.9 points). The paper also reports stronger performance on the 7-task Math dataset, where average accuracy increased from 27.4% to 29.8% zero-shot and from 30.6% to 31.3% few-shot.
finding.measure: Task accuracy on math reasoning benchmarks (AMPS 10-task average; Math dataset 7-task average)
finding.study_size: AMPS: 10 tasks; Math: 7 tasks; underlying example counts vary by task, not_reported at aggregate level

finding.finding_summary: The method improved performance on the logical reasoning tasks studied in the paper, including LSAT-style reasoning and date understanding. In the non-mathematical reasoning benchmark table, average zero-shot CoT accuracy rose from 54.0% to 66.0%, and few-shot CoT accuracy rose from 63.5% to 67.1% with Learning-to-Plan.
finding.measure: Reasoning-task accuracy on LSAT logical reasoning, date understanding, and related non-mathematical benchmarks
finding.study_size: 6 tasks in the non-mathematical benchmark table; individual datasets have not_reported sizes in the table excerpt

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates whether learning a task plan improves higher-order reasoning and structured problem solving, which maps most closely to durable skills such as planning and metacognition. Across several reasoning benchmarks, the learned plan consistently outperformed zero-shot CoT, self-plan, and APE baselines, indicating better procedural reasoning and stepwise problem decomposition.
finding.measure: Accuracy on reasoning tasks requiring step-by-step problem solving and plan-following
finding.study_size: 8 datasets across mathematical, causal, logical, symbolic, and combinatorial reasoning

finding.finding_summary: The central contribution is an LLM prompting method intended to improve task completion efficiency by learning reusable plans, but the paper does not measure human time savings or teacher workload directly. It does report that the method improves model performance over direct prompting and over baseline prompt-engineering methods, suggesting better operational efficiency for LLM-mediated task solving, though this is only indirect evidence for productivity.
finding.measure: Model task-solving accuracy as a proxy for efficiency/productivity gains

paper_profiles.title: Large Language Models to the Rescue: Reducing the Complexity in Scientific Workflow Development Using ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether ChatGPT can support researchers working with scientific workflows, especially for comprehension, modification, and extension of workflow scripts. The authors motivated the work by noting that scientific workflows are difficult to understand and adapt because they combine multiple tools, data formats, and distributed execution details, while domain experts often lack deep software-engineering knowledge.

The study uses three user studies in two scientific domains: biomedicine and Earth observation. Experts were given workflow descriptions or partial scripts and asked to evaluate ChatGPT outputs for understanding the workflow purpose, suggesting alternative tools, rewriting workflow steps, and extending partial workflows. The paper does not test a classroom or school intervention; its participants are adult domain experts (postdocs and PhD students), so the educational relevance is indirect and not K-12-focused.

Overall, the authors find that ChatGPT performs best on reconstructive tasks such as explaining workflows and listing alternative tools, with generally high expert ratings for comprehension. Performance drops for more demanding, exploratory, or generative tasks such as selecting appropriate tool substitutions in context, rewriting workflow code, and extending partial workflows. The paper concludes that general-purpose LLMs may improve human productivity in workflow analysis and adaptation, but they are not yet reliable for complex workflow modification without human correction.

finding.finding_summary: Across three user studies with adult domain experts, ChatGPT was judged to improve efficiency mainly for reconstructive workflow-support tasks such as explaining workflows and listing alternative tools. Experts rated comprehension positively (mean rating µ=4.7, σ=0.68), and the authors conclude that the system can save time when users are analyzing or searching for replacements for workflow components, though exact time savings were not quantified.
finding.measure: Expert ratings of workflow comprehension, tool exploration, and qualitative judgments of time-saving/productivity

paper_profiles.title: Exploring Teachers’ Perception of Artificial Intelligence: The Socio-emotional Deficiency as Opportunities and Challenges in Human-AI Complementarity in K-12 Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 teachers perceive artificial intelligence (AI) as a complement to human teachers across a broad set of school roles and tasks. The central question is not whether AI improves test scores directly, but which teacher responsibilities teachers believe AI can automate, augment, or struggle with, especially given growing interest in human-AI collaboration in schools.

The study used a mixed-methods design with a survey of 100 elementary school teachers in South Korea and follow-up semi-structured interviews with 12 teachers. The survey used an Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) to derive perceived AI complementarity scores across eleven teacher tasks, while interviews explored why teachers saw AI as suitable or unsuitable for particular duties. Teachers viewed AI as especially well-suited to administrative work, automation, and data-driven planning, and least suited to socio-emotional tasks such as life guidance and parent-teacher relationships.

A major conclusion is that teachers see AI’s advanced analytical ability as useful, but its lack of socio-emotional capability creates both limits and opportunities. Teachers expected AI to help with personalized learning, automated scoring, and administrative efficiency, while also fearing that AI cannot reliably handle nuanced communication, guidance, and relationship-building. The authors argue that future AI adoption in schools should be tailored to teacher concerns and task-specific complementarity rather than treated as a single, uniform solution.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers perceived AI as most complementary for administrative and automation-related work. In the AHP survey of 100 elementary teachers, school administration had a summed PCS of 0.820 versus 0.180 for educational tasks, with administrative affairs alone scoring highest (PCS=0.437), indicating strong perceived productivity gains for AI in fixed, standardized tasks such as document processing and budget planning.
finding.measure: Perceived AI Complementarity Score (PCS) from Analytic Hierarchy Process survey across teacher tasks

finding.finding_summary: Teachers believed AI could support institutional decision-making, policy administration, task allocation, and leadership, but also recognized risks around authority and interpersonal dynamics. Interview data (12 teachers; 68 meaningful comments) suggested AI could provide fairer, non-authoritative decisions and reduce conflict in schools, yet human judgment remained seen as important for politically and socially complex interactions.
finding.measure: Perceived AI roles in school governance, decision-making, task assignment, and leadership from survey and interviews

finding.finding_summary: Teachers perceived AI as weak for socio-emotional tasks such as life guidance, parent-teacher relationships, emotional recognition, persuasion, and non-verbal communication. In the AHP results, the socio-emotional task group had low perceived complementarity, and life guidance (PCS=0.007) and parent-teacher relationships (PCS=0.009) were among the lowest-rated tasks.
finding.measure: Perceived AI complementarity for socio-emotional teacher tasks

finding.finding_summary: Teachers saw AI as potentially useful for some reflective and analytical aspects of teaching, such as data-driven planning and objective feedback, but not for nuanced judgment, adaptability, or complex social interpretation. The study’s task-ability mapping and clustered task groups showed analytical tasks as the most AI-complementary, while perceptual/instructional tasks were least complementary, suggesting uneven perceived support for higher-order professional skills.
finding.measure: Perceived AI complementarity for analytical and reflective teacher tasks from PCS and task-ability mapping

finding.finding_summary: Teachers anticipated AI could contribute to personalized learning, individualized feedback, AI-powered instruction, and curriculum planning. Survey and interview evidence indicated support for AI in tailoring learning materials, providing daily check-ups and feedback, and contextualizing curriculum planning based on school and national data, but these were perceptions rather than direct student outcome measures.
finding.measure: Perceived AI complementarity for teaching, student assessment, training, and curriculum planning

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conceptual article examines how artificial intelligence is changing classroom practice and academic work, with a focus on higher education. The paper asks what knowledge and skills are needed for students and educators to use AI responsibly and productively, and it centers three capabilities: AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking.

The paper is built around a case study from Kalaidos University of Applied Sciences in Switzerland, where the institution developed internal AI guidelines in response to widespread student use of ChatGPT and related tools. The author combines informal discussions with students and staff and a narrative literature review to propose a middle-ground policy: AI should be permitted, but only with transparency, critical evaluation, and clear boundaries against uncritical copy-paste use.

A second part of the paper discusses classroom uses of AI, such as AI experiments, case study construction, curriculum support, gamification, and immersive technologies. Rather than evaluating a specific intervention empirically, the article argues that schools should build an AI culture through workshops, updated guidance, dedicated budgets, and staff support. Its main conclusion is that AI can support learning and teaching, but only if users are trained to understand limitations, verify outputs, and use prompt engineering thoughtfully.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that institutional AI guidelines, workshops, dedicated budgets, and paid AI support roles would improve how schools govern AI use and build an AI culture. This is a conceptual recommendation based on a Swiss university case study and narrative literature review, not an empirical test, so no effect size or sample-based outcome is reported.
finding.measure: Institutional AI policy and governance practices

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that AI tools can help teachers create curricula, generate case studies, and support classroom preparation, but it also cautions that prompting and refinement can sometimes take as long as doing the task manually. The discussion is qualitative and illustrative rather than experimental, so no quantitative time-savings estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workflow, curriculum creation, and classroom preparation efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally argues that prompt engineering and AI literacy can strengthen critical thinking by requiring users to evaluate outputs, detect hallucinations, and compare AI responses against evidence. The claim is supported by narrative review and examples, not a direct intervention study, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, AI literacy, and prompt engineering skill development

paper_profiles.title: JALT Editorial 6(1): Fully automated luxury communism or Turing trap? Graduate employability in the generative AI age
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This editorial reflects on the changing meaning of work in the age of generative AI, using historical, philosophical, and contemporary examples to frame a debate between reduced work/fully automated futures and the risks of a "Turing trap" in which AI is used to automate human labor rather than augment it. The paper is not an empirical study of a single intervention; instead, it synthesizes commentary and cites emerging reports and examples about generative AI's effects on productivity, employment, and higher education.

A substantial portion of the editorial considers implications for higher education and graduate employability. It argues that generative AI may dramatically reshape white-collar knowledge work, including education-related tasks, and that this could increase inequality and threaten the meaning of work for students, educators, and professionals. The piece also briefly surveys the issue’s articles, including several on generative AI in higher education, but does not report original data from K-12 classrooms or teacher productivity studies.

Because the article is an editorial and conceptual discussion rather than a primary research study, it offers no experimental design, sample, or effect estimates. Its main contribution is interpretive: it situates generative AI within broader debates about labor, automation, and the future of higher education, and it raises questions about whether educators will flourish or be displaced as AI adoption increases.

paper_profiles.title: AI to the rescue: Exploring the potential of ChatGPT as a teacher ally for workload relief and burnout prevention
paper_profiles.venue: Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning
paper_profiles.population: Secondary school teachers (students aged 12-18 in lesson-plan examples)
paper_profiles.extended_summary: This paper examines whether ChatGPT can serve as a teacher assistant to reduce workload and help prevent burnout in secondary education. The authors frame teacher burnout as strongly linked to heavy workload and time-consuming non-teaching tasks, especially lesson planning and content development. Rather than testing effects on students, the study evaluates whether ChatGPT can generate useful lesson plans and related instructional content for common secondary-school subjects.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that ChatGPT can generate lesson plans, revisions, differentiated supports, and content ideas that may reduce teacher preparation time, but the first output often required substantial human review and iterative prompting. The authors conclude that the tool can relieve workload and free time for other teaching responsibilities, yet the gross time savings are reduced by the need for verification, refinement, and prompt engineering; no quantitative time-saving measure was reported.
finding.measure: Quality of ChatGPT-generated lesson plans and supporting materials for planning/content development tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that reducing lesson-planning workload with ChatGPT may help mitigate teacher burnout and improve work-life balance. This is an indirect, conceptually supported finding rather than a measured effect: the study does not administer burnout scales or report pre-post changes, but it concludes that ChatGPT has potential to support burnout prevention through workload relief.
finding.measure: Teacher workload/burnout relevance inferred from qualitative evaluation of ChatGPT-supported planning

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT was able to generate and improve lesson plans for math, science, and English, including content development tasks such as real-life examples and formative assessment prompts. The study’s subject-specific lesson-plan evaluations found that revised outputs aligned better with the 5Es instructional model and were more comprehensive and student-centered, though this was based on expert review rather than learner outcomes.
finding.measure: Lesson plan quality across math, science, and English using the 5Es instructional model

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests ChatGPT can support teachers’ planning, customization, and iterative refinement through prompt-based human-AI collaboration. The main durable-skill implication is improved task management and iterative problem solving for educators, but the study does not directly measure teacher collaboration, metacognition, or time-management outcomes.
finding.measure: Prompt iteration and human-AI collaboration during lesson planning

paper_profiles.title: A systematic literature review of empirical research on ChatGPT in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the rapid emergence of ChatGPT in education and asks how students and teachers have initially used it, along with the main findings from empirical studies published through April 10, 2023. The authors conducted a systematic literature review of 14 empirical studies, following PRISMA 2020 and Okoli’s review procedures, and synthesized results across learning and teaching contexts.

The review covers mostly higher-education settings, with one elementary-school study and several studies spanning multiple countries. It finds that students used ChatGPT as a virtual intelligent assistant for on-demand answers, feedback, explanations, writing support, translation, and self-directed learning; educators used it to create lesson plans, quizzes, and other teaching resources. Across the reviewed studies, ChatGPT was generally associated with improved productivity, efficiency, and learning support, but the review also highlights concerns about inaccurate outputs, overreliance, reduced innovative capacity, weaker collaborative skills, and threats to academic integrity. The authors conclude that effective use depends on training, clear guidelines, and ongoing research and policy dialogue.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, ChatGPT was used to support writing and language-related tasks such as generating ideas, composing essays, summarizing, paraphrasing, translating, and checking grammar. The review reports that students in several studies found it helpful for improving writing proficiency and producing more developed written work, but the paper does not report a pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Writing tasks, essay generation, summarizing, paraphrasing, translation, grammar checking

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies studies in mathematics education where ChatGPT supported students’ problem-solving and understanding of problem-solving processes. The underlying studies reported improved efficiency and learning experience in solving mathematics problems, but the review does not provide a quantitative synthesis or effect estimate.
finding.measure: Mathematics problem-solving tasks and related learning experiences

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT was used across multiple non-literacy/non-math subject areas, including journalism, construction, computer engineering, early education, English education, and social sciences. The reviewed studies generally found that it helped with content understanding, idea generation, hazard recognition, and task completion, but the paper does not report a pooled quantitative effect.
finding.measure: Subject-specific learning tasks across journalism, construction, engineering, early education, and social sciences

finding.finding_summary: The review reports positive indications for critical thinking, reasoning, and problem-solving in some studies, but also notes negative effects when ChatGPT was overused, including reduced innovative capacity and weakened collaborative learning competencies. Because the paper synthesizes both beneficial and harmful findings without a quantitative overall estimate, the net direction is mixed.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, reasoning, problem-solving, innovation, and collaborative learning competencies

finding.finding_summary: A central finding of the review is that educators used ChatGPT to create lesson plans, generate quizzes, provide additional resources, and answer student questions, which improved productivity and efficiency and reduced workload. The review specifically states that teachers used it to save time and that participants’ productivity and work efficiency were significantly enhanced, but it does not provide a pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Teacher productivity, work efficiency, workload, and time use

finding.finding_summary: Several reviewed studies reported improved learning engagement, motivation, and overall learning experience, especially when ChatGPT supported self-directed or personalized learning. At the same time, the review warns that frequent use may reduce students’ motivation to attend classes, so the overall evidence summarized in the paper is mixed rather than uniformly positive.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, and learning experience

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (position paper discussing K-12, higher education, and professional development contexts)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities and challenges of large language models (LLMs), especially ChatGPT, for education. Rather than testing a specific intervention, it synthesizes early examples and theoretical arguments about how LLMs may support learning and teaching across educational levels, from primary school to professional training.

The paper discusses potential uses for students, such as generating practice questions, explanations, summaries, and conversational support, and for teachers, such as lesson planning, personalized feedback, assessment support, and content creation. It also reviews current research on LLMs and related NLP systems in education, including examples of automated quiz generation, adaptive feedback, and answer evaluation.

A major emphasis of the paper is on risks and implementation constraints: bias, hallucinations, plagiarism, privacy, cost, lack of transparency, overreliance by students and teachers, and difficulty distinguishing machine-generated from human-generated text. The authors conclude that LLMs may be valuable educational tools, but only when paired with human oversight, critical thinking, fact-checking, governance, and careful design of policies and workflows.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can save teachers time on tasks such as lesson planning, generating quizzes, producing feedback, and semi-automated grading. It cites prior work reporting that NLP-based feedback generation could reduce grading effort by up to 85% in large courses, but this paper itself is a position paper and does not present a new empirical estimate for K-12 teacher productivity or gross versus net time savings after verification and editing.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading effort, lesson-planning and feedback production efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes that successful educational use of LLMs depends on institutional policies for privacy, copyright, bias mitigation, verification, and responsible use. It does not test policy interventions, but it argues that governance, training, and school-level workflows are necessary to integrate these systems safely and effectively.
finding.measure: Institutional governance, privacy/security practices, responsible-use procedures

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly notes that LLMs may support critical thinking, problem-solving, and fact-checking when used as a supplement, but may also weaken these skills if learners or teachers rely on the model too heavily. No original empirical data are reported; the claims are conceptual and based on the authors' synthesis of prior work and examples.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, fact-checking, metacognitive use of AI

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes strong potential for LLMs to support reading and writing through summaries, outlines, grammar corrections, style improvement, and writing assistance. These benefits are presented as plausible educational uses rather than as results from a new study, so no effect size or sample size is reported.
finding.measure: Reading comprehension, writing quality, summaries, outlines, grammar/style support

paper_profiles.title: Teachers and AI: Understanding the factors influencing AI integration in K-12 education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines what psychological and pedagogical factors shape K-12 teachers’ readiness to integrate artificial intelligence into classroom practice. The authors ask how teachers perceive AI’s value, what supports their adoption of AI, and what barriers make integration difficult, with particular attention to a Turkish K-12 context and a school-based professional development program.

The study used an exploratory qualitative design with 66 teachers from 11 disciplines at a private school in Türkiye participating in a 14-week AI-in-education professional development course. Data came from online discussion forums and AI-supported learning activity design tasks, then were analyzed through inductive thematic analysis. Teachers most often described AI as useful for efficiency, lesson planning, differentiated instruction, student engagement, and adaptive learning, while also raising concerns about technical access, workload, curriculum misalignment, language/cultural fit, and ethical issues such as privacy and plagiarism.

Overall, the paper concludes that AI has strong perceived promise for improving K-12 teaching productivity and enriching instruction, but successful integration depends on support structures, better alignment with curricula and local context, and clearer ethical guidance. Because the study is qualitative and context-specific, it offers insights into teacher perceptions and implementation conditions rather than causal evidence of student outcomes or time savings.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers consistently perceived AI as improving efficiency and reducing workload, especially for lesson planning, content creation, and preparing presentations. However, they also reported that technical issues, trial-and-error learning, and curriculum adaptation demands can offset gross time savings, so the practical net productivity gain depends on verification, editing, and contextualization work.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions and qualitative themes from discussion forums and AI-supported learning activity design tasks
finding.study_size: n=66 teachers; 59 designed activities analyzed; 133 forum messages and 240 reflection messages

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that AI-supported activities increased student excitement, curiosity, and engagement, and made lessons more enjoyable and interactive. These claims were based on qualitative observations across the 66 participating teachers rather than standardized engagement measures.
finding.measure: Teacher observations of student excitement, interest, and engagement

finding.finding_summary: Teachers described AI as supporting critical thinking, collaboration, inquiry, creativity, and problem solving through classroom activities such as group work, questioning, and interactive tasks. At the same time, they worried that student overreliance on AI could reduce creativity, effort, and independent thinking, producing a mixed picture of durable-skill development.
finding.measure: Teacher-designed AI learning activities and qualitative reflections on student skill development

finding.finding_summary: Teachers believed AI could support subject-specific instructional work across non-core areas such as history, literature, social sciences, presentation tasks, and creative writing. The evidence is qualitative and centered on perceived instructional usefulness rather than measured achievement gains.
finding.measure: Teacher-designed learning activities and perceived usefulness across subject areas

paper_profiles.title: How Can ChatGPT Facilitate Teaching and Learning: Implications for Contemporary Education
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (general education context; no specific study sample)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a review-and-argumentative article that examines how ChatGPT may be used to facilitate teaching and learning across educational settings. Rather than testing an intervention empirically, it synthesizes recent literature on generative AI and chatbots to outline potential benefits, risks, and implications for educational practice and leadership.

The paper argues that ChatGPT can support students through personalized tutoring, individualized feedback, practice materials, self-directed learning, and support for 4C skills (collaboration, communication, critical thinking, creativity). For teachers, it may help generate lesson plans, presentations, assessment items, rubrics, and feedback, thereby saving time and enriching instruction. The authors also emphasize that effective use requires digital leadership, policy guidance, and ethical safeguards so that schools can build a digital-friendly ecology while avoiding misuse, plagiarism, and overreliance on AI.

Because the article is conceptual and literature-based, it does not report original participants, measures, or effect sizes. Its main contribution is a balanced discussion of opportunities and pitfalls of ChatGPT in education, with practical implications for educators, school leaders, and policymakers rather than empirical claims about outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT can help teachers save a significant amount of time by assisting with lesson planning, content generation, presentation design, assessment item creation, rubric development, and feedback generation. No original data, sample size, or effect size are reported; this is a conceptual claim based on reviewed literature rather than a measured productivity outcome.
finding.measure: Teacher time savings / workload reduction (conceptual discussion)

finding.finding_summary: The article claims ChatGPT can support students' critical thinking, creativity, communication, and collaboration by prompting questions, enabling debate, and providing interactive conversations and peer-assessment opportunities. These claims are presented as literature-informed expectations rather than results from a direct empirical study.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, creativity, communication, collaboration (conceptual discussion)

finding.finding_summary: The paper states that ChatGPT may increase student motivation, self-confidence, and self-regulation while reducing anxiety by providing personalized tutoring and immediate feedback. No empirical sample, effect size, or confidence interval is reported because the article is a review and argument piece.
finding.measure: Motivation, self-confidence, anxiety, self-regulation (conceptual discussion)

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT: Bullshit spewer or the end of traditional assessments in higher education?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the emergence of ChatGPT and its implications for higher education, especially assessment, learning, and teaching. The authors ask whether ChatGPT represents a disruptive advance in AI that may undermine traditional written assessments, while also positioning it within the broader history of educational technology and Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIEd).

The paper uses a desktop literature review and informal experimentation with ChatGPT rather than a formal empirical study. It reviews early peer-reviewed articles and preprints on ChatGPT, then reports a series of demonstrations showing ChatGPT’s strengths and limitations: it can generate coherent explanations, short essays, and translations quickly, but it can also produce generic, inaccurate, poorly cited, or low-quality output, especially for higher-order analytical writing and low-resource languages like Chinese.

The paper’s main conclusion is that ChatGPT should not be treated as a reliable substitute for human judgment or as a reason to abandon all traditional assessment. Instead, educators and institutions should adapt assessment design, teaching practices, and policy to account for AI text generators. The authors argue that ChatGPT is best understood as part of a broader ecosystem of AI writing and assessment tools, with both opportunities and risks for students, teachers, and institutions.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT can save time for teachers and students by generating explanations, drafts, and rewrites within about 60-120 seconds, and by supporting feedback, revision, and other writing-related tasks. However, the paper also emphasizes that any time savings are offset by the need for verification, correction, and adaptation of assessments, so the productivity gains are presented as possible but limited rather than measured directly.
finding.measure: Observed speed and usability of ChatGPT for drafting, explaining, translating, and rewriting text in author demonstrations

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT produced coherent prose and short essays quickly, but the output was often generic, descriptive, shallow, or inaccurate, and it struggled with higher-order academic writing such as critical analysis and proper citation. In the authors’ demonstrations, a requested 2000-word essay instead produced roughly 500 words and five references after repeated attempts, and the Chinese composition was grammatically weak and ill-structured.
finding.measure: ChatGPT-generated essays, explanations, citations, and Chinese composition quality

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that ChatGPT can communicate conversationally and generate text in languages other than English, but its performance was weaker in Chinese than in English. The authors report that the Chinese composition was awkward, illogical in parts, and seemed directly translated from English, suggesting limited fluency for low-resource or distant languages.
finding.measure: Quality of ChatGPT-generated Chinese composition and multilingual response capability

finding.finding_summary: In the paper’s demonstration, ChatGPT gave a clear and sensible explanation of mean, standard deviation, and z-scores, and provided a worked real-world example with step-by-step calculations. The authors note, however, that the system hit a character-limit problem while elaborating the example, so the result is presented as capable but not robust.
finding.measure: Quality of explanations and worked examples for statistical concepts

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT may force institutions to rethink assessment policy, plagiarism detection, and academic integrity practices, because current detectors may fail to identify AI-generated text. At the same time, the authors suggest institutions can respond by redesigning assessments, updating policies, and adapting teaching and learning strategies rather than banning the tool outright.
finding.measure: Policy and institutional implications discussed in literature review and author analysis

paper_profiles.title: What if the devil is my guardian angel: ChatGPT as a case study of using chatbots in education
paper_profiles.population: Educators and other early adopters of ChatGPT in education (including students, developers, and AI freelancers); context is higher education/adult users rather than K-12
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines concerns about using ChatGPT in education, asking what risks and limitations arise when early adopters use an advanced chatbot for teaching and learning. Rather than testing a formal intervention, the authors use ChatGPT as an instrumental case to explore public discourse, stakeholder perceptions, and hands-on user experiences.

The study uses a three-stage qualitative design: (1) social network analysis and sentiment analysis of 2,330 tweets about ChatGPT and education, (2) content analysis of 19 publicly recruited interviewees who had used ChatGPT in educational contexts, and (3) educator-led user experience testing across 10 educational scenarios. The contexts are largely adult and higher-education oriented, including educators, students, developers, and AI freelancers; the paper does not study K-12 students directly, but it discusses implications for schooling and teaching practice more broadly.

Across all three stages, the paper finds that public and participant sentiment is generally optimistic but tempered by substantial concerns. ChatGPT is seen as potentially useful for generating learning materials, supporting instructional design, and reducing workload, but the paper highlights recurring issues with accuracy, fairness, cheating, privacy, manipulation, and lack of emotional/human qualities. The authors conclude that ChatGPT should be adopted cautiously, with stronger guidance, policy, and design principles for responsible use, rather than simply banned.

finding.finding_summary: Participants repeatedly described ChatGPT as useful for preparing teaching materials, generating quizzes, and providing immediate feedback, suggesting potential workload reduction for educators. However, the study is qualitative and does not report a quantified time-savings estimate, so the finding is based on perceived productivity gains rather than measured efficiency outcomes.
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness for instructional design, content generation, quiz creation, and immediate feedback
finding.study_size: n=19 interviewees; n=3 educators in user-experience scenarios

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests ChatGPT can support baseline knowledge-building and stimulate understanding, but it may also reduce learners’ critical thinking if used as an easy substitute for independent work. The main durable-skill concern is that overreliance on ChatGPT could weaken critical thinking, question asking, and reflective judgment, while careful use could support these skills.
finding.measure: Perceptions and observed scenario-based concerns about critical thinking, prompt skill, and reflective judgment

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that ChatGPT can help students write essays and answer short-answer questions, which may support writing tasks, but it can also facilitate cheating and produce inaccurate or misleading written content. No writing-performance scores were reported; the evidence is based on qualitative user experiences and examples of generated text.
finding.measure: Essay generation, short-answer generation, and writing support in educational scenarios

finding.finding_summary: The study argues that ChatGPT is already affecting school and university policy discussions, including bans, concerns about cheating, privacy, and the need for new teaching philosophies and responsible-AI guidelines. The evidence is qualitative and conceptual, but the paper clearly treats institutional response, governance, and policy adaptation as central outcomes.
finding.measure: Policy and governance implications discussed in relation to cheating, privacy, responsible use, and teaching reform
finding.study_size: n=2330 tweets; n=19 interviewees; n=3 educators

finding.finding_summary: Some users found ChatGPT fun, exciting, and emotionally engaging, but others reported disappointment because it cannot provide real empathy or emotional value. The paper also raises concerns that emotional attachment to ChatGPT may be misleading because the system lacks genuine feelings or reflective engagement.
finding.measure: Perceptions of enjoyment, emotional attachment, empathy, and engagement with ChatGPT

paper_profiles.title: Exploring High School EFL Teachers' Experiences with Magic School AI in Lesson Planning: Benefits and Insights
paper_profiles.venue: Voices of English Language Education Society
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This exploratory case study examines how Indonesian high school EFL teachers experienced using MagicSchool AI for lesson planning after a workshop on AI-assisted lesson planning. The paper asks what benefits and challenges teachers encounter when integrating a generative AI tool into routine planning work, with particular attention to efficiency, differentiation, and the need for teacher oversight.

The study involved 38 high school EFL teachers in Central Java, Indonesia, using an open-ended questionnaire and focus group interviews, with stimulated recall used in the group sessions. Teachers generally reported that MagicSchool AI helped them generate lesson materials and assessments faster, produced ideas for differentiated instruction, and sparked new teaching ideas, but they also stressed that the outputs were often not ready to use without substantial editing.

A central conclusion is that the apparent time savings of AI are conditional rather than automatic: teachers repeatedly described the need for follow-up prompting, refinement, and contextual adaptation, which reduced or sometimes offset gross time savings. The paper reframes efficiency as not just saving minutes, but producing pedagogically sound, contextually appropriate materials, and argues that effective AI use depends on prompt-engineering skills, critical evaluation, and human oversight.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that MagicSchool AI sped up initial lesson material and assessment preparation, especially when using its structured fields and prompts, and helped reduce workload. However, many also said the outputs required follow-up prompting, editing, and contextual adaptation, which reduced or sometimes negated the net time savings (e.g., Rosa said it was 'not as fast as I expected').
finding.measure: Teacher-reported time efficiency, workload, and ease of lesson planning/material and assessment preparation

finding.finding_summary: Teachers said MagicSchool AI helped them generate and adapt lesson materials, reading texts, activities, and assessments aligned to EFL lesson planning needs. The tool was especially useful for producing differentiated materials and varied question types, though many outputs still required teacher refinement before classroom use.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported usefulness of AI-generated lesson materials, activities, and assessments for EFL lesson planning

finding.finding_summary: The paper highlights prompt engineering, critical evaluation, and adaptive decision-making as essential teacher skills for using generative AI effectively. Teachers emphasized that success depended on crafting the right prompt and judging whether AI outputs fit classroom dynamics and pedagogical goals.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported perceptions of prompt engineering, critical thinking, and adaptive judgment in AI use

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks Middle School
paper_profiles.population: Middle School (7th grade mathematics teachers and students)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether and how teachers should remain in the loop when using generative AI to personalize mathematics tasks for middle school students. The authors focus on a practical question relevant to K-12 AI productivity: whether ChatGPT can meaningfully reduce teacher workload while helping teachers adapt existing curriculum materials to students’ interests, and whether the resulting tasks are actually appealing to students.

Seven 7th-grade mathematics teachers in six U.S. schools were trained to use ChatGPT (GPT-4o) to modify Illustrative Mathematics problems in two units: proportional relationships/percentages and expressions/equations/inequalities. Over two sessions, teachers created 143 personalized problems for 521 students. The study analyzed teacher prompts, chatbot interactions, time spent per problem, and student survey feedback (closed- and open-ended) about interestingness, closeness to interests, and accuracy/realism.

Findings suggest that teachers used the LLM in nuanced ways, balancing breadth of interest personalization, realism, mathematical clarity, and ownership of the content. Students generally preferred narrower, more specific popular-culture references rather than broad categories, but they focused more on surface-level interest matches than on deeper realism issues. In terms of productivity, personalizing a single problem took about 4 minutes on average, and teachers did not become more time-efficient over time; in fact, they became slower and used more prompts in the second unit. The study concludes that teacher-in-the-loop personalization may support professional learning and quality control, but it does not reliably produce gross time savings once verification and editing are included.

finding.finding_summary: Teacher-in-the-loop personalization was time-intensive rather than time-saving. Across 143 problems, teachers used 558 prompts (3.2 prompts per problem on average) and spent an average of 246 seconds per problem (SD=165.7), and time increased rather than decreased from Unit 4 to Unit 6 (204 seconds vs. 286 seconds per problem; B=70.4, p=0.0189).
finding.measure: Teacher time per personalized problem; number of prompts per problem
finding.effect_size: B=70.4 seconds increase from Unit 4 to Unit 6; B=1.26 more prompts per problem
finding.std_deviation: SD=165.7 seconds per problem; prompts SD=2.6

finding.finding_summary: The study centers on personalizing middle school mathematics problems and shows that teachers could successfully produce mathematically usable tasks with ChatGPT, though they often had to revise realism and quantities. Student ratings of the personalized math problems were modest overall, but were higher when teachers used 3-5 prompts to refine a task; this prompt range was associated with about 0.24 points higher ratings on a 5-point scale (B=0.240, SE=0.085, p=0.0073).
finding.measure: Quality of personalized mathematics problem posing; student ratings of interestingness and closeness for math problems
finding.study_size: n=143 problems; student ratings for 52-53 problems, 446-454 responses on open-ended items

finding.finding_summary: Students responded variably to the personalized problems in terms of interest. Across 454 responses to the interestingness item, 163 implied the problem was interesting and 243 implied it was not, with mean ratings of 2.46/5 for interestingness and 2.53/5 for closeness to interests. Problems personalized with 3-5 prompts received the highest student ratings, suggesting a moderate level of refinement was most engaging.
finding.measure: Student survey ratings of interestingness and closeness to interests
finding.study_size: n=521 students; ratings collected for 52-53 problems; 454 interestingness responses and 449 closeness responses

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that teachers developed prompting skill and professional judgment through iteration with ChatGPT, especially in deciding how much control to give the model and how to improve realism, readability, and age appropriateness. However, this growth was not accompanied by greater efficiency; the second round required more prompts and more time, even though student ratings improved.
finding.measure: Teacher prompting practices and iterative refinement of AI-generated problems
finding.effect_size: B=1.26 more prompts per problem from Unit 4 to Unit 6; B=70.4 seconds more time per problem

paper_profiles.title: LLMs to Support K–12 Teachers in Culturally Relevant Pedagogy: An AI Literacy Example
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a large language model–powered tool, CulturAIEd, can help K–12 teachers adapt AI literacy activities so they better reflect culturally relevant pedagogy (CRP). The motivation is that teachers often want to implement CRP but face barriers such as limited time, insufficient training, and a lack of culturally responsive AI literacy resources.

The authors built a demo system that combines student demographic information, a CRT checklist, rubric-based feedback, and a chatbot for just-in-time pedagogical support. In an exploratory pilot, four secondary teachers from North America and East Asia completed a sequence of adaptation tasks in a 90–120 minute Zoom session: first independently, then with a CRT checklist, and finally with CulturAIEd. The study used qualitative thematic analysis of interviews and descriptive analysis of survey responses.

Findings suggest that CulturAIEd increased teachers’ confidence in identifying opportunities for cultural responsiveness and in making culturally responsive modifications to AI literacy lessons. Participants also perceived the tool as streamlining CRP work by integrating demographics, generating actionable suggestions, and reducing the time and research burden of lesson adaptation. The authors conclude that LLMs may support efficient CRP integration in AI literacy instruction, but emphasize that the evidence is preliminary and based on a very small pilot sample, so larger controlled studies are needed.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that CulturAIEd reduced the time and research burden involved in adapting AI literacy lessons for culturally relevant pedagogy. In the post-survey, 3/4 participants strongly agreed that the tool saved time, and participants explicitly described it as solving the problem of time and research needed for CRP.
finding.measure: Post-survey time-saving ratings; interview perceptions of workflow efficiency and reduced planning burden

finding.finding_summary: The tool increased teachers’ confidence in identifying opportunities for cultural responsiveness in learning activities and making culturally responsive modifications. Pre-survey confidence was reported as 3-5 on a 5-point scale, and post-survey confidence increased to 5/5 for all participants on identifying opportunities for cultural responsiveness.
finding.measure: Self-reported confidence in CRP integration and cultural responsiveness on pre/post surveys

paper_profiles.title: Shiksha Copilot: Teacher-AI Collaboration for Curating and Customizing Lesson Plans in Low-Resource Schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether and how an AI-assisted lesson-planning system can help teachers in low-resource, multilingual public schools create and adapt lesson plans, while also reducing workload and supporting classroom practice. The central problem is that teachers in such settings face heavy administrative burdens, time scarcity, multilingual instructional demands, and limited access to high-quality materials, all of which make lesson planning both difficult and time-consuming.

The authors designed and deployed Shiksha Copilot in government schools across Karnataka, India. The system used LLMs plus retrieval-augmented generation and human-in-the-loop curation: curators first reviewed and refined AI-generated learning objectives and lesson plans, then teachers customized the curated plans for their own classrooms. The deployment involved 1,043 teachers and 23 curators, with interviews, surveys, system logs, and log-based analyses used to study collaboration patterns, content quality, time use, stress, and workflow changes.

Findings show that teachers used the system for both instructional and bureaucratic tasks. The tool reduced lesson-planning and record-keeping burden, lowered teaching-related stress, and supported a shift toward more activity-based pedagogy, but the gains were uneven across language contexts: English lesson plans were generally high quality with few edits, whereas Kannada translations required extensive linguistic revision. The study concludes that teacher-AI systems can be useful in low-resource settings, but only when they preserve human oversight, support local language quality, and fit existing institutional workflows and constraints.

finding.finding_summary: Shiksha Copilot reduced teacher workload by easing bureaucratic record-keeping and reducing lesson-planning time. The paper reports measurable reductions in weekly lesson-planning time and teaching-related stress, and notes that teachers used the system to prepare LPs for both classroom delivery and administrative documentation.
finding.measure: Weekly time spent on lesson planning and administrative tasks; teacher stress (Teacher Stress Scale); system logs and interviews about workload
finding.study_size: n=406 matched survey responses; n=5,544 teacher-created lesson plans in logs; n=22 teacher interviews

finding.finding_summary: The system lowered teaching-related stress, suggesting a beneficial effect on teacher well-being. The paper reports pre/post survey evidence using the Teacher Stress Scale, with improved scores after deployment, though exact effect sizes are not provided in the text excerpt.
finding.measure: Teacher Stress Scale (teaching demands and school-based support subscales)

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that Shiksha Copilot supported administrative documentation and curricular compliance in government schools, and that its use was shaped by staffing shortages, mandated 5E lesson-plan formats, and school/district implementation constraints. The tool also enabled organizational-level workflows involving mentors, curators, and government officials, indicating institutional rather than purely individual effects.
finding.measure: Interviews, deployment process, and usage/log patterns relating to record-keeping and compliance-oriented lesson-plan use

paper_profiles.title: New Curriculum, New Chance – Retrieval Augmented Generation for Lesson Planning in Ugandan Secondary Schools. Prototype Quality Evaluation.
paper_profiles.venue: Ndejje University Second Annual Research Dissemination Symposium 2024
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This working paper evaluates whether a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) prototype can generate technically strong lesson plans for Ugandan secondary schools under the new competency-based curriculum. The authors frame the problem as one of teacher workload, outdated lesson plans, and limited access to quality planning materials, especially in rural schools, and ask whether AI-generated plans based on government-approved textbooks meet required standards for classroom use.

The prototype, called the NDU Lesson Plan Generator, uses Cohere embeddings, a Cohere LLM, LangChain, and textbook vector stores built from three Secondary 1 textbooks (ICT, Mathematics, and History). The system generated 24 lesson plans, which three independent raters evaluated using an adapted Lesson Plan Analysis Protocol (LPAP). The paper reports average technical quality scores of roughly 75-80% ("very good") and notes that even excluding structural checklist items, the average remained about 75%.

The study is situated in Uganda and focuses on secondary-school lesson planning rather than student learning outcomes. The main conclusion is that the generated plans meet the technical standards for implementation in Ugandan classrooms and appear to outperform human-created lesson plans reported in comparable LPAP-based East African studies. The paper also highlights a key limitation of hallucination: when the source textbook had too little information on a topic, the model produced an incorrect lesson plan, underscoring the need for teacher verification and plausibility checks before use.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that the RAG-based lesson plan generator produced lesson plans efficiently enough to be judged technically implementable, with 24 generated plans averaging about 75-80% on the LPAP and none scoring below 65%. The authors argue this suggests teachers could save time in lesson planning, but they do not measure actual time saved, time-on-task, or net savings after verification/editing.
finding.measure: Technical quality of AI-generated lesson plans on the Lesson Plan Analysis Protocol (LPAP)

finding.finding_summary: The intervention is presented as supporting faster and more efficient implementation of Uganda's new curriculum by providing context-aligned lesson plans based on government-approved textbooks. The paper concludes that the tool can contribute to curriculum rollout and teacher support, although this is an inferred institutional implication rather than a direct policy evaluation.
finding.measure: Compatibility of generated lesson plans with the Ugandan competency-based curriculum and government lesson-plan format

paper_profiles.title: Personalized Auto-Grading and Feedback System for Constructive Geometry Tasks Using Large Language Models on an Online Math Platform
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of providing scalable, timely, and pedagogically useful grading and feedback for open-ended and constructive geometry tasks in K-12 mathematics. The authors focus on the gap between automated assessment systems and teacher-quality formative feedback, especially for tasks where students can use multiple valid solution paths and where human grading is time-consuming.

The study presents a personalized auto-grading and feedback system deployed on the Algeomath online geometry platform. The system combines rule-based grading for closed-ended and construction-based tasks with few-shot GPT-4 grading for open-ended written explanations, plus attempt-aware feedback generated from teacher-authored exemplars. Students could revise answers across up to three or four attempts, and feedback adapted based on correctness and remaining attempts.

The field study involved 79 middle-school students in four classes in South Korea completing 18 geometry tasks. Results showed strong agreement with teacher judgments for rule-based items and substantial agreement for LLM-graded explanation items, though some items suffered from terminology mismatches and partial-credit ambiguities. Feedback was generally rated as pedagogically serviceable, and about 36.7% of initially incorrect responses were corrected on the next attempt, suggesting short-term learning support. However, the study found limited evidence that feedback-driven corrections transferred to later problems, and it highlighted issues such as answer leakage, overly generic hints, and tone escalation.

finding.finding_summary: The system’s auto-grading and feedback supported learning on constructive geometry tasks, with 36.7% of initially incorrect responses corrected on the subsequent attempt (260/708). Across the 18-item task set, first-attempt correctness ranged roughly from 0.42 to 0.91, and cumulative success rose from about 0.60 on the first attempt to about 0.80 by the fourth attempt, indicating meaningful short-term improvement on math tasks.
finding.measure: Correctness on constructive geometry tasks; attempt-level learning curves; post-feedback correctness conversion rate

finding.finding_summary: The feedback system appeared to support persistence and re-engagement, as many students improved after retries and the survey ratings were generally positive (average ratings around 4.1–4.5 on a 5-point scale). However, qualitative feedback indicated that overly directive or discouraging messages such as final-chance wording could undermine the supportive climate.
finding.measure: Attempt-by-attempt correction patterns; student survey ratings; qualitative comments on feedback tone and usefulness

finding.finding_summary: The iterative tasks and feedback were associated with improved conceptual explanation and refinement of reasoning, especially when students moved from vague answers to more precise, domain-specific justifications. For example, the paper reports qualitative improvement in explanation quality as feedback guided students toward equidistance and other geometric concepts, indicating gains in structured reasoning and metacognitive revision.
finding.measure: Iterative answer refinement in open-ended explanations; qualitative rubric-based evaluation of explanation quality

finding.finding_summary: The system substantially automated grading and feedback generation for geometry tasks. Rule-based grading achieved 100% agreement with teacher judgments on closed-ended and CGT items, and LLM grading on open-ended items reached 0.866 agreement with teachers (Cohen’s κ=0.737 across 878 responses). This indicates strong potential to reduce teacher workload for routine grading and formative feedback delivery, although the paper does not directly measure time savings in minutes or hours.
finding.measure: Agreement with teacher grading; automated feedback evaluation; proportion of responses handled by automated system

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s survey and task design included broader mathematical understanding of geometric concepts and applications in real-life contexts beyond routine numeracy. Students generally endorsed the activities, with average self-assessment ratings around 4.1–4.5 on a 5-point scale for understanding circumcenter properties, using digital tools, explaining the circumcenter’s location, and applying the ideas in everyday contexts.
finding.measure: Five-item student Likert survey on understanding and application of circumcenter concepts

paper_profiles.title: SimPal: Towards a Meta-Conversational Framework to Understand Teacher’s Instructional Goals for K-12 Physics
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the Eleventh ACM Conference on Learning @ Scale (L@S ’24)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a teacher-facing problem in simulation-based science instruction: many K-12 physics simulations come with predesigned conversational AI agents whose instructional goals (IGs) are difficult for teachers to modify, making it hard to align the agent with a teacher’s evolving pedagogy. The authors propose SimPal, a meta-conversational framework in which teachers describe their instructional goals in natural language and the system maps those goals to relevant physical variables and relationships that can be used to prompt an underlying conversational agent.

The system is evaluated as a variable-extraction task for physics simulations rather than in a classroom deployment. The authors test ChatGPT-3.5 and PaLM 2 on 63 simulations from PhET and Golabz, with prompts structured according to the TELeR prompt taxonomy at different levels of detail. Gold-standard variables are created by combining simulation webpages, teacher resources, and a CK-12 physical science textbook, and outputs are compared using precision, recall, and micro-F1.

Results show that prompt design materially affects performance, with Level 2 and Level 3 prompts generally outperforming Level 4, and ChatGPT-3.5 often outperforming PaLM 2 in F1 under the evaluated conditions. The main conclusion is that SimPal can generate meaningful variable lists aligned to teacher goals, but its accuracy depends strongly on prompt structure and simulation source. The study is technical and exploratory, and it does not measure actual teacher time savings or classroom outcomes; instead, it provides an early-stage method for helping teachers customize AI-supported simulations.

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes SimPal as a teacher-facing meta-conversational framework intended to reduce the difficulty of customizing simulation-based conversational agents to teachers’ instructional goals. In evaluation on 63 physics simulations (32 PhET, 31 Golabz), the system showed moderate-to-high variable-extraction performance depending on prompt level and model, with micro-F1 scores in the roughly 0.52–0.60 range in the main simulation experiments, indicating promise for streamlining the customization task but not measuring actual teacher time savings.
finding.measure: Precision, recall, and micro-averaged F1 for extracted instructional-goal variables; prompt format accuracy
finding.study_size: n=63 simulations (final evaluation); n=5 simulations (preliminary prompt study)

paper_profiles.title: AI in Pakistani Schools: Adoption, Usage, and Perceived Impact among Educators
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K–12 educators in Pakistan are adopting and using AI tools, and how they perceive AI’s effects on teaching and students. The authors frame the study as a response to the limited evidence base on AI adoption in developing-country school systems, where access, infrastructure, and training may shape whether AI is used at all and for what purposes.

The study uses a descriptive online survey of 125 Pakistani educators collected in July 2025. The questionnaire covered AI familiarity, frequency of use, use cases such as lesson planning, content creation, grading, and tutoring, and perceptions of impact on student engagement, performance, workload, teaching strategies, and equity. Results show broad openness to AI: about two-thirds of respondents were willing to adopt AI with support, around 30% were active users, and content generation and personalized learning were the most common applications, while grading and tutoring were used less often.

Perceived benefits centered on efficiency and instructional support. Teachers reported that AI reduced routine task time, improved engagement, and helped student-centered teaching, but they also expressed concern that unequal access to devices and infrastructure could leave some students behind. The paper concludes that AI adoption in Pakistani schools is still early and uneven, with enthusiasm tempered by training and equity barriers, and argues for stronger professional development and infrastructure support before deeper integration can occur.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that AI reduced the time they spend on routine teaching tasks, especially grading and content creation. In the survey, 73% agreed that AI tools reduced workload, and the overall average agreement with positive AI impact statements was 3.7/5 among N=125 educators.
finding.measure: Perceived reduction in time spent on routine teaching tasks / teacher workload Likert items

finding.finding_summary: Educators perceived AI as supporting student engagement. About 67% agreed that using AI tools in the classroom improved students’ engagement levels, based on survey responses from n=125 Pakistani educators.
finding.measure: Perceived student engagement Likert item

finding.finding_summary: Teachers also reported perceived improvements in student performance from AI integration. Approximately 60% agreed that they had observed better student performance as a result of AI tool use, but this was self-reported perception rather than an objective achievement measure.
finding.measure: Perceived student performance Likert item

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds uneven AI adoption across school types and highlights institutional barriers related to access and infrastructure. Private-school teachers showed more polarized AI use, public-school teachers tended toward occasional experimentation, and many respondents worried that unequal device access could widen disparities.
finding.measure: Reported AI adoption/familiarity by school type; perceived equity/access concerns

paper_profiles.title: T-TExTS (Teaching Text Expansion for Teacher Scaffolding): Enhancing Text Selection in High School Literature through Knowledge Graph-Based Recommendation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem that high school English Literature teachers often lack the time and resources to curate diverse, thematically aligned text sets. The authors argue that this planning burden can limit teachers’ ability to build instruction around culturally relevant, pedagogically coherent literature selections, especially for novice educators.

To support text selection, the paper presents T-TExTS (Teaching Text Expansion for Teacher Scaffolding), a recommendation system built on a domain-specific ontology and knowledge graph. The team manually curated a dataset of 100 English Literature books using educator input, syllabi review, text-complexity tools, and qualitative rubrics, then converted the ontology to RDF triples and generated embeddings with DeepWalk, biased random walk, and a hybrid of both. The system was evaluated with link-prediction and recommendation metrics such as AUC, MRR, Hits@K, and nDCG.
