The main conclusion is that the knowledge-graph-based approach can support more informed and inclusive curricular decisions by helping teachers identify related texts. DeepWalk performed best on most metrics, reaching an AUC of 0.9431, while the hybrid model was more balanced and the biased random walk underperformed on several metrics. However, the paper evaluates the recommendation model’s technical performance rather than measuring teacher time savings or classroom outcomes, so it provides evidence about recommendation quality and potential utility, not direct evidence of productivity gains in practice.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the T-TExTS recommendation system can help ease the burden of high school English Literature text selection for educators, but this is an asserted benefit rather than a measured time-savings outcome. The empirical evaluation focused on recommender performance, with DeepWalk achieving AUC=0.9431, MRR=0.3882, and Hits@10=0.5789 on the task of recommending literature texts, suggesting the system may be practically useful for reducing planning effort.
finding.measure: Recommendation quality metrics for literature-text retrieval (AUC, MRR, Hits@K, nDCG@10)

paper_profiles.title: Partnering with AI: A Pedagogical Feedback System for LLM Integration into Programming Education
paper_profiles.population: Secondary school computer science teachers in Germany
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how large language models (LLMs) can be used to generate pedagogically sound feedback for programming education, with an emphasis on adaptive feedback rather than one-size-fits-all prompting. The authors argue that existing LLM feedback systems often overlook important instructional principles such as learner mastery, task progress, and the presence or absence of student input.

To address this gap, the paper proposes a pedagogical feedback framework for LLMs and implements it in a web-based Python programming system. The system uses multiple LLM agents, including teacher-style feedback agents, an expert programmer agent for error analysis, and pedagogical validators to check whether generated feedback meets the framework’s requirements. The system was evaluated through mixed-method semi-structured interviews with eight secondary-school computer science teachers in Germany, who reviewed synthetic student requests and pre-generated LLM responses across recursion tasks.

The study finds that teachers generally viewed the framework-aligned LLM feedback as pedagogically sound, comprehensive, and effective, especially for supporting high-performing students and for quickly detecting small code errors. Teachers also felt the system could complement human teaching by handling routine feedback and saving teacher time. However, they emphasized important limitations: the system cannot adapt well to classroom context, lacks real-time interaction, and cannot use visual/interactive teaching strategies that teachers rely on. Overall, the paper concludes that LLMs can augment but not replace teacher judgment in feedback generation, and that adaptive, pedagogically informed prompting is preferable to generic prompting.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the LLM system would be significantly faster than human teachers for identifying small code errors and routine feedback, suggesting potential time savings in programming instruction. One teacher explicitly noted that the AI might find such errors in about 5 minutes of teacher effort, and the study’s teacher ratings indicated high correctness (91.7% correct, 55/60 responses; 8.3% partially correct, 5/60).
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of feedback speed/efficiency; correctness ratings of LLM feedback responses

paper_profiles.title: Comparative Analysis of STEM and non-STEM Teachers’ Needs for Integrating AI into Educational Environments
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 teachers in STEM and non-STEM subjects want AI to be integrated into block-based programming and educational platforms. The authors focus on three teacher workflow areas: assessment, course/resource development, and student monitoring/support. The central question is not whether AI improves student outcomes directly, but what AI features teachers perceive as most useful for making educational platforms more effective, adaptable, and usable across disciplines.

The study uses semi-structured interviews with eight K-12 teachers from North and South Carolina in the United States: four STEM teachers and four non-STEM teachers. Interviews were conducted via Zoom, transcribed, and analyzed using thematic analysis with two independent coders. Across both groups, teachers wanted AI support for customizable rubrics, more detailed feedback, integrity/plagiarism checks, curriculum and resource generation, personalized learning materials, and student monitoring tools such as help notifications, reminders, and distraction prevention. Non-STEM teachers additionally emphasized authenticity, creative/simulation-based assessment, and support for more qualitative evaluation, while STEM teachers more often emphasized grading and code-tracing support. The paper concludes that AI-enhanced educational platforms should be more adaptable to subject area differences, especially to better serve non-STEM classrooms.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers across STEM and non-STEM groups reported that AI features could reduce time and effort in assessment, course planning, and monitoring by streamlining rubrics, generating materials, and consolidating platform workflows. However, this paper is qualitative and does not report measured time savings, effect sizes, or experimental comparisons, so the evidence is based on teacher perceptions rather than quantified productivity gains.
finding.measure: teacher interview themes about perceived productivity, grading efficiency, resource creation, and workflow integration

finding.finding_summary: Teachers said AI tools should integrate better with LMSs, school platforms, single sign-on systems, and privacy/security requirements so they can be adopted safely and fit institutional workflows. The study identifies platform and governance needs—such as privacy settings, interoperability, and access control—but does not measure institutional outcomes directly.
finding.measure: teacher interview themes about LMS integration, SSO, privacy, and platform interoperability

paper_profiles.title: Youth as Advisors in Participatory Design: Situating Teens’ Expertise in Everyday Algorithm Auditing with Teachers and Researchers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how high school teens can be positioned as expert advisors in participatory design sessions with teachers and researchers who are developing classroom lessons on algorithm auditing. The core question is not whether an instructional intervention improves test scores, but how youth expertise can be elicited and used productively when adults are designing learning activities about generative AI and algorithmic bias.

The study centers on a two-hour advisory session in which three teens (ages 16–18) who previously participated in an earlier algorithm-auditing workshop reviewed and critiqued teachers’ audit reports. The broader project involved a prior youth workshop on everyday algorithm auditing practices and a week-long teacher PD workshop, all focused on designing high school computer science lessons around auditing TikTok filters and related systems. The researchers collected video data from preparation meetings and the advisory session, then conducted thematic analysis to understand what knowledge teens shared and which facilitation choices supported their advisory role.

Findings show that teens contributed substantive expertise in TikTok use, audit design, dataset consistency, and the practical constraints of filter testing. They also offered personally meaningful curriculum suggestions, such as auditing music recommendation systems, local search results, and shopping platforms, and reflected on how auditing changed their views of algorithmic systems and their own online behavior. The paper concludes that teens can serve as valuable advisors when adults intentionally prepare them for the role, explicitly recognize their expertise, and structure conversations to support authentic dialogue and shared reflection. The authors offer design recommendations for researchers, facilitators, and teachers who want to make youth advisory roles feasible and productive in PD contexts.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that teens developed and demonstrated critical thinking, metacognition, and collaborative discussion skills through the advisory process. In the two-hour session, three teens used prior auditing experience to critique teachers’ TikTok filter audits, explain data-quality issues such as glare and inconsistent inputs, and build on others’ ideas in dialogue, indicating growth in reflective and analytic reasoning rather than content knowledge alone.
finding.measure: Video-recorded participatory design discussion; thematic analysis of teens’ advisory contributions and reflections

finding.finding_summary: The teens reported increased engagement and personal relevance around algorithm auditing, moving from seeing TikTok as casual entertainment to treating it as something worth critically analyzing. The paper describes the advisory session and preparatory meetings as helping teens feel more confident and valued in speaking with teachers, though no quantitative measure was reported.
finding.measure: Observed participation, reflective comments about motivation and relevance, and researchers’ thematic coding of discussion

finding.finding_summary: The teens demonstrated scientific-reasoning-like practices in the context of algorithm auditing, including formulating hypotheses, identifying variables, evaluating input consistency, and interpreting outputs from TikTok filters. The study reports that teens drew on prior workshop experience to advise on how to structure audits and improve validity, but it does not present a formal achievement measure or statistical effect.
finding.measure: Algorithm audit practices and critique of audit reports

paper_profiles.title: Integration of AI in STEM Education – Addressing Ethical Challenges in K-12 Settings
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the ethical challenges and opportunities associated with integrating artificial intelligence into K-12 STEM education. Rather than reporting new empirical results, it synthesizes recent literature on AI-powered instructional tools such as intelligent tutoring systems, automated assessments, predictive analytics, and surveillance technologies, with particular attention to algorithmic bias, privacy, accountability, and equity concerns.

The paper’s central contribution is a conceptual framework for responsible AI integration in K-12 STEM settings. It proposes a three-phased implementation roadmap (pilot, capacity building, systemic transformation) and a four-phase professional development model for teachers grounded in TPACK and critical algorithmic literacy. The framework emphasizes equity-centered design, low-tech adaptations for under-resourced schools, culturally responsive pedagogy, and policy alignment with standards such as UNESCO guidance.

The context is K-12 schooling, especially STEM classrooms, and the intended users are educators and school systems responsible for implementing AI tools. The paper argues that AI can improve personalization, feedback, and operational efficiency, but only if schools pair deployment with ethical safeguards, teacher preparation, data governance, and ongoing equity audits. Its conclusions are normative and synthesis-based: AI should augment, not replace, human judgment, and implementation must prioritize student agency, transparency, and fairness.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI tools such as intelligent tutoring systems and automated assessments can enhance operational efficiency by personalizing instruction, providing immediate feedback, automating scoring, and reducing teacher workload. However, these claims are drawn from cited literature rather than original empirical analysis, and the paper does not report new effect sizes for time savings after verification or editing.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, assessment automation, and instructional efficiency discussed conceptually

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes a phased implementation roadmap, tiered professional development model, policy alignment, and mandatory ethics/equity audits as mechanisms for institutional change in K-12 AI adoption. Its main finding is that responsible AI integration requires governance structures, data protocols, and school-level capacity building, but these are framework recommendations rather than measured outcomes.
finding.measure: Policy alignment, professional development structures, and institutional implementation roadmap

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes AI ethics literacy, critical algorithmic literacy, and teachers’ ability to interrogate AI systems, all of which are framed as supporting critical thinking and ethical reasoning. It cites prior work and curricular examples, but does not provide original quantitative evidence for gains in durable skills.
finding.measure: AI ethics literacy, critical thinking, and ethical reasoning

finding.finding_summary: The paper notes that AI tools may improve student engagement through personalization and real-time feedback, but also raise concerns about surveillance, privacy, and reduced student agency. Its discussion is conceptual and synthesis-based, with no original measurement of motivation or engagement outcomes.
finding.measure: Student engagement and agency discussed conceptually

paper_profiles.title: A Tabu Search Algorithm with Efficient Diversification Strategy for High School Timetabling Problem
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Computer Science & Information Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of constructing feasible and high-quality high school timetables, which is described as a difficult scheduling task involving classes, teachers, subjects, rooms, and special lesson blocks. The authors note that manual timetabling is time-consuming and can take weeks, and they propose an automated approach tailored to Iranian high schools, where block structures such as half-switch and double-lessons are common.

The proposed method has three phases: a preprocessing step that detects and groups block sessions using graph search, a greedy constructive phase that creates an initial feasible timetable, and an optimization phase based on tabu search. The tabu search uses two move types (out-in and intra moves), a tabu list, aspiration criteria, and a frequency-based diversification strategy to escape local optima. The algorithm is evaluated on three real Iranian high-school instances and compared across variants of tabu search components; results show that diversification substantially improves the cost function, and the combined use of diversification and intra moves produces the best results overall.

Although the paper is framed as a timetabling optimization study rather than an educational intervention, its main contribution is operational: it demonstrates that the proposed algorithm can generate acceptable timetables and detect most block sessions in real school data. The study concludes that the approach is effective for school scheduling and may generalize to other timetabling problems.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the proposed tabu search system substantially improves timetable quality relative to the initial solution, reducing the cost function by 66%-96% depending on the school instance and algorithm variant. Across the three real high-school datasets, the full method with diversification and intra moves (TSDI) achieved the lowest costs (e.g., DE: 26,000 to 1,050; TA: 37,000 to 2,650; AL: 61,000 to 2,880), and the authors state that manual timetabling is typically tedious and takes several weeks.
finding.measure: Timetable cost function F(Q), percentage reduction in cost, and detection of block sessions

paper_profiles.title: Enabling Multi-Agent Systems as Learning Designers: Applying Learning Sciences to AI Instructional Design
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a practical problem in K-12 AI use: teachers can prompt large language models to generate instructional materials, but simple prompting often produces shallow, generic, or pedagogically weak outputs, and more sophisticated prompting is time-consuming. The authors ask whether multi-agent systems guided by a learning-sciences framework can produce higher-quality learning activities than a simple single-agent baseline.

The study compares three generation architectures for secondary math and science learning activities: a single-agent baseline (SAS), a sequential role-based multi-agent system (MAS-Roles), and a collaborative multi-agent system with conquer-and-merge discussion (MAS-CMD). The systems embed the Knowledge–Learning–Instruction (KLI) framework into the generation process. Ten curriculum-aligned learning objectives from ORISE were used, generating 30 activities for human review and 120 activities for LLM-as-a-judge evaluation. Twenty practicing U.S. secondary math and science teachers evaluated the outputs using adapted Quality Matters K-12 criteria, and their written feedback was thematically analyzed.

Quantitatively, the teacher ratings showed only small and often statistically insignificant differences, although MAS-CMD performed best overall and was significantly better than MAS-Roles on the active-learning criterion. Inter-rater reliability was low. Qualitatively, however, teachers strongly preferred MAS-CMD, describing it as more creative, contextually relevant, and classroom-ready, with better completeness and teacher usefulness than the baseline systems.

The paper concludes that embedding pedagogical theory into LLM architectures can improve the perceived quality of generated instructional materials, but that the more effective collaborative multi-agent design comes with substantially higher computational cost. The authors also argue that standard rubrics and LLM-as-a-judge methods may miss educator-valued qualities such as creativity, utility, and classroom readiness.

finding.finding_summary: The study found a clear quality–efficiency trade-off across generation systems. SAS was fastest and lightest at 25±16 seconds, about 3.4k tokens, and 1 request, while MAS-Roles took 77±45 seconds and 22,497±7,157 tokens, and MAS-CMD took 272±168 seconds and 71,638±25,222 tokens with 13 requests. The authors interpret this as higher-quality collaborative generation coming at substantially greater computational cost, not net time savings.
finding.measure: Generation time, tokens used, and number of model requests per learning activity
finding.study_size: n=10 learning objectives per system; 30 human-evaluated activities and 120 total LLM-evaluated activities
finding.std_deviation: 25±16 sec; 3,376±1,601 tokens; 1.00±0.00 requests (SAS); 77±45 sec; 22,497±7,157 tokens; 5.42±1.13 requests (MAS-Roles); 272±168 sec; 71,638±25,222 tokens; 13.00±0.00 requests (MAS-CMD)

finding.finding_summary: For math-generated activities, expert teachers generally rated the systems similarly on QM standards, with MAS-CMD receiving the highest mean total score (10.05 overall across all criteria) and MAS-Roles the lowest. The only statistically significant human-rated difference was on QM criterion 5.2 (active learning), where MAS-CMD was rated higher than MAS-Roles, F(2,38)=4.75, p=.014, ηp²=.20. However, the total-score omnibus test was not conventionally significant, indicating limited evidence of a robust mathematics-specific quality advantage.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of generated secondary math learning activities on Quality Matters K-12 rubric criteria and total score
finding.study_size: n=20 teachers (11 math, 9 science); 10 learning objectives total, 5 math and 5 science

finding.finding_summary: The paper also evaluated science learning activities, but results were pooled with math rather than reported separately. Across the combined secondary math and science sample, MAS-CMD tended to receive the highest expert scores, yet most criterion-level omnibus tests were non-significant and inter-rater agreement was low. This suggests only weak evidence that the KLI-guided multi-agent designs improved science-activity quality in a way detectable by the rubric.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of generated secondary science learning activities on Quality Matters K-12 rubric criteria and total score
finding.study_size: n=20 teachers (11 math, 9 science); 10 learning objectives total, 5 math and 5 science
finding.effect_size: ηp²=.20 for QM criterion 5.2 (combined math/science sample)
finding.std_deviation: MAS-CMD total M=10.05, 95% CI [9.42, 10.68] across the combined sample

finding.finding_summary: Teacher qualitative feedback emphasized student engagement, active learning, and motivation as valued features of the generated lessons. MAS-CMD was repeatedly described as more creative and engaging, and the paper notes that all systems were praised when they involved students through relevant topics, investigation, and movement. This is qualitative evidence that the designs supported engagement-related social-emotional outcomes, though no direct student outcome data were collected.
finding.measure: Thematic analysis of teacher written feedback regarding engagement, interest, and active learning in generated activities

finding.finding_summary: The study’s qualitative results suggest that the collaborative MAS-CMD more effectively supported higher-order design features such as creativity and pedagogical coherence, which teachers valued as indicators of stronger instructional quality. However, no direct student measures of critical thinking, metacognition, or collaboration were collected; the finding is based on educator judgments about the activities’ design rather than student performance.
finding.measure: Teacher qualitative assessments of creativity, coherence, and instructional soundness in AI-generated learning activities

paper_profiles.title: AI and Machine Learning for Next Generation Science Assessments
paper_profiles.venue: Machine learning, natural language processing and psychometrics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book chapter examines how artificial intelligence and machine learning can support next-generation science assessment in K-12 settings. The central problem is that traditional assessment formats, especially multiple-choice items, do not adequately capture three-dimensional science learning or students’ scientific reasoning, modeling, and argumentation. The chapter argues that performance-based tasks are better aligned to the Framework for K-12 Science Education, but they create substantial scoring burdens for teachers because open-ended written and drawn responses are time-consuming to evaluate.

To address this problem, the chapter reviews machine-learning-based automatic scoring approaches for science assessments, including supervised, unsupervised, semi-supervised, pretrained models such as BERT, zero-shot methods, and fine-tuned ChatGPT. It summarizes the general workflow for developing and validating scoring models, and proposes a framework for understanding what factors affect machine-human score agreement, including assessment features, examinee characteristics, training/validation approach, and algorithmic design. The chapter also discusses validity, fairness, generalizability, and data imbalance as key challenges for deployment.

The paper is not an empirical classroom intervention study; it synthesizes prior science-assessment research and uses examples drawn from middle school, high school, and teacher PCK scoring studies. Its main conclusion is that ML can reduce teacher scoring burden and provide timely feedback, but performance depends strongly on item design, training data, and model choice. The chapter ultimately frames ML-based scoring as promising for next-generation science assessments, while emphasizing the need for careful validation, fairness analysis, and user guidelines before widespread adoption.

finding.finding_summary: The chapter argues that machine learning-based assessments are well suited to science tasks that capture three-dimensional learning, including modeling, explanation, and argumentation. Across the cited studies, supervised ML and pretrained models produced satisfactory to strong scoring accuracy for written science responses, and a fine-tuned GPT-3.5 model outperformed fine-tuned BERT by an average of 9.1% accuracy across six science assessment tasks.
finding.measure: Machine-human agreement and scoring accuracy on science explanation, argumentation, investigation, and model-based constructed-response tasks

finding.finding_summary: The chapter presents science assessments as measuring students’ scientific thinking, problem-solving, and knowledge-in-use, which are durable skills central to performance-based science tasks. It does not report a single new effect size for these skills, but it synthesizes evidence that ML scoring can validly support assessment of these higher-order competencies through open-ended responses.
finding.measure: Scientific thinking, problem-solving, modeling, explanation, and argumentation in performance-based assessment tasks

finding.finding_summary: A major claim of the chapter is that automatic scoring can alleviate teacher workload by replacing time-consuming manual scoring of open-ended science responses. The chapter gives a concrete example: scoring one middle-school item may take about 1 minute per student, so a teacher with 100 students would spend about 100 minutes per task; ML systems are presented as a way to provide timely and objective feedback with reduced grading burden.
finding.measure: Teacher scoring time / workload for open-ended science assessment responses

finding.finding_summary: The chapter argues that ML-based assessment could reshape science assessment practice at scale by enabling timely feedback, broader adoption of performance tasks, and more feasible implementation of NGSS-aligned assessment systems. It also highlights that deployment requires institutional attention to validity, fairness, privacy, and user guidelines, indicating system-level implications beyond individual classrooms.
finding.measure: Feasibility and implementation considerations for ML-based science assessment systems

paper_profiles.title: Human or AI? Comparing Design Thinking Assessments by Teaching Assistants and Bots
paper_profiles.population: Secondary school and pre-university teachers (MOE Singapore)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This exploratory study examines whether an AI grader can reliably assess design-thinking journey maps that combine visual and textual elements, and how teachers perceive AI-, TA-, and hybrid scoring. The paper is motivated by the workload and inconsistency challenges of rubric-based assessment in large design-thinking classes, especially when assessing creative artifacts that are difficult to score consistently by humans.

The researchers developed a GPT-4o-based journey map grader calibrated with rubric descriptors and example-scored samples. They compared instructor benchmark scores against AI and TA scores on 10 student samples across three dimensions: empathy and user understanding, identification of pain points and opportunities, and visual communication. They also asked 33 Singapore in-service teachers to choose which of three anonymized scores (AI, TA, hybrid) they agreed with most for another set of 10 samples, and collected open-ended survey and focus-group feedback.

Results showed low agreement between instructor and AI/TA scores on empathy and pain-point dimensions, with slightly better alignment for visual communication. Teachers preferred TA scores in 6 of 10 samples, AI scores in 4, and did not prefer hybrid scores for any sample. Qualitative feedback suggested teachers saw AI as fast and potentially useful for formative feedback and self-reflection, but not yet trustworthy for summative assessment because it struggled with contextual nuance, creative judgment, and visual interpretation. The authors conclude that AI may be most appropriate as a complementary tool in hybrid assessment models rather than a replacement for human judgment.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the AI grader was much faster than manual scoring and could provide rationale for scores, suggesting potential workload reduction and quicker formative feedback. However, the study did not measure actual time saved or productivity gains directly; these benefits were qualitative and framed as perceived advantages rather than quantified outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of speed, labor intensity, and usefulness for formative feedback
finding.study_size: n=33 teachers; 10 student samples per task

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests AI could support scalable assessment practices in large multi-section design-thinking classes, but teachers were cautious about its validity for high-stakes grading. The paper recommends hybrid models, calibration with instructor scoring, and professional development, indicating potential institutional adoption with safeguards rather than full automation.
finding.measure: Teacher acceptance/preference for AI, TA, and hybrid scoring; qualitative feedback on adoption readiness

paper_profiles.title: PhysicsAssistant: An LLM-Powered Interactive Learning Robot for Physics Lab Investigations
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of providing timely, individualized support in K-12 physics laboratories, where teachers may struggle to assist every student during hands-on experiments. The authors propose PhysicsAssistant, a multimodal educational robot that combines YOLOv8-based object detection, speech-to-text, GPT-3.5-turbo generation, response validation, and text-to-speech output to answer students’ physics questions in real time.

The system was tested in a user study with ten 8th-grade students performing a projectile-motion lab. Students asked a set of five questions across the lab session, and a human expert rated responses from PhysicsAssistant and GPT-4 using Bloom’s taxonomy dimensions: factual, conceptual, procedural, and metacognitive knowledge. PhysicsAssistant showed strong factual performance and much faster response times than GPT-4, but it scored lower on conceptual and procedural knowledge. The main conclusion is that PhysicsAssistant is promising as a real-time lab assistant that can offload repetitive teacher support tasks, though it still needs improvement on higher-order reasoning and deeper conceptual responses.

finding.finding_summary: In a study with n=10 8th-grade students during a projectile-motion lab, PhysicsAssistant was evaluated on physics understanding using a Bloom’s-taxonomy rubric. It achieved strong factual performance but weaker conceptual and procedural performance than GPT-4, indicating it can support some scientific understanding but is less effective for deeper reasoning.
finding.measure: Human expert ratings of student-question responses on Bloom’s taxonomy dimensions (factual, conceptual, procedural, metacognitive knowledge)

finding.finding_summary: The paper explicitly evaluates conceptual, procedural, and metacognitive knowledge as part of students’ interaction with the system. PhysicsAssistant performed well on factual recall but less well on conceptual and metacognitive dimensions, suggesting limited support for higher-order thinking overall.
finding.measure: Human expert ratings of conceptual, procedural, and metacognitive knowledge

finding.finding_summary: PhysicsAssistant was significantly faster than GPT-4 in delivering responses. Across five questions, average response time was 1.64 ± 0.24 s for PhysicsAssistant versus 3.54 ± 0.87 s for GPT-4, with a paired-samples t-test showing a significant difference (t(4) = -6.847, p = .002).
finding.measure: Response time from student query to verbal response
finding.std_deviation: 0.24 sec (PhysicsAssistant total response time); 0.87 sec (GPT-4 total response time)

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that the faster responses and real-time interaction improve the user experience and help maintain student engagement during lab sessions. However, engagement was not directly measured with a validated instrument; this conclusion is inferential rather than based on a direct outcome test.
finding.measure: Not directly measured; inferred from response-time and interaction-flow observations

paper_profiles.title: EDUMATH: Generating Standards-aligned Educational Math Word Problems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a practical K-12 teaching problem: teachers often lack the time to create math word problems (MWPs) tailored to students’ interests, grade-level math standards, and ability levels. The authors argue that large language models (LLMs) could reduce this burden, but only if they can generate problems that are solvable, accurate, educationally appropriate, and aligned to specific standards rather than just broad math topics.

To study this, the paper builds a teacher-annotated dataset of standards-aligned educational MWPs for grades 3-5 in Virginia, called STEM. The authors first label and repair a subset of ASDIV with VA SOL standards and readable chain-of-thought solutions, then generate a larger synthetic dataset annotated by teachers and filtered with a second LLM-based annotator. They use this data to fine-tune and filter open models, producing EDUMATH 12B and EDUMATH 30B, and evaluate them against open and closed baselines using teacher-aligned criteria and automatic metrics.

The paper also includes a small classroom study with 3rd-5th grade students at two elementary schools. Students solved both human-written and customized LLM-generated MWPs and reported which they preferred. The authors conclude that their models substantially improve standards-aligned MWP generation, can reduce teacher workload, and produce problems that students like and solve similarly to human-written ones, with EDUMATH 30B performing best overall.

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central claim is that LLMs can reduce teacher burden by generating customized, standards-aligned math word problems. The authors show that teacher-annotated data plus filtering improves model quality, with EDUMATH 30B reaching 94.6 MaC% (meets all criteria) on 1,000 generated MWPs, suggesting a practical route to faster MWP creation for educators, though no direct teacher time-savings study or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Meets-all-criteria (MaC) rate for generated math word problems; teacher annotation/labeling workflow; model quality for problem generation
finding.study_size: n=1,000 MWPs per model for evaluation; n=1,372 teacher annotators for synthetic-data labeling

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates whether generated math word problems are usable for elementary math instruction by checking solvability, accuracy, educational appropriateness, and standards alignment. EDUMATH 30B achieved the highest MaC rate (94.6%) and students solved its problems similarly to human-written problems, indicating strong performance for math practice generation, but the paper does not report learning gains or standardized math achievement effects.
finding.measure: Solvability/accuracy/educational appropriateness/standards-alignment (MaC); student worksheet performance on generated vs human-written MWPs
finding.study_size: n=1,000 MWPs per model in model evaluation; n=82 fourth graders and n=12 3rd-5th grade intervention students in classroom study

finding.finding_summary: In the classroom study, students preferred the LLM-generated problems over human-written ones, largely because they liked the topics, suggesting increased interest/engagement with the customized problems. This is a preference and enjoyment finding rather than a direct measure of motivation or persistence, and no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Student preference reports and brief explanations of preference after solving worksheets
finding.study_size: n=82 fourth graders; n=12 3rd-5th grade intervention students

paper_profiles.title: Co-Designing Interdisciplinary Design Projects with AI
paper_profiles.population: Secondary and pre-university in-service teachers (Singapore MOE schools)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem that designing interdisciplinary, project-based learning experiences is cognitively demanding and time-consuming for teachers, especially when they must align activities to curriculum standards, integrate multiple subjects, and maintain coherent sequencing. The authors ask whether a GPT-based planning assistant can improve the quality of teacher-created interdisciplinary design project plans compared with manual planning.

To study this, they developed IDPplanner, a custom GPT-based co-design tool grounded in SUTD’s Design Innovation framework, Singapore’s MOE syllabuses, and 21st-century competencies. In a within-subject, counterbalanced workshop, 33 in-service teachers from Singapore secondary and pre-university schools each created manual and AI-assisted versions of the same interdisciplinary design project plan under 30-minute constraints. Plans were evaluated with a six-dimension rubric and supplemented by self- and peer-reflection data, making the study mixed-methods in nature.

Quantitatively, AI-assisted plans scored significantly higher on Curriculum Alignment (M=4.08 vs. 3.67, p=.036, d=0.54), Design Thinking Application (M=3.85 vs. 3.00, p=.005, d=0.81), and Coherence & Flow (M=4.00 vs. 3.42, p=.035, d=0.64). Assessment Strategies showed a large but non-significant advantage (d=0.92), while Clarity of Learning Objectives and Interdisciplinary Integration were not significant. Qualitative findings suggested that AI improved structure, sequencing, and idea generation, but that contextualization to local syllabuses, class profiles, and deeper interdisciplinary integration still required teacher judgment. The authors conclude that AI is best used as a pedagogical planning partner in hybrid teacher-AI workflows rather than as a replacement for teacher expertise.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that the AI-assisted IDPplanner improved the efficiency and quality of teachers’ planning process by reducing the cognitive and structural burden of interdisciplinary project design. Teachers reported that the tool helped with organization, sequencing, and idea generation, and the authors argue it can reduce planning complexity and workload, although teachers still need to verify, contextualize, and refine outputs.
finding.measure: Teacher reflections on planning support; rubric-rated project plan quality under manual vs AI-assisted conditions
finding.study_size: n=33 teachers (19 project plans formally scored; 13 AI-assisted, 6 manual)
finding.effect_size: d=0.64 to d=0.92 across quality dimensions, depending on rubric criterion
finding.std_deviation: Manual vs AI rubric SDs reported per dimension (e.g., Curriculum Alignment SD=0.65 manual, 0.48 AI)

finding.finding_summary: AI-assisted planning improved design-thinking-related planning skills, especially the ability to structure projects through the Discover–Define–Develop–Deliver sequence. It also supported teachers’ collaborative planning and sequencing of interdisciplinary activities, though deeper conceptual integration and iterative refinement still depended on human expertise.
finding.measure: Rubric scores for Design Thinking Application, Coherence & Flow, and teacher qualitative reflections
finding.effect_size: d=0.81 for Design Thinking Application; d=0.64 for Coherence & Flow
finding.std_deviation: Design Thinking Application SD=1.04 manual, 1.07 AI; Coherence & Flow SD=0.79 manual, 0.57 AI

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests AI-assisted planning can support institutional curriculum alignment and interdisciplinary implementation within schools. AI-assisted plans were rated higher for Curriculum Alignment, and teacher comments indicated the tool could help bridge subject-specific knowledge gaps and support school-level interdisciplinary curriculum design, though local adaptation by school leaders remained necessary.
finding.measure: Rubric score for Curriculum Alignment; teacher reflections on curriculum fit and school implementation

paper_profiles.title: Aligning technology with cognitive development: a five-tiered framework to generative AI in K-12 education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This perspective paper addresses the problem of how to integrate generative AI (GenAI) into K-12 education without either banning it outright or allowing unrestricted use. The author argues that current debates are polarized and insufficiently attentive to child development, cognitive load, and ethical risks such as cognitive offloading, hallucinations, bias, privacy, and dependency.

To respond to this, the paper proposes a developmentally aligned five-tier framework spanning ages 3–18. The framework is built from developmental psychology theories (Piaget, Vygotsky, Erikson, Kohlberg, Bronfenbrenner) and a best-fit framework synthesis of developmental neuroscience and recent GenAI/education studies. It specifies age bands, intended educational purposes, daily time limits, and minimum student-independence ratios, ranging from zero direct use in preschool to more autonomous and critical use in senior secondary school.

The paper is not an empirical evaluation of a GenAI intervention; instead, it is a theory-driven conceptual model meant to guide policy and classroom practice. The author concludes that GenAI should be used as a scaffold calibrated to developmental stage, with strong adult mediation in early years and increasing but still regulated autonomy in later grades. The paper calls for future longitudinal research to test and refine the proposed cut-off values and to adapt the framework across cultural and socioeconomic contexts.

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes a policy and governance framework for school systems, arguing that GenAI adoption in K-12 should be regulated through age-based usage limits, age-locks in tools, teacher training, and coordinated roles for policymakers, educators, developers, and parents. It does not report empirical effect sizes; instead, it offers a conceptual governance model intended to shape institutional AI policy and implementation.
finding.measure: Policy framework / governance recommendations

finding.finding_summary: The framework is explicitly designed to protect and develop durable skills such as critical thinking, metacognition, independent reasoning, and ethical judgment while allowing limited, developmentally appropriate GenAI use. The paper synthesizes prior studies suggesting risks of cognitive offloading, hallucination acceptance, and dependency, but it does not generate new quantitative outcomes itself.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, metacognition, independent reasoning, ethical judgment

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that GenAI can reduce teacher workload and support productivity, especially through administrative automation and teacher-facing content generation such as differentiated materials, story prompts, and phonics games. These claims are drawn from cited literature and examples rather than original empirical testing, so no effect size or sample size is reported in this article.
finding.measure: Teacher administrative workload / productivity

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes both potential benefits and risks for social-emotional development: GenAI may support engagement and autonomy when carefully scaffolded, but overuse may contribute to dependency, reduced self-regulation, and emotional reliance on AI agents. The article is conceptual and cites prior evidence; it does not present new direct measurements or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Engagement, autonomy, self-regulation, dependency risk

paper_profiles.title: Technological Literacy in the AI Era
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how the concept of technological literacy has evolved in the AI era and argues for a school-based framework to develop AI-relevant competencies across K–12 education. Using an integrative literature review of standards, policy documents, curriculum guidelines, and prior research, it synthesizes definitions and frameworks such as ITEEA’s Standards for Technological Literacy and the European Commission’s DigComp model.

The paper does not test a new intervention experimentally; instead, it proposes a developmental roadmap for age-appropriate technological and AI literacy. It argues that elementary grades should emphasize basic digital fluency and ethical awareness, middle school should introduce structured AI concepts, data reasoning, and algorithmic thinking, and high school should deepen students’ understanding through interdisciplinary, project-based learning focused on machine learning, bias, and societal implications.

The review identifies common barriers to implementation, including digital infrastructure gaps, limited teacher preparedness, fragmented curricula, and policy/funding constraints. It also highlights promising practices such as scaffolded instruction, modular curriculum design, project-based learning, inclusive access strategies, and targeted teacher professional development. Overall, the paper concludes that integrating AI literacy into K–12 schooling is both necessary and feasible, but it requires coordinated changes in curriculum, policy, and educator training.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that integrating AI literacy into K–12 systems is necessary and feasible, but implementation is constrained by infrastructure gaps, limited teacher preparedness, fragmented curricula, and weak policy support. It synthesizes literature and framework comparisons rather than reporting a single empirical effect, so the finding is conceptual and system-level rather than causal.
finding.measure: Curriculum and policy framework analysis; literature synthesis of K–12 AI literacy implementation barriers and enablers

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly frames AI literacy as supporting durable skills such as algorithmic thinking, critical thinking, collaboration, problem solving, and ethical reasoning. It proposes grade-band scaffolds and exemplar modules (e.g., bias detection and climate data analysis) designed to build these competencies, but it does not provide original quantitative outcome data.
finding.measure: Conceptual competency roadmap and exemplar classroom activities targeting critical thinking, collaboration, and ethical reasoning

finding.finding_summary: A central theme is improving educator capacity and reducing implementation barriers through teacher professional development, modular curricula, open educational resources, and low-bandwidth/offline alternatives. The paper suggests these design choices can make AI literacy instruction more practical and scalable, but it does not measure teacher workload or productivity directly.
finding.measure: Proposed teacher professional development pathway; implementation design features intended to support scalable classroom adoption

paper_profiles.title: Real Intelligence: Teaching in the Era of Generative AI
paper_profiles.population: Undergraduate; High School (adaptable); earlier grades mentioned as transferable principles
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book is a practitioner-oriented guide for educators responding to the rise of generative AI, especially large language models such as ChatGPT. Its central question is how teaching and learning should adapt when students can use AI to generate plausible text, summaries, and other coursework outputs, and when educators may be tempted to rely on AI for instruction, grading, or task design.

The authors explain how LLMs work, emphasizing their statistical, pattern-based nature, limitations, and tendency to fabricate or mislead when treated as knowledge systems. They then propose a series of assignment designs and pedagogical strategies that preserve the core learning goals of humanities education while making inappropriate AI use harder or less useful. Although the book is written primarily for humanities professors in higher education, it explicitly argues that many ideas transfer to high school and earlier grades, and it frames the guidance as broadly applicable to educators across disciplines.

The book does not report an empirical study, intervention trial, or systematic evaluation of outcomes. Instead, it offers conceptual explanation, examples, and practical teaching recommendations meant to help educators redesign assignments, focus on process, and use AI in limited, meaningful ways. Its main conclusion is that generative AI is not a substitute for human learning, but it does require pedagogical adaptation so that students continue developing writing, reasoning, and disciplinary understanding.

finding.finding_summary: The book does not present empirical evidence that generative AI improves or worsens literacy outcomes. Instead, it argues that writing, reading, and revision tasks should be redesigned so students still perform the core literacy work themselves, rather than outsourcing it to LLMs.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: No direct empirical effect is reported, but the book substantively focuses on preserving durable skills such as critical thinking, reasoning, metacognition, and independent problem-solving in the presence of AI tools. The authors argue that assignments should be structured to keep students doing the intellectual work required to build these skills.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The book argues that several AI-aware assignment designs can reduce teacher workload by making AI misuse harder to police and by shifting assessment toward process-based evidence of learning. However, this is a conceptual recommendation rather than a measured productivity outcome, so no effect size or sample size is reported.
finding.measure: teacher workload / grading and assignment management (conceptual discussion)

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI in K-12 Education: The CyberScholar Initiative
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a generative AI writing assistant, CyberScholar, can support K-12 students’ writing in classroom settings. The core question is how students and teachers experience AI-generated formative feedback when it is aligned with teachers’ rubrics, instructional materials, and expectations.

The study piloted CyberScholar across four public schools in the United States: one middle school and three high schools, in diverse socioeconomic contexts (underserved, university laboratory, rural mid-poverty, and mid-poverty settings). The tool was used in English Language Arts, Social Studies, and Modern World History classes in Grades 7, 8, 10, and 11. Data came from observations, surveys, and interviews with 121 students and 4 teachers, with post-survey responses from 54 students and 3 teachers and interviews from 8 students and 1 teacher.

Findings from thematic qualitative analysis suggest that students generally perceived the tool as helpful for writing development. They valued the detailed and specific feedback, the ability to interact with the tool and ask follow-up questions, the perception that their writing improved, and the rubric-aligned ratings. Some students also reported concerns about inconsistent ratings. The authors conclude that CyberScholar has potential to support student writing and may shift teachers’ roles toward guiding AI feedback processes rather than serving only as evaluators, but they emphasize that it should complement rather than replace teacher feedback.

finding.finding_summary: Students across four schools reported that CyberScholar helped improve their writing through detailed, specific, and rubric-aligned formative feedback. The study is qualitative, but the authors report that 19 students explicitly praised the detailed feedback, 23 students said the tool helped them perceive improvements in writing quality, and some students reported rubric score gains after revision (e.g., one student improved a “Compare”/“Contrast” score from 0 to 2).
finding.measure: Student perceptions of writing improvement; rubric-based writing revisions and scores

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that CyberScholar supported metacognition and self-regulation by helping students revise drafts, reflect on feedback, and ask follow-up questions. The qualitative findings emphasize that students used the tool to identify specific weaknesses, revise iteratively, and better understand how to improve their writing, which the authors connect to metacognition and cyber-social learning.
finding.measure: Student reports of revision behavior, reflection, and follow-up questioning

finding.finding_summary: Students generally found the AI feedback engaging and motivating, with some reporting that the tool made writing feel more interactive and encouraged them to use it again. However, a subset of students was hesitant to reuse the tool, and some disliked inconsistent ratings, so the affective response was positive but not uniform.
finding.measure: Student survey comments and interview responses about engagement, motivation, and willingness to reuse the tool
finding.study_size: n=54 post-survey respondents; n=8 interview participants

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests the tool may improve efficiency by providing fast, detailed feedback and reducing the time needed for students to identify revision needs. Students explicitly described the tool as quicker and easier to work with than peer or self-analysis, and the authors also note possible teacher workload benefits because CyberScholar can support feedback processes aligned to rubrics.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of speed and ease of feedback; author discussion of teacher workload support

paper_profiles.title: VLM@school – Evaluation of AI image understanding on German middle school knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a new benchmark, VLM@school, for evaluating vision-language models on German middle-school content. The authors argue that current multimodal benchmarks are often English-language, heavily multiple-choice, and insufficiently reflective of real-world reasoning; in response, they build a dataset of 486 images and 2,038 open-ended questions grounded in school-textbook material across nine domains, including math, history, biology, geography, arts, music, physics, religion, and sports.

The study does not test a classroom intervention; instead, it evaluates thirteen open-weight VLMs on the benchmark using automated judging with multiple LLM evaluators. The population/context is German middle school level (grades 8-10), with questions and answers authored in German native language and drawn from German school materials and related books. The paper reports that even the strongest models achieve under 45% overall accuracy, with particularly weak results in music, math, and adversarial questions that are intentionally unanswerable from the image alone.

The main conclusion is that middle-school multimodal tasks are substantially harder for current open-weight VLMs than their scores on popular public benchmarks would suggest. Performance varies by domain and model family, and the authors find notable gaps between benchmark performance (e.g., MMMU) and performance on their German, open-ended, visually grounded tasks. They also conclude that models struggle to say “no” on misleading questions and that German-language, non-translation-based evaluation exposes limitations not captured by standard English benchmarks.

finding.finding_summary: Models performed poorly on math questions that required visual interpretation, counting, and basic calculation. The best overall model on the benchmark reached only 34.09% accuracy on math (Qwen2.5VL 32B), while the strongest models overall still struggled with geometry, area, circumference, and identifying shapes correctly.
finding.measure: Open-ended accuracy on math questions

finding.finding_summary: Performance was weak on physics and biology items that required interpreting diagrams, tables, labels, and domain concepts. The paper reports that the best models often failed on explanation-based physics questions and on biology tasks involving technical term identification, with best reported physics accuracy reaching 47.65% for Qwen2.5VL 32B and biology accuracy reaching 48.53% on the main results table.
finding.measure: Open-ended accuracy on physics and biology questions

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark shows that VLMs struggle across non-STEM school subjects such as arts, geography, history, music, religion, and sports. Best-domain accuracies remained modest, e.g. history at 54.36% in Table 3, religion at 52.92% in Table 4, and music at 31.03% for the best model, with many errors involving map reading, art-style identification, chord recognition, and sports-game interpretation.
finding.measure: Open-ended accuracy across arts, geography, history, music, religion, and sports questions
finding.study_size: arts n=286; geography n=251; history n=264; music n=166; religion n=206; sports n=154 questions

finding.finding_summary: The paper documents weaknesses in reasoning-related abilities such as interpreting diagrams, combining visual and background knowledge, and handling adversarial or misleading questions. The authors specifically note that models often failed to infer when an image could not support an answer, suggesting limited metacognitive-like judgment about unanswerability rather than a direct instructional outcome measure.
finding.measure: Accuracy on adversarial and reasoning-heavy open-ended questions
finding.study_size: n=2038 questions overall; adversarial subset included within dataset

finding.finding_summary: The paper's main contribution is the creation of a new German-language benchmark for multimodal evaluation, which the authors argue fills a gap in existing AI evaluation infrastructure. They show that this benchmark differentiates among models differently than public leaderboards like MMMU and may better reflect real-world, non-English educational settings, suggesting institutional value for model evaluation and procurement decisions.
finding.measure: Creation and comparative evaluation of a new benchmark dataset and protocol

paper_profiles.title: Envisioning the Applications and Implications of Generative AI for News Media
paper_profiles.venue: CHI ’23 Workshop on Generative AI and HCI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This workshop paper examines how generative AI might be incorporated into newsroom workflows and what tensions such systems raise for journalism. The authors ask which tasks across the news production pipeline could benefit from generative support, how such tools might affect journalistic agency and creativity, and what editorial values should shape system design.

Rather than evaluating a specific deployed intervention, the paper synthesizes prior research and industry reports to envision possible applications for generative AI in newsgathering and production. It argues that generative models may be useful for tasks such as summarizing unstructured documents, querying text, drafting story leads, revising copy, and generating social media versions of articles, but that these uses must be constrained by concerns about hallucination, confidentiality, bias, cost, and over-reliance.

The paper is grounded in the adult professional context of journalists and editors, especially in newsrooms experimenting with AI. Its main conclusion is that generative AI is promising as a supplement to human newsroom labor, but only if systems are designed with human oversight, transparency, and value-sensitive interaction patterns that preserve journalistic judgment and control.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI could improve newsroom productivity by helping journalists summarize unstructured documents, draft copy, revise text, and generate social media outputs, but it also notes important efficiency costs. In particular, the authors highlight that experimentation, prompt engineering, and human review can add time, and cite evidence that AI-generated stories at CNET were produced rapidly but took longer to edit than human-written work.
finding.measure: Conceptual assessment of newsroom workflow efficiency; cited examples of story drafting and editing time in news production

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes broader institutional implications for journalism organizations, including confidentiality, editorial independence, bias, and governance of AI use in newsrooms. It frames generative AI as a socio-technical issue affecting newsroom norms, values, and work routines, and argues for inclusive, value-sensitive design processes rather than simple automation.
finding.measure: Theoretical analysis of newsroom norms, editorial values, and organizational implications

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI Toolkit - A Framework for Increasing the Quality of LLM-Based Applications Over Their Whole Life Cycle
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This preprint addresses a software engineering problem rather than an education research question: how to improve the development, testing, deployment, and monitoring of LLM-based applications across their full life cycle. The authors argue that current workflows for LLM applications are manual, slow, and trial-and-error driven, and they propose the Generative AI Toolkit as an automation framework to improve quality, shorten release cycles, and support continuous monitoring.

The paper describes toolkit features including automated agent creation, user-defined metrics, repeatable evaluation cases, model/prompt permutation testing, CI/CD integration, infrastructure-as-code deployment, a debugging GUI, and logging/monitoring via traces. It is illustrated with several representative adult industry use cases: text-to-SQL, a restaurant RAG agent, an in-vehicle personal assistant, and model comparison experiments. The paper reports qualitative benefits such as reduced manual work, improved test coverage, faster iteration, and easier identification of optimization opportunities, but it does not present a controlled empirical study or K-12 context.

The population is software developers/DevOps teams building LLM applications, not students or K-12 educators. Although the paper mentions educationally relevant concepts like testing, prompts, and automation, it does not study teacher productivity, grade bands, subject areas, or school context. As a result, it provides no direct evidence for K-12 teacher AI productivity, and its conclusions are framed as framework capabilities and illustrative use cases rather than measured educational outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims the toolkit automates manual, trial-and-error workflows for LLM application development and monitoring, thereby reducing manual work and shortening cycle times. However, the paper does not report a controlled experiment or quantitative effect estimate; the benefits are described qualitatively across illustrative use cases rather than measured with a sample size or statistical comparison.
finding.measure: Developer workflow efficiency, manual work reduction, cycle time, test automation, and monitoring/debugging efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The toolkit is positioned as a DevOps/CI-CD framework that standardizes and automates LLM application development, deployment, logging, and monitoring, which could support organizational workflows and governance. The paper does not measure institutional outcomes directly; the evidence is descriptive and implementation-focused rather than empirical.
finding.measure: DevOps workflow automation, CI/CD integration, infrastructure-as-code, logging/monitoring infrastructure

paper_profiles.title: Making AI-Enhanced Videos: Analyzing Generative AI Use Cases in YouTube Content Creation
paper_profiles.venue: Extended Abstracts of the CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI EA ’25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative AI tools are being used by YouTube content creators across the video production workflow. The authors ask what specific use cases GenAI supports during planning, production, editing, and uploading, because existing research had not yet mapped these uses in detail.

The study analyzes 274 English-language YouTube how-to videos posted over a six-month period in 2023–2024. Using thematic analysis of 2,829 transcript segments, the authors identify recurring GenAI practices such as topic ideation, script generation, prompt refinement, image/video creation, voiceover generation, lip-syncing, upscaling, subtitle generation, and title generation.

The paper’s main contribution is a conceptual framework organizing GenAI uses into four phases of video creation. The authors argue that GenAI is already streamlining creator workflows and reducing creative labor, but they also raise concerns about over-reliance, originality, authenticity, transparency, and the labeling of AI-generated content. The discussion concludes with design and research implications for future GenAI tools that support content creation and prompt-based workflows.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that GenAI is widely used to streamline creator workflows across planning, production, editing, and uploading. In 274 YouTube how-to videos, creators used GenAI for scriptwriting (n=85), prompt refinement (n=16), AI image/video generation (n=167), voiceovers (n=93), upscaling (n=17), subtitle generation (n=28), and title generation (n=6), indicating broad productivity support rather than a single narrow use case.
finding.measure: Observed GenAI use cases in YouTube how-to videos across the video production workflow

paper_profiles.title: Making Physical Objects with Generative AI and Robotic Assembly: Considering Fabrication Constraints, Sustainability, Time, Functionality and Accessibility
paper_profiles.venue: GenAICHI: CHI 2025 Workshop on Generative AI and HCI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This workshop paper examines how 3D generative AI can be paired with fabrication methods to produce physical objects, arguing that progress in text-to-3D generation alone is not sufficient unless the downstream making process can accommodate real-world constraints. The authors frame the problem around five considerations for physical making with generative AI: fabrication constraints, time, sustainability, functionality, and accessibility.

As a case study, the paper presents a prompt-to-production system that combines text-to-3D generation (using Meshy.AI) with discrete robotic assembly on a UR10 robotic arm. The system converts AI-generated meshes into component-level representations, then applies algorithmic checks such as overhang detection, connectivity search, and robotic reachability analysis to enable feasible assembly. The paper reports demonstrations of assembling multiple objects from modular parts and uses these demonstrations to analyze fabrication time, reuse of components, object functionality, and cost barriers.

The study is not an educational intervention and does not involve K-12 participants. Its main conclusion is that discrete robotic assembly can better align with generative AI’s speed and support sustainable reuse and rapid fabrication, but accessibility remains limited by equipment cost and the need for specialized hardware. The paper is primarily conceptual and demonstrative, offering a framework for assessing how physical fabrication methods align with generative AI capabilities rather than testing user learning or educational outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The system is designed to reduce the time and expertise needed to turn generative AI outputs into physical objects. The authors report that nearly all assembled objects were fabricated in under five minutes from the user's prompt, showing that prompt-to-physical production can be rapid relative to conventional fabrication workflows.
finding.measure: Fabrication/assembly time from user prompt to completed physical object

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that discrete robotic assembly can improve sustainability by reusing the same modular parts to produce multiple distinct objects, which the authors present as a more responsible alternative to wasteful one-off fabrication. Using 40 modular components, they successfully assembled seven distinct objects, demonstrating repurposability at the system level.
finding.measure: Number of distinct objects produced from a fixed set of modular components; reuse/disassembly capability

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI and Firm Productivity: Field Experiments in Online Retail
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether generative AI can raise productivity at the firm level, and through what mechanisms. Rather than focusing on worker-level task completion, the authors study whether GenAI increases revenue-based productivity in a large cross-border online retail platform by improving existing customer-facing workflows.

The study evaluates seven GenAI-enabled workflow changes, including a pre-sale service chatbot, search query refinement, product description generation, marketing push message creation, Google Shopping ad title optimization, chargeback defense, and live-chat translation. Each workflow was tested with large randomized field experiments over roughly six months in 2023–2024, mostly at the consumer level and one at the product level, with treatment conditions holding prices and inputs constant. This design allows the authors to interpret changes in sales as productivity gains.

The main conclusion is that GenAI often increases sales and conversion rates, with effects ranging from no detectable change to gains as large as 16.3% in sales depending on the workflow. The strongest effects appear in customer service and search-related applications, while some advertising-related applications show little or no effect. The paper also finds that the mechanism is mainly demand-side: GenAI increases conversion and reduces friction in the customer journey, but does not worsen returns or customer ratings. Heterogeneity analyses suggest larger benefits for less experienced consumers, and weaker or imprecisely estimated differences by seller type. The paper’s setting is not K-12 education, but it is relevant to AI productivity evidence because it offers causal evidence from large-scale randomized experiments.

finding.finding_summary: GenAI adoption improved workflow and revenue productivity in seven large-scale randomized field experiments at an online retail platform. Across the four applications with positive sales effects, treatment effects ranged from 0% to 16.3% in sales, with the largest gains in the pre-sale service chatbot and search-related workflows; the authors estimate an annual incremental value of about $4.6–$5 per consumer.
finding.measure: Sales value (total consumer expenditure), conversion rates, cart value, workflow success rates, consumer satisfaction
finding.study_size: n=44,614; n=1,849,382; n=4,772,937; n=13,715,528; n=1,244,016; plus about 30,000 and about 200,000 for two non-granular experiments
finding.effect_size: 0% to 16.3% sales lift; 1% to 22% conversion-rate increases; 15% higher chargeback-defense success; 5.2% higher live-chat satisfaction

paper_profiles.title: Clinical Productivity System – A Decision Support Model
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Productivity and Performance Management
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a data-driven clinical productivity system can improve organizational performance in a large behavioral health provider. The central problem is that traditional productivity metrics in healthcare rely on arbitrary weighting schemes and do not fully align clinician behavior with revenue, quality, compliance, and access goals.

The proposed intervention is a value-per-unit (VPU) decision support system built on electronic health record and billing data, with daily feedback to clinicians and management. The system incorporates revenue, clinical percentage, treatment plan completion, licensure/compliance constraints, and other modifiers into a productivity metric intended to replace traditional weighted productivity models.

The setting is Centerstone, a large community-based behavioral health organization serving more than 75,000 clients annually in Tennessee and Indiana. The paper reports pre-post implementation changes over a short time window, including improvements in revenue, treatment plan completion, case management eligibility, and access time, with reductions in variation across metrics. The evidence is presented as a real-world implementation study rather than a controlled experiment, and the author argues that EHR-derived decision support can make productivity systems more actionable and better aligned with quality and outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: In a pre-post implementation analysis over 3 months, the VPU system was associated with improved productivity-related metrics. Actual revenue increased 28% from December 2008 to March 2009 (March mean $7,528 per staff vs. December mean $5,409; t(344)=-14.071, p<.001), while total staff time rose only 2.1%. The paper also reports a 25% increase in treatment plan completion and a 23% decrease in access time.
finding.measure: Actual revenue per staff, staff time, treatment plan completion, access time

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the productivity system improved organization-level functioning, including compliance/audit issues, outcomes collection, case management eligibility, and access. Case management eligibility rose from 79.4% (SD=7%) in September 2008 to 96.3% (SD=1%) by March 2009, with a significant paired t-test result (t(157)=-11.325, p<.001), and eligible clients exceeded baseline total caseload by 10.6%.
finding.measure: Case management eligibility, compliance/audit issues, outcomes collection, access time, caseload eligibility
finding.std_deviation: SD=7% at baseline; SD=1% at follow-up

finding.finding_summary: This paper is not an education study and does not evaluate student learning outcomes. It focuses on healthcare productivity and organizational performance rather than academic outcomes, so no direct evidence is reported for literacy, language, math, or science outcomes.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Natural Language Query Engine for Relational Databases using Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem that non-technical users often cannot effectively query relational databases because SQL knowledge is required. The author proposes a generative-AI-based natural language query engine that translates user questions into SQL, validates the SQL syntactically and semantically, incorporates business rules and domain knowledge via a vector database, and then generates a natural-language response from the retrieved data.

The system is prototyped with IBM watsonx.data, watsonx.ai, Milvus, and Python orchestration. It is evaluated on the BIRD-SQL benchmark and by a small group of nontechnical users. The paper reports that more than 50% of queries were translated correctly on the first attempt (over 58% for simple queries), and that natural-language responses were judged excellent in 90% of the tested cases. The main conclusion is that combining LLM-based SQL generation with iterative validation and vector-retrieved business rules can improve the usability and apparent correctness of natural-language database interfaces for enterprise users.

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central claim is that the proposed natural-language interface improves productivity for non-technical database users by removing the need to know SQL and by automating query generation, validation, and response generation. In the prototype evaluation, more than 50% of benchmark queries were translated correctly on the first attempt (more than 58% for simple queries), and iterative refinement increased success further.
finding.measure: SQL translation accuracy and user-facing response generation efficiency in BIRD-SQL prototype evaluation

paper_profiles.title: Transforming Software Development with Generative AI: Empirical Insights on Collaboration and Workflow
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative AI tools such as ChatGPT and GitHub Copilot are changing software developers’ daily work, learning, and collaboration. The central question is how GenAI affects individual workflow and team dynamics in software development, particularly whether it improves productivity without harming knowledge sharing and agile teamwork.

The authors conducted an exploratory multi-case qualitative study using semi-structured interviews with 13 participants across software-related roles: developers, data scientists, managers, designers, frontend developers, CTOs, and architects. Participants described using GenAI for getting unstuck, learning, creating virtual environments, copywriting, boilerplate code, and working with existing code such as refactoring, debugging, and test generation.

The main findings are that GenAI often makes work faster, more efficient, and more enjoyable by reducing repetitive tasks and supporting rapid learning. However, it can also reduce human-to-human interaction, decrease pair programming and knowledge sharing, and disrupt the feedback loops that support teamwork in agile development. The paper concludes that GenAI may boost individual productivity while potentially weakening collaborative processes, making tool integration, prompt skill, and team practices important mediators of its impact.

finding.finding_summary: Interviewees consistently reported that GenAI reduced time spent on repetitive or tedious tasks and improved day-to-day efficiency. Examples included generating boilerplate code, drafting bids in about 20 minutes instead of much longer, and speeding up debugging, refactoring, and test writing; the study is qualitative and does not report effect sizes.
finding.measure: Self-reported productivity, time saved on coding and writing tasks, and perceived workflow efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The study found that GenAI supported learning, problem-solving, and metacognitive reflection by acting like a tutor or rubber duck, helping participants get unstuck and explore problems in new ways. At the same time, it appeared to reduce some peer collaboration behaviors such as pair programming and asking coworkers for help, so the collaboration-related effects were mixed.
finding.measure: Interview-reported learning speed, problem-solving support, and collaboration practices

finding.finding_summary: Participants said GenAI increased enjoyment, motivation, and fun by removing boring work and giving immediate feedback. They also reported lower friction and less social discomfort than asking colleagues, which made it easier to seek help and stay engaged in work.
