The authors conclude that AI deployment in education requires careful policy and design calibration rather than a one-size-fits-all approach.
finding.measure: Perceptions of global utility, justice, confidence, risk, and intention to use AI across stakeholder groups and vignette scenarios

finding.finding_summary: The study touches operational efficiency through perceptions of AI for grading, answering questions, and supporting students, but it does not measure actual productivity or workload. In the Correct-AI vignette, teachers reported higher explainability was associated with greater perceived global utility (β=0.7161) and perceived usefulness (β=0.6634), both of which increased intention to use; however, higher agency often reduced acceptance. This suggests AI may be viewed as potentially efficiency-enhancing, but only when it is sufficiently understandable and not overly autonomous.
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness, global utility, and intention to use AI tools for grading, Q&A, and support

finding.finding_summary: A central vignette, Emotion-AI, concerned AI used to support or monitor students' emotional health, making this a substantive social-emotional outcome. For students, explainability increased global utility, which in turn increased intention to use; for teachers, privacy significantly lowered confidence in Emotion-AI (β=-0.6581), and confidence then increased intention to use (β=0.4744). The paper indicates that acceptance of emotionally supportive AI depends on trust-related perceptions rather than direct positive reactions to the tool itself.
finding.measure: Acceptance of an AI system for emotional support/monitoring, via confidence, global utility, and intention to use

paper_profiles.title: Shadows and light: navigating teachers’ time poverty and blended teaching acceptance with social support and job satisfaction in EFL teachers’ voyage
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether teachers’ perceived time poverty is associated with their acceptance of blended teaching, and whether job satisfaction mediates that relationship and social support moderates it. The authors frame blended teaching as a technology-infused instructional approach that requires substantial teacher time and effort, and argue that time scarcity may reduce willingness to adopt it.

The study surveyed 793 English teachers from universities in eastern China (Fujian, Jiangxi, and Guangdong). Using regression and moderated mediation analysis, the authors found that time poverty was negatively associated with blended teaching acceptance and job satisfaction, and that job satisfaction partially mediated this relationship.

Social support was positively associated with both job satisfaction and blended teaching acceptance, but it did not function as a simple buffer. Instead, social support strengthened the positive link between job satisfaction and blended teaching acceptance, while unexpectedly intensifying the negative associations between time poverty and both job satisfaction and blended teaching acceptance. The paper concludes that support systems need to be context-sensitive and well-aligned with teachers’ needs rather than assumed to be universally protective.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers’ perceived time poverty was significantly and negatively associated with blended teaching acceptance (β = -0.125, p < .001) and job satisfaction (β = -0.374, p < .001) in a sample of 793 Chinese university EFL teachers. The study also found a significant indirect effect of time poverty on blended teaching acceptance through job satisfaction (indirect effect = -0.127, bootstrapped 95% CI [-0.174, -0.086]).
finding.measure: Teachers’ Time Poverty Scale; Teacher’s Blended Teaching Acceptance Scale; job satisfaction scale
finding.confidence_interval: 95% bootCI [-0.174, -0.086] for indirect effect; not_reported for direct effects

finding.finding_summary: Job satisfaction was positively associated with blended teaching acceptance (β = 0.339, p < .001), and time poverty negatively predicted job satisfaction (β = -0.374, p < .001). Social support was also positively associated with job satisfaction (β = 0.433, p < .001), but its moderation effects were mixed: it strengthened the job satisfaction-to-acceptance link (β = 0.081, p < .01) while intensifying the negative effects of time poverty on job satisfaction and blended teaching acceptance (interaction betas = -0.110 and -0.104, both p < .001).
finding.measure: Job satisfaction; social support; blended teaching acceptance

paper_profiles.title: TIMSS 2027 Assessment Frameworks
paper_profiles.venue: Boston College, TIMSS & PIRLS International Study Center
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This publication presents the TIMSS 2027 assessment frameworks for mathematics and science, along with the contextual and assessment design frameworks that guide the next international cycle. Rather than testing an intervention, it specifies the construct definitions, content domains, cognitive domains, item design principles, and background questionnaires used to measure student achievement and learning contexts across participating countries.

The paper describes the transition to a fully digital assessment and the resulting innovations, including adaptive group design, performance-based routing, interactive problem-solving and inquiry tasks, and expanded automated scoring. It also documents the inclusion of new contextual questionnaire topics such as digital technologies, artificial intelligence use in education, family involvement, and school leadership practices.

The population of interest is fourth- and eighth-grade students participating in TIMSS, with related background data collected from parents, teachers, and school leaders. The framework concludes that TIMSS 2027 will preserve trend comparability while improving measurement precision, engagement, and contextual understanding of mathematics and science learning internationally. As a framework document, it does not report empirical effects of an intervention or relationship, but instead provides the measurement and design foundation for future TIMSS studies.

finding.finding_summary: This is a framework document, not an empirical study, so it does not report an observed effect on mathematical numeracy. It defines the mathematics content and cognitive domains for TIMSS 2027 (e.g., number, algebra, geometry/measurement, data/probability) and the grade-specific assessment blueprint for fourth and eighth grades.
finding.measure: TIMSS mathematics content and cognitive framework specification

finding.finding_summary: The science framework specifies what TIMSS 2027 will measure in science, including cognitive domains aligned with knowing, applying, and reasoning, plus environmental knowledge as a distinct subscale. No empirical outcome effects are reported because the paper is a measurement framework rather than a results study.
finding.measure: TIMSS science content and cognitive framework specification

finding.finding_summary: The document argues that the move to a fully digital, adaptive TIMSS assessment will enhance operational efficiency and reporting, and that automated scoring will streamline administration of constructed-response items. However, it provides no empirical estimate of the magnitude of these efficiency gains.
finding.measure: Assessment design features affecting logistics, routing, and automated scoring

finding.finding_summary: The framework is intended to support cross-country monitoring of education systems, benchmarking curricula, and informing policy and practice through richer contextual data. It adds new questionnaire content on AI tools, digital devices, family involvement, and school leadership to improve institutional insight, but it does not report causal effects.
finding.measure: TIMSS contextual framework and system-level questionnaire design

paper_profiles.title: Measuring the Effectiveness of Transfer of Learning Constructs and Intent to Transfer in a Simulation-Based Leadership Training Program
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This dissertation examines a long-standing problem in training and human resource development: whether what people learn in simulation-based leadership training actually transfers to the workplace. The study is grounded in Holton’s HRD evaluation model and uses the Learning Transfer System Inventory (LTSI) to investigate four transfer-related constructs—ability, motivation, work environment, and learner readiness—along with intent to transfer.

The empirical study was conducted with mid-level managers in a global telecommunications organization in Princeton, New Jersey. Participants completed self-report surveys, and the researcher supplemented the quantitative data with interviews and observations to better understand transfer conditions in the simulation-based training context. The sample was small (n=22), which the author notes limits generalizability.

The main conclusion is that transfer-related constructs were meaningfully associated with intent to transfer, supporting the use of simulation-based leadership training as a potentially viable approach for developing managerial skills. The dissertation reports a strong relationship between ability and motivation, moderate relationships between work environment and both ability and motivation, and a moderate relationship between learner readiness and ability. Overall, the findings suggest that organizational support and learner preparedness matter for transfer, but the evidence is correlational rather than causal.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that transfer-related constructs were associated with intent to transfer in a simulation-based leadership training context, with a strong relationship reported between ability and motivation and moderate relationships involving learner readiness. These findings suggest the training supported managerial learning processes related to problem solving, application, and transfer readiness, but the evidence is correlational and not an outcome test of skill gain.
finding.measure: Self-report Learning Transfer System Inventory (LTSI) constructs and intent to transfer

finding.finding_summary: Participants' motivation, learner readiness, and intent to transfer were central variables in the study, and the results indicate these affective and self-regulatory factors were positively related in the simulation training setting. The dissertation reports a strong relationship between ability and motivation and moderate relationships involving work environment and motivation, supporting the idea that readiness and motivation are important for transfer.
finding.measure: Self-report LTSI motivation, learner readiness, and intent to transfer scales

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly targets transfer of learning to work performance, which is framed as a productivity and performance-improvement issue in managerial training. Although it does not report objective productivity gains, it concludes that stronger transfer-related constructs are associated with greater intent to apply newly learned skills in the workplace, implying potential efficiency benefits from the simulation-based program.
finding.measure: Intent to transfer and transfer of learning constructs as proxies for workplace application

paper_profiles.title: Mandatory Gamified Security Awareness Training Impacts on Texas Public Middle School Students: A Qualitative Study
paper_profiles.venue: Issues in Informing Science and Information Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This qualitative study examines expert beliefs about the impacts of implementing a mandatory gamified security awareness curriculum in Texas public middle schools. The authors ask whether such training could improve students’ long-term security behaviors, when it should be introduced, and whether teachers and schools are prepared to deliver it.

The study uses semi-structured Zoom interviews with 12 cybersecurity awareness training experts and educators recruited through the CyberTexas Foundation and snowball sampling. Participants discussed middle school as a potentially ideal time for habit formation because students are increasingly independent with technology, but some argued that cybersecurity instruction should begin even earlier. Respondents generally supported mandatory training for student safety and future workforce readiness, while also noting practical barriers such as limited teacher expertise, crowded schedules, student maturity differences, and curriculum maintenance challenges.

Participants believed gamification could help shape cybersecurity habits because middle school students respond positively to game-like activities, but only if the games are relevant, hands-on, and sustained over time. They emphasized that one-off lessons would likely fade, whereas repeated, long-term reinforcement combined with traditional instruction could produce more durable behavior change. Because the paper is qualitative and based on expert perceptions rather than student outcome data, its conclusions are suggestive rather than causal.

finding.finding_summary: Interviewed experts believed gamified security awareness training could improve middle school students’ motivation, engagement, and willingness to participate in cybersecurity learning. Ten participants said middle schoolers respond positively to game-based activities, and several argued that gamification can sustain interest and encourage repeated practice of desired habits over time.
finding.measure: Expert interview themes about student engagement, interest, and willingness to participate in gamified cybersecurity training
finding.study_size: n=12 experts interviewed (15 recruited; 12 interviewed per abstract, though the body text also references 15 participants)

finding.finding_summary: The study centrally argues that gamified cybersecurity instruction may help shape long-term habits, behavioral self-regulation, and practical decision-making. Participants repeatedly stated that security behaviors become more lasting when taught in middle school, reinforced over time, and connected to real-world scenarios; single lessons were viewed as insufficient.
finding.measure: Expert interview themes about habit formation, long-term security behavior, and application of cybersecurity concepts

finding.finding_summary: Participants believed teachers could potentially deliver cybersecurity awareness lessons and that instruction could fit into the school day without major schedule changes, but they also identified substantial implementation burdens. The study reports both feasibility claims and barriers, including teacher training needs, lack of technical expertise, time constraints, and the effort required to build and update curricula.
finding.measure: Expert interview themes about teacher preparedness, scheduling, and curriculum implementation feasibility

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses strongly on institutional feasibility and policy implications of making cybersecurity awareness training mandatory in middle schools. Participants generally supported mandatory implementation for student safety and future societal benefits, while also noting institutional barriers such as staffing, scheduling, student special education needs, and parental pushback.
finding.measure: Expert interview themes about mandatory curriculum adoption, school implementation, and policy feasibility

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing college students’ AI literacy through generative AI use: a mixed-methods investigation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how college students’ use of generative AI relates to the development of AI literacy, addressing a perceived gap between rapid AI adoption and students’ deeper understanding, ethical judgment, and practical competency. The authors argue that existing AI literacy frameworks are too static and insufficiently explain how usage behaviors translate into improved literacy.

The paper uses an exploratory sequential mixed-methods design. In phase one, semi-structured interviews with 30 Chinese undergraduates were analyzed using grounded-theory style coding to build a four-part model: cognition, practice, evaluation, and social environment. The qualitative findings suggest AI literacy develops as a spiral process in which students move iteratively through cognition, practice, and evaluation, with many participants showing awareness of algorithmic bias and privacy risks.

In phase two, a survey of 590 undergraduates tested the model using structural equation modeling. The quantitative results indicate that the social environment influences practice indirectly through perceptual impressions, and that collective/group needs fully mediate one key pathway from social environment to use. Perceived ease of use and technological expectations also predict AI adoption and future-oriented literacy. Overall, the study concludes that AI literacy development is ecological and recursive rather than linear, and that interventions should combine cognitive scaffolding, ethical education, and skill training.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly focuses on AI literacy development among undergraduate students and reports that generative AI use is associated with improved AI literacy through iterative cognition-practice-evaluation cycles. In the qualitative phase (n=30), 82% of participants showed critical awareness of algorithmic bias and privacy risks, suggesting growth in AI-related knowledge and judgment rather than only tool use.
finding.measure: AI literacy interview themes; qualitative coding of cognition, practice, evaluation, and awareness of bias/privacy
finding.study_size: n=30 qualitative interviews; n=590 survey respondents

finding.finding_summary: A central finding is that GenAI use supports higher-order thinking, reflection, and critical evaluation. The paper describes a spiral-ascending literacy model built around cognition-practice-evaluation, and the quantitative model shows perceived usefulness and ease of use are linked to interactive application and future-oriented literacy (e.g., perceived ease of use β=0.477; technological expectations β=0.284).
finding.measure: AI literacy dimensions related to critical evaluation, reflective cognition, and future-oriented literacy; structural equation model paths
finding.study_size: n=30 qualitative interviews; n=590 survey respondents

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that social environment and institutional context shape students’ GenAI use, and that educational policy and peer/institutional norms matter for literacy cultivation. The model shows social environment indirectly drives application practice via perceptual impression (path coefficient=0.294, p<0.001), and the authors recommend AI-integrated curricula, institutional support, and multi-dimensional interventions.
finding.measure: Perceived social environment, institutional/peer influence, and AI literacy development model

paper_profiles.title: Learning Factors in AI-Augmented Education: A Comparative Study of Middle and High School Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how four student perception dimensions—experience, clarity, comfort, and motivation—relate to one another in AI-mediated learning environments, and whether those relationships differ between middle school and high school students. The authors motivate the study by noting that most prior work on AI in education has focused on higher education, leaving K-12 learners underexamined, especially in terms of how learning-perception dimensions interact rather than simply whether students like or dislike AI tools.

The study was conducted in extracurricular computer science classes where students used AI tools during programming-related activities. The sample included 53 students total: 25 middle school students (ages 10–13) and 28 high school students (ages 15–20). Middle school students used Teachable Machine in an introductory AI course, while high school students worked on Python applications using vibe coding and LLMs such as Gemini and Claude. Data came from a 17-item questionnaire with Likert-scale items and open-ended responses; analyses included descriptive statistics, Mann-Whitney U tests, Spearman correlations, and text mining.

Results showed generally positive perceptions of AI across both age groups, but with a statistically significant difference in perceived ease of use: high school students rated the tools as easier to use than middle school students (U=192.00, p=0.0013). Correlation patterns also differed strongly by age. Middle school students showed tightly interconnected and mostly strong positive correlations across dimensions, suggesting a holistic evaluation pattern, whereas high school students showed weaker and more differentiated relationships, suggesting they assessed clarity, comfort, and motivation more independently. The authors conclude that AI-supported learning design should be developmentally responsive, emphasizing clarity and scaffolding for younger learners and more nuanced usability and motivational supports for older learners.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies students' perceptions of AI tools in computer science programming activities, which falls under academic learning outside literacy, math, or science-specific reasoning. Across both groups, students reported generally positive experiences with AI-supported programming, with high school students especially rating the tools as easy to use (67.9% "very much" easy; mean 3.68) compared with middle school students (24.0%; mean 3.16), and the groups differed significantly on ease of use (U=192.00, p=0.0013).
finding.measure: Questionnaire measures of overall experience, ease of use, clarity, learning support, comfort, and intention to use AI in other courses during programming learning activities

finding.finding_summary: This is a central outcome of the paper: the authors examine experience, clarity, comfort, and motivation as learning-perception dimensions. Students across both groups reported generally positive motivation and comfort, and the correlational structure shows that middle school students had strong positive links among dimensions (e.g., Experience-Clarity ρ=0.79; Clarity-Motivation ρ=0.60), while high school students showed weaker or near-zero links (e.g., Experience-Motivation ρ=0.02), indicating different motivational and comfort-related responses to AI-mediated learning.
finding.measure: Likert-scale questionnaire items on experience, clarity, comfort, and motivation; Spearman correlations among items and aggregated dimensions
finding.std_deviation: 0.85 total Cronbach's alpha; subgroup alpha=0.81 middle, 0.89 high

finding.finding_summary: The study also substantively addresses students' evaluative and analytical judgment about AI tools, which is relevant to durable skills such as metacognition and critical appraisal. High school students exhibited a more differentiated and technically sophisticated pattern of evaluation, with weaker correlations between experience and motivation/comfort, suggesting more independent judgment, while open-ended responses emphasized explanation, code, and thinking; middle school students showed more holistic but less differentiated appraisals.
finding.measure: Spearman correlations between perception dimensions; open-ended responses about AI's influence on learning

paper_profiles.title: Business Intelligence for Service Optimization in U.S. Education and Customer-Facing Enterprises: A Prisma Systematic Review of KPI Frameworks
paper_profiles.population: U.S. education and customer-facing enterprises (mixed service-sector organizations; includes education institutions such as K-12/higher education and non-education customer-facing enterprises)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how Business Intelligence (BI) capability is associated with service optimization outcomes, and whether the quality of KPI frameworks helps explain those relationships. Using a PRISMA-guided systematic review, the author synthesized 92 peer-reviewed quantitative studies from U.S. education and customer-facing enterprises and coded them as evidence records for structured analysis.

The review focuses on how BI is operationalized in the literature (for example, information quality, system quality, usage intensity, analytics maturity) and how KPI frameworks are structured (for example, Balanced Scorecard, service-quality KPI systems, operations KPIs, and commercial outcome KPIs). The paper does not evaluate a single intervention; instead, it compares patterns across studies and examines how BI-related constructs relate to outcomes such as satisfaction, efficiency, retention/loyalty, responsiveness, and equity/access.

The main conclusion is that BI capability is positively associated with service optimization outcomes across the reviewed studies, with the strongest average standardized effects for satisfaction (β̄=0.33) and efficiency (β̄=0.31), followed by retention/loyalty (β̄=0.29) and responsiveness (β̄=0.28). When KPI framework quality is included in models, the average BI coefficient declines from β̄=0.30 to β̄=0.22, while KPI quality itself remains positively associated (β̄=0.27), suggesting that BI works best when its outputs are embedded in coherent and well-governed KPI systems.

The review also argues that education studies emphasize retention, progression, and equity/access, while customer-facing enterprise studies emphasize satisfaction and loyalty. Reliability reporting is concentrated in SEM and PLS-SEM studies, with Cronbach’s alpha generally ranging from 0.82 to 0.88. Overall, the paper presents BI as a measurable organizational capability whose service benefits depend partly on the design and governance of KPI frameworks.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed quantitative studies, BI capability showed a positive association with efficiency outcomes, with a mean standardized effect of β̄=0.31. When KPI framework quality was included in extended models, the average BI coefficient declined from β̄=0.30 to β̄=0.22, while KPI framework quality remained independently positive (β̄=0.27), indicating that coherent KPI systems help translate BI into operational gains.
finding.measure: Efficiency / service optimization indicators

finding.finding_summary: The review found that BI capability is positively associated with broader institutional/service optimization outcomes when paired with quality KPI frameworks. Across 92 studies, adding KPI framework quality increased explanatory power by an average ΔR² of 0.09, and models with governance maturity and organizational enablers produced cumulative ΔR² increases up to 0.16.
finding.measure: Institutional/service performance outcomes; model explanatory power (ΔR²)
finding.effect_size: ΔR²=0.09 (average increase with KPI quality); cumulative ΔR² up to 0.16

finding.finding_summary: The paper synthesizes studies where satisfaction is a central service outcome, especially in customer-facing enterprises and education service contexts. The strongest mean standardized effect reported in the review was for satisfaction (β̄=0.33), suggesting that BI-enabled KPI systems are associated with improved user/customer/student experience, although the outcome is aggregated across sectors rather than isolated to one population.
finding.measure: Satisfaction / service experience surveys and indices

finding.finding_summary: The review reports positive associations for responsiveness and retention/loyalty outcomes, which can reflect persistence and self-management at the institutional/service level. The mean standardized effect for responsiveness was β̄=0.28, and KPI-supported BI systems were also associated with retention/loyalty (β̄=0.29), indicating stronger performance on continuity-related outcomes when analytics outputs were embedded in KPI frameworks.
finding.measure: Responsiveness; retention/loyalty outcomes

finding.finding_summary: Education studies in the review particularly emphasized retention, progression, and equity/access, indicating institutional-level effects in education systems rather than individual learning outcomes. Equity or access outcomes showed a positive but weaker association (β̄=0.22), and the paper notes that these outcomes appeared predominantly in education studies.
finding.measure: Equity/access outcomes in education; retention and progression indicators

paper_profiles.title: A Review on Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Healthcare: Why, How, and When?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a PRISMA-style scoping/systematic review of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) in healthcare, focused on why XAI is needed, how XAI methods work, and when different forms of explanation are most appropriate. The authors review literature published from January 2012 to February 2022 and synthesize major XAI methods including dimension reduction, knowledge distillation/rule extraction, feature importance methods, attention mechanisms, and surrogate representations.

The paper does not evaluate a single intervention in a primary empirical study; instead, it maps the healthcare XAI literature and discusses benefits, limitations, and evaluation criteria for trustworthy AI. The review emphasizes that explainability is important for acceptance, accountability, and clinical deployment, but also notes that explanation quality is hard to assess and that explainability alone is insufficient without good data quality, validation, governance, and legal oversight. The context is adult healthcare and medical decision-making, not education.

For the K-12 teacher AI productivity question, this paper provides only indirect analogical evidence: it argues that interpretable/explainable AI can support adoption in high-stakes professional settings, but it does not study teachers, classrooms, or productivity outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that XAI can improve trust, transparency, accountability, and acceptability of AI in healthcare, but also stresses that explainability alone is insufficient and must be paired with data-quality checks, external validation, and governance. No primary effect sizes are reported because this is a literature review rather than an intervention study.
finding.measure: Reported themes from the healthcare XAI literature (trust, transparency, accountability, validation, governance)

paper_profiles.title: Artificial Intelligence Framework for Simulating Clinical Decision-Making: A Markov Decision Process Approach
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to support better sequential decision-making in complex, uncertain healthcare environments where costs are high, outcomes vary over time, and clinicians must make treatment decisions with incomplete information. The authors propose a general-purpose artificial intelligence framework intended to simulate clinical decision-making and to serve as the basis for adaptive clinical decision support.

The approach combines Markov decision processes, partially observable Markov decision processes, dynamic decision networks, and a multi-agent structure. The framework is trained and evaluated on electronic health record data from an outpatient mental health setting at Centerstone, using 5,807 patients in the underlying dataset and simulation runs of 500 randomly selected patients. The main comparison is between the proposed MDP-based approach and simpler treatment-as-usual analogs such as fee-for-service and case-rate/hard-stop policies.

The study reports that the AI framework is feasible and can outperform these baseline decision rules on cost-effectiveness. In particular, an MDP model using a global transition model achieved lower cost per unit change than the raw-effect fee-for-service analog ($189 vs. $497) and produced about 30–35% better patient outcomes; with outcome scaling, the authors report roughly 50% more improvement for about half the cost. Because this is a simulation study using retrospective EHR-derived parameters rather than a prospective evaluation, it provides indirect evidence about AI-enabled decision support rather than direct evidence in K-12 education.

finding.finding_summary: The proposed AI/MDP framework improved cost-effectiveness relative to treatment-as-usual analogs in simulation. Using a global transition model, the MDP achieved CPUC = $189 compared with $497 for the raw-effect fee-for-service baseline, and the authors report about a 30–35% increase in patient outcomes; with outcome scaling, they report roughly 50% more improvement for roughly half the costs.
finding.measure: Cost per unit change (CPUC) and simulated outcome delta on CDOI-ORS
finding.study_size: n=500 simulated patients (from EHR dataset of 5,807 patients)

paper_profiles.title: Study on the Helpfulness of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to evaluate the helpfulness of explainable AI (XAI) methods in a human-centered way. The authors argue that many existing XAI evaluations rely on subjective user impressions or automatic proxy benchmarks that do not capture whether explanations actually help people make better decisions. They propose an objective methodology in which users perform a proxy task whose accuracy reflects whether the explanation helps them judge an AI system’s output.

To demonstrate the approach, the authors ran a user study with 139 participants who judged whether image-classification predictions were correct based on the original image, ground-truth label, and one of six explanation types: LRP, Grad-CAM, LIME, SHAP, Integrated Gradients, or confidence scores. Participants answered questions across two ImageNet-based models (AlexNet and VGG16), and the study measured accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity as proxies for judging, trusting, and questioning AI decisions.

The results showed that all methods performed above chance on overall accuracy, but confidence scores produced the highest accuracy and were significantly better than the other methods. Grad-CAM, confidence scores, and LRP were best for helping users trust correct decisions, while SHAP was best for helping users question incorrect decisions. The authors conclude that no single explanation method worked best across all objectives, and they recommend more diverse, interactive explanation frameworks rather than relying on one monolithic XAI approach.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly measured users’ ability to judge whether an AI image-classification decision was correct, which is a form of critical thinking / evaluative judgment. Across 139 participants, all six XAI methods produced accuracy above the random baseline of 0.5, with confidence scores highest at mean accuracy ≈0.698 and effect size d=0.84 (p<.001).
finding.measure: Accuracy in judging whether the AI prediction was correct

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central aim was to assess whether XAI helps users perform a decision task more effectively, which is directly relevant to task efficiency/productivity. Confidence scores enabled the best task performance for judging model correctness (mean accuracy ≈0.698, d=0.84), while Grad-CAM, LRP, SHAP, LIME, and Integrated Gradients all also exceeded chance but with smaller effects.
finding.measure: Decision-task accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity when using XAI explanations
finding.effect_size: d=0.84 (accuracy for confidence scores); other methods d=0.46, 0.40, 0.28, 0.20, 0.15

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes an objective methodology for evaluating XAI in human-centered settings and argues this could improve how XAI is selected and validated for real-world, safety-relevant applications. This is primarily methodological rather than institutional outcome measurement, but it has direct implications for evaluation practice and governance of XAI systems.
finding.measure: Proposed objective human-centered XAI evaluation methodology; comparison of XAI methods

paper_profiles.title: Gathering Strength, Gathering Storms: The One Hundred Year Study on Artificial Intelligence (AI100) 2021 Study Panel Report
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report is the 2021 installment of the One Hundred Year Study on Artificial Intelligence (AI100), a long-running expert review of the state of AI and its societal influences. Rather than evaluating a single intervention, it synthesizes developments in AI research and deployment over the prior five years and organizes the findings around standing questions about technical progress, public sentiment, governance, labor markets, and the role of academia and industry.

The report is authored by a multidisciplinary study panel and draws on prior AI100 materials, workshop outputs, and the AI Index report. It covers domains such as language processing, computer vision, robotics, mobility, health, finance, recommender systems, public policy, and caregiving, emphasizing both opportunities and risks. Its central conclusion is that AI has made major technical progress and is increasingly embedded in real-world systems, but that many applications still face limits related to robustness, bias, transparency, governance, and sociotechnical integration.

Because this is an expert synthesis rather than an empirical study of a bounded sample, it does not report original participant data or treatment effects. Instead, it provides high-level assessments of the state of the field and offers policy-oriented guidance on responsible development and deployment.

finding.finding_summary: The report argues that AI is increasingly improving task efficiency and automation across multiple domains, including healthcare, finance, robotics, and recommender systems. However, it does not provide a single original effect estimate; instead it describes broad gains such as faster image-processing pipelines (e.g., ImageNet tasks reportedly running 100x faster than three years earlier) and automation of documentation, scheduling, and monitoring tasks.
finding.measure: Expert synthesis of productivity, automation, and task-efficiency applications across sectors

finding.finding_summary: The report substantially focuses on AI’s institutional and policy implications, emphasizing that successful deployment depends on governance, regulation, public oversight, and integration into organizations. It notes that over 60 countries have pursued national AI initiatives, that few have AI-specific regulations, and that impact assessments are emerging as a policy tool, but it does not estimate causal effects.
finding.measure: Policy and governance developments, institutional responses, and regulatory initiatives

paper_profiles.title: Conceptual Modeling and Artificial Intelligence: Mutual Benefits from Complementary Worlds
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an editorial preface for the 3rd International Workshop on Conceptual Modeling Meets Artificial Intelligence (CMAI'2021). It frames the workshop’s central question: how conceptual modeling and artificial intelligence can mutually benefit one another, especially by combining the interpretability and formal structure of conceptual models with the data-driven capabilities of AI.

The paper does not report an empirical study or an intervention. Instead, it introduces a research framework that organizes CMAI work into four categories: exaptation, CM-driven CMAI, AI-driven CMAI, and CM- & AI-driven CMAI. It briefly summarizes the invited papers in the workshop program and maps each to the framework, illustrating example directions such as using conceptual models to improve machine learning, using AI to modularize models, and hybrid AI/modeling approaches.

The context is an academic workshop in information systems / conceptual modeling, not a K-12 educational setting. The main conclusion is that conceptual modeling can improve explainability, integration of domain knowledge, and structure in AI systems, while AI can help scale or automate aspects of conceptual modeling. The article is conceptual and programmatic rather than empirical, so it provides no direct evidence about educational outcomes or teacher productivity.

paper_profiles.title: Certifiable Artificial Intelligence Through Data Fusion
paper_profiles.venue: AAAI FSS-21: Artificial Intelligence in Government and Public Sector
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual review and position paper about how artificial intelligence and machine learning systems can be certified for deployment. The authors argue that AI adoption depends on more than model performance alone; it also requires procedures for verification, validation, documentation, and managing expected use, especially in safety-critical human-machine teaming contexts.

The paper proposes the Multisource AI Scorecard Table (MAST) as a framework for assessing AI systems across sourcing, uncertainty, interpretability, transparency, consistency, accuracy, and visualization. It also outlines a notional certification process with four stages: conceptual idea, processing design, implementation testing, and managed deployment. The discussion is anchored in examples from aviation, autonomous systems, and image fusion, but it does not study K-12 settings, teachers, or educational productivity.

A small illustrative example uses multimodal image fusion for automatic target recognition to show how performance bounds might support certifiable AI. The example compares anisotropic diffusion and CNN-based fusion methods using image-quality metrics such as mutual information, PSNR, SSIM, gradient-based fusion performance, standard deviation, and spatial frequency. The main conclusion is that certification should be based on intended use, robust performance bounds, and documented limitations rather than on raw algorithmic capability alone.

paper_profiles.title: Artificial Intelligence for Sustainable Wine Industry: AI-Driven Management in Viticulture, Wine Production and Enotourism
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how artificial intelligence could support sustainability and efficiency in the wine industry, with a focus on viticulture, wine production, and enotourism in Poland. The authors frame the study around the three pillars of sustainability: environmental, economic, and social, and ask how AI tools might help wine enterprises reduce resource use, improve business operations, and strengthen community relations.

Empirically, the study combines an electronic questionnaire survey of 75 Polish vineyards with a qualitative coding of open-ended responses and a conceptual mapping of AI applications to the issues raised by respondents. The survey was distributed to all actively operating vineyards registered in Poland at the time, and the authors report that 75 vineyards responded. The paper is not an evaluation of a deployed AI intervention; rather, it is an observational and applied conceptual study that interprets winemakers’ current sustainability practices and then proposes AI methods such as drone monitoring, predictive analytics, chatbots, route optimization, and virtual tasting systems.

The main conclusion is that Polish winemakers already show strong awareness of sustainability, especially in environmental care, local economic support, and positive community relations. The authors argue that AI could reinforce these practices by optimizing irrigation, production, supply chains, and tourism services while helping preserve sustainability as the sector grows. They also caution that most Polish winemakers are not yet using advanced AI tools, and future work should test long-term effects, climate adaptation strategies, and broader stakeholder perspectives.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI can improve operational efficiency in the wine industry by optimizing vineyard monitoring, irrigation, fermentation control, quality control, waste reduction, logistics, and tourism operations. This is based on a survey of 75 Polish vineyards plus a structured synthesis of AI methods; however, the paper does not report an experimental effect size or a causal estimate of productivity gains.
finding.measure: Survey responses about sustainability/operations plus conceptual mapping of AI tools to vineyard, production, and tourism processes

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that Polish vineyards contribute to local development, community relations, and cultural heritage, and it positions AI as a tool that could support these institutional and regional outcomes. The evidence comes from the full-population survey of 75 vineyards and qualitative responses describing local hiring, local purchasing, collaboration with residents, and tourism-related community benefits, but no quantitative policy or governance effect is estimated.
finding.measure: Survey items on local development, cooperation with residents, and enotourism benefits

paper_profiles.title: Enterprise AI Canvas: Integrating Artificial Intelligence into Business
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper proposes the Enterprise AI Canvas, a structured framework for helping organizations think through the adoption of artificial intelligence in business settings. The author argues that integrating AI is more complex than conventional analytics because it changes how decisions are made, who makes them, what organizational roles are affected, and what data and technical constraints must be addressed.

The canvas is organized into two parts: a business view and a model/data view. The business side covers value, success metrics, decision optimization, organizational change, sponsorship, and domain expertise; the technical side covers prediction and action, features, data sources and processing, data quality, constraints, and evaluation/monitoring. The paper is primarily conceptual and illustrative, using a supermarket replenishment example to show how the canvas can be applied to demand forecasting and automated ordering.

The paper does not study K-12 education, teachers, or students, and it does not report empirical results. Instead, it offers a design-oriented management framework intended to facilitate cross-functional planning between business experts and data scientists when deploying AI systems in enterprises. Its main conclusion is that AI projects should be evaluated jointly from business, operational, organizational, and technical perspectives to avoid mismatches between model performance and actual decision quality.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI-based decision systems can improve operational efficiency by optimizing business decisions such as replenishment order quantities. In the supermarket example, the proposed AI system is described as reducing waste of perishable goods, lowering inventory, and decreasing stock-out situations, but no empirical effect sizes or study data are reported.
finding.measure: Operational KPIs such as waste rate, stock-out rate, and overall inventory

finding.finding_summary: A central claim of the paper is that AI adoption requires organizational transformation, including change management, new role definitions, management sponsorship, and coordination across departments. The framework emphasizes that decisions formerly made by humans may shift to AI systems, which has implications for governance and institutional workflow, but these claims are conceptual rather than empirical.
finding.measure: Organizational roles, decision workflows, sponsorship, and change management requirements

paper_profiles.title: Augmented Computational Design
paper_profiles.venue: Artificial Intelligence in Performance-Driven Design: Theories, Methods, and Tools Towards Sustainability
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter proposes a conceptual and mathematical framework called Augmented Computational Design (ACD) for using AI in performance-driven generative design. The paper argues that many design problems can be reframed as two dual tasks: mapping from many design decisions to a few performance outcomes, and navigating backward from desired outcomes to feasible design decisions.

The approach is developed for architectural and building design in the architecture, engineering, and construction (AEC) domain, not for education. The chapter formalizes design spaces as decision and performance vector spaces, discusses Jacobian-based approximation and pseudo-inversion, and situates probabilistic and possibilistic AI methods within a spectrum of generative design methods. It emphasizes interpretability, explainability, and the tradeoff between predictive power and transparency.

A worked example uses a Bayesian Belief Network meta-model to approximate the Dutch NTA 8800 building energy calculation tool. The case study samples 20,000 quasi-random configurations, applies sensitivity analysis to reduce 269 inputs to 15 influential parameters, and then trains a shallow BBN to predict three energy performance outputs (BENG 1–3). The main conclusion is that ACD can support efficient, partially reversible, data-driven design exploration in complex high-dimensional settings, especially where direct simulation is expensive or hard to interpret.

finding.finding_summary: The chapter argues that the proposed ACD/BBN surrogate model improves computational efficiency for building energy design by replacing a 269-parameter simulation problem with a tractable meta-model using only 15 influential inputs. The authors report that these 15 parameters account for 90.45% to 92.30% of the final energy performance score, enabling faster exploration and approximate reverse design, but they do not report a quantitative validation effect size for productivity or workload reduction.
finding.measure: Meta-model tractability / surrogate modeling efficiency for building energy performance prediction
finding.study_size: n=20000 simulation samples; 269 original input parameters reduced to 15 inputs

paper_profiles.title: Modular Belief Updates and Confusion about Measures of Certainty in Artificial Intelligence Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines conceptual confusion in artificial intelligence research about two different kinds of uncertainty measures: absolute belief and belief updates (changes in belief). The authors formalize a property they call modularity for belief updates, showing that a modular update depends only on a hypothesis and new evidence, not on prior evidence, and then contrast this with more general updating schemes that depend on prior context.

The paper is not an empirical study of learners or teachers; instead, it is a theoretical/analytical discussion grounded in examples from expert systems, especially MYCIN and INTERNIST-I. The authors argue that both systems implicitly assumed modular belief updates while eliciting quantities that were actually closer to absolute beliefs, leading to inconsistency and potential inference errors. They further discuss historical roots of the confusion in probability and philosophy of science, using these examples to motivate better care in defining and eliciting uncertainty measures.

The main conclusion is that AI systems should distinguish clearly between measures of belief and measures of belief change, and that assumptions of modularity must align with how quantities are elicited from experts. While the paper is influential for uncertainty reasoning in expert systems, it does not present educational intervention evidence, student outcomes, or teacher productivity data.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that using the wrong form of uncertainty measure in expert systems can create serious flaws in reasoning and make knowledge acquisition and maintenance more cumbersome. Although it does not report a quantitative productivity study, it directly discusses operational consequences such as increased complexity, misleading elicitation of certainty values, and potential inference errors in systems like MYCIN and INTERNIST-I.
finding.measure: Expert system knowledge elicitation and reasoning procedure design

paper_profiles.title: Bias Amplification in Artificial Intelligence Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues that the most urgent risks of AI are not hypothetical future scenarios such as killer robots or mass job loss, but the present-day amplification of bias embedded in training data and algorithmic systems. It defines several types of bias in machine learning (dataset, association, automation, interaction, and confirmation bias) and explains how these can scale harm across marginalized groups in domains such as hiring, advertising, criminal justice, healthcare, and public services.

The paper is not an empirical evaluation of a specific intervention; rather, it is a policy-oriented analytic essay drawing on examples from journalism, prior research, and public controversies (e.g., COMPAS, Google ad delivery, Tay chatbot, facial recognition, and healthcare algorithms). Its central recommendation is that government and public-sector institutions should set data standards, promote transparency, regulate algorithmic accountability, and support more diverse datasets and discrimination-aware machine learning. The context is broad public-sector and commercial AI deployment, with an emphasis on governance and institutional responsibility rather than a specific educational setting.

Because the paper is primarily conceptual and argumentative, it does not report original sample-based findings, effect sizes, or direct outcomes. Its main conclusion is that bias mitigation must be treated as a policy and governance problem, and that failure to address dataset and algorithmic bias will continue to produce representative and allocative harms at scale.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI systems can amplify existing bias at scale and that public-sector governance is needed to reduce harm. It does not present original empirical effect estimates; instead, it uses illustrative cases to claim that regulation, transparency, and data standards are necessary to prevent representative and allocative harms.
finding.measure: Policy analysis / conceptual discussion of AI governance and bias amplification

paper_profiles.title: Human-in-the-loop Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues that current AI systems create a form of "knowledge theft" by extracting value from the everyday interactions of workers and other users without compensating them. The author frames this as a future labor-market and fairness problem, especially as AI systems increasingly automate tasks previously done by humans.

Rather than presenting an empirical study or evaluation, the paper proposes Human-in-the-loop AI (HIT-AI) as a normative paradigm for fairer AI. The proposal emphasizes explainable AI, traceability of knowledge sources, symbolic and distributed representations, trusted technologies, virtual identity protocols, privacy-preserving mechanisms, and possible copyright extensions so that people whose data/behavior trains AI systems can be identified and rewarded.

The context is broad and non-educational: examples include call centers, driving, medicine, translation, image recognition, and chatbots. Education is mentioned only briefly as one domain where chatbots and MOOCs might replace teachers and professors, but the paper does not study teachers, schools, students, or any K-12 setting. Its main conclusion is a policy and ethics argument: AI systems should be designed so that revenue generated by AI can be traced back and partially redistributed to the original knowledge producers.

finding.finding_summary: This is a conceptual proposal, not an empirical study, so it does not report measured institutional effects. The paper argues that AI systems should incorporate explainability, identity tracking, privacy-preserving protocols, and copyright extensions to redistribute profits to knowledge producers, but provides no outcome data, sample, or effect size.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Engaging Teachers to Co-Design Integrated AI Curriculum for K-12 Classrooms
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2020 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '20) / arXiv preprint
paper_profiles.population: K-12 teachers (with curriculum design focused on K-12 classrooms)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how AI education can be designed so that K-12 teachers can more readily integrate it into core classroom subjects. The authors argue that AI curricula are often presented as standalone computing activities, which can make them difficult for non-CS teachers to adopt, especially when teachers already face time, content, and classroom-management constraints.

To explore this problem, the authors ran a two-day remote co-design workshop with 15 K-12 educators from varied subject areas, including English language arts, science, social studies, ESL, history, library science, STEM, and computer science. Teachers completed pre-work, participated in presentations introducing AI concepts and tools, and then worked in small groups with researchers to design integrated AI lesson plans. The workshop produced three draft curricula: one for social studies, one for ESL, and one for literacy for students with learning disabilities.

The paper’s main contribution is a qualitative account of what teachers value when designing AI-integrated lessons. Across the workshop, teachers emphasized four practical considerations: evaluation, engagement, logistics, and collaboration. They also identified three main ways to integrate AI into core curriculum: using data from classroom activities, using reflection activities to connect subject content with AI concepts, and embedding ethics discussions. The authors conclude that teacher co-design can surface useful design requirements for accessible AI curricula and may help broaden AI education beyond computing classrooms, but the findings are exploratory and based on a small, remote workshop rather than classroom implementation.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers co-designed an ESL curriculum that integrated AI into pronunciation practice and an AI-powered pronunciation app. The paper reports that participants viewed this integration as a viable way to support students’ language learning, but it does not provide student outcome data or effect sizes because the work stops at curriculum design.
finding.measure: Curriculum design for ESL pronunciation practice and language-learning application

finding.finding_summary: Teachers co-designed a literacy curriculum for students with learning disabilities that embedded AI into vocabulary learning using images and classification models. The paper reports the curriculum as implementable and conceptually aligned with literacy goals, but no learner achievement outcomes were measured.
finding.measure: Curriculum design for vocabulary instruction in literacy

finding.finding_summary: One exemplar curriculum integrated AI with physics through a paper-airplane activity, where students would collect design and flight data to train a model and then reflect on model behavior and bias. This shows a proposed linkage between AI and scientific reasoning, but the paper does not test student learning outcomes.
finding.measure: Curriculum design for physics activity and model-based prediction

finding.finding_summary: The workshop produced integrated curricula in social studies, ESL, and literacy, showing that teachers could meaningfully embed AI into non-computing subjects. The strongest direct evidence in this category is the social studies curriculum, which centered on the CROWN Act, government policy, and classification ethics, but the paper reports no student outcome measures.
finding.measure: Curriculum design for social studies, ESL, and literacy integration

finding.finding_summary: Teachers repeatedly identified engagement as a key design need and built activities meant to motivate students through real-world anchors, student choice, competition, and gamification. The paper also reports that teachers felt more confident and more familiar with AI after the workshop (familiarity 4.8/7 to 5.8/7; confidence 5.6/7 post-workshop), but these are teacher self-reports rather than student outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher self-reported familiarity/confidence; curriculum design for student engagement

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally studies collaboration, reflection, and evaluation as design considerations and shows that teachers intentionally built these into the co-designed curricula. Teachers proposed group work, reflection on data and ethics, and conversational/qualitative assessment methods, suggesting strong emphasis on durable skills like collaboration and metacognition, though no student-level outcome data were collected.
finding.measure: Curriculum design emphasizing collaboration, reflection, and non-traditional evaluation

finding.finding_summary: A central finding is that teachers need additional scaffolding, explicit tool guidance, and ready-to-use lesson structures to make AI curriculum practical in classrooms. The paper also reports increased teacher confidence about integrating AI into curriculum after the workshop (mean 5.6/7), but it does not measure workload reduction or time savings directly.
finding.measure: Teacher confidence and qualitative reports about implementation logistics and scaffolding needs

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that integrating AI into core subjects could broaden access to AI education beyond CS classrooms and help address institutional barriers to adoption. It presents teacher-generated curricula and implementation considerations as a pathway toward more scalable and equitable AI education, but no policy or institutional outcome data were collected.
finding.measure: Qualitative evidence about adoption barriers, accessibility, and cross-curricular integration

paper_profiles.title: Need of AI in Modern Education: in the Eyes of Explainable AI (xAI)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book chapter argues that AI is essential for modern education, but emphasizes that its use must be transparent, explainable, and fair. Rather than studying a classroom intervention, the paper uses explainable AI (xAI) methods to probe how model predictions can be interpreted and whether common feature-importance tools are sufficient to detect bias in high-stakes decisions.

Empirically, the authors train an XGBoost classifier on the Adult Census Income dataset to predict whether an individual earns more than $50K, treating income as a proxy for educational access for children in the authors’ broader argument. They compare multiple explanation approaches—permutation importance, SHAP, LIME, a decision-tree surrogate, and FairML—to show that feature importance methods consistently highlight variables such as marital status, education, age, capital gain, sex, race, and nationality, but that bias may be missed by some explainers and revealed by FairML. The paper’s main conclusion is methodological: feature importance alone is not enough to establish fairness, LIME can be unstable, SHAP and surrogate models can approximate model behavior, and explicit fairness auditing is necessary to uncover discriminatory dependencies in the model.

The context is not K-12 instruction itself, but an adult socioeconomic proxy intended to analogize how parental income can affect children’s educational opportunities. As such, the paper is best understood as indirect evidence about AI governance and fairness in education-related decision support rather than direct evidence of teacher productivity or student learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that explainable AI methods can reveal that an income-prediction model depends on sensitive attributes such as race, nationality, and sex, implying unfair or discriminatory decision logic in an education-relevant socioeconomic context. Using FairML on an XGBoost model trained on the Adult Census Income dataset, the authors report that the model is more likely to predict income above USD 50K for White, U.S.-nationality, and male individuals, while SHAP and feature-importance methods did not consistently expose these biases.
finding.measure: Model bias / fairness audit using FairML, SHAP, permutation importance, and surrogate-model comparisons on Adult Census Income predictions

paper_profiles.title: Designing for human–AI complementarity in K-12 education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how human teachers and AI tutoring systems can be designed to work together more effectively in K-12 classrooms. The authors argue that successful human–AI partnerships depend on participatory design with teachers, iterative measurement of teacher decision-making in context, and a theory of complementarity that identifies what humans and AI each do best.

The paper presents the design and evaluation of Lumilo, mixed-reality smart glasses that give teachers real-time analytics about students’ learning, metacognition, and behavior while students work with an AI math tutor. Across formative co-design work, pilot studies, and a field experiment in middle school classrooms, teachers used Lumilo to identify students needing support, redirect attention toward lower-performing students, and make brief, targeted interventions. In the randomized classroom study (n=286 analyzed students across 18 classrooms, 8 teachers, 4 schools/districts), students in the Glasses + Analytics condition outperformed both a business-as-usual no-glasses condition and a glasses-only condition, indicating that the analytics-enabled teacher support tool improved math learning and reduced the tendency for higher-performing students to benefit disproportionately.

finding.finding_summary: In a randomized classroom field study on linear equation solving, students in the Glasses + Analytics condition showed greater pre/post learning gains than students in the No Glasses business-as-usual condition and than students in the Glasses-only condition. The analysis used data from 286 students (after excluding 57 absences) across 18 classrooms, 8 teachers, and 4 schools/districts; the paper reports a positive effect on post-test math learning but does not provide a numeric effect size in the excerpted text.
finding.measure: Pre/post test scores on linear equation solving

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that Lumilo helped teachers redirect attention toward students with lower initial knowledge and support them with brief, encouraging interactions. Although the main outcome is academic, the observed mechanism included improved teacher attention allocation and student engagement/motivation cues during AI-supported class sessions, suggesting a positive influence on classroom engagement-related behaviors.
finding.measure: Teacher attention allocation and observed in-the-moment student interactions

finding.finding_summary: Teachers using Lumilo made richer, complementary judgments by combining AI alerts with their own observations to infer underlying student needs and decide how to respond. The paper presents this as evidence of improved teacher-mediated metacognitive/diagnostic decision-making in context, but it does not report a formal effect size for a durable-skill measure.
finding.measure: Teacher decision-making / attention allocation based on AI alerts and classroom observation

finding.finding_summary: Lumilo improved the efficiency and targeting of teacher support during AI-supported lessons. Teachers spent about 24 seconds per visit on average and, in the analytics condition, allocated substantially more time to students with lower initial knowledge, indicating more efficient prioritization of limited teacher attention; the paper does not report a numeric effect size for workload reduction or time savings.
finding.measure: Teacher time allocation across students during class; classroom monitoring/awareness
finding.study_size: 14 teachers in pilots; 8 teachers and 18 classrooms in field study

finding.finding_summary: The study also examines learning with the AI tutor in the context of classroom orchestration, including the effect of teacher mediation on students’ trajectories through the software. The main academic outcome remains mathematics, but the paper additionally reports that Lumilo reduced post-test knowledge gaps by helping lower-pretest students gain more, showing a beneficial effect on learning progression rather than a different subject domain.
finding.measure: Reduction in knowledge differences between lower- and higher-pretest students

paper_profiles.title: Shiksha Copilot: Teacher-AI Collaboration for Curating and Customizing Lesson Plans in Low-Resource Schools
paper_profiles.population: Educators in government K-12 schools (Grades 5–10), primarily teachers in Karnataka, India
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether and how a human-in-the-loop LLM system can support teachers in low-resource, multilingual K-12 settings. The central problem is that teachers in Karnataka, India face heavy administrative burdens, limited instructional resources, and substantial time pressure when preparing lesson plans, yet lesson planning is also required for compliance and accountability. The authors investigate how an AI-assisted workflow can help teachers and curators create curriculum-aligned, context-sensitive lesson plans in English and Kannada.

The intervention, Shiksha Copilot, combines retrieval-augmented generation, bilingual translation, and human curation. Curators first review and refine AI-generated learning objectives and lesson plans; teachers then customize curated plans for their own classrooms and can optionally use additional AI tools such as lesson chat and question generation. The system was deployed in 757 schools across 35 districts, with 1,043 teachers and 23 curators involved; the evaluation includes system logs, surveys, and 43 interviews with curators, teachers, and mentors.

The paper finds that the tool was useful for both pedagogical and bureaucratic purposes. It substantially reduced lesson-planning and record-keeping burden, lowered teacher stress, and supported a shift toward activity-based pedagogy, but broader instructional change was constrained by staffing shortages and administrative demands. English lesson plans were generally high quality and required few edits, while Kannada outputs often needed substantial linguistic revision, showing the limits of literal translation in low-resource language contexts. Overall, the study suggests that teacher-AI collaboration can improve productivity and access to curated instructional materials, but only when paired with human expertise, contextual adaptation, and institutional support.

finding.finding_summary: Shiksha Copilot reduced teacher workload by easing bureaucratic record-keeping and lesson planning. In the survey and interview data, teachers reported measurable reductions in lesson planning time and stress, and log analysis showed that 5,542 lesson plans were created from curated base plans, indicating substantial workflow uptake; the paper also reports only 85/5,542 (1.53%) teacher-made platform edits, suggesting many teachers used the system as a time-saving planning aid.
finding.measure: Lesson planning time, administrative workload/record-keeping, teacher stress, platform usage logs
finding.study_size: n=1,043 teachers (surveys analyzed on n=406 matched responses; interviews n=22 teachers)

finding.finding_summary: The tool lowered teaching-related stress, especially by reducing the burden of lesson planning and record-keeping. The paper states that surveys found measurable reductions in teacher stress after deployment, but it does not report a specific effect size in the provided text.
finding.measure: Teacher Stress Scale (TSS), including teaching demands and school-based support subscales

finding.finding_summary: Shiksha Copilot fit existing administrative workflows and supported documentation requirements, but systemic constraints limited broader pedagogical change. Teachers used AI-generated lesson plans both for classroom instruction and for compliance/record-keeping, and the authors conclude that staffing shortages and administrative demands constrained institutional transformation even as the tool improved workflow alignment.
finding.measure: Teacher reports, interviews, platform adoption across 757 schools and 35 districts

paper_profiles.title: From Teacher to Colleague: How Coding Experience Shapes Developer Perceptions of AI Tools
paper_profiles.venue: GenAICHI: CHI 2025 Workshop on Generative AI and HCI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether coding experience is related to developers’ awareness of, adoption of, and mental models about AI-assisted development tools. The authors frame the study around two research questions: whether more experienced coders are more likely to know about or use AI tools, and whether experience shapes the role developers assign to AI in their workflow.

The study analyzes survey responses from a subset of JetBrains’ 2024 State of Developer Ecosystem survey. From the cleaned developer sample, 8,073 participants answered questions on AI awareness/experience, and 3,380 participants answered the role-perception item. The authors use Spearman correlations and logistic regression to test associations between coding experience and AI awareness/experience, and between coding experience and specific role labels such as teacher, junior colleague, content generator, and none of the above.

The main finding is that coding experience does not meaningfully predict AI adoption or AI experience, and its association with AI awareness is statistically significant but negligible (Spearman’s ρ=0.031, n=8073). However, coding experience does shape perceived roles: more experienced developers are more likely to see AI as a junior colleague, a content generator, or as having no role, while less experienced developers are more likely to describe AI as a teacher. The authors conclude that AI tool design should better align with differing expertise levels and mental models rather than assuming more experienced users will be more likely adopters.

finding.finding_summary: The paper examines whether coding experience relates to AI tool awareness, AI experience, and the roles developers assign to AI tools in their workflow. Coding experience did not predict AI experience (Spearman’s ρ=-0.005, n=8073, p=0.652), and it had only a negligible relationship with AI awareness (ρ=0.031, n=8073, p=0.005). However, more experienced developers were more likely to characterize AI as a junior colleague, content generator, or as having no role, while less experienced developers were more likely to call AI a teacher.
finding.measure: Survey measures of AI awareness, AI experience, and perceived AI role in development workflow
finding.study_size: n=8073 for awareness/experience analyses; n=3380 for role analyses
finding.effect_size: ρ=0.031 for AI awareness vs coding experience; ρ=-0.005 for AI experience vs coding experience; odds ratios: 1.170 (junior colleague), 1.087 (content generator), 0.883 (teacher), 1.380 (none of the above)
finding.confidence_interval: Junior colleague 95% CI [1.053, 1.299]; content generator [1.025, 1.152]; teacher [0.814, 0.958]; none of the above [1.180, 1.614]

paper_profiles.title: DeBiasMe: De-biasing Human-AI Interactions with Metacognitive AIED (AI in Education) Interventions
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of Workshop: AI Augmented Reasoning (CHI ’25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper addresses a growing problem in AI-enabled learning: students’ cognitive biases in human-AI interactions, such as automation bias, anchoring bias, and confirmation bias, and how these biases can degrade critical thinking and learning quality. The author argues that most AI literacy efforts emphasize technical and ethical competence while neglecting metacognitive support for recognizing and regulating human bias during AI use.

The paper proposes DeBiasMe, a metacognitive AI literacy intervention for university students, built around deliberate friction, bi-directional intervention across both prompt formulation and output interpretation, and adaptive scaffolding. It describes an illustrative prototype with two main components: a prompt refinement tool that flags possible biases before submission and a bias visualization map that helps users interpret AI-generated outputs. The paper also reports initial mixed-methods user research with university students (surveys and interviews) identifying three support needs: bias awareness, AI understanding, and critical thinking.

Overall, the paper is conceptual and design-oriented rather than an outcome study. Its main conclusion is that effective AI literacy tools should move beyond automation support and incorporate metacognitive mechanisms that make biases explicit, encourage reflection, and support learners in making more intentional choices about when and how to use AI. The paper positions DeBiasMe as an early-stage framework and prototype for future evaluation, not as a validated intervention with measured learning gains.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that metacognitive AI literacy interventions may improve students’ critical thinking, bias awareness, and self-regulation when interacting with AI, but it does not report controlled outcome data. The only empirical basis described is initial mixed-methods user research with university students (surveys and interviews) identifying three support needs—bias awareness, AI understanding, and critical thinking—and an earlier prototype review using usability heuristics, think-aloud studies, and expert reviews that suggested potential usefulness.
finding.measure: Surveys, interviews, usability heuristics, think-aloud studies, expert reviews

paper_profiles.title: Meaningful human control: actionable properties for AI system development
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how to translate the philosophical idea of meaningful human control over autonomous AI systems into concrete design guidance for researchers and engineers. The authors argue that current discussions of meaningful human control are too abstract to support practice, especially in safety- and rights-sensitive domains where responsibility gaps can arise when AI systems act autonomously.

Using abductive reasoning across interdisciplinary perspectives, the paper proposes four actionable properties for AI systems: an explicit moral operational design domain (moral ODD), mutually compatible human and AI representations of the system and context, appropriate alignment between ability, authority, and responsibility, and explicit links between AI actions and responsible human decisions. The authors illustrate these properties with two non-education application scenarios: automated vehicles and AI-based hiring.

The paper is conceptual rather than empirical; it does not test an intervention or report outcome data. Its main contribution is a framework meant to help designers, developers, and policymakers evaluate whether a human-AI system can plausibly be said to remain under meaningful human control, while emphasizing that meaningful human control is necessary but not sufficient for ethical AI.

paper_profiles.title: Privacy and Copyright Protection in Generative AI: A Lifecycle Perspective
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2024 IEEE/ACM 3rd International Conference on AI Engineering - Software Engineering for AI (CAIN)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
