finding.measure: Not reported; conceptual claims about feedback delivery speed, grading automation, and educator workload

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses GenAI’s ability to support assessment across domains by grading coding assignments, producing adaptive assessments, and creating authentic tasks, but it emphasizes that validity and reliability remain unresolved. These claims are supported by citations to prior work rather than new data from this paper.
finding.measure: Not reported; assessment and grading tasks across subjects such as coding and authentic assessment

paper_profiles.title: Incorporating AI in foreign language education: An investigation into ChatGPT’s effect on foreign language learners
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how undergraduate foreign language learners experienced the use of ChatGPT in an online English course and what they perceived as its strengths, limitations, and recommendations for improvement. The study was motivated by the rapid emergence of ChatGPT and a gap in understanding its practical role in foreign language learning, especially in real classroom contexts.

The authors implemented ChatGPT over four weeks with 13 preparatory-class students at a Turkish university. ChatGPT was embedded into reading, writing, grammar, and vocabulary activities, including brainstorming, creative writing, social-media style tasks, vocabulary practice, and written feedback. Data came from semi-structured interviews and were analyzed thematically.

The main findings are based on student perceptions rather than performance measures. Students reported that ChatGPT supported writing, grammar, and vocabulary learning, increased motivation and engagement, and saved time in research and idea generation. At the same time, participants raised concerns about over-reliance, technical/connectivity problems, limited usefulness for speaking and listening, and the risk of shortcuts or misuse. Overall, the paper concludes that ChatGPT can be a useful supplementary tool for language learning, but it should complement rather than replace human instruction and authentic communicative practice.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that ChatGPT improved writing skills and supported grammar and vocabulary acquisition during the four-week intervention. The evidence is qualitative and perception-based from 13 preparatory-class students; the paper does not report test scores or other quantitative learning gains.
finding.measure: student interview perceptions of writing, grammar, and vocabulary learning

finding.finding_summary: Participants described limited benefit for speaking and no effect on listening. Specifically, speaking was seen as only marginally helped by ChatGPT, while listening was reported as unaffected in the interview data from 13 students.
finding.measure: student interview perceptions of speaking and listening support

finding.finding_summary: Students consistently reported increased motivation and engagement when using ChatGPT in online language activities. The paper describes the tool as making learning more engaging and accessible, but these outcomes are based on self-reported perceptions rather than standardized engagement measures.
finding.measure: student interview perceptions of motivation and engagement

finding.finding_summary: Students said ChatGPT supported creative writing, interactive learning, and efficient idea generation, which the authors frame as enhancing creativity and some aspects of learner autonomy. However, the same interviews also raised concerns about dependency and shortcuts, suggesting mixed implications for higher-order and self-regulatory skills.
finding.measure: student interview perceptions of creativity, independence, and learning strategies

finding.finding_summary: Participants repeatedly reported that ChatGPT saved time and made research and idea generation faster, indicating perceived productivity gains. The study does not quantify time saved, compare against human-only or non-AI digital alternatives, or report turnaround measures.
finding.measure: student interview perceptions of time-saving and efficiency

paper_profiles.title: The application of AI technologies in STEM education: a systematic review from 2011 to 2021
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a systematic review of empirical research on artificial intelligence applications in STEM education published from 2011 to 2021. The authors ask how AI has been used across STEM learning contexts, what other educational system elements it interacts with (subject, information, medium, environment), and what educational and technological effects have been reported.

Using PRISMA-guided search and content analysis, the review synthesized 63 peer-reviewed empirical studies. The paper classifies AI-STEM applications into six categories: learning prediction, intelligent tutoring systems, student behavior detection, automation, educational robots, and other applications such as AI textbooks and group formation. It also maps where these applications appear across disciplines, learner levels, instructional strategies, media, and environments.

The review concludes that AI in STEM education is most often applied in higher education, especially in technology and science, and is frequently embedded in face-to-face and computer-based environments. Across the reviewed studies, AI generally showed positive educational effects on learning performance, affective perception, and higher-order thinking, while also offering technological benefits such as improved prediction accuracy and automation efficiency. However, the authors emphasize that STEM education is a complex system and that effective AI integration requires attention to instructional context and system interactions, not just the AI technique itself.

finding.finding_summary: The review includes mathematics-focused AI-STEM studies and reports generally positive effects for AI-enabled tutoring and recommendation in math learning, but the paper does not provide a pooled effect size specific to mathematics. Mathematics was a smaller share of the corpus (n=3 learning-content studies focused on mathematics), and the reported findings are descriptive rather than meta-analytic.
finding.measure: Mathematics learning performance, problem-solving, and related course outcomes across included studies

finding.finding_summary: Across the 63 reviewed studies, AI applications in STEM education were reported to improve science-related learning outcomes in most cases. The review states that 20 of 22 studies examining learning performance found significantly positive effects, with examples including geoscience achievement gains in a context-aware ubiquitous learning system and improved biology/evolutionary explanation scoring with automated assessment tools.
finding.measure: Learning performance/achievement in science and STEM courses; automated assessment of science explanations

finding.finding_summary: The review synthesizes AI applications across engineering, programming, computer science, and cross-disciplinary STEM courses and reports generally positive academic outcomes in these areas. Examples include improved programming performance with intelligent tutoring, automated feedback, and behavior analytics, as well as positive effects in engineering writing and course outcomes; however, the paper does not provide a single pooled effect size for these domains.
finding.measure: Programming achievement, engineering course performance, computer science outcomes, and related STEM academic measures

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that many studies found positive effects on affective outcomes such as attitude, interest, motivation, and satisfaction. Specifically, 17 reviewed studies addressed affective perception, and examples include positive student feedback for learning analytics, satisfaction with adaptive learning systems, and increased interest/motivation in personalized learning environments.
finding.measure: Affective perception surveys, attitudes, interest, motivation, satisfaction

finding.finding_summary: The review reports positive effects on higher-order thinking skills, including problem-solving, computational thinking, self-regulated learning, and argumentation. Seven studies are summarized in this category, with examples such as better problem-solving performance in a flowchart-based ITS and stronger computational thinking with deep-learning-supported AR.
finding.measure: Problem-solving ability, computational thinking, self-regulated learning, argumentation

finding.finding_summary: This review directly addresses AI-enabled productivity and efficiency gains, especially through automation and assessment tools that reduce instructor workload and speed feedback. It reports that AI systems automatically graded open-ended physics questions, generated multiple-choice tests, and provided immediate feedback, and it characterizes these technological effects as generally favorable in terms of efficiency and accuracy, though no net time-saved estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Automated assessment/grading performance, feedback immediacy, question-generation efficiency, algorithm accuracy

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI-STEM integration must be understood as a system-level issue involving subject, information, medium, environment, and technology, but it does not report institutional or policy outcomes directly. Its contribution here is conceptual: it proposes a general system theory framework for analyzing how AI interacts with instructional systems across STEM contexts.
finding.measure: System-level framing of AI-STEM integration and distribution of AI across educational system elements

paper_profiles.title: Exploring Applications of ChatGPT to English Language Teaching: Opportunities, Challenges, and Recommendations
paper_profiles.venue: The Electronic Journal for English as a Second Language
paper_profiles.population: Undergraduate and graduate international students in higher education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the emerging role of ChatGPT in English language teaching (ELT), focusing on both opportunities and challenges for classroom use. The authors situate ChatGPT within broader debates about generative AI, academic integrity, human-in-the-loop teaching, and the need for AI literacy, then review early scholarship on ChatGPT in education and ELT.

The paper is primarily a conceptual and practice-based discussion, but it also includes the authors’ own classroom experiments at Northeastern University in spring 2023. They used ChatGPT in an undergraduate public speaking course and a graduate academic listening and speaking course for international students, where students generated and evaluated ChatGPT outputs related to persuasive argumentation and presentation skills. Student reflections were collected through short surveys and class discussion, revealing generally positive engagement but also skepticism about accuracy, overreliance, and the need for human judgment.

Overall, the authors conclude that ChatGPT can support language instruction as a tool for brainstorming, comparison, and reflection, but it should not replace teachers or authentic interaction. They recommend collaboration among educators, reflection with students about responsible use, and redesign of learning activities and assessments to emphasize critical thinking, process, and human oversight rather than simple product generation.

finding.finding_summary: In the authors’ classroom implementation with undergraduate public speaking and graduate academic listening/speaking students, ChatGPT appeared to support speaking-related engagement and discussion, but the paper does not report quantitative fluency gains. Students were asked to analyze ChatGPT-generated responses and compare them with their own ideas; the authors observed increased talkativeness and enthusiasm, alongside skepticism about accuracy and usefulness.
finding.measure: Classroom participation, student reflections, and comparison of ChatGPT output with students’ ideas in speaking-related activities

finding.finding_summary: The classroom examples suggest ChatGPT increased student engagement and motivation during ELT activities. The authors report that students seemed more talkative and enthusiastic, and student quotations described the activities as creative, fun, and attention-grabbing, although some students remained cautious about accuracy and appropriate use.
finding.measure: Student engagement, motivation, and attitudes captured through classroom observation and short survey/reflection comments

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally frames ChatGPT as a tool for fostering critical thinking, evaluation, and comparison of information rather than as a substitute for student work. In the reported classroom activities, students compared their own ideas with ChatGPT output, analyzed persuasive constructs, and evaluated presentation advice, which the authors interpret as promoting critical digital literacy and evaluative judgment.
finding.measure: Critical analysis of AI-generated text, comparison tasks, and reflective evaluation of output quality/accuracy

finding.finding_summary: The article repeatedly claims that ChatGPT may save teachers time by generating lesson materials, worksheets, assessments, and ideas for instruction, but it does not provide any direct time-saved measurement, comparison to human-only alternatives, or net productivity estimate after review and adaptation. The evidence is therefore conceptual rather than empirical, with no effect size or turnaround data reported.
finding.measure: Teacher planning/materials creation efficiency (discussed conceptually, not measured empirically)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that institutions should develop responsible-use policies, professional development, and human-centered guidance for AI use in education. These recommendations are based on the authors’ experience and literature review rather than institutional outcome data, so the finding is about anticipated policy and governance implications rather than measured impact.
finding.measure: Institutional policy guidance, professional collaboration, and responsible-use recommendations

paper_profiles.title: La nueva realidad de la educación ante los avances de la inteligencia artificial generativa / The new reality of education in the face of advances in generative artificial intelligence
paper_profiles.venue: RIED-Revista Iberoamericana de Educación a Distancia
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article examines the implications of generative artificial intelligence, especially ChatGPT, for education at a moment of rapid technological change. The paper asks what generative AI tools can do in educational contexts, what risks and limits they pose, and how academic and institutional responses are evolving. Rather than presenting a single empirical intervention, it offers a systematic review of early literature and a structured reflection on tools, uses, benefits, risks, and policy challenges emerging in the first months after ChatGPT's release.

The authors review generative AI tools with potential educational uses and conduct a rapid review of articles indexed in Web of Science and Scopus up to early April 2023. The corpus includes studies across several levels and disciplines, including pre-university education, higher education, medicine, writing, and other fields. The paper highlights possible benefits such as content generation, personalized learning, student support, and reduced teacher workload, but also stresses major risks including hallucinations, bias, privacy problems, plagiarism, and unreliable AI-text detection.

Overall, the article concludes that generative AI should neither be ignored nor banned, but incorporated thoughtfully through teacher and student training, curriculum updates, ethical guidance, and assessment redesign. Its emphasis is primarily strategic and conceptual, with a strong institutional and pedagogical orientation rather than direct measurement of learning outcomes. It is especially relevant for educators and decision-makers seeking to understand how generative AI may affect teaching, learning, assessment, and governance in K-12 and higher-education settings.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI can improve teacher productivity by reducing time spent answering repeated student questions and grading written work, thereby freeing educators to focus on higher-level support and feedback. This is presented as a potential benefit across the reviewed literature, but the article itself does not report a direct experimental estimate, sample size, or measured turnaround-time outcome.
finding.measure: teacher workload, grading time, response efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that generative AI is driving institutional concern, policy development, and assessment redesign, while also exposing gaps in preparedness, ethics guidance, and governance. The main conclusion is that institutions should not ban these tools outright, but instead develop codes of ethics, staff training, and assessment alternatives to manage their use responsibly.
finding.measure: institutional policies, governance responses, assessment strategy changes

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, generative AI is described as having potential to support critical thinking and creativity by giving feedback on tasks and helping students develop ideas, but it also may undermine independent thinking and creativity if used uncritically. The paper synthesizes these arguments qualitatively rather than reporting a direct empirical effect estimate.
finding.measure: critical thinking, creativity, independent thinking

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that some studies suggest generative AI can increase engagement, motivation, and collaboration, especially through asynchronous communication and virtual instructors. However, this is a synthesis of early studies and commentary, not a single measured intervention effect in the paper itself.
finding.measure: motivation, engagement, collaboration

paper_profiles.title: Ethical principles for artificial intelligence in education
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (policy/guideline synthesis; no direct study population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether there is a global consensus on ethical principles for artificial intelligence in education (AIED). Rather than evaluating a classroom intervention or AI product, it conducts a thematic analysis of international ethics policies and guidelines related to AI and education, including UNESCO, OECD, and European Union documents.

The authors identify and synthesize 39 codes into 7 overarching ethical principles for AIED: governance and stewardship, transparency and accountability, sustainability and proportionality, privacy, security and safety, inclusiveness, and human-centered AIED. They discuss how these principles should guide the design, deployment, and regulation of AI in education across stakeholders such as students, teachers, developers, policymakers, and institutional decision-makers.

The paper’s contribution is conceptual and normative: it offers a framework for ethical and trustworthy AIED and argues that current guidelines share substantial overlap but are not yet standardized into a universal consensus. It does not report empirical effects of AI on learning, teacher workload, or turnaround time, and it does not study K-12 implementation outcomes directly.

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not test an intervention or measure institutional outcomes; instead, it synthesizes ethical principles from international policy and guideline documents. Its main contribution is conceptual: a proposed framework of 7 ethical principles for governing AIED, based on thematic analysis of UNESCO, OECD, and EU guidance rather than outcome data.
finding.measure: Thematic analysis of policy and guideline documents

paper_profiles.title: Teacher’s Perceptions of Using an Artificial Intelligence-Based Educational Tool for Scientific Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This qualitative study examines how in-service STEM teachers perceived an AI-enhanced scaffolding system for scientific writing after using it themselves in a course setting. The authors focused on whether the system could support argumentation, evidence-based writing, and higher-order thinking, and on what concerns teachers had about AI use in classrooms.

Participants were nine K-12 teachers enrolled in a doctoral program in the southeastern United States. They completed a short instructional sequence about AI in education, then interacted with an artificial intelligence-enhanced scaffolding system (AISS) built on GPT-2 to produce a scientific essay about an authentic air-quality problem. Teachers first wrote an initial draft independently, then used AI-generated sentence/paragraph completion and reflection prompts, and finally participated in post-task interviews.

The analysis found broadly positive perceptions of the tool as an individualized expert model that provided immediate, high-quality scaffolding for scientific writing. Teachers reported that the system helped them think more deeply about claims, evidence, and reasoning, and many viewed it as especially useful for middle and high school students. At the same time, they raised concerns about AI transparency, accuracy, and the possibility that AI could reduce teachers’ roles in instruction. The study concludes that hands-on experience with AI can increase teacher receptiveness, but that implementation will require clearer guidance, explainability, and professional development.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the AI-enhanced scaffolding system helped with scientific writing by generating well-written sentences and paragraphs, giving individualized examples that served as models for improved writing. The system was described as useful for sentence structure, sequencing, and revision, but the study did not report standardized writing scores or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of scientific writing support; interview themes about sentence structure, paragraph sequencing, and revision

finding.finding_summary: Teachers said the AISS strengthened argumentation, evidence-based writing, and reasoning by prompting them to justify claims with stronger evidence and reflect on their thinking process. The qualitative data indicate the tool acted as expert modeling for scientific problem solving, but no quantitative performance outcome was measured.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of argumentation, evidence use, and reasoning in a scientific writing task

finding.finding_summary: Participants frequently described the system as supporting higher-order thinking, metacognition, and problem-solving. Teachers noted that interacting with the AI encouraged reflection on their mental process and comparison of alternative claims, but these were subjective perceptions rather than measured skill gains.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of higher-order thinking, metacognition, and problem-solving support

finding.finding_summary: Teachers emphasized the immediacy and individualized nature of the AI-generated feedback, noting that sentences were generated in under 45 seconds and that the tool could provide prompt support that would otherwise be difficult for a teacher to deliver at scale. The paper did not quantify time saved versus human-only or other digital alternatives, so operational gains are based on perception only.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of immediacy, individualized feedback, and workflow efficiency

paper_profiles.title: The Promises and Challenges of Artificial Intelligence for Teachers: a Systematic Review of Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper systematically reviews empirical research on how teachers use artificial intelligence (AI) in teaching and how teachers participate in the development and validation of AI systems. The authors focus on questions about the kinds of data collected from teachers, the roles teachers play in AI-based research, the benefits AI offers teachers, the challenges teachers face, and the AI methods used in the included studies.

The review screened Web of Science journal articles published over the prior 20 years and retained 44 empirical studies related to pre-service and in-service teachers, with an emphasis on K-12 contexts. Across the studies, teachers most often contributed self-report data and grading data, and they commonly served as training models for AI systems or as validators of automated assessment. The review concludes that AI can support planning, implementation, and assessment by helping teachers monitor student activity, provide immediate feedback, reduce workload, and automate scoring, but current systems are limited by reliability, technical capacity, infrastructure constraints, and contextual fit. The authors also note that pre-service teachers are underrepresented and that multimodal data and deeper teacher involvement in AI design remain important future directions.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, AI was reported to support teacher productivity by reducing workload, enabling timely monitoring, providing immediate feedback, and assisting with automated assessment. The review specifically notes that AI-based peer tutor recommendation systems and automated scoring tools helped teachers save time for other activities, but it does not report net time-saved estimates after review/adaptation versus human-only or non-AI digital alternatives.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, monitoring efficiency, feedback turnaround, automated scoring/assessment support
finding.study_size: 44 studies reviewed; specific efficiency estimates not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Several included studies concerned writing and text-related literacy tasks, especially automated essay scoring, readability classification, and text complexity analysis. The review concludes that AI can make essay scoring more effective and more objective, but it does not synthesize a pooled effect size; for the literacy-related studies, sample sizes and quantitative effects are inconsistently reported in the review text.
finding.measure: Essay scoring accuracy/objectivity, text readability classification, writing-related assessment

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies AI support for engagement-related and interaction-related teacher functions, including monitoring student concentration, tracking progress, and informing timely interventions. Some studies used AI to predict or model teacher engagement, and the authors describe these systems as helping teachers respond more quickly to students' needs; however, the review does not report pooled effects for engagement outcomes.
finding.measure: Student/teacher engagement, concentration monitoring, interaction analytics, job satisfaction/engagement prediction

finding.finding_summary: A subset of the reviewed work used AI to support teachers in detecting authentic questions, guiding collaborative learning, and identifying critical moments for intervention, which the authors frame as supporting higher-order instructional processes such as monitoring and adaptive decision-making. The evidence is descriptive rather than comparative, and the review does not provide effect sizes or pooled estimates.
finding.measure: Teacher decision-making, monitoring of collaborative learning, adaptive intervention support

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that teachers are important contributors to AI system development, serving as data sources, model providers, and validators of automated assessment systems. It also notes institutional barriers to AI adoption, including limited infrastructure, technical capacity, and contextual applicability, but overall frames teacher participation as essential for successful AI integration in schools.
finding.measure: Teacher participation in AI development/validation; implementation barriers and adoption conditions
finding.study_size: 44 studies reviewed; specific institutional outcome measures not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing education with AI: Exploring the transformative potential of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (literature review; not an empirical K-12 sample)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article is a narrative review of the educational uses, benefits, and risks of artificial intelligence, with a special focus on chatbots and ChatGPT. Rather than testing a specific intervention, the authors synthesize recent literature to explain what AI systems can do in education, why they matter, and what ethical and practical issues arise when schools and universities adopt them.

The paper discusses applications such as personalized learning, instant feedback, automated grading, tutoring, student support, and administrative assistance. It argues that AI may improve learning outcomes, engagement, and teacher productivity, but it also emphasizes concerns about bias, privacy, academic integrity, overreliance, and the need for teacher training and responsible implementation.

The discussion is broad and largely conceptual, drawing examples from prior studies across educational settings, including K-12 and higher education, but it does not report original data from a specific student sample or an intervention evaluation. Its main conclusion is that AI and chatbots have strong potential to support teaching and learning, yet successful adoption requires ethical safeguards, pedagogical alignment, and further empirical research.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI tools such as automated grading systems and chatbots can reduce teacher workload and speed up assessment and feedback processes. It gives examples like Gradescope, Autolab, AutoGradr, and Repl.it, but reports no original effect size, sample size, or turnaround-time data.
finding.measure: Teacher workload; grading/scoring/feedback productivity

paper_profiles.title: Interpreting Black-Box Models: A Review on Explainable Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (review paper; no human study population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a broad review of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) focused on the longstanding problem that many high-performing machine learning and deep learning models behave as black boxes. The authors argue that opacity limits trust, accountability, debugging, and adoption, especially in high-stakes domains.

The review surveys core XAI concepts, interpretability types, design principles for interactive explanations, and major implementation families such as model extraction, rule extraction, model distillation, feature importance, and local explanation methods including LIME, Anchors, and Shapley-based approaches. It also discusses where XAI has been applied, with examples from transportation, medicine, and finance, but it does not evaluate an AI intervention in schools or conduct a K-12 empirical study.

The paper’s main conclusion is that XAI is important for transparency, fairness, and responsible deployment, but the field still faces unresolved challenges in evaluation, user-centered design, and balancing accuracy with interpretability. Because it is a narrative survey rather than an empirical education study, it provides conceptual guidance rather than direct evidence about educational outcomes or teacher productivity.

paper_profiles.title: Teachers’ AI digital competencies and twenty-first century skills in the post-pandemic world
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conceptual paper addresses the question of what AI-related digital competencies teachers need in the post-pandemic era, especially as AI-enabled tools become more common in online and blended teaching. The authors focus on how AI can support teaching, learning, assessment, and administrative tasks, while also introducing challenges related to technical readiness, ethical concerns, and overreliance on AI systems.

Rather than testing a specific intervention, the paper synthesizes research examples and existing frameworks to propose how teachers’ AI competencies can be aligned with DigCompEdu and the P21 framework for twenty-first century learning. It argues that teacher preparation should go beyond basic technical skills to include pedagogical, ethical, collaborative, and life/career competencies, and it outlines a broader conceptual model for teacher professional engagement, instructional support, content choices across disciplines, and students’ learning competencies.

The paper is framed around educators in higher education and K-16 contexts, but it is primarily aimed at teachers and school leaders generally. Its main conclusion is that AI should be treated as part of a holistic competency profile rather than as a stand-alone technical domain, and that professional development and policy guidance are needed to help educators use AI responsibly and effectively in teaching, learning, and assessment.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI-driven tools can reduce teacher workload by automating operational tasks such as grading, feedback, repetitive paperwork, and resource recommendation. However, this is presented as a conceptual synthesis based on cited literature rather than as a directly measured effect, and no net time-saved estimate, sample size, or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading and feedback automation, administrative task efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The article proposes revising educator competency frameworks (DigCompEdu and P21) to incorporate AI, and argues that teacher education programs, standards, and professional development should be updated accordingly. This is a framework and policy-oriented contribution rather than an empirical test, so no quantitative effect is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher competency frameworks, educational standards, and professional development guidance

paper_profiles.title: Editorial: Insights in assessment, testing, and applied measurement: 2022
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (editorial covering studies across K-12 and higher education)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This editorial introduces and synthesizes a Frontiers Research Topic on assessment, testing, and applied measurement. Rather than reporting a single empirical study, it summarizes 20 manuscripts published across 2022–2024 and highlights themes in assessment validity, teacher assessment competence, scale development, and emerging innovations such as AI-enabled formative assessment and personalized classroom assessment.

The piece’s main purpose is to orient readers to what the collection says about the state of the field and future directions. It emphasizes that assessment practices are becoming more complex, that teacher-made assessments and feedback can be problematic, and that AI may eventually support feedback, automated scoring, and tutoring, but current teacher capacity and implementation challenges remain substantial.

The editorial also summarizes several empirical papers in the research topic, including studies on teacher assessment literacy, peer feedback training, dynamic assessment, and AI-related assessment innovations. In relation to AI, it notes potential classroom uses such as automated essay scoring and generating feedback, but does not present a standalone evaluation of AI productivity gains or turnaround time in K-12 settings.

finding.finding_summary: The editorial discusses operational efficiency only indirectly through one cited study on synchronous self-assessment in written exams and a broader discussion of AI’s possible role in reducing teacher workload. In the cited Spanish teacher educator study, four instructors reported that marking was less tedious because students completed different tasks and weighting choices gave clues to competence, but this is qualitative and does not quantify time saved.
finding.measure: Instructor-reported marking burden / grading tedium in synchronous self-assessment exams

paper_profiles.title: Training writing skills: A cognitive developmental perspective
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how writing skill develops across childhood, adolescence, and adulthood from a cognitive-developmental perspective. The central problem is not how to teach writing as a school subject in a narrow sense, but how writers move from early knowledge-telling to knowledge-transforming and ultimately to knowledge-crafting, a professional-level form of writing that requires managing author, text, and reader representations simultaneously.

The article is a conceptual and theoretical review rather than an intervention study. Kellogg argues that progress in writing depends on the maturation of executive attention and working memory, along with extensive practice, domain knowledge, and training methods that reduce cognitive load. He discusses implications for writing education, including deliberate practice, cognitive apprenticeship, spaced practice, and feedback, and notes that automated essay scoring may offer timely feedback, though the paper itself does not evaluate such tools empirically.

The context spans school-aged writers through university students and professional adult writers, with examples drawn from prior research on revision, composing strategies, and writing instruction. The main conclusion is that effective writing development requires reducing working-memory demands so that planning, generating, and reviewing can be coordinated more efficiently; however, the article is primarily argumentative and synthesizes existing research rather than testing an intervention in K-12 settings.

finding.finding_summary: The paper synthesizes evidence that writing skill improves across development and that training can reduce the cognitive demands of composing, planning, and revising. It does not report a single new effect estimate, but it argues that deliberate practice, cognitive apprenticeship, and strategies such as outlining or delayed revision can improve writing quality and depth; e.g., it cites prior studies showing improved revisions for 5th and 9th graders and college students when prompted to 'read-as-the-reader.'
finding.measure: Writing quality, revision quality, composing skill, and writing fluency across developmental stages

finding.finding_summary: A major focus is the role of executive attention, working memory, and self-regulation in writing development. The paper argues that writers must coordinate planning, translating, and reviewing, and that training can help reduce cognitive load so these higher-order control processes are more available during composition.
finding.measure: Executive attention, working memory demands, self-regulation in composing

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that training writers to use outlines, organized notes, spaced practice, and delayed revision can improve composing efficiency by reducing momentary working-memory load. It also discusses the promise of automated essay scoring as a way to provide timely, individualized feedback, but notes that the field had not broadly embraced these systems at the time and does not present new turnaround-time data.
finding.measure: Composing efficiency, working-memory load, feedback timeliness, and writing productivity

paper_profiles.title: AI-generated feedback on writing: insights into efficacy and ENL student preference
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether GPT-4-generated writing feedback can support English as a new language (ENL) students as effectively as feedback from a human tutor, and whether students prefer AI-generated feedback over human-generated feedback. The study is motivated by growing interest in generative AI as a tool for automated writing evaluation (AWE) and the practical question of how such tools might be incorporated ethically and effectively into writing instruction.

The paper reports two longitudinal studies conducted at a small liberal arts university in the Asia–Pacific region during a six-week Spring 2023 semester. In Study 1, 48 ENL university students completed weekly writing tasks in a quasi-experimental repeated-measures design: one group received GPT-4 feedback and the other received feedback from a trained human tutor. Writing was assessed with pre- and post-tests scored on an analytic rubric. The results showed no significant difference in writing gains between the AI and human feedback groups, with both groups improving similarly over time.

In Study 2, a separate group of 43 ENL students received both AI and human feedback on weekly assignments and completed repeated preference surveys. Students were nearly evenly split in preference between human and AI feedback, though the human tutor was rated slightly higher on satisfaction, clarity, helpfulness, and preference. Qualitative comments suggested that human feedback was valued for personal interaction and follow-up opportunities, while AI feedback was valued for clarity, specificity, and availability. The authors conclude that AI-generated feedback can be used without harming learning outcomes, but a blended approach combining AI and human strengths may be most effective.

finding.finding_summary: In Study 1, GPT-4-generated writing feedback did not produce significantly better writing gains than human tutor feedback for ENL university students. Both groups improved from pretest to posttest over six weeks, but the group-by-time interaction was not significant (F=3.094, p=0.085, ηp2=0.063), and the between-group effect was also non-significant (F=0.241, p=0.626, ηp2=0.005).
finding.measure: Analytic rubric scores for writing pretest and posttest (content, coherence, language use, sources and evidence; max score 40)
finding.effect_size: ηp2=0.063 for time x group; ηp2=0.005 for group effect; Cohen's d=0.520 at pretest and d=-0.156 at posttest

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI-generated feedback can reduce teacher workload and turnaround time because GPT-4 can produce individualized feedback for each assignment quickly, with feedback emailed within two working days. However, this was a conceptual/practical inference rather than a direct time-and-motion comparison, and the study did not measure net time saved versus human-only feedback or other digital tools.
finding.measure: Teacher feedback turnaround/workload discussion; no direct timing metric reported

paper_profiles.title: Implementation Considerations for Automated AI Grading of Student Work
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how an AI-powered grading platform was implemented in real K–12 classroom settings, with a focus on whether teachers found it useful for rubric generation, grading, and feedback. The authors are especially interested in the practical conditions under which automated grading can support classroom workflows without undermining teacher judgment or pedagogical goals.

The study used a seven-week co-design pilot with 19 teachers from four public school districts and one independent school in the Puget Sound region of Washington state. Teachers used Colleague AI to create rubrics, generate AI feedback, and in some cases let students view AI feedback and resubmit work. The evidence comes from platform usage logs, teacher surveys, group discussions, and interviews, making this a mixed-methods implementation study rather than an efficacy trial.

Across 33 classrooms and 58 assessment records, the platform produced high AI grading coverage on submitted work (median 92.2%), and teachers often used the system as a first-pass formative feedback tool. Teachers valued the speed and narrative specificity of AI-generated comments, but they distrusted automated scores, frequently made minor edits to rubrics, and emphasized the need for human oversight before final grading. Students generally appreciated quick turnaround and revision-oriented feedback, but some were skeptical of AI-only grading and some found the interface or feedback volume challenging.

The main conclusion is that AI grading tools may be useful in K–12 primarily as formative scaffolds that speed up feedback cycles, not as replacements for teacher judgment. The paper argues that teacher mediation, editable feedback, and usability improvements are essential for trustworthy adoption, and it highlights that time savings only matter if the AI output is accurate enough to avoid substantial rework by teachers.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers and students reported that the platform produced rapid, first-pass narrative feedback and could streamline grading workflows, with one teacher noting students preferred getting feedback immediately rather than waiting 2–3 weeks. Platform logs show high automation coverage: across 58 assessment records in 33 classrooms, the median AI grading coverage on submitted work was 92.2%, and over 75% of classrooms had more than 80% of submitted work AI-scored.
finding.measure: Platform usage logs; teacher survey/interview reports of turnaround time and workflow usefulness
finding.study_size: n=19 teachers; 33 classrooms; 58 assessment records; 936 student works submitted

finding.finding_summary: The tool was used for classroom assessment and grading across ELA, math, science/programming, Spanish, and other high school subjects, but the paper does not report learning gains on subject-matter achievement. Instead, it shows that AI-generated narrative feedback was often seen as pedagogically useful for identifying misconceptions and next steps, while numerical scoring was viewed as inconsistent or misaligned with rubrics.
finding.measure: Teacher survey and qualitative judgments about assessment feedback quality across classroom subjects
finding.study_size: n=19 teachers; 33 classrooms; 936 student works submitted

finding.finding_summary: Students generally welcomed quick feedback and some struggling learners felt more confident using pre-submission feedback, but others were confused, overloaded by the amount of feedback, or skeptical of AI-only grading. Teacher interviews suggest that timely feedback could support revision and confidence, but the emotional and relational benefits depended on teacher framing and interface usability.
finding.measure: Teacher interview and survey reports of student reactions to AI feedback; resubmission behavior
finding.study_size: n=19 teachers; student experience observed in 33 classrooms

finding.finding_summary: The system supported revision-oriented workflows and iterative learning by allowing students to resubmit work after seeing AI feedback, and 8.7% of students resubmitted work on average. However, the paper does not measure durable-skill gains directly; it reports qualitative evidence that the tool may scaffold self-assessment and revision, while some students struggled to interpret feedback or navigate the interface.
finding.measure: Resubmission rates; qualitative reports of revision behavior and feedback use

paper_profiles.title: Human or AI? Comparing Design Thinking Assessments by Teaching Assistants and Bots
paper_profiles.population: Secondary school teachers and pre-university educators in Singapore; student work from secondary Design Thinking/Design and Technology context
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This exploratory study examines whether an AI grader can assess design-thinking posters as reliably as teaching assistants (TAs) in a Singapore secondary-school context. The authors focus on a common assessment problem in creative, multimodal assignments: rubric-based grading of posters that combine visual and textual evidence is time-consuming, labor-intensive, and inconsistent when multiple assessors are involved.

The intervention/approach was a GPT-4o-based custom grader calibrated with rubric descriptors and exemplar scores from previously assessed student journey maps. The study used ten anonymized samples for score-alignment comparison and a separate set of ten samples for a teacher preference task. Thirty-three in-service teachers from Singapore secondary schools and pre-university institutions participated in a workshop, first manually scoring samples and then judging AI, TA, and hybrid scores in randomized order.

Quantitatively, AI and TA scores showed low agreement with instructor benchmarks on empathy and user understanding and on identification of pain points/opportunities, with somewhat better agreement on visual communication. Qualitatively, teachers appreciated AI’s speed, consistency, and formative-feedback potential, but worried that it missed contextual nuance and creative judgment. Teachers preferred TA-assigned scores more often than AI or hybrid scores, and hybrid averaging was not favored. The paper concludes that AI may be useful for formative support and workload reduction, but it is not yet ready to replace human judgment in summative assessment of creative design-thinking artefacts.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers consistently described manual rubric-based scoring as slow, tedious, labor-intensive, and time-consuming, while the AI grader was perceived as much faster and capable of giving immediate rationales for scores. The paper does not report a formal time-saved estimate or net productivity calculation, but qualitative evidence suggests AI could reduce grading burden if sufficiently calibrated.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of grading speed, labor, and feedback turnaround; qualitative comments about AI-assisted scoring workflow
finding.study_size: n=33 teachers; n=10 samples per task

finding.finding_summary: The AI grader and TA scores aligned poorly with instructor benchmarks on the more interpretive rubric dimensions, especially empathy/user understanding and identification of pain points/opportunities (20% raw agreement with negative/near-zero Cohen’s kappa). This suggests limitations in AI support for nuanced judgment and interpretation, though visual communication showed somewhat better alignment (50% raw agreement, κ=0.242).
finding.measure: Agreement between instructor, AI, and TA scores on three rubric dimensions; Cohen’s kappa and percent agreement
finding.study_size: n=10 student samples per scoring comparison

finding.finding_summary: Teachers expressed cautious openness to AI-assisted assessment as a complementary tool, but they preferred TA scores in 6 of 10 samples and did not favor hybrid averaging. The paper argues that adoption in public education systems will require human oversight, calibration, and professional development before AI can be trusted for high-stakes assessment.
finding.measure: Teacher preference among AI-assigned, TA-assigned, and hybrid scores; qualitative attitudes toward AI adoption in assessment

paper_profiles.title: LLMs to Support K–12 Teachers in Culturally Relevant Pedagogy: An AI Literacy Example
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a large language model (LLM)-supported tool can help K–12 teachers adapt AI literacy activities to better reflect culturally relevant pedagogy (CRP). The authors frame the problem as a practical implementation gap: teachers value CRP but often lack the time, training, and resources to integrate students’ cultural backgrounds into lesson planning, especially in the emerging area of AI literacy.

To address this, the paper introduces CulturAIEd, an LLM-powered prototype that combines demographic student information, CRT checklist guidance, rubric-based feedback, and just-in-time chatbot support. The study used an exploratory pilot with four secondary teachers from different contexts (three from North America and one from East Asia) in 90–120 minute Zoom sessions that included baseline lesson adaptation, checklist-guided adaptation, and CulturAIEd-supported refinement. The study used qualitative thematic analysis and descriptive survey data.

Findings suggest the tool improved teachers’ confidence in identifying culturally responsive opportunities and making culturally responsive modifications, while also being perceived as time-saving and useful for streamlining CRP integration. Participants especially valued the integration of student demographics, actionable feedback, and the ability to generate more concrete culturally responsive examples. However, the evidence is preliminary, based on a very small sample and no comparison group, and the authors frame the results as promising rather than conclusive. Future work is needed to test whether these perceived efficiency and instructional benefits hold in larger, controlled studies.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers perceived CulturAIEd as reducing planning burden and streamlining culturally responsive lesson adaptation. In the pilot with n=4 secondary teachers, participants described the system as solving the time and research needed for CRP and reported that 3/4 strongly agreed it saved time; the paper characterizes this as high implementation efficiency, but no objective time-on-task measure was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived time saved / implementation efficiency in lesson adaptation; post-survey Likert responses and interview feedback

finding.finding_summary: The tool was positioned as a way to help schools and teachers incorporate culturally relevant pedagogy into AI literacy instruction more feasibly, potentially addressing institutional barriers such as limited support, training, and resources. Evidence is limited to a four-teacher exploratory pilot and qualitative reports of better fit with CRP implementation, so the effect is suggestive rather than demonstrated at scale.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of CRP implementation barriers and tool usefulness for institutionalized CRP integration

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that CulturAIEd helped teachers identify opportunities for cultural responsiveness and make more thoughtful pedagogical modifications, which can be interpreted as supporting reflective practice and instructional decision-making. However, the study does not directly measure durable skills with validated instruments; evidence comes from survey shifts and interviews with n=4 teachers.
finding.measure: Teacher confidence in identifying opportunities for cultural responsiveness and making modifications; qualitative reflections

paper_profiles.title: Personalized Auto-Grading and Feedback System for Constructive Geometry Tasks Using Large Language Models on an Online Math Platform
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether a large language model (LLM)-based auto-grading and feedback system can support scalable formative assessment for constructive geometry tasks in K-12 mathematics. The core problem is that open-ended and geometry-construction tasks are difficult to grade quickly and consistently, and teachers often cannot provide timely individualized feedback in online settings. The authors therefore designed an automated system integrated into the Algeomath platform that combines rule-based grading for closed-ended and construction tasks with GPT-4-based few-shot grading and feedback generation for open-ended explanations.

The system was piloted in four middle school classes in South Korea with 79 students across 18 math tasks. The study compared automated judgments with teacher judgments, evaluated the pedagogical quality of generated feedback using expert ratings, and analyzed student revision patterns across multiple attempts. Results showed strong alignment with teachers for rule-based items and substantial agreement for LLM-graded explanatory items (overall agreement 0.866, Cohen’s κ=0.737). Expert review found feedback to be generally serviceable but uneven in quality, with issues such as answer leakage, imprecise terminology, and overly generic or overly revealing prompts.

The paper also examined learning dynamics from the feedback process. Students often corrected errors after feedback: 36.7% of initially incorrect responses were converted to correct on the next attempt (260/708), with higher conversion for closed-ended items than for CGT and open-ended tasks. However, evidence for longer-term transfer to later questions was inconclusive, as no significant carry-over effects were found. Overall, the study suggests that LLMs can provide teacher-aligned, scalable formative feedback in middle school geometry, but the feedback design still needs refinement to avoid revealing answers and to better scaffold mathematical reasoning.

finding.finding_summary: The system supported learning on constructive geometry tasks and open-ended geometry explanations. Across all questions, 36.7% of initially incorrect responses were converted to correct on the subsequent attempt (260/708), and overall attempt-level learning curves rose from about 0.60 correct on the first attempt to about 0.80 by the fourth attempt, indicating meaningful short-term gains in geometry problem solving.
finding.measure: Attempt-level correctness on constructive geometry tasks and open-ended geometry explanations; post-feedback conversion rate
finding.study_size: n=79 students; 708 feedback-supported incorrect attempts for conversion analysis

finding.finding_summary: Students generally responded well to the iterative feedback environment, with broad improvement after retries and survey ratings near the upper end of the scale (average about 4.1 to 4.5 on five-point Likert items). The feedback system appears to support persistence and willingness to revise answers, although the paper does not provide a separate causal estimate for motivation or engagement.
finding.measure: Student survey ratings, retry behavior, and revision of incorrect answers after feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central contribution is an automated grading and feedback workflow intended to reduce teacher workload and speed turnaround on complex geometry tasks. The system achieved 100% agreement on rule-based closed-ended and CGT items and substantial agreement on LLM-graded explanations (κ=0.737 overall), suggesting it can reliably automate much of the grading process, though the paper does not report direct time-saved metrics.
finding.measure: Automated grading agreement with teacher judgments; system scalability for grading and feedback generation

finding.finding_summary: The feedback process helped some students refine explanations and reason more precisely, especially on geometry justification tasks. Expert review and the iterative refinement examples show that students moved from vague responses to more conceptually accurate answers after feedback, but the paper found no statistically significant evidence that these feedback-driven corrections transferred to later, more complex questions.
finding.measure: Quality of student written explanations, iterative answer refinement, and transfer to later target questions

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI in K-12 Education: The CyberScholar Initiative
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether CyberScholar, a generative AI writing assistant, can support K-12 students’ writing through formative feedback aligned to teacher rubrics and classroom materials. The study responds to a practical question in AI-assisted instruction: whether an AI tool can provide useful, timely, and pedagogically aligned feedback for students writing in authentic school settings.

The authors piloted CyberScholar across four public schools in the Midwestern and Northwestern United States, involving students in grades 7, 8, 10, and 11 (with some school context spanning grades 6-12) and 4 teachers. The tool was customized using retrieval-augmented generation and prompt engineering so that feedback reflected teachers’ rubrics, instructional resources, and expectations, and students could revise drafts and ask follow-up questions. Data came from observations, surveys, and interviews, and were analyzed qualitatively.

Findings suggest that students viewed CyberScholar as helpful for writing development because it provided detailed, specific, and rubric-aligned feedback, supported interactive clarification, and helped students notice improvements in grammar, transitions, clarity, and overall writing quality. Students also valued the feedback process as faster and, in some cases, easier to work with than peer or self-review. However, some participants reported inconsistent scoring across repeated submissions, indicating that the ratings were not always stable or trusted.

Overall, the study concludes that GenAI can support formative writing feedback in K-12 contexts when carefully aligned with teacher expectations and used as a complement to, not a replacement for, teacher feedback. The paper is exploratory and qualitative, so it offers early evidence of potential rather than causal estimates of impact or rigorous productivity gains.

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers reported that CyberScholar provided detailed, specific, rubric-aligned feedback that helped students revise writing drafts. Across the 121 participating students, 19 explicitly praised the detailed feedback, and some students reported rubric score improvements after revision (e.g., one student improved a "Compare" and "Contrast" rubric score from 0 to 2 after receiving AI feedback and revising).
finding.measure: Student interviews, post-survey responses, rubric-based writing feedback and scores
finding.study_size: n=121 students, n=4 teachers; post-survey n=54 students, n=3 teachers; interviews n=8 students, n=1 teacher

finding.finding_summary: Students described the feedback process as motivating and confidence-building, saying it helped them realize they could improve their writing and encouraged them to submit revised drafts. Some students also said the star ratings motivated them to earn more stars on subsequent revisions, suggesting increased engagement and persistence during the writing process.
finding.measure: Post-survey comments and interview responses about motivation, engagement, and perceived improvement

finding.finding_summary: The tool supported metacognitive and revision-oriented practices by prompting students to reflect on their writing, ask follow-up questions, and make iterative improvements. Students reported that the feedback helped them think more carefully about transitions, grammar, structure, and clarity, and the paper argues that CyberScholar fostered a more dialogic, self-regulated revision process.
finding.measure: Observations, student reflections, follow-up question use, iterative draft revisions

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that students perceived CyberScholar as quicker and easier to use than peer or self-analysis, and that it quickly identified areas for improvement. However, the study does not provide measured time-on-task, turnaround time, or net time saved after review and adaptation versus human-only or other digital alternatives, so evidence of productivity gains remains qualitative and unquantified.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of speed, ease of use, and feedback turnaround
finding.study_size: n=121 students; specific efficiency comments from a subset of respondents

paper_profiles.title: Personalized Multimodal Feedback Using Multiple External Representations: Strategy Profiles and Learning in High School Physics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether students’ use of elaborated feedback in a computer-based high school physics platform is associated with better learning outcomes, and whether different patterns of using multiple external representations (MERs) relate to performance. The authors are motivated by the promise of adaptive feedback and intelligent tutoring systems, especially as multimodal large language models make personalized multimodal feedback more feasible.

The study followed 661 German 10th- and 11th-grade students over 16–24 weeks in authentic classroom settings. After each multiple-choice physics exercise, students received verification feedback and could optionally open elaborated feedback in verbal, graphical, and mathematical forms. The researchers used linear mixed-effects models to test associations between feedback use and post-test performance, and clustering/ANCOVA analyses to identify feedback-selection strategies.

Results showed a small positive association between more frequent use of elaborated feedback and higher post-test scores in both cohorts, independent of prior knowledge, platform score, and confidence. However, because the design was observational, the authors do not claim causality and note possible confounding by motivation or interest. Clustering suggested three main feedback strategies among students who used elaborated feedback: consistently using all representations, using them more selectively, or favoring verbal feedback; time-resolved sequences did not reveal additional meaningful strategy differences. Overall, the paper supports adaptive multimodal feedback design, but it does not provide evidence on grading or turnaround-time productivity gains.

finding.finding_summary: Elaborated multirepresentational feedback was associated with higher post-test performance in high school physics. In the mixed-effects models, feedback frequency had a small positive standardized association with post-test score in Cohort 1 (β=0.13, 95% CI [0.05, 0.22], n=351) and Cohort 2 (β=0.08, 95% CI [0.00, 0.16], p=.054, n=310), controlling for pre-test score, platform score, exercises solved, and confidence.
finding.measure: Physics post-test score on kinematics assessments
finding.study_size: n=661 total; n=351 Cohort 1; n=310 Cohort 2

finding.finding_summary: The study measured average response confidence and examined whether it moderated or correlated with elaborated feedback use. Average confidence was a small, non-significant predictor of post-test performance in both cohorts (Cohort 1: β=0.07; Cohort 2: β=0.09), and feedback frequency was not meaningfully correlated with confidence (r=0.00 in Cohort 1; r=0.10 in Cohort 2).
finding.measure: Average response confidence (1-5 scale) and its relation to feedback use/performance

finding.finding_summary: The paper links elaborated feedback use with representational competence and feedback-selection strategies, which are relevant to metacognitive and representational-processing skills. Students who more frequently accessed elaborated feedback tended to select all three MERs more often, and in Cohort 1 no statistically significant differences in baseline representational competence were found across feedback-strategy clusters (Pillai’s trace=0.018, F=0.74, p=.67).
finding.measure: Representational competence scores and MER-feedback strategy clusters

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks Middle School
paper_profiles.population: Middle School (7th grade mathematics teachers and students)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether teachers should remain in the loop when using generative AI to personalize mathematics tasks, and what that means for task quality, student reactions, and teacher efficiency. The authors focus on context personalization in middle school math, where teachers use ChatGPT/GPT-4o to adapt existing Illustrative Mathematics problems to students’ interests such as sports, food, brands, games, and social media references.

The study involved 7 seventh-grade mathematics teachers across 6 U.S. schools and 521 students. Teachers first received training, then used ChatGPT in recorded sessions to personalize 143 problems across two curriculum units (Unit 4 and Unit 6). The researchers coded teacher prompts, analyzed student closed- and open-ended feedback, and modeled relationships among prompting, time, and student ratings. The paper concludes that teacher-in-the-loop personalization can improve task quality through teacher judgment about realism, readability, and mathematical clarity, but it is not especially time efficient: teachers took about 4 minutes per problem on average, and efficiency did not clearly improve over time. Students generally preferred finer-grained, specific popular-culture references, while teachers often worked at broader grain sizes; student ratings were highest when teachers used about 3–5 prompts. When teachers iterated after reviewing Unit 4 student feedback, they used more prompts and more time in Unit 6, and student interest/closeness ratings improved modestly. The authors argue that teacher-in-the-loop GenAI personalization has benefits for professional learning and quality control, but the time cost and mismatch between teacher-made broad personalization and student preferences remain major limitations.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined personalization of middle school mathematics problems, but it did not measure student achievement or learning outcomes. It does report that student ratings of the math problems’ interestingness and closeness to interests improved from Unit 4 to Unit 6, and that 3–5 prompts per problem was associated with higher ratings (B=0.240, SE=0.085, t=2.84, p=0.0073).
finding.measure: Student ratings of personalized mathematics problems (interestingness and closeness to interests)
finding.std_deviation: SD=1.24 (interestingness), SD=1.28 (closeness); problem creation time SD=165.7 seconds, prompts SD=2.6

finding.finding_summary: Student interest and perceived relevance were the main learner outcomes. Students rated personalized problems moderately low overall (mean interestingness=2.46/5, mean closeness=2.53/5), but ratings were significantly higher in Unit 6 than Unit 4 (interestingness 2.27 to 2.56; closeness 2.28 to 2.66; B=0.33, SE=0.095, p=0.0012).
finding.measure: Student survey ratings of interestingness and closeness to personal interests
finding.study_size: n=521 students; 52 problem ratings for the closed-ended survey subset
finding.std_deviation: SD=1.17 to 1.29 across unit-level ratings; overall SD=1.24 and 1.28

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studied whether teacher-in-the-loop GenAI saved time when personalizing math tasks, and found that it did not appear time efficient. Teachers spent an average of 246 seconds per problem (about 4 minutes; SD=165.7), used 3.2 prompts per problem on average, and actually became slower and used more prompts from Unit 4 to Unit 6 (time increased by 70.4 seconds, p=0.0189; prompts increased by 1.26, p=0.0025).
finding.measure: Teacher time spent creating each personalized problem and number of ChatGPT prompts used
finding.effect_size: B=70.4 seconds (time increase from Unit 4 to Unit 6); B=1.26 prompts (prompt increase from Unit 4 to Unit 6)
finding.std_deviation: SD=165.7 seconds per problem; SD=2.6 prompts per problem

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests teachers engaged in iterative prompting, problem refinement, and reflective adjustment, which are durable skills related to metacognition and problem solving. Teacher prompting was associated with better student ratings at an intermediate level of effort (3–5 prompts), indicating that effective use of GenAI required strategic revision rather than accepting initial outputs.
finding.measure: Teacher prompting patterns and iterative refinement during task design

paper_profiles.title: AI as a Teaching Partner: Early Lessons from Classroom Codesign with Secondary Teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report examines early classroom implementation of a generative AI platform, Colleague AI Classroom, in secondary school settings. The central question is how teachers design, adapt, and experience AI-assisted tools for instruction, assessment, feedback, and student support, and what conditions make those tools useful in real classrooms.

Over seven weeks in spring 2025, 21 in-service teachers across five Washington State schools integrated four features: Teaching Aide, Assessment & AI Grading, AI Tutor, and Student Growth Insights. The study used teacher surveys, planning/reflection forms, interviews, group meetings, and platform logs to understand implementation patterns and perceived value. Teachers used AI mainly as a scaffolded, human-overseen tool rather than a replacement for teacher judgment.

The report concludes that AI can support classroom instruction when teachers provide clear framing, rubrics, and monitoring. Teachers reported stronger student engagement and formative feedback loops when activities were structured and aligned to instructional goals, and they valued narrative feedback more than automated numeric scores. The most consistent practical benefit was reduced teacher burden and faster feedback/insight turnaround, especially through AI-assisted grading and Student Growth Insights, though the findings are exploratory and based largely on self-report and usage logs rather than direct outcome measures.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the platform reduced burden and sped up formative feedback workflows. In the assessment feature, 92.2% median AI grading coverage on submitted work (58 classroom assessment records; 936 submissions across 33 classrooms) and teacher reports that AI-generated rubrics and narrative comments were useful indicate substantial automation of first-pass feedback, though teachers commonly reviewed and adjusted outputs. Student Growth Insights were also described as saving teachers hours of scanning for common questions and misconceptions, but no direct time-on-task study or net time-saved estimate was reported.
finding.measure: AI grading coverage; teacher-reported usefulness of AI rubrics/feedback; teacher-reported time saved from Student Growth Insights
finding.study_size: n=21 teachers overall; assessment logs from 58 classroom-level records across 33 classrooms; 936 student submissions

paper_profiles.title: Overview of AI Grading of Physics Olympiad Exams
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the challenge of automating grading for high school physics exam questions, with a focus on the Australian Physics Olympiad. The central problem is that physics assessments include multiple response formats—numerical, algebraic, short answer, plots/graphs, and diagrams—each requiring different automated marking techniques, and the paper asks what AI-enabled approaches are available and how they align with ethical principles.

The paper is a systematic literature review conducted in December 2024. It describes search and screening procedures across multiple databases, then synthesizes prior work on rule-based grading, computer algebra systems, hand-crafted feature methods, and large language / multimodal models for different physics question types. The paper does not present a new experimental evaluation in classrooms; instead, it summarizes what the literature suggests about feasibility, limitations, and likely fit of each approach. For numeric responses, rule-based systems are straightforward when inputs are constrained, while algebraic and diagram-based responses remain difficult and often require more sophisticated reasoning or multimodal methods.

The main conclusion is that no single approach currently solves automated grading across all physics item types. The paper argues that future systems should likely combine LLMs with external verification tools in an LLM-modulo framework, and that practical deployment should prioritize explainability, privacy, local execution, and minimal training burden on teachers. Its contribution is primarily conceptual and synthetic rather than empirical evidence of classroom impact or turnaround-time savings.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that automated grading could reduce teacher workload, but it provides no original time-savings data from an implemented system in K-12 settings. Its evidence is a literature review of methods that may support faster marking, with the strongest practical case for rule-based numeric grading and the weakest for complex algebraic, diagrammatic, and LLM-based marking where reliability and nuance remain concerns.
finding.measure: teacher workload / grading efficiency (reviewed literature, not a new empirical measure)

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on automated grading of high school physics problems, including numeric, algebraic, plotted, diagrammatic, and short-answer responses that require scientific reasoning to assess. It synthesizes prior work showing that simpler response types can often be graded reliably with rules or symbolic tools, while complex reasoning embedded in algebraic proofs and diagrams remains difficult for current AI systems.
finding.measure: physics problem-response grading accuracy / feasibility across response types

paper_profiles.title: Machine-Assisted Grading of Nationwide School-Leaving Essay Exams with LLMs and Statistical NLP
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models (LLMs) and statistical NLP tools can support grading of high-stakes national essay exams in Estonia. The central question is not which model is best in an absolute benchmark sense, but whether machine-assisted grading can approximate human scoring closely enough to be useful in a rubric-driven, human-in-the-loop examination workflow.

The study uses two full national cohorts of digitally produced Estonian school-leaving essays from 2024: 781 grade 9 essays and 764 grade 12 essays. The authors prompt several commercial LLMs (GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, o4-mini, Gemini 2.0 Flash, Gemini 1.5 Pro) in a zero-shot rubric-scoring setup, compare their scores with human panel scores, and also build supervised statistical NLP regressors for selected rubric dimensions. They evaluate performance with mean absolute error, agreement with human score ranges, bias, and robustness to prompt injection. The paper also explores whether an LLM can generate high-scoring essays and whether the resulting subscores could be used for systematic feedback.

Overall, the paper concludes that current LLMs can score these essays at near-human levels on many dimensions, though they show some bias, are vulnerable to prompt injection, and do not fully replace human judgment. Statistical NLP models performed slightly better on lower-level language mechanics such as punctuation and orthography. The authors argue that a principled hybrid workflow is feasible for national-scale assessment, with potential productivity gains, more consistent grading, and richer feedback, but only if human oversight, rubrics, and security safeguards remain central.

finding.finding_summary: The paper provides evidence that LLM-assisted grading can reduce assessor workload by enabling rapid, rubric-based scoring of national exam essays. On the 9th-grade dataset (n=781) and 12th-grade dataset (n=764), models produced near-human scores and the authors explicitly argue that the workflow could support faster, more consistent evaluation; however, the paper does not directly measure net time saved versus human-only or non-AI digital alternatives.
finding.measure: Essay scoring throughput and proximity of automated scores to human panel scores; implied grading productivity/workflow efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The main substantive focus is automated assessment of student writing, including content, argumentation, vocabulary, syntax, punctuation, orthography, and structure.
