Across the two datasets (n=781 and n=764), LLMs achieved total-score MAE values ranging from 2.66 to 4.97 on the 0–27 scale, and several category-level regression models achieved around 0.4 MAE on specific language-mechanics categories; this indicates that machine scoring can approximate human judgments on authentic K-12 writing tasks, though not perfectly.
finding.measure: Essay rubric scores, mean absolute error on writing subscores and total scores

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLM-assisted scoring could be implemented at national scale in Estonia’s examination system while preserving human oversight and compliance with emerging regulations. It situates the work in the transition to digital examinations and reports that the method is viable for high-stakes assessment in a small-language context, with potential implications for national policy, exam governance, and institutional exam modernization.
finding.measure: Feasibility of national-scale human-in-the-loop exam scoring; policy/regulatory fit and operational viability

finding.finding_summary: The rubric and subscore profiles target higher-order writing qualities such as argumentation, coherence, and textual organization, which the authors link to critical thinking and structured reasoning. The paper does not directly measure student durable-skill growth, but it does show that LLMs can score these constructs in authentic essays with moderate-to-strong agreement relative to human raters, suggesting these dimensions are assessable at scale.
finding.measure: Rubric categories for argumentation, coherence, structure, and related higher-order writing dimensions

paper_profiles.title: Designing for human–AI complementarity in K-12 education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how to design effective human–AI partnerships in K-12 classrooms, focusing on the challenge of helping teachers make better in-the-moment decisions while students work with AI tutors. The authors argue that successful AI in education should complement, not replace, teachers, and present a participatory design process for developing Lumilo, mixed-reality smart glasses that provide teachers with real-time analytics about student learning, metacognition, and behavior during AI-supported math lessons.

The intervention was developed through iterative co-design with teachers, replay-based prototyping, and pilot studies in real classrooms. The main field evaluation compared three conditions across 343 middle school students in 18 classrooms: no glasses, glasses without analytics, and full Lumilo glasses with analytics. Students worked for two class sessions with the Lynnette AI tutor on linear equation solving, and their teachers used the wearable tool to monitor and support them. The study found that Lumilo improved student learning relative to both business-as-usual and a reduced-glasses condition, suggesting that real-time analytics helped teachers direct attention to students who most needed support.

The paper’s broader conclusion is that human–AI complementarity can produce measurable gains when AI systems are designed around teachers’ real workflows and information needs. In this case, the glasses led teachers to spend more time with lower-performing students and reduced the usual pattern in which higher-performing students benefit disproportionately from AI tutoring. The authors also emphasize that the benefit came partly from the analytics and partly from the wearable form factor itself, which enabled teachers to remain oriented to the classroom rather than to a separate screen.

finding.finding_summary: In a randomized classroom study, students who learned linear equation solving with a teacher using Lumilo (mixed-reality glasses plus analytics) showed greater pre/post learning gains than students in the no-glasses business-as-usual condition and the glasses-without-analytics condition. The study included 343 middle school students across 18 classrooms (286 analyzed after absences) and used a pre-test/post-test on linear equation solving; the paper reports a positive effect but does not provide the numeric effect size in the excerpted text.
finding.measure: Pre-test and post-test scores on linear equation solving

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that, with Lumilo, teachers spent more time supporting lower-initial-knowledge students and that students in this condition showed greater growth if they began with lower pre-test scores. This suggests an improvement in equitable attention and responsiveness during class, though the primary measured outcomes were academic rather than student self-report engagement or motivation.
finding.measure: Teacher attention allocation by student pre-test level; downstream differential student gains

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests that Lumilo helped teachers use complementary evidence from the AI system and their own observations to make better in-the-moment judgments about student needs. The main data source was classroom observation and logged teacher attention allocation, indicating that the tool supported teacher metacognition and decision-making during instruction, although no formal durable-skills test was administered.
finding.measure: Classroom observation and teacher decision-making/attention allocation
finding.study_size: n=8 teachers in the main field experiment; n=14 teachers in pilot studies

finding.finding_summary: Lumilo appears to improve teacher orchestration efficiency by helping teachers identify which students most needed help and by enabling brief, targeted visits. In pilot observations, teachers spent an average of about 24 seconds per visit with each student, and the system shifted attention toward students with lower initial knowledge; however, the paper does not report net time saved versus alternatives or a formal workload reduction metric.
finding.measure: Teacher attention allocation / time per student visit
finding.study_size: n=14 teachers, 15 classrooms, 304 students in pilots; n=8 teachers, 18 classrooms, 343 students in main study

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that participatory, theory-driven design of human–AI partnerships can improve deployment in real K-12 settings and offers design recommendations for future educational AI systems. This is primarily a conceptual and design contribution informed by field evidence, not a policy or governance evaluation, so the institutional impact is indirect.
finding.measure: Design/process implications from iterative field deployment

paper_profiles.title: AI-Generated Rubric Interfaces: K–12 Teachers’ Perceptions and Practices
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K–12 teachers perceive and use AI-supported rubric generation tools, with a focus on assessment design and feedback practices in block-based programming contexts. The authors were motivated by the fact that rubric creation is time-consuming, cognitively demanding, and often difficult to align precisely with instructional goals and student grade level expectations.

The study was conducted during summer 2025 professional development workshops with 25 middle- and high-school teachers. Participants used MagicSchool.ai to generate rubrics for a sample Snap! programming task, compared AI-generated rubrics with manually created rubrics, and then used both an AI-generated rubric and a chatbot (Raina/Reina) to produce feedback on the same work. Data sources included pre- and post-workshop surveys, open-ended responses, exit tickets, and discussion notes, which were analyzed using thematic analysis and descriptive survey statistics.

Findings suggest that teachers viewed AI-generated rubrics as strong starting drafts that improved structure, clarified vague criteria, and could save time, but they also emphasized substantial editing needs, limited editability, occasional misalignment with learning goals, and the need for teacher oversight. Survey responses were generally positive on clarity, alignment, and transparency, while usability—especially the ability to add, remove, or revise criteria—was the weakest area. Overall, hands-on exposure increased teachers’ willingness to consider AI rubric tools, but adoption was conditional on preserving teacher control and improving workflow integration.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers consistently reported that rubric creation is time-consuming and that AI-generated rubrics can reduce the effort of drafting rubrics from scratch by providing a structured first draft. In post-workshop surveys, they also viewed the rubric as a flexible starting point (M=3.5625, SD=1.31) and a tool that could help communicate expectations efficiently, though editing and criterion revision remained difficult (M=2.75, SD=1.23).
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of rubric creation time, workload, usability, and flexibility; post-survey Likert ratings and open-ended reflections

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests AI rubric tools may influence classroom assessment workflows and teachers’ future adoption intentions, especially when tools support teacher control, alignment with standards, and easy integration into existing grading systems. Teachers explicitly requested LMS integration, better exporting, and clearer scaffolds, indicating that institutional and workflow design features shape whether such tools can be adopted at scale.
finding.measure: Teacher adoption intentions, workflow fit, and recommendations for tool/institutional design from surveys and qualitative responses

paper_profiles.title: Integration of AI in STEM Education – Addressing Ethical Challenges in K-12 Settings
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a critical conceptual review of artificial intelligence integration in K-12 STEM education, with a particular emphasis on the ethical challenges that arise when AI tools such as intelligent tutoring systems, automated assessment, predictive analytics, and surveillance technologies are introduced into classrooms. The authors argue that AI offers potential benefits like personalized learning, immediate feedback, and operational efficiency, but they caution that these gains may be offset by algorithmic bias, privacy violations, reduced pedagogical flexibility, and widening inequities.

Rather than reporting original empirical results, the paper synthesizes literature from 2016–2025 and proposes a framework for responsible AI adoption in K-12 STEM. The framework combines a three-phased implementation roadmap with a four-phase professional development model grounded in TPACK and critical algorithmic literacy. It recommends low-tech adaptations, culturally responsive pedagogy, bias and equity audits, and governance structures to support ethical, human-centered AI use.

The paper’s intended audience is primarily educators and school systems considering AI adoption. Its main conclusion is that AI should be integrated gradually and with strong human oversight, professional development, and policy safeguards; otherwise, the technology risks reinforcing existing educational inequities and undermining the broader goals of STEM education.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI-powered automated assessments and intelligent tutoring systems can reduce teacher workload, provide immediate feedback, and increase scalability in K-12 STEM contexts. However, this is a synthesis claim rather than a direct empirical result, and the paper does not report its own measured time savings, turnaround times, or net productivity after implementation and adaptation versus human-only or non-AI digital alternatives.
finding.measure: teacher workload; feedback turnaround; operational scalability

finding.finding_summary: The review states that AI-driven guidance and intelligent tutoring can improve knowledge integration, revision behaviors, and achievement in STEM subjects, and it specifically notes benefits for scientific argument refinement through immediate diagnostic feedback. These claims are drawn from cited studies rather than new data in this paper; no pooled effect size or sample size is reported for the review itself.
finding.measure: knowledge integration, revision behaviors, scientific argument quality, STEM achievement

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes that AI ethics and AI literacy activities can support critical thinking, ethical reasoning, and critical engagement with algorithms. It cites project-based and role-playing approaches as effective for developing these durable skills, but the paper itself provides no direct outcome data, effect sizes, or sample sizes.
finding.measure: critical thinking, ethical reasoning, AI literacy, algorithmic literacy

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper is institutional and policy-level implementation: phased adoption, educator certification, mandatory ethics and equity audits, and student data governance. The paper proposes these governance structures as mechanisms to improve responsible AI integration, but it does not present empirical evaluation of institutional outcomes.
finding.measure: policy alignment, equity audits, governance structures, program retention, implementation roadmap

paper_profiles.title: On the Graded Identities for Elementary Gradings in Matrix Algebras over Infinite Fields
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies graded polynomial identities of the matrix algebra Mn(K) over an infinite field K of positive characteristic, focusing on elementary gradings where the neutral component is the diagonal of the matrix algebra. The central question is to describe a basis for the G-graded identities in this setting and to extend prior results, which were known for characteristic 0 and for some special cases, to infinite fields of characteristic p > 0.

The paper does not study an educational intervention or any AI-enabled system; rather, it is a pure algebraic mathematics paper. The author constructs generic matrices and uses them to analyze the relatively free algebra associated with the grading, proving that the same generators of the graded identity ideal known in characteristic 0 also work over infinite fields of positive characteristic, together with a finite set of additional monomial identities whose length is bounded by a function of n. The main theorem characterizes the graded identities for these elementary gradings and shows that, under pairwise distinct grading elements, a basis consists of three universal identities plus finitely many bounded-length monomial identities.

paper_profiles.title: Shiksha Copilot: Teacher-AI Collaboration for Curating and Customizing Lesson Plans in Low-Resource Schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether and how an LLM-based, human-in-the-loop lesson planning system can support teachers in low-resource K–12 schools. The central problem is that teachers in government schools in Karnataka, India face heavy administrative burdens, limited instructional materials, multilingual classrooms, and little time for lesson planning, yet are still expected to produce curriculum-aligned, compliant lesson plans.

The authors designed and deployed Shiksha Copilot, a teacher-AI collaboration system that generated draft learning objectives and lesson plans from the state curriculum, routed them through expert human curators, translated them into Kannada, and then let teachers further customize the curated plans for classroom use. The deployment involved 1,043 teachers and 23 curators across 757 schools, with evidence drawn from system logs, 43 interviews, and pre/post surveys. Teachers generally found the tool helpful for reducing bureaucratic workload and lesson planning time, while curators reported that English plans were mostly high quality but Kannada translations often required substantial linguistic editing.

Overall, the paper concludes that AI can productively augment teacher workflows when it is embedded in a human-in-the-loop, curriculum-grounded process rather than used as a standalone generator. The strongest benefits were operational: less time spent on lesson planning and record-keeping, and lower teaching-related stress. However, the paper also shows clear limits, especially for low-resource language generation and for deeper pedagogical change, which remained constrained by staffing shortages, administrative demands, and the need for teachers to adapt outputs to local classroom realities.

finding.finding_summary: Shiksha Copilot reduced teachers’ workload by easing bureaucratic record-keeping and lesson-planning effort. The paper reports measurable reductions in lesson planning time and teacher stress in a mixed-methods deployment with 1,043 teachers, and teachers repeatedly described the tool as saving time because they could start from curated, curriculum-aligned plans rather than creating plans from scratch.
finding.measure: Weekly time spent on lesson planning and administrative tasks; teacher stress scale; qualitative reports of workload reduction
finding.study_size: n=406 matched survey respondents; n=1,043 deployed teachers; qualitative interviews n=22 teachers, n=4 mentors, n=17 curators

finding.finding_summary: The system helped teachers meet administrative documentation requirements and fit into existing school compliance practices, especially the mandated 5E lesson-plan format in Karnataka. The paper also suggests organizational change at the workflow level, but broader institutional transformation was constrained by staffing shortages and administrative demands.
finding.measure: Teacher reports and interview themes on bureaucratic documentation, compliance, and workflow integration
finding.study_size: n=1,043 teachers; qualitative interviews n=22 teachers, n=4 mentors, n=17 curators

paper_profiles.title: HARQ Feedback in Spectrum Sharing Networks
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper analyzes hybrid automatic repeat request (HARQ) feedback in spectrum-sharing wireless networks. The main question is how two HARQ protocols—repetition time diversity (RTD) and incremental redundancy (INR)—affect throughput and outage probability when a secondary user shares spectrum with a primary user under power and interference constraints.

The study is entirely theoretical and simulation-based, not an educational intervention study. It derives closed-form expressions for throughput and outage under continuous and bursting communication models, assuming Rayleigh fading channels and imperfect secondary-to-primary channel state information at the transmitter. The paper also incorporates constraints on secondary-user peak transmit power and primary-user received interference, and examines how the results change with retransmission limits.

The main conclusion is that HARQ does not necessarily increase throughput, especially depending on channel conditions and communication model, but it consistently reduces outage probability. INR outperforms RTD in both throughput and outage probability, and continuous communication generally yields higher throughput than bursting communication. Because the paper is about wireless communications rather than K-12 education, it does not provide evidence relevant to AI-enabled grading, feedback turnaround, or school-based productivity outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Common Problems and Effects of Feedback on Fun When Programming Ozobots in Primary School
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 17th Workshop in Primary and Secondary Computing Education (WiPSCE '22)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates what kinds of problems primary school children encounter while programming Ozobot Evo robots and how different forms of corrective feedback relate to students’ experienced fun. The authors focus on a practical classroom question: when children get stuck during introductory programming with robots, which kinds of teacher support are most helpful, and which kinds may reduce enjoyment and motivation.

The study was conducted in seven workshops with 116 third- and fourth-grade students (ages 8–10) in primary school. Children completed seven Ozobot activities, mostly in pen-and-paper mode and one digital OzoBlockly activity. Supervisors recorded students’ problems and the feedback provided, while children reported fun after each activity using the Fun Toolkit (Smileyometer and Again Again Table). The analysis identified eight common problem categories and six feedback types. The paper finds that urgent problems and feedback delivered as direct instruction can lower fun ratings, while hints are associated with better fun ratings. Overall fun was high, and there were no major gender differences in enjoyment or problem frequency, though mixed groups needed more help with directional movement. The paper concludes that prepared hints, stickers, and advance materials may help teachers support students without undermining motivation.

finding.finding_summary: Across seven Ozobot workshops with 116 primary school children, overall fun was high (mean 1.9/2 on the Again Again Table; 3.72/4 on the Smileyometer). However, fun ratings varied by problem type and feedback type: receiving feedback on urgent problems such as task misunderstanding (P1) or app use (P7) was associated with significantly worse Smileyometer ratings (P1: p=.001, rpb=0.18; P7: p=.022, rpb=0.11), while hints were associated with better ratings (Smileyometer p=.001, rpb=-0.17).
finding.measure: Fun / enjoyment ratings using the Fun Toolkit (Smileyometer and Again Again Table)
finding.effect_size: rpb=0.18 (P1 on Smileyometer), rpb=0.11 (P7 on Smileyometer), rpb=-0.17 (hints on Smileyometer); other reported means

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly examines how feedback affects students’ ability to proceed through programming tasks, including debugging, understanding task constraints, and using directions/sequence logic. Some supports such as hints and guiding questions helped children solve problems independently, whereas direct instruction was less motivating; mixed groups showed a significant difficulty with directional movement (P6: p=.029, η2=0.1).
finding.measure: Observed problem categories during Ozobot programming activities and associated feedback strategies
finding.effect_size: η2=0.1 for group-constellation difference on directional movement problems; rpbs reported for specific problem-feedback associations

finding.finding_summary: The study is partly about efficient teacher support for common classroom problems, especially how to prepare feedback in advance and what types of support can resolve issues quickly. The authors report that many problems were handled with explanations, stickers, hints, or direct instruction, and they argue that prepared hints and auxiliary materials can reduce time spent on repeated troubleshooting, though no direct time-saved metric was measured.
finding.measure: Recorded frequency of problem types and tutoring feedback types during classroom workshops

paper_profiles.title: Automated Assignment Grading with Large Language Models: Insights from a Bioinformatics Course
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models (LLMs) can serve as practical graders for written student assignments in a university bioinformatics course, with particular attention to grading accuracy and the quality of feedback students receive. The authors are motivated by the common challenge of providing timely, individualized feedback at scale and evaluate whether LLMs can reduce teaching-assistant workload while preserving or improving the student experience.

The study was conducted in the 2024/25 Introduction to Bioinformatics course at the University of Ljubljana, involving 119 students and five take-home assignments with many short written responses. Student text answers were randomly assigned to one of six LLM graders (including GPT-4o, several Llama 3 variants, and Nvidia-70B) or human TA-based grading conditions used for rubric refinement and comparison. The paper uses a structured grading-rubric prompt plus TA-graded examples, and compares LLM and human performance on grading criteria accuracy, grading bias, and student feedback ratings.

Results indicate that, except for the smallest model (Llama-8B), the LLMs achieved grading accuracy roughly comparable to human TAs, with classification accuracy around 85%–90% on matched grading criteria. The inclusion of both a grading rubric and graded examples produced the most balanced grading behavior, and quantization had little apparent effect on performance. Students generally rated LLM-generated feedback about as favorably as TA feedback, with slightly higher preference for LLM feedback in some cases, especially when responses were correct and LLMs provided more elaborated feedback. The authors conclude that well-designed LLM graders can be viable in real course settings, especially when paired with human review options and carefully structured prompts.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that LLMs can automate grading of written assignments with performance comparable to human TAs, suggesting potential reductions in staff workload. Across 670 manually evaluated submissions used as the gold standard, most models reached 85%–90% classification accuracy on grading criteria, and the authors argue this makes automated grading feasible for real course workflows, though they do not report a direct time-saved measure.
finding.measure: LLM grading accuracy / classification accuracy on TA-defined grading criteria
finding.study_size: n=670 manually evaluated submissions; 119 students in the course

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates written assignment grading and feedback for university bioinformatics coursework, showing that LLM-generated grades and feedback can align closely with human TA judgments. For the 1,527 feedback ratings collected, students generally did not prefer TA feedback over LLM feedback, and feedback satisfaction was comparable across graders, indicating that the system can support assessment of written academic work.
finding.measure: Assignment grading accuracy and student feedback satisfaction ratings
finding.study_size: n=119 students; 1,527 rated answers; 670 manually evaluated submissions

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests a positive effect on the feedback environment relevant to metacognition and self-improvement, because students received individualized written feedback on their responses and rated LLM feedback as comparable to TA feedback. However, the paper does not directly measure durable skills outcomes such as critical thinking or self-regulation, so this assignment is only moderate-confidence and indirect.
finding.measure: Student satisfaction with assignment feedback

paper_profiles.title: The Hands-Up Problem and How to Deal With It: Secondary School Teachers’ Experiences of Debugging in the Classroom
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates secondary school computing teachers’ experiences of teaching and supporting debugging in text-based programming classrooms. The authors focus on the practical classroom problem that arises when many students encounter errors and immediately raise their hands for help, creating what they term the “hands-up problem.”

Using semi-structured interviews with nine teachers, the study examines teachers’ perspectives on the barriers to successful debugging, the emotional experiences students have when debugging, and the ways teachers scaffold and model debugging. The paper is not an intervention study; rather, it is an exploratory qualitative analysis of classroom experiences and teaching practices in lower secondary computing contexts.

The teachers described a range of challenges, including limited lesson time, students’ lack of resilience or motivation, difficult syntax in text-based programming languages, and confusing Python error messages. They also described strategies to reduce dependence on the teacher, such as requiring students to try independently first, using peer support, modeling debugging, explicitly teaching how to interpret error messages, and building a positive classroom error culture.

The authors synthesize these findings into the concept of the hands-up problem and argue that less confident or less experienced teachers are more vulnerable to it. They conclude by recommending further work on debugging-specific pedagogical content knowledge, professional development, and classroom strategies that encourage independent debugging and improve students’ resilience.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that debugging frequently evokes negative emotions in students, including frustration, anxiety, disappointment, and disengagement when they get stuck; they also observed positive emotions such as excitement and pride when students finally solve an error. No effect size was reported because this was a qualitative interview study with nine teachers (n=9).
finding.measure: Teachers’ interview reports of students’ emotional reactions, resilience, motivation, and disengagement during debugging

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that some teacher strategies appeared to improve students’ debugging independence, resilience, and problem-solving habits over time, such as asking students to explain their thinking, modeling debugging, and requiring independent effort before help is given. Because the study is qualitative, these are reported perceptions rather than quantified effects.
finding.measure: Teachers’ observations of students’ debugging strategies, resilience, independent problem-solving, and metacognitive reflection

finding.finding_summary: Teachers consistently described debugging in class as creating a heavy workload: many students raise their hands at once, lessons become “busy” or “chaotic,” and teachers feel pressure to debug many students’ code simultaneously. The study does not quantify time saved or turnaround gains; instead it highlights the inefficiency of teacher-dependent debugging in classes of roughly 25-30 students.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, lesson busyness, and capacity to provide debugging support during class

finding.finding_summary: The study centers on debugging in text-based programming rather than on tested academic achievement outcomes. Teachers reported that students struggle with syntax, logical errors, and interpreting Python error messages, but also that instructional strategies and repeated practice can improve debugging performance and independence over time.
finding.measure: Debugging ability, error detection, and success in resolving programming errors

paper_profiles.title: Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education – where are the educators?
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.population: Undergraduate and postgraduate higher education students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a systematic review of research on artificial intelligence (AI) applications in higher education published between 2007 and 2018. The authors ask how AI research has developed over time, how AI is conceptualized and ethically discussed, and what kinds of AI applications are being studied in higher education.

The review screened 2,656 records and included 146 peer-reviewed journal articles. The synthesis organizes applications into four main areas: profiling and prediction, assessment and evaluation, adaptive systems and personalisation, and intelligent tutoring systems. Most studies used quantitative methods and focused on undergraduate settings, with far fewer studies coming from education researchers than from computer science researchers.

The paper concludes that AI research in higher education is growing, but is dominated by technical work rather than educational or pedagogical perspectives. It also finds very limited critical discussion of ethics, privacy, costs, and risks. Across the included studies, AI systems were often reported to work well for prediction, grading, and feedback, and sometimes reduced workload or improved efficiency, but the review notes that many studies were short-term, lacked longitudinal evidence, and rarely compared AI against human tutoring in a rigorous way.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed higher-education studies, AI applications were repeatedly framed as reducing workload and improving efficiency for administrative and teaching tasks such as admission decisions, course scheduling, grading, feedback, plagiarism detection, and student support. The review reports that machine-learning systems often achieved high classification accuracy and that automated essay scoring and other assessment tools could reduce the cost and time associated with human assessors, although many systems required calibration and were more suitable for large-enrollment courses.
finding.measure: Prediction accuracy, grading agreement with human raters, and qualitative reports of workload/time savings
finding.study_size: n=146 included studies; multiple studies contributed to this outcome

finding.finding_summary: The review found substantial use of AI for institutional and administrative functions, including admissions, course scheduling, retention monitoring, counseling, library services, and matching students to competencies or career needs. These applications were presented as enabling institutional decision-making and policy support, but the paper also highlights ethical and governance concerns such as privacy, data protection, and the risk of replacing human labor with automated systems.
finding.measure: Descriptive synthesis of institutional AI use cases and reported ethical concerns
finding.study_size: n=146 included studies; 48 studies primarily on administrative/institutional services

finding.finding_summary: AI was frequently used to support academic outcomes outside the core literacy, numeracy, or science categories, especially in course-level prediction, adaptive learning, and tutoring across disciplines such as computer science, business statistics, medicine, and engineering. The review reports that these tools often produced accurate predictions or satisfactory preliminary results, but evidence was typically short-term and concentrated in technical fields.
finding.measure: Prediction accuracy and preliminary performance outcomes across subject-matter applications
finding.study_size: n=146 included studies; numerous course-level studies across disciplines

finding.finding_summary: Several studies targeted engagement, motivation, self-regulation, and persistence-related outcomes, such as identifying low-engaged students, predicting academic motivation, or supporting collaboration. The review notes mostly positive or satisfactory preliminary results, but one ITS study reported negative results on the support provided, and the authors caution that novelty effects were often not controlled.
finding.measure: Engagement, motivation, and self-regulation indicators; course-level behavioral data and preliminary system evaluations

finding.finding_summary: A smaller subset of studies examined collaboration, peer interaction, and related higher-order learning processes, including collaborative learning discussions, collaborative writing, and problem-solving dialogue with agents. The review characterizes these applications as promising for supporting collaboration and interactive learning, while emphasizing that the evidence base is still sparse.
finding.measure: Collaborative learning outcomes, dialogue quality, and process indicators in small-scale studies

paper_profiles.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence in Educational System
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Scientific Research in Science and Technology
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and higher education (not specifically sampled; general educational system)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative review of artificial intelligence (AI) in education, discussing how AI may transform teaching, learning, assessment, and administration. It asks what benefits and challenges AI presents for educational systems, with particular attention to personalized learning, intelligent tutoring systems, automated grading and assessment, chatbots, and teacher-student collaboration.

The paper does not report an original empirical study or sample; instead, it synthesizes prior literature and examples to argue that AI can improve efficiency, provide personalized support, speed up grading, and generate data-driven insights for educators. It also emphasizes risks such as bias, privacy, over-reliance on technology, cost, and reduced human interaction. The conclusions are broadly optimistic but cautious, recommending balanced adoption of AI with attention to ethics, equity, and privacy.

Because the paper is a descriptive review rather than a controlled evaluation, it does not provide direct evidence of quantified effects in K-12 classrooms. Its discussion is relevant to educators and institutions considering AI tools for instructional and administrative purposes, but it does not compare AI-enabled workflows against human-only support or non-AI digital tools using original data.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI can streamline administrative tasks such as grading, scheduling, enrollment management, and responding to common inquiries, thereby freeing teachers to focus more on teaching and mentoring. This conclusion is descriptive and based on cited literature rather than original data; no sample size, effect size, or statistical uncertainty is reported.
finding.measure: Administrative task efficiency, grading speed, scheduling/enrollment support, teacher time savings

finding.finding_summary: The review claims AI can improve data analysis for educational decision-making and support broader institutional functions such as school operations, logistics, and access to education. These claims are presented as general benefits from prior work, without an empirical estimate or original comparison group.
finding.measure: Data-driven decision-making, school operations, institutional support

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT: Bullshit spewer or the end of traditional assessments in higher education?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article examines the emergence of ChatGPT and situates it within broader artificial intelligence in education (AIEd) research, with a particular focus on assessment, learning, and teaching in higher education. The paper asks what ChatGPT is, how it works, what its strengths and limitations are, and what its arrival may mean for teaching, learning, and assessment practices.

The authors use a desktop analysis and literature review approach, supplemented by informal experimentation with ChatGPT. Rather than evaluating a formal intervention, they review the small body of early peer-reviewed and preprint literature on ChatGPT, compare it to prior AI writing tools such as Grammarly and Wordtune, and discuss teacher-facing, student-facing, and system-facing AIEd applications. They argue that ChatGPT is especially relevant to teacher-facing uses such as writing support, feedback, assessment, and administration, but they emphasize that it is unreliable for higher-order reasoning, citation accuracy, and some languages.

The paper’s main conclusion is that ChatGPT is an important and disruptive development, but not a magical replacement for human judgment or existing educational practice. The authors suggest that educators and institutions should adapt assessments, policies, and teaching strategies rather than simply banning the tool, and they recommend leveraging AI to support innovation in learning, feedback, and assessment design.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that ChatGPT can generate coherent prose quickly and can support drafting, explanation, and basic writing tasks, but its written output is often generic, shallow, and unreliable for academic standards. In the authors’ own tests, ChatGPT produced an approximately 500-word essay in about 120 seconds rather than the requested 2000 words and failed to provide accurate in-text and end references; the paper also notes that it can be useful for simple language tasks but weak in critical/analytical writing.
finding.measure: Quality of generated essays, drafting assistance, citation/references, and general writing performance

finding.finding_summary: In the authors’ demonstrations, ChatGPT provided a clear and sensible explanation of statistical concepts and could work through an example of standard deviation with step-by-step calculations. The paper reports that responses were produced within roughly 60 seconds and were judged usable for conceptual explanation and basic calculation support, although no formal performance metric was reported.
finding.measure: Explanations and worked examples involving mean, standard deviation, and z-scores

finding.finding_summary: The article includes a Chinese composition task and concludes that ChatGPT can produce a relevant response, but the output was poorly structured, grammatically weak, and apparently translated too literally from English. The authors link this to existing findings that ChatGPT performs better on high-resource languages than on lower-resource or distant languages such as Chinese and Romanian.
finding.measure: Chinese-language composition generation and language quality

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT may support higher-order learning only indirectly, and its own testing suggests limited competence in critical and analytical thinking tasks. The authors conclude that ChatGPT can help with basic explanations but is less competent for work requiring deeper reasoning, and they recommend using AI-involved tasks to foster creativity and critical thinking rather than relying on the tool for such capabilities.
finding.measure: Ability to handle higher-order thinking tasks, critical and analytical reasoning in essay generation

finding.finding_summary: The strongest teacher-facing implication in the paper is that ChatGPT and related AI tools can reduce workload by automating or supporting drafting, feedback, administration, and other productivity tasks. The authors explicitly state that teachers may use teacher-facing AIEd to reduce workloads and that ChatGPT can function as a fast drafting and brainstorming aid, though they do not report a formal productivity study or effect size.
finding.measure: Teacher workload reduction, administrative support, drafting speed, and feedback/assessment support

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT is likely to affect institutional assessment policy, plagiarism detection, and broader educational governance, but these claims are based on conceptual analysis rather than direct institutional measurement. The authors discuss the need for universities to revise assessment methods and policies because ChatGPT can evade plagiarism detectors and challenge conventional written assignments.
finding.measure: Assessment policy implications, plagiarism detection, and institutional adaptation to AI

paper_profiles.title: A systematic literature review of empirical research on ChatGPT in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how students and teachers have initially used ChatGPT in educational settings and what empirical studies report about its effects. The authors conducted a systematic literature review of 14 empirical studies published through April 10, 2023, using PRISMA 2020 and Okoli’s review steps to identify, screen, appraise, and synthesize studies from Dimensions.ai, Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, and Lens.

The reviewed studies were mostly in higher education, with one elementary-school study and several studies that did not specify level. Across qualitative, quantitative, and mixed-methods designs, the paper synthesizes evidence that students used ChatGPT as a virtual intelligent assistant, writing/language aid, and personalized learning resource, while educators used it to create lesson plans, quizzes, and additional resources. The review concludes that ChatGPT may improve productivity, efficiency, and some learning supports, but it also raises concerns about inaccuracies, reduced collaborative learning, weakened innovative capacities, academic integrity, and the need for training, guidance, and clear rules for responsible use.

Because the underlying evidence base is small and heterogeneous, the paper emphasizes that conclusions are preliminary. It argues that effective adoption in education will require teacher training, policy guidance, and continued research on accuracy, equity, assessment, and long-term learning effects.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, ChatGPT was used to support writing-related tasks such as generating ideas, composing essays, summarizing, paraphrasing, translating, and checking grammar. The review synthesizes these studies as showing improved writing and language proficiency, especially in English education contexts, but it does not report a pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Writing tasks, essay composition, summarization, paraphrasing, translation, grammar checking, writing proficiency

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that ChatGPT supported language-related activities such as translation, conversational practice, and changing linguistic tone or style. These uses were presented as helping learners access content more easily and improve language use, though the paper does not provide quantitative estimates.
finding.measure: Language proficiency tasks, translation, conversation, linguistic tone/style changes

finding.finding_summary: Several included studies, especially in mathematics education, found that ChatGPT helped students understand concepts and solve geometry and problem-solving questions. The review describes gains in problem-solving ability and understanding of the problem-solving process, but no pooled statistics are reported.
finding.measure: Mathematics problem-solving, geometry operations, understanding of mathematical concepts

finding.finding_summary: The review includes evidence from non-math, non-literacy contexts showing ChatGPT supported learning in computer engineering, construction education, journalism, social sciences, and early education. Reported uses included generating ideas, supporting hazard recognition, offering explanations, and enabling personalized learning, but no overall effect size is given.
finding.measure: Disciplinary learning tasks in engineering, journalism, social sciences, early education, and general concept understanding

finding.finding_summary: The review reports positive student experiences such as increased engagement, motivation, and more supportive self-directed learning environments, but also notes concerns that overuse may reduce collaborative learning competencies and motivation to attend classes. Overall, the direction is mixed because the paper synthesizes both benefits and drawbacks without quantitative pooling.
finding.measure: Engagement, motivation, self-directed learning, collaborative learning competencies

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT was reported to improve critical thinking, reasoning, hazard recognition, and problem-solving in some studies, but overuse was also associated with weaker innovative capacities, collaborative skills, and higher-order thinking. The review is clear that the evidence base points to both benefits and risks, but it does not report a pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, reasoning, problem-solving, collaboration, innovation, higher-order thinking

finding.finding_summary: Teachers used ChatGPT to create lesson plans, generate quizzes, provide additional resources, preplan activities, answer questions, and search for information, and the review states that this improved productivity and efficiency while reducing workload and time demands. The paper synthesizes these effects qualitatively and does not report a pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Teacher productivity, efficiency, workload reduction, time savings, content generation

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that effective use of ChatGPT depends on training, support, clear rules and regulations, and collaboration with policymakers and stakeholders. It also raises concerns about academic integrity, plagiarism, assessment validity, and the need to redesign evaluation practices, but these are synthesized as implications rather than measured outcomes.
finding.measure: Training needs, policy guidance, academic integrity, assessment practices, stakeholder collaboration

paper_profiles.title: Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup as an Evaluation Domain for Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.venue: AAAI-2019 Workshop on Games and Simulations for Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues that Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup (DCSS), a complex single-player roguelike game, is a promising evaluation domain for artificial intelligence and cognitive systems. The authors focus on why DCSS is attractive as a benchmark: it is partially observable, dynamic, stochastic, open-ended, and highly complex in both state and action space, yet it is turn-based and does not penalize slow reaction times.

Rather than testing a specific educational intervention or classroom technology, the paper describes the properties of the game and outlines an API under development to enable AI agents to play DCSS, receive structured state representations, and issue commands. The authors also discuss possible research questions the domain could support, such as planning, explainability, knowledge extraction, reinforcement learning, and human-agent interaction.

The paper includes descriptive evidence from prior DCSS tournaments to motivate the benchmark, noting that thousands of players participate, average winning playtimes are long, and human win rates are low. It concludes that DCSS could serve as a useful testbed for evaluating AI systems that require deliberate reasoning, long-horizon planning, and natural-language interaction, but it does not present an experimental evaluation of any intervention or educational outcome.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not evaluate any productivity intervention, but it does propose DCSS as a domain for studying AI systems that can act without time pressure and maintain action histories for performance metrics. It reports descriptive tournament statistics only, such as an average winning human playtime of about 8.5 hours, a fastest run of 41 minutes, about 2500 human competitors, and an overall win rate slightly above 2%; these are context-setting observations rather than evidence of productivity gains.
finding.measure: Human tournament playtime, win rate, and benchmark metrics proposed for AI agents
finding.study_size: n=2500 human tournament players; average winning games and thousands of games overall

paper_profiles.title: Probability Judgment in Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual discussion of how probability should be represented and combined in artificial intelligence systems, contrasting Bayesian probability with Dempster-Shafer belief functions. Shafer argues that the two formalisms differ not just technically but in the kind of problem they are suited to model: Bayesian methods model uncertainty about the answer to a question, while belief functions model uncertain evidence bearing on that answer.

The paper uses simple illustrative examples involving Fred's testimony and a thermometer to show how belief functions can represent incomplete probability models and how Dempster's rule combines independent evidence. It argues that belief-function approaches can be more convincing than Bayesian arguments when the evidence needed for full Bayesian conditioning is unavailable or weak. The paper then connects these ideas to expert systems, explaining why modularity and evidence combination made belief functions attractive to AI designers, while also emphasizing that neither Bayesian nor belief-function methods fully capture the flexibility of human probability judgment.

Although the paper is not about education, schools, or classroom interventions, it is relevant only at a very general level to AI system design and uncertainty reasoning. It does not evaluate any educational technology, teacher workflow, student outcomes, or productivity gains in K-12 settings.

paper_profiles.title: Conceptual Modeling and Artificial Intelligence: Mutual Benefits from Complementary Worlds
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an editorial preface for the 3rd International Workshop on Conceptual Modeling Meets Artificial Intelligence (CMAI’2021). It is not an empirical study of educational technology or K-12 practice; instead, it frames the intellectual relationship between conceptual modeling (CM) and artificial intelligence (AI), arguing that each field can contribute to the other. The author contrasts AI’s data-driven, often black-box outputs with CM’s human-interpretable, formal representations, and motivates the need for combining the two.

The paper proposes a research framework that organizes CMAI work into four categories: exaptation, CM-driven, AI-driven, and CM- & AI-driven research. It then summarizes the invited papers in the workshop program and maps them to these categories, describing how they address topics such as concept modeling for machine learning, conceptual models to augment ML training data, and hybrid AI techniques for model search. The piece concludes by positioning the workshop as a community-building venue and discussing future workshop directions.

Because the paper is an overview/editorial rather than a study, it does not report any participant population, intervention, or outcome data. It provides conceptual and programmatic context only, with no direct evidence about productivity, teacher workload, or K-12 educational outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Certifiable Artificial Intelligence Through Data Fusion
paper_profiles.venue: AAAI FSS-21: Artificial Intelligence in Government and Public Sector
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how artificial intelligence and machine learning systems can be certified for use, with emphasis on adopting standards, testing, and evaluation practices that bound performance and clarify intended use. The authors argue that AI certification should address not only algorithms, but also data provenance, uncertainty, explainability, interpretability, and the human-machine system in which AI operates.

The paper proposes the Multisource AI Scorecard Table (MAST) as a conceptual framework for evaluating AI systems across sourcing, uncertainty, distinguishing, analysis of alternatives, customer relevance, logical argumentation, consistency, accuracy, and visualization. It also outlines a four-stage certification process: conceptual idea, processing design, implementation test, and managed deployment, framed within verification and validation practices.

A notional image-fusion use case is presented to illustrate certifiable AI for automatic target recognition, comparing anisotropic diffusion and CNN-based fusion methods across performance metrics such as mutual information, PSNR, SSIM, and spatial frequency. The discussion concludes that certification should be tied to performance bounds, robustness, and documentation of limitations; however, the paper is primarily a conceptual and review-oriented discussion rather than an empirical study of K-12 educational settings or teacher productivity.

paper_profiles.title: From Statistical Relational to Neurosymbolic Artificial Intelligence: a Survey
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a survey of two related areas of AI research: statistical relational AI (StarAI) and neurosymbolic AI (NeSy). It asks how learning and reasoning are integrated in these approaches, and proposes a shared framework for comparing systems across seven dimensions, including inference style, logic syntax, semantics, learning scope, representation, paradigm, and task class.

The survey is methodological rather than empirical: it does not test an educational intervention or evaluate outcomes in classrooms. Instead, it reviews representative systems such as ProbLog, Markov Logic Networks, TensorLog, DeepProbLog, NeuralLP, Logic Tensor Networks, Semantic Loss, and others, showing how logical rules can be compiled into probabilistic graphical models or neural architectures. It also explains how first-order and relational structure support parameter sharing, grounding, and efficient learning, and how model-based approaches use logic as a loss function while proof-based approaches use logic to define network structure.

The paper’s main conclusion is that StarAI and NeSy share deep conceptual parallels despite different historical traditions, and that these parallels enable cross-fertilization between the fields. It emphasizes the tradeoff between control/interpretability and scalability, especially for NeSy systems, and outlines open challenges in combining symbolic reasoning with neural learning. No K-12 population, teacher workflow, or educational productivity study is reported.

paper_profiles.title: Intelligent Clinical Documentation: Harnessing Generative AI for Patient-Centric Clinical Note Generation
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Innovative Science and Research Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the burden of clinical documentation on healthcare professionals and explores whether generative AI can streamline note-taking by producing structured SOAP and BIRP clinical notes from patient-clinician interactions. The authors frame clinical documentation as a time-consuming administrative task that contributes to burnout, errors, and reduced time for direct care.

Using synthetic therapy-session videos from YouTube, the study transcribes audio with ASR tools and then experiments with multiple LLMs (GPT-3.5 Turbo, GPT-4 Turbo, Claude V3, Mixtral 8x7b, and Llama-3 70B) to generate notes under basic, zero-shot, one-shot, and JSON-structured prompting regimes. The paper also tests speaker diarization approaches, including GPT-3.5-based utterance classification, and compares model outputs using human grading and ROUGE-1 F1 scores across 20 SOAP/BIRP note samples.

The main conclusion is that generative AI can help produce structured draft clinical notes and may save time, but quality varies substantially by model and prompting strategy. GPT-4 performed best in note generation, while the paper emphasizes that human oversight remains necessary because of errors, hallucinations, privacy concerns, and inconsistent note quality. The authors argue that AI-assisted documentation may alleviate administrative burden and improve workflow efficiency, but they do not present evidence from real K-12 settings or teachers.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI can reduce the administrative burden of clinical documentation by transcribing encounters and generating draft SOAP/BIRP notes, potentially saving time and allowing professionals to focus more on direct patient care. However, the reported evidence is limited to a small case-study style comparison of note generation quality across models, not a measured productivity trial in practice.
finding.measure: ROUGE-1 F1 scores on generated SOAP/BIRP notes; human quality grading; qualitative assessment of documentation workflow and time savings claims

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses broader institutional implications of deploying generative AI for documentation, including privacy, security, regulatory compliance, liability, and the need for human oversight. It concludes that responsible deployment could transform documentation practices, but also stresses unresolved governance and risk-management challenges.
finding.measure: Qualitative discussion of deployment considerations and ethical/regulatory issues

paper_profiles.title: Transforming Software Development with Generative AI: Empirical Insights on Collaboration and Workflow
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how generative AI tools, especially ChatGPT and GitHub Copilot, are changing day-to-day work in software development. The authors ask how GenAI is being used, what effects it has on individual workflow and productivity, and how it may alter collaboration within teams.

The study uses an exploratory multi-case qualitative design based on semi-structured interviews with 13 professionals in software-related roles, including developers, data scientists, managers, designers, and technical leaders. The tools were used for a range of tasks: getting unstuck, learning, creating virtual environments, copywriting, boilerplate code generation, and working with existing code. Participants described GenAI as making routine tasks faster, more efficient, and more enjoyable, while also reducing interruptions and sometimes lowering the need to consult coworkers.

The main conclusion is that GenAI appears to improve individual productivity and satisfaction by automating tedious or repetitive work, but it may also reduce human-to-human knowledge sharing and alter team dynamics. The authors argue that this creates a tradeoff: more efficient individual work versus possible disruption to the learning loop and collaborative performance of teams. They also note important limitations such as privacy concerns, weak tool integration, and the need for prompt engineering and post-editing of AI outputs.

finding.finding_summary: Participants consistently reported that GenAI made routine and repetitive work faster, reducing time spent on tasks such as boilerplate code, email drafting, bid writing, refactoring, test generation, and general problem solving. One manager said a bid that would normally take a lot of time was completed in about 20 minutes, and several informants described ChatGPT/Copilot as helping them get unstuck and work more efficiently (n=13).
finding.measure: Self-reported productivity, time saved on workflow tasks, and perceived efficiency in coding and non-coding work

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports both gains and losses for durable skills such as learning, problem solving, and collaboration. GenAI supported faster learning, rubber-ducking, and more precise thinking, but it also reduced pair programming and some peer-to-peer consultation, suggesting a tradeoff between individual metacognition and collaborative knowledge sharing (n=13).
finding.measure: Interview-reported changes in learning behavior, collaboration patterns, and problem-solving practices

finding.finding_summary: Informants described GenAI as increasing enjoyment, motivation, fun, and work satisfaction because it removed tedious tasks and made progress feel faster. Participants also said interacting with ChatGPT felt more natural and less socially burdensome than interrupting coworkers, which reduced friction in getting help (n=13).
finding.measure: Self-reported motivation, enjoyment, work satisfaction, and reduced social friction in help-seeking

paper_profiles.title: Engaging Teachers to Co-Design Integrated AI Curriculum for K-12 Classrooms
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the ACM conference article (arXiv preprint version provided)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how K-12 teachers can be supported to design AI curriculum that is integrated into core non-computing subjects, rather than taught only as standalone computer science content. The authors argue that AI education is often inaccessible to many teachers and learners, especially in non-CS classrooms, and they seek to identify what teachers value and need when incorporating AI into existing curricula.

To investigate this, the authors ran a two-day remote co-design workshop with 15 K-12 educators from diverse grade levels and subject areas. Participants received introductory presentations on AI, used several AI tools, completed pre-work, and then co-designed integrated lesson plans in small groups with researcher support. The resulting curricula connected AI with social studies, ESL, and literacy for students with learning disabilities, and the analysis focused on teachers’ design considerations: evaluation, engagement, logistics, collaboration, and ethics/scaffolding.

The main conclusion is that teachers see clear opportunities to embed AI into core subjects through data, reflection, and ethics, but they need stronger scaffolding, clearer tool guidance, and classroom-ready supports to do so confidently. The study does not test student learning outcomes or productivity gains; instead, it contributes design insights showing how teacher co-design can make AI education more accessible and more likely to fit real classroom constraints.

finding.finding_summary: The paper is centered on teacher workflow and curriculum-design process, but it does not measure productivity gains, time savings, or workload reduction from AI tools versus human-only support or non-AI digital tools. Instead, it reports that teachers valued scaffolding, clearer guidance on tools, and logistical supports while co-designing curricula, based on workshop discussion and post-workshop reflections (n=15).
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of curriculum design process, logistics, and tool support during a co-design workshop

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported higher confidence and greater comfort teaching AI after the workshop, with confidence about integrating AI into their curriculum averaging 5.6/7 at post-workshop, and familiarity with AI increasing from 4.8/7 to 5.8/7. This reflects increased self-efficacy and perceived readiness rather than a tested student outcome.
finding.measure: Self-reported familiarity with AI and confidence in integrating AI into curriculum (pre/post workshop ratings)
finding.std_deviation: pre-post means reported; SD not reported

finding.finding_summary: A central finding is that teachers valued and designed for student collaboration, reflection, and critical discussion as part of integrated AI lessons. The paper reports these as design priorities from the co-design process, but does not provide direct student outcome evidence or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Teacher-identified curriculum design priorities and lesson components (collaboration, reflection, discussion)

finding.finding_summary: Teachers successfully co-designed integrated AI lesson plans for social studies, ESL, and literacy, showing feasibility of embedding AI concepts into non-computing core subjects. The paper reports three draft curricula produced by the 15 teachers, but it does not evaluate student academic achievement on these topics.
finding.measure: Co-designed curriculum drafts integrating AI into social studies, ESL, and literacy

paper_profiles.title: Shiksha Copilot: Teacher-AI Collaboration for Curating and Customizing Lesson Plans in Low-Resource Schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how teachers in low-resource public schools in Karnataka, India used an LLM-based lesson-planning system, Shiksha Copilot, to generate, curate, translate, and customize curriculum-aligned lesson plans. The authors focus on a key practical question in teacher-facing AI: whether and how a human-in-the-loop system can support both pedagogical work and administrative documentation in multilingual, resource-constrained settings.

Shiksha Copilot combined curriculum ingestion, retrieval-augmented generation, expert curation, translation, and teacher-facing customization tools. First, curators reviewed AI-generated learning objectives and lesson plans, then translated and refined English lesson plans into Kannada; teachers later used the curated plans for classroom adaptation. The deployment involved 1,043 field teachers across 757 schools, with mixed-methods data from logs, surveys, and 43 interviews (teachers, curators, and mentors). The study emphasizes the full workflow rather than a simple chatbot: AI generated drafts, human experts improved them, and teachers used them for both instruction and record-keeping.

The main conclusions are that the tool was highly useful for reducing bureaucratic workload and lesson-planning time, while also lowering teacher stress and supporting activity-based pedagogy. English lesson plans were generally reliable with only minor edits, but Kannada translations required substantial linguistic correction, showing that multilingual quality remains a major challenge. Teachers often used the system pragmatically to satisfy documentation requirements, but they also adapted plans using their own expertise and off-platform resources. Overall, the study suggests that AI can improve teacher productivity in low-resource settings, but effective deployment depends on human curation, curriculum alignment, and attention to local language and institutional constraints.

finding.finding_summary: Shiksha Copilot reduced teachers’ lesson-planning and record-keeping burden. The paper reports measurable reductions in lesson planning time and teacher stress, and notes that teachers used the tool to meet administrative documentation needs as well as classroom preparation. In usage logs, 60.8% of users were single-day users (n=622), indicating the system supported concentrated planning workflows rather than requiring frequent incremental use.
finding.measure: Lesson planning time, time spent on administrative/record-keeping tasks, and teacher-reported workload/stress
finding.study_size: n=406 matched survey respondents; n=1,043 teachers in deployment; n=622 single-day users

finding.finding_summary: The intervention reduced teacher stress, which is one of the paper’s central survey outcomes. The authors state that Shiksha Copilot led to measurable reductions in teacher stress, assessed with the Teacher Stress Scale, alongside reduced workload and planning burden. However, the paper excerpt provided does not report the exact pre-post effect size or confidence interval.
finding.measure: Teacher Stress Scale (stress from teaching demands; stress from limited school-based support)

finding.finding_summary: The system supported creation of curriculum-aligned lesson plans across Science, Mathematics, Social Science, and English for grades 5–10, helping teachers prepare instructional materials for classroom use. The paper’s evidence is primarily about teacher-facing content creation rather than student learning outcomes; it shows that curated English lesson plans were largely classroom-ready, with 96.13% of English content blocks rated suitable for use and only 4.1% requiring edits.
finding.measure: Quality/rating of lesson plans and curriculum-aligned instructional content
finding.study_size: 991 curated lesson plans; 5,544 teacher-created lesson plans

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that the AI system helped teachers comply with administrative documentation requirements and fit into school and district workflows. It also reports broader organizational effects, including shifts in lesson-planning practices and constraints from staffing shortages and administrative demands that limited further pedagogical change. Because the system was deployed with government-school teachers and designed around mandated 5E lesson-plan formats, the institutional relevance is central to the study.
finding.measure: Administrative documentation use, workflow integration, and organizational/implementation effects
finding.study_size: n=1,043 teachers across 757 schools in 35 districts

paper_profiles.title: TerraGen: A Unified Multi-Task Layout Generation Framework for Remote Sensing Data Augmentation
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (remote sensing imagery / computer vision datasets, not human participants)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of task-isolated generative data augmentation in remote sensing. The authors argue that existing layout-conditioned generation methods are fragmented across tasks such as object detection, semantic segmentation, building extraction, road extraction, and flood detection, and that they often fail to model geographic constraints and cross-task structure in remote sensing scenes.

To address this, the paper proposes TerraGen, a unified layout-to-image diffusion framework that accepts task type, spatial layout (bounding boxes or masks), and text prompts as conditions. The model uses a geographic-spatial layout encoder, multi-scale layout injection into a Stable Diffusion U-Net, and an adaptive mask-weighted training loss to preserve both coarse structure and fine-grained spatial detail. The authors also construct a new multi-task remote sensing dataset of about 45k samples and a 1k-image benchmark for standardized evaluation.

Experiments compare TerraGen to remote-sensing-specific baselines and general controllable generation methods. TerraGen achieves the best or near-best image quality and layout-consistency scores across tasks, and the paper reports downstream data-augmentation gains in full-data and few-shot settings. Overall, the study concludes that a single unified layout representation can support cross-task knowledge transfer and improve synthetic data usefulness for remote sensing models.

finding.finding_summary: TerraGen is presented as a universal data-augmentation engine that reduces the need to train separate generative models for different remote sensing tasks, supporting an "annotate once, benefit multiple tasks" workflow. The paper reports that synthetic data generated by TerraGen improved downstream model performance across object detection, semantic segmentation, building extraction, road extraction, and flood detection, indicating practical gains in training efficiency and data scalability; however, no direct teacher or administrator workload study was conducted.
finding.measure: Downstream model performance after synthetic-data augmentation; cross-task utility of generated layouts

paper_profiles.title: Byzantine-Resilient SGD in High Dimensions on Heterogeneous Data
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies distributed stochastic gradient descent (SGD) in a master-worker architecture when some workers are Byzantine (malicious or faulty) and when workers hold heterogeneous local datasets. The core question is how to robustly aggregate worker gradients so the master can still optimize a global empirical risk objective under adversarial corruption, without assuming that workers’ data come from the same distribution.

The proposed approach uses a robust gradient estimation (RGE) procedure based on outlier filtering from robust mean estimation, combined with mini-batch SGD. The authors derive a new matrix concentration bound to justify this filtering step in the heterogeneous-data setting, and prove convergence guarantees for both smooth strongly-convex and non-convex objectives. They show the method tolerates up to 1/4 Byzantine workers, and that increasing the mini-batch size reduces stochastic variance and improves the approximation error up to a term driven by data heterogeneity.

They also extend the method to compressed communication, where workers send random k coordinates of their gradients. Under mild conditions, this preserves the convergence rate and approximation error up to order-wise constants while reducing communication and decoding cost by a factor of d/k. The paper is methodological and theoretical, aimed at distributed learning and federated-learning-style settings rather than K-12 educational practice; there is no empirical study of teachers, students, or schools.

paper_profiles.title: Juxtaposing Controlled Empirical Studies in Visualization with Topic Developments in Psychology
paper_profiles.venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a state-of-the-art survey that compares controlled and semi-controlled empirical studies in visualization with topic developments in psychology. Its main question is how visualization experiments relate to established psychological research themes, and whether visualization researchers can draw on psychology to better frame perceptual and cognitive questions. The authors assemble and taxonomically analyze 129 controlled empirical studies in visualization and juxtapose them with a text-mining analysis of major psychology journal topics from 1978 to 2017.

The visualization side of the paper focuses on how empirical studies can be categorized by study purpose, knowledge scope, visualization tasks, behavioral measures, and related design variables. The psychology side uses Voyant Tools, tag clouds, temporal tag clouds, and ThemeRiver visualizations to track keyword trends in Behavioral and Brain Sciences and Psychological Review. The paper concludes that many visualization experiments map to established psychological topics, while some visualization-specific tasks and contexts still require new empirical work. It also proposes a general taxonomy for empirical studies in visualization that can accommodate controlled, semi-controlled, and uncontrolled studies.

Because this is a survey and taxonomy paper rather than an intervention study, it does not evaluate K-12 classroom outcomes or AI-enabled productivity tools for teachers. Its contribution is methodological and conceptual, aimed at organizing empirical research rather than testing educational effectiveness in schools.

paper_profiles.title: KubeAdaptor: A Docking Framework for Workflow Containerization on Kubernetes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a systems problem in cloud-native workflow execution: when workflow systems are migrated to Kubernetes, the Kubernetes scheduler may execute task pods in an order that does not match the workflow scheduler’s optimized task order. The authors argue that this mismatch reduces workflow execution efficiency and makes it difficult for existing workflow engines to realize the benefits of their own scheduling algorithms.

To solve this, they propose KubeAdaptor, a docking framework that integrates workflow systems with Kubernetes while preserving the workflow scheduling order. The framework uses a workflow injection module, Kubernetes resource monitoring via Informer, event-triggered creation and deletion of pods and namespaces, and dynamic storage provisioning through StorageClass/PVC/NFS so that tasks can share data within a workflow namespace. The system is evaluated on four scientific workflows—Montage, Epigenomics, CyberShake, and LIGO—running on a six-node Kubernetes cluster. The comparison is against Argo and batch-job submission methods, not against human support or educational tools.

The experimental results show that KubeAdaptor maintains consistency between workflow scheduling and pod execution order and improves workflow execution efficiency. Reported gains include reductions in average task-pod execution time versus Argo of up to 24.45%, 47.57%, 23.72%, and 24.65% across the four workflows, along with reductions in average workflow lifecycle of up to 43.44%, 43.65%, 44.86%, and 48.98%. The paper concludes that the proposed architecture reduces Kubernetes apiserver pressure and improves resource usage for containerized workflows.

finding.finding_summary: KubeAdaptor improved workflow execution efficiency relative to Argo and Batch Job submission by reducing average task pod execution time and average workflow lifecycle across four workflows.
