Reported reductions versus Argo reached up to 24.45% (Montage), 47.57% (Epigenomics), 23.72% (CyberShake), and 24.65% (LIGO) for task-pod execution time, and up to 43.44%, 43.65%, 44.86%, and 48.98% for workflow lifecycle.
finding.measure: Average task pod execution time; average workflow lifecycle; resource usage rate
finding.study_size: n=4 workflows, 100 runs each per workflow submission approach

paper_profiles.title: A 20 Gbps Data Transmitting ASIC with PAM4 for Particle Physics Experiments
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes the design, fabrication, and bench testing of GBS20, a custom data-transmitting ASIC intended for particle physics detector readout links. The motivation is to double per-fiber bandwidth relative to existing lpGBT/VTRx+ systems used in high-energy physics experiments, thereby reducing fiber count and simplifying detector data transmission infrastructure.

The authors present the architecture of the first prototype, GBS20v0, which integrates two serializers, a shared PLL, and a PAM4 encoder/VCSEL driver chain. A 65 nm CMOS prototype was fabricated and tested up to 20.48 Gbps using an internal PRBS generator, but the results exposed nonlinearity, limited dynamic range, and layout-related noise issues. Based on these test results, the team proposes a second prototype, GBS20v1, with higher supply voltage for the PAM4 stage, separate gain control paths, stronger output peaking, and a programmable source load to improve eye quality and increase output current.

The paper is an engineering R&D report for detector electronics, not an education study. It does not involve K-12 learners, teachers, schools, or administrative workflows in educational settings, and it reports no outcomes relevant to AI-enabled productivity in education.

paper_profiles.title: Connecting Feedback to Choice: Understanding Educator Preferences in GenAI vs. Human-Created Lesson Plans in K-12 Education – A Comparative Analysis
paper_profiles.population: K-12 mathematics educators (elementary, middle, and high school)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether K-12 educators prefer lesson plans generated by generative AI models or by human curriculum designers, and which parts of a lesson plan are most favored. The authors address a practical problem in AI adoption for education: lesson planning is time-consuming, but it is unclear whether GenAI can produce instructional materials that teachers would actually want to use.

The study compares lesson plans produced by a customized GPT-4 model, a fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model, and human-authored plans retrieved from open lesson-plan repositories. Twenty experienced K-12 mathematics educators evaluated 529 lesson-plan pairs across four dimensions: warm-up, main tasks, cool-down, and overall quality. The study combines pairwise preference analysis with qualitative thematic analysis of 2,979 educator comments.

Results show that human-created lesson plans were generally preferred overall, especially for elementary-grade instruction and for components requiring pedagogical nuance, student discourse, group work, and scaffolding. GenAI performed comparatively better on cool-down activities and was more competitive at higher grade levels, with the fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b sometimes outperforming human plans in high school comparisons. The authors conclude that GenAI is best viewed as a collaborative planning assistant rather than a replacement for educator expertise, with particular promise for structured lesson components and potential workload reduction.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that GenAI lesson-plan generation can reduce educator workload by assisting with a time-consuming planning task, and concludes that it can serve as an efficient planning assistant rather than a replacement for teacher expertise. However, the study measures educator preferences and perceived usefulness, not actual time saved, so the evidence is indirect rather than a direct productivity experiment.
finding.measure: Educator preferences for AI-generated versus human-created lesson plans; qualitative comments about usefulness and workload reduction potential
finding.study_size: n=20 educators; 529 lesson plan pairs; 2,116 pairwise evaluations; 2,979 comments

paper_profiles.title: Data Encoding for Byzantine-Resilient Distributed Optimization
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (distributed optimization / machine learning systems study, not a K-12 human population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies how to make distributed optimization robust to Byzantine adversaries—worker machines that may behave arbitrarily or send corrupted updates—while preserving computational efficiency. The core problem is how a master node can correctly compute gradients and coordinate-descent updates when some workers are untrusted, and how to do so with low storage, communication, and decoding overhead.

The authors propose data-encoding schemes based on sparse real-valued error-correcting codes for two settings: proximal gradient descent / gradient descent and coordinate descent. Their approach encodes the data matrix across workers, enables exact recovery of matrix-vector products despite up to nearly half the workers being corrupt, and extends to stochastic gradient descent and streaming data. They provide theoretical guarantees and complexity bounds, plus experiments showing the method’s efficiency on linear regression tasks under corruption.

The paper is not an education intervention study and does not involve K-12 students or teachers directly. It is best understood as a systems / optimization methods paper about reliable distributed computation, with implications for large-scale learning infrastructure rather than instructional practice.

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central contribution is an exact Byzantine-resilient distributed optimization scheme that reduces the inefficiency of corrupted-worker settings. For gradient computation, the authors show exact recovery with per-worker computation O((1+ϵ)nd/m), master computation O((1+ϵ)(n+d)m), and constant-factor storage overhead when tolerating up to about m/3 corrupt workers; for coordinate descent, similar constant-overhead guarantees are provided when each worker updates τ coordinates. The experiments are reported as demonstrating the efficiency of the proposed schemes on linear regression under varying numbers of corrupt workers, but no numerical effect size is given in the excerpt.
finding.measure: Storage, computation, communication, and runtime efficiency of distributed optimization / matrix-vector multiplication under Byzantine corruption

paper_profiles.title: TPS-BENCH: Evaluating AI Agents’ Tool Planning & Scheduling Abilities in Compounding Tasks
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces TPS-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating large language model (LLM) agents on compound, multi-step tasks that require both tool selection and execution scheduling. The authors argue that existing agent benchmarks emphasize whether a task can be solved, but under-measure how efficiently an agent plans tool use and orders tool calls when multiple subtasks have dependencies or can be parallelized.

TPS-Bench contains 200 compound tasks built from 141 tools across 15 MCP servers, spanning activities such as web search, map navigation, calendar checking, weather queries, and other everyday workflows. The benchmark has two difficulty levels: TPS-Bench-Easy, with simpler and weakly related subtasks, and TPS-Bench-Hard, with tighter dependencies and more complex scheduling demands. Performance is evaluated using LLM-as-a-judge for task completion and tool selection, plus token usage, turns, and wall-clock time for efficiency.

The paper evaluates several closed- and open-source LLMs and finds a clear trade-off between effectiveness and efficiency. Models that schedule more sequentially, such as GLM-4.5, achieve the highest completion rates but at much higher time and token cost, while models that parallelize aggressively, such as GPT-4o, are faster but complete fewer tasks. An RL fine-tuning experiment on Qwen3-1.7B using only 100 samples improves completion rate by 6% and reduces execution time by 14%, suggesting that scheduling behavior can be improved with post-training.

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark shows a strong trade-off between task success and efficiency in LLM agent workflows. On TPS-Bench-Hard, GLM-4.5 achieved the highest task completion rate (64.72%) but required 217.8 seconds, 12.6k input tokens, and 35.0 tool-call turns per task, whereas GPT-4o finished faster (76.84s, 2.5 turns) but completed only 45.08% of tasks. After GRPO training on 100 samples, Qwen3-1.7B improved task completion by 6% and reduced execution time by 14% (from 42.0s to 36.1s).
finding.measure: Task completion rate, input/output tokens, tool-call turns, and end-to-end execution time
finding.study_size: n=7 models on TPS-Bench; RL ablation n=1 model with 100 training samples

paper_profiles.title: The Promises and Challenges of Artificial Intelligence for Teachers: a Systematic Review of Research
paper_profiles.population: Elementary (PreK-5th) to High School; mixed K-12 teacher populations
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This systematic review synthesizes empirical research on how teachers use artificial intelligence (AI) in K-12 education and what roles teachers play in AI-based research. The authors screened Web of Science journal articles from the past 20 years and retained 44 empirical studies focused on in-service K-12 teachers and, in a few cases, pre-service teachers, examining AI applications such as automated scoring, intelligent tutoring, prediction models, and classroom sensing tools.

The review asks what kinds of data are collected from teachers, how teachers contribute to AI development, what benefits AI provides, what challenges arise in implementation, and which AI methods are most common. Across the studies, teachers most often appeared as data sources for training AI systems, grading/validation, or providing pedagogical guidance; AI was most often reported to help with planning, timely monitoring, feedback, intervention, and assessment. The review also found persistent limitations in AI reliability, technical capacity, infrastructure, contextual transferability, and teachers’ AI-related knowledge. The subject areas most represented were STEM, mathematics, English, and primary education, while pre-service teacher participation was notably limited.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, AI was generally reported to reduce teacher workload and improve efficiency in planning, monitoring, feedback, intervention, and assessment. The review synthesized 44 studies and noted the most common implementation benefit was timely monitoring of learning processes (f=12), along with reduced workload (f=8) and automated essay/exam scoring (f=7).
finding.measure: Teacher workload, planning efficiency, monitoring timeliness, automated scoring, and feedback provision as reported across primary studies

finding.finding_summary: The review focused substantively on AI used to support instructional content and assessment across subjects such as English, mathematics, primary education, and STEM. It found AI could help teachers choose appropriate learning content and automate assessment, but also that AI systems sometimes failed on text complexity, image-containing texts, and context-dependent tasks, indicating mixed instructional utility rather than a uniform benefit.
finding.measure: Instructional planning support, content readability classification, and automated assessment/essay scoring across subject areas

finding.finding_summary: The review identified AI supports for student engagement and teacher responsiveness, including timely feedback, monitoring of student concentration, and tracking of student progress. These functions were discussed as enabling teachers to respond earlier and more effectively to learners’ needs, with several studies specifically modeling engagement-related outcomes.
finding.measure: Engagement, concentration, and student progress indicators modeled or monitored by AI

paper_profiles.title: Teachers’ AI digital competencies and twenty-first century skills in the post-pandemic world
paper_profiles.population: K-16 educators (with emphasis on teachers; not limited to K-12)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conceptual paper addresses a growing problem in post-pandemic education: teachers are increasingly expected to use AI-enabled tools for teaching, assessment, communication, and administration, yet many lack clear guidance on the competencies needed to do so effectively and ethically. The authors ask what AI digital competencies educators need and how existing competency frameworks can be adapted to AI-rich teaching environments.

Rather than testing an intervention, the paper synthesizes prior research, policy documents, and framework literature to propose an expanded model. It adapts the DigCompEdu educator digital competence framework and the P21 twenty-first century learning framework, and relates them to existing AI competency work and a revised TPACK lens. The paper argues that AI competency for teachers should include not only technical skills, but also instructional design, content choices across disciplines, ethical judgment, collaboration, communication, creativity, and life/career skills.

The context is the post-pandemic shift toward online and blended learning, where AI tools are increasingly used for personalized support, learning analytics, automatic feedback, grading, resource recommendation, and administrative support. The paper’s main conclusion is that teachers need ongoing professional development, policy guidance, and subject-sensitive support to integrate AI in ways that improve teaching and learning while protecting against privacy, bias, overreliance, and other ethical risks. It is a framework-building and recommendation paper, not an empirical evaluation of student or teacher outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues, based on cited examples and prior literature, that AI tools can reduce teacher workload by automating routine administrative tasks such as grading, repetitive paperwork, feedback generation, and some assessment and data-analysis work. However, this is a conceptual synthesis rather than a direct empirical test, so no effect size or sample size is reported.
finding.measure: teacher workload, administrative task automation, grading and feedback efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on institutional and policy implications, arguing that universities, schools, professional organizations, and policymakers should develop standards, guidelines, and professional development to support AI competency in education. It proposes adapting the DigCompEdu and P21 frameworks and emphasizes governance concerns such as ethical use, privacy, and responsible AI integration; no empirical effect size is reported.
finding.measure: framework adaptation, policy guidance, professional development standards, institutional guidance for AI integration

finding.finding_summary: A major substantive focus of the paper is that AI competency should include durable skills such as critical thinking, collaboration, communication, creativity, self-regulation, and problem solving. The paper does not report a new empirical study of these skills; instead it synthesizes prior work and argues that AI integration should be designed to strengthen them across disciplines.
finding.measure: critical thinking, collaboration, communication, creativity, self-regulation, problem solving

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses social-emotional and motivational outcomes mainly in relation to teachers’ and students’ use of AI tools, including self-efficacy, self-regulation, motivation, and attitudes toward AI. These claims are supported through literature examples rather than original data, so no effect size or sample size is available.
finding.measure: self-efficacy, self-regulation, motivation, attitudes toward AI

paper_profiles.title: AI literacy in K-12: a systematic literature review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper systematically reviews how artificial intelligence (AI) literacy is being integrated into K-12 education worldwide. The authors searched Scopus and screened 750 records, ultimately reviewing 179 documents that covered both learning experiences and broader theoretical/implementation perspectives. The review was motivated by the rapid growth of AI and the need for education systems to prepare students to understand, use, and critically evaluate AI technologies from early schooling onward.

The paper organizes the literature into two major streams: hands-on learning experiences and theoretical/implementation proposals. Learning experiences include activities to help students recognize AI artifacts, understand how AI works, use AI tools, and think critically about AI's societal implications. Implementation-oriented papers focus on curriculum design, AI as a subject, student perspectives, teacher training, support resources, and gender diversity. Across the literature, the authors find that K-12 AI education is still early-stage and often limited to technical or applied skills in narrow domains, with very few studies rigorously assessing learning outcomes.

The review concludes that AI literacy should be interdisciplinary, competency-based, and integrated into existing subjects rather than treated as a standalone AI course. It emphasizes the importance of curricular guidance, modular and context-sensitive design, ethical and social considerations, and especially teacher co-design and teacher preparation. The paper highlights national and institutional efforts in places such as the U.S. and China, but argues that stronger evidence is still needed on what students learn, how teachers are prepared, and how these initiatives function across contexts.

finding.finding_summary: The review finds substantial policy and curriculum activity around K-12 AI literacy, especially in the U.S. (AI4K12) and China (national compulsory secondary curriculum), but also notes that implementation remains uneven and not yet widespread. The paper argues that AI literacy initiatives need competency frameworks, modular curricula, and teacher co-design to be effective, indicating important institutional momentum but limited mature system-level evidence.
finding.measure: Presence and characterization of national/curricular implementation proposals, policy guidelines, and institutional initiatives

finding.finding_summary: The review repeatedly emphasizes AI literacy as a means to build critical thinking, ethical reasoning, and problem-solving around AI, although most included studies did not directly measure these outcomes rigorously. The literature described includes proposals aimed at helping students critically evaluate AI, understand its social consequences, and engage in real-world problem solving.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, ethical reflection, problem-solving, and related competency-oriented AI literacy goals

finding.finding_summary: Several studies in the review examined student interest, attitudes, and intentions to learn AI, and the authors note that motivation can be supported by real-world and social-good framing. However, the review also indicates that these affective outcomes are usually discussed more than empirically measured, so evidence is suggestive rather than strong.
finding.measure: Student interest, attitudes, behavioral intention, and motivation toward learning AI

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that AI literacy can enhance the teaching of disciplinary subjects by integrating AI into existing classroom processes and potentially improving instructional practice, but it does not report direct productivity or workload measures. It also stresses that teacher training, co-design, and appropriate resources are necessary conditions for any efficiency gains to materialize.
finding.measure: Teacher preparation, curriculum integration, and instructional use of AI to support teaching processes

paper_profiles.title: Understanding K–12 teachers’ technological pedagogical content knowledge readiness and attitudes toward artificial intelligence education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study investigates K–12 teachers’ readiness to teach artificial intelligence (AI) and their attitudes toward AI education, addressing a gap in the literature on teacher preparedness for AI instruction. The authors focus on AI-specific technological pedagogical content knowledge (TPACK) and two attitude dimensions: perceived importance of teaching AI and interest in teaching AI.

The study surveyed 1,664 K–12 teachers from multiple provinces in Mainland China using adapted AI-specific TPACK and teacher-attitude questionnaires. Analyses included descriptive statistics, cluster analysis, t-tests, ANOVAs, and multinomial logistic regression to examine overall readiness, patterns of teacher profiles, and differences by gender, teaching subject, teaching grade, teaching experience, and prior experience teaching AI.

Results showed that teachers rated their pedagogical knowledge higher than their AI content and technological knowledge, indicating a notable gap in AI-related CK and TK. Five distinct readiness-attitude clusters emerged, including groups with high readiness/high attitudes and others with low readiness but differing attitudes. Demographic patterns suggested that male teachers, primary school teachers, and teachers with prior AI-teaching experience generally reported stronger TPACK readiness; prior AI-teaching experience was the most consistent predictor of higher readiness and more positive attitudes. The paper concludes that AI teacher professional development should be age-appropriate, pedagogically differentiated, and supported by clearer policy and guidance.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly examines implications for AI teacher professional development, curriculum guidance, and policy support rather than measuring a student outcome. Based on a survey of 1,664 K–12 teachers, the authors argue that clearer age-appropriate AI standards, guidance, and organizational learning structures are needed to improve teachers’ readiness and attitudes toward AI education.
finding.measure: Teacher survey of AI-specific TPACK, attitudes, and demographic predictors; policy/professional development implications derived from these measures

finding.finding_summary: The study focuses on teacher readiness for AI instruction, which is closely tied to implementation capacity and instructional efficiency rather than direct productivity metrics. Teachers with prior experience teaching AI reported higher scores on all seven AI-specific TPACK factors than those without such experience, suggesting better preparedness to implement AI teaching effectively; however, no direct workload or time-savings measure was reported.
finding.measure: AI-specific TPACK readiness (CK, PK, TK, TPK, TCK, PCK, TPACK)

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively measures teachers’ attitudes toward AI education, including perceived importance and interest, which are motivational/affective constructs. Teachers reported high average attitudes overall (importance M=3.953, interest M=3.885), and teachers with prior AI-teaching experience had significantly higher attitudes than those without such experience, indicating stronger willingness to engage with AI teaching.
finding.measure: Perceived importance of teaching AI; interest in teaching AI

finding.finding_summary: The study does not measure student durable skills directly, but it does assess teachers’ perceived pedagogical readiness and AI-specific knowledge, including comprehensive knowledge for integrating AI technology, pedagogy, and content. Teachers scored higher on pedagogical knowledge than on AI content and technological knowledge, suggesting uneven capacity to support higher-order AI instruction; no direct effect on student critical thinking or collaboration was measured.
finding.measure: AI-specific TPACK dimensions related to pedagogical and integrative knowledge

paper_profiles.title: How should we change teaching and assessment in response to increasingly powerful generative Artificial Intelligence? Outcomes of the ChatGPT teacher survey
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how educators believe teaching and assessment should change in response to increasingly powerful generative AI such as ChatGPT, and what motivates those changes. It was written in the immediate aftermath of ChatGPT’s release and is positioned as a baseline study for later comparison as teacher beliefs evolve.

The authors used a mixed-methods survey with 318 educators drawn from elementary/primary, secondary/high school, and university settings. The survey collected Likert-scale ratings of perceived AI impact on teaching and assessment, plus open-ended responses about desired changes and motivations for change. Quantitative analyses modeled perceived impact against demographics and contextual factors such as teaching level, region, experience, gender, and AI awareness; qualitative thematic analysis coded suggested curricular, pedagogical, and assessment changes, as well as motivations using the UTAUT2 framework.

The main conclusion is that most educators expected generative AI to have a major or profound impact on both teaching and assessment, but perceptions varied by AI awareness, region, gender, and teaching level. Teachers most often recommended teaching students how to use AI, understand how it works, think critically about AI outputs, and use AI ethically. For assessment, they favored more oral, supervised, authentic, higher-order, and process-oriented tasks, while some suggested embedding AI into assessment workflows. Motivations for change were dominated by performance expectancy, especially improving student learning and maintaining fair, authentic assessment.

finding.finding_summary: Educators overwhelmingly argued that teaching should shift toward durable skills such as critical thinking, creativity, collaboration, and ethical judgment in response to generative AI. In the qualitative coding of teaching changes, 38 responses emphasized teaching students to critically evaluate AI outputs and 26 emphasized ethical and responsible AI use; the discussion concludes that these suggestions center on higher-order thinking and process-oriented learning rather than rote content delivery.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses on how teaching should change; thematic coding of curricular and pedagogical changes

finding.finding_summary: Teachers frequently expected generative AI to improve their own and their students' performance and reduce effort in teaching and assessment work. Performance expectancy dominated the motivation codes (teaching: n=233; assessment: n=264), with many respondents saying AI would improve workflow, help create resources, make assessment easier, and support faster feedback and plagiarism checking.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses on motivations to change teaching and assessment; thematic coding under UTAUT2 performance expectancy and effort expectancy

finding.finding_summary: The study found strong perceived impact on teaching and assessment practices across subject areas, with teachers proposing subject-specific AI uses and changes to classroom tasks. Examples included using ChatGPT to translate Latin texts, support Spanish instruction, explain code or statistics, and create differentiated resources; however, these were primarily perceptions and suggestions rather than outcome measures.
finding.measure: Perceived impact ratings and open-ended examples of subject-specific teaching/assessment adaptation
finding.std_deviation: 0.9 for teaching-impact scale; 0.9 for assessment-impact scale (Likert-response SDs reported in paper)

finding.finding_summary: Teachers repeatedly framed AI-related changes as a way to boost student engagement, authenticity, and readiness for an AI-saturated future, which maps to motivation and engagement rather than test achievement alone. In the motivation coding, many responses stressed that students should 'not be missing out,' 'be made aware,' and 'be ready,' indicating a perceived need to sustain student motivation and engagement through AI-informed teaching and assessment.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses on motivations for change and perceived pedagogical shifts

paper_profiles.title: What Explains Teachers’ Trust in AI in Education Across Six Countries?
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.population: K-12 teachers (middle school, junior high, high school, upper secondary)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks what explains K-12 teachers’ trust in AI-based educational technology (AI-EdTech) across six countries: Brazil, Israel, Japan, Norway, Sweden, and the USA. The authors frame trust as a key condition for teachers’ willingness to adopt AI tools in classrooms, and examine whether trust is related to perceived benefits, concerns, demographic and professional characteristics, AI self-efficacy, AI understanding, cultural values, and geographic location.

The study uses an anonymous survey of 508 teachers and multiple regression models. Teachers reported trust in AI-EdTech, perceived benefits, perceived concerns, AI-EdTech self-efficacy, AI understanding, cultural values, age, gender, education, subject area, years in education, and years teaching with technology. The analysis also included country fixed effects to compare national samples.

The main finding is that trust in AI-EdTech is strongly associated with perceived benefits and lower concerns. Teachers with higher AI-EdTech self-efficacy and better understanding of AI reported more perceived benefits, fewer concerns, and higher trust; however, these effects on trust were largely mediated by benefits and concerns in the combined model. Cultural values also mattered: higher uncertainty avoidance predicted higher trust, and in the combined model higher masculinity and collectivism were additional predictors of trust. By contrast, age, gender, education level, subject taught, and years of teaching with technology were not significant predictors. The authors conclude that professional development and teacher training that improve basic AI understanding, self-efficacy, and culturally responsive guidance may support adoption of AI-EdTech in K-12 settings.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies teachers’ perceived benefits of AI-EdTech, including productivity- and workflow-related uses, and finds that higher AI-EdTech self-efficacy and better AI understanding predicted more perceived benefits. In the regression model for perceived benefits (n=508), AI-EdTech self-efficacy was positively associated with benefits (b=0.18, p<0.001) and AI understanding was also positive (b=0.11, p<0.05).
finding.measure: Perceived benefits of AI-EdTech index (7-item Likert scale), including teacher productivity/planning/support items
finding.effect_size: b=0.18 for self-efficacy; b=0.11 for AI understanding

finding.finding_summary: The study directly addresses institutional adoption conditions for AI in K-12 education by examining trust in AI-EdTech across countries and by discussing teacher training and policy guidance. Teachers’ trust varied significantly by country, with Brazilian, Israeli, and Japanese samples generally reporting higher trust than Norwegian, Swedish, and US samples, and the authors argue that AI competency development, transparency, and culturally sensitive guidance are important for adoption.
finding.measure: Trust in AI-EdTech index and country fixed effects in regression models

paper_profiles.title: Students’ perceptions of using ChatGPT in a physics class as a virtual tutor
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how undergraduate students perceive ChatGPT when used as a virtual tutor in an introductory physics class. The authors focus on three questions: ChatGPT’s accuracy in answering physics problems, whether students’ trust depends on answer accuracy, and how trust shapes perceptions of usefulness, ease of use, and future intention to use ChatGPT.

The intervention/approach involved 40 students using ChatGPT to help complete a makeup assignment for missed points on a second exam in a 16-week introductory physics course. Students asked ChatGPT about questions they had answered incorrectly, compared its answers with the exam key, and then completed a survey; a subset also submitted drawings representing their perceptions of ChatGPT. The study combines quantitative analyses of answer accuracy, trust group differences, and survey responses with qualitative coding of student drawings to characterize misconceptions and anthropomorphic views of AI.

Overall, ChatGPT answered physics questions with 85% accuracy, but many students trusted its answers even when incorrect. Trust was associated with more positive perceptions of ease of use and a higher likelihood of future use, and drawing data suggested that many students viewed ChatGPT as a robot/machine, sometimes with super-intelligent or magical qualities. The paper concludes that students need stronger AI literacy and critical thinking skills, and that educational use of GenAI should be accompanied by explicit caution, prompt engineering guidance, and designs that avoid excessive anthropomorphism.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT answered 307 of 362 physics questions correctly (85% accuracy) for undergraduate students in an introductory physics class, but performance varied across items and sometimes changed after follow-up prompts. The paper does not report a formal learning gain, but it does show that ChatGPT can answer many physics-concept questions correctly while remaining error-prone on science content.
finding.measure: Accuracy of ChatGPT responses to physics exam questions (light, radioactivity, and related concepts)
finding.study_size: n=40 students; 362 ChatGPT question-answer instances (46 unique questions)

finding.finding_summary: Students’ trust in ChatGPT was significantly associated with their perceptions of the tool: the Trust group rated ChatGPT as easier to use than the Partial Trust group, and showed a borderline higher intention to use it in the future. However, many students trusted ChatGPT even when its answers were wrong, indicating weak critical evaluation and susceptibility to blind trust.
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and intention to use; trust group differences; agreement with ChatGPT answers
finding.effect_size: eta2=0.175 for MANOVA on perception by trust level; eta2=0.257 for ANOVA on answer accuracy by trust level

finding.finding_summary: The study found that students’ trust patterns shaped their willingness to accept ChatGPT’s answers and their reported perceptions of the tool, suggesting affective reliance and confidence in the AI system. Many participants agreed with ChatGPT even when incorrect, which the authors interpret as blind trust rather than calibrated skepticism.
finding.measure: Trust in ChatGPT; agreement with answers; perceived usefulness/ease of use; intention to use

paper_profiles.title: JIME Special Issue on Reusing Online Resources: Commentary and Debate on Reusing Online Resources: A Sustainable Approach to eLearning
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Interactive Media in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This special issue is a commentary and debate forum built around the book *Reusing Online Resources: A Sustainable Approach to eLearning*. Rather than reporting a single empirical study, it assembles editorials, chapter introductions, and expert commentaries that discuss the promise and limits of reusable online learning resources (often framed as learning objects) in e-learning.

Across the included essays, the core question is how digital learning resources can be designed, described, shared, and reused effectively across courses, disciplines, institutions, and countries. The contributors argue that reuse is not just a technical issue of metadata and standards; it also depends on pedagogical design, resource granularity, contextual information, interoperability, and institutional change. Several pieces emphasize that learning objects alone are insufficient unless combined with activities, dialogue, learning design, and human judgment.

The context is higher education and online learning broadly, with some discussion of schools and further education, but the paper is not an intervention study and does not evaluate student outcomes. Its main conclusion is that reuse is feasible only if technical standards are matched by support for teachers, learners, repositories, and institutional practices that make reuse practical and pedagogically meaningful.

finding.finding_summary: The issue argues that reusable online resources could reshape institutional roles, staff collaboration, and cross-institutional sharing, but it does not report empirical outcome data. Contributors emphasize that implementation depends on standards, metadata, repositories, copyright policy, staff development, and organizational change across schools, colleges, and universities.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of institutional roles, standards, staff development, repositories, and sharing practices

paper_profiles.title: A Differentiated Discussion About AI Education K-12
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual and descriptive overview of the emerging field of AI education for K-12, organized around four dimensions: formal versus informal education, collaboration among AI researchers, education researchers, and teachers, the level of education, and concepts/tools for teaching AI. Rather than evaluating a single intervention, it surveys a range of national and international initiatives and argues that AI literacy is becoming important for younger learners because AI increasingly shapes daily life, society, and the economy.

The paper contrasts formal efforts such as AI4K12, AI Singapore programs, Chinese and South Korean curriculum initiatives, Australian curriculum mapping, and European teacher-training projects with informal approaches such as Elements of AI and the Technovation AI Family Challenge. It emphasizes that formal programs often provide curricula, guidelines, certification, or train-the-trainer models, while informal programs are more agile and scalable. The article also highlights the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration and teacher support, noting that advanced K-12 AI education is difficult to implement without strong academic background, adequate school support, and well-prepared teachers.

In addition, the paper reviews pedagogical concepts and tools used in K-12 AI education, including constructivist approaches, unplugged activities, block-based environments, Python-based tools, and no-code machine learning platforms such as Teachable Machine. Its main conclusion is that the field is growing quickly but remains fragmented, with a need for curated, quality-assessed repositories and stronger evidence from larger, longer-term deployments across grade bands. The paper does not report original empirical evaluation results; it primarily synthesizes examples and implementation lessons from the literature and initiatives it cites.

finding.finding_summary: This paper argues that K-12 AI education is expanding through both formal and informal institutional efforts, but implementation depends heavily on curricula, guidelines, teacher training, and school support. It reports that national initiatives and teacher-certification models can provide structure and reach, while also noting that advanced programs are only feasible in privileged settings with strong infrastructure and well-prepared teachers. No original effect size or sample-based outcome evaluation is reported.
finding.measure: Policy, curriculum, teacher-training, and institutional implementation conditions for K-12 AI education

finding.finding_summary: The article describes several teacher-facing initiatives and tools intended to make AI education easier to deploy, such as train-the-trainer programs, ready-to-use materials, repositories, and low-barrier tools like block-based environments and no-code machine learning platforms. The central claim is that these supports can improve scalability and reduce the burden of introducing AI content in schools, but the paper does not provide quantified workload or productivity results.
finding.measure: Teacher preparation, usability of tools, and scalability of instructional delivery

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly emphasizes constructivist and project-based AI learning as a way to build understanding, problem solving, and the ability to analyze AI systems. It treats these as design principles for K-12 AI education rather than as outcomes of a controlled study, so the evidence is conceptual and illustrative rather than empirical.
finding.measure: Problem solving, understanding, and analysis of AI concepts through constructivist activities

paper_profiles.title: Transitioning to Online Teaching During the COVID-19 Pandemic: an Exploration of STEM Teachers’ Views, Successes, and Challenges
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Science Education and Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how K-12 STEM teachers in a Canadian province experienced the abrupt shift to online/distance teaching during COVID-19 school closures. The authors were interested in teachers’ views and attitudes toward online teaching, as well as the successes and challenges they encountered while teaching remotely, with interpretation guided by self-efficacy theory and the TPACK framework.

Data came from an online questionnaire administered to 70 Grade 1–12 science/STEM teachers between May and July 2020. The study used a convergent mixed-methods design, combining Likert-scale responses with open-ended survey responses. The sample included elementary/middle and secondary teachers, with varied teaching experience and educational backgrounds.

Overall, teachers reported mostly negative experiences with emergency remote teaching. Many said the transition was not smooth, workload was unfair, and online teaching was challenging for both teachers and students. At the same time, some teachers reported benefits such as greater student engagement for quieter or anxious students, improved autonomy, increased use of digital tools, and opportunities for differentiated instruction. The paper concludes that teachers’ technological competency, self-efficacy, and prior exposure to digital tools helped somewhat, but were not enough to offset the broader challenges. The authors recommend stronger professional development, better support, clearer direction from leadership, and more coherent policy and infrastructure for future online learning efforts.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that online teaching had both positive and negative effects on student engagement and autonomy. While 59% said online platforms increased engagement for quieter or anxious students and 37% said student autonomy improved, most teachers still described engagement as a major challenge (49%) and a generally negative feature of emergency remote teaching.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported student engagement, autonomy, and participation from survey Likert items and open-ended responses

finding.finding_summary: Teachers described gains in student self-pacing, ownership, and independent work habits, indicating some support for durable skills such as self-regulation and autonomy. However, these benefits were uneven and often constrained by weak engagement and limited accountability in the remote setting.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported student independence, self-pacing, and responsibility for learning

finding.finding_summary: The transition to online teaching substantially increased teacher workload and time burden. In the survey, 51.4% said the workload was unfair, and open-ended responses described 8+ hour workdays, constant monitoring across platforms, and substantial time spent recreating lessons and assessing work. No effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, time use, and perceived efficiency during online teaching

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that institutional supports and policy direction did not match expectations, with unclear Ministry guidance, changing requirements, and insufficient support for implementation. The paper also notes that access, platform provision, and professional development were uneven, creating systemic barriers to effective emergency remote teaching.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported support from leadership/administration, Ministry guidance, and institutional readiness

paper_profiles.title: A systematic review of teaching and learning machine learning in K-12 education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper systematically reviews the K-12 machine learning (ML) education literature to map the field’s current focus and identify research gaps. The authors asked what areas of ML teaching and learning have been studied in K-12 and what issues and future directions emerge from that literature. They screened 43 conference and journal articles and coded them into four focus areas: curriculum development, technology development, pedagogical development, and teacher training/professional development.

The review shows that most K-12 ML work has centered on pedagogical development and tool development, with relatively little attention to teacher professional development. The literature is concentrated in high school and formal settings, while kindergarten, middle school, informal settings, and non-computing subject areas are underrepresented. The authors also found recurring limitations in prior studies, including small samples, limited intervention duration, inadequate resources, and technical constraints. They conclude that the field needs more curricula across grade bands, more integrated subject-area approaches, and much more teacher training and professional development to support broader and more sustainable ML implementation in schools.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, the paper found that AI/ML tools and curricula were often designed to support teaching, but evidence for productivity gains was limited and uneven. Teacher-related work was especially sparse: only four papers focused on teacher training/professional development, and one study (Zhou et al., 2021) explicitly aimed to support ML-powered scientific discovery without extra ML training for teachers and learners. The review does not report a pooled effect size, but it repeatedly notes limited teacher training, limited resources, and implementation constraints as barriers to sustained efficiency gains.
finding.measure: Teacher training/professional development, resource demands, implementation burden, and reported need for extra ML training
finding.study_size: n=43 studies reviewed; teacher-focused studies n=4

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s main contribution is a field-level synthesis showing that K-12 ML education is still emerging and unevenly developed across curriculum, tools, pedagogy, and teacher preparation. It identifies structural gaps such as the lack of teacher professional development, limited integration beyond computing subjects, and underrepresentation of younger grade bands and informal contexts, and it calls for more curricula, policy support, and teacher resource development. No effect size is reported because this is a review of descriptive and design-oriented studies, not an intervention meta-analysis.
finding.measure: Presence/absence of curricula, teacher training programs, subject integration, and implementation gaps across the K-12 ML literature

paper_profiles.title: Engaging Teachers to Co-Design Integrated AI Curriculum for K-12 Classrooms
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (CHI-style publication / ACM paper)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how K-12 teachers can be supported to design and implement AI-integrated curriculum inside regular classroom subjects. The authors argue that AI education is often treated as a standalone computing topic, which makes it difficult for teachers of English, social studies, science, ESL, and other core subjects to adopt. To explore this issue, they ran a two-day remote co-design workshop with 15 K-12 teachers, combining short presentations on AI concepts and ethics with guided co-design tasks.

Participants first completed pre-work to identify a current curriculum and an AI tool that might be integrated with it. In the second workshop session, teachers and researchers split into small groups and collaboratively produced three draft integrated curricula: a social studies lesson about government policy and data, a literacy lesson for students with learning disabilities, and an ESL lesson focused on pronunciation. The study is based on workshop discussions, participant questionnaires, and artifacts from the co-design process, analyzed thematically.

The main contribution is qualitative evidence about what teachers need in order to teach integrated AI lessons: clear scaffolding, especially for evaluation and ethics discussions; engaging and authentic classroom anchors; logistical support for selecting tools and structuring lessons; and collaboration structures that support group work. The paper also shows several ways AI can be integrated into core subjects through data collection, reflection, and ethics. It does not test student learning outcomes or provide causal evidence of impact; instead, it offers design guidance for making AI curriculum more accessible to K-12 teachers and students outside computing classes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not evaluate literacy achievement outcomes; instead, it presents a co-designed literacy curriculum for students with learning disabilities that integrates AI through vocabulary words, image classification, and discussion of bias. Evidence is limited to design artifacts and teacher discussion, so no effect on reading or writing performance is reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The ESL curriculum draft centered on pronunciation practice and an AI-powered pronunciation application, but the study did not measure student speaking, listening, or pronunciation outcomes. The findings are about teachers’ design preferences and implementation considerations, not learner fluency effects.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Science content appears in the exemplar physics curriculum, where students would use paper-airplane data to train a model, but the paper does not report any student science learning or reasoning outcomes. The evidence is confined to curriculum co-design and teacher reflections.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively focuses on integrating AI into non-CS subjects such as social studies, ESL, and literacy, but it does not measure academic attainment in those subjects. Findings show that teachers could connect AI to subject content through data, reflection, and ethics, yet no learner outcome data are reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Teachers repeatedly emphasized student engagement, motivation, and interest as central design goals, and several curriculum ideas explicitly used anchors, student choice, and gamification to support engagement. The study reports teacher perceptions rather than measured student outcomes, but the workshop suggests these design features were viewed as likely to support engagement in K-12 AI lessons.
finding.measure: teacher perceptions of engagement-oriented design

finding.finding_summary: The co-design process emphasized reflection, collaboration, and critical thinking as core elements of integrated AI lessons. Teachers proposed group work, peer discussion, and reflective prompts about data, bias, and real-world implications, but the paper does not measure skill gains; it documents design recommendations and teacher judgments about how AI lessons could support these durable skills.
finding.measure: teacher-designed curriculum artifacts and workshop discussion

finding.finding_summary: Teachers identified logistics, scaffolding, and ready-made exemplars as important supports that would make AI lessons easier to implement, but the paper does not quantify workload reduction or productivity gains. The findings indicate that clear tools, templates, and guidance could improve feasibility for teachers, especially those with little prior AI experience.
finding.measure: teacher perceptions of implementation logistics and feasibility

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that integrated AI curriculum can broaden access beyond computing classrooms and supports teacher buy-in as a condition for adoption. It also highlights the value of ethics, standards alignment, and cross-subject integration as institutional considerations, but it does not evaluate policy change or school-wide implementation effects.
finding.measure: teacher perspectives on curriculum adoption and standards alignment

paper_profiles.title: Understanding Opportunities and Risks of Synthetic Relationships: Leveraging the Power of Longitudinal Research with Customised AI Tools
paper_profiles.venue: CONVERSATIONS 2024 (8th International Workshop on Chatbots and Human-Centred AI)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper argues that research on human-AI synthetic relationships is currently limited by short-term, one-off study designs that miss subtle effects that unfold over time. The authors define synthetic relationships as ongoing associations between humans and AI tools that influence thoughts, feelings, and actions, and they focus on both the opportunities (e.g., support in education, health, and work) and the risks (e.g., manipulation, privacy loss, and reduced autonomy) of such relationships.

Rather than testing a specific intervention, the paper proposes a methodological agenda for studying these relationships more rigorously. The core recommendation is to use customised AI tools that researchers can control and modify, combined with longitudinal behavioural data and experience sampling methods. This would allow researchers to observe how users’ trust, emotional dependence, decision-making, and social behaviour evolve over time and to better separate AI influence from reciprocal adaptation.

The paper is not an empirical study of K-12 classrooms or teachers. It uses examples from companion AI, mental health, and workplace management, and briefly mentions education as a domain where AI tutors could personalize learning and improve outcomes. Its main conclusion is that longitudinal research with transparent, custom-built AI systems is needed to understand both the benefits and harms of sustained human-AI interaction, but it does not present data on teacher productivity, training conditions, grade bands, subject areas, or implementation policies.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI tools can improve productivity by streamlining decision-making and administrative tasks, freeing humans to focus on more strategic work. This is a conceptual claim rather than an empirical result, and no effect size, sample size, or outcome metric is reported.
finding.measure: productivity / administrative task efficiency

paper_profiles.title: Privacy and Copyright Protection in Generative AI: A Lifecycle Perspective
paper_profiles.venue: 2024 IEEE/ACM 3rd International Conference on AI Engineering - Software Engineering for AI (CAIN)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of privacy and copyright protection in generative AI, especially the risks created by large-scale training datasets that may contain personal data or copyrighted content. The authors argue that existing approaches such as differential privacy, machine unlearning, and data poisoning are useful but fragmented, and they propose a lifecycle perspective that organizes privacy/copyright challenges across stages of the AI data lifecycle.

Rather than evaluating a specific intervention empirically, the paper develops a conceptual framework mapping key issues—consent and license acquisition, transparency and data access, consent modification and withdrawal, provenance and attribution, side effects, continuous monitoring, and downstream distribution—to the stages of data collection, training, deployment, and distribution. The paper draws on legal frameworks (GDPR and US copyright law), related technical work, and examples from generative AI systems to argue for integrated protections, including lifecycle-aware guardrails, machine forgetting, and an AI bill of materials.

The paper is aimed at the broader AI engineering and policy community, not a K-12 population, and it does not study teachers, students, or schools. Its main conclusion is that privacy and copyright protection in generative AI cannot be handled reliably by isolated technical fixes; instead, they require coordinated, end-to-end governance and engineering practices across the full data lifecycle.

paper_profiles.title: Shiksha Copilot: Teacher-AI Collaboration for Curating and Customizing Lesson Plans in Low-Resource Schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether and how a teacher-facing generative AI system can support lesson planning in low-resource public schools. The core problem is that teachers in Karnataka, India face heavy administrative burdens, limited instructional materials, multilingual classrooms, and little time for planning, making it difficult to produce high-quality, curriculum-aligned lesson plans.

The authors designed and deployed Shiksha Copilot, a human-in-the-loop lesson planning system that uses retrieval-augmented generation, bilingual English-Kannada support, and a two-stage workflow: expert curators first review and refine AI-generated learning objectives and lesson plans, then teachers customize the curated plans for their classrooms. The deployment involved 1,043 field teachers across 757 government schools in Karnataka, plus 23 curators and 4 mentors, and used logs, interviews, and pre/post surveys to study usage and outcomes.

The main findings are that the system substantially eased workload: it reduced lesson planning time, lowered teaching-related stress, and helped teachers meet bureaucratic documentation requirements while also supporting classroom instruction. The curated English lesson plans were generally high quality with minimal edits, but Kannada translations often required extensive linguistic revision, showing that language support remains a major bottleneck in low-resource multilingual settings. Teachers did not simply accept AI outputs; they adapted them using their own expertise and professional networks, and more experienced teachers especially relied on off-platform planning practices. The paper concludes that effective AI for teachers depends on human curation, curriculum alignment, bilingual support, and integration with existing teacher communities and workflows.

finding.finding_summary: Shiksha Copilot reduced teachers’ planning and administrative burden. In the matched survey sample (n=406), teachers reported lower weekly lesson-planning time and lower teaching-related stress after deployment, and log/interview data showed the system was also used for record-keeping and faster LP preparation. The paper describes the effect as measurable but does not report a single pooled effect size for time savings in the excerpt provided.
finding.measure: Weekly time spent on lesson planning and administrative tasks; Teacher Stress Scale; platform logs of lesson-plan creation and customization
finding.study_size: n=406 survey; n=5,544 teacher-created lesson plans in logs; n=1,043 deployed teachers

finding.finding_summary: The intervention improved alignment with institutional documentation and curriculum requirements, but broader pedagogical change was constrained by school system conditions. Teachers used the tool to satisfy bureaucratic record-keeping demands and the state-mandated 5E instructional format, yet staffing shortages and administrative pressures limited deeper transformation in practice.
finding.measure: Teacher interviews, usage patterns, and qualitative analysis of workflow change and compliance-oriented use
finding.study_size: n=22 teacher interviews; n=4 mentor interviews; n=1,043 deployed teachers

paper_profiles.title: Designing for human–AI complementarity in K-12 education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how to design human–AI partnerships in K-12 classrooms so that teachers and AI tutors complement one another rather than operate separately. The authors present Lumilo, a pair of mixed-reality smart glasses that give teachers real-time analytics about students’ learning, metacognition, and behavior while students work with an AI tutor. The paper combines participatory design, iterative prototyping, and field piloting to develop the tool with teachers who already used AI tutors in their classrooms.

The central empirical study is a randomized classroom field experiment in middle school math classrooms. Across 18 classrooms, 8 teachers, 4 schools/districts, and 343 students (286 analyzed after absences), classrooms were assigned to business-as-usual AI tutoring, a glasses-only monitoring condition, or glasses plus analytics. Students completed pre- and post-tests on linear equation solving after two class sessions with the AI tutor Lynnette. The results indicate that the full Lumilo system improved student learning relative to both control conditions, and that the analytics were responsible for part of the benefit beyond the monitoring hardware itself.

The paper also reports mechanism evidence: teachers using Lumilo spent more time with students who entered with lower prior knowledge, and these lower-pretest students showed greater learning gains. In the glasses-plus-analytics condition, the usual “rich get richer” pattern was attenuated, suggesting that the tool helped redistribute teacher attention more equitably during AI-supported instruction. Overall, the paper argues that effective AI use in classrooms depends on participatory design, real-world piloting, and a theory of complementarity between teacher judgment and AI-generated signals.

finding.finding_summary: In the randomized field study, students in the Glasses + Analytics condition showed greater learning gains on linear equation solving than students in both the No Glasses and Glasses-only conditions. The study analyzed 286 middle school students (from 343 enrolled) after two class sessions with the Lynnette AI tutor; the paper reports that the intervention improved pre/post test performance, but the exact effect size is not reported in the provided text.
finding.measure: Pre-test and post-test scores on linear equation solving

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies teacher attention allocation and classroom orchestration as a mechanism for improving learning with AI tutors. With Lumilo, teachers spent more time with lower-pretest students, and the system appears to have helped teachers target brief, high-value interventions more efficiently; the paper reports an average of about 24 seconds per visit per student, but does not give a formal efficiency effect size.
finding.measure: Teacher time allocation across students and classroom monitoring behavior

paper_profiles.title: BERT4beam: Large AI Model Enabled Generalized Beamforming Optimization
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to use large AI models to solve generalized beamforming optimization problems in wireless communications. The authors argue that conventional optimization and small deep learning models struggle with dynamic, large-scale wireless settings, and they propose a BERT-inspired framework, BERT4beam, to recast beamforming as a token-level sequence learning problem.

The paper introduces two models. The first, BERT, uses CSI tokenization, an embedding block, transformer encoder blocks, and a power-adaptive output layer for single-task beamforming. The second, UBERT, uses finer element-wise tokenization plus antenna encoding and task embeddings to support multi-task beamforming across system utilities such as sum rate, min rate, and energy efficiency. Both models are trained with supervised pre-training and fine-tuning strategies, and evaluated through simulation against optimization and neural baselines.

The experiments are conducted on synthetic multi-user MISO wireless communication settings, not an education population. Results show that BERT and UBERT achieve near-optimal performance relative to CVX/SCA baselines, with strong generalization across user counts, power budgets, and task types. UBERT is especially strong in preserving pre-trained knowledge across tasks because its architecture does not need to be reconfigured during fine-tuning.

finding.finding_summary: The paper studies computational efficiency and deployment utility of AI models for beamforming optimization, showing that BERT and UBERT can achieve near-optimal solutions with real-time inference after pre-training. In simulation, both models performed close to CVX/SCA baselines across sum-rate, min-rate, and energy-efficiency tasks, with BERT often within 0-3% of SCA and UBERT similarly close.
finding.measure: Beamforming performance relative to CVX/SCA baselines; simulated inference quality for beamforming optimization tasks

paper_profiles.title: Generalized Planning with Deep Reinforcement Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether deep reinforcement learning can learn generalized planning policies that transfer from small planning instances to much larger ones. The central question is whether a graph neural network-based policy, trained on small classical planning problems, can learn reusable decision rules that remain effective far outside the training distribution.

The authors propose a state representation based on PDDL planning graphs with node, edge, and global features, and train policies with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). They compare two graph network blocks (GN and GNAT), represent actions via their effects, and also introduce a search procedure, GBFS-GNN, that combines the learned policy and value function with greedy best-first search at inference time.

Experiments are conducted on five classical planning domains: Blocksworld, Satellite, Logistics, Gripper, and Ferry. The paper reports that the learned policies generalize well to much larger instances in four domains, often requiring little search, but fail to generalize well in Logistics. Because the study is about automated planning for AI benchmarks rather than education, it does not address K-12 teachers, schools, or instructional use directly.

paper_profiles.title: Expansive Participatory AI: Supporting Dreaming within Inequitable Institutions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how participatory AI (PAI) processes can better support young people in imagining socially just futures, rather than simply eliciting feedback for pre-specified technologies. The authors argue that many co-design efforts are constrained by institutional norms and power dynamics, which can reproduce inequities even when they include stakeholder participation.

To address this, the paper proposes a set of design principles for "expansive" co-design: desettling institutional assumptions, treating AI as a means rather than an end, removing feasibility constraints early in the process, and embracing contradictory youth perspectives. These principles are illustrated through a Learning Futures Workshop with high-school-aged youth, who first imagined ideal collaboration in non-school settings and then re-imagined how such aspirations might translate into classrooms.

The paper is primarily conceptual and practice-oriented rather than evaluative. Its main conclusion is that participatory AI with youth should begin from expansive dreaming about desirable institutions and social relations, because this can surface more transformative possibilities than conventional classroom-focused co-design. The workshop example suggests that youth can imagine AI-enabled tools aligned with their aspirations when facilitators deliberately shift attention away from existing school constraints, but the paper does not present quantitative outcome evidence or a comparative assessment of productivity gains.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that participatory AI processes can either reinforce or challenge institutional power dynamics depending on how co-design is structured. In the Learning Futures Workshop, youth were able to re-imagine classroom goals and norms, but the paper is conceptual and illustrative rather than an empirical evaluation of institutional change, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Youth-generated visions and workshop observations related to classroom norms, goals, and AI's role in institutional redesign
finding.study_size: n=high-school-aged youth participants (exact number not reported)

finding.finding_summary: The workshop encouraged youth to collaboratively dream, negotiate contradictory ideas, and co-create future collaboration spaces, which the authors frame as supporting expansive sense-making and collaboration. However, these are qualitative observations from a single workshop rather than measured skill gains, and no standardized outcomes or effect sizes are reported.
finding.measure: Collaborative dreaming, idea generation, and negotiation of classroom futures during the workshop
finding.study_size: n=high-school-aged youth participants (exact number not reported)

paper_profiles.title: Model-Based AI Planning and Execution Systems for Robotics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a review and position-style survey of model-based planning and execution systems for robotics (MPERs). It asks why these systems have recently become more important, what technical design choices they involve, and how existing systems differ in modeling, decision making, state representation, integration, and practical impact.

The paper compares several robotics systems, including ROSPlan, CLIPS Executive, PlanSys2, and SkiROS2. It discusses how they use planning formalisms such as PDDL, RDDL, and behavior trees; how they handle sensing, replanning, and multi-robot coordination; and how their APIs and interfaces affect usability and integration effort.

The context is autonomous robotics rather than education. The main conclusion is that MPERs provide a transparent, controllable, and flexible way to combine planning with robot skills, but they remain difficult to build and integrate well, especially when dealing with uncertainty, partial observability, and non-trivial software engineering requirements. The paper does not report empirical results on K-12 teachers or education outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Educational futures of intelligent synergies between humans, digital twins, avatars, and robots - the iSTAR framework
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a conceptual gap in the literature on AI in education: how human teachers and intelligent machines can collaborate in a safe, responsible, and pedagogically useful way. Rather than studying a specific intervention, the authors propose the iSTAR framework (Intelligent human-machine Synergy in collaborative teaching), which organizes collaboration around three enabling technologies: digital twins, avatars/agents, and physical robots.

The paper synthesizes prior work from human-machine collaboration, intelligent tutoring systems, robotics, virtual reality, and AI ethics to propose levels of collaboration ranging from simple tool use to complex multi-machine ecosystems. It also introduces DELTA considerations—design, ethics, learning, teaching, and assessment—to guide responsible implementation. The framework is intended for educators and education designers working in AI-rich settings, especially where teachers remain central and machines augment rather than replace human agency.

The paper does not report primary empirical data, and its conclusions are theoretical and normative: future AI-enabled education should emphasize human-centered design, role clarity, data governance, transparency, fairness, and AI literacy. It argues that machines can support teaching, assessment, and collaborative learning, but only if their roles are carefully bounded and aligned with educational goals and ethical constraints.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues conceptually that AI-enabled systems such as digital twins, avatars/agents, and robots can improve teacher productivity by supporting collaborative teaching, remote operation, monitoring, and task management. However, no primary data, sample size, or effect estimates are reported; the claims are illustrative rather than empirical.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of teacher-task support, remote teaching, and workflow augmentation

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively focuses on institutional design and governance issues for AI in education, including responsible use, data privacy, fairness, transparency, accountability, and AI literacy. These are presented as framework components (DELTA) needed for safe and ethical adoption across educational systems, but no empirical institutional outcomes are measured.
finding.measure: Conceptual framework for governance, ethics, and institutional implementation of AI in education

paper_profiles.title: A Review of AI Tools: Definitions, Functions, and Applications for K-12 Education
paper_profiles.venue: AI, Computer Science and Robotics Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review article surveys artificial intelligence tools and platforms relevant to K-12 education, aiming to give teachers a practical reference for selecting and using AI. It defines major AI categories and functions, then organizes educational AI tools into instructional, administrative, and analytical uses. The paper also discusses implementation concerns, especially data privacy, algorithmic bias, plagiarism, and the risk of overreliance on AI.

The article is not an empirical intervention study; rather, it synthesizes prior literature and vendor/product information on tools such as ChatGPT, MagicSchool, Copilot, Diffit, DreamBox, Eduaide.AI, Khanmigo, Canva Magic Design, PowerBuddy, and SchoolAI. Across examples, it argues that AI can support personalized instruction, automated assessment, and teacher productivity, including administrative tasks like parent communication and lesson planning. The paper’s conclusions are broadly favorable toward AI adoption in K-12 settings, while emphasizing that teachers and administrators should use these tools cautiously and with attention to ethics, equity, and privacy.

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that AI tools can improve teacher productivity by automating or accelerating administrative work such as lesson planning, grading, generating assessments, translating materials, and communicating with parents. Examples given include ChatGPT for drafting emails and documents, Copilot for parent communication and lesson planning, MagicSchool for parent communication and other time-saving tasks, and SchoolAI for automating assessment and behavior intervention plans. No quantitative effect sizes or study-level sample sizes are reported because this is a narrative review of tools rather than an empirical comparison study.
finding.measure: Teacher productivity, administrative task support, parent communication, lesson planning, assessment generation

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses school- and district-level implications of AI adoption, including data privacy, security, algorithmic bias, compliance (e.g., FERPA/COPPA), and the need for policies governing use on school devices and in classrooms. It also notes that some platforms offer district agreements, monitoring, and privacy protections, but stresses that institutional decisions about adoption, storage, and governance remain critical. These are descriptive claims from a review, not outcomes from an evaluation study.
finding.measure: Policy, governance, privacy protections, institutional adoption considerations

paper_profiles.title: The role of digital technologies in supporting quality improvement in Australian early childhood education and care settings
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Child Care and Education Policy
paper_profiles.population: Early childhood education and care (ECEC) / Long day care services
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how digital technologies are referenced in Australian early childhood education and care (ECEC) settings that improved their National Quality Standard (NQS) rating, and what purposes these technologies serve across quality areas. The authors analyze secondary documents from a national quality-improvement project: 60 Quality Improvement Plans (QIPs) and 60 Assessment and Rating (A&R) reports from 60 long day care services that moved from Working Towards NQS to Meeting or Exceeding NQS.

Using keyword searches and thematic analysis, the study identifies where technology appears in planning, documentation, communication, leadership, and governance. Digital tools were most frequently referenced in Quality Area 1 (educational programme and practice), Quality Area 6 (collaborative partnerships with families and communities), and Quality Area 7 (governance and leadership). Common uses included digital documentation, communication with families, online professional development, sharing information, and management/administrative tasks.

The main conclusion is that digital technologies were broadly embedded in everyday ECEC operations and were positively associated with quality improvement, especially for communication, documentation, and leadership support. The authors argue for a more holistic view of technology as part of the whole organizational system, while also noting that the study is descriptive and does not establish causal effects of technology on quality ratings.

finding.finding_summary: Digital technologies were widely used to streamline planning, documentation, communication, and management in the 60 ECEC services studied. The paper reports that 47 of 60 centres (78%) used some form of digital technology, with frequent references to online platforms, email, websites, tablets, and social media supporting administrative and pedagogical workflows.
finding.measure: Frequency and thematic analysis of references to digital technologies in QIPs and A&R reports; documented uses in planning, documentation, communication, and administrative tasks
finding.study_size: n=60 services (120 documents: 60 QIPs, 60 A&R reports)

finding.finding_summary: The study shows that technology was embedded across organizational quality areas, especially governance and leadership, family/community partnerships, and educational practice.
