References to technology were highest in QA1 (n=74), QA6 (n=111), and QA7 (n=107), and the authors conclude that digital tools support quality improvement at the institutional level, including policy communication, leadership functions, and service-wide management.
finding.measure: Frequency and thematic analysis of technology references across the seven NQS quality areas; association of technology use with quality-improvement documents and ratings

paper_profiles.title: Dimensions of artificial intelligence on family communication
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This cross-sectional survey study examines how seven dimensions of artificial intelligence—accessibility, personalization, language translation, privacy, bias, dependence, and safety—relate to family communication. The paper is motivated by the rapid spread of AI-enabled tools such as voice assistants, translation apps, and ChatGPT-style messaging support, and by the author’s claim that there is limited research on AI’s effects within family life.

The study used a convenience sample of 300 participants recruited through social media, email newsletters, and family-oriented forums. Respondents completed a 18-item Likert survey; the analysis used descriptive statistics, multiple regression, and ANOVA to test whether AI dimensions predicted family communication and whether responses differed by gender and number of AI tools used. The paper reports statistically significant positive associations for accessibility, personalization, and language translation, along with concerns about privacy, bias, safety, and dependence.

Overall, the paper concludes that AI has a positive influence on family communication by improving access, customization, translation, and speed, but that increased use of multiple AI tools is associated with greater privacy, bias, safety, and dependence concerns. The study does not compare AI against human-only help or non-AI templates, and its findings are based on self-reported perceptions rather than behavioral or causal outcomes. The author recommends more robust future research, including mixed-method and longitudinal designs, to better understand AI’s long-term effects on family communication.

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported that AI tools increased access to communication, improved speed, and saved time in family interactions. In the regression analysis, accessibility (p=0.001), personalization (p=0.001), and language translation (p=0.016) significantly predicted family communication, and respondents generally agreed that AI improved communication efficiency and interpersonal perceptions.
finding.measure: Self-reported family communication accessibility, efficiency, speed, and time savings on a 5-point Likert survey; multiple regression on AI dimensions

finding.finding_summary: The paper found that greater use of multiple AI tools was associated with higher concerns about bias and privacy (p=0.015) and safety and dependence (p=0.049). The study also reported that respondents lacked knowledge and transparency about AI data storage and privacy policies, indicating governance and policy concerns around AI-enabled communication systems.
finding.measure: Self-reported privacy, bias, safety, and dependence concerns; association with number of AI tools used

paper_profiles.title: Research Methods in Machine Learning: A Content Analysis
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Computer and Information Technology
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable / not reported (paper is a content analysis of machine learning research articles, not a human-subject study)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how machine learning research is being conducted by analyzing 100 recent articles published since 2019 in IEEE journals. The authors aim to identify common research methods, recurring methodological themes, and implications for the machine learning field. Their analysis focuses on the research design, data sources, preprocessing practices, algorithm selection, training/testing strategies, evaluation metrics, and tools used in the sampled studies.

The study finds that machine learning research in the sampled corpus is overwhelmingly quantitative and experimental in design. Most papers used secondary datasets, often from repositories such as UCI, and nearly all used more than one algorithm to compare performance. Data preprocessing was universal, with cleaning, normalization, and noise reduction common; feature selection was less common but associated with improved performance in the studies that used it.

Across the reviewed papers, the most common evaluation approach was the confusion matrix, often supplemented by processing time, and Python with Scikit-Learn was the dominant implementation environment. The authors conclude that several recurring themes are shaping contemporary machine learning research: preference for algorithms that can handle both classification and prediction, use of multiple algorithms to improve reliability, growing attention to optimal feature selection, interest in algorithm submodules rather than only whole algorithms, and increasing use of processing-time metrics alongside accuracy-oriented measures. This paper is best understood as a methodological overview of machine learning scholarship rather than a study of educational interventions or learner outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Development of Digital Education in the Age of Digital Transformation: Citing China’s Practice in Smart Education as a Case Study
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and higher education systems in China (broad national context)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article is a policy and practice-oriented case study of China’s digital education transformation, framed around the global rise of digital education and the 2023 World Digital Education Conference. The paper asks why digital education matters for educational reform and how China’s smart education initiatives illustrate a path toward more equitable, personalized, and high-quality education.

Rather than testing a specific intervention, the authors synthesize policy developments, infrastructure investments, platform construction, and examples of national and local digital education systems (for example, smart education cloud platforms and resource banks). The paper emphasizes the role of AI, big data, online platforms, and teacher digital literacy training in reshaping teaching, learning, governance, and resource sharing across basic, vocational, and higher education.

The main conclusion is that digital education has become a strategic necessity for educational modernization, equity, and lifelong learning in China. The article argues that China’s smart education practices show how digital infrastructure, centralized resource platforms, and teacher training can support personalized learning, continuity during disruptions such as COVID-19, and broader systemic improvements in educational quality and efficiency.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that digital education and AI-enabled platforms improve teacher productivity, instructional efficiency, and education management. It cites national and local platform use cases where digital tools supported lesson planning, homework, teacher training, home-school communication, and analytics, but it does not report a controlled estimate of effect.
finding.measure: Teacher productivity, instructional efficiency, platform use, and education management processes

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central focus is the institutional transformation of China’s education system through national policy, infrastructure, cloud platforms, and resource banks. It reports large-scale adoption indicators such as 72.51 million registered users on the Smart Primary and Secondary Education platform, but these are descriptive implementation figures rather than causal effect estimates.
finding.measure: Policy implementation, platform adoption, resource sharing, and system-level digital transformation

paper_profiles.title: Exploring corporate reputation and crisis communication
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how corporate reputation and crisis communication are related during a major global crisis, using the COVID-19 pandemic as the focal context. The authors combine a literature review with opinion mining, automated classification, and manual human coding of media coverage for selected Nasdaq Helsinki-listed companies to understand how crisis events affect reputation and what communication components matter most.

The empirical part analyzes 115,914 media hits (57,335 editorial news documents and 58,579 social media posts) from January 2020 through mid-2021, with a smaller manual sample used to validate the automated sentiment results. The study finds that crisis effects on corporate reputation were generally minimal or neutral, though some companies and sectors saw slight positive reputation effects when they responded quickly, implemented preventive measures, or introduced alternative operations and new digital services.

The paper also synthesizes crisis management theories to identify three critical components of crisis communication: monitoring, tactics of responding, and response management. It argues that these components are important for managing reputational risk in digitally mediated environments and suggests that AI tools can support crisis communication tasks, especially monitoring and response handling, although current practice still requires human oversight.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI can support crisis communication by improving monitoring, response tactics, and response management, but the empirical evidence is primarily descriptive rather than causal. In the media-analysis case study, companies that reacted rapidly and adapted operations during COVID-19 were described as managing the crisis rather well, with some operational changes such as remote service delivery and new digital platforms associated with slightly positive reputation outcomes.
finding.measure: Media hit sentiment and content analysis of company crisis responses; qualitative assessment of AI support potential for monitoring and response management
finding.study_size: n=115,914 media hits (57,335 editorial news documents; 58,579 social media posts)

finding.finding_summary: The study synthesizes crisis communication theories into a framework linking monitoring, response tactics, response management, and corporate reputation, with an explicit discussion of how AI could support these institutional communication functions. It concludes that AI has potential to enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of crisis communication at the organizational level, but should be used with human involvement and oversight.
finding.measure: Conceptual/theoretical synthesis and AI-assisted query probing of crisis communication functions

paper_profiles.title: Digitalization of health indicators for fitness aerobics teams
paper_profiles.venue: Scientific research of the SCO countries: synergy and integration (International Conference Proceedings)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conference paper examines whether new digitalized criteria can better assess the readiness of university fitness aerobics teams competing in different event categories (step aerobics and aerobics). The authors argue that conventional pedagogical control systems emphasize physical, technical, tactical, and psychological indicators, while health indicators are often missing or conflated with physical fitness measures.

The approach is a university-based comparative study of two student teams at Moscow City Pedagogical University: a step aerobics team and an aerobics team. The paper proposes a set of health and psychological indicators and reports that these indicators are applicable for evaluating team members’ health status and psychological preparedness. The context is student sports training and scientific support for a university team, with the main conclusion that digitalized health metrics can improve assessment of readiness in competitive fitness aerobics.

Although the article discusses digitalization, the evidence presented is descriptive rather than experimental: it compares teams and argues for the usefulness of the proposed metrics. The paper’s main contribution is methodological, offering a framework for monitoring athlete readiness in university sports settings rather than testing a causal intervention with quantified effects.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that newly proposed digitalized health and psychological indicators are applicable for evaluating the readiness of university fitness aerobics teams in two event categories (step aerobics and aerobics). The study is descriptive and comparative, based on team data from Moscow City Pedagogical University; no effect size, confidence interval, or statistical test results are reported.
finding.measure: Health status and psychological preparedness indicators for university fitness aerobics teams

paper_profiles.title: Технології моніторингу стану будівельних конструкцій в умовах експлуатації: на прикладі сенсорних систем
paper_profiles.venue: Innovative Approaches in Modern Science and Technology: Collection of Scientific Papers with Proceedings of the 2nd International Scientific and Practical Conference
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper discusses the need for continuous, high-precision monitoring of building structures during operation, arguing that traditional visual inspections and manual measurements are too slow, subjective, and poorly suited to detecting hidden defects early. It presents sensor-based monitoring as a more modern alternative for tracking deformation, stress, temperature, humidity, vibration, acceleration, and crack development in real time.

The paper focuses on two major technology families: fiber-optic sensors, including Bragg grating systems, and wireless sensor networks (WSNs). It explains how these systems can be embedded in or attached to structures to improve safety, support predictive maintenance, and extend service life, while also reducing maintenance and repair costs. The context is architectural and civil engineering practice, with examples framed around bridges, foundations, and historic buildings rather than a K-12 education setting.

The article is descriptive and conceptual rather than empirical; it does not report an experimental study, sample, or measured performance outcomes. Its main conclusion is that combining sensor systems with cloud analytics and AI-enabled anomaly detection can improve lifecycle management of buildings and infrastructure and support more sustainable, reliable construction practice.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that sensor-based monitoring improves operational efficiency in building management by enabling continuous, real-time detection of defects and anomalies, which can reduce reliance on labor-intensive manual inspections. It states that these systems help optimize maintenance and repair spending, but it reports no sample size, effect size, or quantitative evaluation.
finding.measure: Building-structure monitoring efficiency, maintenance burden, and defect detection capability

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims that adopting sensor systems changes lifecycle management practices in construction by shifting organizations from planned-preventive maintenance toward predictive strategies. It emphasizes improved safety, longer service life, and more sustainable infrastructure management, but provides no empirical institutional outcome data.
finding.measure: Lifecycle management approach, maintenance strategy, and infrastructure safety/sustainability implications

paper_profiles.title: Editorial: Digital participation and communication disorders across the lifespan
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (editorial; discusses children, adolescents, and adults with communication disorders across the lifespan)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This editorial introduces a Frontiers research topic on digital participation and communication disorders across the lifespan. It frames participation as a human right and argues that digitization creates both opportunities and barriers for people with speech, language, and communication impairments. The authors organize the topic around the International Classification of Functioning (ICF), emphasizing how digital tools can support communication, daily activities, and social participation.

Rather than reporting one primary empirical study, the editorial summarizes the contributions included in the research topic. These include work on video-based self-rating in children with developmental disabilities, voice assistants for people with aphasia, digital participation in autism, communication aids, telepractice, and other digital tools for assessment and therapy. Across these examples, the editorial argues that digital participation should be understood as the ability to perform meaningful activities in the digital world, not merely having access to devices or software.

The piece concludes that digital technologies can both facilitate and constrain participation, depending on the impairment, context, and design of the tool. It also highlights ethical and practical issues such as accessibility, privacy, and the need for communication supports that fit diverse user needs. Because this is an editorial, it does not present original outcome data or empirical effect estimates.

finding.finding_summary: The editorial argues that digital participation should be treated as a substantive institutional and therapeutic issue in speech-language services, not just as device access. It synthesizes examples across the research topic to show that digital tools can expand participation, but also introduce accessibility and privacy concerns that institutions must address.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: European Medical Physics News (Winter 2022 / Winter 2023 issue)
paper_profiles.venue: European Medical Physics News / EFOMP Newsletter
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This issue of the EFOMP newsletter is a professional society publication containing editorials, reports, interviews, and company articles related to medical physics. It does not report a single empirical study; instead, it presents commentary on EFOMP activities, policy and organizational updates, education and training initiatives, conference and school reports, and an interview with Professor Ben Heijmen about teaching and medical physics education.

The parts most relevant to education and productivity are descriptive rather than experimental. The interview with Ben Heijmen discusses teaching practices, the value of conceptual instruction, the importance of good teachers, and how international teaching experiences shape pedagogical practice. Other pieces describe EFOMP’s online educational platform, an AI-in-medical-physics school, and reports on professional projects, but none provide measurable outcomes or comparisons of interventions.

Because the document is a newsletter and not a research article, it does not present participant-level data, intervention effects, or formal methods. It is best understood as a professional communications piece summarizing current activities and viewpoints within the European medical physics community.

finding.finding_summary: The newsletter discusses administrative and educational activities aimed at improving efficiency, including plans for an online educational platform, hybrid schools, and other workflow-supporting initiatives, but it does not report empirical evaluation of productivity gains. No sample, effect size, or outcome measure is provided.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Promoting Real-Time Reflection in Synchronous Communication with Generative AI
paper_profiles.venue: AIREASONING-2025-01 (ACM Workshop on Human-AI Interaction for Augmented Reasoning)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper asks how generative AI can support real-time reflection during synchronous communication. The authors argue that reflection is difficult in live interaction because speakers have limited cognitive bandwidth, weak feedback signals, and little opportunity to pause and review what is happening. The paper is motivated by communication settings such as online meetings, lectures, presentations, and practice talks, with special attention to educational contexts where instructors may need to adjust their communication in the moment.

Rather than reporting a new user study or experiment, the paper reviews 11 recent systems for supporting reflection in synchronous communication and synthesizes their design patterns. The review covers approaches such as audience-feedback simulation, aggregation of audience status, real-time summaries, and expert suggestions, including systems that use generative AI for role-playing audiences or tutors. The authors organize these systems by how they support reflection, what role generative AI plays, and how information is delivered to users (user-initiated, system-initiated, or continuous display).

The main conclusion is that generative AI can extend existing reflection tools beyond simple aggregation toward nuanced, contextual, and multimodal feedback, including natural-language summaries, inferred conversation structure, and expert-like suggestions. The paper also identifies design challenges, especially interpretability, proactiveness without disruption, and the limitations of role-play agents when persona design or contextual grounding is weak. Overall, the paper is conceptual and synthesizing rather than empirical, offering design implications for future AI systems that scaffold real-time reflection in live communication.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI can reduce user workload in synchronous communication by proactively monitoring context, summarizing ongoing dialogue, and providing timely suggestions. However, these claims are based on a review of prior systems and design analysis rather than a new empirical evaluation; no study size, effect size, or confidence interval is reported.
finding.measure: User workload, interaction efficiency, and ability to monitor communication context in real time

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on real-time reflection, communication strategy adjustment, and agenda tracking, which are core metacognitive and self-regulatory skills. It concludes that AI-supported reflection may help speakers stay on track and improve communication performance, but these are synthesis-level claims with no direct quantitative outcomes reported.
finding.measure: Real-time reflection, metacognitive monitoring, and communication-strategy adjustment

finding.finding_summary: The paper is directly concerned with synchronous speaking and listening contexts such as lectures, presentations, online meetings, and practice talks. It suggests that generative AI can improve how speakers adapt their live communication through real-time summaries, audience feedback, and expert-like suggestions, but it provides no empirical language-performance data.
finding.measure: Live oral communication performance and conversational feedback in synchronous settings

paper_profiles.title: Designing for human–AI complementarity in K-12 education
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction / CHI-related conference paper (venue not explicitly stated in provided text)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues that effective human–AI partnerships in education require participatory design, iterative piloting in authentic settings, and explicit theorizing about complementarity between human and machine strengths. It uses the development of Lumilo, a pair of mixed-reality smart glasses for teachers, as a case study to show how teacher-facing AI support can be designed to help educators act on real-time information from AI tutoring systems.

The intervention was tested in K-12 math classrooms where students used an AI tutor for linear equation solving. Teachers wore Lumilo in a multi-condition field experiment comparing business-as-usual instruction, a reduced-glasses monitoring condition without analytics, and full glasses with real-time analytics. The study involved 343 middle school students across 18 classrooms, 8 teachers, and 4 schools/districts; 286 students were included in the final analyses. Results showed that full Lumilo support improved student learning relative to both controls, with the analytics condition outperforming the no-analytics glasses condition as well. Observational and process analyses suggested that Lumilo shifted teachers’ attention toward lower-performing students, helping reduce the usual tendency for higher-performing students to benefit more from AI tutoring.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers using Lumilo in AI-supported math classrooms produced higher student learning gains on linear equation solving than teachers in the control conditions. The paper reports significant benefits for the Glasses + Analytics condition over both business-as-usual (No Glasses) and the minimal-monitoring Glasses condition; analyses were conducted on n=286 students after exclusions.
finding.measure: Pre/post test scores on linear equation solving

finding.finding_summary: The paper treats teacher attention allocation and classroom orchestration as a central outcome of the tool. Lumilo helped teachers redirect time toward students with lower initial knowledge, with teachers spending more time on those students in the Glasses + Analytics condition; the paper also notes that teachers spent about 24 seconds per student visit on average while using the system.
finding.measure: Teacher attention allocation / time spent with students during class sessions
finding.study_size: n=8 teachers; n=286 students in final analysis

finding.finding_summary: Although the main academic outcome was math learning, the paper also directly studies classroom performance in AI-supported learning environments more broadly through the tool’s impact on students’ interaction with the tutor and teacher support. The findings indicate that better teacher orchestration improved students’ progress through the AI tutor, but the outcome is still substantively tied to mathematics rather than a separate domain.
finding.measure: Student progress in AI tutor sessions / learning behavior in the math tutor

paper_profiles.title: Human-AI communication for human-human communication: Applying interpretable unsupervised anomaly detection to executive coaching
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues for a design pattern for AI systems that support highly contextual human-human communication: use unsupervised anomaly detection to surface potentially meaningful cues, but leave interpretation and decision-making to human experts. The authors motivate this approach by discussing their prior and ongoing work in executive coaching, where conventional supervised or rule-based methods were found to oversimplify behavior and to be ignored when they contradicted coaches’ intuition.

The paper centers on two systems, REsCUE and INWARD. REsCUE detects outlying nonverbal behavior during coaching sessions and presents it in an interpretable way so expert coaches can decide whether a cue matters. INWARD builds on those cues for video reflection, asking novice and expert coaches to annotate and explain the same detected events; the discrepancy display is intended to support meta-reflection and learning.

The context is adult executive coaching and professional human assessment, not K-12 schooling. The main conclusion is conceptual rather than causal: interpretable anomaly detection can better fit complex interpersonal settings than supervised classification, because it preserves nuance, supports expert judgment, and can even create educational opportunities for novices by prompting explanation and discussion. The paper reports prior experimental/user-study evidence for the two tools but does not present a new controlled evaluation of educational or productivity outcomes in this article.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that interpretable anomaly-detection outputs can support coaches’ interpretive judgment and meta-reflection in complex one-on-one communication. In the INWARD workflow, novice and expert coaches annotated detected cues and discussed discrepancies, which the authors report helped novices construct their own hypotheses and learn how experts interpret subtle nonverbal behavior; no numerical effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Interpretation, annotation, and meta-reflection during coaching-session review

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents REsCUE and INWARD as tools that reduce the burden of observing and reviewing nuanced behavioral cues during coaching sessions by automating cue detection while leaving interpretation to humans. The authors claim the design improved the efficiency and effectiveness of executive coaching support, but this article provides no new quantitative productivity estimate (e.g., time saved or workload reduction).
finding.measure: Perceived efficiency/effectiveness of coaching support and session review

paper_profiles.title: Engaging Teachers to Co-Design Integrated AI Curriculum for K-12 Classrooms
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2020 ACM Conference (CHI-related workshop/arXiv preprint)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how K-12 teachers’ values and classroom constraints can be incorporated into the design of AI curriculum, and how AI concepts can be integrated into core subjects rather than isolated computer science lessons. The authors argue that making AI education more accessible requires teacher-centered co-design, scaffolding, and lessons that fit real classroom contexts.

To investigate this, the authors ran a two-day remote co-design workshop with 15 K-12 educators from diverse subject areas. Teachers first learned about AI concepts and tools, then completed pre-work and worked in small groups with researchers to draft integrated curricula. The workshop produced three exemplar lesson plans: a social studies unit on data and government policy, an ESL pronunciation app using machine learning, and a literacy unit for students with learning disabilities.

The main findings are qualitative: teachers valued evaluation, engagement, logistics, and collaboration when designing AI lessons, and they connected AI to core subjects through data, reflection, and ethics. The paper concludes that AI curriculum is more likely to be adoptable when it is embedded in existing subjects, comes with clear scaffolding for teachers, and explicitly supports ethical discussions and classroom implementation needs.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers co-designed a literacy curriculum for students with learning disabilities that integrated AI through vocabulary, image collection, and model training. The lesson plan was intended to support vocabulary learning and literacy concepts, but the paper reports design outcomes rather than student learning results; no effect sizes or student outcome data were reported.
finding.measure: Co-designed literacy curriculum for students with learning disabilities; vocabulary/image classification activities
finding.study_size: n=15 teachers (design workshop); student sample not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Teachers co-designed an ESL curriculum centered on pronunciation practice and an AI-powered pronunciation app. The paper describes how students would record correct and incorrect pronunciations to train a classifier, but it does not report student performance outcomes, so the evidence is limited to curriculum design rather than measured language gains.
finding.measure: ESL pronunciation curriculum / pronunciation app design
finding.study_size: n=15 teachers (design workshop); student sample not_reported

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper was integrating AI into non-CS core subjects, especially social studies, with one curriculum draft on data and government policy. The paper shows that teachers could successfully design integrated lessons connecting AI to history, government, and other subject content, but it does not measure student academic outcomes in these domains.
finding.measure: Social studies / history-integrated AI curriculum design

finding.finding_summary: Teachers identified engagement as a central design priority and repeatedly emphasized hooks, student interest, gamification, and real-world relevance to sustain motivation. The workshop also increased teachers’ comfort and familiarity with AI (reported familiarity rose from 4.8/7 to 5.8/7, and confidence integrating AI was 5.6/7 post-workshop), suggesting improved teacher self-efficacy, though no student-level social-emotional outcomes were measured.
finding.measure: Teacher familiarity with AI, teacher confidence integrating AI, and perceived engagement strategies
finding.std_deviation: familiarity SD=11.6 for age only; AI outcome SD not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally finds that AI-integrated curricula can support durable skills such as collaboration, reflection, and critical thinking. Teachers intentionally built group work, reflection prompts, and ethical discussion into the lesson drafts; however, the study reports design artifacts and teacher perceptions rather than direct student outcome measures.
finding.measure: Co-designed lesson plans emphasizing collaboration, reflection, and ethics

finding.finding_summary: A key teacher concern was logistics, including lesson structure, tool choice, and how to make AI activities manageable in class. The paper suggests that integrated AI curricula and clearer scaffolding can reduce implementation barriers and make classroom adoption easier, but it does not measure teacher workload or time savings directly.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported logistics/implementation concerns and perceived classroom usability

finding.finding_summary: The study argues that integrating AI into core K-12 subjects can broaden access to AI education beyond computing classrooms and improve institutional adoption by aligning with teacher needs and standards. Evidence is based on a small co-design workshop and teacher reflections, not on policy outcomes or system-level implementation data.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of adoptability, accessibility, and curriculum integration

paper_profiles.title: Competing Visions of Ethical AI: A Case Study of OpenAI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how OpenAI has publicly framed AI ethics over time, asking whether its discourse emphasizes explicit ethics language or instead shifts toward adjacent terms such as safety, alignment, risk, and governance. The authors treat organizational language as a window into ethics-in-practice, arguing that public discourse can signal what kinds of concerns are made visible, institutionalized, or sidelined.

The study uses a mixed-methods case study design combining computational text analysis with qualitative content analysis. The corpus includes 424 OpenAI website articles and 30 OpenAI-authored or co-authored publications (with the broader review covering 454 documents), spanning December 2015 through July 2025. The authors quantify term frequencies, inspect tagging practices and term usage in context, and compare web articles with academic-style publications to understand how ethics vocabulary differs across audience and venue.

The main conclusion is that explicit ethics language is rare in OpenAI’s public web communications and is often superficial when present, while safety, risk, responsibility, and alignment dominate. Publications contain somewhat more ethics language than website articles, especially in academic or collaborative contexts, but even there ethics often appears in peripheral or rhetorical ways rather than as a central analytic frame. The authors interpret these patterns as evidence of discursive narrowing and possible ethics-washing, with implications for governance, accountability, and how AI organizations shape the boundaries of responsible practice.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds a strong discursive shift in OpenAI’s public communication away from explicit ethics vocabulary and toward safety, risk, alignment, and governance framing. Across 424 web articles, only 16 (3.8%) contained an ethics-related term, while safety peaked at 687 mentions and risk at 386 mentions in 2024; the authors argue this pattern signals ethics-washing and a reorientation of institutional priorities.
finding.measure: Computational and qualitative discourse analysis of OpenAI web articles and publications; keyword frequencies, tagging practices, and contextual coding of ethics-related language
finding.study_size: n=454 documents total; n=424 web articles; n=30 publications

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not directly evaluate AI-enabled drafting, translation, or message-management productivity for teachers, but it does discuss how discourse shapes internal design process, policy drafting, and product safety processes within OpenAI. These are organizational productivity-related implications rather than measured effects, so no causal impact on efficiency is established.
finding.measure: Observed discourse about internal organizational processes and priorities

paper_profiles.title: On the Effect of Information Asymmetry in Human-AI Teams
paper_profiles.venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’22), Workshop on Human-Centered Explainable AI (HCXAI)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies when human-AI collaboration can achieve complementary team performance, meaning the human-AI team performs better than either the human or AI alone. The authors argue that a prerequisite for this outcome is complementarity potential, and specifically test whether information asymmetry—where the human has access to contextual information that the AI does not—helps people use AI advice more effectively.

To test this, they run an online experiment in the domain of real-estate appraisal. Participants recruited through Prolific estimate house prices either with or without access to a house image (the unique human contextual information), then see a random-forest model’s price prediction and uncertainty estimate, and finally adjust the prediction. The AI is trained only on tabular features and never sees the image. The study includes 101 analyzed participants (53 no-UHCI, 48 UHCI), with 15 appraisal cases per participant.

Results show that participants with unique human contextual information perform better on their own and improve the AI’s predictions more effectively than participants without that information. In the UHCI condition, the human-AI team achieves lower mean absolute error than the AI alone, demonstrating complementary team performance; in the no-UHCI condition, the team improves over humans alone but does not significantly beat the AI. The paper concludes that information asymmetry can create the conditions for effective human-AI teaming and suggests future XAI systems should be designed around human-centered complementarity, not only explanation quality or trust calibration.

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that adding unique human contextual information (a house image) improves the effectiveness of human-AI teaming for a judgment task. Participants in the UHCI condition achieved a lower MAE when adjusting AI predictions (MAE=$148,009) than participants without UHCI (MAE=$160,095), a significant difference of $12,086 (t=2.9571, p=0.0155).
finding.measure: Mean absolute error (MAE) in house-price prediction after human adjustment of AI predictions
finding.study_size: n=101 analyzed participants; 15 appraisal instances per participant

paper_profiles.title: Can You Explain That? Lucid Explanations Help Human-AI Collaborative Image Retrieval
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether AI-generated explanations can improve human performance in a collaborative task, and whether explanation quality matters. The authors introduce Explanation-Assisted Guess Which (ExAG), a Twenty Questions-style image retrieval game in which a human tries to identify a secret image by asking a VQA system questions and optionally viewing explanations of the system’s answers.

Two experimental settings are studied. In an at-will setting, participants choose whether to request explanations, and in a controlled setting they receive one of several explanation modes: attention visualizations, related question-answer pairs (RelQAs), both together, or no explanations. The task was run with adult human participants on Amazon Mechanical Turk and in a smaller competitive team setting, with outcomes including win rate, score, question count, and subjective helpfulness/correctness ratings.

The main finding is that explanations generally improve collaborative task performance, especially text-based related question-answer explanations. Across the controlled setting, explanations increased win rate and score overall, indicating that participants needed fewer questions to identify the secret image. Helpfulness ratings strongly tracked performance, and incorrect explanations could hurt performance, while a few correct explanations were especially valuable when the VQA system’s answers were often wrong. The paper concludes that ExAG is a useful framework for evaluating explanation efficacy in human-AI collaboration.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly evaluates human-AI collaboration performance in a question-asking image retrieval game, showing that explanations help users build a better mental model of the system and make better follow-up decisions. In the controlled setting, explanation modes improved win rate and score overall, with related question-answer explanations performing best; for example, the overall win rate rose from 63.85% without explanations to 69.29% with explanations in the aggregated analysis.
finding.measure: Game win rate, game score, and number of questions needed to identify the secret image
finding.study_size: n=69 AMT workers in the controlled setting; n=206 games in the at-will setting; n=1469 games in the controlled setting

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that participants increasingly chose to use explanations over time in the at-will setting, suggesting growing perceived usefulness and engagement with the tool despite an added point penalty. In that setting, explanation use increased from 61.2% in the first half of plays to 91.3% in the second half (z-test p < 10^-5).
finding.measure: Proportion of games in which participants chose to use explanations; self-rated helpfulness of explanations

paper_profiles.title: Advantages of Multimodal versus Verbal-Only Robot-to-Human Communication with an Anthropomorphic Robotic Mock Driver
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how an anthropomorphic humanoid robot mounted on top of a mobile robot—the "Anthropomorphic Robotic Mock Driver" (ARMoD)—can communicate intent to nearby humans in shared workplace environments. The core question is whether a multimodal communication style, combining speech with gaze, head movement, and pointing gestures, improves human attention and task response compared with verbal-only communication.

The authors ran two experiments with adult participants in controlled laboratory settings. In Experiment A, participants worked with a robotic forklift in a corridor, and in Experiment B, they interacted repeatedly with a mobile robot in a more open workspace. Across both experiments, participants experienced verbal-only and multimodal ARMoD conditions; the study measured eye-gaze behavior, fixation duration, reaction time to instructions, and subjective questionnaire ratings of trust and robot perception.

The main findings were that multimodal communication shifted participant attention toward the ARMoD, increased fixation on the robot’s face, and reduced reaction times to robot instructions by about 1.0–1.3 seconds relative to verbal-only communication. Subjective ratings were not significantly different between conditions, though multimodal interaction tended to receive slightly higher medians on some questionnaire subscales. The study concludes that multimodal, anthropomorphic communication can improve efficiency and engagement in human-robot collaboration, especially when intent must be registered in space.

finding.finding_summary: Multimodal ARMoD communication improved task efficiency by reducing the time to first fixation on the target after instructions. In Experiment A, reaction time decreased from M=2317 ms (SD=853) in verbal-only to M=1237 ms (SD=524) in multimodal; in Experiment B, it decreased from M=2505 ms (SD=1095) to M=1232 ms (SD=436). Both differences were statistically significant (p=0.03) with small effects (Cohen’s d=0.39 and 0.41).
finding.measure: Time from ARMoD instruction to first fixation on the target point/object; reaction time to communicated instructions

finding.finding_summary: The multimodal interaction style increased attentional engagement with the robot and appeared to support more natural interaction. Participants fixated longer on the ARMoD face in Experiment B (M=278 ms, SD=192) than in verbal-only (M=212 ms, SD=136), a statistically significant difference (p=0.01, Cohen’s d=0.34), and fixation patterns shifted toward the robot’s face in the multimodal condition. Questionnaire results did not show significant differences, but medians were slightly higher for multimodal on several perception subscales.
finding.measure: Fixation duration on ARMoD face; gaze distribution/heatmaps; trust and Godspeed questionnaire subscales

paper_profiles.title: Human-centred Test and Evaluation of Military AI
paper_profiles.venue: Responsible AI in the Military Domain (REAIM 2024)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a session summary from REAIM 2024 focused on the challenge of test and evaluation (T&E) for AI systems that operate with humans, especially in military human-machine teams. The central problem is that conventional AI evaluation methods often measure algorithmic performance in isolation, but real-world outcomes depend heavily on how humans interact with, monitor, correct, or override AI-enabled systems.

The session argues that responsible AI deployment requires a human-centred TEVV (test, evaluation, verification, and validation) approach that incorporates human behavior, operational context, accountability, and governance throughout the system lifecycle. Across the talks, the authors emphasize that current T&E practices are insufficient for predicting operational performance, that metrics should include human factors and system-level outcomes, and that TEVV must be ongoing rather than a one-time technical check.

The context is defense and military policy, not K-12 education. The audience discussion highlights broad interest in operationalizing responsible AI through standards, oversight, confidence-building, and cross-functional collaboration. The overall conclusion is that human-centered T&E is essential for safe, accountable, and contextually reliable AI-enabled systems, but there remain major methodological, organizational, and policy challenges.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that human-centred T&E/TEVV is necessary to operationalize responsible AI governance, accountability, and oversight for AI-enabled systems. It emphasizes that policies, standards, and deployment decisions should be grounded in rigorous evaluation of human-machine teams across the lifecycle, rather than algorithm-only testing.
finding.measure: Workshop/session discussions, audience responses, and expert perspectives on T&E/TEVV, governance, and responsible AI implementation

finding.finding_summary: A recurring claim is that AI-enabled systems can improve operational effectiveness only when human interaction, training, and context of use are accounted for; otherwise realized performance may be lower than algorithmic metrics suggest. The session does not report a direct productivity effect size, but it repeatedly frames T&E as essential for assessing actual system performance, human workload implications, and the ability to deploy systems reliably over time.
finding.measure: Operational performance, TEVV adequacy, and human-machine team effectiveness in context

paper_profiles.title: ACE, Action and Control via Explanations: A Proposal for LLMs to Provide Human-Centered Explainability for Multimodal AI Assistants
paper_profiles.venue: CHI Workshop on Human-Centered Explainable AI ’24
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This short position paper proposes ACE (Action and Control via Explanations), a human-centered explainability approach for multimodal AI assistants. The paper argues that LLMs can generate explanations not as technical system descriptions, but as structured, user-actionable “semantic frames” that help end users supply the missing information a multimodal system needs to align vision, audio, and document inputs.

The concrete setting is MARIE (Multimodal Activity Recognition in an Industrial Environment), an in-development system for supporting technicians performing intricate cleaning tasks in manufacturing facilities. The authors describe participatory design challenges in training MARIE, including missing context in speech, temporal misalignment between speech and action, and variable process sequences. They propose using LLM-generated explanations to prompt users to fill in semantic frame slots (e.g., action, tool, receiver, extent), thereby improving grounding across modalities and enabling better task support.

The paper is primarily conceptual and design-oriented, drawing on prior research and empirical observations from ongoing system development rather than reporting a controlled study. Its main conclusion is that semantic-frame-based explanations may reduce cognitive load, improve collaboration between humans and the AI assistant, and lead to more accurate multimodal understanding and better task performance support. It does not present quantitative evidence of effectiveness in K-12 education contexts.

paper_profiles.title: Expansive Participatory AI: Supporting Dreaming within Inequitable Institutions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how participatory AI co-design can better support youth in imagining socially just futures within institutions such as schools. The authors argue that many participatory AI processes remain technocentric and constrained by institutional norms, which can limit the ability of impacted communities to imagine transformative uses of technology.

To address this, the paper proposes co-design principles for “expansive” participatory AI: desettling institutional assumptions, treating AI as a means to an end, removing feasibility constraints during ideation, and making space for contradictory youth voices. The authors illustrate these principles through the Learning Futures Workshop, a co-design workshop with high-school-aged youth in which participants first dreamed about ideal collaboration in non-school settings, then envisioned technology to support those dreams, and finally reconsidered how such ideas might translate into classrooms.

The main contribution is conceptual and methodological rather than evaluative: the workshop reportedly helped youth reimagine school goals and opened up broader technological possibilities. The paper concludes that participatory AI can be used not only to design specific tools, but also to surface and challenge inequitable institutional logics that shape what kinds of tools and futures seem possible.

finding.finding_summary: The workshop is reported to have supported youth in re-imagining key goals of school and in questioning the taken-for-granted classroom norm that work must be the primary goal. The authors argue that this expansive co-design process opened space for alternative institutional purposes, including dreaming alongside work, but no quantitative effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Youth re-imagining of school goals and classroom norms during the Learning Futures Workshop

paper_profiles.title: Should I Follow AI-based Advice? Measuring Appropriate Reliance in Human-AI Decision-Making
paper_profiles.venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '22), Workshop on Trust and Reliance in AI-Human Teams (trAIt)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a foundational measurement problem in human-AI decision-making: how to quantify whether people rely on AI advice appropriately rather than over- or under-relying on it. The authors argue that existing metrics such as advice utilization or task performance do not capture whether users can distinguish correct from incorrect AI advice and act on that distinction. They therefore propose a two-dimensional construct of appropriate reliance (AR) consisting of relative positive AI reliance and relative positive self-reliance.

The paper is primarily conceptual and theoretical, but it includes an illustrative behavioral user study to demonstrate how the proposed metric works in practice. In the study, 200 adult participants on Prolific completed a deceptive hotel-review classification task in two sequential steps: first classifying reviews on their own, then receiving either plain AI advice or AI advice with LIME-based explanations and optionally revising their decisions. This setup allowed the authors to compute AR separately for cases where AI advice was correct versus incorrect.

Results from the illustration showed under-reliance in the plain AI condition: participants had high self-reliance and low positive AI reliance. Adding explanations increased positive AI reliance significantly without reducing self-reliance, suggesting that explanations can reduce under-reliance rather than simply inducing blind compliance. The main conclusion is that AR should be measured case-by-case using the proposed two-dimensional framework, which may better support future experimental work on AI explanations and human-AI decision-making.

paper_profiles.title: Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup as an Evaluation Domain for Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.venue: AAAI-2019 Workshop on Games and Simulations for Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues that Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup (DCSS), a complex turn-based rogue-like video game, is a valuable evaluation domain for artificial intelligence and cognitive systems research. The authors focus on why DCSS is attractive as a testbed: it is partially observable, dynamic, stochastic, open-ended, text-rich, and difficult for humans, while also offering substantial existing human performance data for comparison.

The paper describes the game’s state and action complexity, including the large number of monsters, spells, items, levels, and possible character configurations. It also proposes an API that would let AI agents receive structured game-state information, issue actions, and be evaluated in custom scenarios, with an emphasis on supporting planning, learning, explainability, knowledge extraction, and human-agent interaction.

The context is AI experimentation rather than educational deployment. The authors discuss potential research questions such as goal reasoning, explainable planning, curriculum RL, and intelligent tutoring in a game setting, but do not evaluate an educational intervention or report results on students, teachers, or schools. The main conclusion is that DCSS could fill a useful gap among simulation environments for AI research because it combines high complexity with deliberative, non-real-time decision making.

paper_profiles.title: Reporting and Reviewing LLM-Integrated Systems in HCI: Challenges and Considerations
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks what authors and reviewers in HCI should consider when reporting and evaluating papers that involve LLM-integrated systems. The central problem is not whether LLM systems work in a classroom setting, but how the research community should judge their credibility, transparency, rigor, and contributions amid uncertainty about model behavior and intense hype around AI.

The authors conducted an interview study with 18 HCI scholars who had authored and reviewed LLM-integrated system papers, then synthesized additional feedback from six expert HCI researchers. The study focuses on the practices, tensions, and review norms surrounding LLM-integrated systems: how authors design and iterate on prompts and models, how much detail to report, when to use technical evaluations, and how to frame LLM use in titles and abstracts. The context is HCI conference research (especially CHI and UIST), not K-12 classroom implementation.

Main conclusions are that uncertainty in LLM behavior has weakened traditional trust-building norms in HCI, leading reviewers to demand more extensive technical evaluation and reporting than they often did for non-LLM systems. Participants argued that prompt reporting should be selective and context-dependent, that appendices/repositories can carry detailed documentation, and that authors should clearly justify LLM use while foregrounding interaction or user-behavior contributions when appropriate. The paper also highlights a broader clash between HCI and more technical ML/NLP review norms, and it proposes considerations for authors, reviewers, and the community rather than evaluating an educational intervention.

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not evaluate productivity gains or workload reductions from AI tools; instead, it qualitatively examines how researchers report and review LLM-integrated systems. The relevant finding is about reporting and peer-review practices, not measured efficiency outcomes, so no effect size or task-level productivity measure is reported.
finding.measure: reporting and peer review practices around LLM-integrated systems
finding.study_size: n=18 interview participants, plus feedback from 6 expert HCI researchers

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that LLM uncertainty and hype are reshaping institutional review norms in HCI, with reviewers increasingly expecting technical evaluations, more detailed reporting, and explicit justification for LLM use. Participants also describe venue-level policy responses and community tensions, including concerns about desk-reject standards and clashes between HCI and ML/NLP expectations.
finding.measure: reported experiences with peer review norms, reporting guidelines, and conference policy practices
finding.study_size: n=18 interview participants, plus feedback from 6 expert HCI researchers

paper_profiles.title: Probability Judgment in Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines two frameworks for probability judgment in artificial intelligence: Bayesian probability and belief functions (Dempster-Shafer theory). Shafer argues that these are different languages for expressing uncertainty, and that the right choice depends on how evidence is structured and what can be plausibly modeled as known chance versus partially related evidence.

The paper uses conceptual examples rather than empirical data, especially a running example involving Fred's testimony about whether the streets are slippery and a thermometer's reading. These examples illustrate how belief functions can represent incomplete evidence more modularly than Bayesian methods, and how Dempster's rule combines independent items of evidence. Shafer then discusses why expert systems in AI often favored belief functions or quasi-Bayesian methods: modularity, the ability to add or remove evidence, and the difficulty of specifying all required Bayesian probabilities.

The main conclusion is philosophical and methodological rather than empirical: Bayesian and belief-function approaches each have niches, but neither fully captures the flexibility of human probability judgment. The paper does not study educational settings, teachers, or administrative workflows, and it provides no evidence about AI productivity gains in K-12 contexts.

paper_profiles.title: Artificial Intelligence for Sustainable Wine Industry: AI-Driven Management in Viticulture, Wine Production and Enotourism
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how artificial intelligence could support sustainability and efficiency in the wine industry, with a focus on viticulture, wine production, and enotourism in Poland. The authors frame the study around three sustainability pillars—environmental, economic, and social—and ask both what Polish winemakers currently do and where AI tools might plausibly add value. The paper is not an intervention study; instead, it combines a questionnaire survey of Polish vineyards with a conceptual mapping of AI methods to industry tasks.

The empirical component is a full-population electronic survey sent to all active vineyards identified in Poland, with 75 respondents completing the questionnaire. The survey collected winemakers’ self-reported practices related to environmental stewardship, local economic support, social relations, and tourism offerings. The authors also conducted a literature-based analysis of AI methods such as predictive analytics, machine learning, computer vision, chatbots, recommendation systems, and geospatial analysis, and then linked these to use cases in vineyard management, production optimization, workforce planning, community engagement, and tourist services.

Main findings indicate that many Polish winemakers already report sustainability-oriented practices: 77% said they consider environmental issues in wine production, 96% reported actions supporting local economic development, and most described good relations with nearby residents. In enotourism, 83% of respondents offered or planned tourist visits, and they cited benefits such as increased wine sales, brand promotion, and additional income. The paper concludes that AI could support sustainable winemaking mainly by improving resource management, production efficiency, marketing, and tourism personalization, but it also notes that most wineries are not yet using advanced AI tools and that broader adoption will depend on scale, local fit, and future demand.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI can improve operational efficiency in viticulture, wine production, and enotourism by optimizing irrigation, reducing waste, forecasting yields, automating fermentation monitoring, and streamlining customer-facing tourism processes. However, these are proposed applications rather than tested effects; the empirical survey does not report productivity gains or effect sizes from AI use. The study describes current practices among 75 Polish vineyards and concludes that most are not yet using advanced AI, so the operational impact remains conceptual rather than measured.
finding.measure: Survey of winemakers’ current practices plus conceptual mapping of AI applications to vineyard, production, and tourism workflows

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that Polish winemakers already contribute to local development, community relations, and cultural heritage, and it proposes AI tools to strengthen these institutional and regional functions. Survey results show strong self-reported support for local economies (96%) and good relations with residents, while the authors argue that AI could enhance supply chains, community engagement, and sustainable tourism governance. These are descriptive and prospective findings, not causal estimates.
finding.measure: Self-reported survey responses on local economic, social, and tourism-related practices; conceptual AI use-case analysis

paper_profiles.title: Blue Sky Ideas in Artificial Intelligence Education from the EAAI 2017 New and Future AI Educator Program
paper_profiles.population: Secondary school; early undergraduate; university faculty / future educators
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a collection of short perspective essays written for the EAAI 2017 New and Future AI Educator Program. It asks participants to respond to three broad questions: how to incorporate ethics into AI curricula, how to teach AI topics at early undergraduate or secondary-school levels, and how to make AI education more interdisciplinary so it benefits non-engineering fields.

The contributions do not report an intervention study or empirical evaluation. Instead, they propose ideas such as peer-learning across disciplines, Montessori-inspired student discovery, early exposure to non-arithmetic AI concepts, ethics threaded throughout AI courses, real-world problem-based instruction, and video-game-based or blended learning formats. The intended audiences include secondary school students, early undergraduates, and educators/faculty designing AI instruction.

The paper’s main conclusion is that AI education should be more interdisciplinary, more ethically grounded, and more accessible to younger learners. The authors argue for active, project-based, and student-centered approaches, but provide no experimental evidence or measured outcomes. As a result, the paper functions as a conceptual and agenda-setting piece rather than an empirical study.

paper_profiles.title: Conceptual Modeling and Artificial Intelligence: Mutual Benefits from Complementary Worlds
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an editorial preface for the 3rd International Workshop on Conceptual Modeling Meets Artificial Intelligence (CMAI’2021). Its central purpose is to frame the relationship between conceptual modeling and artificial intelligence, explain why the two fields have complementary strengths and weaknesses, and justify the workshop’s role in bringing them together.

The paper argues that AI systems can efficiently learn from data but are often opaque and difficult to explain, while conceptual modeling produces human-comprehensible and formal representations but may struggle with scale and complexity. To organize the emerging research area, the author proposes a framework with four categories of CMAI research: exaptation, CM-driven, AI-driven, and CM- & AI-driven. The remainder of the paper summarizes the invited papers in the workshop program and places each in this framework.

Because this is an editorial overview rather than an empirical study, it does not evaluate an intervention, population, or measurable educational outcome. It provides conceptual guidance and a field-mapping perspective on how conceptual modeling can contribute to AI and vice versa, with examples drawn from machine learning, optimization, and predictive business process management.

paper_profiles.title: From Statistical Relational to Neurosymbolic Artificial Intelligence: a Survey
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a survey of two related branches of AI: statistical relational AI (StarAI) and neurosymbolic AI (NeSy). Its main purpose is conceptual rather than empirical: it organizes the literature around shared dimensions such as inference style (proof-based vs. model-based), logic syntax, semantics, learning, representations, paradigms, and task types. The survey argues that these dimensions help explain how symbolic reasoning can be integrated with probabilistic graphical models and neural networks.

The paper reviews representative StarAI and NeSy systems, including ProbLog, Markov logic networks, probabilistic soft logic, DeepProbLog, Neural Theorem Provers, Logic Tensor Networks, Semantic Loss, and related approaches. It explains how proof-based systems use logical proofs to shape neural architectures, while model-based systems use logical constraints to shape loss functions. The paper also compares propositional, relational, and first-order formulations, and discusses Boolean, fuzzy, and probabilistic semantics.

This is not a study of K-12 settings, educators, or students, and it does not evaluate an educational intervention. Its conclusions are methodological: the survey identifies common structure across the two AI subfields and highlights tradeoffs between interpretability, control, and scalability in neurosymbolic methods. It also outlines open challenges and opportunities for cross-fertilization between symbolic and neural approaches.

paper_profiles.title: Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education – where are the educators?
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This systematic review examines the state of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education from 2007 to 2018, with particular attention to how AI is conceptualized, what ethical concerns are raised, and how AI is used across the student life cycle. The authors screened 2656 records, ultimately including 146 peer-reviewed journal articles for synthesis.

The review organizes AI uses into four major application areas: profiling and prediction, assessment and evaluation, adaptive systems and personalization, and intelligent tutoring systems. Across the literature, most studies were quantitative and concentrated in computer science and STEM, with relatively little participation from educators or educational researchers. The authors conclude that AI in higher education has been explored mainly for student-facing functions such as prediction, automated assessment, and tutoring, while teacher-facing and critically reflective work remains scarce.

The paper’s main conclusions are that AI applications can support administrative and instructional processes, particularly by improving prediction, feedback, and automation at scale, but the field lacks strong pedagogical grounding and critical reflection about ethics, privacy, and risks. The review also highlights that educators are underrepresented in the AI-in-education literature and that more research is needed on teacher-facing applications, governance, and ethically informed implementation.

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that AI applications are frequently used to reduce workload and automate administrative or instructional tasks such as admission decisions, course scheduling, assessment, feedback, plagiarism detection, and student support. Across 146 studies, teacher-facing systems were explicitly described as supporting teachers by automating tasks and reducing workload, but the paper is a synthesis and does not report a single pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Literature synthesis of AI applications for administration, assessment, feedback, and teacher support

finding.finding_summary: The review shows that a substantial share of studies (48/146, 32.8%) addressed administrative and institutional services, including admission decisions, course scheduling, dropout prediction, student profiling, and institutional decision support. The evidence suggests AI is being used to inform institutional management and policy-relevant decisions, but the paper does not estimate an overall effect size.
finding.measure: Literature synthesis of institutional and administrative AI applications

finding.finding_summary: Several studies in the review focus on engagement, motivation, and self-regulation, especially through predictive models that identify low-engagement students and through intelligent tutoring systems that support self-regulatory processes. The review characterizes many results as positive or satisfactory, but also notes at least one negative study and emphasizes that no longitudinal evidence base exists; no pooled effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Student engagement, motivation, self-regulation, and related learner-behavior measures
finding.study_size: n=146 studies (subset focused on engagement/motivation/self-regulation not separately aggregated)

finding.finding_summary: The review includes studies on collaboration, problem solving, and metacognitive/self-regulatory support, especially within intelligent tutoring systems and collaborative-learning tools. Reported findings are generally positive at the study level, but the paper does not synthesize a quantitative effect size for these durable-skill outcomes.
finding.measure: Collaboration, problem solving, and self-regulatory/metacognitive supports in AI tools
finding.study_size: n=146 studies (subset focused on durable skills not separately aggregated)

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies a substantial body of work on automated essay scoring, writing feedback, and reading comprehension support. For example, one AES study reported agreement between computer scoring and human raters of 94.6% to 98.2%, and other studies found that automated feedback can encourage revisions and provide useful writing support, though feedback quality concerns remain.
finding.measure: Automated essay scoring, writing feedback, and reading comprehension support

finding.finding_summary: A smaller subset of studies addressed second-language learning and feedback in language-learning contexts, including intelligent tutoring and automated feedback for language tasks. The review indicates generally positive or promising results, but the evidence base is limited and not quantitatively pooled.
finding.measure: Second-language learning / language-learning feedback

finding.finding_summary: Multiple studies applied intelligent tutoring systems and adaptive systems to mathematics, statistics, and related quantitative courses. The review reports mostly positive preliminary results and notes that these systems can support course content delivery and feedback, but it does not provide a meta-analytic effect estimate.
finding.measure: Performance in mathematics, business statistics, and related quantitative coursework

finding.finding_summary: The review covers AI applications in a wide range of non-core subjects, including computer science, medicine, business, engineering, and virtual laboratories. Across these areas, studies were generally described as promising or satisfactory, especially for content delivery and feedback, but no overall effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Course learning outcomes across varied disciplines (e.g., computer science, medicine, business, engineering)
finding.study_size: n=146 studies (discipline-specific subsets not separately aggregated)

paper_profiles.title: An overview of clinical decision support systems: benefits, risks, and strategies for success
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review surveys clinical decision support systems (CDSS) in medicine, focusing on how computerized tools embedded in electronic health records and related workflows can improve clinician decision-making, reduce errors, and streamline work. The paper is motivated by the rapid growth of CDSS and AI-enabled systems, alongside persistent concerns about alert fatigue, workflow disruption, maintenance burdens, user distrust, interoperability problems, and financial sustainability.

The authors synthesize prior literature across many CDSS functions, including patient safety, guideline adherence, cost containment, administrative documentation, diagnostic support, imaging, laboratory interpretation, and patient-facing decision support. They emphasize that the strongest evidence exists for more mature, knowledge-based CDSS integrated into computerized provider order entry and EHR workflows, while AI/ML-based systems are emerging but face implementation and explainability challenges.

The review’s main conclusion is that CDSS can improve care quality and efficiency when carefully designed, integrated into existing workflows, and maintained over time. At the same time, poorly implemented systems can create new risks such as alert fatigue, overreliance, and inaccurate documentation. The paper closes with design and governance recommendations aimed at maximizing benefits and minimizing harm as AI and decision support become more common in healthcare.

finding.finding_summary: The review concludes that CDSS can automate and expedite administrative and workflow tasks, including diagnostic code selection, automated documentation, note auto-fill, ordering, and other steps that reduce provider workload. The evidence summarized in the paper suggests these systems can improve efficiency and reduce time spent on tedious tasks, but the review does not report a single pooled effect size for administrative productivity gains.
finding.measure: Administrative workflow efficiency, documentation automation, ordering/workload reduction

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes organization-level effects of CDSS, including improved adherence to guidelines, reduced duplicate testing, lower costs, and better integration of clinical workflows into electronic records. It also emphasizes institutional challenges such as maintenance, interoperability, implementation cost, and governance requirements, indicating that the impact depends heavily on system-level adoption and support.
finding.measure: Guideline adherence, cost/resource utilization, workflow integration, interoperability

paper_profiles.title: Transforming Rural and Underserved Schools with AI-Powered Education Solutions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI-powered education tools can improve learning and reduce workload in underserved, resource-constrained K-12 schools. The central problem is that rural and underserved schools often face limited infrastructure, teacher capacity constraints, and high administrative burden, making it difficult to provide individualized learning support at scale.

The authors propose an AI-based inclusive learning framework with three main components: a personalized learning platform, an intelligent tutoring system, and automated management tools. The system is designed for low-bandwidth, low-hardware environments using lightweight models, edge computing, and differential privacy. The study describes a 12-week experiment with 200 students aged 12 to 15 from three underserved public schools, comparing an experimental group using the AI system with a control group receiving traditional instruction.

Results reported in the paper indicate that the experimental group outperformed the control group on standardized academic measures, especially in mathematics and science, showed stronger engagement, and experienced reduced teacher workload. The automated management tools were reported to streamline administrative tasks such as attendance tracking, grade management, and course scheduling. Overall, the paper concludes that AI can support both student learning and school operations in underserved settings, though the authors note limitations including the small sample size and unresolved issues around privacy, long-term stability, and broader scalability.

finding.finding_summary: Students in the experimental group improved more than the control group in mathematics over the 12-week study. Table 1 reports a 23% performance improvement for the experimental group versus 6% for the control group on standardized tests.
finding.measure: Standardized mathematics test performance improvement

finding.finding_summary: The AI intervention produced stronger gains in science than the traditional condition. Table 1 reports an 18% performance improvement in the experimental group compared with 4% in the control group on standardized science tests.
finding.measure: Standardized science test performance improvement

finding.finding_summary: The paper also reports gains in language and arts achievement, which it classifies as part of the broader academic effect of the AI system.
