Table 1 shows 20% improvement in language and 19% in arts for the experimental group versus 5% and 3% in the control group, respectively.
finding.measure: Standardized subject test performance improvement in language and arts

finding.finding_summary: The intervention increased student learning engagement and motivation. The experimental group’s online learning time increased by 125% versus 35% in the control group, and classroom discussion participation increased by 80% versus 20%, suggesting stronger engagement and intrinsic motivation.
finding.measure: LMS engagement logs and classroom discussion participation

finding.finding_summary: Automated management tools reduced teacher workload, especially in lesson preparation and administrative tasks. The paper reports a 40% reduction in lesson preparation time and a 30% reduction in administrative tasks for the experimental group, compared with 10% and 15% reductions in the control group.
finding.measure: Teacher survey ratings of lesson preparation time and administrative task load

paper_profiles.title: Evaluation Report on Large Language Models Solving High School Mathematics Questions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report evaluates how well several large language models (LLMs) can solve high school mathematics exam questions and whether they might be useful in educational settings. The paper frames LLMs as potentially helpful tools for teaching, feedback, and automated answering, but focuses specifically on mathematics problem-solving rather than classroom instruction or administrative use.

The study uses college entrance examination mathematics papers from 2019–2023 as the evaluation dataset and tests at least eight LLMs, including GLM-4-Flash, ERNIE-Speed-128K, Spark Lite, Hunyuan-lite, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, gemma-2-9b-it, Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and Yi-34B. It compares models on response time, accuracy, logical reasoning, guidance responsiveness, and creative multi-solution output. The paper reports that models differ substantially by metric: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and ERNIE-Speed-128K perform best on accuracy, Spark-lite is fastest on some tasks, GLM-4-Flash produces the most and most complex multiple solutions, and Hunyuan-lite performs well in guidance and logic. The authors conclude that LLMs show promise for educational applications but still need improvement in reasoning and creativity.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates LLM performance on high school mathematics exam questions and finds substantial variation across models and task types. In single-solution settings, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and gemma-2-9b-it were fastest on several question types (e.g., 0.43s and 0.32s on multiple-choice and fill-in-the-blank respectively), while ERNIE-Speed-128K and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct showed the highest comprehensive-question accuracy (0.950 and 0.850 in Table 12).
finding.measure: Accuracy, response time, logical reasoning, and multi-solution creativity on high school mathematics questions

paper_profiles.title: Research on the Application of Large Language Models in Automatic Question Generation: A Case Study of ChatGLM in the Context of High School Information Technology Curriculum
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether the Chinese large language model ChatGLM can generate high school information technology exam questions that are comparable to human-written questions. The authors focus on whether AI-generated questions match textbook content, align with core competencies, are clear, and are acceptable to teachers for classroom use.

The intervention/approach is prompt-engineered question generation using ChatGLM. Questions were generated from two compulsory high school information technology chapters (“Data and Information” and “Algorithm Basics”) and compared against human-produced questions. Five experienced high school information technology teachers rated 20 human questions and 20 ChatGLM questions on hitting, fitting, clarity, and willingness to use, each on a 1–5 scale.

Results show that ChatGLM performed similarly to human questions on hitting and fitting, slightly better on clarity, and substantially better on teachers’ willingness to use the questions. Welch’s ANOVA found no significant differences for hitting (p=.067), fitting (p=.891), or clarity (p=.149), but a significant difference for willingness (p<.001), favoring ChatGLM (M=3.98) over human questions (M=3.05). The authors conclude that ChatGLM may reduce teacher workload and improve the efficiency of question generation, though further optimization is needed to preserve content alignment while improving usability.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGLM improved teacher-perceived usability and was framed as a way to reduce workload in question generation. Five teachers rated ChatGLM-generated questions substantially higher than human questions on willingness to use (M=3.98, SD=0.568 vs. 3.05, SD=0.539), and the difference was statistically significant (Welch’s ANOVA p<.001).
finding.measure: Teacher-rated willingness to use generated exam questions

finding.finding_summary: ChatGLM-generated questions were comparable to human-written questions in content alignment and core competency alignment, with slight advantages in clarity. Human questions had a slightly higher hitting mean (4.32 vs. 4.17), while ChatGLM had a slightly higher clarity mean (4.14 vs. 4.03); neither difference was statistically significant for hitting, fitting, or clarity.
finding.measure: Expert ratings of hitting, fitting, and clarity of high school information technology exam questions
finding.std_deviation: Hitting: Human SD=0.584, ChatGLM SD=0.570; Fitting: Human SD=0.567, ChatGLM SD=0.461; Clarity: Human SD=0.502, ChatGLM SD=0.569

paper_profiles.title: AI in Pakistani Schools: Adoption, Usage, and Perceived Impact among Educators
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how Pakistani K–12 educators are adopting and using AI tools, and how they perceive AI’s effects on teaching and learning. The authors are motivated by the limited evidence on AI adoption in developing-country school systems, where infrastructure constraints, uneven access, and limited professional development may shape whether AI can actually support classroom practice.

The study uses an online descriptive survey of 125 in-service educators across public and private schools in Pakistan. The questionnaire asked about AI familiarity, attitudes toward adoption, current usage patterns, and perceived impacts on student engagement, student performance, teacher workload, teaching strategies, and access equity. The most common uses were lesson planning, content creation, and personalized learning; grading and tutoring bots were less common. Teachers generally viewed AI positively, with many reporting reduced workload and improved engagement, but they also raised concerns about unequal access and the risk that some students could be left behind.

Overall, the paper concludes that AI adoption in Pakistani schools is still early and uneven, but educator sentiment is cautiously optimistic. It highlights the need for training, infrastructure, and equity-focused implementation if AI is to move beyond occasional experimentation and produce broader instructional benefits.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that AI reduced routine teaching workload, with 73% agreeing that AI tools reduced the time they spend on routine teaching tasks such as grading and content creation. In the discussion, the authors also note that many teachers use AI primarily for lesson planning and content creation, suggesting perceived productivity gains rather than fully automated administrative workflow transformation.
finding.measure: Likert-scale survey item on whether AI tools reduced time spent on routine teaching tasks; reported AI use in lesson planning/content creation

finding.finding_summary: Educators perceived AI as improving student engagement: 67% agreed that using AI tools in the classroom improved students' engagement levels. This is a self-reported perception from the survey rather than an objective outcome measure, but it was one of the paper’s central findings about classroom impact.
finding.measure: Likert-scale perception of student engagement

paper_profiles.title: Shiksha Copilot: Teacher-AI Collaboration for Curating and Customizing Lesson Plans in Low-Resource Schools
paper_profiles.population: Educators in grade 5–10 public schools in Karnataka, India
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether and how an AI-assisted lesson planning system can support teachers working in low-resource schools. The central problem is that teachers in such settings face heavy workloads, limited instructional materials, multilingual demands, and administrative documentation requirements, all of which make high-quality lesson planning difficult and time-consuming.

The authors designed and deployed Shiksha Copilot, a human-in-the-loop lesson planning system for English and Kannada-medium public schools in Karnataka, India. The system used retrieval-augmented generation to draft curriculum-aligned lesson plans, a curation workflow for expert teachers to review and refine outputs, and a distribution platform that allowed teachers to customize plans for their own classrooms. The deployment involved 23 curators and 1,043 teachers, with quantitative log analysis, pre/post surveys, and 43 interviews used to study adoption, editing behavior, stress, and workflow change.

The main findings are that AI-generated English lesson plans were generally high quality and required few edits, while Kannada outputs needed extensive linguistic correction and localization. Teachers used the tool not only for instruction but also for bureaucratic documentation, and the system reduced lesson-planning time, record-keeping effort, and teaching-related stress. At the same time, broader pedagogical change was limited by structural constraints such as staffing shortages and ongoing administrative burdens, showing that AI can ease workload but does not by itself resolve institutional constraints.

finding.finding_summary: Shiksha Copilot reduced lesson-planning and record-keeping burden for teachers in Karnataka public schools. The study reports measurable reductions in lesson planning time and teaching-related stress, and interviews/logs indicate teachers used the system to speed up administrative documentation as well as classroom preparation; however, the paper does not report a single aggregate effect size for time savings in the excerpt provided.
finding.measure: Weekly time spent on lesson planning and administrative tasks; teacher stress scale; system logs of LP creation/editing
finding.study_size: n=406 matched survey responses; 5,544 teacher-created lesson plans in logs; 22 teacher interviews

finding.finding_summary: The tool supported compliance-oriented documentation and fit into existing school workflows, but broader organizational change was constrained by staffing shortages and administrative demands. The paper argues that AI integration influenced teacher workflows and administrative processes, yet systemic barriers limited the extent of pedagogical change.
finding.measure: Interview and thematic analysis of workflow/organizational change; observations of use for bureaucratic documentation
finding.study_size: n=1043 teachers deployed; 43 interviews; log data from curation and distribution platforms

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported lower teaching-related stress after using Shiksha Copilot. The post-survey measured stress with the Teacher Stress Scale, and the paper states that the tool led to measurable reductions in teacher stress, consistent with reduced workload and easier access to ready-made lesson plans.
finding.measure: Teacher Stress Scale (teaching demands and school-based support subscales)
finding.std_deviation: teaching demands α=.79 pre, .83 post; school-based support α=.70 pre, .83 post

finding.finding_summary: The system supported curriculum-aligned lesson planning across Science, Mathematics, Social Science, and English for grades 5–10, but this paper does not evaluate student learning outcomes directly. Instead, it shows that curated English lesson plans were usually suitable for classroom use (96.13% of content blocks rated suitable) and that teachers adapted plans for instructional delivery.
finding.measure: Curator ratings of lesson-plan content blocks; teacher ratings of lesson plans
finding.study_size: 991 curated lesson plans; 5,544 teacher-created lesson plans

paper_profiles.title: Do Tutors Learn from Equity Training and Can Generative AI Assess It?
paper_profiles.venue: LAK 2025 (Proceedings of the 15th International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether undergraduate tutors learn to respond more effectively to students who may be experiencing educational inequities, and whether generative AI can reliably assess those tutors’ open-ended responses. The authors situate the work in learning analytics and tutor training, arguing that equity-related competencies are important but difficult to assess at scale because they are expressed in nuanced language rather than easily scored right-or-wrong content knowledge.

The intervention is a short scenario-based lesson in which 81 paid remote tutors completed pretest and posttest activities involving two student scenarios (Jeremiah and Alexis). Tutors answered multiple-choice and open-ended prompts about how to respond to possible inequities, and their responses were coded by human raters. The study then evaluated GPT-4o and GPT-4-turbo, using zero-shot and few-shot prompting, to determine whether LLMs could grade the open responses comparably to human coders.

Results showed marginally significant learning gains on tutor performance from pretest to posttest, along with a significant increase in self-reported confidence and high perceived ability to apply the lesson content. The LLMs performed well, especially with few-shot prompting, and GPT-4o few-shot offered the best balance of accuracy, cost, and speed. The authors conclude that scenario-based equity training can improve tutor knowledge and confidence, and that generative AI may support scalable assessment of nuanced tutor responses, though some subjective scoring disagreements remain.

finding.finding_summary: Tutors reported significantly higher confidence after the lesson. Mean self-reported confidence increased from 3.44 (SD=1.09) pretest to 4.51 (SD=0.56) posttest among the 35 tutors who completed the post-survey, with a paired-sample t-test showing t(34)=6.82, p<.001. Tutors also reported high confidence in applying what they learned (M=4.71, SD=0.46).
finding.measure: Self-reported confidence in knowledge about responding to students experiencing potential inequities; self-reported confidence in applying learned skills
finding.study_size: n=35 for post-lesson confidence survey; n=81 total tutors
finding.std_deviation: SD=1.09 pretest, SD=0.56 posttest, SD=0.46 application confidence

finding.finding_summary: The lesson produced marginally significant improvements in tutors’ ability to choose and justify appropriate responses in equity-related scenarios, indicating gains in applied judgment and reasoning. Mixed-effects ANOVA showed a main effect of time, F(1,79)=3.20, p=.078, and a significant scenario-by-time interaction, F(1,79)=4.31, p=.041; post-hoc contrasts showed significant learning gains in one scenario order condition (M=0.12, SE=0.04, t(79)=3.07, p=.001).
finding.measure: Open-ended and multiple-choice tutor responses on scenario-based assessments of how to respond to possible inequity
finding.effect_size: beta=0.42 (Rasch model time effect, discussed in robustness analysis)

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates whether GPT-4o and GPT-4-turbo can automate scoring of open-ended tutor responses, aiming to reduce the cost and time of human grading. GPT-4o few-shot achieved strong performance (predict: Acc.=0.89, AUC=0.88, F1=0.92; explain: Acc.=0.88, AUC=0.87, F1=0.89) and was estimated to cost $8.85 and take 3.5 hours to assess 1,000 lesson completions, versus roughly 16.7 hours and about $500 for human graders.
finding.measure: Model grading accuracy, AUC, F1, estimated processing time, and estimated cost for scoring tutor responses
finding.study_size: n=81 tutor responses used for evaluation; cost/time extrapolated to 1,000 lesson completions

paper_profiles.title: Excited, Skeptical, or Worried? A Multi-Institutional Study of Student Views on Generative AI in Computing Education
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 25th Koli Calling International Conference on Computing Education Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how students from different educational contexts use and perceive generative AI tools in computing education. The authors note that prior work has largely focused on single institutions or higher education, leaving a gap in understanding how high school, vocational college, and university students differ in their use patterns, perceptions, ethics, and attitudes toward GenAI.

To address this, the researchers ran a multi-institutional survey in the Netherlands with 410 computing students from 23 institutions: 7 high schools, 7 vocational colleges, and 9 research universities. The survey, adapted from prior GenAI education instruments, asked about frequency of use for tasks such as learning and programming, perceptions of usefulness and risk, institutional policies, ethical views, attitudes, help-seeking, and whether GenAI influenced study choice. Analyses used descriptive statistics, nonparametric group comparisons, chi-square tests, and Spearman correlations.

The main conclusion is that student experiences and perceptions differ substantially by educational level. High school students reported more frequent use for text and learning tasks, greater trust in GenAI, fewer negative emotions, and more permissive ethical views, while college and university students used GenAI more for programming and expressed more skepticism, worry, and concern about learning effects. Across groups, GenAI was commonly viewed as helpful for learning and explanation, but not appropriate for exams or graded work. The authors conclude that educators should tailor GenAI guidance and literacy support to students’ educational context, especially as students transition from high school to higher education.

finding.finding_summary: The study primarily examines GenAI use in computing education tasks such as text generation, programming, bug fixing, and learning support. High school students reported frequent use for text and learning (e.g., 54.6% at least weekly for text tasks; 57% for learning), while college students most often used GenAI for programming-related tasks (e.g., 69% at least weekly for finding and fixing bugs).
finding.measure: Self-reported frequency of GenAI use across text, learning, and programming tasks

finding.finding_summary: Students across all groups reported emotional responses to GenAI, including excitement, optimism, gratitude, worry, skepticism, stress, and fear. High school students showed fewer negative emotions and greater trust than higher-education students; for example, 68.7% of high school students felt excited, and only 36.1% agreed they felt worried, compared with 49.8% of college students and 58.6% of university students agreeing they felt worried.
finding.measure: Likert-scale attitude ratings and self-reported emotion statements about GenAI

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that higher GenAI use is associated with lower concern about learning and greater confidence in GenAI guidance among college and university students, suggesting a relationship with metacognitive/help-seeking judgments. However, students also voiced concerns about overreliance, reduced thinking for oneself, and possible weakening of critical thinking, indicating both beneficial and potentially detrimental durable-skill implications.
finding.measure: Spearman correlations between GenAI usage and agreement with statements about learning, guidance, and overreliance; open-ended responses about learning impacts

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examines institutional GenAI policies, perceived policy clarity, and ethical judgments about permissible use. College students reported clearer and more permissive policies than high school and university students, and across all groups most students supported allowing GenAI for learning but not for exams or graded assignments.
finding.measure: Survey responses on institutional policy clarity, policy allowance, and ethical permissibility of GenAI use

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI in Modern Education Society
paper_profiles.population: Not reported; broad education context spanning school and higher education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews the role of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in modern education, framing the field as a transition from Education 1.0 to Education 5.0. It asks how GenAI is being integrated into teaching, learning, assessment, research, and broader educational administration, and what challenges and future directions emerge from this transition.

The paper is a narrative literature review rather than an empirical study. It synthesizes prior work on GenAI tools and models such as ChatGPT, LLMs, prompt engineering, and AI-driven learning platforms, describing their uses in content creation, tutoring, assessment, adaptive learning, collaboration, accessibility, educational research, and some administrative tasks. The review emphasizes that GenAI can support personalized learning, automate some routine educational workflows, and assist teachers and researchers, while also raising concerns about privacy, bias, academic integrity, overreliance, and the erosion of human social interaction.

The population discussed is broad and includes students, teachers, administrators, and researchers across school and higher education settings, with some references to K-12 contexts. The main conclusion is that GenAI has substantial promise for improving educational practices and productivity, but effective adoption requires careful attention to ethics, training, equitable access, and the preservation of human-centered learning. The paper offers conceptual guidance and future research directions, not direct experimental evidence of effects.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that GenAI can automate tedious educational and administrative processes, freeing teachers and management teams to focus on higher-value work. It specifically mentions uses such as generating draft emails and proposals, data analysis, report generation, automating grading, and streamlining lesson planning and instructional activities, but it does not present new empirical results or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Narrative synthesis of reported use cases for automation, grading, report generation, and educational administration

finding.finding_summary: The review frames GenAI as reshaping education systems, policies, and institutional practices at the level of Education 5.0. It highlights implications for curriculum design, assessment systems, teacher roles, governance, and future research directions, but these claims are conceptual rather than empirically tested in this paper.
finding.measure: Narrative review of institutional and policy implications of GenAI adoption

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating Large Language Models on Financial Report Summarization: An Empirical Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates whether large language models can improve automated financial report summarization, a task requiring accuracy, informativeness, and coherence in a high-stakes domain. The authors compare three models—GLM-4, Mistral-NeMo, and LLaMA3.1—using prompt engineering and few-shot prompting to generate summaries from a dataset of 1,000 financial news articles collected from TradingView and MSN across English, Chinese, and Japanese content.

The study uses a benchmark-style observational comparison rather than a human-subject experiment. Model outputs are evaluated with ROUGE-1, BERTScore, and an LLM-based scoring scheme across accuracy, informativeness, and coherence, along with iteration time as a proxy for efficiency. Results suggest a trade-off: LLaMA3.1 generally achieves the strongest summarization quality but is much slower, Mistral-NeMo is fastest but weaker on some quality dimensions, and GLM-4 offers a middle ground balancing speed and quality.

The paper’s main contribution is methodological and evaluative: it proposes a structured framework for assessing LLM summarization in finance and provides an open dataset for further research. The findings support the broader claim that prompt engineering and domain-adapted evaluation can make LLMs more viable for real-world financial summarization, but they do not address K-12 educational workflows or teacher administrative tasks.

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that LLMs can substantially speed up financial report summarization while preserving useful quality, though there is a quality-speed tradeoff across models. In particular, Mistral-NeMo had the fastest iteration time (3.02s for accuracy evaluation; 2.99s for informativeness; 3.04s for coherence), while LLaMA3.1 was much slower (63.35s, 23.72s, and 25.04s) but generally achieved the highest ROUGE/BERT scores. The authors conclude that prompt-engineered LLMs can reduce manual scanning time for finance analysts and investigators.
finding.measure: Iteration time for summarization; ROUGE-1, BERTScore, and LLM-based quality scores

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating the Ability of Large Language Models to Identify Adherence to CONSORT Reporting Guidelines in Randomized Controlled Trials
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This methodological evaluation study asks whether contemporary large language models can accurately assess adherence to the CONSORT 2010 reporting guidelines in randomized controlled trials. The authors argue that manual CONSORT checking is time-consuming and labor-intensive, making it a plausible target for AI-assisted workflow support in research and editorial settings.

The study constructed a gold-standard benchmark of 150 published RCT full texts from 2020-2025, annotated by expert methodologists across 37 CONSORT items. Sixteen LLMs were tested in a zero-shot setting, and performance was evaluated using macro-F1 and Cohen’s kappa. The best models reached only modest agreement with expert consensus (macro-F1 0.634; kappa about 0.28), performing well on clearly reported items but poorly on missing or inapplicable items.

The main conclusion is that current LLMs can help as preliminary screening tools for CONSORT checks, but they are not reliable for autonomous use because they frequently miss reporting omissions and confuse “not reported” with “not applicable.” The paper supports a human-in-the-loop workflow in which AI can reduce some repetitive checking work, but expert review remains necessary for high-stakes methodological appraisal.

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests LLMs can modestly improve workflow efficiency by serving as preliminary screening assistants for CONSORT checks, reducing some of the manual burden of reviewing RCT reports. However, the benefit is limited because the models still perform poorly on detecting omissions and methodological flaws, so they cannot replace expert review.
finding.measure: Macro-averaged F1-score and qualitative assessment of CONSORT guideline checking performance

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates whether LLMs can support institutional workflows in peer review and evidence synthesis by automating CONSORT adherence checking. Results show only fair agreement with expert consensus (best macro F1=0.634; Cohen’s kappa≈0.28), implying limited institutional usefulness without human oversight.
finding.measure: Agreement with human expert consensus on CONSORT checklist adherence

paper_profiles.title: From Co-Design to Metacognitive Laziness: Evaluating Generative AI in Vocational Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study investigates whether a generative AI proof-of-concept can improve lecturers’ workflows and student learning in a vocational education context. The core problem is not just whether AI can answer student questions, but whether an AI chatbot can reduce repetitive teaching tasks, support individualized feedback, and improve the overall efficiency of exam-preparation support.

Using a user-centred, three-phase mixed-methods design, the researchers co-developed an AI chatbot called StudyBuddy with 20 vocational education lecturers in Singapore. The tool was deployed with students during exam preparation periods, and the study combined surveys, interviews, chat-log analysis, and exam performance comparisons across AI-assisted and non-AI cohorts. Lecturers reported reduced repetition, improved confidence in providing feedback, and streamlined workflows, suggesting clear productivity gains for educators.

However, the student learning results were more mixed. Exam data showed little to no overall score improvement from AI use, though some groups exhibited more consistent performance and in some cases stronger students used the tool more strategically than weaker students. Chat logs also suggested substantial dependency and superficial use patterns, including short direct-answer requests and copying behaviors. Overall, the paper concludes that generative AI can improve teaching processes and operational efficiency, but those gains do not automatically translate into better learning outcomes, raising concerns about dependency, equity, and metacognitive offloading.

finding.finding_summary: Lecturers reported that the StudyBuddy chatbot reduced repeated questions, streamlined workflows, and improved the efficiency of feedback delivery during exam preparation. In post-implementation surveys, confidence in providing personalized feedback increased from M=2.15 to M=4.10, and lecturers described the tool as enabling them to focus on higher-value teaching activities rather than routine support.
finding.measure: Lecturer surveys, interviews, and reported workflow efficiency during exam preparation

finding.finding_summary: In exam-performance comparisons, AI-assisted student cohorts showed either parity with or small differences from non-AI cohorts rather than consistent score gains. In the SDP module, the AI group scored 30.98/45 versus 30.60/45 for one non-AI cohort and 23.11/45 for a lower-performing cohort; in AIEB, the AI tool group scored 17.04/45 versus 17.43/45 for controls, indicating no significant overall improvement.
finding.measure: Module exam scores (MCQ and short-answer/application sections)
finding.study_size: SDP AI group n=103; AIEB group sizes not_reported
finding.std_deviation: SDP AI group SD=7.27; AIEB AI group SD=4.70

finding.finding_summary: Lecturers reported that students using StudyBuddy appeared more confident and less anxious during exam preparation. The paper also notes improved study consistency and stronger confidence in navigating course content, though these benefits were accompanied by concerns about dependency for weaker students.
finding.measure: Lecturer reports, post-implementation interviews, and student behavior observed through chat logs
finding.study_size: n=20 lecturers; 269 unique conversations in chat logs

finding.finding_summary: The study found some evidence of improved metacognitive support for stronger students, but also substantial metacognitive offloading and dependency behaviors. In chat logs, 40.1% of user messages contained dependency-indicating phrases, and many queries were extremely short or direct-answer seeking, suggesting that AI use often replaced rather than strengthened self-regulation and deep thinking.
finding.measure: Chat-log indicators of dependency, metacognitive offloading, and engagement quality

finding.finding_summary: Within vocational education exam contexts, the AI tool did not produce broad learning gains, but it sometimes improved consistency and reliability of performance. For example, in SDP the AI group’s score variability was lower than one non-AI cohort (SD 7.27 vs. 8.77), while in AIEB the AI group showed slightly lower mean scores but reduced variability (SD 4.70 vs. 5.15).
finding.measure: Exam score distributions, SD, Cronbach's alpha, SEM across vocational education modules
finding.study_size: SDP AI group n=103; AIEB group sizes not_reported
finding.std_deviation: SDP AI group SD=7.27; Non-AI A SD=8.77; AIEB AI group SD=4.70; Control SD=5.15

finding.finding_summary: The deployment appears to have increased engagement and time on task, but not necessarily productive learning. In the AIEB module, the AI group took longer to complete the paper (median 37.18 minutes vs. 33.28 minutes for controls), suggesting greater engagement or verification behavior, though this did not translate into higher scores.
finding.measure: Median paper completion time and lecturer interpretation of engagement
finding.study_size: AIEB control and AI tool groups; exact n not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Improving Primary Healthcare Workflow Using Extreme Summarization of Scientific Literature Based on Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI can reduce the time and cognitive effort required to screen scientific literature in primary healthcare contexts. The authors frame the problem as a workflow bottleneck for healthcare professionals who need to stay current with evidence-based practice and propose extreme summarization of abstracts as a way to speed up literature review tasks.

The study compared three conditions across two simulated use cases related to preventive care and behavior change: participants read full abstracts, AI-generated short summaries, or short summaries with the option to expand to the full abstract. A total of 113 university students from Slovenia and the United States were randomized into the three groups and answered content questions about 10 abstracts per use case. The main findings were that AI summaries significantly reduced the time needed to answer questions, especially for EU students, but also reduced accuracy when full abstracts were not available.

Overall, the paper concludes that generative AI-based extreme summarization can improve workflow efficiency for screening literature, but at a cost in comprehension accuracy. The authors suggest the approach has promise for supporting learning health systems and reducing information overload for healthcare professionals, while emphasizing the need for further refinement and human evaluation before broader deployment.

finding.finding_summary: Using AI-generated short abstracts reduced the time needed to answer literature-screening questions compared with full abstracts, but it also lowered accuracy when the full abstract was not available. For EU students, time was significantly lower in the AI-summary groups in both use cases (e.g., G1 vs G3; F=13.466, p<0.001 and F=9.705, p<0.001), while accuracy was also significantly lower for G2/G3 than G1 (e.g., χ2=48.349, p<0.001 and χ2=23.14, p<0.001).
finding.measure: Time to read abstracts and answer content questions; accuracy in answering abstract-based questions

paper_profiles.title: Can Large Language Models Make the Grade? An Empirical Study Evaluating LLMs Ability to Mark Short Answer Questions in K-12 Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language models, especially GPT-4, can reliably grade open-ended short-answer responses in K-12 settings. The motivation is practical: formative assessment is educationally valuable but time-consuming and expensive to scale, so the authors investigate whether LLMs can reduce teacher workload while maintaining accuracy close to human raters.

The study uses a newly assembled dataset of 1,710 student responses to short-answer questions in Science and History from the Carousel quizzing platform, spanning Key Stages 2-4 (roughly ages 5-16). Expert teachers first established ground-truth labels, with disagreements resolved by a third rater. The authors then evaluated GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 under zero-shot and few-shot prompting, comparing model judgments to human labels using accuracy, precision, recall, F1, percent agreement, and Cohen's kappa.

Results showed that GPT-4 with few-shot prompting performed best, reaching Cohen's kappa of 0.70 versus human interrater kappa of 0.75. GPT-4 substantially outperformed GPT-3.5, and few-shot prompting provided a small additional gain. Performance was relatively consistent across subject, grade level, and question difficulty. The authors conclude that LLMs may be useful for low-stakes formative assessment tasks in K-12 education and could offer meaningful teacher time savings, though human judgment remains important for ambiguous edge cases.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that GPT-4 could substantially reduce the time needed to mark short-answer student responses while maintaining near-human agreement. The authors estimate that grading 1,700 responses manually would take at least 11 hours, whereas using GPT-4 after a simple script setup took about 2 hours, with Cohen's kappa of 0.70 versus 0.75 for human raters.
finding.measure: Teacher grading time for 1,700 short-answer responses; agreement with human raters (Cohen's kappa)

paper_profiles.title: The Effects of Access to Credit on Productivity: Separating Technological Changes from Changes in Technical Efficiency
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether access to subsidized agricultural credit increases productivity among rice-producing farm households in Bangladesh, and whether any productivity gains come from improved technology adoption or from better technical efficiency. The authors motivate the study by noting that credit constraints can limit poor farmers’ ability to buy complementary inputs and adopt higher-yield technologies, but prior evidence has struggled to separate frontier-shifting technological change from efficiency improvements.

The study uses a clustered randomized control trial conducted by BRAC’s BCUP program. Treatment communities received access to subsidized credit, while control communities did not; the analysis follows 4,301 households surveyed at baseline in 2012 and at follow-up in 2014, with the main analytic sample focused on rice-producing farms. The authors estimate intent-to-treat effects on input use and rice yields, then apply a stochastic frontier model to decompose the overall productivity effect into a frontier shift and a change in technical efficiency.

The main finding is that access to credit increases rice output by about 13.5–14 percent on average. Roughly 11 percent of this gain is attributed to technological change/frontier shift, and about 3 percent to improved technical efficiency. The effects are concentrated among modern hybrid and high-yielding rice varieties, are essentially absent for traditional rice, and are larger for tenant and mixed-tenant households than for owner-cultivators. The paper concludes that subsidized credit can raise farm productivity by enabling adoption of modern inputs and improving resource management, especially for more resource-constrained farmers.

finding.finding_summary: Access to subsidized credit improved farm productivity and efficiency among rice-producing households in Bangladesh. Using a baseline of 4,301 households and a 24-month follow-up, the authors estimate that treatment households produced about 13.5–14 percent more rice per decimal than controls, with roughly 3 percent of the gain coming from improved technical efficiency. The average efficiency gain is larger for modern hybrid rice producers (about 9 percent) and is negligible for traditional rice varieties.
finding.measure: Rice yield per decimal; technical efficiency from stochastic frontier model
finding.effect_size: about 14% increase in yield; about 3% increase in technical efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates a government-linked microfinance intervention implemented by BRAC and shows that subsidized credit can shift farming practices and improve output in a low-income agricultural setting. The intervention’s broader implication is that credit policy and program design can materially affect farm productivity, especially for tenant and mixed-tenant farmers who are typically underserved by formal finance.
finding.measure: Program-level impact of BCUP credit access on productivity and efficiency

paper_profiles.title: Guardrails for avoiding harmful medical product recommendations and off-label promotion in generative AI models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines a safety and regulatory failure mode of generative AI in medical settings: the tendency of large multimodal language models to recommend medical products for off-label uses. The author argues that because GenAI systems are trained on broad internet-scale corpora with limited human oversight, they can internalize unvetted product-indication relationships and surface them in generated responses, potentially leading to harmful or illegal promotional content.

The paper proposes a post-hoc detection method for identifying off-label promotion in model outputs. The method standardizes user queries, applies biomedical named entity recognition, matches entities to FDA labeling data, and then checks whether product-indication pairs are FDA-approved; if not, a zero-shot T5-large classifier determines whether the response is a recommendation. The approach is demonstrated on Anthropic Claude 3 Sonnet in a shopping-style product question-answering setup using 35 pharmaceuticals and 14,300 synthetic queries generated from templates. The system flagged off-label indications in 15.4% of responses, and on a 2,000-sample human-annotated evaluation the detection pipeline achieved precision 85.75%, recall 80.47%, and F1 83.02%. The main conclusion is that guardrails are needed to monitor and filter model outputs before users see them, especially in regulated domains like healthcare.

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents evidence that generative AI models can produce off-label medical product recommendations and argues for post-hoc guardrails to reduce regulatory and public-health risk. In a synthetic evaluation of 35 pharmaceuticals and 14,300 queries, 15.4% of responses contained off-label indications, and the proposed detection pipeline achieved precision of 85.75%, recall of 80.47%, and F1 of 83.02% on a 2,000-sample human-annotated set.
finding.measure: Off-label promotion detection in MLLM responses; precision/recall/F1 of the detection pipeline; proportion of responses flagged as off-label
finding.study_size: n=14300 synthetic queries; n=2000 human-annotated sample

paper_profiles.title: Artificial Intelligence and Economic Theories
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter examines how artificial intelligence may change core concepts in economics and economic theory. Rather than reporting an empirical study, it develops a conceptual argument that AI-driven systems can alter pricing, market efficiency, rational choice, rational expectations, bounded rationality, game theory, mechanism design, portfolio theory, and causality by improving prediction, optimization, adaptation, and multi-agent modeling.

The paper is framed around broad economic examples and illustrative analogies, not a specific educational or classroom intervention. It argues that as AI increasingly participates in economic decision-making, markets may become more individualized and efficient, information asymmetry may decline, and decision processes may become more consistent and less uncertain. The chapter does not present original data, a sampled population, or experimental results; instead it synthesizes prior theory and asserts plausible implications of AI for economic behavior and modeling.

Because the text is a conceptual economics chapter and not an education study, it does not provide evidence about K-12 teachers, implementation conditions, training, templates, policy guidance, subject area, grade band, or teacher experience. It also does not contain empirical findings with measurable outcomes. Its relevance to the retrieval question is therefore indirect and theoretical rather than evidentiary.

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the Evidence-Based SE Beliefs of Generative AI Tools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks what generative AI tools ‘believe’ about evidence-based software engineering (SE) claims and what kinds of evidence they use to justify those beliefs. The authors conceptually replicate prior work on human software engineers by prompting five chat-based AI tools—ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot, Gemini, Blackbox AI, and Claude—with 17 empirical SE claims and then asking how the tools arrived at their answers.

The study is not about a classroom intervention; it is an analysis of AI system behavior in professional software-development contexts. The tools were evaluated using zero-shot prompts and the responses were coded as yes, no, ambiguous, or not applicable, with follow-up analysis of whether responses cited research, training data, reasoning, or prior conversation. Blackbox AI was the most accurate and the only tool that consistently provided explicit evidence, but most evidence came from blogs and Q&A sites rather than scholarly research.

Overall, the paper finds that generative AI tools often agree with empirical SE claims, but many responses are ambiguous and most lack credible evidence. The authors conclude that practitioners should be cautious about using AI outputs as evidence in development workflows, and they recommend future work on evidence-grounded training data, layered workflows, and AI-based dissemination of research findings. The paper’s contribution is primarily about reliability, evidence use, and implementation of AI tools in software engineering practice rather than educational outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates whether generative AI tools can support software engineering work by giving evidence-based responses to development-related claims. Across 85 coded responses (5 tools × 17 claims), 64.7% were positive, 10.6% negative, and 25.9% ambiguous, indicating that these tools can sometimes support productivity but often provide unclear or unsupported guidance.
finding.measure: Coded agreement with 17 empirical software engineering claims; evidence presence in responses

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examines whether generative AI tools can surface and justify empirical research claims for practitioners, which has implications for the translation of research into practice and evidence-based decision making in software organizations. Most AI-generated responses lacked clear evidence, and the authors argue this limits trustworthy adoption in development workflows.
finding.measure: Presence/type of evidence cited in AI responses; prompted explanations of how answers were generated

paper_profiles.title: The Role of Generative AI in Software Development Productivity: A Pilot Case Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This pilot case study examines how generative AI tools affect the productivity of software professionals in a large software company. The authors focus on the early adoption of tools such as ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot, OpenAI API, and Midjourney and ask how these tools influence work across different roles and activities.

The study uses questionnaires with open-ended questions and observation of workplace communication channels to gather reports from 13 participants after one participant withdrew. Participants included software engineers, designers, data scientists, a QA specialist, and an agile coach, with a mix of mid-level, senior, principal, and management experience. The tools were used for generating and reviewing artifacts, ideation, code-related questions, and formal writing. Reported benefits centered on time savings, knowledge acquisition, and versatility, while challenges included reliability, precision, and security concerns.

Overall, participants reported a generally positive perceived effect on productivity, mainly because the tools helped them work faster, consolidate tasks, and produce useful content more efficiently. However, the authors emphasize that the evidence is preliminary, qualitative, and based on a small sample from one company, so the findings are not statistically generalizable. The paper concludes that generative AI appears promising for software work, but better training, support, and future research are needed to address reliability and integration challenges.

finding.finding_summary: Participants generally reported that generative AI improved their perceived productivity by saving time and streamlining work. In the final sample of 13 professionals, the tools were described as helping with faster text writing, debugging, research, code generation, and consolidation of multiple tools into one workflow, although the evidence is qualitative and not quantified with effect sizes.
finding.measure: Perceived productivity, time optimization, task efficiency, and workflow consolidation reported in open-ended questionnaire responses

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that generative AI supported knowledge acquisition, ideation, and problem solving across tasks, which the authors connect to improved efficiency and flow. Participants said the tools helped them learn new things, validate knowledge, and generate ideas, but the findings are based on self-reports rather than direct skill measures.
finding.measure: Self-reported learning, ideation support, problem-solving support, and knowledge validation

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing Productivity in Database Management Through AI: A Three-Phase Approach for Database
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how generative AI can improve productivity in PostgreSQL database management by automating several routine and analytical tasks. The authors propose a three-phase framework: (1) natural-language-to-SQL query generation and optimization, (2) iterative data analysis and anomaly detection with contextual explanation, and (3) automated question generation and report summarization. The system is positioned as a productivity tool for database administrators and analysts working with enterprise datasets.

The approach combines GPT-4o/CodeLlama-style generative models with schema-aware attention, statistical anomaly detection, forecasting models, and transformer-based summarization. The paper evaluates the framework on enterprise-style database benchmarks and reports improvements in query latency, SQL syntax accuracy, schema-linking precision, root-cause analysis time, and DBA workload. However, the evidence is presented as a technical systems paper rather than a controlled study of educational use, and no K-12 context, teacher population, or classroom implementation is described.

Overall, the paper concludes that AI-assisted database tooling can substantially reduce time and effort for routine database tasks while maintaining high SQL accuracy. It also notes limitations related to complex schemas, training-data bias, and execution-cost awareness, and suggests future work on query-planner integration, knowledge graphs, adaptive learning, and security safeguards.

finding.finding_summary: The AI system reduced DBA workload by 70% for routine queries and reduced analytical report generation time by 40%. It also improved query latency, with tabled results showing AI-generated queries taking 120 ms vs. 200 ms for simple SELECTs, 450 ms vs. 900 ms for JOIN + aggregation, and 600 ms vs. 1500 ms for nested subqueries.
finding.measure: DBA workload, report generation time, query latency

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI-based database automation can improve enterprise data workflows by reducing human intervention, improving query optimization, and supporting faster decision-making. It also discusses governance-relevant issues such as role-based access control, data privacy, and security safeguards for automated query execution, but does not present a policy evaluation or institutional adoption study.
finding.measure: enterprise workflow efficiency and security considerations

paper_profiles.title: The relationship among research productivity, research collaboration, and their determinants
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how research productivity and collaboration relate to one another, and how both are shaped by personal and organizational characteristics. The authors ask whether different forms of collaboration—intra-university, domestic, and international—have different effects on productivity, and whether productivity in turn predicts later collaboration. They also study whether academic rank, cohort (birth year), and gender have direct and indirect effects on both productivity and collaboration.

The study uses longitudinal bibliometric data from Italian university professors in science and economics fields, spanning four three-year periods from 2001-2003 through 2010-2012. Collaboration is measured by the share of publications that are coauthored within university, domestically, or internationally; productivity is measured by Fractional Scientific Strength, a field-normalized citation-based indicator. The authors estimate cross-lagged panel models with structural equation modeling to address reciprocal relationships and unobserved heterogeneity.

The main finding is that collaboration and productivity are mutually related, but not symmetrically. Collaboration at the intra-university and domestic levels has a positive effect on subsequent research productivity, whereas international collaboration does not show a significant positive productivity effect in the full sample. At the same time, prior productivity strongly predicts later collaboration across all forms, and academic rank, cohort, and gender also shape both productivity and collaboration. The paper concludes that the net value of collaboration depends on collaboration type, with lower-cost local collaboration appearing more productivity-enhancing than international collaboration in this context.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies research productivity and collaboration as mutually reinforcing processes among Italian university professors (n=16,823). In the main cross-lagged panel model, intra-university collaboration (CI, b=0.102, p<0.001) and domestic collaboration (CED, b=0.081, p<0.001) positively predicted later Fractional Scientific Strength, while international collaboration (CEF, b=-0.029, n.s.) did not show a significant positive productivity effect. Prior productivity also strongly predicted later collaboration across all collaboration types (e.g., FSS -> CI b=0.005, p<0.001; FSS -> CED b=0.002, n.s./small; FSS -> CEF b=0.003, p<0.05).
finding.measure: Fractional Scientific Strength (FSS) and propensity to collaborate within university, domestically, and internationally

finding.finding_summary: The paper examines how academic rank, cohort, and gender jointly shape productivity and collaboration, and it discusses implications for university policy and management. In the full model, rank and cohort significantly predicted later academic rank (e.g., lagged rank b=0.215, p<0.001; cohort b=0.026, p<0.001), while gender differences were evident in several collaboration models (e.g., male coefficient for CI b=-0.266, p<0.001 in Model D). The authors argue that the findings can inform policy by showing that the payoffs to collaboration differ by collaboration type and by institutional context.
finding.measure: Academic rank, cohort (birth year), and gender effects in cross-lagged panel models

paper_profiles.title: How do you define and measure research productivity?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a methodological problem in research evaluation: how to define and measure research productivity in a way that is consistent with microeconomic theory. The authors argue that commonly used indicators such as publications per researcher, the h-index, and average normalized citation impact do not properly capture productivity because they either ignore output quality, fail to account for co-authorship, or do not normalize output by labor input.

To address this, the paper proposes Fractional Scientific Strength (FSS), an indicator that combines publication output, citation impact, and fractional contribution by authors, while also normalizing by labor cost or staff size. The authors present formulas for individual, field, department, university, region, and nation-level productivity, and then compare Italian university rankings produced by FSS versus simpler publication-count indicators. The comparison shows that rankings can shift substantially depending on the metric, especially in fields such as physics where large-team authorship is common.

The study is set in the Italian higher education and research system, using field classifications unique to Italy (Scientific Disciplinary Sectors and University Disciplinary Areas) and publication/citation data from 2006–2010. Its main conclusion is that productivity assessments should account for both quantity and quality of output, as well as field structure and co-authorship patterns, or else rankings can be misleading. The paper is primarily a conceptual and methodological contribution for research administrators and policy makers rather than an evaluation of an educational intervention.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that Fractional Scientific Strength (FSS) is a more valid measure of research productivity than publications per researcher because it normalizes output by labor input and weights publications by citation impact and fractional authorship. In comparisons of Italian universities (n=61 overall in the final cross-UDA analysis), rankings changed for 85.2% of universities when using FSS instead of simple publication counts, indicating that the alternative metric captures efficiency differences that the conventional metric misses.
finding.measure: Research productivity / efficiency indicators for universities and researchers (FSS vs publications per researcher; FSS vs fractional publications per researcher)
finding.study_size: n=61 universities in overall comparison; field-level samples ranged from n=27 to n=50 universities per UDA

finding.finding_summary: The authors show that the choice of productivity metric materially changes institutional rankings and therefore has implications for research policy, management, and evaluation. In the overall comparison, the Spearman correlation between FSS and simple publication-based rankings was 0.933, yet 52 of 61 universities changed position and 18.8% dropped from the top quartile to a lower quartile, demonstrating substantial institutional consequences of metric choice.
finding.measure: University ranking shifts and rank correlations across productivity indicators
finding.study_size: n=61 universities overall; UDA-specific samples reported in Table 1 and Table 2
finding.effect_size: Spearman rho=0.933 (FSS vs publications per researcher); Spearman rho=0.952 (FSS vs fractional publications per researcher)

paper_profiles.title: Engaging Teachers to Co-Design Integrated AI Curriculum for K-12 Classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 teachers can co-design AI curriculum that is integrated into non-computing core subjects, rather than taught only as standalone computer science content. The authors argue that AI education is often inaccessible to teachers and students, especially in core subjects, and that more scaffolding and teacher collaboration are needed to make AI instruction practical in real classrooms.

To explore this, the researchers ran a two-day remote co-design workshop with 15 K-12 teachers from diverse subject areas and grade bands. Teachers first learned about AI concepts and tools, then completed pre-work and worked in small groups to design integrated lesson plans using AI in social studies, ESL, and literacy for students with learning disabilities. The workshop also included discussion of AI ethics and diversity, and the researchers analyzed workshop audio, questionnaires, and participant deliverables.

The main findings were that teachers valued four implementation supports: evaluation, engagement, logistics, and collaboration. Teachers especially wanted scaffolding for defining AI learning objectives, using AI tools in classroom-friendly ways, choosing age-appropriate structures, and designing ethics discussions. The co-designed curricula showed three main integration pathways: using classroom-generated data to train models, having students reflect on subject content and AI outputs, and embedding AI ethics within core subject lessons. The study concludes that integrated AI curriculum is feasible when teachers are given explicit supports, but that broader adoption will require more tool guidance and curricular scaffolding.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers co-designed a literacy curriculum for students with learning disabilities in which vocabulary words and images were used to train a classification model. The paper reports that the group successfully produced an implementable integrated curriculum draft, but it does not evaluate student literacy outcomes, so the evidence is about design feasibility rather than learning gains.
finding.measure: Co-designed literacy curriculum draft integrating AI with vocabulary and image classification

finding.finding_summary: An ESL curriculum draft was co-created in which students record correct and incorrect pronunciations to train a pronunciation classification app. The paper indicates the curriculum was viewed as implementable and that teachers saw pronunciation practice as a useful AI integration point, but no student language-fluency outcomes were measured.
finding.measure: Co-designed ESL curriculum draft using pronunciation recordings and an AI-powered pronunciation app

finding.finding_summary: The workshop produced an exemplar physics-and-AI curriculum in which students would use paper airplane design data and time-of-flight measurements to train a model and reflect on model improvement. The paper documents successful curriculum design and teacher discussion of scientific/engineering concepts, but does not report student science achievement.
finding.measure: Co-designed physics/engineering curriculum draft using paper-airplane data and model prediction

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s core contribution is the co-design of integrated AI lessons in social studies, ESL, and literacy, including a social studies unit centered on the CROWN Act and AI bias, plus history and career-related connections discussed by participants. The workshop produced first-draft curricula that teachers judged implementable, demonstrating cross-disciplinary integration rather than measured student attainment.
finding.measure: Co-designed integrated curriculum drafts and teacher discussions across social studies, history, career exploration, and literacy-related subjects

finding.finding_summary: Teachers repeatedly emphasized that the integrated lessons should increase student engagement by using real-world hooks, student interests, gamification, and meaningful contexts. The paper reports teachers' perceived need for engagement supports and notes that the workshop increased teachers' enthusiasm for AI integration, but it does not measure student engagement directly.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of engagement supports; workshop feedback and discussion

finding.finding_summary: Teachers highlighted collaboration, reflection, and critical thinking as central design considerations, and the co-designed curricula explicitly built in group work and reflective discussions. The paper reports that these supports helped make AI concepts accessible and curriculum drafts implementable, but it does not quantify gains in durable skills.
finding.measure: Teacher-coded workshop discussions and co-designed lesson-plan features emphasizing collaboration and reflection

finding.finding_summary: A major finding was that teachers needed logistical support, clearer tool guidance, and explicit scaffolding to make AI curriculum easier to run in class. The workshop also produced an increase in teachers’ self-rated confidence integrating AI into their curriculum from 5.6/7 after the workshop (the paper does not report a pre-workshop baseline for confidence), suggesting improved readiness rather than measured time savings.
finding.measure: Teacher self-ratings of confidence integrating AI; qualitative reports about logistics and tool selection

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI should be embedded across K-12 subjects and that teachers need curriculum, ethics, and policy-like guidance to do so effectively. It reports that teachers valued AI ethics discussions and that the co-designed curricula explicitly addressed bias, fairness, and social justice issues, but it does not evaluate institutional adoption or policy change outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher discussions of ethics, diversity, and cross-subject AI curriculum integration

paper_profiles.title: AI as a Teaching Partner: Early Lessons from Classroom Codesign with Secondary Teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report examines how secondary teachers implemented and co-designed generative AI tools for classroom use, with a focus on what conditions made the tools useful or difficult to use. The central question is not whether AI improves test scores, but how AI can function as a teaching partner when teachers remain in control of framing, monitoring, and grading.

Over seven weeks in spring 2025, 21 in-service teachers from five Washington State schools and districts used four Colleague AI features: Teaching Aide, Assessment & AI Grading, AI Tutor, and Student Growth Insights. Teachers planned lessons, implemented AI-supported activities, and provided weekly reflections, surveys, interviews, and usage logs. The sample covered grades 6-12 and multiple subjects, including math, science, ELA, social studies, Spanish, and other courses.

The main conclusion is that AI was most effective when teachers provided strong scaffolding, clear goals, concise prompts, and active supervision. Prior AI experience, teacher belief in AI’s usefulness, grade band, and subject area all shaped implementation quality and student engagement. The report finds strongest promise for formative feedback, conversation scaffolds, and teacher-facing analytics, while also noting limits such as inconsistent AI scoring, overly long responses, and weaker fit in some math, earth science, and younger-student contexts.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that Colleague AI reduced workload by speeding up feedback, streamlining rubric creation, surfacing class-wide misconceptions, and saving time on scanning student work. For AI grading, the median AI grading coverage was 92.2% across submitted assessments (58 assessments; 936 submissions), and teachers frequently described narrative feedback as a helpful first draft that reduced the burden of writing comments.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported workload, AI grading coverage, rubric generation, and feedback turnaround; platform usage logs
finding.study_size: n=21 teachers overall; n=19 teachers in assessment phase; 58 assessments; 936 student submissions

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that AI-supported activities often increased student engagement, confidence, and willingness to participate, especially when teacher framing and scaffolding were strong. In the Teaching Aide feature, 35% of teacher-reported sessions indicated that the tool helped most students learn, while 62% indicated that some students learned from it.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of student engagement and learning during AI-assisted conversations; exit tickets and surveys
finding.study_size: n=18 teachers for Teaching Aide phase

finding.finding_summary: The report suggests AI can support inquiry, revision, and reflective thinking, but effects depended heavily on teacher scaffolding, subject area, and grade band. Teachers reported that structured AI conversations could prompt deeper thinking, but weak framing led to shallow exchanges or off-task use; no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher observations and ratings of student-AI conversation quality, revision behavior, and inquiry depth
finding.study_size: n=18 teachers for Teaching Aide phase; n=19 teachers for assessment phase

finding.finding_summary: In ELA and Spanish, teachers reported useful support for writing-related tasks such as brainstorming, prewriting, revision, and ACTFL-aligned proficiency feedback. However, results were mixed overall because some teachers found responses generic or off-topic, and no standardized writing outcome measure or effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher reports of writing support, prewriting, revision, and language-feedback use in ELA and Spanish

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that multilingual learners and Spanish students benefited from AI conversations and feedback that helped them participate more confidently and receive proficiency-oriented feedback. The evidence is qualitative and implementation-based rather than a formal fluency outcome, and no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher reports of student participation, conversational practice, and proficiency feedback in language-learning contexts

finding.finding_summary: Math teachers used the tools for conversations and feedback, but the report describes more variable outcomes than in some other subjects because the AI struggled with diagrams, technical reasoning, and flexible problem solving. Teachers noted some value for concept talk and inquiry, but trust and accuracy were recurring concerns; no quantitative learning effect was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher reports of implementation quality and learning value in math classes

finding.finding_summary: Science teachers reported that AI-supported conversations could aid inquiry, culturally relevant discussion, and formative feedback, but results varied by topic and task type. Earth science and some technical science contexts were harder for the AI because of diagrammatic and technical-reasoning demands; no standardized science achievement measure was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher reports of inquiry support and science-class implementation quality

finding.finding_summary: The pilot suggests AI adoption depends on institutional supports such as district MOUs, privacy policies, voluntary teacher participation, and professional learning structures. Teachers with prior AI use and stronger AI beliefs implemented more successfully, indicating that implementation conditions and staff capacity matter for scaling; however, no formal policy outcome was measured.
finding.measure: Implementation conditions, district partnership structures, and teacher-reported readiness/experience
finding.study_size: n=21 teachers; 5 Washington State school organizations

paper_profiles.title: Dual-Role Dynamics in Prompting: Elementary Pre-service Teachers’ AI Prompting Strategies for Representational Choices
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how elementary pre-service teachers use generative AI to choose representations for explaining science concepts, and whether their prompting changes when they are cast in a teacher role versus a student role. The authors focus on a dual-role framing: participants used AI to help explain wave velocity to elementary students while acting as teachers, and the Ideal Gas Law to an English teacher while acting as students.

The study was conducted in a physical science course for elementary education majors at a large midwestern U.S. university. Participants first generated representations without AI and then interacted with Microsoft Copilot Pro to generate or refine representations. The researchers analyzed the prompts qualitatively and identified three main differences across roles: participants were more likely to explicitly name the audience, specify the representation in advance (prescriptive prompting), and generate a wider variety of representations when acting as teachers than when acting as students.

The main conclusion is that the teacher role appeared to elicit more agentic and more focused AI prompting, whereas the student role led to more exploratory prompting. The authors argue that teacher preparation programs could use these patterns to support pre-service teachers’ AI literacy, representational competence, and science learning by encouraging multiple representations and more reflective use of AI in both teaching and learning contexts.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that pre-service teachers’ prompting behavior differed by role in ways that reflect representational competence and agency. When acting as teachers, participants were more explicit about the audience, more prescriptive about the representation, and produced a broader variety of representations than when acting as students (n=20).
finding.measure: Qualitative coding of AI prompts for explicit target audience, prescriptive versus exploratory prompting, and diversity of representations

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studied how pre-service elementary teachers used AI to represent and communicate physics concepts, specifically wave velocity and the Ideal Gas Law. Prompting patterns suggested stronger conceptual framing in the teacher role, including more frequent specification of elementary students as the audience and more varied representational choices (pictures, cartoons, analogies, graphs, equations, stories) across the two tasks (n=20).
finding.measure: AI prompts and generated representations for wave velocity and the Ideal Gas Law

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests AI could support pre-service teachers in quickly generating or refining instructional representations, reducing the burden of deciding how to present content. Participants used Microsoft Copilot Pro to obtain representations for explanations, and the authors frame this as a support for teacher preparation and instructional planning rather than a measured productivity outcome (n=20).
finding.measure: Use of AI to generate instructional representations

paper_profiles.title: LLMs to Support K–12 Teachers in Culturally Relevant Pedagogy: An AI Literacy Example
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a practical implementation problem in K–12 education: teachers often want to use culturally relevant pedagogy (CRP), but they lack time, training, and ready-to-use resources to adapt lessons in culturally responsive ways. The authors focus on a particularly underexplored context: AI literacy instruction, where culturally responsive materials are especially scarce.

To address this gap, the paper introduces CulturAIEd, a large language model (LLM)-powered tool that uses student demographic information, a culturally responsive teaching checklist, rubric-based feedback, and just-in-time chatbot support to help teachers adapt AI literacy activities. The authors ran an exploratory pilot with four secondary teachers from different regions and subject areas (science, music education, and information technology), asking them to adapt AI literacy lessons across several stages: without guidance, with a CRT checklist, and with CulturAIEd support.

Findings from surveys and interviews suggest that CulturAIEd improved teachers’ confidence in identifying opportunities for cultural responsiveness and making culturally responsive modifications to lessons. Teachers valued the tool’s ability to streamline demographic integration, provide immediate actionable feedback, and reduce the time needed for CRP-related planning. The study concludes that LLMs may help teachers implement CRP more efficiently, but the evidence is preliminary and based on a very small qualitative-dominant pilot, so the authors frame the results as promising rather than conclusive.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that CulturAIEd saved time and reduced planning burden by streamlining demographic integration, offering immediate actionable feedback, and helping them make culturally responsive lesson modifications more efficiently. In the post-survey, 3/4 participants strongly agreed the tool saved time and inspired new ideas, and the authors describe the tool as solving the problem of time and research needed for CRP.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of time savings, workflow efficiency, and planning burden from post-surveys and interviews

finding.finding_summary: The tool increased teachers’ confidence in identifying opportunities for cultural responsiveness in AI literacy activities and in making culturally responsive modifications. Reported confidence for identifying opportunities rose from pre-survey ratings of 3-5 to 5/5 for all participants post-intervention, indicating improved pedagogical judgment and reflective planning.
finding.measure: Teacher self-rated confidence in identifying opportunities for cultural responsiveness and making CRP modifications

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that CulturAIEd may help address institutional barriers to CRP implementation, including gaps in training, lack of resources, and inconsistent school support. However, the evidence is indirect and based on teacher perceptions rather than policy or organizational outcome measures; the authors also note the need for effective training and integration into professional development.
finding.measure: Teacher reports of school support, professional development exposure, and perceived barriers/opportunities for CRP implementation

paper_profiles.title: AI-Generated Rubric Interfaces: K–12 Teachers’ Perceptions and Practices
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K–12 teachers perceive and use AI-supported rubric generation tools, focusing on rubric authoring and AI-assisted feedback in a block-based programming context. The motivating problem is that rubric creation is time-consuming and cognitively demanding, especially when teachers need clear performance-level distinctions and alignment with instructional goals. The authors ask whether an LLM-based tool can help teachers generate rubrics more efficiently while still preserving teacher judgment, alignment, and fairness.

The study was conducted in summer 2025 with 25 middle- and high-school teachers in professional development workshops. Teachers used MagicSchool.ai to generate rubrics for a sample Snap! block-based programming task, compared AI-generated rubrics to their own manually created versions, and also used an AI chatbot to generate rubric-based feedback. Data sources included pre/post surveys, open discussions, exit tickets, and thematic analysis of qualitative responses. The workshop versions differed slightly by grade band in task selection and scaffolding, but the core workflow was the same.

Across both survey and qualitative results, teachers generally viewed AI-generated rubrics as useful starting drafts that improved structure, clarity, and speed, but not as final products. Teachers repeatedly emphasized the need for oversight, easy editing, grade-appropriate language, and alignment with curriculum and classroom priorities.
