Concerns centered on generic wording, occasional misalignment, fairness/equity, privacy, and workflow limitations, while adoption intentions were conditional on maintaining teacher control and better customization support. Overall, the paper concludes that teacher-facing AI rubric tools are most promising when they support, rather than replace, teacher agency.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers consistently reported that AI-generated rubrics saved time and reduced the effort of drafting rubrics from scratch. In the post-survey, they rated the rubric as a flexible starting point (M=3.5625, SD=1.31) and generally agreed it was easy to modify for classroom needs (M=3.5, SD=1.26), though adding/removing criteria remained a weakness (M=2.75, SD=1.23).
finding.measure: Perceived usability, flexibility, and workload/time savings from AI-generated rubric creation and editing

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined policy and institutional constraints affecting classroom use, including district AI restrictions, school blocks on AI access, LMS integration barriers, and concerns about privacy and transparency. Teachers’ adoption intentions were shaped by whether institutional policies and workflows allowed them to use AI tools while retaining control over assessment decisions.
finding.measure: Survey and open-ended responses درباره policy constraints, access barriers, privacy concerns, and adoption conditions

finding.finding_summary: Teachers said AI-generated rubrics clarified criteria and performance-level distinctions, which they believed could support students’ understanding of expectations and improve assessment transparency. The strongest related survey result was that the rubric could help students understand how their work would be evaluated (M=4.12, SD=0.95).
finding.measure: Perceived student understanding of evaluation, clarity of criteria, and performance-level differentiation

paper_profiles.title: Using Transformers to Provide Teachers with Personalized Feedback on their Classroom Discourse: The TalkMoves Application
paper_profiles.population: K-12 teachers in grades 3-12; underlying data from kindergarten through 12th grade math lessons
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of giving K-12 mathematics teachers timely, actionable feedback on their classroom discourse, especially their use of “talk moves” that support productive mathematical discussion. The authors argue that current expert human coding approaches are too expensive and slow to scale, and propose an AI-based pipeline that automatically analyzes classroom recordings and produces individualized feedback for teachers.

The core intervention is the TalkMoves application, which combines automated speech recognition with transformer-based natural language processing models to classify teacher utterances into six accountable-talk categories plus a none label. The system is trained on 501 manually coded math lesson transcripts drawn from K-12 classrooms and is deployed in a web dashboard that summarizes talk-move frequency, teacher versus student talk, wait time, and related discourse indicators. The best model, RoBERTa-Large, achieved F1 = 79.33% and MCC = 0.7779 on the held-out test set, improving over an earlier BiLSTM baseline (F1 = 65%).

The application was piloted with a small group of 21 teachers in two midwestern U.S. school districts during the 2019-2020 academic year, with teachers in grades 3-12 recording lessons, viewing feedback, and completing surveys/interviews. The paper’s main conclusion is that transformer-based NLP can approximate expert coding closely enough to power an end-to-end teacher feedback system, but substantial implementation challenges remain, particularly noisy classroom speech, uneven label distribution, and under-recognition of young children’s speech by ASR. The paper is primarily a systems/model-development study rather than an outcomes study of teacher or student learning.

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that an automated TalkMoves pipeline can classify teacher discourse moves with substantially better performance than the prior baseline, reducing reliance on time-consuming expert hand-coding. The best model (RoBERTa-Large) reached F1 = 79.33% and MCC = 0.7779 on the test set, compared with the earlier BiLSTM baseline at F1 = 65%, indicating improved productivity for feedback generation rather than a direct classroom outcome.
finding.measure: Model performance for automated talk-move classification; comparison to prior manual-coding workflow and baseline model
finding.study_size: n=501 transcripts; 176,757 sentences (115,418 teacher sentences, 61,339 student sentences)

paper_profiles.title: The Hands-Up Problem and How to Deal With It: Secondary School Teachers’ Experiences of Debugging in the Classroom
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines secondary school computing teachers’ experiences of teaching and supporting debugging in text-based programming classrooms. The authors ask what teachers experience, what they observe about students’ debugging behavior, and what classroom conditions make debugging difficult, especially in contexts where time is limited and students frequently need help.

Using semi-structured interviews with nine teachers, the study identifies recurring barriers to successful debugging: limited lesson time, students’ negative attitudes and emotions, difficult syntax in Python, and hard-to-interpret error messages. A central finding is the “hands-up problem,” where many students raise their hands for teacher help at the same time, making it impossible for one teacher to support everyone effectively. Teachers described a range of responses, including insisting students try independently first, using peer support, modeling debugging strategies, teaching students to interpret programming error messages, and fostering a positive error culture.

The population is secondary school computing teachers teaching text-based programming, mostly in lower secondary / Key Stage 3–equivalent settings, with Python as the main language and some additional TBPLs such as Swift. The paper concludes that debugging-specific pedagogical content knowledge and professional development may help less confident teachers reduce teacher dependence and build student resilience. It frames the hands-up problem as a classroom-level challenge and argues that debugging can become more manageable when teachers use explicit scaffolds and norms that promote independent problem-solving.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that debugging-related hand-raising created a highly busy and sometimes chaotic classroom environment, with too many simultaneous requests for one teacher to handle effectively. The paper does not report a quantitative effect size, but the qualitative evidence from nine interviews indicates that teacher time and attention were stretched by having to potentially debug many students’ programs in a single lesson (e.g., classes of 25–30 students).
finding.measure: Teacher-reported classroom workload and ability to support multiple students during debugging

finding.finding_summary: Teachers described frequent frustration, anxiety, disappointment, and disengagement when students encountered debugging problems, especially when students repeatedly hit a wall and stopped trying. Teachers also observed positive emotions such as excitement and pride when errors were finally resolved, suggesting debugging can produce both negative and positive affect depending on student persistence and success.
finding.measure: Teacher observations of student emotions, resilience, motivation, and disengagement during debugging

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on students’ independent problem-solving, resilience, and metacognitive debugging strategies, showing that some students relied heavily on the teacher while others learned to reflect, test incrementally, and interpret errors themselves. Teachers reported that explicit scaffolding, modeling, and repeated practice helped students become more independent debuggers, but the evidence is qualitative and based on teacher reports from nine interviews.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported student debugging independence, resilience, and use of problem-solving/debugging strategies

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that limited curriculum time, class size, and professional knowledge constraints shape teachers’ ability to teach debugging effectively, and it recommends debugging-specific professional development and better dissemination of teaching approaches. These are institutional and implementation-level findings rather than measured impacts, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Institutional and implementation conditions affecting debugging instruction (time, class size, curriculum constraints, professional development needs)

paper_profiles.title: Exploring K-12 Physical Education Teachers’ Perspectives on Opportunities and Challenges of AI Integration Through Ideation Workshops
paper_profiles.venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how in-service K-12 physical education (PE) teachers in South Korea perceive the opportunities, challenges, and implementation conditions for AI integration in PE classes. The authors argue that AI research in K-12 has focused heavily on classroom STEM subjects, while PE remains underexplored despite its distinctive instructional demands, such as large open spaces, safety monitoring, heterogeneous student abilities, and heavy assessment burdens.

To surface teacher perspectives, the study conducted in-person focus group ideation workshops with 17 secondary PE teachers. Participants first discussed classroom challenges, then received a short AI literacy-oriented lecture on core AI capabilities, and finally sketched and storyboarded potential AI-supported PE scenarios. The workshop format was used to elicit ideas for AI rather than test a deployed system, so the paper is a qualitative exploration of needs, envisioned roles, and concerns.

Teachers imagined AI taking four supportive roles: operational assistant, personal trainer, group coach, and evaluator. These roles were meant to help with class management, personalized feedback, team formation, and multidimensional assessment. At the same time, teachers emphasized major implementation barriers, including limited institutional support, inadequate infrastructure, differences in teachers’ technology proficiency and motivation, misalignment with PE educational goals, overreliance on AI, and privacy/data security concerns. The paper concludes that successful AI integration in PE will require clear pedagogical guidance, robust infrastructure, and teacher-centered design that supports rather than replaces educators.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers overwhelmingly expected AI to reduce workload and streamline PE class operations, including environment setup, student monitoring, safety management, and assessment/data handling. Across the 17-participant qualitative workshop, they described AI as an operational assistant and evaluator that could save class time, automate record keeping, and allow teachers to focus more on student guidance, but these are anticipated benefits rather than measured outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher-perceived workload, class management burden, and assessment/record-keeping efficiency in focus group discussions and ideation artifacts

finding.finding_summary: Participants identified substantial institutional barriers to AI adoption in PE, including low subject priority, inadequate funding and space, lack of Wi-Fi or durable devices, maintenance burdens, and the need for coherent curriculum and policy guidance. They also raised concerns about consent, privacy, and data security, indicating that successful implementation depends on broader governance and institutional support rather than teacher effort alone.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported implementation barriers, institutional support needs, and policy/privacy concerns in workshop discussions

paper_profiles.title: Reflective Diary for Professional Development of Novice Teachers
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 50th ACM Technical Symposium on Computer Science Education (SIGCSE ’19)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a practical professional-development problem in university computer science teaching: novice teaching assistants often have strong technical knowledge but limited pedagogical training, and institutions may lack enough expert mentors to provide frequent individualized feedback. The authors argue that delayed reflection after teaching limits its usefulness, so they designed a structured reflective diary to help novice teachers reflect shortly after lessons and connect that reflection to ongoing teacher-training sessions.

The intervention is a paper-based, semi-structured diary used in the authors’ Teaching Lab at Masaryk University. The diary includes weekly pre-lesson and post-lesson prompts, a teacher self-assessment rubric, and a handbook summarizing concepts and tools covered in training. It was piloted with 25 novice teaching assistants and also offered to a small number of experienced university teachers and some high-school teachers. Data came from focus-group discussion and e-mail feedback, making this a qualitative case study of implementation and user experience rather than an outcome-effect study.

The authors report overwhelmingly positive responses from novice teachers: the diary served as a reminder and trigger for reflection, supported lesson preparation, and helped bridge teacher-training content with actual classroom practice. Participants also valued its use as a shared reference point for discussion with peers and mentors. At the same time, the paper identifies implementation challenges, including irregular use, clashes with existing planning/reporting tools, and limited fit for some non-weekly class formats. Overall, the paper concludes that a structured reflective diary can support novice CS teachers’ professional development and may transfer beyond the original faculty context, though its evidence is primarily experiential and descriptive.

finding.finding_summary: The diary was reported to improve reflective practice and metacognitive awareness among novice teachers. In a pilot with 25 novice teaching assistants plus about five additional staff users, participants said the diary acted as a “kick” to think about lessons, helped them analyze what worked and what did not, and strengthened their ability to connect teaching actions with future improvement. No quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Reflective practice / metacognitive self-reflection as reported in focus group and e-mail feedback
finding.study_size: n=30 (approximately 25 novice TAs and about 5 staff members)

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported that the diary improved lesson preparation and helped organize teaching notes in one place, suggesting a productivity benefit for teachers. The paper does not report a quantified workload or time-savings measure, but qualitative feedback indicates the diary helped teachers remember what to include before lessons and reduced loss of information across weeks.
finding.measure: Lesson preparation, note organization, and perceived teaching workflow efficiency
finding.study_size: n=30 (approximately 25 novice TAs and about 5 staff members)

finding.finding_summary: The diary helped connect teacher-training sessions with actual teaching practice and also stimulated discussion among peers and mentors in the Teaching Lab. The paper further reports broader institutional spillover: interest from other university staff, other faculties, teacher-training centers at three Czech universities, and some secondary-school teachers, indicating possible institutional adoption beyond the original context. No quantitative institutional outcome was measured.
finding.measure: Reported institutional uptake, discussion quality, and transfer beyond the original faculty
finding.study_size: n=30 direct users, plus additional interested external adopters mentioned qualitatively

paper_profiles.title: How Can Video Generative AI Transform K-12 Education? Examining Teachers’ Perspectives through TPACK and TAM
paper_profiles.population: K-12 teachers (predominantly Elementary, plus one High School teacher and one former elementary teacher/data analyst)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 teachers perceive the educational use of video generative AI (Video GenAI), a rapidly emerging AI technology capable of producing videos from natural-language prompts. The study is motivated by the lack of research on how such tools might be integrated into real classrooms, especially given their potential for creating customized visual materials, supporting authentic tasks, and reducing teachers’ preparation burden.

Using TPACK and TAM as analytic frameworks, the authors conducted semi-structured interviews and hands-on experimentation with Luma Dream Machine, a publicly available video generation tool. Ten participants were purposefully selected because they had relatively high interest and experience with educational technology and AI; eight were elementary teachers, one was a high school English teacher, and one was a former elementary teacher working as a data analyst. Participants first used the tool, then reflected on its usability, usefulness, classroom applications, and limitations.

The study finds that teachers viewed Video GenAI as promising for visualizing abstract content, supporting creative expression, enriching project-based learning, and enabling more varied assessment and instructional design. At the same time, they raised substantial concerns about rendering quality, language limitations (especially Korean), safety, age restrictions, copyright, unclear policy guidance, and lack of teacher-monitoring features. The paper concludes that successful adoption will depend on stronger technical performance, clearer institutional and national guidance, and targeted professional development focused on prompt use, ethics, and pedagogical integration.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that Video GenAI could help explain and visualize content in subjects such as science, history, Korean language, and arts, especially for abstract or hard-to-film topics. The evidence is qualitative and based on interviews with n=10 teachers after hands-on use of Luma Dream Machine; no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Teachers’ interview reports of subject-specific instructional applications and perceived value for content comprehension

finding.finding_summary: Teachers believed Video GenAI could increase student engagement, motivation, and interest through dynamic visual content and creative participation. The finding is based on qualitative interview data from n=10 teachers; no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Teachers’ perceptions of student engagement, motivation, and interest

finding.finding_summary: Teachers described Video GenAI as supporting creative expression, divergent thinking, prompt formulation, and project-based learning, with students iterating on ideas and exploring multiple outcomes. These are qualitative perceptions from n=10 teachers, with no reported effect size or quantitative measure.
finding.measure: Teachers’ reports of creativity, divergent thinking, composition/prompt-writing, and project-based learning use

finding.finding_summary: Teachers said Video GenAI could reduce preparation time by quickly generating visual materials and supplementary resources, but they also noted slow rendering, short video length, and the need for extensive editing, which limited practical efficiency. This qualitative evidence comes from interviews with n=10 teachers; no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Teachers’ perceptions of preparation time, generation speed, and workflow efficiency

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper is policy and institutional readiness for Video GenAI, including age restrictions, parental consent, copyright, safety filtering, infrastructure, and national guidance. Teachers and experts argued that adoption would require clearer governance, training, and school-level support; the evidence is qualitative from n=10 interview participants and related discussion, with no effect size reported.
finding.measure: Teachers’ and experts’ views on policy, governance, infrastructure, and institutional support needs

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks Middle School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether teachers should remain “in-the-loop” when using generative AI to personalize mathematics tasks for students, and what the efficiency and instructional tradeoffs look like in that model. The authors focus on context personalization, specifically adapting existing middle school mathematics problems to students’ interests using ChatGPT/GPT-4o, while examining teacher prompting behavior, teacher time, and student reactions.

Seven 7th-grade mathematics teachers from six U.S. schools participated after a 2-hour training on personalization, bias, readability, and cultural relevance, followed by two problem-authoring sessions using Illustrative Mathematics curriculum materials (Unit 4 and Unit 6). Teachers created 143 personalized problems for 521 students, with prompt logs, video, time data, and student survey ratings/open-ended feedback analyzed. The study found that teachers often used GenAI to broaden or narrow the grain size of personalization, but they spent substantial effort correcting realism and tailoring details. Students generally preferred more specific, fine-grained references, while teachers tended to work at broader class-level interests. Personalizing a problem took about 4 minutes on average, and the process did not become clearly more time-efficient over time; in fact, teachers used more prompts and spent more time in Unit 6 than Unit 4, although students rated Unit 6 problems higher. The authors conclude that teacher-in-the-loop personalization can support professional learning and quality control, but it is time-consuming and may not deliver the small-grain personalization many students prefer.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers used generative AI to personalize 143 middle school mathematics problems, and student ratings of the personalized problems improved from Unit 4 to Unit 6. Mean interestingness increased from 2.27 to 2.56 and mean closeness to students’ interests increased from 2.28 to 2.66 on 5-point scales; mixed-effects models found this unit-level improvement was statistically significant (B=0.33, SE=0.095, t=3.49, p=0.0012).
finding.measure: Student ratings of problem interestingness and closeness to interests for personalized middle school mathematics tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that personalized mathematics tasks increased student interest, a key social-emotional outcome, though ratings were modest overall. Across 53 problems with closed-ended survey data, the average interestingness rating was 2.46/5 (SD=1.24), and students more often said specific popular-culture references—not broad topic labels—made problems interesting. The study reports that using 3-5 prompts was associated with higher student ratings by about 0.24 points on a 5-point scale (B=0.240, SE=0.085, t=2.84, p=0.0073).
finding.measure: Student self-reported interestingness ratings and open-ended feedback
finding.study_size: n=521 students; ratings collected for 52-53 problems depending on measure

finding.finding_summary: The study found that teacher-in-the-loop personalization was time-consuming and did not become clearly more efficient with experience. Teachers used an average of 3.2 prompts per problem and about 246 seconds per problem overall, with substantial variability; from Unit 4 to Unit 6, prompt use increased from 3.2 to 4.6 prompts per problem and time increased from 204 to 286 seconds per problem, both statistically significant. The authors conclude that this workflow does not yet save teachers time and likely requires broad-grain personalization to remain feasible.
finding.measure: Teacher time to create each personalized problem; number of prompts per problem

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests that working with ChatGPT supported teacher learning, reflection, and iterative improvement in prompting, which are durable skills related to metacognition and problem solving. Teachers improved at crafting more interesting problems over time and engaged in reflective adjustment after student feedback, though this came with increased time and more prompts rather than greater efficiency.
finding.measure: Teacher prompting practices, iteration over time, and reflective refinement of tasks

paper_profiles.title: Teacher training in the age of AI: Impact on AI Literacy and Teachers' Attitudes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether a short online professional development course can improve in-service teachers’ AI literacy and their attitudes toward using AI in teaching. The motivating problem is that teachers are being expected to understand and use AI tools in classrooms even though many have limited preparation, and the authors argue that structured training may reduce fear and increase readiness for adoption.

The intervention was a four-week certificate course offered by the German platform fobizz, combining synchronous webinars, self-paced modules, optional deep-dive sessions, and a project in which teachers created an AI-supported lesson plan. The course was designed mainly for in-service primary and secondary teachers, though some participants from adult education, higher education, and administration also took part. Participants completed pre-post questionnaires measuring AI literacy (N=291) and attitudes toward AI use and integration (N=436), with all analyses limited to paired respondents.

Results showed statistically significant gains in overall AI literacy (mean 13.15 to 15.13, d=0.37) and significant improvements in 10 of 14 AI literacy competencies, though the effects were generally small. Teachers also reported substantially more frequent AI use in daily life and for lesson/material creation, greater intention and preparedness to integrate AI into teaching, and stronger belief that AI can support students. At the same time, small increases in concern about AI being a threat or replacing teachers were observed, which the authors interpret as possibly reflecting more realistic risk awareness rather than simple resistance. The paper concludes that structured AI-focused teacher training can improve both competence and confidence, but that longer-term follow-up and more subject- or context-specific training are needed.

finding.finding_summary: The training increased teachers’ confidence and willingness to use AI in pedagogical practice. Agreement with the item “I feel well-prepared to integrate AI technologies into my teaching” rose from M=1.03 (SD=0.77) to M=2.28 (SD=0.74), with a large effect (d=1.65, p<0.001; n=436 for attitudes).
finding.measure: Teacher self-reported preparedness/confidence to integrate AI into teaching (4-point Likert item)

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported more frequent AI use for lesson planning/material creation and for assessment/grading after the course. Agreement with using AI to create lessons and teaching materials increased from M=1.27 (SD=0.92) to M=2.35 (SD=0.71), d=1.32, and using AI for assessments/grading increased from M=0.41 (SD=0.69) to M=1.04 (SD=1.11), d=0.67 (both p<0.001; n=436).
finding.measure: Self-reported AI use for lesson creation, teaching materials, assessments, and grading (Likert items)
finding.std_deviation: Lesson/materials: Pre SD=0.92; Post SD=0.71. Assessment/grading: Pre SD=0.69; Post SD=1.11.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined whether a teacher training program improves AI literacy and AI integration readiness as a professional development intervention. Overall AI literacy increased from M=13.15 (SD=5.46) to M=15.13 (SD=5.14), d=0.37 (p<0.001; n=291), and 10 of 14 competencies improved significantly, indicating that structured training can shift institutional teacher capacity for AI adoption.
finding.measure: Overall AI literacy score and 14 AI literacy competency areas; pre-post teacher attitudes toward AI integration

paper_profiles.title: A Pilot Study on Teacher-Facing Real-Time Classroom Game Dashboards
paper_profiles.population: Middle School and High School (grades 6-12) teachers and classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This pilot study addresses a design and implementation question: how can a real-time dashboard help teachers facilitate classroom use of an educational video game, and what kinds of game-state information do teachers want to see? The authors note that teachers often have to monitor students’ gameplay by walking around and inspecting individual screens, which is inefficient and makes it hard to provide timely support. To explore a dashboard solution, they used participatory design with teachers and stakeholders to gather requirements and then built a prototype for the educational game Lakeland.

The study proceeded in two phases. In the first, twelve teachers and teaching mentors participated in a workshop using prompt cards and mockups to generate desired dashboard models and visualizations. In the second, the authors implemented a teacher-facing, real-time dashboard that visualized student gameplay data and piloted it in authentic classroom settings. Four teachers used the prototype across several classes (including one teacher with 12 planned sessions), with students in grades 6-12 and class sizes of up to 20; most sessions were online because of COVID-19 disruptions.

Findings were based on artifact analysis, surveys, and interviews. Teachers saw clear evidence that their workshop input shaped the prototype, reported that setup and use were generally easy, and said the dashboard often helped them notice struggling or inactive students and understand gameplay progress. At the same time, they identified bugs, occasional data mismatches, and the need for class-level overview views and clearer visual encodings. Overall, the paper concludes that participatory design can produce a useful teacher-facing dashboard for classroom game facilitation, though the prototype still needs refinement for reliability and usability.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the dashboard was generally easy to set up and use, and that it helped them monitor students without constantly checking individual screens. Survey results were favorable (n=4 teachers): setting up a class code and getting students connected scored 5/5, the dashboard itself was easy to use (4/5), and teachers said they would use and recommend the tool again (both 5/5).
finding.measure: Teacher survey ratings and post-session interviews on usability, setup, and classroom monitoring

finding.finding_summary: The dashboard helped teachers notice student disengagement, inactivity, and progress in real time, which supported timely intervention during gameplay. Teachers specifically mentioned using the tool to identify students who were 'inactive' or 'clicking randomly' and to determine when students were making progress, suggesting improved engagement monitoring rather than direct student outcome measurement.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of student engagement/inactivity during game sessions

paper_profiles.title: NiCE Teacher Workshop: Engaging K-12 Teachers in the Development of Curricular Materials That Utilize Complex Networks Concepts
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2018 CompleNet / Complex Networks conference context
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes the NiCE (Networks in Classroom Education) teacher workshop, created to introduce K-12 educators to network science and support them in developing lesson plans and curricular materials that use network concepts. The core problem addressed is the lack of accessible, classroom-ready network science resources and the need for teacher ownership, support, and collaboration when adapting new interdisciplinary concepts for schools.

The intervention was a four-day workshop held at West Point in July 2017 with 21 K-12 teachers from diverse subject areas and grade bands. The workshop combined introductory presentations, hands-on activities, discussions, standards mapping (especially to NGSS), and collaborative lesson-design sessions paired with network scientists. Participants were given pre-workshop videos, a small stipend, and post-workshop support, with the goal of producing publicly available curricular resources.

The paper reports workshop outputs and participant reflections rather than a formal experimental evaluation. Teachers generated 13 resources in total, including 10 lesson plans and 3 broader education projects, spanning elementary through high school and multiple subjects. Survey responses and descriptive feedback indicate strong enthusiasm, increased understanding of network science, and greater likelihood of using network concepts in classrooms, suggesting the workshop was effective as a professional development and curriculum-development model.

finding.finding_summary: The workshop was designed to help teachers create classroom materials more efficiently by giving them content knowledge, collaborative support, and standards alignment tools. The paper reports that participants produced 13 resources (10 lesson plans and 3 projects), and that the workshop aimed to ease teachers' workload by providing ready-to-use, adaptable curricular materials; however, no formal productivity metric or controlled comparison was reported.
finding.measure: Number of lesson plans/projects produced; participant reports about usefulness for lesson design and workload reduction

finding.finding_summary: The workshop explicitly targeted curriculum development aligned with standards, especially NGSS, and encouraged teachers to map network science ideas onto governing standards and interdisciplinary grade-level standards. The paper reports that participants created publicly available materials and that the authors view the workshop as a proof-of-principle for integrating network science into K-12 education, but it does not provide quantitative institutional outcome measures.
finding.measure: Development of standards-aligned curricular resources; alignment to NGSS and interdisciplinary standards

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the workshop was helping teachers learn network science concepts and translate them into classroom instruction. The paper states that teachers showed large pre/post increases in knowledge of network-related concepts and in their likelihood of using them in lessons, based on workshop surveys using 1–6 ratings, but exact numeric results, effect sizes, and statistical tests are not reported in the text provided.
finding.measure: Self-rated knowledge of network science concepts; self-rated likelihood of using network concepts in the classroom

paper_profiles.title: Do Teachers Dream of GenAI Widening Educational (In)equality? Envisioning the Future of K-12 GenAI Education from Global Teachers’ Perspectives
paper_profiles.venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’26)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 teachers in the United States, South Africa, and Taiwan think about teaching students about generative AI (GenAI) in ways that promote educational equality rather than widen existing divides. The authors ask how teachers integrate GenAI education into their classrooms, what structural barriers they encounter, and what broader support they believe is needed to make GenAI education more equitable.

The study is based on 30 semi-structured interviews with active K-12 teachers (10 per country) who were already teaching GenAI or incorporating it into subject instruction. Teachers described a range of practices, including teaching students what GenAI is, using it for hands-on activities, and embedding it into subjects such as English, science, social studies, math, and IT/CS. Across contexts, teachers framed GenAI as both a tool for reducing inequality—by expanding access, supporting struggling learners, and compensating for scarce resources—and a source of new risks, such as shortcut use, bullying, cultural bias, and overreliance on AI for emotional support.

The paper concludes that teachers are actively and thoughtfully using GenAI education to address pre-existing inequities, but their efforts are constrained by infrastructural gaps, limited training, unclear curricular guidance, and social or cultural norms. The authors argue that equitable GenAI education requires more than individual teacher initiative; it needs coordinated support from schools, policymakers, communities, and technology companies, including better training, better localized tools, and policies that recognize the systemic nature of educational inequality.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that GenAI education could be used to widen access and support more equal learning opportunities, but they also emphasized that systemic barriers limited what individual teachers could do. Across 30 interviews (n=30), the most persistent constraints were unequal infrastructure, insufficient professional training, and unclear or restrictive curricular/policy guidance.
finding.measure: Teacher interview accounts of institutional conditions, policy guidance, infrastructure, and support needs for GenAI education

finding.finding_summary: Teachers described GenAI education as a way to foster critical thinking, verification, and reflective use rather than shortcut behavior. Examples included comparing AI outputs with textbooks, analyzing deepfakes and scams, and teaching students to critically assess bias and representation; no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher-described classroom practices aimed at critical engagement, verification, and reflective GenAI use

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported using GenAI education to support self-regulation and planning for marginalized learners, especially students with disabilities, while also warning against overreliance on AI for emotional support. One example described using ChatGPT to help students plan study time for an upcoming exam; another emphasized maintaining human care and relational support instead of substituting AI for interpersonal relationships.
finding.measure: Teacher interview accounts of self-regulated learning, emotional support, and relationship-oriented classroom norms

finding.finding_summary: Teachers across subject areas reported using GenAI education to support learning in non-language, non-math domains such as science, social studies, history, economics, IT, and special education. Reported benefits included compensating for scarce textbooks, supporting science learning and examples, and adapting tasks for students with disabilities, but the study did not provide quantitative achievement data.
finding.measure: Teacher-described subject-area instructional uses of GenAI in K-12 classrooms

finding.finding_summary: Teachers frequently described using GenAI in English, writing, and language-related instruction to help students access materials, generate ideas, and complete classroom tasks. The paper is qualitative and does not report test scores or effect sizes, but it documents teachers’ perceptions that GenAI could support literacy learning while requiring critical guidance to prevent shortcut use.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported use of GenAI in English, writing, and language arts contexts

finding.finding_summary: Teachers, especially in science-related contexts, described using GenAI to help students learn examples, clarify concepts, and extend limited textbooks. One South African teacher reported using GenAI to improve science learning access and examples, but the study provides no quantitative evidence of gains in scientific reasoning.
finding.measure: Teacher interview accounts of GenAI use in science learning and examples

paper_profiles.title: LearnLens: An AI-Enhanced Dashboard to Support Teachers in Open-Ended Classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem that teachers in exploratory learning environments have difficulty quickly understanding students’ open-ended responses and identifying misconceptions in time to adjust instruction. The authors argue that existing classroom tools often organize student data but do not summarize it into actionable insights, creating a gap for teachers working in open-ended science classrooms.

To address this, the paper presents LearnLens, a generative AI-enhanced teacher-facing dashboard that ingests digital student responses from check-ins, exit tickets, and formative assessments and presents multiple views of the data, including verbatim responses, word clouds, bar charts, and AI-generated summaries of collective understanding and misconceptions. The dashboard was co-designed with teachers during professional development and implemented as a high-fidelity prototype in a 15-lesson middle school Earth science curriculum.

The study used semi-structured interviews with two 6th-grade science teachers with extensive STEM teaching experience to evaluate the dashboard’s usability and instructional relevance. Teachers reported that the visualizations were helpful and that the AI-generated summaries were especially useful for spotting gaps and misconceptions, but they were cautious about prescriptive recommendations that went beyond the data. Overall, the paper concludes that GenAI-supported dashboards can help teachers make sense of open-ended student work and inform instruction, while still requiring human judgment for instructional decisions.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that LearnLens made it easier to interpret open-ended student responses and reduced the effort needed to surface gaps and misconceptions compared with their usual tools, which mainly organized data without summarizing it. In interviews, both teachers valued the dashboard’s glanceable visualizations and AI-generated summaries as timely supports for instructional decision-making, though no formal efficiency metric was reported.
finding.measure: teacher interview perceptions of dashboard usability, interpretability, and instructional support

paper_profiles.title: The Promises and Challenges of Artificial Intelligence for Teachers: a Systematic Review of Research
paper_profiles.population: K-12 teachers (in-service and pre-service); studies included elementary, primary, middle school, high school, and kindergarten contexts
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper systematically reviews empirical research on how teachers use artificial intelligence (AI) in K-12 and teacher-education contexts. The authors ask what kinds of data have been collected from teachers, what roles teachers play in AI research, what advantages AI offers teachers, what challenges arise in implementation, and which AI methods are most commonly used. The review covers 44 journal articles published in Web of Science-indexed journals from 2004 through September 2020.

Across the reviewed studies, the authors find that teachers are commonly used as sources of data for training and validating AI systems, particularly through self-reports, grades, observations, and videos. Teachers most often appear as models for AI training, providers of data about their professional development, and raters who check the accuracy of automated assessment. The review concludes that AI can support teachers mainly in planning, implementation, and assessment by helping them identify student needs, monitor learning, give immediate feedback, reduce workload, and automate scoring.

The paper also highlights limitations: AI systems are often context-dependent, can be technically weak in handling complex inputs, may provide slow or limited feedback, and are not yet robust across settings. The authors argue that teacher involvement in AI development is still limited and call for more multimodal data, more pre-service teacher research, and closer collaboration among teachers, researchers, and developers to build pedagogically useful AI systems.

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that AI is generally reported to improve teachers’ efficiency by supporting planning, monitoring, feedback, intervention, and assessment. Across the 44 studies, AI was described as helping reduce teacher workload, with examples including timely monitoring of learning (f=12), reduced workload (f=8), immediate feedback (f=7), and automated assessment/essay scoring (f=7).
finding.measure: Teacher workload, monitoring efficiency, feedback timeliness, and automated assessment/essay scoring across reviewed studies
finding.study_size: 44 studies reviewed; no single pooled sample size reported

finding.finding_summary: The review focuses partly on AI-supported assessment and instructional support in subject learning, but it does not synthesize direct learning gains. It reports that AI helped with scoring, feedback, and selecting/adapting learning content across subjects such as English, mathematics, STEM, and early childhood, but the paper does not provide a pooled estimate of student academic outcomes.
finding.measure: Automated scoring, instructional feedback, and content selection across subject-specific studies
finding.study_size: 44 studies reviewed; no pooled sample size reported

finding.finding_summary: Several reviewed studies examined teacher monitoring of student engagement, concentration, and behavioral risk, suggesting AI can support social-emotional monitoring and responsive intervention. The review notes examples such as AI-based detection of student concentration and learner behavior, but it does not report a pooled effect size or common outcome metric.
finding.measure: Student engagement, concentration, behavioral indicators, and related teacher monitoring

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the potential of artificial intelligence tools in educational measurement and assessment
paper_profiles.venue: EURASIA Journal of Mathematics, Science and Technology Education
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (conceptual review; no specific study population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review examines how artificial intelligence tools, especially large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, can support educational measurement and assessment. The paper focuses on the assessment pipeline: determining test purpose, developing test blueprints, generating items, preparing instructions, assembling items, administering tests, scoring, interpreting results, analyzing test quality, and reporting results.

The article is not an empirical study of a specific intervention in schools; instead, it synthesizes prior literature and provides a conceptual discussion of AI’s potential benefits and limitations in assessment. It argues that AI can improve efficiency, consistency, personalization, and feedback in assessment workflows while also raising concerns about bias, transparency, privacy, limited scope, and the need for human oversight.

The context is K-12 and broader educational assessment practice, with an emphasis on how teachers remain central in AI-supported assessment systems. The paper concludes that AI should complement, not replace, educators, and that successful adoption requires transparent algorithms, stakeholder participation, training, and ethical safeguards.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI/LLMs can save teachers time and reduce workload across assessment tasks such as generating test items, preparing instructions, scoring, interpreting results, and reporting. No original effect size or study sample is reported because this is a conceptual review rather than an empirical evaluation.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, time savings, assessment-process efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The review highlights institutional implications of AI adoption in assessment, including the need for stakeholder participation, transparency, ethical algorithms, training, data privacy protections, and integration with existing systems. It concludes that AI may transform educational assessment practices, but also notes significant governance and implementation risks; no empirical institutional outcome is reported.
finding.measure: Assessment governance, policy/implementation considerations, ethical and privacy concerns

paper_profiles.title: A meta systematic review of artificial intelligence in higher education: a call for increased ethics, collaboration, and rigour
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a tertiary review (review of reviews) that maps the state of artificial intelligence in higher education research. The authors ask what kinds of evidence syntheses have been conducted, where they are published, who is doing the work, what methods and technologies are used, what quality those reviews have, and what AI applications and findings dominate the literature.

The review screened 5,609 records and included 66 evidence syntheses focused solely on higher education or continuing education, published in English from 2018 to July 2023. The corpus was dominated by systematic literature reviews, with smaller numbers of scoping reviews, meta-analyses, mapping reviews, integrative reviews, bibliometric analyses, and mixed-methods reviews. The paper synthesizes publication patterns, collaboration patterns, and methodological quality using a DARE/AMSTAR-2-informed rubric.

Substantively, the review shows that higher education AI research mainly centers on adaptive systems and personalisation, profiling and prediction, and assessment/evaluation, with chatbots, recommender systems, personalized content, and facial recognition/mood detection among the common applications discussed. Many reviews focus on teaching and learning support, but fewer address administrative or institutional uses such as admissions, attendance, quality assurance, and course scheduling. The authors conclude that the field needs stronger reporting, more rigorous methods, broader ethical reflection, and more interdisciplinary collaboration.

finding.finding_summary: This tertiary review found that AI in higher education is frequently discussed as a way to support efficiency-related tasks, especially administrative and institutional workflows such as admissions, examinations, attendance, quality assurance, course scheduling, and large-scale data analysis. However, this paper is a review of reviews and does not estimate a direct effect size for productivity or workload reduction.
finding.measure: Frequency and thematic coding of reviewed AI applications related to administrative and institutional workflows

finding.finding_summary: The corpus shows meaningful attention to institution-level uses of AI, including quality assurance, admissions, course scheduling, and broad administrative support, but these topics were less common than teaching-and-learning applications. The review concludes that AI has potential at the institutional level, yet the literature is still comparatively thin and uneven across contexts.
finding.measure: Thematic coding of institutional and administrative AI applications across included reviews

paper_profiles.title: Teachers’ AI digital competencies and twenty-first century skills in the post-pandemic world
paper_profiles.population: Educators (K-12 and higher education teachers; conceptual focus with K-16 references)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conceptual paper examines what AI-related digital competencies teachers need in the post-pandemic world, when AI-enabled tools have become more common in teaching, assessment, and administrative support. The authors argue that the pandemic accelerated digital transformation in education, but many teachers lack the technical, pedagogical, and ethical competencies needed to use AI effectively and responsibly.

Rather than testing a specific intervention, the paper synthesizes research examples and existing competency frameworks to propose an expanded view of teacher AI competency. It adapts the European DigCompEdu framework and the P21 twenty-first century skills framework, and relates them to prior work on AI competencies and TPACK to outline four broad domains: professional engagement, instructional support, content choices across disciplines, and student learning competencies.

The paper emphasizes that AI can support teaching efficiency, assessment, feedback, communication, collaboration, and personalized learning, while also introducing risks related to bias, privacy, misinformation, and overreliance on automated judgments. Its main conclusion is that teachers need broader AI literacy—not just technical skill, but also ethical judgment, interdisciplinary understanding, and the ability to design learning environments that use AI wisely and human-centeredly.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI tools can improve teacher productivity by automating routine administrative and instructional tasks such as grading, generating assessments and feedback, processing data, repetitive paperwork, and supporting communication and resource management. No new empirical study is reported; the paper synthesizes prior literature and examples to support the claim that AI can save teachers time and enhance efficiency.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading and feedback automation, routine administrative task support

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes AI as supporting learner motivation, self-regulation, and self-efficacy through personalized support, timely feedback, and adaptive learning environments. These are framed as benefits drawn from prior studies, but the article itself does not present original outcome data.
finding.measure: Motivation, self-regulation, self-efficacy, engagement

finding.finding_summary: A central focus of the paper is the development of durable skills such as collaboration, communication, critical thinking, creativity, problem solving, and metacognition in AI-rich learning environments. The paper synthesizes prior work to argue that AI can strengthen these skills through collaborative learning, feedback, analytics, and authentic problem-solving tasks, but it reports no original quantitative effect estimates.
finding.measure: Collaboration, communication, critical thinking, creativity, problem solving, metacognitive/self-regulated learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI competency frameworks can inform educational standards, professional development, curriculum design, and broader digital transformation across schools and higher education systems. It does not evaluate policy outcomes empirically; instead, it proposes that adopting DigCompEdu- and P21-informed AI competency frameworks can guide institutional decision-making and teacher preparation.
finding.measure: Educational standards, professional development, curriculum and framework alignment

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence in intelligent tutoring systems toward sustainable education: a systematic review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This systematic review examines how artificial intelligence and information technology are being used in intelligent tutoring systems (ITSs) to support sustainable education. The paper is organized around four questions: the main challenges of sustainable education implementation, the ways AI/IT are incorporated into ITSs, the outcomes reported in the literature, and future research directions. The review is grounded in PRISMA and analyzes 29 studies on AI-enabled ITSs plus additional papers on sustainable education challenges.

The paper finds that the dominant AI use cases in ITSs are performance prediction, learning behavior analysis, engagement/dropout prevention, instructor support, personalization/adaptation, and explainability. Most systems rely on supervised learning for prediction and unsupervised learning for behavior analysis, often using system logs and learner interaction data. Across the reviewed studies, reported outcomes are generally positive: high prediction accuracy, identification of learner behaviors, improved participation or learning after interventions, and some gains from personalized learning paths or AI interaction.

The review also highlights major barriers to sustainable education and AI adoption, including uneven access to devices/connectivity, teacher ICT skills, privacy and security, fairness/bias, and the need for explainable and trustworthy systems. The authors argue that future work should focus on larger and better datasets, portability across systems, stronger links to educational theory, human-centered design, and explainable AI so that educators can trust and act on AI-driven recommendations. Although the review is not specifically about K-12 administrative productivity, it does note that AI can reduce teacher workload through tasks like monitoring, intervention support, and routine reminders.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed ITS studies, AI-based systems were reported to improve engagement, reduce dropout risk, and support self-regulation-related outcomes. The review summarizes 5 studies on engagement/dropout prevention and 2 studies on self-regulation learning improvement, but does not provide a single pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Engagement/dropout risk, self-regulation survey measures, participation rates

finding.finding_summary: The review includes behavior-analysis and adaptation studies that aimed to support learners' decision-making, personalization, and learning strategies, which are adjacent to durable skills such as self-regulation and metacognition. However, these outcomes are not measured consistently enough to support a precise quantitative estimate.
finding.measure: Learning behavior clusters, intervention timing, personalized learning process

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly argues that AI-enabled ITSs can offload teachers' routine workload, especially for grading feedback, monitoring, remediation, and intervention support. In the reviewed studies, AI was used for performance prediction (13 studies), behavior analysis (9), instructor support (4), and automated reminders/interventions, indicating clear productivity and efficiency benefits, but no pooled effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload reduction, automated monitoring, reminders, feedback and intervention support
finding.study_size: 29 studies reviewed; outcome counts reported across studies

finding.finding_summary: The review treats sustainable education as a system-level issue and identifies institutional challenges such as unequal access, policy/regulation, privacy/security, fairness, and explainability. Its main conclusion is that AI-enabled ITSs can support more equitable and sustainable education systems if institutions invest in infrastructure, governance, and human-centered implementation.
finding.measure: Institutional challenges and implementation considerations for sustainable education systems

paper_profiles.title: La nueva realidad de la educación ante los avances de la inteligencia artificial generativa / The new reality of education in the face of advances in generative artificial intelligence
paper_profiles.venue: RIED-Revista Iberoamericana de Educación a Distancia
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article examines the sudden rise of generative AI in education following the public release of ChatGPT. The authors aim to move beyond extreme pro- and anti-AI positions by reviewing both the available tools and the early scientific literature that emerged in the first months after ChatGPT’s launch. The paper is framed as a systematic/rapid review and a reflective synthesis rather than an intervention study.

The article first maps generative-AI tools with potential educational use, including chatbots, writing assistants, translation-related tools, search and summarization tools, and office-productivity integrations such as Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 Copilot. It argues that these tools can support content generation, language learning, search, and productivity, but also warns about hallucinations, bias, privacy risks, plagiarism, and the unreliability of AI-text detectors.

The review of early literature shows that most studies in 2023 focused on education, medicine, and other disciplines, with a general consensus that generative AI should not simply be banned. Instead, institutions should train teachers and students, update curricula, revise assessment practices, and establish ethical guidelines and governance. The paper concludes that generative AI is likely to become embedded in educational practice, but its use must be cautious, critically evaluated, and supported by clear institutional policies.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI can improve teacher productivity by reducing time spent answering repeated student questions, grading written work, and completing routine tasks, thereby freeing teachers to focus on higher-level support and feedback. This is presented as a synthesis of early literature rather than a single empirical estimate, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher productivity / time saved on repetitive instructional and administrative tasks

finding.finding_summary: The review finds strong institutional attention to generative AI, but emphasizes that most institutions lacked clear policies at the time and that governance responses were still emerging. The main conclusion is that schools and universities should develop ethical codes, institutional guidelines, and coordinated policies rather than prohibit the tools outright.
finding.measure: Institutional policies, governance recommendations, and strategic responses to generative AI

paper_profiles.title: AI in Education: A Systematic Literature Review of Emerging Trends, Benefits, and Challenges
paper_profiles.venue: Seminars in Medical Writing and Education
paper_profiles.population: K-12, Higher Education, Vocational Training, Adult
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the rapidly expanding but fragmented literature on artificial intelligence (AI) in education, asking what trends, benefits, challenges, and research gaps are visible across recent peer-reviewed studies. The review follows PRISMA 2020 methods and synthesizes 39 studies published from January 2020 to August 2024 across K-12, higher education, vocational training, and corporate/professional learning contexts.

The review is not an intervention study; instead, it aggregates evidence on how AI is being used for personalized learning, assessment and feedback, instructional support, and administrative tasks. Across the included literature, the authors report recurring benefits such as improved engagement and learning outcomes, more efficient teaching and administrative workflows, and greater attention to AI literacy for educators and students. They also identify persistent barriers including limited infrastructure, inadequate teacher training, algorithmic bias, privacy concerns, and inequities in access.

For the K-12-relevant question about teacher productivity and administrative communication workflows, the review provides broader supportive evidence that AI is being used to automate routine school tasks like grading, scheduling, and attendance, thereby reducing teacher workload. However, it does not report a focused empirical evaluation of teacher emails, newsletters, translation, attendance messaging, documentation, or clerical support compared with specific alternatives. Overall, the paper concludes that AI has substantial promise in education, but responsible adoption will require better infrastructure, professional development, governance, and more empirical classroom-based research.

finding.finding_summary: Across the synthesized literature, AI was reported to reduce administrative workload and improve teaching efficiency. The review summarizes 20 of 39 included studies as identifying enhanced teaching efficiency or instructional support, and specifically notes automation of routine tasks such as grading, scheduling, and attendance, which frees time for direct student interaction. No pooled effect size was reported because this was a systematic literature review rather than a meta-analysis.
finding.measure: Administrative workload, teaching efficiency, and automation of routine school tasks (e.g., grading, scheduling, attendance)
finding.study_size: n=39 studies reviewed; 20 studies noted enhanced teaching efficiency/instructional support

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies institutional-level implications of AI adoption, including the need for infrastructure investment, teacher professional development, AI literacy integration, and ethical/governance frameworks. It also reports barriers such as inadequate infrastructure, insufficient training, algorithmic bias, and data privacy concerns as major system-level constraints on adoption and equity.
finding.measure: Institutional readiness, governance, infrastructure, teacher training, and ethical/privacy concerns

finding.finding_summary: The synthesis reports that AI-enhanced systems were associated with improved student engagement and more interactive learning environments. The review states that 31 of 39 studies (79%) found measurable improvements in student engagement or learning outcomes, although this is not a pooled causal estimate and the underlying evidence is heterogeneous.
finding.measure: Student engagement and related learning outcomes
finding.study_size: n=39 studies reviewed; 31 studies reported improved engagement or learning outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The review notes that AI applications, especially in higher education and teacher education, were linked to critical thinking, creativity, problem-solving, and AI literacy. It also emphasizes that AI literacy for educators and students is increasingly recognized as important for effective and ethical use, but the review does not provide a single quantitative estimate of these effects.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, creativity, problem-solving, and AI literacy

paper_profiles.title: From Statistical Relational to Neurosymbolic Artificial Intelligence: a Survey
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a survey of two related areas of artificial intelligence: statistical relational AI (StarAI) and neurosymbolic AI (NeSy). Its central question is how logic, probability, and neural computation can be integrated, and how different systems in these subfields can be categorized along shared dimensions such as inference style, syntax, semantics, learning, representation, paradigms, and task type.

The paper does not study an educational intervention or school-based population. Instead, it synthesizes a large body of AI research, explaining proof-based versus model-based reasoning, propositional versus relational versus first-order representations, Boolean versus fuzzy/probabilistic semantics, and structure versus parameter learning. It also reviews major frameworks such as ProbLog, Markov Logic Networks, Semantic Loss, DeepProbLog, LTN, SBR, TensorLog, NTP, and related approaches.

Because it is a conceptual survey, the paper’s main contribution is theoretical rather than empirical: it clarifies correspondences between StarAI and NeSy and argues that techniques can be transferred across the two fields. The authors conclude that proof-based systems offer architectural control and modularity, while model-based systems often scale better through differentiable loss functions, leaving an open tradeoff between interpretability/control and scalability.

paper_profiles.title: Conceptual Modeling and Artificial Intelligence: Mutual Benefits from Complementary Worlds
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an editorial preface for the 3rd International Workshop on Conceptual Modeling Meets Artificial Intelligence (CMAI’2021). It frames the growing intersection between conceptual modeling and AI, arguing that the two fields have complementary strengths: AI can efficiently derive outputs from large data but often lacks transparency and reproducibility, while conceptual modeling offers human-comprehensible, explicit representations but can struggle with scale and complexity.

The paper does not report an empirical study, intervention, or evaluation with a specific participant population. Instead, it introduces a research framework that positions CMAI work into four categories: exaptation, CM-driven CMAI, AI-driven CMAI, and CM- & AI-driven CMAI. It then briefly summarizes the invited workshop papers and explains how each fits within the framework, emphasizing opportunities for mutual benefit between conceptual modeling and AI research.

Because the piece is a workshop preface and overview, it has no K-12 population, no educational intervention, and no empirical findings related to teacher productivity or school operations. Its main conclusion is conceptual: integrating CM and AI may improve explainability, development, and problem-solving across domains, but the paper itself does not test these claims.

paper_profiles.title: Certifiable Artificial Intelligence Through Data Fusion
paper_profiles.venue: AAAI FSS-21: Artificial Intelligence in Government and Public Sector
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual review of challenges in certifying artificial intelligence and machine learning systems, framed around systems engineering, verification and validation, and human-machine teaming. The authors argue that AI adoption depends not only on technical performance but also on certifiability, trust, explainability, interpretability, accountability, and documentation of intended use.

The paper proposes the Multisource AI Scorecard Table (MAST) as a checklist-style framework for evaluating AI systems across input, uncertainty, output, and lifecycle dimensions. It discusses certification processes and standards from safety-critical domains such as aviation and defense, then illustrates the ideas with a notional and empirical image-fusion example using airborne imagery. In that example, anisotropic diffusion and CNN-based fusion methods are compared using metrics such as mutual information, PSNR, SSIM, standard deviation, and spatial frequency, with a tradeoff observed between speed and accuracy. The overall conclusion is that certifiable AI requires domain-specific performance bounds, robust testing, and clear documentation, but the paper does not study K-12 education or teacher productivity workflows.

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes a technical image-fusion example that compares anisotropic diffusion (ADF) and CNN methods on an ATR image database, emphasizing a tradeoff between speed and accuracy. ADF was typically fastest (e.g., 0.054 s at distance 1), while CNN was slowest (e.g., 40.783 s at distance 1); performance metrics such as MI, PSNR, SSIM, SD, and SF were otherwise relatively similar across methods.
finding.measure: Image-fusion performance and runtime metrics (MI, PSNR, GB, SSIM, SD, SF; processing time)

paper_profiles.title: Recent Advances in Generative AI and Large Language Models: Current Status, Challenges, and Perspectives
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a broad обзор of generative AI and large language models (LLMs), focused on their technical foundations, capabilities, applications, and open research challenges. Rather than evaluating a specific educational intervention, it synthesizes developments in generative modeling, including GANs, VAEs, autoregressive models, mixture-of-experts systems, diffusion models, multimodal models, and modern transformer-based LLMs.

The paper discusses where these models are used, including machine translation, text summarization, question answering, code completion, personalization, image and video generation, and other language-centric tasks. It argues that LLMs and generative AI are transforming NLP and can support productivity and communication across many domains, but it does not study K-12 schools, teachers, or students directly. The main conclusions emphasize that these systems offer substantial capabilities, while unresolved issues such as bias, fairness, interpretability, privacy, computational cost, limited context windows, and human-AI collaboration remain major barriers to responsible deployment.

For the education context, the paper is relevant only at a conceptual level: it notes that generative video and language tools may affect education and training, and that machine translation and text generation are important application areas. However, it does not present empirical evidence about teacher productivity, school workflows, or K-12 administrative communication tasks. Because it is a general technical survey, it provides background rather than outcome evidence for educational adoption.

paper_profiles.title: Learning From Failure: Integrating Negative Examples when Fine-tuning Large Language Models as Agents
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language models can learn from failed interaction trajectories when fine-tuned as agents, rather than discarding negative examples and training only on successful trajectories. The motivation is to improve low-resource agent tuning, where collecting only successful tool-use data is expensive and discarding failures wastes data.

The authors propose Negative-Aware Training (NAT), a simple reformatting strategy that appends a prompt suffix indicating whether a trajectory is supposed to be correct or incorrect. They collect trajectories with GPT-3.5 across math and question-answering tasks, label them as positive or negative by comparing outputs to ground truth, and fine-tune LLaMA-2-Chat 7B/13B models on mixes of positive and negative examples.

Across GSM8K, ASDiv, SVAMP, MultiArith, HotpotQA, StrategyQA, and a CoT math setup, NAT generally outperforms training on positive examples only and also outperforms naively mixing in negative examples without differentiation. The paper concludes that negative trajectories can be useful training data if their quality is controlled and they are explicitly distinguished from positive samples; most of the gain appears to come from better reasoning/planning rather than better tool actions. The study is about general LLM agent tuning, not K-12 education workflows.

finding.finding_summary: On math word-problem tasks, adding negative trajectories with NAT improved LLaMA-2-7B/13B performance over using positive examples only and over naively mixing negatives. For example, with 2k positive examples, NAT improved average accuracy from 55.90 to 64.64 for LLaMA-2-7B, and with 5k positives from 64.17 to 67.42; the paper reports gains across GSM8K, ASDiv, SVAMP, and MultiArith.
finding.measure: Math word-problem accuracy on GSM8K, ASDiv, SVAMP, and MultiArith
finding.study_size: n=4 benchmark datasets; training sets of 2k or 5k positive examples plus negative examples

finding.finding_summary: The paper also reports improved performance on HotpotQA and StrategyQA, which are multi-hop and strategic question-answering tasks rather than literacy or numeracy. NAT improved HotpotQA EM/F1 and StrategyQA accuracy relative to both positive-only training and naive inclusion of negatives, indicating better general agent reasoning in QA settings.
finding.measure: HotpotQA exact match/F1 and StrategyQA accuracy

finding.finding_summary: A central analysis in the paper suggests that NAT mainly improves reasoning and planning, not just action selection. Compared with Vanilla and NUT, NAT reduced action error rates while increasing task accuracy on GSM8K, implying better thought quality and more effective problem solving under tool-use conditions.
finding.measure: Action error rate, average turns, and task accuracy in agent trajectories
finding.study_size: n=1 benchmark task analyzed in depth (GSM8K)

paper_profiles.title: Augmented Computational Design
paper_profiles.venue: In Artificial Intelligence in Performance-Driven Design: Theories, Methods, and Tools Towards Sustainability (Wiley book chapter)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book chapter argues for a framework called Augmented Computational Design (ACD) that treats design as a decision-making problem and uses artificial intelligence to connect many design variables to a smaller set of performance outcomes. The paper’s central concern is how AI can support generative design by separating two dual tasks: mapping from decisions to outcomes (evaluation) and navigating from desired outcomes back to decisions (derivation).

The chapter develops a mathematical framework based on decision spaces and performance spaces, then discusses how local linear approximations, Jacobians, singular value decomposition, and pseudo-inverses can help represent and invert complex design relationships. It reviews statistical AI approaches such as Bayesian Belief Networks, Variational Autoencoders, and diffusion models, but focuses on a shallow Bayesian Belief Network example.

The demonstration case is not K-12 education; it uses Dutch building energy modelling (NTA 8800) with 269 inputs and three energy-performance outputs (BENG 1, BENG 2, BENG 3). The authors sample 20,000 quasi-random configurations, run simulations, conduct sensitivity analysis to reduce the model to 15 influential parameters, and train/validate a Bayesian Belief Network using cross-validation, NRMSE, and MAPE. The main conclusion is that the ACD approach can create an approximate, more tractable, and potentially reversible surrogate model for complex performance-driven design problems, improving explainability and decision support in AEC and policy analysis rather than education settings.

finding.finding_summary: The chapter presents an AI-based surrogate-modelling workflow for building energy policy analysis, arguing that a Bayesian Belief Network can approximate the Dutch NTA 8800 model to support building code compliance, subsidy policy making, and sustainability planning. In the demonstration, 20,000 quasi-random samples were used, 269 inputs were reduced to 15 influential parameters, and those parameters were reported to explain 90.45% to 92.30% of the final energy performance score, indicating strong potential for institutional decision support.
finding.measure: Building energy performance policy-analysis workflow; BENG 1, BENG 2, and BENG 3 outputs from the NTA 8800 model

paper_profiles.title: Modular Belief Updates and Confusion about Measures of Certainty in Artificial Intelligence Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines a conceptual problem in artificial intelligence research: the confusion between absolute measures of belief and measures of belief change (updates) under uncertainty. The authors define a property they call modularity for belief updates and explain how modular updates differ from absolute probabilities, arguing that these two ideas were frequently conflated in the AI literature.

The paper focuses on historical and theoretical analysis rather than an empirical intervention.
