The authors suggest that human skills remain important for effectively complementing AI and that educational systems should adapt to these implementation realities.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT improved Thai writing-analysis performance on average, but effects were heterogeneous. Among 121 students, the mean score improved by 0.43 points on a 10-point scale and time decreased by 1.73 minutes; however, 34% of participants did not improve, and higher-ability students (proxied by econometrics grades) performed worse with ChatGPT on writing tasks.
finding.measure: Expert-rated writing-analysis score out of 10 and completion time for Thai writing tasks
finding.std_deviation: 1.98 for score diff; 3.43 for time diff

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT improved math and data-analysis task performance on average. Across 121 students, the mean score increased by 1.65 points on a 10-point scale and completion time decreased by 0.99 minutes, though 42% of participants still did not improve. The study also found that students with stronger digital skills benefited more from ChatGPT on these tasks.
finding.measure: Expert-rated math/data-analysis score out of 10 and completion time for Stata-based tasks
finding.std_deviation: 3.67 for score diff; 2.90 for time diff

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly measures productivity through task completion time and finds ChatGPT reduced time spent on both task types. In writing analysis, time fell by 1.73 minutes on average (n=121); in math/data analysis, time fell by 0.99 minutes on average (n=121). This indicates a clear efficiency gain, although the gains were uneven across students.
finding.measure: Task completion time in minutes
finding.std_deviation: 3.43 for writing time diff; 2.90 for math/data time diff

paper_profiles.title: Environmental large language model Evaluation (ELLE) dataset: A Benchmark for Evaluating Generative AI applications in Eco-environment Domain
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (LLM benchmark; no human participants studied)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents the Environmental large language model Evaluation (ELLE) Q&A benchmark, a domain-specific dataset created to evaluate the performance of generative AI and large language models in ecological and environmental sciences. The authors argue that although LLMs and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems are increasingly being used for environmental monitoring, data analysis, educational support, and policy-related tasks, there is no unified, reliable framework for assessing how well these systems perform in this specialized domain.

To address this gap, the authors constructed 1,130 question-answer pairs spanning 16 environmental subject areas. The dataset was built from expert questionnaires and manually curated open-source materials such as textbooks, examination questions, and professional consultations. Each item was categorized by subject domain, difficulty level, and question type (knowledge, calculation, reasoning), and the benchmark is designed to evaluate model responses along three dimensions: professionalism, clarity, and feasibility.

The paper describes the data collection, validation, and evaluation protocol for the benchmark, including multi-round expert cross-review and a staged release process for answers and leaderboard results. The work is not an intervention study on learners or educators; rather, it is a methodological contribution aimed at standardizing evaluation of domain-specific AI systems. The main conclusion is that ELLE provides a comprehensive and trustworthy benchmark for comparing LLMs in environmental science tasks and may support more robust development and assessment of specialized AI applications.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not test student learning; instead, it creates a benchmark for evaluating how well LLMs answer scientific questions in environmental science. The benchmark contains 1,130 QA pairs across 16 subjects, including knowledge, calculation, and reasoning items, but no effect size or human outcome is reported.
finding.measure: LLM benchmark performance on environmental science question-answer tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper is centered on evaluation infrastructure rather than direct productivity outcomes, but it substantively addresses the need for standardized AI assessment tools that could support more efficient comparison of model capabilities. No teacher workload, time savings, or productivity effects were measured.
finding.measure: Benchmarking protocol / evaluation framework for LLMs

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that ELLE fills a methodological gap by providing a standardized, transparent benchmark for domain-specific AI evaluation. This is positioned as an institutional contribution to the standardization and comparison of environmental AI systems, but no policy or organizational outcomes are empirically measured.
finding.measure: Development of a standardized domain benchmark and leaderboard protocol

paper_profiles.title: Better Late Than Never: Meta-Evaluation of Latency Metrics for Simultaneous Speech-to-Text Translation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how well commonly used latency metrics measure user-relevant delay in simultaneous speech-to-text translation systems. The authors argue that existing metrics can be inconsistent and biased, especially when speech is artificially segmented in short-form evaluation or when long-form audio is resegmented poorly.

To address this, the paper proposes new evaluation tools: YAAL for short-form settings, LongYAAL for long-form settings, and SOFTSEGMENTER for more robust resegmentation. The study compares these against established metrics such as AL, LAAL, DAL, AP, ATD, and StreamLAAL using systems from IWSLT shared tasks across English-German, English-Japanese, English-Chinese, and Czech-English directions.

The paper is methodological rather than an intervention study. It shows that short-form evaluation can reward degenerate simultaneous policies and that long-form evaluation requires accurate resegmentation to produce meaningful latency scores. Across extensive pairwise comparisons, YAAL and LongYAAL perform best or near-best in approximating the paper’s automatic estimate of true latency, with SOFTSEGMENTER improving long-form evaluation accuracy over the standard resegmentation tool. The main conclusion is that segmentation practices strongly shape latency measurement, and that the proposed metrics better align automatic evaluation with actual translation delay.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that the proposed latency metrics and resegmentation procedures improve the reliability of evaluating simultaneous speech translation systems, which is directly relevant to operational efficiency in translation workflows. YAAL achieved 98% pairwise accuracy against true latency in short-form evaluation, and LongYAAL reached 94% accuracy in long-form evaluation, outperforming the standard metrics and the prior StreamLAAL approach.
finding.measure: Pairwise accuracy of latency metrics against true latency; resegmentation accuracy for latency evaluation
finding.study_size: n=4900 system pairs (short-form) and n=594 system pairs (long-form)
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CI reported around accuracies but exact values not reported in extracted text

paper_profiles.title: What is essential is visible to the eye: Saliency in primary school ranking and its effect on academic achievements
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether students’ relative rank within their primary-school class affects later academic achievement, and whether that effect depends on whether the rank is visible to students. The authors argue that prior rank studies can be biased because ranks built from standardized test scores are not fully separated from ability peer effects, so they develop a new identification strategy using two scores: teacher grades, which are visible to students, and standardized test scores, which are not.

Using a large administrative panel of Italian public-school students and a companion student survey, the paper compares a visible rank based on reported class grades with an invisible rank based on unreported standardized test scores. The main specification adds extensive controls and student fixed effects, and the invisible rank becomes small and insignificant while the visible rank remains strongly predictive of later performance. The authors interpret this as evidence that saliency matters: students respond to the rank they can see, likely through changes in perception, self-esteem, and school attitudes.

The study follows cohorts of Italian students from grade 5 into grades 8 and 10, with outcome data from national standardized tests in Italian and math. The paper finds sizable positive associations between higher visible rank in primary school and later test performance, along with evidence that higher-ranked students choose higher-achieving high schools and report more positive school perceptions and self-esteem. Overall, the paper concludes that rank saliency affects achievement, but that being in a stronger peer environment has an even larger positive effect than rank itself.

finding.finding_summary: Higher visible class rank in grade 5 is associated with substantially better later academic performance. In the main specification, ranking at the top of the primary-school class versus the bottom predicts gains of 8.5 percentile points in grade 8 and 7.7 percentile points in grade 10 on national standardized tests, while the invisible rank based on unreported test scores is close to zero and not significant.
finding.measure: National standardized test percentile scores in grade 8 and grade 10 (Italian and math)
finding.study_size: n=387,614 combined across the two main cohorts after sample selection

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that a higher visible rank improves students’ perceptions of school and their self-esteem, and it increases perceived recognition by peers. Using the 2018 questionnaire, the authors report that these psychological channels are consistent with the visible-rank effect on later achievement, though they do not report a single unified effect size for these survey outcomes.
finding.measure: Student survey responses on self-esteem, perceived school experience, perceived peer recognition, and related attitudes on a 6-point Likert scale

finding.finding_summary: The study shows that higher-ranked students self-select into high schools with significantly higher average student achievement, indicating that primary-school rank affects later educational sorting decisions. The paper also finds that class quality matters much more than rank: a one-standard-deviation increase in class quality raises later test scores by about 13 national percentiles, versus about 2.2 and 1.9 percentiles for a one-standard-deviation increase in rank in middle and high school, respectively.
finding.measure: High-school enrollment choices and class-quality/class-rank associations with later standardized test performance
finding.study_size: n=387,614 combined across the two main cohorts after sample selection

paper_profiles.title: AI and the EU Digital Markets Act: Addressing the Risks of Bigness in Generative AI
paper_profiles.venue: ICML 2023 (Proceedings of the 40th International Conference on Machine Learning)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether the European Union’s Digital Markets Act (DMA) is sufficient to govern the rise of generative AI platforms and prevent market concentration, gatekeeping, and reduced contestability. The authors argue that while the DMA was designed for established digital platform services, it does not explicitly cover generative AI systems, even though these systems may increasingly function as core platform services and gateways to downstream applications.

The paper develops a policy analysis of how generative AI firms could be treated under the DMA, focusing on OpenAI-like model providers, API-based platforms, and integrated AI services. It discusses sources of market power in generative AI—computing power, early-mover advantage, data resources, and integrated ecosystems—and explains how these could create entrenched gatekeeper positions. The paper also surveys specific DMA obligations that might already apply to generative AI in indirect ways, while arguing that explicit amendments would better support fairness, contestability, and diversity in the market.

The context is EU digital regulation rather than an educational setting, and the paper does not study schools, teachers, or students. Its conclusions are normative and institutional: generative AI should be incorporated into the DMA’s core platform service framework, and some developers should be designated as gatekeepers to limit anti-competitive conduct and preserve user choice. The paper does not report original empirical data or experimental outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI is becoming structurally important enough to warrant treatment under the EU Digital Markets Act, but it also notes that the current DMA framework is not explicitly designed for these services. The conclusion is normative rather than empirical: without amendments, market concentration and gatekeeping may increase; with regulatory updates, contestability and fairness could be better protected.
finding.measure: Policy and regulatory analysis of the EU Digital Markets Act as applied to generative AI

paper_profiles.title: The Most Considered Type of Student Characteristics by Primary School Teachers
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal on Integrating Technology in Education (IJITE)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks which student characteristic primary school teachers consider most when planning instruction, and whether paying attention to that characteristic is associated with better student learning outcomes. The authors frame the issue as an instructional-planning problem: teachers often cannot deeply assess every relevant student characteristic, so the study aims to identify the priority characteristic most commonly used in practice.

The study surveyed 37 class teachers from grades 4 to 6 in seven primary schools in South Bangka, Indonesia. Teachers completed a questionnaire about how they identify and use student characteristics in learning, and the authors also reviewed instructional planning documents to verify reported practices. The study then compared midterm exam averages between classes whose teaching was developed based on student intelligence-level information and classes whose teaching was not.

The main finding is that teachers most often prioritized student intelligence level over motivation, cognitive style, learning style, prior knowledge, and socio-cultural conditions. Observations of planning documents indicated a higher level of identification and use of intelligence-level information than for other characteristics. Classes taught with attention to intelligence level had higher average midterm scores across subjects (overall average 72.67 vs 68.20; gain 6%), leading the authors to conclude that considering intelligence level in planning may improve learning outcomes in primary school.

finding.finding_summary: Instruction developed based on student intelligence level was associated with better midterm exam performance in primary school. Across subjects, the class average increased from 68.20 to 72.67 overall (a 6% gain), with gains reported in Indonesian language (71.00 to 78.00), mathematics (63.67 to 71.00), social science (65.00 to 67.67), natural science (69.67 to 73.00), and art-culture-craft (71.67 to 73.67).
finding.measure: Midterm exam scores across subjects

finding.finding_summary: The study centers on how teachers prioritize and use student-characteristic information in instructional planning, which is an instructional management and planning efficiency issue. Teachers most frequently identified intelligence level and used it at a high level in planning, while other characteristics were used at medium or low levels, suggesting a practical prioritization strategy for classroom decision-making.
finding.measure: Teacher questionnaire responses and instructional planning document review on use of student-characteristic information

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that teachers viewed intelligence-level information as relevant to student motivation and comfort in learning, and discusses differentiation intended to help students feel comfortable understanding the material. However, this outcome is secondary and not measured directly with a dedicated social-emotional instrument.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions reported in questionnaire and discussion of learning comfort/motivation

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the effectiveness of ChatGPT-based feedback compared with teacher feedback and self-feedback: Evidence from Chinese to English translation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether ChatGPT-based feedback can improve translation performance as effectively as conventional teacher feedback (TF) and self-feedback (SF). The authors frame ChatGPT as a general-purpose large language model tool that may provide rapid, personalized feedback, and they test it against human and self-generated revision processes in a Chinese-to-English translation task.

The study was conducted with 45 advanced Chinese Master of Translation and Interpreting (MTI) students at a top university in China. Students translated a 424-character government press release and revised their drafts under three conditions: SF, TF, and ChatGPT-based feedback. The researchers evaluated the resulting translations using BLEU scores for overall translation quality and Coh-Metrix indicators for lexicon, syntax, and cohesion. They also used CFA and SEM to validate the scoring model and estimate relationships between feedback type and language outcomes.

Overall, teacher feedback and self-feedback produced higher translation quality than ChatGPT-based feedback on the BLEU measure. However, ChatGPT-based feedback improved lexical features more than TF and SF, especially word length, verb specificity, and referential cohesion. In contrast, TF was stronger for syntax-related gains, including verb phrase density and agentless passive voice, while cohesion showed no overall significant improvement across conditions. The paper concludes that ChatGPT is useful as a supplementary tool, but not a replacement for teacher feedback in advanced translation practice.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined translation performance, a writing-related literacy outcome, among 45 advanced MTI students. Teacher feedback produced the highest overall BLEU scores (TF=0.501) compared with self-feedback (0.485) and ChatGPT-based feedback (0.472), indicating ChatGPT underperformed on overall translation quality. However, ChatGPT improved lexical indicators more than TF and SF, including longer word length and more specific verbs.
finding.measure: Chinese-to-English translation quality (BLEU score) and linguistic features from Coh-Metrix
finding.study_size: n=45 (135 revised texts across 3 feedback conditions)

paper_profiles.title: EXPTRIALMNG: A Universal Experiment Trial Manager for AR/VR/MR Experiments Based on Unity
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents ExpTrialMng, a Unity library designed to reduce the programming burden involved in building and managing VR/AR/MR experiments. The authors identify two main problems for researchers using immersive environments: the high entry barrier of Unity programming for non-experts and the risk of experiment disruption due to hardware or tracking errors.

The proposed approach is a general-purpose trial manager that reads pre-generated CSV trial files, assigns and randomizes trials, saves results after each trial, and can resume an interrupted experiment from a specific trial number. The library is intended for researchers in psychology, cognitive science, HCI, and related design-oriented fields, rather than K-12 educators or students.

The paper is primarily a systems/tool paper describing implementation and intended utility, with no empirical evaluation of user outcomes reported in the text provided. Its main conclusion is that a lightweight, reusable Unity-based trial manager can lower barriers to conducting VR/AR experiments and reduce data loss from unexpected interruptions.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ExpTrialMng improves experiment-building productivity by reducing the coding required to implement trial assignment, result saving, and recovery from interruptions. However, no empirical evaluation, sample size, or effect size is reported; the claimed benefit is based on system design rather than measured outcomes.
finding.measure: Implementation efficiency / programming burden for experiment setup and resumption

paper_profiles.title: Investigating Decoder-only Large Language Models for Speech-to-text Translation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how to adapt decoder-only large language models (LLMs) for the speech-to-text translation (S2TT) task. The authors focus on architectural choices, parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods, and task formulations for combining a speech encoder with a decoder-only text model, motivated by the idea that LLMs’ fluency and generalization may improve speech translation performance.

The proposed system uses a W2v-BERT speech encoder and a LLaMA-2 decoder, with continuous speech representations fed directly into the decoder rather than discretized speech tokens. The paper compares decoder-only and encoder-decoder architectures, as well as LNA fine-tuning versus LoRA, using public speech translation datasets (CoVoST 2, Common Voice 11, VoxPopuli) and evaluating on CoVoST 2 and zero-shot FLEURS. The main finding is that the decoder-only design with LNA fine-tuning performs best, outperforming encoder-decoder baselines and prior public-data-only systems on BLEU and COMET, while fine-tuning the speech encoder is crucial and LoRA underperforms LNA in this setting.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies speech-to-text translation performance, a language-fluency outcome, and reports strong gains from the proposed decoder-only LLM architecture. On CoVoST 2, the model achieved an average BLEU of 37.1 on 21 X-En directions, outperforming public-data baselines such as W2vBERT+NLLB (33.8 BLEU) and the public-data-only AudioPaLM variant (33.1 BLEU).
finding.measure: Speech-to-text translation quality on CoVoST 2 and FLEURS, measured with corpus BLEU and COMET

paper_profiles.title: Speculative Futures on ChatGPT and Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI): A Collective Reflection from the Educational Landscape
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable; the paper is not an empirical study of a specific K-12 sample. It reflects on educational contexts broadly, including K-12, higher education, and lifelong learning.
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the promises and pitfalls of ChatGPT and generative AI in education through a speculative, collective storytelling methodology rather than empirical testing. The authors assemble a globally diverse group of education scholars to write fictional future narratives that imagine both positive and negative educational futures involving conversational AI. The goal is to provoke critical reflection on how AI may reshape teaching, learning, assessment, access, ethics, and the human role in education.

The paper does not evaluate a specific intervention or produce causal evidence. Instead, it analyzes the narratives thematically to identify recurring concerns and opportunities. Positive scenarios emphasize personalized learning, language support, accessibility, automated assessment, teacher time savings, and enhanced collaboration. Negative scenarios stress algorithmic bias, privacy, inequity of access, dependence on technology, loss of creativity and human agency, academic dishonesty, and possible teacher replacement.

The context spans multiple educational settings and levels, with many examples referencing universities and online learning, but the discussion explicitly extends to K-12 and education systems more generally. The main conclusion is that generative AI can support education in meaningful ways, but its integration is highly context-dependent and requires careful attention to ethics, equity, assessment redesign, and the centrality of human educators. The authors frame the paper as an intellectual exercise, not as a source of empirical findings or generalizable effects.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI can support writing and language-related literacy by helping learners draft text, receive instant feedback, and improve grammar and vocabulary. In the speculative narratives, ChatGPT-like tools are presented as useful for writing support, translation, and producing tailored language practice, but no empirical study or effect estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Speculative narrative discussion of writing support, grammar, vocabulary, and translation uses

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly presents conversational AI as beneficial for language learning, especially speaking, pronunciation, and multilingual communication. Examples include real-time interpretation, voice recognition, text-to-speech/captioning, and simulated conversation partners; however, these are illustrative claims from fictional scenarios rather than measured outcomes.
finding.measure: Speculative narrative discussion of oral/written communication, pronunciation, and translation support

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses AI as a source of educational content support across subjects, including helping with concept explanation, tailored learning pathways, and question generation. These are framed as possible future affordances of ChatGPT-like tools rather than results from a study of a specific subject area.
finding.measure: Speculative narrative discussion of content explanation, lesson design, and learning pathway support

finding.finding_summary: The narratives suggest AI can increase motivation, confidence, and engagement by offering encouragement, immediate support, and personalized interaction, but they also warn about frustration, dependency, and dehumanization. No empirical measurement is reported; the findings are thematic and speculative.
finding.measure: Speculative narrative discussion of motivation, engagement, confidence, and affective support

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests generative AI may support critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, and metacognitive reflection when used well, but it may also weaken creativity, independent thinking, and human agency if over-relied upon. These conclusions are based on speculative future narratives rather than quantitative evidence.
finding.measure: Speculative narrative discussion of critical thinking, collaboration, creativity, and agency

finding.finding_summary: A central theme is that ChatGPT-like tools can save educator time by drafting emails, generating lesson plans, improving course outlines, creating test questions, and automatically grading assignments. The paper does not report measured productivity effects, but it explicitly positions AI as a time-saving tool for teacher workflow and administrative tasks.
finding.measure: Speculative narrative discussion of lesson planning, grading, email drafting, and course design efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI may reshape assessment policy, curricular design, access, equity, and the role of institutions in supporting AI literacy. It also warns about ethics, privacy, ownership, surveillance, and the possibility that institutions could widen inequality if access is uneven or AI is used in harmful ways.
finding.measure: Speculative narrative discussion of assessment policy, curriculum, access, equity, privacy, and governance

paper_profiles.title: AI in Education: Rationale, Principles, and Instructional Implications
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article is a conceptual review of generative AI in schooling, with a particular emphasis on how teachers should think about when and how to use large language models and related AI tools. Rather than testing a specific intervention, it synthesizes cognitive, ecological, and distributed-cognition perspectives to argue that AI use in education should be guided by pedagogical purpose, student prerequisites, and the need to preserve genuine learning effort.

The paper contrasts AI-supported productivity with learning-oriented uses of AI, warning that easy access to answers can undermine deep processing, perseverance, and long-term retention. It discusses classroom examples and tool types such as ChatGPT-like chatbots, educational platforms (e.g., SchoolAI, Canvas, Khanmigo), and GPT Tutor, but explicitly notes that empirical evidence in K-12 is limited. The main conclusion is that AI can be useful as a supplement to instruction, especially when it provides hints, explanations, or personalized support, but it should not replace student cognitive effort or teacher judgment.

The paper is written for teachers and school leaders and is framed around school settings, especially primary and secondary education and preparatory programs. It does not report original data collection; instead, it offers theoretical and practical guidance on using AI in ways that support learning with understanding, critical source evaluation, and appropriate levels of challenge. The article also stresses that different educational stages, subjects, and learner characteristics require different AI-use decisions, and that schools need clear rules and professional judgment rather than one-size-fits-all guidance.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI can increase productivity for teachers and students by helping produce text, provide examples, and support task completion more quickly than standard digital tools. However, this is presented as a conceptual claim rather than an original empirical result, and the paper also cautions that productivity gains may come at the expense of learning if AI is used as a shortcut.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The article argues that AI use can either support or weaken motivation, self-discipline, and perseverance depending on how it is implemented. It cites studies and examples suggesting that direct-answer chatbots may encourage shortcuts and procrastination, whereas hint-based tools may preserve effort and support persistence; no original effect size is reported.
finding.measure: motivation, self-discipline, perseverance, procrastination, engagement with learning tasks

finding.finding_summary: A central claim of the paper is that AI can support or undermine durable skills such as critical thinking, metacognition, and source evaluation. The article emphasizes that tools like ChatGPT can produce superficial or inaccurate answers and that students need strong critical judgment; conversely, Socratic-style bots and hint-giving tools may foster deeper reasoning and self-reflection.
finding.measure: critical source competence, critical thinking, metacognitive self-reflection, deeper processing of instructional material

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses heavily on school-level governance and policy questions, arguing that AI use should be shaped by educational stage, subject matter, exam rules, and professional teacher judgment. It concludes that schools need clear rules and context-dependent guidance because there is too little empirical evidence for universal policies.
finding.measure: school rules, exam regulations, educational policy guidance, teacher professional judgment

paper_profiles.title: AI in Education: Shaping the Future of Teaching and Learning
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Current Educational Studies
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review article examines the role of artificial intelligence in education, with a particular emphasis on higher education teaching, learning, and administration. The paper asks how AI can improve instructional practice, personalize learning, support at-risk students, and reduce educator workload, while also considering ethical concerns such as privacy, bias, equity, and diminished human interaction.

The article is based on a selective literature review and conceptual analysis rather than original empirical data. It synthesizes prior research and presents several illustrative case studies describing AI-driven analytics, early warning systems for at-risk students, curriculum design support, peer feedback platforms, and AI grading systems. Across these examples, the author argues that thoughtful AI adoption can make education more personalized, efficient, and responsive, but only if institutions provide training, protect data, and ensure equitable access.

Although the paper is framed around higher education, many of its claims are relevant to educators more broadly, including the use of AI as a teaching assistant and for administrative automation. The central conclusion is that AI has strong potential to enhance teaching and institutional effectiveness, but its benefits depend on careful implementation, ethical governance, and sustained professional support for instructors.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI streamlines repetitive educator tasks such as grading, scheduling, communication, and data analysis, thereby freeing instructors to spend more time on mentoring and direct student interaction. In the case study of an AI grading system at a mid-sized public university, graded turnaround time decreased by an average of 50%, and instructors gained additional time for teaching and student support.
finding.measure: Grading turnaround time; time spent on administrative and instructional tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents AI as improving institutional processes such as student retention, curriculum alignment, and data-informed decision-making. In the case studies, AI-driven analytics were associated with improved retention rates, better curriculum responsiveness, and more equitable learning opportunities, though these are descriptive claims from illustrative examples rather than controlled estimates.
finding.measure: Retention rates; curriculum relevance; institutional decision-making quality

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims AI-supported personalization and early-warning systems increased student engagement and satisfaction, especially when students received tailored support and prompt feedback. In the case examples, tailored instruction and AI-based interventions were described as improving engagement, motivation, and perceived support, but no standardized effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Student engagement, satisfaction, and participation

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes AI-supported collaboration and peer-feedback tools as improving critical thinking, evaluative skill, problem-solving, and collaboration. In one case study, students using an AI-assisted feedback platform reportedly improved their ability to assess their own and peers’ work and produced higher-quality projects, but the paper provides no formal statistical test or effect size.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, peer evaluation quality, collaboration, project quality

paper_profiles.title: A Multidisciplinary Research Agenda for Artificial Intelligence, Education, Learning, and Instruction
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (expert panel / research agenda paper; no direct study population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article addresses the rapidly growing but fragmented body of research on artificial intelligence in education, learning, and instruction (AI&ED). Rather than testing a specific AI intervention, it asks what challenges, opportunities, and transformations experts see as most important for building a sustainable multidisciplinary research agenda in this field.

The paper uses a collective writing methodology with an expert panel of eleven internationally recognised scholars, plus two additional commentaries, to generate ten standalone reflections and then thematically analyse them. The resulting agenda is organised around macro, meso, and micro levels and highlights challenges such as rapid technological change, unequal access, ethical and assessment issues, weak empirical bases, and limited readiness among instructors and institutions.

The paper’s main conclusion is that AI should be treated as a socio-technical assemblage embedded in educational ecologies, not as a stand-alone tool or a purely technical solution. It argues for human-centred, critical, and multidisciplinary research that supports equity, democratic values, professional development, and responsible redesign of education in postdigital societies.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI&ED research and implementation are currently fragmented, under-theorised, and often too tool-specific, and it calls for coordinated large-scale, longitudinal, multidisciplinary research. It highlights institutional issues such as leadership, governance, professional development, policy, and safe experimentation as central to responsible AI adoption in education, but it does not report empirical effect sizes.
finding.measure: Expert thematic analysis of challenges, opportunities, and transformational ideas for AI&ED research and implementation

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims AI can automate repetitive and tedious tasks such as grading, feedback, and administrative work, thereby freeing instructors to focus on more complex and creative educational activities. However, these are agenda-level claims rather than measured productivity outcomes, so no quantitative effect estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Proposed uses of AI for grading, feedback, administrative work, and instructor workload reduction

finding.finding_summary: A recurring theme is that AI may both support and undermine durable skills such as critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, metacognition, and AI literacy. The paper warns that overreliance on AI may weaken critical thinking and assessment skills, while also arguing that AI can be used to foster AI literacy, reflective use, and human-AI co-orchestration.
finding.measure: Expert thematic analysis of critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, regulation of learning, and AI literacy

finding.finding_summary: The article discusses AI’s potential to support academic writing, collaborative writing, and genre-based writing development, especially through large language models used as tutors or research assistants. At the same time, it cautions that AI may reshape authorship, literacy norms, and reading/writing practices in ways that require critical and ethical attention; no direct student outcome data are reported.
finding.measure: Proposed impact on academic writing, collaborative writing, reading/writing practices, and authorship norms

finding.finding_summary: Language-related opportunities are discussed through examples such as GenAI, chatbots, and natural language processing for translation, which are presented as potentially useful for language education and communication. However, the paper is conceptual and does not report empirical measures of speaking, listening, or language proficiency.
finding.measure: Proposed uses of GenAI, chatbots, and translation/NLP tools in language education

finding.finding_summary: Beyond literacy and language, the paper discusses AI uses in broader academic contexts such as arts and humanities, assessment, curriculum design, and disciplinary learning. It suggests AI could enable creative, meaningful instructional designs and support disciplinary knowledge production, but also warns about harms to cultural, aesthetic, and disciplinary norms if AI is adopted uncritically.
finding.measure: Conceptual treatment of disciplinary learning, arts/humanities education, and curriculum/assessment redesign

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly frames AI as affecting learner motivation, engagement, confidence, and regulation of learning, including self-regulation and socially shared regulation. It argues that AI may support real-time detection and prompting for learning processes, but warns that overreliance may reduce persistence and intrinsic engagement; no empirical estimates are provided.
finding.measure: Conceptual analysis of motivation, engagement, confidence, and regulation of learning

paper_profiles.title: Technostress and generative AI in the workplace: a qualitative analysis of young professionals
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how young professionals experience technostress when using generative AI (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT in the workplace. The authors ask how young employees perceive GenAI-related stress and what new stressors emerge beyond the classic technostress dimensions described in prior research.

The study uses 15 semi-structured interviews with young professionals aged 26 to 35 in research and development, IT, finance, and marketing organizations that were piloting or using GenAI. A structured qualitative content analysis was applied to identify both established technostress dimensions (e.g., techno-insecurity, techno-uncertainty, techno-overload, techno-complexity, techno-invasion) and additional GenAI-specific concerns.

The findings suggest that GenAI can create both strain and benefit. Participants reported concerns about rapid model changes, workload compression, increased responsibility for verification, data protection, copyright, dependence, and potential skill degradation, but also efficiency gains, learning opportunities, intrinsic motivation, and idea generation. The authors conclude that GenAI extends existing technostress frameworks and that organizations need stronger governance, AI literacy, and supportive work design to reduce negative stress while enabling productive use.

finding.finding_summary: Participants frequently described GenAI as improving efficiency, saving time, and helping them complete work faster, but they also reported workload compression, higher pace, and additional pressure to maintain quality. For example, interviewees said GenAI helped them generate outputs with less input and shift toward more complex work, yet faster completion sometimes led to more assignments and greater overload.
finding.measure: Interview-reported perceptions of efficiency, time savings, workload, and productivity in workplace tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively examines critical thinking, knowledge verification, and skill development in relation to GenAI use. Respondents described both benefits, such as learning opportunities and support for more complex work, and risks such as dependency, reduced independent thinking, and possible skill degradation or loss of expertise over time.
finding.measure: Interview-reported cognitive and skill-related effects, including critical thinking, dependency, and skill development

finding.finding_summary: The interviews show both positive and negative social-emotional effects of GenAI use. Participants reported intrinsic motivation, enjoyment, curiosity, and learning-related eustress, but also stress, pressure to keep up, and frustration when GenAI made work feel faster or more demanding.
finding.measure: Interview-reported motivation, enjoyment, curiosity, and stress responses to GenAI

finding.finding_summary: The study centrally focuses on organizational and institutional issues such as compliance, governance, regulation, data protection, copyright, and role changes triggered by GenAI adoption. Participants emphasized the absence of clear organizational rules, uncertainty about acceptable use, and the need for governance structures to manage risk and support responsible implementation.
finding.measure: Interview-reported concerns about governance, regulation, compliance, data protection, copyright, and organizational role change

paper_profiles.title: Academics as adopters of generative AI: an application of diffusion of innovations theory
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines why academic staff adopt ChatGPT, using Rogers’ Diffusion of Innovations (DOI) theory as the explanatory framework. The authors focus on five perceived innovation attributes—relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, trialability, and observability—plus personal innovativeness as a predictor of actual use. The paper addresses a practical question relevant to higher education: which perceptions and individual traits drive faculty members’ willingness to use generative AI in academic work.

The study surveyed 640 academics from ten major Polish universities, with data collected via an online questionnaire. Using PLS-SEM, the authors tested seven hypotheses linking DOI factors to behavioral intention and actual use. Relative advantage, compatibility, and perceived complexity all significantly increased intention to use ChatGPT, with complexity showing the strongest effect (β=0.383), while trialability had a small positive effect (β=0.071) and observability was non-significant. Behavioral intention strongly predicted actual use (β=0.558), and personal innovativeness also positively predicted actual use (β=0.209).

The main conclusion is that academics adopt ChatGPT when they perceive it as useful, compatible with existing workflows, and relatively easy to use. The authors argue that institutions aiming to support generative-AI adoption should emphasize tangible benefits, provide low-risk opportunities to try the tool, and support faculty members who are more willing to experiment with new technologies. The paper is about higher-education faculty rather than K-12 teachers, but it offers evidence on AI-tool adoption conditions and perceived productivity benefits.

finding.finding_summary: Academics perceived ChatGPT as improving productivity and work efficiency, and this perception was a central driver of adoption. In the PLS-SEM model, relative advantage (β=0.240), complexity (β=0.383), compatibility (β=0.214), and behavioral intention (β=0.558) all positively predicted use, with the model explaining 45.0% of variance in actual usage (R²=0.450) among 640 academics.
finding.measure: Behavioral intention to use ChatGPT; actual use frequency; perceived efficiency/productivity in academic work

finding.finding_summary: The paper highlights institutional conditions that support adoption of generative AI in higher education, including compatibility with existing technologies, perceived institutional resources, and low-risk trial opportunities. Although it does not test policy interventions, it argues that universities should provide training, institutional support, and clear AI policies to accelerate diffusion and responsible use.
finding.measure: Perceived compatibility/resources; adoption intention and use in institutional context

paper_profiles.title: Who is Helping Whom? Student Concerns about AI-Teacher Collaboration in Higher Education Classrooms
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how students perceive AI-assisted classroom analysis and intervention systems, with a focus on AI that observes students, interprets behavioral and affective data, and alerts teachers to provide targeted support. The authors ask how students understand the collaborative dynamics among AI, teachers, and students, especially in settings where AI is used for monitoring, evaluation, prediction, and intervention.

The study uses the Story Completion Method with 65 participants recruited from China and Australia who were currently or recently in higher education. Participants responded to speculative scenarios based on emerging AIEd technologies such as facial/emotion recognition, gaze tracking, real-time behavior analysis, automatic evaluation, predictive early warning, and adaptive recommendations. The analysis is qualitative and thematic, aiming to surface students’ concerns before such systems become widespread.

The main findings suggest that students worry AI tools can decontextualize learning, oversimplify complex classroom situations, and create unfair evaluations by relying on quantification and historical data. Participants also expressed concern that AI may shift teacher authority, introduce bias, and create power imbalances in teacher-AI decision-making. A further theme was that surveillance-like monitoring can change student behavior in ways that reduce trust and may even undermine the effectiveness of the AI systems themselves.

At the same time, students saw some potential benefits: AI could help teachers notice struggling students, provide more equal attention, and improve pedagogical processes when used as a supportive tool rather than as an authoritative decision-maker. Overall, the paper argues that effective and ethical AIEd requires context-sensitive design that preserves human judgment, accounts for situated classroom dynamics, and considers unintended behavioral responses from students.

finding.finding_summary: Students anticipated both positive and negative social-emotional effects from AI classroom monitoring. On one hand, some saw AI as introvert-friendly and helpful for identifying students needing support; on the other, many described fear, anxiety, performativity, disengagement, and resistance in response to surveillance-like monitoring (n=65).
finding.measure: Story completion narratives about perceived emotional and behavioral responses to AI-enabled classroom monitoring and intervention

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that students believed AI monitoring could alter interaction patterns, self-presentation, and strategic behavior in ways that affect collaboration and self-regulation. Participants described pretending, gaming the system, and adapting behavior to surveillance, but also noted that AI might prompt students to seek help or communicate needs more effectively (n=65).
finding.measure: Qualitative story completion themes about collaboration, self-regulation, strategic behavior, and student-teacher interaction

finding.finding_summary: Participants believed AI could improve teaching efficiency by directing teacher attention, supporting targeted intervention, and giving teachers more usable data, but they also expected students’ behavior changes to contaminate data and reduce system effectiveness. The paper frames AI as potentially making support more efficient while also risking inefficiency through mistrust, gaming, and distorted inputs (n=65).
finding.measure: Perceived efficiency of teacher intervention, evaluation, and AI-assisted classroom support in speculative narratives

finding.finding_summary: Students raised broad institutional concerns about fairness, bias, governance, and authority in AI-mediated education. Narratives suggested that AI could improve objectivity and standardization, but also amplify designer bias, normalize surveillance, and distort institutional decision-making when teachers rely on AI as evidence or when predictions shape student treatment (n=65).
finding.measure: Perceived fairness, bias, power, and governance implications of AI in education

paper_profiles.title: The University in Transition
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book-length work reflects on the historical development of the university and argues that universities are in a period of transition toward Open Science. The authors trace how universities evolved from theological and civic institutions into research universities, and how later pressures from massification, neoliberal governance, external funding, metrics, and internationalization created tensions between research, teaching, autonomy, and societal relevance.

The central intervention is conceptual rather than experimental: the book advocates Open Science as a way to reconnect universities with society through Open Access, FAIR data, Public Engagement, team science, and revised recognition-and-reward systems. It is written for a broad higher-education audience, especially university leaders, staff, and policy stakeholders, and draws heavily on historical analysis, policy discussion, and examples from Dutch and European higher education. The main conclusion is that Open Science is presented as a fundamental and irreversible cultural shift that should reshape how universities organize education, research, and their societal mission.

finding.finding_summary: The book argues that the Open Science movement is already reshaping university governance, evaluation, and institutional mission. It contends that reforms such as Open Access, FAIR data, Public Engagement, and new recognition-and-reward systems are needed to realign universities with societal needs and collaborative team science, but it does not report empirical effect sizes or a study sample.
finding.measure: Historical and policy analysis of university systems, governance, and Open Science reforms

finding.finding_summary: The text discusses how bureaucratization, efficiency pressures, and performance metrics have increased workload and reduced autonomy in universities, especially after student massification and austerity-driven funding constraints. It does not evaluate an intervention quantitatively, but it presents a normative claim that Open Science and team-based recognition systems could improve the functioning of academic work without reporting numerical outcomes.
finding.measure: University workload, bureaucracy, efficiency, and staff autonomy as discussed in historical and policy analysis

paper_profiles.title: Prospect of using AI-integrated smart medical textiles for real-time vital signs monitoring in hospital management & healthcare industry
paper_profiles.venue: American Journal of Advanced Technology and Engineering Solutions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews the emerging use of AI-integrated smart medical textiles for continuous, real-time vital signs monitoring in healthcare settings. The central problem addressed is how wearable textile-based sensors, when combined with AI, can improve physiological monitoring compared with conventional bedside devices while also reducing staff workload and improving hospital operations.

Using PRISMA-guided systematic review methods, the authors synthesized 152 peer-reviewed articles spanning biomedical engineering, computer science, and healthcare management. The review focuses on textile-embedded sensing technologies, AI-based signal preprocessing and classification, and the operational integration of these systems into hospital information infrastructure such as electronic health records and clinical alerting workflows.

The paper concludes that AI-enhanced smart textiles can achieve monitoring accuracy comparable to conventional devices while offering advantages in comfort, mobility, and continuous data capture. It also reports that hospitals adopting these systems may experience reduced nurse workload, improved alarm management, earlier detection of deterioration, fewer adverse events, shorter lengths of stay, and fewer readmissions. The authors emphasize that successful deployment depends on interoperability, staff training, workflow fit, and compliance with regulatory standards such as FDA, EMA, ISO, and IEC frameworks.

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that AI-integrated smart textiles can reduce nurse workload and improve alarm management by automating continuous vital-sign capture and alerting. Across the 152-article synthesis, hospitals implementing these systems were described as benefiting from expanded monitoring coverage and less manual data collection, but the paper does not provide a single pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Nurse workload, alarm management, manual vital-sign checking burden, monitoring coverage

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes that adoption depends on interoperability with EHRs, clinical workflows, regulatory compliance, and governance structures for safety, cybersecurity, and lifecycle management. It argues that these institutional conditions determine whether smart textiles function as standalone devices or as embedded components of the hospital digital ecosystem.
finding.measure: Interoperability with EHRs, workflow integration, regulatory compliance, governance/cybersecurity readiness

paper_profiles.title: OECD Digital Economy Outlook 2024 (Volume 1): Embracing the Technology Frontier
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (cross-country OECD economies; no K-12 study population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This OECD report examines broad trends in digital transformation across OECD countries and partner economies, with chapters on ICT sector growth, the future of AI, digital technology diffusion, next generation wireless networks, virtual reality, and mental health in digital environments. The paper is not an education intervention study; rather, it synthesizes descriptive evidence, official statistics, and model-based estimates to characterize the digital economy and associated policy issues.

The chapter most relevant to this retrieval question is the AI chapter, which discusses the technology frontier, emerging risks, governance, and the diffusion of AI-related tools and incidents. However, it does not evaluate specific AI tools for K-12 teacher productivity, nor does it compare general-purpose language models, education-specific products, LMS-integrated tools, auto-grading systems, or speech/translation tools in schools. Instead, it provides high-level policy and measurement context about AI adoption, trust, and diffusion across economies.

Overall, the report’s conclusions emphasize that digital technologies and AI are advancing rapidly, but adoption is uneven and policy frameworks need to support trustworthy innovation, inclusion, and better measurement. For the education-related retrieval focus, the report offers only indirect context about AI diffusion and productivity, with no direct empirical evidence on K-12 teacher productivity outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Redefining Teacher Leadership in the Age of ChatGPT: Instructional Practices, Ethical Challenges, and Professional Agency in Moroccan High Schools
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Language and Literary Studies
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how Moroccan high school teachers are using ChatGPT in their instructional work and how that use is reshaping teacher leadership and professional agency. The paper asks how teachers incorporate a generative AI tool into lesson design, activity creation, and feedback, what motivates those choices, and how teachers negotiate the balance between AI support and their own judgment in a context where national AI-specific guidance is still limited.

Using a mixed-methods design, the authors surveyed 87 high school teachers in the Casablanca-Settat region, interviewed 12 teachers, and analyzed lesson plans created with ChatGPT. Quantitative results showed that teachers used ChatGPT most often for lesson planning (64.4%), followed by activity generation (51.7%) and feedback drafting (41.4%), suggesting that adoption was strongest for planning and content creation tasks and more cautious for evaluative tasks. Qualitative findings indicated three main themes: teachers experienced time-saving and creative benefits, but also worried about plagiarism, student overreliance, and occasional inaccuracies in AI-generated content.

The study concludes that ChatGPT is not replacing teachers but is changing how they exercise leadership in the classroom. Teachers described themselves as critical filters or ethical gatekeepers who review and adapt AI outputs before use, preserving pedagogical integrity while leveraging AI for efficiency. The paper argues for AI literacy professional development and clearer policy guidelines in Moroccan schools to support responsible integration of generative AI.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that ChatGPT improved instructional efficiency, especially for lesson planning and activity creation. In the survey of 87 Moroccan high school teachers, 64.4% used ChatGPT for lesson planning, 51.7% for activity generation, and 41.4% for drafting feedback, with interview data emphasizing time savings and reduced planning fatigue.
finding.measure: Self-reported ChatGPT use for lesson planning, activity generation, and feedback drafting; interview reports of time-saving and planning efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT is reshaping teacher leadership and professional agency, but it is not a direct institutional intervention study. Teachers positioned themselves as ethical gatekeepers who mediate AI use, and the authors call for professional development and policy guidelines on AI literacy, responsible use, and academic integrity in Moroccan high schools.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of leadership, professional agency, and ethical mediation; discussion of policy and professional development needs

finding.finding_summary: The study reports both opportunities and risks for durable skills, especially critical thinking and judgment. Teachers said ChatGPT could support creativity and idea generation, but they also worried it might encourage student overreliance, plagiarism, and weaker critical thinking unless teachers actively filtered outputs and modeled responsible use.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes on creativity, critical thinking, overreliance, and ethical mediation

paper_profiles.title: Using ChatGPT for Science Learning: A Study on Pre-service Teachers' Lesson Planning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks how pre-service elementary science teachers can integrate ChatGPT into lesson planning, what kinds of science content and instructional strategies they choose, how well they align ChatGPT with TPACK-based planning criteria, and what benefits and concerns they perceive. The paper is positioned against a backdrop of rapid enthusiasm for generative AI but limited empirical evidence on actual classroom-use cases, especially for K-12 science instruction.

The authors worked with 29 pre-service elementary teachers in a Korean teacher education program. After four instructional sessions introducing ChatGPT, its functions, and science teaching strategies, participants wrote lesson plans for a typical 45-minute elementary science class and attached simulated ChatGPT conversations. The plans were evaluated with a modified TPACK-based rubric (TIAR) and analyzed alongside open-ended survey responses. Teachers most often applied ChatGPT to biology, chemistry, and earth/environmental science, and commonly paired it with cooperative learning, POE, learning cycle, analogy generation, concept mapping, and experimentation.

Results suggest that participants saw ChatGPT as broadly useful for questioning, individualized support, formative assessment, and supporting instructional design, but they were less skilled at selecting the most appropriate ChatGPT functions for specific lesson purposes. The average rubric score was 3.29/4 (SD=.91), with stronger performance in matching ChatGPT to curriculum goals and instructional strategies than in function selection. Qualitatively, participants also warned about inaccuracies, hallucinations, and student over-dependence, and many proposed safeguards such as using multiple information sources, structured group interaction, and teacher feedback. Overall, the paper concludes that pre-service teachers anticipate meaningful pedagogical value from ChatGPT, while also recognizing the need for AI literacy and more targeted professional development.

finding.finding_summary: Pre-service teachers judged ChatGPT to be useful for supporting scientific inquiry, prediction, explanation, and concept understanding in elementary science lesson plans. Across 29 lesson plans, ChatGPT was integrated into multiple science domains and instructional strategies, and the average TIAR score was 3.29/4 (SD=.91), suggesting generally strong alignment between ChatGPT use and science-learning objectives. However, this is based on lesson-plan quality and teacher perceptions rather than student achievement.
finding.measure: Modified TPACK-based Technology Integration Assessment Rubric (TIAR) applied to lesson plans; qualitative lesson-plan coding of science domains and instructional strategies

finding.finding_summary: Participants believed ChatGPT could increase motivation, interest, active participation, and self-directed learning in science lessons. In the survey, many teachers described ChatGPT as supporting individualized learning and prompt feedback, which they expected would improve student engagement and self-paced learning, though these were anticipations rather than measured student outcomes.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses about perceived usefulness and anticipated outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly examined how pre-service teachers expected ChatGPT to support critical thinking, questioning, and self-directed learning, and how they designed safeguards against over-dependence. Teachers repeatedly framed ChatGPT as a tool for continuous questioning and deeper thinking, while also recommending comparative checking across sources, peer discussion, and teacher feedback to preserve critical engagement.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses; lesson-plan analysis of ChatGPT integration and mitigation strategies for over-reliance

finding.finding_summary: Participants saw ChatGPT as a productivity aid for lesson planning and classroom management, especially for generating, summarizing, and adapting instructional materials within a 45-minute class. The average lesson-plan rubric score was 3.29/4, and teachers explicitly described ChatGPT as useful for role-play scripting, providing additional explanations, and delivering quick feedback, indicating perceived gains in planning and instructional efficiency rather than measured workload reduction.
finding.measure: Lesson-plan analysis (TIAR) and open-ended survey responses about usefulness for planning and instruction

finding.finding_summary: The study also found that pre-service teachers used ChatGPT across several specific science content areas, including biology, chemistry, earth science, physics, environmental science, and ecological balance. This shows broad content applicability in elementary science lesson design, but the paper does not evaluate achievement in non-science subjects or provide student outcome measures.
finding.measure: Descriptive coding of lesson-plan content domains

paper_profiles.title: Engaging Teachers to Co-Design Integrated AI Curriculum for K-12 Classrooms
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2020 ACM Conference (arXiv preprint / CHI-related publication metadata not fully specified in provided text)
paper_profiles.population: K-12 teachers (with curricula targeting middle school and high school students)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how K-12 teachers’ values, needs, and classroom contexts can shape the design of AI-integrated curricula for non-computing subjects. The authors argue that many AI education tools are presented as standalone products or computer-science extensions, which limits accessibility for teachers in core subjects such as English, social studies, science, and ESL.

To investigate this, the researchers ran a two-day remote co-design workshop with 15 K-12 educators and educational directors. Participants received introductory AI presentations, explored several AI learning tools, completed pre-work using a selected tool with their own curriculum, and then worked in small groups with researchers to design integrated lesson plans. The workshop produced draft curricula for social studies, literacy for students with learning disabilities, and ESL, and the authors analyzed workshop transcripts, questionnaires, and participant deliverables using thematic coding.

The main findings are that teachers need scaffolding around four practical design concerns: evaluation, engagement, logistics, and collaboration. Across the co-designed curricula, integration points consistently centered on data, reflection, and ethics. The paper concludes that embedding AI into core subject instruction is feasible and potentially broadens access to AI education, but successful classroom adoption requires teacher-centered co-design, clearer implementation guidance, and stronger support for ethics instruction.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the co-design workshop increased engagement with AI curriculum design and slightly increased their familiarity and confidence. Across the workshop, perceived helpfulness was highest for the presentations (11 votes) and co-design activity (9 votes), and participants described renewed interest in AI as a pathway to broader learning opportunities.
finding.measure: Workshop surveys and participant feedback on helpfulness, familiarity with AI, and confidence integrating AI

finding.finding_summary: A central result was that teachers identified and applied durable-skill considerations when designing AI-integrated lessons, especially collaboration, reflection, and evaluation of student understanding. The paper reports that all groups discussed collaboration and that the co-design process generated usable curriculum drafts emphasizing critical thinking about AI data, bias, and ethics.
finding.measure: Thematic analysis of co-design workshop transcripts and curriculum drafts

finding.finding_summary: One of the three curriculum drafts focused on ESL, and it integrated AI into pronunciation practice and language learning. Teachers designed an AI-powered pronunciation application in which students would record correct and incorrect pronunciations to train a classification model, linking language practice to AI concepts.
finding.measure: Co-designed ESL curriculum draft and workshop discussion

finding.finding_summary: The workshop produced a literacy curriculum for students with learning disabilities that used vocabulary words and associated images to train a classification model. The paper presents this as a feasible way to connect reading/vocabulary instruction with AI concepts such as data literacy, ML steps, and human role in AI.
finding.measure: Co-designed literacy curriculum draft

finding.finding_summary: Teachers successfully co-designed integrated AI curricula for social studies, ESL, and literacy, showing that AI concepts can be embedded in non-computing subjects. The social studies curriculum centered on the ethics of the CROWN Act and algorithmic classification of outfits and hairstyles, while other drafts linked AI to core subject content through data, reflection, and ethics.
finding.measure: Co-designed curriculum drafts and workshop analysis

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests that co-design with teachers can improve the accessibility and likely adoption potential of AI curricula in K-12 settings by making them more aligned with classroom realities. Teachers emphasized the need for scaffolding, explicit tool guidance, and ethics supports, indicating that institutional uptake depends on implementation conditions rather than tool availability alone.
finding.measure: Thematic analysis of workshop discussions about implementation, adoption, and classroom feasibility

paper_profiles.title: Shiksha Copilot: Teacher-AI Collaboration for Curating and Customizing Lesson Plans in Low-Resource Schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how teachers in low-resource government schools in Karnataka, India collaborated with an LLM-based lesson-planning system, Shiksha Copilot. The research addresses a practical problem common in many K–12 systems: teachers face heavy administrative documentation burdens, limited instructional materials, multilingual classrooms, and time scarcity, all of which make lesson planning difficult. The authors ask how teachers work with AI in lesson planning, what implementation challenges arise in non-English-medium classrooms, and how the tool reshapes everyday teaching work.

Shiksha Copilot combined retrieval-augmented generation, human curator review, translation, and teacher customization. The system first generated and curated curriculum-aligned lesson plans in English, then translated and curated them into Kannada, and finally allowed teachers to adapt the plans for their own classrooms. The deployment included 1,043 teachers and 23 curators across public schools in Karnataka, with interviews, surveys, and log analysis used to study use patterns and effects.

The study finds that the tool reduced lesson-planning time, eased bureaucratic record-keeping, and lowered teacher stress, while also supporting a modest shift toward activity-based pedagogy. English lesson plans were generally high quality and required only minor edits, but Kannada translations often needed substantial linguistic revision. Teachers used the system both for instructional planning and administrative documentation, but broader pedagogical change was limited by systemic constraints such as staffing shortages and ongoing administrative demands. Overall, the paper argues that teacher-AI collaboration can be effective when systems are curriculum-aligned, human-in-the-loop, and adapted to local linguistic and institutional conditions.

finding.finding_summary: Shiksha Copilot reduced lesson-planning burden and record-keeping work for teachers in low-resource schools. The paper reports measurable reductions in lesson planning time and teacher stress, and notes that teachers used the system for both classroom instruction and bureaucratic documentation (n=1,043 teachers deployed; 406 matched survey responses; 5,544 teacher-created LPs analyzed).
finding.measure: Lesson-planning time, administrative/record-keeping workload, and teaching-related stress (Teacher Stress Scale subscales; time-use survey items; platform logs)
finding.study_size: n=1043 deployed teachers; n=406 matched survey respondents; n=5544 teacher-created lesson plans

finding.finding_summary: The system helped teachers meet state-mandated documentation and curriculum-compliance requirements, showing institutional utility beyond classroom use. However, the paper also finds that systemic constraints such as staffing shortages and administrative demands limited broader pedagogical change, suggesting institutional impact was meaningful but bounded.
finding.measure: Teachers’ use of AI-generated lesson plans for bureaucratic documentation and curricular compliance; interview and survey evidence

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported lower teaching-related stress after using Shiksha Copilot. The post-survey measured stress with the Teacher Stress Scale, and the authors state that lesson planning time and teacher stress both decreased after adoption (matched survey sample n=406).
finding.measure: Teaching-related stress (Teacher Stress Scale: teaching demands and school-based support subscales)

paper_profiles.title: To what extent is ChatGPT useful for language teacher lesson plan creation?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can help foreign language teachers create lesson plans, and whether more specific prompts lead to better, more consistent output. The authors focus on zero-shot prompting in ChatGPT 4.0 and examine how prompt specificity affects the quality and variability of generated lesson plans.

The study used five prompts of increasing specificity to generate 50 Spanish lesson plans for a high school Level I classroom (10 outputs per prompt). The outputs were scored against a rubric aligned with ACTFL proficiency guidelines, world-readiness standards, and edTPA-style lesson plan expectations. The authors analyzed rubric scores, word counts, and output dissimilarity using ANOVA, PERMANOVA, ANOSIM, Jaccard distances, and hierarchical clustering.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT can produce generally high-quality lesson plans and may reduce teacher workload, but greater prompt specificity does not reliably improve quality in a linear way. Adding a lesson template sometimes lowered scores, while adding a checklist of required criteria produced the best average outputs. The paper also finds substantial non-determinism: the same prompt could yield strongly different lesson plans, including some that reflected outdated pedagogical practices (for example, behaviorist or audiolingual approaches). The authors argue that teachers need AI literacy to critically evaluate and revise generated materials rather than using them uncritically.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT was generally useful for generating foreign language lesson plans and could streamline lesson planning, but performance depended on prompt design. Across 50 outputs (5 prompts x 10 iterations), lesson plans were often high quality, with mean rubric scores ranging from 19.6/25 to 21.6/25 and the best average output occurring when a checklist of required criteria was added.
finding.measure: Lesson plan rubric score; lesson plan word count; presence/absence of 25 required lesson components

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks Middle School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether teachers should remain in the loop when using generative AI to personalize mathematics tasks for students, and what that implies for efficiency, task quality, and student reactions. The authors focus on context personalization: adapting existing middle school math problems to students’ interests using ChatGPT (GPT-4o). They are especially interested in how teachers prompt the model, how much time the process takes, whether teachers become more efficient over time, and what students think about the resulting tasks.

Seven 7th-grade mathematics teachers from six U.S. schools participated. After training on personalization, bias, readability, and cultural relevance, teachers modified Illustrative Mathematics problems in ASSISTments using ChatGPT. They personalized problems across two units (Unit 4 and Unit 6), creating 143 personalized problems for 521 students, and the researchers analyzed ChatGPT logs, teacher talk, and student survey responses. The study is observational/mixed-methods rather than experimental.

The main findings were that teachers used LLMs to vary grain size and ownership of personalization, often asking for broad popular-culture topics at first and then refining with specific references, realism checks, age/location tailoring, and readability fixes. Students generally preferred smaller-grain, specific references when those matched their own interests, but often found broad personalization or mismatched specific references uninteresting. Personalizing one problem took about 4 minutes on average, and the process did not become clearly more time-efficient over time; in fact, teachers used more prompts and spent more time in Unit 6 than Unit 4. However, student ratings of interestingness and closeness improved in Unit 6, and using about 3–5 prompts per problem was associated with better student ratings than using fewer or many more prompts.
