The authors conclude that teacher-in-the-loop GenAI personalization can support teacher learning and task quality checks, but it is time-intensive and still struggles to match the fine-grained preferences students want.

finding.finding_summary: The study centered on middle school mathematics task personalization using ChatGPT, examining the creation of personalized proportional relationships, percentages, expressions, equations, and inequalities problems. While the paper did not measure achievement or learning gains directly, it did find that personalized math problems could be generated and iteratively improved, and that student ratings of the problems increased from Unit 4 to Unit 6 (interestingness and closeness both improved significantly), suggesting improved task quality in math contexts.
finding.measure: Student ratings of interestingness and closeness for personalized mathematics problems; teacher problem-posing process for math tasks
finding.study_size: n=7 teachers; n=521 students; 143 personalized problems
finding.effect_size: B=0.33 for Unit 6 vs Unit 4 on combined student ratings; B=0.240 for 3-5 prompts vs other prompt counts on ratings

finding.finding_summary: Students’ reactions indicated that personalized problems could increase situational interest when the context matched their preferences, especially with specific popular-culture references. Average student ratings were modest overall (interestingness M=2.46, closeness M=2.53 on a 5-point scale), and ratings were higher in Unit 6 than Unit 4 (interestingness 2.56 vs 2.27; closeness 2.66 vs 2.28), showing a positive shift in perceived relevance and engagement.
finding.measure: 1-5 student survey ratings of interestingness and closeness to interests; open-ended student feedback
finding.study_size: n=521 students; ratings available for 52-53 problems depending on measure
finding.effect_size: B=0.33 for Unit 6 vs Unit 4 on combined ratings; B=0.240 for 3-5 prompts vs other prompt counts
finding.std_deviation: SD=1.24 (interestingness average), SD=1.28 (closeness average); Unit 4/6 SDs reported in paper

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that teachers improved their ability to craft interesting problems in partnership with generative AI over time, indicating growth in prompting, reflection, and iterative problem revision. However, this growth was not clearly reflected in efficiency gains, and the benefits appeared tied to reflective iteration rather than reduced effort.
finding.measure: Teacher prompting patterns, iterative revision behavior, and changes from Unit 4 to Unit 6
finding.effect_size: B=1.26 more prompts per problem from Unit 4 to Unit 6; B=70.4 seconds more per problem from Unit 4 to Unit 6

finding.finding_summary: The study found that teacher-in-the-loop personalization was time-consuming rather than time-saving. Teachers used 558 prompts to create 143 problems, averaging 3.2 prompts and about 246 seconds per problem, and they did not become more efficient over time; instead, they used more prompts and spent more time in Unit 6 than Unit 4.
finding.measure: Number of prompts per problem; time spent creating each personalized problem

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that teacher-in-the-loop GenAI personalization has implications for professional learning, teacher role preservation, and how schools might implement AI-supported curriculum adaptation. It suggests that teacher-facing systems could support learning but warns that student-facing automation without safeguards may raise ethical and institutional concerns; these are conceptual conclusions grounded in the study’s evidence rather than direct institutional measurement.
finding.measure: Teacher reflections, implementation process, and discussion of deployment implications

paper_profiles.title: Is ChatGPT a Good Teacher Coach? Measuring Zero-Shot Performance for Scoring and Providing Actionable Insights on Classroom Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can serve as an automated teacher coach by generating classroom-observation scores and feedback that are useful for instructional improvement. The authors focus on three generative-AI coaching tasks: (A) scoring transcript segments using established observation rubrics, (B) identifying highlights and missed opportunities in instructional practice, and (C) giving actionable suggestions for eliciting more student mathematical reasoning.

The study uses the NCTE Transcript dataset of U.S. elementary mathematics classrooms (1,660 transcripts from 317 teachers in 4 districts) and evaluates GPT-3.5/ChatGPT in zero-shot mode. For the quantitative scoring task, the model is prompted to predict selected CLASS and MQI observation-item scores; for the qualitative feedback tasks, expert math teachers rate model outputs for relevance, faithfulness, insightfulness, actionability, and novelty. The model is tested on sampled transcript segments rather than the full dataset because of context-length and cost constraints.

Results show that ChatGPT performs poorly as a scorer: correlations with human ratings are low across all observed CLASS and MQI items, and adding rubric descriptions or chain-of-thought-style reasoning does not meaningfully help. For feedback generation, teachers often judged responses as relevant or actionable, but frequently not insightful or novel; for Task C, 82% of suggestions merely restated what the teacher was already doing. The paper concludes that ChatGPT may be a useful starting point for scalable teacher support, but current models are not yet reliable as standalone teacher coaches, especially for producing faithful, insightful, and non-redundant instructional feedback.

finding.finding_summary: Across selected CLASS and MQI math-instruction items, ChatGPT’s zero-shot score predictions had low Spearman correlations with human ratings. For the MQI mathematics items, correlations were near zero to small at best (e.g., EXPL 0.02, REMED 0.05, LANGIMP 0.00, SMQR 0.17 under direct-answer prompting), indicating poor alignment with expert judgments of instructional quality in elementary math transcripts.
finding.measure: Spearman correlation between ChatGPT-predicted observation scores and expert human rubric scores on CLASS and MQI mathematics instructional items
finding.study_size: n=100 transcript segments for quantitative scoring; 317 teachers in source dataset
finding.effect_size: Spearman rho near 0 to 0.17 depending on item and prompt

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT could potentially provide scalable, cost-effective teacher feedback, but the empirical results show substantial limitations. For qualitative coaching tasks, responses were often relevant and actionable, yet 82% of suggestions repeated what the teacher already did, and teachers frequently rated outputs as not insightful or not relevant, especially for MQI-related feedback.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of model-generated highlights, missed opportunities, and actionable suggestions; novelty/redundancy rate of suggestions
finding.study_size: n=216 CLASS examples, n=288 MQI examples, n=36 suggestion examples
finding.effect_size: 82% redundant suggestions; qualitative human ratings on 3-point scales

finding.finding_summary: In the feedback-generation tasks, ChatGPT often failed to produce genuinely insightful or novel pedagogical advice, suggesting weak support for higher-order reflective practice. For CLASS and MQI highlights/missed opportunities, teachers rated many responses as not insightful (roughly 50-70% 'No'), and for suggestion generation the model mostly reproduced existing transcript content rather than generating new instructional ideas.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of insightfulness and novelty for model-generated feedback
finding.study_size: n=216 CLASS examples, n=288 MQI examples, n=36 suggestion examples
finding.effect_size: Novelty failure rate 82% for suggestions; 'No' insightfulness roughly 50-71% depending on task/instrument

paper_profiles.title: AI-Generated Rubric Interfaces: K–12 Teachers’ Perceptions and Practices
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K–12 teachers perceive and use AI-supported rubric generation for assessment and feedback, with a focus on block-based programming assignments. The authors ask whether a large language model tool can help teachers create rubrics, support grading, and influence teachers’ intentions to adopt AI rubric tools in future classroom practice.

The study was conducted in summer 2025 with 25 middle- and high-school teachers in professional development workshops. Teachers used MagicSchool.ai to generate rubrics, compared AI-generated rubrics with manually created ones, and then used the AI-generated rubrics to assess a sample programming task. They also used the platform’s chatbot feedback feature and completed pre/post surveys, open-ended questions, exit tickets, and discussions. Quantitative survey items measured clarity, alignment, usability, fairness, and confidence; qualitative thematic analysis captured teachers’ experiences and concerns.

Overall, teachers viewed AI-generated rubrics as useful starting drafts that saved time, improved structure, and clarified vague criteria, but they emphasized that the tool required substantial teacher oversight and editing. Survey results were generally positive for clarity, assignment alignment, and transparency, while usability for modifying criteria was the weakest area. Teachers’ adoption intentions increased after hands-on use, but only conditionally: they wanted stronger editability, better LMS integration, grade-appropriate language, clearer prompting support, and continued teacher control over assessment decisions.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers consistently reported that AI-generated rubrics reduced the time and cognitive effort needed to draft rubrics from scratch. In the post-survey, they rated the rubric as a flexible starting point (M=3.5625, SD=1.31) and said it helped them save time, improve structure, and scale feedback, though they also noted substantial editing was still required. The sample size was n=25 middle- and high-school teachers.
finding.measure: Perceived rubric-generation efficiency, workload reduction, and usability of AI-generated rubric drafting/editing

finding.finding_summary: The paper documents how AI rubric tools fit into existing school workflows and institutional constraints, including Google Classroom, Canvas, district policies, privacy concerns, and incomplete LMS integration. Teachers explicitly recommended better LMS integration and export options, and noted that school AI restrictions could limit adoption even when the tool itself was useful. The study is primarily about teacher perceptions, but institutional fit is a substantive theme.
finding.measure: Teachers’ reported workflow fit, LMS integration needs, privacy/policy barriers, and adoption constraints

paper_profiles.title: LessonPlanner: Assisting Novice Teachers to Prepare Pedagogy-Driven Lesson Plans with Large Language Models
paper_profiles.venue: UIST '24 (ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether and how a large language model (LLM)-based system can help novice teachers prepare lesson plans more efficiently and with better pedagogical structure. The authors argue that lesson planning is time-consuming and that generic chat interfaces like ChatGPT make it difficult for teachers to organize generated content into a coherent, theory-informed lesson plan.

To address this, they develop LessonPlanner, a web-based authoring tool built on GPT-4 that structures lesson planning around Gagne’s Nine Events of Instruction and Bloom’s Taxonomy. The system supports teachers in generating lesson goals, outlining lessons, suggesting instructional activities and materials, refining sections with contextual prompts, and exporting a markdown lesson plan. The design is informed by formative interviews and co-design sessions with novice teachers and teaching assistants.

The paper evaluates LessonPlanner in a within-subjects study with 12 university students acting as teachers and a baseline condition using the standard ChatGPT web app plus a markdown editor and Bing search. It also includes expert interviews with six teachers across university, elementary, and high school contexts. Results suggest LessonPlanner improves the quality of lesson plans and reduces perceived workload relative to the baseline, while also helping users produce more organized, pedagogy-aligned plans. Participants still expressed concerns about factual reliability and the need to verify LLM outputs, especially for subject-specific content.

finding.finding_summary: In a within-subjects study (n=12), LessonPlanner significantly improved the quality of outcome lesson plans and eased users’ workload during lesson preparation compared with a baseline ChatGPT web app plus markdown editor and Bing search. Participants also reported that the tool reduced mental effort by organizing prompts, structuring the lesson plan, and lowering the burden of generating and refining content from scratch.
finding.measure: Lesson plan quality ratings by an experienced teacher; NASA-TLX workload survey; user interview reports on process burden

finding.finding_summary: The system was designed to support pedagogical planning, prompting, and refinement, which are closely tied to teachers’ planning and decision-making skills. In expert interviews and formative feedback, participants said the tool helped them think through instructional strategies more effectively and made it easier to adapt generated content to specific teaching events.
finding.measure: Interview feedback on planning support and instructional strategy guidance
finding.study_size: n=6 expert interviews; formative study n=6

paper_profiles.title: LLMs to Support K–12 Teachers in Culturally Relevant Pedagogy: An AI Literacy Example
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a large language model (LLM)-based tool can help K-12 teachers adapt AI literacy activities to be more culturally responsive. The motivation is that culturally relevant pedagogy (CRP) is valuable but difficult for teachers to implement because of limited time, training, and access to appropriate resources. The authors also frame the work as responding to a gap in culturally responsive AI literacy materials for diverse classrooms.

The study introduces CulturAIEd, a prototype LLM-powered system that uses student demographic information, a CRT checklist, rubric-based feedback, and just-in-time chatbot support to help teachers revise AI literacy lessons. In an exploratory pilot, four secondary teachers from North America and East Asia completed adaptation tasks and interviews across baseline, checklist-guided, and tool-supported phases. Participants also had access to ChatGPT and internet resources, so the study compared a structured LLM-supported workflow against unguided and checklist-only approaches rather than against a pure no-AI condition.

Findings are qualitative and descriptive, but they consistently suggest that the tool improved teachers’ confidence, reduced planning burden, and made it easier to identify and implement culturally responsive modifications. Teachers especially valued the integration of demographic information and the immediate actionable feedback, which they felt could improve implementation efficiency. The authors conclude that LLMs may be useful as teacher-support tools for CRP in AI literacy contexts, while noting important cautions about bias, overreliance, and the need for larger controlled studies before making efficacy claims.

finding.finding_summary: In an exploratory pilot with 4 K-12 teachers, CulturAIEd was perceived to reduce planning burden and make CRP adaptation more efficient by streamlining demographic integration, content customization, and feedback. The paper reports that 3/4 participants strongly agreed the tool saved time and inspired new ideas, but these are self-report perceptions rather than objective time-on-task measures.
finding.measure: Teacher self-reports of time saved, perceived efficiency, and workflow ease during culturally responsive lesson adaptation

finding.finding_summary: The tool appeared to strengthen teachers’ ability to identify opportunities for cultural responsiveness and to make culturally responsive modifications, which the authors describe as improvements in pedagogical decision-making and reflective practice. Pre-survey confidence for identifying cultural responsiveness was 3-5/5 and rose to 5/5 for all participants post-use of CulturAIEd.
finding.measure: Teacher confidence ratings and interview evidence related to identifying and implementing CRP strategies

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that LLM-supported tools could help address institutional barriers to CRP implementation, especially where teachers lack training, time, or access to culturally responsive resources. Participants also noted that the tool’s demographic integration and structured rubric could support more consistent CRP implementation, but the study does not test school- or policy-level outcomes.
finding.measure: Perceptions of institutional support barriers and usefulness of an LLM tool for CRP implementation

paper_profiles.title: From Teacher to Colleague: How Coding Experience Shapes Developer Perceptions of AI Tools
paper_profiles.venue: GenAICHI: CHI 2025 Workshop on Generative AI and HCI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how coding experience relates to developers’ awareness, adoption, and mental models of AI tools used in software development. The authors ask whether more experienced coders are more likely to adopt AI tools and whether experience shapes the role developers assign to AI in their workflow.

The study analyzes survey data from 3,380 developers drawn from JetBrains’ 2024 State of Developer Ecosystem survey, with a larger subset of 8,073 respondents used for awareness/experience analyses. Coding experience, AI awareness, AI experience, and chosen AI “roles” were examined using Spearman correlations and logistic regression. The authors find essentially no relationship between coding experience and AI tool adoption/experience, and only a negligible relationship with awareness (r=0.031).

However, coding experience does significantly shape perceptions of AI’s role. More experienced developers are more likely to view AI as a junior colleague or content generator, or to say it has no role, while less experienced developers are more likely to see AI as a teacher. The paper concludes that adoption is not driven by experience alone, but that tool design and positioning should align with users’ expertise levels and expectations.

finding.finding_summary: The study found no meaningful association between coding experience and AI tool adoption/usage for development. In the subset used for awareness/experience analyses (n=8,073), Spearman’s rho between coding experience and AI experience was -0.005 (p=0.652), and the correlation with AI awareness was only 0.031 (p=0.005), indicating a negligible relationship.
finding.measure: Survey measures of AI experience and AI awareness among developers

finding.finding_summary: Coding experience significantly predicted the roles developers assigned to AI tools, suggesting differences in mental models rather than differences in performance outcomes. More experienced developers were more likely to describe AI as a junior colleague (OR=1.170, p-adj=0.017) or content generator (OR=1.087, p-adj=0.020), while less experienced developers were more likely to call it a teacher (OR=0.883, p-adj=0.017); the analysis of role assignment used n=3,380 respondents.
finding.measure: Survey responses selecting the role of AI in developers’ workflow

paper_profiles.title: How Can Video Generative AI Transform K-12 Education? Examining Teachers’ Perspectives through TPACK and TAM
paper_profiles.population: K-12 Teachers (predominantly Elementary; some High School)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper explores how K-12 teachers perceive the educational potential and limitations of video generative AI (Video GenAI), a rapidly emerging form of AI that can create realistic videos from natural-language prompts. The authors frame the study with TPACK and TAM to understand how teachers judge the tool’s usefulness, ease of use, pedagogical fit, and institutional feasibility.

The study uses semi-structured interviews and hands-on experimentation with Luma Dream Machine, a public video-generation platform, with 10 participants: eight elementary teachers, one high school teacher, and one former elementary teacher/data analyst. Participants reviewed an educational guide, generated videos themselves, and then reflected on likely classroom uses. The paper is not an impact evaluation of student outcomes; instead, it is a qualitative study of teacher perspectives and implementation conditions.

Teachers generally viewed Video GenAI positively for creating visuals that could support comprehension, creative expression, project-based learning, and alternative assessment. They also saw potential for reducing preparation time and for helping students develop AI literacy and language precision through prompt writing. However, they raised substantial concerns about rendering speed, output instability, hallucinations, weak Korean-language support, safety risks, age restrictions, copyright, lack of monitoring features, and the need for clear policy and professional development.

Overall, the paper concludes that Video GenAI has promise as a pedagogical tool in K-12 settings, but practical adoption depends on stronger technical performance, multilingual support, safety guardrails, teacher oversight functions, and institutional/policy support. The authors emphasize that effective integration requires more than access to the tool itself; it also requires teacher training, ethical guidance, and alignment with instructional goals.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers perceived Video GenAI as potentially reducing preparation time for instructional materials and enabling faster creation of supplementary videos for class use. However, this benefit was qualified by concerns about slow rendering, short video length, and the need for substantial editing, which limited immediate productivity gains.
finding.measure: Teacher interviews about perceived usefulness, preparation time, and classroom workflow efficiency

finding.finding_summary: Teachers believed Video GenAI could increase student engagement and motivation by making learning more visual, creative, and immersive. They also described potential benefits for students’ creative expression and interest in project-based tasks, though these were perceived possibilities rather than measured outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of student engagement, motivation, and creative participation

finding.finding_summary: Teachers expected Video GenAI to support divergent thinking, imagination, sentence formulation, and AI literacy, especially when students generate and refine prompts. At the same time, they warned that students might overtrust AI outputs or need explicit instruction on ethical and critical use, so the durable-skills impact was seen as beneficial but conditional.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of critical thinking, divergent thinking, prompt formulation, and AI literacy development

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that turning literary or non-literary texts into short videos could strengthen comprehension and engagement in language arts, and that prompting students to translate ideas into precise text may improve sentence formulation. These claims were based on participant reflections rather than direct assessment of reading or writing outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of reading comprehension and writing/sentence formulation

finding.finding_summary: Teachers said Video GenAI could help visualize scientific experiments and phenomena, support explanation of complex concepts, and compensate for limited laboratory facilities. No student learning gains were measured; the evidence is qualitative and based on teachers’ expectations about science instruction.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of science visualization, experiment simulation, and conceptual understanding

finding.finding_summary: Teachers identified strong potential for history, art, social studies, and Korean-language instruction, especially for reenacting historical events, visualizing abstract content, and creating subject-specific materials. These potential applications were described as ways to improve comprehension and engagement across non-core subjects, but no direct student outcomes were measured.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of subject-specific instructional applications outside literacy, math, and science

finding.finding_summary: Teachers identified major institutional and policy barriers to adoption, including age restrictions, parental consent, copyright and ownership uncertainty, lack of national guidelines, infrastructure gaps, and subscription costs. They argued that adoption would require policy reform, funding support, clearer governance, and professional development, indicating substantial institutional dependence for implementation.
finding.measure: Teacher interviews on policy, governance, infrastructure, consent, copyright, and implementation supports

paper_profiles.title: Foundations of GenIR
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter-style paper surveys the foundations of generative AI for information access (IA), focusing on how large language models (LLMs) change both information generation and information synthesis. The authors contrast modern generative models with traditional AI and retrieval systems, arguing that generative AI enables new paradigms for producing tailored outputs directly from user instructions and for synthesizing external information into grounded responses.

The paper is not an education study and does not evaluate a K-12 intervention or product. Instead, it provides a conceptual overview of model architectures, scaling laws, training stages, prompt optimization, multimodal applications, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), generative retrieval, and domain-specific modeling. The central conclusion is that generative AI can improve information access by enabling direct, instruction-following responses and by integrating external knowledge through retrieval and synthesis, but major challenges remain around hallucination, controllability, efficiency, and domain adaptation.

finding.finding_summary: The chapter argues that generative AI can improve operational efficiency in information access systems by producing tailored outputs directly, synthesizing retrieved evidence, and reducing the need for manual multi-step information processing. However, this is a conceptual claim rather than an empirical result; the paper does not report effect sizes or a study evaluating productivity gains.
finding.measure: conceptual discussion of information access workflow efficiency and response generation efficiency

paper_profiles.title: Exploring K-12 Physical Education Teachers’ Perspectives on Opportunities and Challenges of AI Integration Through Ideation Workshops
paper_profiles.venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how in-service secondary school physical education (PE) teachers in South Korea think about integrating AI into K-12 PE. The authors focus on a context that is underexplored in AI-in-education research: PE, where teachers face distinct challenges related to class management, individualized feedback, team formation, safety, and assessment in large, open, and physically active learning environments.

To study this, the researchers conducted focus-group ideation workshops with 17 PE teachers. The workshop included a brief AI literacy lecture, individual sketching of AI ideas, group discussion, storyboarding, and role-play around imagined AI-enabled PE scenarios. Participants were not evaluating a finished product; rather, they were generating concepts and discussing needs, barriers, and concerns for future AI integration. Because of this, the paper is primarily about teachers’ perceptions, envisioned use cases, and implementation conditions rather than measured effects on students or teachers.

Teachers described AI as potentially useful in four roles: operational assistant, personal trainer, group coach, and evaluator. Across these roles, they imagined AI supporting class logistics, personalized movement feedback, balanced team formation, and multidimensional assessment. At the same time, they emphasized important barriers and risks, including weak institutional support, insufficient infrastructure, uneven teacher technical proficiency, possible overreliance on AI, misalignment with PE educational goals, and privacy/data-security concerns. The paper concludes that AI for PE should be designed as a supportive tool that complements, not replaces, teachers, and that successful adoption will require co-design with teachers and attention to pedagogical fit and implementation constraints.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers strongly believed AI could improve operational efficiency in PE classes by reducing workload related to environment setup, student monitoring, safety management, and record keeping. In the ideation sessions with 17 in-service secondary PE teachers, all participants envisioned AI as an operational assistant, and many said it could save time and let teachers focus more on instruction and individualized support. This was a perception study rather than a tested intervention, so no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Teachers’ workshop ideas and perceptions of AI support for class operations, workload, attendance/monitoring, safety, and data handling

finding.finding_summary: Participants identified important institutional and infrastructural barriers to adopting AI in PE, including low subject priority, limited school resources, lack of Wi-Fi or space for equipment, maintenance burdens, and the need for broader administrative support. They also raised concerns about policy-relevant issues such as consent, privacy, data leakage, and the need for coherent curriculum and guidelines to align AI with PE goals. No quantitative impact was measured.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported concerns about institutional support, infrastructure, governance, privacy, and implementation conditions

finding.finding_summary: Teachers envisioned AI helping students’ motivation, confidence, and emotional support, especially through personalized encouragement and psychologically supportive feedback. One example was a 'Warm Advice AI' concept intended to help nervous students cope with competition pressure; however, these were speculative design ideas rather than evaluated outcomes, so no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher-anticipated student motivation, encouragement, confidence, and emotional support in imagined AI use cases

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests AI could support collaboration and teamwork through balanced team formation and tactical analysis, which teachers believed might create more inclusive and cooperative PE activities. At the same time, teachers worried that overreliance on AI could reduce student autonomy and self-directedness. These findings come from qualitative ideation and concern elicitation, not outcome measurement.
finding.measure: Teacher-perceived collaboration/team formation and concerns about autonomy/self-directed learning

paper_profiles.title: Exploring Teachers’ Perception of Artificial Intelligence: The Socio-emotional Deficiency as Opportunities and Challenges in Human-AI Complementarity in K-12 Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how elementary school teachers perceive AI as a complement to human teachers across a wide range of school roles and tasks. The authors ask which teacher responsibilities are seen as suitable for AI, and what opportunities and challenges teachers associate with AI’s capabilities and limitations, especially in relation to socio-emotional skills.

The study uses a mixed-method design with a survey of 100 elementary school teachers in South Korea and semi-structured interviews with 12 teachers. The survey uses an Analytic Hierarchy Process to compare AI complementarity across eleven teacher tasks, while the interviews probe teachers’ reasoning about AI’s strengths and weaknesses. Teachers generally view AI as most suitable for administrative work and analytical tasks, and least suitable for socio-emotional work such as life guidance and parent-teacher relationships.

A central conclusion is that teachers see AI as useful for automating standardized administrative tasks, supporting personalized learning, and enabling fairer or more objective assessment and decision-making. At the same time, they believe AI lacks the socio-emotional understanding needed for teaching, guidance, and relationship-based work. The paper argues that AI adoption in schools should be tailored to educators’ preferences and concerns, and that AI’s socio-emotional limitations can be interpreted both as a constraint and as a source of potential value in reducing bias and hierarchy.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers strongly perceived AI as useful for operational work, especially administrative affairs, policy administration, educational administration, and external relations. In the AHP survey of 100 elementary teachers, administrative affairs received the highest perceived AI complementarity score (PCS=0.437), and the summed PCS for school administration was 0.820 versus 0.180 for educational tasks, indicating AI is viewed as much more suitable for productivity and workload reduction than for direct teaching.
finding.measure: Perceived AI complementarity scores (PCS) for teacher tasks; survey using Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP)

finding.finding_summary: Teachers saw AI as potentially useful for school-level governance and institutional decision-making, including policy administration, task allocation, and leadership roles. Interview data from 12 teachers suggested AI could support fairer, less authoritarian decisions and reduce conflict in school management, though these were perceptions rather than measured institutional outcomes.
finding.measure: Perceptions of AI roles in decision-making, task assignment, leadership, and school governance from survey and interviews

finding.finding_summary: Teachers viewed AI as weak in socio-emotional capacities, especially for life guidance, parent-teacher relationships, emotion recognition, non-verbal communication, persuasion, and interpersonal support. In the AHP results, socio-emotional tasks had the lowest perceived complementarity, and qualitative comments emphasized that AI’s lack of emotional understanding can hinder guidance and relationship-building, even while some teachers saw that same lack of emotion as useful for fairness.
finding.measure: Perceived AI complementarity for socio-emotional teacher tasks; interview themes on emotion, guidance, and relationships

finding.finding_summary: The paper indicates AI is perceived as moderately helpful for analytical and reflective work, but not for many higher-order human tasks requiring judgment, metacognition, and adaptive interaction. Teachers associated AI with data-driven planning and objective evaluation, yet remained skeptical about AI’s ability to interpret complex classroom cues or handle nuanced collaboration and guidance.
finding.measure: Perceived AI complementarity across analytical and reflective teacher tasks; task-ability mapping and interview themes

paper_profiles.title: Towards The Ultimate Brain: Exploring Scientific Discovery with ChatGPT AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can be used not just to draft prose, but to participate in a structured scientific-discovery workflow. The author creates a gamified, text-adventure-like environment in which ChatGPT is prompted to define generalized probabilistic theories, compare classical and quantum theories, generate a limerick, evaluate determinants, discuss nonlocal correlations, and then iteratively revise a hypothetical theory called GPT4.

The intervention is not an educational tool trial; it is a human-AI co-creation experiment in which the human author uses prompts and revisions to steer ChatGPT’s outputs. The context is theoretical physics and scientific writing, and the “population” is effectively the model itself rather than human learners or educators. The paper also includes a nested “game within a game” demonstration and a speculative section on predictive power, intended to showcase the model’s generative and reasoning-like capabilities.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT can produce coherent, structured, and sometimes surprisingly creative outputs when heavily guided, but these outputs should not be interpreted as scientifically rigorous or independently validated research. The author emphasizes that the paper is an experiment in generative AI collaboration and text production, not a genuine discovery claim. The paper’s own appendix explicitly notes the limitations, hallucinations, and lack of autonomous scientific contribution, reinforcing that the work is best understood as a demonstration of prompting and co-writing rather than empirical science.

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that ChatGPT can generate scientifically styled explanations, toy derivations, and structured arguments about generalized probabilistic theories, quantum theory, and nonlocal correlations when prompted in a gamified setting. However, the author explicitly states that the resulting “predictions” and “proofs” are not scientifically rigorous or verifiable, so the scientific-reasoning performance is creative but unreliable.
finding.measure: Quality and coherence of generated scientific explanations, toy proofs, and theory comparisons in a prompt-driven gamification environment

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT is shown generating and manipulating mathematical expressions such as determinants, a Cramer-Rao bound, and simple probability formulas within the paper’s simulated environment. The author notes, however, that some derivations contain errors or non-rigorous reasoning, so the demonstrated mathematical ability is partial rather than trustworthy.
finding.measure: Ability to generate and discuss mathematical expressions and calculations (e.g., determinants, probability formulas, bounds)

finding.finding_summary: The paper demonstrates ChatGPT’s ability to generate a limerick and other creative textual artifacts while maintaining the conventions of the fictional game environment. The model is portrayed as able to produce publication-like prose, references, and stylized outputs, although the author notes that the limerick itself does not perfectly satisfy formal poetic rules.
finding.measure: Generation of a limerick, scientific prose, and game-like narrative outputs

finding.finding_summary: A central claim of the paper is that ChatGPT can support creative problem framing, iterative refinement, and prompt-following within a human-AI collaboration loop. The author characterizes this as evidence of dynamic contextual understanding and adaptive co-creation, though the claims are based on qualitative observation rather than formal measurement.
finding.measure: Observed coherence, contextual persistence, and iterative prompt-following during human-AI co-writing

paper_profiles.title: The Most Considered Type of Student Characteristics by Primary School Teachers
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal on Integrating Technology in Education (IJITE)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks which student characteristic primary school teachers consider most important when planning instruction, and whether attention to that characteristic is associated with higher student achievement. The authors frame student characteristics broadly—intelligence level, motivation, cognitive style, learning style, prior knowledge, and socio-cultural background—and argue that teachers must decide which characteristics to prioritize given practical constraints.

The study surveyed 37 class teachers from grades 4–6 in seven Indonesian primary schools and also reviewed instructional planning documents. Teachers completed a questionnaire about which student characteristics they identify and prioritize, and researchers categorized the extent to which each characteristic was considered in practice. The paper reports that intelligence level was the most frequently identified and most prioritized characteristic, while socio-cultural conditions were least attended to.

To examine whether this emphasis mattered for outcomes, the authors compared midterm exam scores for classes whose instruction was developed with attention to students’ intelligence levels versus classes that did not. They report higher average scores in the classes where instruction accounted for intelligence level (72.67 vs. 68.20 average across subjects), with gains of about 3%–10% depending on subject. The authors conclude that primary teachers most commonly focus on intelligence level and that instruction informed by this information is associated with better student achievement, especially in Indonesian language and mathematics.

finding.finding_summary: Classes whose instruction was developed based on students’ intelligence levels scored higher in Indonesian language than classes that did not. The average Indonesian language midterm score increased from 71.00 to 78.00, a 9% gain.
finding.measure: Indonesian language midterm exam scores
finding.study_size: n=37 teachers; student class-level sample size not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Instruction informed by students’ intelligence levels was associated with higher mathematics performance. The average math midterm score increased from 63.67 to 71.00, a 10% gain.
finding.measure: Mathematics midterm exam scores
finding.study_size: n=37 teachers; student class-level sample size not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Across the other subjects reported, classes taught with attention to students’ intelligence levels also showed higher midterm scores. Gains were reported in social science (65.00 to 67.67; 4%), natural science (69.67 to 73.00; 5%), and arts/craft (71.67 to 73.67; 3%).
finding.measure: Midterm exam scores in social science, natural science, and arts-culture-craft
finding.study_size: n=37 teachers; student class-level sample size not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that considering intelligence level helps teachers classify students and tailor instruction, which may support understanding and learning progression, but it does not directly measure durable skills. The closest reported construct is teachers’ identification of cognitive style and prior knowledge, yet the empirical outcome tested is academic achievement rather than durable skills.
finding.measure: Teacher questionnaire and instructional planning use of student characteristics

paper_profiles.title: AI as a Teaching Partner: Early Lessons from Classroom Codesign with Secondary Teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report examines how secondary teachers used a generative AI classroom platform during a seven-week co-design pilot and what implementation conditions shaped its usefulness. The central question is not whether AI improved student outcomes in a causal sense, but how teachers designed, framed, and iterated on AI-supported activities and what kinds of classroom routines made the tools workable.

The pilot involved 21 in-service teachers from five Washington State schools/districts and more than 600 students in grades 6-12. Teachers used four Colleague AI features: Teaching Aide for structured student-AI conversations, Assessment & AI Grading for rubric generation and feedback, AI Tutor for guided student support, and Student Growth Insights for teacher-facing summaries. Data came from planning/reflection forms, surveys, interviews, group meetings, and platform logs.

Across features, the report concludes that AI was most effective when teachers provided clear goals, short prompts, tight monitoring, and strong pedagogical framing. Teachers generally viewed AI as a helpful but limited partner rather than a replacement, with the strongest value in formative feedback, inquiry support, and reducing teacher workload. Results also varied by grade band and subject: younger students needed more scaffolding, math and some STEM contexts were harder to automate reliably, and narrative feedback was valued more than numeric scoring. The study suggests early promise for AI-supported teaching, but emphasizes that teacher AI competency, tool design, and classroom context are decisive implementation conditions.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the AI-supported conversation and assessment tools helped with writing-related tasks, including prewriting, brainstorming, and essay development. In particular, high school English teachers used the Teaching Aide for prewriting and brainstorming, which they said improved essay quality, and many teachers valued narrative feedback for revision.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported classroom implementation outcomes and perceived usefulness for writing tasks/essay quality

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that multilingual learners who had previously hesitated to speak in whole-class settings found their voice through AI conversations. Spanish teachers also used the tool for real-time ACTFL-aligned proficiency feedback, indicating that the platform supported speaking and language development in conversational contexts.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported student participation in AI conversations and language proficiency feedback use

finding.finding_summary: Math classrooms showed both promise and limitations. Teachers used Teaching Aide for concept talk and some middle school math classes saw thoughtful engagement, but outcomes were more variable than in other subjects because the AI struggled with diagrams, technical reasoning, and non-linear problem solving. Assessment and feedback also required precise rubrics and strong trust to work well in math contexts.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported engagement and learning outcomes in math classes; implementation of AI conversations and AI grading in math assessments
finding.study_size: n=21 teachers; math classes included within 33 classrooms

finding.finding_summary: Science classes generally showed favorable use of the platform, with teachers reporting that AI-facilitated conversations supported inquiry, expanded opportunities for culturally relevant content, and helped students engage in formative feedback cycles. The report notes clearer gains in science than in several other subjects, though some earth science cases were more variable because of diagram and technical-reasoning limitations.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported learning and engagement in science classrooms; AI-assisted conversations and assessment feedback use
finding.study_size: n=21 teachers; science classes within 33 classrooms

finding.finding_summary: Across non-core subjects, teachers reported useful applications in Spanish, engineering, business law, programming, and interdisciplinary STEM. Examples included ACTFL-aligned feedback in Spanish and support for individualized skill development and inquiry in other subjects, though some technical and file/OCR/code issues limited performance in more complex STEM settings.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported outcomes across humanities, Spanish, engineering, and other non-core subjects

finding.finding_summary: The strongest and most consistent evidence concerns student engagement, confidence, and persistence. Teachers reported that AI created a lower-pressure environment for some anxious or less confident students, supported visible self-improvement in response to feedback, and increased student willingness to participate. Engagement was especially strong when teachers framed tasks clearly and tied them to meaningful class products.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of student engagement; qualitative reports of confidence, buy-in, and self-improvement behavior
finding.study_size: n=18 teachers for Teaching Aide engagement; n=19 teachers for assessment implementation; n=21 overall

finding.finding_summary: The platform appeared to support higher-order thinking, including inquiry, revision, and evidence-based reasoning. Teachers described AI conversations as helping students explore ideas more deeply, revise work based on feedback, and practice reasoning, especially when prompts were structured around seminar preparation, proof sketches, and formative feedback cycles.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported student inquiry depth, revision behavior, and reasoning during AI-supported activities
finding.study_size: n=18 teachers for Teaching Aide; n=19 teachers for assessment; n=21 overall

finding.finding_summary: This is a central focus of the report. Teachers reported that AI grading streamlined feedback, SGI reduced the burden of scanning student work, and the platform accelerated turnaround for personalized comments. Platform logs showed high automation: median AI grading coverage was 92.2% across 58 assessments and 33 classrooms, and teachers described SGI as saving hours of teacher time.
finding.measure: Platform logs of AI grading coverage and teacher reports of workload reduction/turnaround time
finding.study_size: 58 classroom-level assessment records across 33 classrooms; 19 teachers in assessment phase

finding.finding_summary: The report suggests broader institutional implications for AI adoption, including the need for teacher AI competency, school/district support, privacy agreements, and collaborative implementation models. However, these are implementation recommendations rather than measured institutional outcomes, so evidence here is limited and mainly descriptive.
finding.measure: Teacher reports, implementation conditions, and district-level partnership context

The current result set is dominated by broader generative-AI-in-education discussion and does not yet establish a robust evidence base for the specific productivity workflow question.

Coverage is still too thin for the specific research thread on K-12 communication and administrative workflows. Only one clearly relevant Scopus item is identified, and it appears more about general communication/management in smart EdTech than direct evidence on teacher emails, newsletters, attendance messaging, documentation, reporting, or routine office tasks.
There is no clear empirical comparison against templates, translation tools, or clerical/administrative support, which is a core part of the question.

The sweep lacks evidence from K-12-specific practitioner studies, pilots, or workload/time-savings evaluations focused on parent/family communication, multilingual messaging, attendance/absence outreach, or report/document drafting.
The current results lean on broad secondary claims and vendor/blog-style examples rather than peer-reviewed studies or concrete field evaluations in schools.
The sweep only surfaced a general discussion paper and search failures; it does not yet provide comparative empirical evidence on productivity outcomes for K-12 teachers across tool categories.

No direct studies were found on education-specific products vs general-purpose LLMs vs LMS-integrated tools vs auto-grading systems vs speech/translation tools, so the central comparative question remains unanswered.

Implementation conditions are not covered: there is little or no evidence on school level, subject area, teacher role, training, access, policy, privacy constraints, or workflow integration that affects productivity gains.
Standard digital supports are missing as a comparator, so the sweep cannot distinguish AI-specific productivity effects from ordinary edtech/automation baselines.

The evidence base appears skewed toward conceptual/review material and school-student use cases rather than teacher workload, lesson planning, grading, communication, or admin tasks in actual K-12 settings.
The sweep is heavily weighted toward general generative AI/ChatGPT and broad survey evidence, but it does not yet cover the full comparison requested across AI tool types.
Missing or thin evidence on education-specific products versus general-purpose LLMs, including whether domain-built tools outperform generic tools for teacher productivity.

No clear evidence found on LMS-integrated AI tools (for example, AI embedded in Google Classroom, Canvas, Schoology, Teams, or other LMS platforms) and how implementation conditions affect teacher time savings.
Auto-grading systems are mentioned only indirectly; there is no substantive comparative evidence on grading-specific AI tools versus standard digital grading supports.
Speech or translation tools are not yet covered, though they are a key requested category with likely distinct productivity effects for multilingual communication and accessibility tasks.

The implementation-conditions angle is only partially addressed through professional development; missing are concrete conditions such as workflow integration, data privacy constraints, district policy, subject/grade-level differences, and task-specific fit compared with non-AI digital supports.
